Domain Trusts and the Access Push (18 September)

Within a roughly three-hour window the attacker joined three separate domains with two-way trusts and pushed the backdoor account’s access across the estate. This is the clearest worked example of the hybrid pattern, so it has its own section below rather than being narrated twice here.

Loader Development and Encryption (19 September)

An attempt to remove EDR, a standard step before encryption, ran on the file server as av_remove.ps1, then again as av_remove2.ps1 seven minutes later, and a third revision, av_remove3.ps1, is known from its hash (T1562.001 Impair Defenses). The scripts were aimed at Sophos and Bitdefender, and anti-tampering controls blocked the removal (Bitdefender TechZone, anti-tampering and detection evasion). Also on 19 September, a randomly named executable started by services.exe ran a psexec-ok marker command, which matches RemCom-based execution, the service implementation used by Impacket’s psexec module. A script loader was developed on one workstation through visible iterations and then deployed to about 40 machines using randomly named job*.cmd and cfg*.txt files, in a fixed order, at about 101 seconds per machine, repeating roughly every two hours (T1053.005 Scheduled Task). The ThreeAM encryptor (host.exe) then ran from 05:07 to 05:33, at 12 to 13 seconds per machine, deleting system-state backups as it went with wbadmin (T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact, T1490 Inhibit System Recovery). Three further install attempts (prx, prx2, prx3) followed on one server, and a persistent callback was left on the server running SQL Server.

What the Commands Tell Us About the Model Behind Them

This section addresses claim one only: whether a language model generated the commands. The evidence is presented in order of strength, and the strength is labeled. None of it bears on whether a program or a person carried each result back to the model.

Errors a Writer Makes From Memory, Not From the Manual

The strongest signal is a cluster of mistakes typical of generating commands from recalled knowledge rather than from documentation or trial and error.

The backup-software call is the clearest. It reached for port 9392 with HTTP Basic authentication against the real credentials path, when Veeam’s REST examples use port 9419 and require an OAuth2 token. The specifics are the kind a manual or a working script would have supplied; a writer reconstructing the call from memory gets the shape right and the specifics wrong. We could not confirm whether that resource ever returns passwords at all.

An LSASS-dump one-liner used for /f "tokens=2" over tasklist /fo csv output without specifying delims=",". In plain terms, the command tried to pull the second column of a comma-separated list but, without telling the parser that commas separate the columns, it grabbed the wrong fragment and passed the trailing K" of a memory-size figure where a process ID belonged. It is the kind of delimiter parsing bug that compiles in the writer’s head and fails on the machine. The full command and the resulting rundll32 call, with the stray K", are shown in the credential-dumping section above.

Bash-style \$ escape sequences appeared inside Windows double-quoted PowerShell on 14, 15, and 19 September. That idiom belongs to Unix shells, not Windows ones. Its recurrence on three separate days (14, 15, and 19 September) is the point: this is a habit, not a one-off slip. One example, from 14 September:

Three commands used 2>/dev/null, the Unix way of discarding error output, inside Windows command lines. All three fell in one 51-minute window on 13 September and the idiom never recurs. On its own it would be weak. Alongside the escape errors, it is consistent with a writer whose default register is Unix shell. The 13 September reconnaissance command in the second command block above is one of the three.

Probe, Confirm, Label, and Revise

The commands show a working style built around checking each step before relying on it: test strings and confirmation files such as test123, TASK-OK, psexec-ok, da_proof.txt, and wmi_test.txt, and a scheduled task literally named VEEAMPROBE. One script logged its own numbered progress (1 start through 7 DONE). Output was often self-labeled inside a single command (echo ===TRUSTS===, or a probe script printing == CONNECTIVITY ==, == EXCLUSION ==, and == DOWNLOAD ==) and collapsed into one separator-joined string. Progress and warning output was suppressed ($ProgressPreference='SilentlyContinue', -WarningAction SilentlyContinue), which keeps the output short and clean for whoever, or whatever, reads it next. A single first-move probe tested connectivity to four targets, tried to add a Windows Defender exclusion for C:\Windows\Temp, and downloaded Mimikatz into that folder (T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer); every later artifact lived in that directory.

Numbered revisions of the same task recur throughout: dcboot/dcboot2, av_remove/av_remove2, prx/prx2/prx3, and the loader’s iterations. File hashes show there were more revisions than our command log captured: hop2.ps1, hop3.ps1 and av_remove3.ps1 exist but never appear in the log, and two different versions of grant_lib.ps1 were deployed under the same name. This is diagnose-and-adapt behavior, and it fits either a model revising its own output or a person iterating by hand. One detail matters here: each revision left a new, higher-numbered file behind instead of an edit to the earlier one, which is typical of an agentic loop that writes a new file per generation.

How We Measured Two Authoring Styles

We measured authoring styles across 60 distinct hands-on steps, command length splits into two regimes. Sessions on 13 and 15 September run long, with a median of 365 to 493 characters, bundling reconnaissance and error handling into single commands. Sessions on 12 and 14 September run short, 46 to 86 characters, one tool per command. On the same task, domain discovery, the median was 683 characters on 13 September against 80 on 14 September. This shows two authoring styles. It does not show two authors: the model-style errors above appear in both regimes, so even the short sessions were probably model-written.

What Does Not Point to a Model

For balance, several things cut the other way, and they matter. The encryptor is a conventional commodity binary (host.exe -k <victim ID> -s 15, an anti-debug check, wbadmin backup deletion), consistent with earlier public ThreeAM analyses. The tooling is public throughout: the published Veeam script, Impacket patterns, Mimikatz. No natural-language comments, docstrings, or reasoning text appear in any bespoke payload we can read; the only commented script in the log is the public Veeam tool, carrying its original author’s comments. That absence matters because self-narrating comments were one of the main lines of evidence in the JadePuffer case.

No decision cycle ran faster than about 40 to 60 seconds in the hands-on phase. The fast segments (about 101 seconds and 12 to 13 seconds per machine) are scheduled fan-outs, which are deterministic loops, not decisions. And misspellings are not a reliable signal in either direction: a single misspelling (wevutil for wevtutil) appears in the log, and we draw no conclusion from it either way.

Defender action: Hunt for literal probe and confirmation artifacts on hosts that should never see them: files or scheduled tasks named with strings like test123, psexec-ok, da_proof, or VEEAMPROBE, and scripts that write numbered self-logging output. These are cheap, high-signal, and rarely benign on a production server.

Joining the Domains: How the Attacker Built Two-Way Trusts

The estate’s domains were originally separate. This section is the worked example of the hybrid pattern, because joining domains is fiddly, order-sensitive configuration where one wrong detail stops everything, and the fix is found by reading errors and trying again.

The groundwork came on 13 September, when the attacker enumerated trusts with nltest /domain_trusts and searched SYSVOL for other schools’ names and subnets.

The build ran on 18 September, from 15:39 to 18:37 UTC. Within that window the attacker created two-way trusts between three domains using netdom (the built-in tool for managing domain trusts) and dnscmd (the built-in DNS management tool) (T1484.002 Domain Trust Modification). A two-way trust lets an account from one domain authenticate in the others. It does not grant permissions by itself, which is why the attacker followed the trusts with an explicit access push. The first step was a dnscmd call that created a conditional forwarder, a DNS rule that sends lookups for another domain to that domain’s name servers, so the domains could find each other. The netdom calls then built the trust, first from one side (16:09) and, seven minutes later, from the other (16:16).

The trust commands authenticate as library in three different domains, and as svc_bkpmon in at least one. That tells us the backdoor accounts had already been created in several domains before the trusts were built, which is how the attacker had the rights to build them.

Also inside that same three-hour window, the attacker ran a sequence of diagnostic probes and restarted Netlogon, the Windows service that maintains the secure channel between domains. Three probes (diag_member, diag_nl and lmhosts_test) ran between 16:26 and 16:31, before the access push. A fourth (wb_probe) ran at 17:23, after it, and checked the trusts with netdom trust /verify in both directions between two of the domains. Netlogon was restarted (nl_restart) at 18:36. The probe sequence is the diagnose-and-adapt evidence for the trust build. Because the script bodies are unavailable, we cannot say what the probes returned or whether the first trust attempt succeeded.

The access push began at 16:36 UTC, after the first probes: grant_lib.ps1 was pushed by scheduled task to about 40 machines, 3 to 50 seconds apart, granting the backdoor account access everywhere, with stragglers retried at 17:07 and 17:22 (T1078.002 Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts). About 50 machines were reached from the unmanaged host, and about 37 were encrypted the next morning. That cross-domain encryption suggests the trusts functioned, though we treat it as suggestive rather than as proof.

Conclusion and Recommendations

It is one thing to find anecdotal experiments with AI in attacks, and another to find the approach inside a working ransomware playbook. The affiliate in this case ran its usual sequence: backup credential theft, rogue domain administrators, trusts between domains, removal of endpoint security, encryption. It handed the hands-on work to a hybrid of a person and a model. One case does not make a trend, but the approach looks pragmatic: the model takes the mechanical, repetitive work, and nothing in it needed skill or spend that these attackers did not already have. We will be watching for more cases like this one, and for whether the playbook spreads.

Agentic loops are noisy. A loop that reads each result and tries again keeps repeating itself: the same command re-run unchanged, then a small tweak, then a different tool, numbered script after numbered script, probe files and confirmation strings left on disk, the same reconnaissance from several angles. Here the retries came every 40 to 100 seconds. This noise is easy to discover, and it is often underreported in accounts of AI-operated attacks, but it is the attribute defenders most need to understand. A loop does not make an intrusion quiet or subtle. It makes it repetitive, and repetition is what gives it away.

Prevent, do not race. Detection that depends on spotting enough events quickly enough loses to anything that tries again every minute. Prefer controls that work regardless of volume and speed, because they stop an action the first time and the hundredth:

Keep the administrative accounts of separate domains separate, and never keep privileged credentials for several domains in one place. Creating a trust takes administrative rights in each domain involved. After taking credentials from the backup servers, the attacker created the library account in at least three domains and used it to build the trusts. Put domain trusts and domain-admin accounts behind change control, and alert on every one that appears without it.

Treat backup as a target, and review your backup strategy for malicious intent. Most backup designs assume accidents. This attacker hit the backup layer first (credential theft) and last (deletion of system-state backups). Scope backup accounts per domain, isolate the backup servers, and keep immutable recovery copies that no domain account can delete.

Restrict remote execution and administrative shares. WMI, remote registry, scheduled-task creation and ADMIN$ access were the attacker’s movement fabric. Limit them to known management hosts.

Block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them. Portable Python and PowerShell on ordinary workstations ran the attacker’s tooling.

Put an endpoint agent on every machine. The staging host here was unmanaged, which is why we cannot say who or what drove the commands.

Nothing here is new. We have seen nothing novel or creative in this attack: built-in tools, a few public ones and a commodity encryptor. The security practices that stop conventional ransomware stop this too, and they should be adopted. What a model changes is not what works, but what the traces look like.

IOCs and How to Follow Our Research

The full indicator set for this research is available from our GitHub IOC repository to support other researchers and the wider defender community. The same indicators are also delivered through Bitdefender IntelliZone, our threat intelligence platform, alongside the broader context around this activity.

This research is part of Ctrl-Alt-DECODE, Bitdefender’s threat intelligence initiative.

Supermarkets across at least nine European countries have reportedly been impacted by a cyber-attack on their refrigeration systems, resulting in food stock being destroyed.

Reports and official statements emerged about the incident on November 1 from supermarket retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden.

At the time of writing, there is no confirmation about how the incident occurred or the perpetrators. However, the incident appears to be similar in nature to the cyber-attack on refrigeration systems providers Danfoss and Copeland in October 2026, which led to hackers changing temperatures on internet connected refrigerators across several chains of supermarkets in France.

Refrigerator temperatures were reportedly programmed to reach as high as 50°C (122°F), ruining food held in the affected fridges.

Among the retailers impacted in the latest incident is Ireland-based supermarket chain SuperValu. The Irish Times cited a spokesperson from the retailer, who confirmed the “cyber incident” affected a “specific model” of refrigerator used in SuperValu stores. The firm removed chilled and frozen products from shelves in 13 stores as a precautionary measure, the report added.

Among the Swedish retailers impacted were the ICA Sweden, with The Guardian reporting that one store had posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50°C.

Sweden’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said it was monitoring incidents that have affected freezer and refrigeration systems in the grocery trade in a release published on November 2.

“The centre is in contact with affected businesses and also has exchanges with its counterparts in several Nordic and other European countries,” the agency wrote.

Ikea is another company whose refrigeration units are reportedly impacted by the incident. A report by Agence France-Presse on November 3 cited a spokesperson who said the retailer’s outlet in Mons, Belgium, was hit by a cyber-attack that caused freezer temperatures to rise.

UK Food Suppliers Also Affected

Reports emerged on November 3 that businesses in the UK’s food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack.

NCSC chief executive Richard Horne told the BBC’s ‘Today’ program that the agency is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."

Horne added that potentially affected companies have been alerted about the threat.

The comments came as the NCSC published its annual review, which warned that AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028.

Attack a “Deliberate Attempt” to Disrupt Food Supplies

Speaking to Politico, EU Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen warned that the latest incidents, alongside the attack on Danfoss in October, “are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it.”

Hansen noted: “Europe’s food supply chain must be prepared for new and evolving threats. The repeated cyber-attacks on supermarkets are deeply concerning, causing economic losses for retailers and empty shelves for consumers.”

He also told the news outlet that the attacks would be discussed at the next meeting of its Security College to assess retailers’ contingency plans and their ability to respond to incidents.

Hansen’s comments suggest that there could be suspicions on nation-state involvement in the series of attacks. So far, no threat actor has claimed responsibility for either the attack on Danfoss or the latest wave.

Speaking about the incident, Amir Preminger, CTO of Claroty, said: “This second wave of attacks on refrigeration systems in Europe highlights a growing trend: threat actors are increasingly targeting widespread, high-impact disruptions to essential services. Heightened geopolitical tensions have driven a surge in activity targeting critical infrastructure, while AI technologies enable attackers to rapidly scan networks for vulnerabilities and weaknesses in access controls.”

b20a52f78d9a.text: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says AI-powered malware is "highly likely" to be a part of a future ransomware attack on Britain's critical national infrastructure between now and 2028. The warning accompanies its annual review and a separate assessment exploring how AI could change cyber threats over the next two years. The cyber arm of signals intelligence agency GCHQ did not provide much detail about what form this AI malware may take. However, it alluded to open source AI security tools that were initially intended to assist security researchers being repurposed for nefarious activity. Attackers are already repurposing such tools. For example, researchers are increasingly seeing widespread abuse of ARTEX, an open source, Chinese-made AI red-teaming platform, in attacks on UK registrar 123 Reg, Microsoft 365, and others since its launch in July. In its pessimistic scenario for 2028, the NCSC envisages "a significant increase in the frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks worldwide," with wider adoption of AI tools making attribution harder. China "has likely played a role" in supplying those tools in this future, "enabling them to hide their activities within the noise," the report states. It also considers a further threat: an autonomous attacker operating beyond its human operator's control. The NCSC says it "is a realistic possibility such an entity could self-replicate and conduct cyberattacks at will, with no apparent motivation or restraint." Such attacks would likely complicate geopolitical relationships, owing again to attribution difficulties, making it easier for countries that order attacks on others to deny their involvement. The UK's plans for AI defense At a time when each Patch Tuesday seems to come loaded with record numbers of bugs, the NCSC acknowledges that AI is already changing vulnerability discovery and patching. The body is also exploring how AI could help defenders keep pace. Project DROMOS began earlier this year with a four-week pilot analyzing government code repositories, before expanding into selected operational environments. The Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) launched the project with the AI Security Institute and other departments. The NCSC says it uncovered hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities. The review also reaffirms plans for Cyber Shield, an agentic cyber defense system first teased in July. Cyber Shield is expected to be delivered in stages over the next five years. It will involve the NCSC providing defensive agents deployed by participating organizations with data that will strengthen national resilience to ongoing cyber threats. The NCSC will be running the scheme alongside the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), but acknowledged that this kind of automated defensive activity currently sits outside many organizations' risk tolerances, meaning it has a role to play in building trust in the system before adoption can go mainstream. As reported last week, the government has set aside £60 million to fund the initiative, and an additional £70 million to support a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre. The NERV Centre's job will be to identify and maintain an ongoing understanding of vulnerabilities across CNI organizations and the wider economy. Per last week's budget, £40 million will fund a National Agentic Security Unit responsible for responding to uncontrolled bots and other agentic mishaps, and £24 million was assigned to strengthen public sector defenses. An undisclosed sum will also help establish a new NCSC-managed AI Cyber Security Centre in Manchester to develop AI security expertise across government. In the meantime, NCSC CEO Dr Richard Horne is calling for organizations to "invest with urgency" in their security and resilience. "For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap," he said today, announcing the annual report. "We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency... And where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. "The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all." Horne said organizations should treat the NCSC's Cyber Essentials certification as the starting point, but scale up resilience efforts in line with organizational size, complexity, and risk. The government also announced a 75 percent discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small, and medium-sized businesses applying for their first certificate. ®

Executive Summary

We investigated a campaign targeting Israeli organizations through phishing emails impersonating the Israel Tax Authority. The activity has been observed since September 2026. Government-themed domains and a verification page lead recipients to ZIP archives containing executables disguised as tax-related documents. The campaign abuses SimpleHelp, a legitimate remote monitoring and management tool, to enable attacker-directed remote access.

The lure exploits a routine business task and can reach finance, accounting, and administrative staff across sectors. We suspect a connection to MuddyWater based on its documented use of SimpleHelp and targeting of Israel.

Key Findings

The campaign uses Israel Tax Authority impersonation and government-themed domains to distribute ZIP archives to Israeli organizations.

The payload is presented as a tax-related document but is a SimpleHelp executable.

Cato telemetry recorded threat prevention alert against campaign web infrastructure. The event demonstrates prevention of that request, without establishing a completed remote-access session.

Attack Flow

Figure 1 summarizes the delivery chain. Remote access depends on successful execution and activation of the SimpleHelp component.

Figure 1. Tax authority impersonation leads to a SimpleHelp executable. The dashed final step represents potential remote access following successful execution.

Technical Details and Analysis

This activity was previously described in public reporting by CyberIL. Our investigation examined the campaign’s delivery infrastructure and use of SimpleHelp.

From a tax themed email to a verification page

The attack begins with a phishing email impersonating the Israel Tax Authority. Recipients attempting to access the supposed personal area are directed to a lookalike site and prompted to complete a CAPTCHA-style verification step before downloading a ZIP archive.

The infrastructure uses names such as document-govil[.]com to resemble the official Israeli government namespace, gov.il. The string govil is part of a separately registered domain and does not indicate government affiliation.

The verification page in Figure 2 displays a checkbox, a Continue button, and the password 123123. This presentation reinforces the appearance of a protected document-delivery process.

Figure 2. Verification interface used in the tax authority lure.

A ZIP archive delivers the executable

Following the verification step, the download is presented as a tax-related archive. Figure 3 shows Israel_Tax_Authority.zip in the browser download history. The investigation also identifies an archive named document.zip.

Figure 3. Download of Israel_Tax_Authority.zip.

The agency-themed naming continues inside the archive. The executable shown in Figure 4 is named רשות המסים בישראל.exe, meaning “Israel Tax Authority.” A recipient expecting a tax document is instead presented with a program to run. The payload inventory also includes document.exe.

Figure 4. Executable named רשות המסים בישראל.exe presented under the tax authority pretext.

SimpleHelp provides the remote access capability

SimpleHelp is legitimate remote support software. In this campaign, it is used as the remote-access component behind the document lure. The research identifies 129.121.120[.]121 as associated command-and-control infrastructure.

Successful deployment can allow an operator to connect to the endpoint and continue the intrusion using the software’s built-in capabilities. The table below maps vendor-documented features to potential attacker use and business impact. It describes capabilities rather than observed post-compromise actions.

Potential attacker use

These capabilities are described in SimpleHelp’s feature documentation, Toolbox Guide, and Remote Access Guide.

The activity involved social engineering and abuse of legitimate RMM functionality. Our findings and SimpleHelp’s assessment are summarized in the disclosure section below.

Mapping the infrastructure with FOFA

We searched FOFA for the two observed HTTP ETag values. The search returned eight service records associated with 129.121.120[.]121, including records for document-govil[.]com and document-govil[.]online, as shown in Figure 5. Both domains displayed “Coming Soon” pages served by nginx.

Figure 5. FOFA results linking the two domains to 129.121.120[.]121. The eight results are service records on one IP.

Public reporting on SimpleHelp abuse

Group-IB previously documented MuddyWater’s use of SimpleHelp, providing context for our attribution assessment. Sophos, CISA, and Huntress have also reported separate ransomware incidents involving SimpleHelp exploitation or abuse.

Attribution Assessment

We suspect MuddyWater involvement based on the combination of Israeli organizational targeting, locally tailored authority impersonation, and delivery of legitimate remote-access software through phishing. HarfangLab documented an October 2023 MuddyWater phishing email linking to a SimpleHelp installer. Proofpoint documented Hebrew payroll lures in March 2024 that led Israeli recipients through PDF links to ZIP archives containing Atera installers.

Earlier campaigns also used institution-themed Egnyte subdomains and Hebrew filenames related to scholarships and tourism. These examples show a recurring approach of adapting recognizable Israeli identities and routine business tasks to persuade recipients to install remote-access software. The current campaign follows a similar pattern through Israel Tax Authority impersonation and tax-themed filenames.

The February 2022 joint government advisory identifies MuddyWater as a subordinate element of Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security.

Disclosure Timeline

SimpleHelp is legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. Based on the evidence reviewed and validation with SimpleHelp, we did not identify exploitation of a SimpleHelp vulnerability or compromise of SimpleHelp’s own infrastructure in connection with this campaign. The activity investigated involved social engineering intended to induce users to deploy SimpleHelp configured to connect to attacker-controlled infrastructure, consistent with the broader abuse of legitimate RMM tools by threat actors.

SimpleHelp confirmed that both samples identify themselves as SimpleHelp Remote Access Client version 5.4.5. Based on the information we provided, SimpleHelp assessed the activity as apparent malicious use of an older release and stated that it had not seen evidence indicating exploitation of a SimpleHelp vulnerability. SimpleHelp offered to investigate associated infrastructure and assess available action, requesting server addresses or hostnames, observation timestamps, and supporting evidence through a private file request. We subsequently shared the relevant server list with SimpleHelp.

Cato automatically blocks the campaign domains and IOCs listed below, protecting Cato customers against these identified threats without requiring manual indicator updates.

In addition, Cato MDR provides 24/7 threat monitoring, investigation, and response for suspicious activity involving remote-access tools and attacker-controlled infrastructure.

A new vulnerability disclosure can set off a familiar chain of work. You check whether or not an application uses the affected component, determine whether the vulnerable code is reachable, find a fixed version, test the upgrade, and get it into production. Then the next advisory arrives.

Known vulnerabilities need to be understood and remediated. But a process built around chasing CVEs one at a time can leave teams reacting to risk after a dependency has already entered their software.

It also leaves important questions unanswered:

Is the package malicious?

Is its license acceptable?

Is the project still maintained?

Can its origin be verified?

Does the dependency meet the organization's requirements?

A CVE is a useful signal, but it is not a complete measure of component trust. Teams need to govern the software dependencies they use across the SDLC, from selection and approval through ongoing monitoring and remediation.

CVE Remediation Is Necessary. It Is Not the Whole Strategy.

The CVE system gives security teams, developers, vendors, and researchers a shared way to identify known vulnerabilities. But a CVE record or score does not show whether vulnerable code is reachable in an application, whether a dependency is direct or transitive, or whether a safe upgrade is available.

Sonatype's analysis of 1,552 open source CVEs found that 64% had no CVSS score, severity categories matched across sources only 19% of the time, and scoring delays averaged six weeks. Those gaps can make it difficult to rank findings and decide where engineering time will reduce the most risk.

Teams need to treat CVEs as one input and weigh them alongside component use, available fixes, and application context.

Disclosure Starts the Remediation Cycle

When vulnerability management centers on incoming CVEs, teams begin responding after disclosure: identifying affected versions, tracing dependencies, and coordinating upgrades. By then, a component may already appear across applications, build environments, and releases, adding to the remediation backlog.

Component risks also extend beyond CVEs. A package may be malicious, poorly maintained, or incompatible with licensing requirements. Finding those issues earlier can help teams avoid broader changes, release delays, and retesting.

AI Is Increasing the Pace of Discovery and Consumption

AI is changing how quickly teams find and use software components. A developer might ask a coding assistant to add a feature, accept its suggestion to use a new library, and move on to the next task. The package can become part of the project before anyone has checked whether it is maintained, allowed by policy, or appropriate for that use. Consequently, teams must absorb a higher volume of vulnerability disclosures while simultaneously tracking which components enter their codebase and why.

A large Spring security disclosure illustrates the downstream scale. In August 2026, Sonatype tracked 91 CVEs across Spring and related projects. At the time of publication, Sonatype Guide reported 148,608 affected components, including components that bundle vulnerable Spring code. The disclosure does not establish that AI caused those vulnerabilities, but it shows how broadly a vulnerability can affect software that depends on an ecosystem.

Teams responding to disclosures at this scale need to determine:

Which applications include the affected components, directly or transitively?

Which vulnerable versions are present or deployed?

Which components pose the greatest risk in their environment?

Which upgrades will address the vulnerabilities without causing unnecessary disruption?

Discovery can move faster than downstream teams can locate, assess, and upgrade affected components. As AI-assisted vulnerability research develops, vulnerability intelligence and remediation processes will need to keep pace.

Teams also need visibility into what is in their software, where it came from, how it is used, and who owns decisions to keep, upgrade, replace, or accept it. That context helps turn a stream of findings into work that can be prioritized and acted on.

Component Risk Goes Beyond Vulnerabilities

A component can create risk even when it has no known CVE. A more complete assessment considers several dimensions:

Malware: Has the package or release been compromised, or does it contain malicious behavior?

Licensing: Is its license compatible with the project's obligations and intended use?

Maintenance: Is the project maintained, and can the team rely on its release and support practices?

Provenance: Can the component's source and history be verified?

Policy: Does it meet the organization's requirements for approved sources, versions, and use cases?

Each scenario demands distinct evidence and action: fixing vulnerable releases, instantly blocking malicious packages, scheduling replacements for unmaintained libraries, legally reviewing licenses, or verifying provenance prior to approval.

Treating every issue as another scanner finding can obscure those differences. Component governance gives teams a way to define which qualities matter, set expectations before adoption, and assign an appropriate response when a component falls outside them.

Govern Dependencies Before and After Adoption

Governance works best when it is part of normal development, rather than a review that begins after a release is ready.

Teams can make it practical by connecting policy to the component lifecycle:

Define acceptable use. Establish requirements for sources, licenses, maintenance, provenance, and known security risks. Set policies that reflect how components will be used and the impact of a failure.

Evaluate before adoption. Check candidate components against those requirements before they become dependencies. Give developers and AI tools clear, approved choices where possible, so the compliant path is also the easy path.

Maintain a record of use. Track component identity and version, origin, dependency relationships, and the applications or releases that include it. This context helps teams understand the reach of a new advisory or policy change.

Monitor for change. A component's status can change after adoption. New vulnerability information may emerge; a project may become inactive; a release may be compromised; or an organization's policy may change. Reassess components as new evidence arrives.

Route decisions to owners. Define who handles upgrades, replacement, license review, and exceptions. Record the reason for an exception and when it should be reviewed again.

Scanning and patching remain essential, but connecting them to a broader decision framework lets teams weigh vulnerabilities against exposure, exploitability, available fixes, and business context. Meanwhile, malware alerts, licensing issues, and maintenance risks can be routed directly to the appropriate decision-makers.

Effective open source policy enforcement aligns with risk severity. Known malware warrants immediate blocking, licensing queries require review before distribution, and unmaintained low-risk components may receive temporary exceptions. Explicit thresholds, designated owners, and time-bound exceptions enable consistent standard application without unnecessary escalations or blanket bans.

Timing is critical. Providing developers and AI tools with trusted, policy-approved component options during dependency selection allows teams to address risk before it is built in. Identifying flagged components later in release pipelines forces teams to reverse decisions already embedded across repositories and applications.

Move From a Findings Queue to Better Decisions

Software teams will continue to receive CVEs, and they should continue to remediate vulnerabilities that put their applications at risk. But a growing list of CVEs is not, by itself, a strategy for choosing and managing software components.

A stronger approach starts earlier and continues after adoption. It helps teams select components that meet their needs, understand where those components are used, detect changes in their risk, and respond according to clear policies. That can reduce avoidable surprises and help engineering teams spend less time reconstructing dependency context during an incident.

The goal is not to eliminate vulnerability work. It is to make that work part of a more complete way to govern software components — one that accounts for security, licensing, maintenance, provenance, and policy throughout the software lifecycle.

Sonatype Nexus One platform helps put that strategy into practice and gives teams the data to assess open source dependencies. With trusted component intelligence and policies built into development workflows, teams can make better decisions about what they use and respond more effectively when the evidence changes. Contact us to learn more about how you can improve your open source governance strategy.

Written by Aaron Linskens

Aaron is a technical writer at Sonatype. He works at a crossroads of technical writing, developer advocacy, and information design. He aims to get developers and non-technical collaborators to work better together in solving problems and building software.

What you will learn

Why audit trails record a developer when an AI agent acted, how entitlement scope differs from action attribution, and the five facts a session record needs to show which agent ran a query and whose credentials it used.

An AI agent ran the query. The audit trail says a person did.

Why does an audit trail attribute AI agent activity to a person?

An AI agent connects with credentials issued to a person, so the audit trail records the person.

For example, at two in the morning, a database connection opens and a query runs against a production table. The audit trail records the username of a developer who was asleep at the time. A coding agent made the connection with the developer credentials while it worked through a task the developer had assigned before logging off.

Nothing in the log entry separates the developer from the agent. By its own standard, the log is complete. It still cannot answer the question an investigator will ask: Who ran that query?

In the Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report: The AI Enforcement Gap, Gal Diskin, Vice President of Research and Head of Delinea Labs, noted that actions taken with AI credentials “are very hard to distinguish between the AI and the human that launched them with existing tools and audit log limitations.”

Access models and audit trails were designed for human actors

Access models assume that the person who holds an account is the person who uses it. Until recently, that assumption held. A username answered two questions at once: Who held the access, and who used it. Audit trails follow the same design, so they record the username as the actor.

AI agents break that assumption. The account holder and the actor can now differ, and security teams need a way to talk about each one.

Entitlement scope is what an identity is permitted to reach. A developer with access to the production customer database has that database in scope, whether the developer or an agent opens the connection. Reviewers settle entitlement scope during an access review, before any session begins.

Action attribution identifies which actor used the entitlement and what that actor did. Attribution separates “the developer ran the query” from “a coding agent ran the query with the developer credentials.” Investigators can settle attribution only from a session record, and they need the answer after the session ends.

The agent never receives an entitlement of its own. It works with the entitlement already issued to the person who started it.

AI agents carry entitlements without the judgment behind them

A person receives an entitlement because someone decided that person could be trusted with access. An agent receives the same entitlement, but nobody made that decision about the agent. Nothing checks the agent against the original approval. The session record is the only place to find out what the agent did with the access it inherited.

How can security teams tell whether an AI agent or a person performed an action?

Security teams can tell only when the session record captures the initiator separately from the username. If the record captures only the username, the person and the agent look identical.

The Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report shows how often agents reach past their tasks. Of the IT and security leaders surveyed, 87% said an AI tool or agent at their organization accessed, or likely accessed, sensitive data beyond what its task required in the past year. Only 36% said their organization can always trace a sensitive AI access event back to a named human authorizer.

Example: overprivileged AI agent access

What happened. A developer asks a coding agent to look into a spike in failed customer logins. The developer has access to the production customer database for on-call work, so the agent has that access too. The agent pulls full customer records, including email addresses and phone numbers, and saves them to a file on the developer laptop. The task needed only login counts.

What the audit trail showed. The database log lists the queries under the developer username.

Why the evidence fell short. The log cannot show who pulled the records, which agent acted, or what instruction the agent followed. Without those facts, the reviewer cannot tell whether a person or an agent decided to export customer data, and the security team cannot decide who owns the response.

What should an AI agent audit trail record about each session?

An authorization record shows who approved an agent. A session record shows what the agent did with that approval; an AI agent audit trail needs both. At a minimum, the session record should capture five facts:

the identity that held the entitlement

whether a person or an AI agent initiated the session, and which agent

the resources the session reached and the actions taken on each resource

each path the agent used to reach a resource, including paths outside the Model Context Protocol (MCP)

a record the security team can reach and search during an investigation

AI agent activity can bypass MCP, so audit coverage cannot depend on MCP-only monitoring. MCP is a common standard for connecting AI agents to tools and data, but an agent with a database credential does not need it. The agent can open a database connection on its own, and a monitoring approach that watches only MCP traffic will never see that connection.

How does Delinea record AI agent activity?

Delinea records AI agent activity at the gateway, where the agent connects to the resource. When Delinea identifies the agent, the session record names both the person who held the entitlement and the agent that acted on behalf of that person. The record captures both names regardless of how the agent reached the resource.

Delinea built agent attribution by extending the gateway that already recorded human sessions. The developer and the coding agent appear in the same record, so investigators can review human and agent activity in one place.

AI agent attribution is the first step toward AI agent guardrails

Frank Vukovits, Chief Security Scientist at Delinea, framed the issue the way an auditor would: “Saying the AI agent did it is not a defensible answer.”

After a session ends, investigators use the session record to learn who ran the query. The gateway identifies the agent when the connection opens, so the same information can limit what the agent can do in the first place. Security teams can write entitlement rules for the agent itself. The developer keeps access to the production customer database, and the coding agent working for that developer does not.

Phil Calvin, Executive Vice President of AI Innovation at Delinea, tested an agent-specific rule which he documented in the blog "Your AI agent doesn't need to go rogue; it just needs you to be over-privileged". The gateway enabled him to write to a database and blocked the agent working for him from doing the same. His results show what a rule written for the agent can do.

In our conversations with security teams, we hear a consistent pattern. Teams want to audit which agent acted and which identity the agent used, but the larger concern is keeping agents out of critical production systems until the organization has a reason to trust them. Until that trust exists, the gateway can keep agents away from the most sensitive resources.

Read how Telnyx and Delinea compare for AI agent access.

Contact Delinea to review what current session records show about AI agent activity.

When an active zero-day like the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability breaks, security tools light up within minutes, flagging critical production risks that demand an immediate fix. And while AI has accelerated how quickly vulnerabilities are discovered, fixing them still waits on human coordination.

However, implementing that fix extends far beyond the security team and becomes an organization-wide initiative. Security teams discover the risk, but they don't own the code, the infrastructure, or the deployment pipelines. Resolving the issue requires coordinating across three distinct teams, each with their own set of priorities:

Security: Wants to eliminate exploitable risk immediately.

Engineering: Wants to maintain shipping velocity without breaking dependencies or spending time figuring out the right fix.

Cloud / Platform Operations: Wants to preserve uptime and infrastructure stability.

With each team working in their own workflows and against their own roadmap, remediation becomes an expensive game of cross-departmental ping pong. Tickets bounce between teams, developers waste hours determining the environment-specific fix, and Mean Time to Remediation (MTTR) grows.

To close this gap, organizations need a bridge between runtime context and developer execution so fixing becomes automated and continuous. Here is how leading teams use Wiz Green Agent to eliminate the three core bottlenecks of remediation, the ROI they achieve, and how that work builds towards a self healing cloud.

The Three Bottlenecks that make remediation hard

Finding the right owner for the Issue

Before a team can investigate or fix a risk, they run into the first hurdle: who actually owns the vulnerable asset? In dynamic multi-cloud, hybrid, or AI environments, that answer is hard to come by. A production container might have been deployed through a shared pipeline, authored by an engineer who switched teams months ago, or spun up across accounts with missing tags and with a CMDB that’s out of date. When ownership isn't clear, Issues sit unassigned in backlog queues or bounce between Platform, DevOps, and AppSec teams trying to determine whose repo or service an issue belongs to.

That delay in finding an owner stretches out remediation cycles before work can even begin.

How Green Agent solves it

Green Agent eliminates the ownership guessing game by connecting signals from across your entire environment. By analyzing repository commit history, Wiz Project assignments, service catalogs, CMDB integrations, and cloud logs, Green Agent automatically identifies the Suggested Assignee: the specific developer or individual best positioned to act.

Security teams can assign the issue to the right owner with one click directly inside the Issue drawer, ensuring Issues land with the person who can actually merge the fix.

This analysis is how teams like Rogo, an enterprise AI platform for financial institutions, eliminate manual cross-team detective work while maintaining rapid development velocity across AWS and GCP:

With the Green Agent it's surfaced automatically in the Wiz Issue and is incredibly valuable in finding the right person so our developers can quickly remediate.

Eric Tu, Product Security Engineer, Rogo

Understanding risk at the root cause

When a critical security Issue hits a developer’s queue, they want clear, actionable answers on what they need to fix, where it lives in code, and how they need to fix it so they can get back to shipping new features. Getting to those answers starts with tracing it back from runtime to code to understand the root cause.

That means confirming the workload is actually exposed, verifying the vulnerable package is reachable, and locating the originating repository, Dockerfile, or commit that introduced it. Doing that forensic legwork by hand for every alert is slow and repetitive, and at cloud scale, with AI pushing more code into production every week, it's where the bulk of triage time goes before the fix can begin.

How Green Agent solves it

Green Agent automates that entire investigation under the hood. For each Issue, it reasons across the Wiz Security Graph to evaluate runtime exposure, identity access, and code-to-cloud mapping to understand the root cause. It confirms whether the risk is truly exploitable and recommends whether to remediate or adjust the severity to keep developers focused on high-priority risks, then pinpoints the exact file and line in the source code responsible for the vulnerability.

As a result of Green Agent’s AI investigation engine, Fireblocks, the digital asset and blockchain infrastructure provider, cut daily operational triage time by more than 70% and now reaches same-day resolution on critical risks.

Green Agent explains the full context; it shows us all of our workloads and the exact remediation path for any issue. All the remediation paths are really clear... Before Red Agent, Green Agent, and the Cloudflare integration, we used to have manual processes for triage. Now, we get clearer findings and faster remediation that reduce the amount of manual hours of operation needed.

Roy Weiss, Principal DevSecOps, Fireblocks

Turning alerts into actionable fixes for developers

Even with the right owner assigned and the root cause identified, the final friction point is execution: turning that Issue into merged code.

Handing an engineer an alert with a link to a generic CVE bulletin forces them to context-switch away from their sprint, research potential patches, and figure out how to write the fix without breaking existing dependencies. Developers are focused on building and shipping product features; for remediation to move at the speed of AI engineering, the specific environmental fix has to meet developers directly in their everyday workflows.

How Green Agent solves it

Green Agent closes that loop by generating prescriptive, environment-specific remediation. It provides code or Terraform changes needed down to the exact line, and surfaces 1-click Pull Requests or handoffs to coding agents so developers can simply review, validate, and merge. For teams building with AI, Green Agent also exposes its remediation context via API and the Wiz Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, allowing developers to pull Green Agent’s remediation recommendations directly inside their agentic IDEs to accelerate fixing.

By meeting developers where they work and removing the manual research burden, project44, the global supply chain visibility platform, accelerated their remediation velocity by 10x while keeping engineering focused on roadmap priorities:

AI has enhanced coding velocity for engineers; the Green Agent from Wiz offers a similar increase in velocity for security engineering work.

Matthew Blackert, Security Operations Manager, project44

Our Wiz enablement with Engineering showed us what's possible when you remove the noise: engineers fixing real risk instead of validating false positives.

Mihajlo Jankovic, Security Operations Analyst II, project44

Closing the Remediation Gap

Remediation speed is no longer limited by how fast security can find risks, it’s defined by how smoothly security context converts into developer action.

By eliminating the context gap, automating ownership attribution, and delivering 1-click code fixes, Wiz Green Agent transforms remediation from a cross-team tax into an automated, closed-loop workflow.

99cce7f47927.text:
Attackers are exploiting an authentication flaw (CVE-2026-58115) in Node-RED, a programming tool built into some industrial control products, to install a Linux bot and backdoors on unprotected servers, VulnCheck has found.

Node-RED is a flow-based programming tool built on Node.js that lets users wire together event-driven applications in a browser-based editor. It can run on small devices such as the Raspberry Pi or in the cloud, and it is used in manufacturing, healthcare, and home and industrial automation.

The tool is also part of critical infrastructure, embedded in commercial ICS/OT products such as Siemens’ SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced, which is affected by the flaw. Siemens disclosed it in August and gave it a CVSS score of 10.0, warning that devices running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed, in versions before V4.3.4.1, are vulnerable.

The bug “could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to create malicious flows and execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with maximum privileges,” Siemens said at the time of disclosure.

Caught by a decoy

More than two months after Siemens’ disclosure, the flaw is being exploited in the wild.

“On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” wrote VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity.

“The attacker’s request was a complete exploit. It deployed a Node-RED flow, triggered it automatically, and pulled a binary from an attacker-controlled server, all behind three layers of encoding,” added Garrity.

“Two built-in node types make this trivial to weaponize. An inject node fires a message on a schedule or once at startup, and an exec node runs a shell command. Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” he explained.

The flow downloaded a file named bot-linux-amd64 from a separate server, saved it under a hidden name in a memory-backed location and ran it in the background. VulnCheck did not retrieve the binary, so the company can’t say whether it is a cryptominer, a DDoS bot, a reverse shell or something else.

One address, eight CVEs

The request came from an IP address in Microsoft’s network that geolocates to Brazil. “It didn’t just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity stated.

The same address went after the Node-RED flaw 16 times between October 30 and November 1, and in VulnCheck’s wider canary data it logged 125 hits against 8 different CVEs, old and new, in Apache Solr, Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik and Joomla.

Garrity describes this as opportunistic mass scanning, and notes that an address in a large cloud provider’s range is usually a rented or compromised virtual machine and says little about who is behind the attacks.

Later requests brought new payloads. One fetched a shell script from the same download server, and another pulled a file from a second server and saved it under a name made to look like a kernel worker thread. Several requests installed webshells that let the attackers come back and run commands at will. The bot is stored in memory and is lost on reboot unless it sets up persistence some other way, while the webshells stay in place after a restart.

The exploitation activity (Source: VulnCheck)

Check your instances

VulnCheck added the flaw to its KEV catalog after spotting the in-the-wild attempt and noted that CISA had not listed it in its own KEV catalog at the time of writing.

“Node-RED instances without adminAuth are being found and exploited automatically,” Garrity warned.

“If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post.

The VulnCheck post lists indicators of compromise, including the IP addresses of the attack source and both payload servers.

The median vulnerability on enterprise network appliances stays unpatched for more than a year, Microsoft’s own telemetry shows, even as the most damaging software flaws are being weaponized within days of disclosure.

Microsoft Security Research reported the findings Monday in an analysis of roughly 383,000 CVEs disclosed from 1999 through September 2026. It shows that the median time to patch a vulnerability exceeds a year for network appliances. The period is more than a month for Windows servers, over 10 weeks for Linux servers and applications running on macOS, and about two weeks for Windows workstations.

“That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest,” Microsoft Security researchers Yair Tsarfaty and Or Begam wrote in a blog post detailing the findings. They were referring to the distance between how fast flaws are exploited and how slowly critical systems are patched.

Patching measured in weeks and months

Microsoft drew its patching figures from 2026 data in its Security Exposure Management product. The median vulnerability is fixed in about two weeks on Windows workstations but takes more than a month on Windows Server, according to the post. The delay stretches beyond 10 weeks on Linux servers and for applications running on macOS, and past a year on network appliances.

Vibhum Dubey, a cybersecurity researcher and red teamer, said the findings reflect what he sees across enterprise environments. In those environments, change approvals, application dependencies, maintenance windows, and legacy infrastructure routinely hold up fixes.

“Network appliances are particularly difficult because firmware upgrades can affect critical business operations,” Dubey said. “In many cases, the challenge is not identifying vulnerabilities, but getting the right teams to remediate them without disrupting business services.”

Exploitation measured in days

Exploitation runs on a far shorter clock, Microsoft wrote in the post. Citing CISA figures, the researchers said the mean time from CVE publication to listing in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. For 2026 through September, the mean has dropped to 20 days and the median to three.

“Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure,” the post said.

The researchers also cited VulnCheck’s State of Exploitation 2026 report, which found that 29% of exploits in 2025 were launched within a day of CVE publication. Industry research points to advances in AI as a significant factor in cutting the time needed to develop exploits, Microsoft wrote in the blog post.

In some cases, defenders have hours rather than weeks, Dubey said. Vulnerabilities can be exploited before public disclosure or before organizations have completed their initial assessment.

He said enterprises need to move away from relying entirely on monthly scans and scheduled patch cycles. In their place, he said, they need continuous monitoring, emergency patching procedures, virtual patching through WAF and IPS controls, and clear remediation ownership.

“The priority should be to reduce the window of exposure, because by the time a vulnerability reaches the regular patching queue, attackers may already be exploiting it,” Dubey said.

Where the exploits land

The vulnerabilities attackers actually use look very different from the CVE population as a whole, the analysis found. Server-side remote code execution (RCE) flaws make up 20% of all published CVEs but 37% of those exploited in the wild. Local privilege escalation climbs from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%.

Cross-site scripting drops from 15% of published CVEs to 4% of exploited ones, and denial-of-service flaws drop from 16% to 7%, according to the researchers. Operating system vulnerabilities make up 23% of the overall population but account for 41% of exploited CVEs.

“These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control,” the researchers wrote.

Together, RCE, authentication bypass, and local privilege escalation account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, the post said. Windows ranks as the most affected platform among exploited CVEs in Microsoft’s data.

Prioritizing by exposure

A vulnerability’s value to an attacker depends on its impact and its exposure, according to Microsoft. Impact is what successful exploitation delivers. Exposure is the identities, privileges, and network connections reachable from the compromised asset.

Servers frequently run service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with more permissions than they need, the post noted. Taking over one of them can open paths to sensitive data, administrative rights, and trusted networks.

“CVSS scores alone are no longer sufficient,” Dubey said. Organizations should prioritize vulnerabilities based on active exploitation, internet exposure, asset criticality, and potential attack paths, he said. “A medium-severity vulnerability on an internet-facing system with a known exploit can present a greater risk than a critical vulnerability on an isolated asset,” he said.

A China-nexus espionage group used AI agents to attack more than 200 organizations in 11 days, CrowdStrike said last week. On Monday, Kaspersky published details of a separate campaign against educational institutions in Africa and Latin America, mounted by Chinese-speaking operators.

Though the campaigns don’t appear to be connected, they are executed the same way: a human picks the targets and sets the goals, and a large language model (LLM) decides which commands to run and sends them to an implant on the victim’s network.

ARTEX widens Vapor Panda’s net

The China-nexus group CrowdStrike tracks as Vapor Panda started using an agentic framework called ARTEX on October 17. Over the next 11 days, a single ARTEX controller was used against organizations in at least 14 countries, the company determined.

Targets included foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia and the Middle East, US defense and semiconductor companies, and telecom providers.

CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organizations, where the group installed the BloodAlchemy backdoor. It also saw password spraying against at least 12 others, including US think tanks and European government bodies.

The ARTEX framework ran mostly on DeepSeek, along with a second commercial LLM that CrowdStrike couldn’t identify. A main agent handed work to planner and worker agents, which keep track of what they’ve learned in a shared graph.

In one intrusion alone, the planning agents went through roughly 1.4 billion input tokens. Recovered transcripts show the operator stepping in at decision points with instructions written in Chinese.

When one route failed, the agents moved on to another, but the techniques they use were familiar.

At one pharma firm, the agent paired an unsigned SAML assertion with an XXE flaw to reach the cloud instance metadata service, then worked its way up to an enterprise admin account.

“Against a Greek government entity, the operator supplied the agent with a 2022 directory export from the organization’s mail server containing authentication keys that had likely not been rotated since the export. The agent used those keys to forge an administrator token and read mailboxes, then used VPN configurations recovered from a user’s sent mail, alongside a VPN client key the operator described as originating from a May 2024 email leak, to reach the internal network,” the company added.

This is the first time CrowdStrike has seen Vapor Panda use AI tooling, and the group’s target list has grown with it. This finding and Microsoft’s recent report about separate ARTEX activity by the Storm-0940 group seems to point to the ARTEX framework catching on among China-nexus groups, Crowdstrike noted.

Domain admin in days

Kaspersky’s report covers a smaller campaign against educational institutions in several African and Latin American countries.

The attackers used CyberStrikeAI, an open-source penetration testing framework written in Go. The LLM runs on the attacker’s command-and-control (C2) server, where it plans the next steps and generates commands. The implant on the victim’s machine has no AI built in and simply executes what it receives.

The attackers broke in “by hand” through a compromised SQL Server, spent about a day on reconnaissance, then went quiet for two weeks. But once the agent was installed, things moved fast: it set up persistence and did local recon within two minutes, then spent about five hours mapping the domain.

A few days later, lateral movement, credential dumping across multiple hosts and a database export took less than an hour. From agent deployment to the compromise of domain admin accounts, the whole thing took three to four days.

Kaspersky didn’t link the activity to a known group, but several clues point to a Chinese-speaking operator: Chinese comments in the scripts, use of the Chinese service dnslog[.]cn, and C2 server restarts that mostly happened during business hours in UTC+8.

“The origin of the tool itself also indirectly points in the same direction: CyberStrikeAI was developed within the Chinese cybersecurity community and is well known there,” Kaspersky researchers added.

What defenders should do now

Until recently, most documented attacker use of AI was preparation: writing phishing emails, fixing code, researching vulnerabilities. In these campaigns, the model is part of the intrusion itself.

“If HexStrike AI and similar tools cover the ‘find and break’ phase, and Sliver/Mythic/Havoc cover the ‘establish a foothold and control’ phase, CyberStrikeAI completes the kill chain: a single server-side process written in Go executes utilities via MCP, handles webshell connections, and assigns tasks to the implant, while the model analyzes the results and decides what to do next,” Kaspersky researchers say.

“The key takeaway is that the introduction of AI into the attack chain does not yet present fundamentally new challenges for detection. All the ‘intelligent’ work remains on the attacker’s side, while the compromised host is subjected to familiar actions: from reconnaissance via Kerberoasting and AS-REP Roasting to LSASS dumps, DCSync, and the Golden Ticket attacks.”

The novelty in these attacks is the speed and ease with which they were executed, they added.

CrowdStrike notes that detection only helps where it’s deployed, and these operators went looking for the gaps. It advises organizations rotate keys and credentials after any suspected exposure, enforce SAML signature validation and IMDSv2, hunt for ARTEX markers, patch internet-facing appliances, and run EDR everywhere.

“China-nexus adversaries will highly likely continue adopting agentic frameworks such as ARTEX over the next 12 months, pairing them with commercially available LLMs, and enabling small teams to quickly scale intrusions across many targets simultaneously,” the company concluded.

Kaspersky researchers also expect the techniques these tools use to grow more sophisticated as models improve, and the operator’s job to shift “from setting tasks to monitoring the model’s actions.”

Google on Monday announced new security updates for Android that resolve more than 200 vulnerabilities, including two dozen critical-severity issues.

The first part of the patches arrives on devices as the 2026-11-01 security patch level and resolves 119 security defects across Android runtime, Framework, and System.

Framework received fixes for the largest number of flaws, namely 65, followed by System with 53. Google resolved one high-severity information disclosure bug in Android runtime.

According to Google’s security bulletin, the most severe of the patched weaknesses resides in the Framework component and is tracked as CVE-2026-58868.

“The most severe of these issues is a critical security vulnerability in the Framework component that could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation,” the company says.

Critical-severity remote code execution (RCE), elevation of privilege (EoP), and denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerabilities were addressed in the System component as well.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Google rolled out patches for 17 of these flaws ahead of the monthly rollout, as part of Google Play system updates.

The second part of Android’s November 2026 security updates arrives on devices as the 2026-11-05 security patch level and fixes 97 bugs in Kernel, Arm, Imagination Technologies, MediaTek, Unisoc, and Qualcomm components.

While most of the fixes target high-severity issues, more than a dozen of them resolve critical-severity weaknesses in subcomponents such as Bluetooth, pKVM, HID, MediaTek modem, and a Qualcomm closed-source component.

“Security patch levels of 2026-11-05 or later address all of these issues,” Google notes.

On Monday, Google also published security bulletins for Android XR and Wear OS. In addition to the bugs described in the November 2026 Android bulletin, the Android XR update resolves a high-severity flaw in Framework, while the Wear OS patch addresses two high-severity issues in Framework and System.

While digital billboards are supposed to grab your attention, recent reports from Egypt, Malaysia, and Brazil described them doing so with explicit footage.

The cyberattacks were claimed by a group called Leakers$, which said it exploited software used to send content to LED displays.

The group said it did not hack into individual billboards to show the pornographic footage, but that it accessed the software used to send the content.

For example, on October 29, explicit footage appeared on a large billboard overlooking one of Egypt’s busiest highways. Videos circulating online showed the attackers’ aliases and a Telegram channel address overlaid on the footage. Some motorists stopped to record it.

Egyptian authorities said the billboard’s operator suffered a website compromise, resulting in unauthorized footage appearing in several countries simultaneously. Similar events were reported in Malaysia and Brazil. The attackers also claimed access to systems in Iraq and China, but those claims are less firmly corroborated.

Speaking to The Cairo Report, a representative of Leakers$ claimed the group found thousands of exposed systems during roughly two hours of automated scanning. The representative described a vulnerability in content-transmission software and weaknesses accessible through the systems’ own web pages and interfaces.

That is the group’s account, but if it is accurate, it helps explain the apparent ease and reach of the attack:

Internet exposure makes targets discoverable. Attackers can scan for reachable management systems rather than physically approach individual screens.

Repeated software weaknesses can scale. Finding a flaw in software used across multiple installations can create opportunities far beyond one billboard.

Content-management access is the prize. Someone who gains control of the system that publishes advertisements may be able to replace legitimate content without touching the display itself.

This is another example of how convenient remote management can expose systems to attack. Recent attacks on refrigerated systems in European supermarkets demonstrated a similar risk. The cooling systems are internet-connected, so mechanics can remotely diagnose and fix problems.

What should be done

The risk of food waste or dangerous traffic situations should be a warning to review what organizations need to do to prevent their systems from being hacked and abused.

Regarding digital billboards, the Out of Home Advertising Association of America’s security guidelines tell operators not to rely on manufacturers’ default passwords or reuse passwords across displays. They also recommend restricting access to management services, using multifactor authentication, and protecting remote connections with a VPN.

But the practical response is less about protecting a giant television and more about securing a remotely managed computer system:

Restrict management access rather than leaving it open to the public internet.

Replace default and reused passwords and enable multifactor authentication.

Keep signage software, controllers, and networking equipment updated.

Check who has access, including suppliers, and how that access is protected.

Monitor systems and rehearse a way to stop unauthorized access quickly.

These same basic rules can be applied to smart household appliances.

AIs Hacking the Law

In both a 2021 essay and my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind, I talk about AIs finding vulnerabilities and exploits—hacking—the legal system.

Here’s some demonstrations of this from Germany:

Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language. Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation.1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place. With highly capable AI systems enabling the discovery of vulnerabilities at unprecedented scale, we believe the latter could change.

In testing this hypothesis, we have identified a substantial number of vulnerabilities in the German legal system using LLMs. To our knowledge, none of these have been previously recorded. We share a selection of vulnerabilities below, and present potential exploits for each. We share only those vulnerabilities whose exploitation we believe would not cause serious harm.

We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems. In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves.

Still in its early stages, but definitely something that’s coming.

Tags: AI, hacking, laws

Chinmay Patel of Digital Boundary Group reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.

Subnet Solutions reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.

Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.

Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. These vulnerabilities are not exploitable remotely.
