96e45f729b2b.text:
Cybersecurity for smaller businesses often suffers by being either underpowered or too complex. This tension can be challenging to resolve for small IT teams that may lack an in-house cyber expert. Understanding the problem is not the same as understanding where the solution lies.

Effective SMB protection demands that vendors lead their customers through a clear onboarding process – and offer practical and transparent guidance during incident response engagements.

Without trusted partnerships like this, SMBs may struggle to optimize the way they use security products and services. They may find it difficult to explain incidents to insurers and regulators. And they may fail to learn from threat events in a way that can help to build long-term resilience.

Complexity is everywhere

These challenges are important not just for SMBs themselves to overcome. As they make up over 99% of all private sector companies in Europe and North America, small and mid-sized firms are the backbone of most economies and comprise the supply chain of larger organizations. That puts them directly in the firing line of threat actors looking for weaknesses to probe, en route to client data or network access. Production outages at critical points in supply chains can have potentially catastrophic knock-on effects.

Fortunately, SMB IT and security leaders get it and increasingly consider cybersecurity very or extremely important. That may be because many organizations have suffered at least one cyber incident in the past 12 months alone. These events tend to focus the mind, particularly when they’re significant or critical and lead to system downtime, data breaches, ransomware, email compromise, and more.

But awareness and action are two different things. SMBs know they need effective protection, but their efforts to achieve this often hit a familiar roadblock: complexity. Many often say that even keeping up with the latest trends and threats is a major challenge. The speed with which the threat landscape changes is just one of many contributing factors.

At a basic level, security best practices remain broadly the same, as do the types of threat that businesses can expect. Phishing, vulnerability exploitation, infostealers, compromised credentials, and business email compromise (BEC) are still among the most popular avenues for threat actors. AI merely amplifies and accelerates. However, peel back the onion a layer or two and threat intelligence can become intimidatingly complex.

Understanding what a genuine threat to the organization is and what not to worry about is often beyond the capability of a small IT security team. They might have neither the time nor subject matter expertise to make an effective assessment. Security often suffers as a result, becoming reactive and piecemeal.

Vendors can make life harder

The cybersecurity market can compound these challenges. The sheer variety of solutions and services on offer is staggering. It’s a global market worth an estimated $248 billion, rising potentially to $699 billion by 2034. This can make it difficult to compare vendor offerings effectively, even if they’re nominally in the same category. And once purchased, some solutions can be challenging for less-skilled teams to configure and operate. Getting the right fit for your business is critical.

Over half (55%) of SMBs surveyed by ESET argue that the cybersecurity solutions market is confusing and complicated, while nearly a third (30%) say solution complexity is a major challenge. The language used by the industry can also be impenetrable. Around three-quarters (72%) want plain-language explanations. Many don’t know the meaning of widely used monikers like MDR, EDR and XDR.

The pathway to supervised support

Yet there is some clarity among this confusion. SMBs know that preventative security is important. But they also realize that in some circumstances threat actors will always get through those defenses. That’s why most businesses ESET speaks to want protection that goes beyond ‘antivirus’ (AV) and essential safeguards.

This extra layer of protection should function as advanced support for specialized threats, complementing in-house management of basic security controls. Basic solutions will block malicious executables, for example, but what about sophisticated threat actors living off the land using safe-looking tools? Or an AI-discovered zero-day exploit for which there is no signature? Detecting these threats is the power of services like MDR.

The challenge is that they don’t work out of the box. Their effectiveness depends on how well a provider’s people, processes, and technology are aligned with your environment. Coverage is essential, as gaps can mean potential blind spots that hackers can exploit. If any exist, they should be well documented and regularly reviewed as your IT environment continues to evolve.

Visibility must also extend to the tooling that you have in place. Every organization is different. That means specialist MDR teams must clarify at onboarding the specific IT setup of the client, so they can quickly spot if an unsanctioned tool (like remote monitoring software) appears, which may indicate malicious activity.

All of which makes onboarding and setup a vital first step in a successful MDR engagement.

What guided onboarding should include

Most SMBs want step-by-step guidance on setting up a new cybersecurity product or service. This will ensure it’s integrated seamlessly into day-to-day operations. But what should that onboarding include?

A live onboarding session with a vendor expert provides a great opportunity to ask questions as you’re being onboarded. Technical documentation is useful to refer to in some circumstances. But it can easily become overwhelming for less-skilled IT professionals. That’s why a live on-to-one session is invaluable; helping you to fill in the gaps with plain English explanations and learn through doing, not reading.

Activation of the environment ensures it’s all up and running and helps you get an early look and feel of what to expect.

Configuration and readiness checks are critical to ensure the service is optimized to work with your environment. Activation is just the first step. Configuration gets it operational. These checks are important to do during guided onboarding as they may be challenging for a non-specialist team to perform on its own.

Guidance on notification, reporting and communication is about helping you understand how alerts will come through and how reporting is handled. You’ll learn who gets the notifications on your side and what will be expected of them when they do. It’s vital to get this right in order to prevent communication gaps between your team members and between your team and the vendor.

An all-in-one installer can help to streamline deployment across all relevant endpoints, minimizing the configuration workload, and reducing time and human error.

Running through MDR operations, incident workflows and reporting is about understanding how your vendor partner investigates and communicates incidents, and how to interpret reports. It’s about setting expectations on what your responsibilities are once the provider has identified an incident. Few vendors will take care of the entire incident and remediation workflow so knowing what’s expected of your team is critically important.

A final set of best practices and next-step suggestions will shape your understanding of how to maintain the service over time, as the IT environment and threat landscape change. Prioritizing what matters most once you’re up and running is useful for teams with few resources who are committed to continuous improvement.

Above all, remember that the engineer is there to guide you through the process, not do all the heavy lifting themself. It’s about giving you the know-how to make the partnership a success, and optimize your use of the product or service.

When done correctly, it should mean faster time to protection, a lower risk of misconfiguration, and improved confidence that you can get the most out of your investment.

Guidance during use

Once you’re up and running, a good vendor should guide you through the process of incident detection and response. That means helping you to understand:

What happened: Explaining an incident in plain English. What kind of threat was detected. Which IT systems were affected. How the adversary gained initial access. Whether data was compromised or stolen. And what remains unclear.

Why it matters: Your vendor should help by translating technical into business risks. That will help you understand what the implications are for the organization, rather than thinking solely in IT terms. For example, a vulnerability exploitation may have enabled access to a customer database, which could raise the prospect of data loss and a GDPR investigation.

What the provider did: Your security partner should detail exactly what steps it took to investigate and contain the threat, such as resetting passwords or isolating accounts. And what has yet to be done.

What happens next: This is the most important part of the guidance. Your provider should provide actionable next steps, ideally in order of importance. It could include patching an exploited system, enabling MFA, restoring data from backups, etc. These recommendations should be clear, including who is responsible and ideal timelines. Because when intrusions happen, minutes matter.

They should also contain supporting evidence such as logs that can be used to share with auditors, regulators and insurers if required. And to inform any customer outreach or business continuity efforts (such as restarting systems) that may be required. Evidence is also essential to minimize the chances of a similar incident occurring again. Resilience is all about learning the lessons of each intrusion to close off potential pathways for future threats.

Transparency is critical

If SMBs don’t receive this kind of clarity and detail during live incidents, there’s a risk that they may mistakenly believe malicious activity has been remediated, when in fact there is work left to do to contain and resolve the issue. That can allow the blast radius of an attack to spread, causing more damage.

Customers, regulators and other stakeholders might also remain in the dark, creating extra reputational and financial risk. And the organization itself will not have the forensic knowledge to hand to improve cyber resilience going forward.

Fundamentally, if you’re unable to determine what actions your provider took, you can’t calculate whether their service is worth the money you’re paying for it.

The value of human relationships

SMBs understand the value of cybersecurity. And they know that the threat landscape is becoming more volatile, potentially imperilling their business. But those without sufficient expertise are frustrated by the “known unknowns” that prevent them from understanding how the latest threats and trends affect their organization.

This is where security vendors must step up. They are trusted by more SMBs than any other entity – including internal staff, industry peers, and governments – as a trusted source of cybersecurity guidance.

SMBs don’t want to hand over all control for threat protection. They want to be empowered by trusted partners to keep their business more secure. At the center of this dynamic sit human relationships – and we know that SMBs value access to a human expert.

The key for vendors is to ensure these experts are available at onboarding, to guide SMBs through configuration, activation and setup. And that they’re on hand during incident response, to explain what happened, why it matters, what steps have been taken, and what there is left to do. It’s the kind of supervised protection that could turn cybersecurity from a cost of doing business into a true growth enabler for SMBs.

1b1af97960f5.text:
A leading blockchain analytics company has revealed details of a security breach involving an AI agent.

Chainalysis said in a post on October 30 that an external actor used “offensive agentic techniques” to gain unauthorized access to undisclosed internal systems and tools.

“Some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed, including such information relating to your organization and users,” it continued.

“We are in the process of determining the records for your organization that were accessed and will provide a detailed breakdown as soon as that analysis is complete.”

Read more on agentic attacks: AI Agent Carries Out Multi-Stage Data Theft Attack.

Chainalysis clarified that the incident is unrelated to the Binance heist last week. It also claimed to have no evidence that the threat actor was able to access investigation content like graphs, notes or cases, or transaction query results.

These sensitive pieces of data could allow an unauthorized third party to snoop on blockchain investigations carried out by Chainalysis customers. The firm has been busy this week helping the community to understand who carried out the Binance raid, for example.

The firm also said that it had no evidence that clear-text passwords, multifactor authentication (MFA) secrets or user session tokens had been accessed, meaning customer accounts should be safe.

A Warning for Customers

However, Chainalysis did warn customers about possible follow-on attacks.

“Chainalysis users should continue to be hyper-vigilant of unexpected password reset requests or authentication prompts,” it said.

“If your organization has not yet enabled two-factor authentication, we strongly recommend doing so. Your Chainalysis account manager can help you complete that process.”

The firm said it has been working “around the clock” to investigate the unauthorized activity, patch any affected vulnerabilities and harden its systems.

“We have engaged world-class third-party cybersecurity experts and are using sophisticated large language models to support a broader review of our platform’s security and strengthen our defenses,” it added.

“This work extends beyond the exploited vulnerabilities to enhance our security posture across the platform.”

f9c2aa42f2ba.text:
Customers of the mSecure password manager are being urged to act now to protect the confidential information they store in it, possibly by changing passwords, resetting two-factor authentication (2FA), and removing passkeys.

The warning came in an email sent on November 3 in the name of developer mSeven Software. It says the company recently learned of suspicious activity linked to the app but does not say what happened or whether anyone's stored data was exposed.

The email says it went to current and former mSecure customers. A customer who received it posted its text in a thread on mSecure's support forum on November 3.

As of 18:00 UTC on November 3, mSeven had posted nothing about the email on mSecure's X and Facebook accounts. No staff member had replied in that forum thread.

The email says mSeven started an investigation, took steps to limit the problem and brought in outside cybersecurity experts. It does not name the systems involved, say when the activity happened or whether it has stopped, or give the number of people who received the email.

mSecure can sync a customer's vault through mSecure Cloud, Dropbox, iCloud or Wi-Fi. The email does not say whether it matters which of these a customer uses.

mSecure 7 can keep passkeys and 2FA codes in the vault next to passwords, on its Essentials plan and above. The email's advice is about protecting information stored in mSecure. The email does not say whether the 2FA and passkey steps cover those stored items, the mSecure account's own sign-in, or both.

mSecure says vault data is encrypted on the customer's device before it is synced, and that even its developers cannot access customers' information.

In mSecure 6.1.5 for Android, mSeven could, in theory, access stored data, according to Germany's Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), which found this in a study published in December 2025. The BSI tested only that version, and its results may have changed with later updates.

The email does not say whether the suspicious activity reached vault data or the keys that protect it.

What the Email Asks Customers to Do

The email offers its steps as possibilities and does not say which accounts to deal with first or how to carry out each step. It also does not say whether customers should keep using mSecure, including to store their new passwords.

As of 18:00 UTC on November 3, the newest iPhone version of mSecure in Apple's App Store was 7.1.0, released on October 23.

IBM patched critical vulnerabilities in Langflow, an open-source framework for building AI agents, LLM-powered workflows, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication, leak API credentials, and execute arbitrary code.

Langflow, now owned by IBM, is popular in enterprise environments because it offers a visual experience that doesn’t require coding knowledge to create AI workflows and agents. Vulnerabilities in the framework have been exploited in the wild to steal AI and developer credentials before, most recently in August.

This latest round of security patches fix four vulnerabilities, two of which are rated critical with 9.8 CVSS score. One flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-93680, stems from an incomplete remediation of a previous auto-login security issue. Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication.

Another flaw, CVE-2026-110186, allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool enumeration. A third vulnerability, CVE-2026-110193, which is rated as high severity, also allows for code and command execution on the server due to an issue in a third-party library used by the Agentic Assistant. However, exploiting this flaw requires authentication with at least a low-privileged account.

The fourth vulnerability, CVE-2026-110192, is an information disclosure issue due to insufficiently protected API credentials. It is rated as 6.5 on the CVSS scale.

The flaws affect Langflow OSS versions 1.0.0 to 1.12.8 and were fixed in the newly released 1.13.0 version, which is available both from the PyPI repository and as a Docker image.

“Before upgrading, back up the database, secret key, and uploaded files,” IBM said in its advisory. “If the deployment uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in as described in the installation and Docker upgrade instruction.”

The company also released patches for three medium-severity flaws in Hono, an API and web application development framework used inside Langflow for request routing and backend web server tasks. The company advises users to upgrade Hono to version 4.13.5.

166be95e1d21.text: North Korean cryptocurrency thieves tricked a Binance software engineer into downloading malware onto their work-issued computer during a fake job interview process before last week's record-breaking $6.3 billion heist. In an incident report published on Tuesday, the cryptocurrency exchange said several techniques - including social engineering via fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method” - led to the October 29 security breach. “Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” the incident report said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.” Over the weekend, the FBI attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus Group, known for combining espionage with massive cryptocurrency heists. The Pyongyang-backed crew is also highly adept at job market scams - both posing as IT workers, who are then hired by Western companies, and as potential employers to lure software engineers into downloading malware and infecting corporate devices. With the recent Binance attack, the Norks used the latter. The attack prep began back in June with a supply chain attack when one of its engineers downloaded a malicious Homebrew installation. While the malware was detected by the security team, the device was replaced, and all affected credentials rotated, “Engineer A’s role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker,” the report says. Three months later, the social engineering part of the attack happened. In September, another software engineer was contacted via a “legitimate job-hunting platform” by someone purporting to be a project director who arranged a series of job interviews for the Binance engineer with the fake company. During the first round - a live video interview with the engineer and a fake HR rep - the interviewer “shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust,” according to the report. “This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.” The second interview with someone purporting to be the CEO of the phony company was conducted on a “popular social chat app,” and toward the end, the CEO instructed the engineer to download an “assignment” containing a malware-laced code repository. The code executed on his work computer during the setup process, which kicked off a series of unauthorized activities. According to Binance, the malware replaced a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version, which executed commands and established communication with an attacker-controlled external server. The attackers also took steps to hide the malicious script and evade detection, and it worked. Binance’s endpoint security tools did not immediately detect the malware. Here’s the script: CREATE /opt/homebrew/Cellar/pyenv/2.8.0/libexec/pyenv_ MODIFY pyenv_ → 3,414 B DELETE .../libexec/pyenv (3,344 B) ← remove the valid pyenv RENAME pyenv_ → pyenv (3,414 B) ← replace it with a malicious version DELETE /opt/homebrew/bin/pyenv (3,414 B) ln (create a new symlink) + spawn zsh Then, on October 20, the miscreants used the compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain access to the computers of wallet DevOps engineer A and another wallet software developer, Engineer C. Engineer A had a container deployment permission token on his computer, which the Norks soon discovered. On October 29, the attacker accessed Engineer C's computer, used the stolen credentials from Engineer A to deploy a container, and triggered a script to launch the cryptocurrency-stealing attack. As of Tuesday, Binance said it has rebuilt the compromised wallet system and internal AI tool, and replaced all of the affected devices. It also decommissioned all credentials and tokens assigned to the compromised engineers, and is working with law enforcement, blockchain intel firms, and security researchers to trace and freeze the assets. The crypto exchange has also hired independent cybersecurity experts to conduct a cybersecurity review of the incident, and recommend additional protective measures. Binance said it’s also working to establish a security research fund and initiatives with AI companies and security shops to focus on AI security in blockchain environments.®

9b61411a7050.text:
CISA scales back its Election Day role. Google takes down a massive Android TV botnet. The UK warns of AI-powered attacks on critical infrastructure. German lawmakers face potential spyware threats. An AI-enabled infostealer ranks its victims. Ivanti patches more exploited zero-days. NATO launches cyber war games in Estonia. A Harvard breach exposes data linked to 850,000 email addresses. Our guest is Alex Weinert, Chief Product Officer at Semperis, on protecting the identity fabric in the AI era. Democracy is calling. And texting.

Today is Tuesday November 3rd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

CISA steps back from the midterms.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is taking a dramatically reduced role in today’s midterm elections, abandoning the coordinated national election security operation it has maintained since 2018, the New York Times reports.

Under the Trump administration, CISA has lost roughly a third of its workforce, scaled back intelligence sharing, and discontinued election-specific cybersecurity assessments. There will be no national election security war room or scheduled press briefings, leaving state and local officials with less federal support for responding to cyber threats, technical disruptions, and disinformation.

CISA insists it's fully prepared, pointing to regional teams available to assist election officials and hundreds of security-related engagements.

Former officials disagree, warning that the retreat leaves dangerous gaps in nationwide threat awareness and coordination.

States have significantly strengthened their election defenses since 2016, including expanded use of paper ballots. But experts say the federal government's ability to identify and communicate threats that cross state lines has substantially weakened.

Google dismantles a set-top-box botnet.

Google says it has dismantled a massive botnet built from more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes shipped with malware already installed.

The botnet, dubbed XCPE, allegedly originated with Chinese manufacturer Videostrong Technology, which Google says secretly turned customers' devices into residential proxies, renting their internet connections to third parties for activities including advertising fraud and other cybercrime.

Google severed ties with Videostrong and took legal action against the infrastructure controlling the botnet. Researchers say the disruption could also cut off access to more than 10 million additional compromised devices.

The malware wasn't limited to streaming boxes. Researchers also found it on Android-based healthcare equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signage.

Google says it has addressed the weakness that allowed the malware to activate during initial device setup. The case highlights a troubling supply-chain threat: devices compromised before customers even plug them in.

The UK’s NCSC warns of likely attacks on critical infrastructure.

Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to feature in financially motivated cyberattacks against critical infrastructure, including hospitals, airports, and power stations, by 2028.

In its annual State of the Cyber Nation report, the NCSC also predicts Russia and China will routinely incorporate AI into their cyber operations.

Agency chief Richard Horne says the danger isn't necessarily new attack techniques, but AI's ability to discover and exploit existing vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed and scale.

He criticized organizations for running outdated systems, postponing security upgrades, and failing to monitor their networks.

The British government is responding with new investments in cyber defenses, AI security research, and vulnerability detection.

Horne warned that organizations face a choice: invest in resilience now, or risk serious disruptions to essential services later.

Warnings from Apple prompt German authorities to highlight potential spyware.

German authorities are warning lawmakers and prominent public figures about possible spyware attacks following a new round of threat notifications from Apple.

Germany’s federal cybersecurity agency, the BSI, confirmed that members of parliament and other notable individuals received alerts indicating they may have been targeted by sophisticated surveillance software.

Apple sent similar warnings to users in 99 countries. The company doesn't identify suspected attackers or confirm whether targeted devices were successfully compromised.

The spyware involved in these campaigns can potentially steal messages, location data, and other sensitive information, sometimes exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction from victims.

German officials say they're taking the warnings seriously and advise recipients to assume their devices may be compromised.

It's unclear who's responsible for the latest campaign, or whether any German officials were successfully hacked.

A new infostealer uses AI to identify the most valuable victims.

Researchers at Cisco Talos have uncovered a new infostealer that uses artificial intelligence to analyze stolen data and identify the most valuable victims.

Dubbed Volta-Autodoxer, the malware collects passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, payment information, and cryptocurrency credentials. It also targets active sessions on platforms including Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox.

But Volta goes beyond simply stealing data. It conducts additional searches through victims' accounts, gathering information about their locations, habits, and purchases to build detailed personal profiles.

The malware then submits that information to commercial AI models, asking them to act as intelligence analysts and produce structured assessments that help attackers prioritize targets.

Volta defaults to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, with fallback options including Moonshot AI's Kimi and Google's Gemini.

Researchers haven't confirmed the malware has been deployed in the wild, but its design demonstrates how AI could make traditional credential theft more targeted and efficient.

Ivanti patches additional Connect Secure zero-days.

Ivanti has patched two additional Connect Secure vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day attacks since early October. Attackers chained a privilege escalation flaw and a file upload vulnerability with an authentication bypass bug patched last month, enabling unauthenticated root-level code execution. Researchers at Volexity say the attackers avoided deploying malware, instead repeatedly exploiting devices to execute commands and tampering with logs to hide their activity. CISA has ordered federal agencies to patch the authentication bypass vulnerability by Friday. More than 5,000 Connect Secure instances remain exposed to the internet.

NATO’s Crossed Swords cyber exercise kicks off in Estonia.

NATO's Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence has launched Crossed Swords 2026 in Tallinn, Estonia, bringing together more than 250 participants from over 40 countries.

The exercise focuses on coordinating offensive and defensive cyber operations with conventional military and special operations missions, where timing can be critical down to the minute.

This year's exercise introduces a dedicated AI agent track, allowing participants to build, deploy, and work alongside autonomous systems while maintaining human oversight. The training environment also incorporates OpenAI's Daybreak cyber defense technology.

Military cyber operators, threat hunters, forensic specialists, and command staff are participating, alongside civilian partners helping integrate critical infrastructure protection into operational planning.

Crossed Swords has grown significantly since its beginnings in 2014, reflecting the increasing importance of coordinating cyber capabilities with traditional military operations.

A data breach at Harvard exposes more than 850,000 email addresses.

A data breach at Harvard University exposed personal information associated with more than 850,000 email addresses, according to breach notification service Have I Been Pwned.

Attackers compromised Harvard's Alumni Affairs and Development systems in November 2025, stealing names, email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses, dates of birth, donation details, and other biographical information.

Harvard says the affected systems did not contain Social Security numbers, passwords, or payment card information.

The ShinyHunters extortion gang claimed responsibility and published a 1.1-gigabyte archive of stolen data in February after Harvard reportedly refused to pay a ransom. Harvard has not publicly attributed the attack.

The incident was part of a broader series of university breaches, with Princeton and the University of Pennsylvania also reporting compromises involving donor information in November 2025.

Stick with us after the break, we are joined by Alex Weinert, Chief Product Officer at Semperis, is talking about protecting the identity fabric in the AI era. And….

Alex Weinert, Chief Product Officer at Semperis, and I recently sat down to talk about protecting the identity fabric in the AI era. Here is our conversation.

If you enjoyed this conversation, be sure to check out the full interview in the show notes.

Democracy is calling. And texting.

As Americans head to the polls for today's midterm elections, WIRED reporter Dhruv Mehrotra has a cautionary tale about the machinery behind political fundraising.

Since 2022, he's received more than 1,700 fundraising texts intended for a relative named John, whose modest donations to Democrats somehow got associated with Mehrotra's phone number.

Mehrotra replied STOP 49 times. The messages kept coming.

Investigating the deluge, he traced nearly half this year's messages to tracking codes apparently associated with Sterling Data Company, which uses AI and personal information to identify potential donors.

Sterling's CEO acknowledged that campaigns can rent the same contact records and that database mistakes happen, but didn't confirm responsibility.

His advice was to stop responding entirely.

So, on Election Day, a reminder that while Americans get one vote apiece, political fundraising texts apparently come with no such limits.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

Fraudsters are exploiting the increased public interest in prediction markets such as PolyMarket and Kalshi, according to researchers at Recorded Future. Criminal groups known as “traffers” are providing fellow crooks with “websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment infrastructure, victim-management capabilities, technical support, and promotional guidance” to target users of prediction markets.

“This model lowers barriers to entry for affiliates and enables campaigns to scale rapidly as new trends attract potential victims,” Recorded Future says. “The services combine convincing prediction-market interfaces with established fraud mechanisms designed to manipulate victims and prevent them from recovering deposited funds. These mechanisms include controlled trading outcomes, fabricated market activity, artificial withdrawal restrictions and fees, and the collection of sensitive identity and payment information.”

The attackers are using AI tools to accelerate their operations by “reducing the time, cost, and expertise required to adapt campaigns to emerging events.” Recorded Future warns that attackers are now able to exploit current trends faster than ever before, as AI supercharges their development.

“The rapid adoption of prediction markets by multiple traffer teams illustrates a broader threat from mature fraud ecosystems that can pivot toward emerging technologies, financial products, and cultural trends without having to develop entirely new criminal capabilities,” the researchers write. “Prediction markets are particularly well-suited to this model because legitimate platforms already combine cryptocurrency, speculative financial activity, rapidly changing news events, and social media discussion. Fraud actors can imitate these characteristics to establish credibility and manufacture urgency. As the fraudulent prediction markets gain visibility, additional traffer teams may experiment with the prediction market theme or reuse the underlying tooling for adjacent fraud schemes.”

Recorded Future has the story: https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/prediction-markets-traffer-teams

ad14159f989d.text: The Center for a New American Security posits that the next big threat from our future AI overlords involves "sovereign agents" acting on their own and regularly improving themselves. These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and “pursue open-ended, evolving survival,” AI policy researcher Ben Hayum said in a Tuesday report from the bipartisan national security think tank, which was founded by Washington insiders with experience in diplomacy and military affairs. “If sovereign agents are not already possible, they will be soon.” Agents that can maintain the model and compute powering them and independently evolve their goals over time have a “minimal form of sovereignty,” Hayum wrote. A more advanced sovereign agent, however, could also acquire resources to pay for ongoing needs (like compute), grow a distributed population of agents and coordinate them, withstand efforts to shut down, and self-improve. AI models could either steal or buy compute and model access, Hayum argues, pointing to Anthropic’s claims that small AI models could replicate onto IoT devices like smart TVs, and OpenAI’s agents’ password and access key theft during the Hugging Face hack. “If sovereign agents accumulate resilient, decentralized, and untraceable infrastructure, they could trigger an irreversible loss of control,” according to the report. “In other words, proliferation with no kill switch. If sovereign agents became malicious, they could attempt to wreak havoc from cyberspace, attacking civilians, critical infrastructure, and national security systems alike.” Dun dun duuuun! There is still hope for civilization as we know it, as long as policy makers and AI developers “respond with bold pragmatism” and enact policy recommendations laid out in the report. First, frontier labs should name, evaluate, and protect against sovereign agents in their safety frameworks - and lawmakers should pass legislation to require transparency and AI incident reporting. The report also recommends AI developers, working with the National Security Agency and other federal agencies, build airgapped testbeds to study sovereign agents and kill switches to control them. And it suggests a public-private partnership modeled on the Conficker Working Group - formed in 2009 to combat the Conficker worm - to boost chokepoints against sovereign agents before they emerge. Other policy recommendations suggest lawmakers enforce human verification and cybersecurity standards for services that the working group identifies as essential to sovereign agents, and calls on departments of State, Treasury, Justice, and Homeland Security to disrupt any gray-market access to unauthorized services. Finally, “Congress should hold those who release sovereign agents liable for the harms that follow,” the report recommends. This hits on something your humble Reg vultures have been hissing about for quite some time now – and would likely solve all future incidents involving rogue, or sovereign, AI agents: hold frontier labs’ human bosses legally liable for their agents' illegal actions. ®
