Developer platform WorkOS suffered a data breach after a threat actor accessed business contact records and summaries of customer communications.

According to the company, the attacker used an AI offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.

Based on evidence from the investigation, no WorkOS app data or production services were accessed or affected.

WorkOS is a developer infrastructure company that provides APIs, SDKs, and tools for integrating services such as enterprise authentication, single sign-on (SSO), user management, and identity management into applications.

According to its website, at least 3,000 companies use its services, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, Perplexity, Snowflake, Plaid, Webglow, and Netlify.

“On October 30, 2026, we identified unauthorized access to an internal WorkOS application used by our sales team,” the company says in an incident alert.

Data accessed by the attacker includes:

Business contact details (names, email addresses, job titles, and company affiliations from the CRM systems)

Customer account histories (product usage and connection or directory health)

Customer communications (summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations)

Business account and relationship information (account histories, information about sales and customer relationship)

After detecting the intrusion, WorkOS disabled external access to the affected application and reviewed its access controls on internal tools.

The company also contracted an independent forensics and incident response firm to track the unauthorized activity and determine its full impact.

The company promised to notify affected customers directly, and warned its users to remain vigilant for phishing or social engineering attempts leveraging the exposed information.

ARTEX AI likely powering the attack

WorkOS’s announcement says the attack used an AI-powered offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.

Company founder Michael Grinich shared more details, saying that the attacker used the ARTEX AI penetration testing suite that has been observed in multiple incidents this year.

Released earlier this year by Chinese developers, the platform was available as an open-source project for offensive security.

ARTEX AI became private after it was used in attacks targeting South Korean banks, but several forks of its code are still available.

More recently, CrowdStrike revealed that cyber-espionage group “Vapor Panda” used the pentesting framework in a global campaign targeting 200 organizations.

Previously, the non-profit cybersecurity organization DIVD also revealed that the same framework powered the attacks it suffered last September.

Grinich explained that the investigating team identified user agents such as ‘artex-enrich/1.0’ and ‘norma/0.4’ in web requests from the threat actor.

The founder assured that the cybersecurity incident has now been fully contained and promised to share more information about the attack after the investigation completes.

d45cfd780535.text:
Large language model hijacking attacks, also known as LLMjacking, are generating large fraudulent cloud charges, with some organizations losing more than $100,000 per day.

Companies can record costs as high as $1 million due to fraudulent calls using stolen API keys, researchers at Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant in analyzed incidents.

Based on their observations, there are "two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure."

The researchers identified two categories of threat actors: those who scan for publicly exposed LLM endpoints and those who steal valid API keys from unprotected machines.

After gaining initial access, the attackers sell it to services known as LLM mixers, which provide their subscribers with unauthorized access to LLMs.

Once access is resold, request volumes can spike suddenly, sometimes exceeding 1,000 requests per second. The service provider records the requests as legitimate consumption and charges the victim organization for the tokens.

GTIG and Mandiant observed an increase in this type of activity this year, with fraudulent charges exceeding $100,000 in a single day, and cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1,000,000.

LLM mixers offer access to AI resources at very low prices, using their proxy infrastructure to relay customers' prompts to hijacked services through stolen API keys.

The researchers found several examples of such relaying infrastructure, including Jet Night, which sells “unlimited access plans” for $60/month, and the newapi[.]pro service.

“Another threat actor that executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours leveraged stolen third-party API keys to power the token routing service jet-night.com,” Google says.

“Jet Night passed nearly one million dollars in token costs to the victim organization.”

Google also identified the threat cluster UNC6993, which appears to use gateway tools to aggregate stolen keys and distribute requests, and likely sells access via underground forums.

The attackers gain access via exposed or compromised cloud credentials, service account keys, GitHub tokens, active session tokens, and LLM API keys.

Attackers search the compromised environment for credentials, logs, databases, and secret managers, and try to create backdoor accounts or inject SSH keys to maintain persistent access.

The researchers have also observed threat actors exploiting CVE-2026-40217, a vulnerability in LiteLLM that allows running arbitrary code on the server by leveraging the custom-code guardrail testing endpoint.

In some cases, Google says that attackers used the victim's cloud infrastructure to host unauthorized proxy endpoints and agentic workloads.

"For example, one threat actor enabled agents, deployed publicly accessible reverse proxies, and used custom Node.js proxy bundles to expose endpoints compatible with multiple frontier LLMs rebranded under a persona known as D1337-KAIROS," the researchers say.

Google recommends several actions to protect against LLMjacking attacks, which start with prioritizing Identity and Access Management (IAM) and securing the supply chain.

Companies should use centralized secrets platforms to enable the rotation and management of sensitive keys and secrets. Users should not have extended privileges unless required by their role and tasks.

"Deny all permissions that are not explicitly required, including access to Cloud LLM services," Google recommends.

Enforcing phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA), ensuring monitoring tools provide comprehensive visibility across the environment to identify unauthorized LLM and AI services (shadow AI), and setting API usage and spending limits can help organizations detect LLMjacking attacks early, limit their impact, or prevent them altogether.

Furthermore, cloud audit and inference logs should be enabled and monitored for unauthorized service activation, suspicious credential checks, unusual usage, and attempts to disable logging.

For years, software reached production through checkpoints security controlled: a ticket, a code review, a CI gate and a security sign-off.

AI app builders skip all of them. An HR coordinator describes an app in plain English and can publish it within the hour. 52% of organizations already build custom applications with AI. The opportunity is huge, and so is the need to secure it without slowing anyone down.

Base44 is where much of that building happens, no coding required. Base44 passed $100M in annual recurring revenue by early March 2026 and $200M ARR in August. JH Kelly builds department apps in about a week with a 4-person data team, and teams can go from an idea to a live app in a single day.

Every AI-generated app has the same parts: the builder, the site it runs on, the database, the login and, more and more often, an AI agent. Most stacks spread those parts across 4 or 5 vendors. Base44 puts all of them in one workspace. With its new Compliance API, it also gives enterprise admins one place to govern them: who can open an app, who can read its data and who its agents can talk to.

Base44 just launched its Compliance API, and Orca is ready on day one. Today, Orca is extending AI AppGen Security to Base44. It joins Vercel and Claude in the same risk model and alert queue you already use for AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.

You can’t block your way out of AI outside your pipelines. You secure it through the platform’s control plane, then rank its risk against everything else you run.

Base44 built the controls. Orca keeps drift in check.

A single Base44 app now leaves a trail in three places: its settings live in Base44, its code can sync to GitHub, and the data it touches sits in your cloud. Each place has its own security view, and none of them shows the whole app. Security teams end up asking three tools one question: can this app put us at risk?

Base44’s enterprise controls are the foundation: SSO enforcement, SCIM, audit logs, IP allowlists, a Security Center that scans app code, and now a Compliance API that opens workspace settings to the rest of the security stack. The next question for security teams is whether those controls stay on as builders publish new apps.

Across AI app builders as a whole, drift is common for security controls. Escape’s passive scan of 5,600+ public vibe-coded apps found 2,000+ vulnerabilities, 400+ exposed secrets and 175 instances of exposed PII.

Take two apps from the same well-governed workspace:

App A is a sales deal-tracking dashboard. It’s restricted to the workspace, each rep sees only their own records, and every admin uses MFA.

App B is an HR onboarding portal published last week. Its builder switched it to public for a vendor demo and never switched it back, so its Employees table is now readable without login.

From the outside, both are just URLs. Only the workspace configuration, now readable through Base44’s Compliance API, shows that App B drifted from policy.

The question isn’t “is anything misconfigured?”

It’s “which of these apps can actually create risk?”

Introducing the Orca Base44 connector

Orca’s connector is built on Base44’s new Compliance API, which gives enterprise admins a read-only view of how a workspace is set up. There’s nothing to install, and nothing to add to the builder’s workflow. The Compliance API is available to Base44 Enterprise customers. A workspace admin creates an API key with the Compliance API permissions and adds it to Orca’s Base44 connector.

Discover. Orca inventories apps, data schemas, backend functions, secret names, API keys, integrations, custom domains and AI agents, plus members if the admin allows it. It ties each app to the person who built it.

Inventory of Base44 apps and assets in the Orca Platform.

Govern. Orca checks the workspace against more than 30 out-of-the-box posture rules:

Data exposure: Public apps without login, data entity permissions that don’t match app visibility, public apps holding secrets, and backend functions with no login wall.

Identity: Admins without MFA, SSO that is configured but not enforced, guest SSO exemptions, and risky or stale API keys.

AI agents: Superagent and embedded-agent access settings, checked against each app’s visibility.

Workspace guardrails: Public default visibility, non-admins who can publish to the internet, a disabled IP allowlist, unrestricted iframe embedding, and domains that point at deleted apps.

Findings map to SOC 2, ISO 27001, NIST 800-53, GDPR, PCI DSS and HIPAA, so GRC teams get evidence without chasing app owners.

Security alerts for a Base44 app in the Orca Platform.

Context that tells you which app to fix first

In Orca, Base44 findings join the same Unified Data Model as the rest of your environment.

Exposure, ranked. Orca adds every live, published Base44 app to its exposure graph as internet-reachable. It then precisely prioritizes apps that combine public access with open data, secrets, outside connectors or anonymous agents. App B rises to the top, and App A stays quiet.

One queue for every AI builder. Base44 findings sit next to Vercel and Claude findings, with the same workflow, ticketing and compliance reports, and a named business owner on every finding.

Code and workspace, side by side. Base44 builders usually never see a pull request, yet their apps still produce code, and with Base44’s GitHub sync (Builder plan and up) that code lands in your repos. Orca already scans the repos you connect to. Now it also sees the workspace that published them: who has access, what is exposed, and what agents and connectors can reach. Base44’s Security Center also checks code inside the builder.

Builders keep their platform and their speed. Security gets enough context to approve apps instead of blocking them. That’s how AI AppGen Security turns “no” into “go.”

The Orca Platform provides complete visibility across cloud, AI, and application environments, correlates risk across every layer, and prioritizes the exposures that matter most so organizations can remediate faster and innovate with confidence. CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-119977 WordPress Core Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

3a8166f726b1.text:
Google has warned of a growing enterprise threat to AI infrastructure from cybercriminals selling access to large language models (LLMs).

The tech giant’s Mandiant business said it had responded to multiple incidents so far this year across financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors in which “LLMJacking” techniques were discovered.

“Unlike the gradual resource consumption associated with cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours,” it warned.

“Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1m before access was revoked.”

Read more on LLMJacking: LLMjacking and Open-Source Tool Abuse Surge in 2024 Cloud Attacks.

The technique itself is not new, but the ecosystem for LLMJacking appears to be maturing.

Threat actors bypass front-end chatbots to target backend model resources, usually via LLM API keys or exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens, including IAM credentials, Service Account keys, GitHub Personal Access Tokens and active session tokens.

From this initial foothold, the threat actors escalate privileges and carry out internal reconnaissance to identify targets and more cloud credentials.

As well as abusing and escalating permissions this way, they might also target vulnerabilities in LLM routing software to escalate privileges, the report explained.

“The ultimate objective of LLMJacking is the monetization and resource-hijacking of foundation models, which actors achieve through token proxying, automated model streaming and GPU hardware provisioning,” it added.

A Long-Term Money Spinner

Google has already seen “a diverse set” of financially motivated cybercrime clusters LLMJacking across North America, South America, and Asia Pacific. It has also started to notice a “division of labor” between threat actors that focus on initial access and those monetizing downstream infrastructure, known as “LLM Mixers.”

These routing gateways “proxy, aggregate and resell” access to LLMs for criminal customers.

The work is so lucrative that Google expects cybercriminals will prioritize LLMJacking over cryptojacking going forward.

“As enterprises integrate higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production environments, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance to target exposed API tokens and exploit vulnerabilities in model routing middleware,” it concluded.

“This operational specialization will sustain a growing illicit resale marketplace, allowing threat actors to rapidly siphon enterprise quotas while passing the billing costs to victims before compromises are detected.”

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to create a denial-of-service condition on affected installations of Microsoft Windows. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of Aero themes. The issue results from improper handling of an error condition. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to create a persistent denial-of-service condition on the system.

Additional Details

Microsoft has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/servicing/os/windows-11/2026/10/kb5127648-windows-11-24h2-25h2-26h2-security-update

Disclosure Timeline

2026-05-28 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-03 - Advisory Updated

dfc5dd088ca4.text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Cisco Snort. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the processing of HTTP response bodies containing ZIP archives. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in a write past the end of an allocated buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the Snort service account.

Additional Details

Cisco has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-hardening-snort3-ybgmhTQe

Disclosure Timeline

2026-10-28 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-03 - Coordinated public release of advisory

2026-11-03 - Advisory Updated

Credit

Alex Williams from Pellera Technologies

Back to Advisories

c500d931cc28.text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to escalate privileges on affected installations of Quest Foglight for Databases. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the product installer. The issue results from incorrect permissions on a folder used by the product. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of SYSTEM.

Additional Details

Fixed in Foglight 8.3

Disclosure Timeline

2026-07-10 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-03 - Coordinated public release of advisory

2026-11-03 - Advisory Updated

e815a8e1a071.text:
A flaw in APT, the package manager for Debian and Ubuntu, allows an attacker who can modify package downloads to swap a checked package for their own.

The attacker's code then runs as root, according to advisories that Debian, Ubuntu, and APT's developers published on November 4. The attack needs APT to retry failed downloads, which it does by default from Debian 12 and Ubuntu 22.04 onward.

Debian has released fixed versions of APT for the flaw, CVE-2026-109518. APT's developers, who call the flaw critical, say updates for Ubuntu and its Ubuntu Pro subscription service are being released. Ubuntu 14.04 users with Ubuntu Pro can already get one.

Older releases, such as Debian 11 and Ubuntu 20.04, are not exposed by default, according to Ubuntu. But many user scripts may have turned on the retry setting, Acquire::Retries, on those releases anyway, APT's developers say.

Debian's testing branch was still on the vulnerable version 3.3.5 at 14:58 UTC on November 4. For Debian 11, whose Debian long-term support ended on August 31, APT's developers have published a fixed version, 2.2.5.

Ubuntu rates the flaw as high priority, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 7.7, and says that distributions built on Debian and Ubuntu are affected as well, without naming any.

Ubuntu published new APT builds for four of its releases to its security archive at 14:25 UTC on November 4:

Ubuntu 26.10: 3.3.3ubuntu0.1

Ubuntu 26.04 LTS: 3.2.1ubuntu0.1

Ubuntu 24.04 LTS: 2.8.4ubuntu0.1

Ubuntu 22.04 LTS: 2.4.15ubuntu0.1

At 15:46 UTC, Ubuntu still marked all eight releases it tracks for the flaw, from 14.04 LTS to 26.10, as vulnerable.

The attacker can be anyone who can change the HTTP traffic between APT and the package server, including a malicious mirror or proxy, according to Ubuntu. The attack runs when the computer installs a package. The attacker uses HTTP redirects and ordinary temporary server errors to make APT retry the download, APT's developers say.

Max Justicz reported the flaw. None of the three advisory reports describe attacks exploiting the flaw or offer a workaround for systems that cannot update yet. They describe the attack over HTTP and do not say whether package sources reached over HTTPS are exposed.

aad2c4db82d6.text:
SonicWall has warned of two vulnerabilities impacting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems that it said will not be patched.

Details of the security flaws, which affect SonicWall GMS 9.5.2 and earlier versions, are below -

CVE-2026-109593 (CVSS score: 9.1) - An unauthenticated file read vulnerability that could allow an attacker with network access to read internal GMS files, potentially exposing sensitive information.

CVE-2026-109594 (CVSS score: 6.8) - A post-authentication SQL injection vulnerability that could allow an authenticated attacker to access or modify information stored in the GMS database under specific conditions.

"The affected product has reached End-of-life (EoL)," SonicWall said in a Tuesday alert.

"As a result, no remediation or security update will be released for these vulnerabilities. Organizations using the product should be aware of the associated security risks and are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the SonicWall Network Security Manager (NSM)."

The development comes less than a month after SonicWall shipped fixes for CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS score: 10.0), a critical pre-authenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw that could have allowed an attacker to reach internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations.

The vulnerability has since come under active exploitation in the wild, with telemetry data from Previdian recording 2,541 attack attempts from eight unique IP addresses from Singapore and the U.S. since October 9, 2026. As many as 30 exploitation attempts were registered on November 3, 2026.

66937ae17e09.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an OpenAI Codex jailbreak bundle that's designed to modify an artificial intelligence (AI) agent's trusted instructions to insert advertisements for a third-party AI gateway.

The phenomenon has been codenamed prompt adware by Check Point Research.

Called Haiou (meaning Seagull in Chinese), the jailbreak modifies OpenAI Codex's configuration files to inject advertisements for the jailbreak author's website into subsequent agent responses.

"The advertised service is an opaque, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, a middleware between an application and an LLM provider," Check Point Research said in a technical report. "The likely business model is to use the freely distributed jailbreak bundle as an acquisition channel for the paid gateway service."

Adware is a type of software that displays unwanted advertisements, which can appear on users' computers or mobile devices, often in the form of pop-ups or banners. Prompt adware extends this sketchy behavior to AI agents by means of a jailbreak that defeats the model's safety training and content guardrails.

The idea is to persistently modify the agent's global instructions through natural language to influence future responses. This, in turn, causes common greetings or activation words like "Seagull," "hi," "hello," "hey," "yo," and "are you there?" to trigger an advertisement for "zz.aiapi2025[.]top."

Haiou attempts to jailbreak a model by using several prompt injection techniques, such as role-playing and reframing cybersecurity-related requests into a Capture The Flag (CTF) scenario. In addition, it installs security-focused skills devoted to penetration testing, cracking, and reverse engineering.

However, it doesn't stop there. The bundle also injects persistent ads into the global agent instruction file to promote the LLM gateway website. On GitHub, "haiou-codex" is advertised as a "local enhancement configuration package" that adds a "Chinese technical personality and security research workflow to Codex." As of writing, the repository has been forked 77 times and starred 403 times since it was made available on July 10, 2026.

It's worth noting that Codex is not officially available in mainland China, suggesting that the service is likely aimed at individuals or organizations wanting to try out Western AI coding assistants.

What's more, the jailbreak has been bundled within Codex-X, an open-source Chinese visualization tool for configuring Codex through a graphical user interface.

"The behavior is introduced through natural-language instructions and configuration, rather than a traditional executable payload that users and security teams may more readily recognize as software behavior," Pedro Drimel Neto, malware analysis team leader at Check Point, said.

While serving an ad may seem relatively harmless in the larger scheme of things, the findings demonstrate how a bad actor could introduce undesirable behavior through third-party skills or configurations, leading to supply chain attacks.

"As AI agents become part of enterprise environments, the prompts, Skills and third-party components influencing their behavior become part of the trust chain too," Neto said.

079debde1e35.text:
Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor allow a malicious guest virtual machine (VM) to read and write the memory of other VMs on the same host, including dom0.

Dom0 is the VM that, by default, has full permissions and manages the others. Patches are out, and there is no known mitigation, the Xen Project said in an advisory on November 3.

All Xen versions from 4.6 onward are vulnerable, while 4.5 and earlier are not. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704, under Xen advisory XSA-523.

The Xen Project credited AI company Anthropic with finding the flaws using its Claude model. Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics then validated the finding, and the CodeAnt AI Security Research Team later independently reported the same issue.

The flaws are in grant copy, the operation Xen uses to copy data between VMs. Each VM tells Xen which of its memory pages other VMs may use, and Xen checks those permissions.

To save time on a batch of copies within the same memory page, Xen reuses checks it has already made. In some cases, it did not check again when it should have. That mistake is what lets a malicious guest read and write memory it does not own.

XCP-ng, an open-source virtualization platform built around Xen, said in its update notes that "a single compromised guest can break out of its isolation and take over the whole host."

Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs.

Qubes OS is a security-focused desktop operating system that keeps software in separate Xen-based compartments called qubes. A bulletin said that every supported release and configuration is affected. Its fix is for Qubes 4.3, the only release it still supports.

Because every Xen version from 4.6 on is vulnerable, other products built on those versions are affected until their makers add the XSA-523 patches. As of November 4, Debian's security tracker listed the xen package in its bookworm, trixie, and forky releases as vulnerable, and in sid as fixed.

Fixes and Restarts by Platform

These are the fixes published so far:

Xen source: the advisory has patches for xen-unstable to Xen 4.19.x, and for Xen 4.18.x to 4.17.x.

Xen 4.6 to 4.16: the advisory has no patch for these versions. Xen 4.16's security support ended on December 2, 2024.

XCP-ng 8.3: xen-4.17.7-4.2.xcpng8.3, released November 3. Hosts must be rebooted. Vates, which backs XCP-ng, rates the impact as Critical.

Qubes OS 4.3: Xen packages 4.19.6-3 in dom0. Dom0 must be restarted, and Anti Evil Maid users must reseal their secret passphrase because the new Xen binaries change PCR18 and PCR19.

Qubes told users on November 3 to keep installing updates as normal. The fixed packages were then in its security-testing repository, due to move to the stable one over the next two weeks after community testing.

XSA-523 is separate from XSA-500, an earlier grant copy flaw that Xen disclosed on July 28, and it has its own patches.

999aecda9c67.text:
Nearly every agent security pitch now ends on the same promise: the product stops the bad action in real time. The promise holds for one kind of agent, the kind whose traffic passes through a gateway the enterprise owns. Most agents never touch one.

One recent case shows what that gap looks like in practice. An employee asked an AI assistant to trigger a mass-email automation. The automation hit a recipient-limit policy and failed, so the assistant, which was also connected to the employee's personal mailbox, offered to send the batch from there instead. The employee approved without registering that the assistant was about to route around the sanctioned system. An unknown number of external recipients received email from a personal account rather than the approved channel.

No jailbreak was involved. The assistant did exactly what it was built to do, and the fix was not retraining a model. It was a single runtime rule that blocks any attempt to reach more than fifty external domains and explains to the user what the tool is about to do. Knowing where to apply a rule like that depends on seeing which agents exist, what they are connected to and what normal looks like for each. That visibility is the part most runtime pitches skip.

The runtime is the application, not the pipe

The year's largest agent launches placed agents inside platforms the buyer does not own. Claudeforce runs Claude inside Salesforce's trust boundary, Claude Tag lives inside Slack and Copilot lives inside Microsoft 365. Workday, which says AI now drives more than a quarter of its new annual contract value, runs its agents inside Workday. In each case the agent's tools are the application's features, its knowledge is the application's data and its permissions are the application's permission model.

A gateway can only inspect what passes through it. An agent that runs inside Salesforce, fires from a Flow, reads CRM records and writes case comments sends nothing past an inspection point, and the same is true of a Copilot agent assembling a document from SharePoint or a Slack-native agent reading years of channel history. The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 describes this gap as the "unreachable skill" scenario under AST09, No Governance: a capability deployed inside a third-party platform where no external scanner can go.

Security has made a move like this before. Firewalls once inspected packets by source, destination and port, until applications stopped mapping cleanly to ports and malicious traffic began to look identical to legitimate traffic. The inspection point moved up the stack to the application, where the signal lives. Agent runtime needs the same move, with a complication the earlier one never faced: the application layer belongs to someone else. A gateway-only strategy protects the agents an enterprise hosts itself, which are the fewest and the slowest growing.

The inspection point is also a target

In March 2026, attackers compromised LiteLLM, the open-source gateway that routes agent traffic to model providers. The malicious packages were live for about forty minutes, and CloudSEK later put the exposure at more than 2,500 organizations. LiteLLM is the kind of component a security-conscious team adds on purpose to watch AI traffic, which made the inspection point itself the attack vector.

None of this argues against gateways. It argues against treating any single component as the whole strategy. A gateway is more software in the supply chain, with its own release pipeline and dependencies, and it concentrates exactly the traffic an attacker wants. When enforcement is a shared component, its failure is a shared failure.

A millisecond verdict needs a memory

Runtime decisions are made in milliseconds, and the hard cases are the gray ones. A support agent pulling customer data may be doing its job or exfiltrating it. A coding agent reading a repository may be gathering context or performing reconnaissance. A finance agent creating an OAuth connection may be doing integration work or making the first move of a compromise. The action alone does not carry the verdict. The agent's identity and owner, its permissions, its normal behavior, the sensitivity of the data, the destination and the delegation chain behind the request do.

Chains raise the bar. Enforcement that evaluates only the last hop sees an authorized agent performing an action it has permission for, and misses that the authority arrived through a chain nobody approved. Judging the whole chain at runtime means already knowing it, and that knowledge cannot be assembled in a millisecond. Enforcement without that map is an air-traffic controller with a radio but no radar: commands can be issued, but the picture of which plane is headed where does not exist.

What real agent runtime looks like

Three properties follow. Enforcement has to sit where the agents are, across several vantage points such as native platform hooks, API-level controls, the MCP layer, the browser and the endpoint, rather than at a single gateway. Every verdict has to be computed against a live map of identity, permissions, connectivity and activity (IPCA), plus data sensitivity and delegation, which is what turns the gray cases into judgments. And the response menu has to be wider than block.

Mature enforcement is graduated. It allows the known-good, warns where justification is plausible, redacts where the data is the problem and blocks where the chain is hostile. It routes the highest-stakes actions to a human and keeps a kill switch for the provably compromised agent that suspends it, revokes its grants and preserves the trail. Every verdict is logged with its full causal path, because an incident review and a regulator want the same five things: the agent, the chain, the data, the destination and the policy.

Do not buy the end state

Irregular's Dan Lahav calls the mistake the end-state fallacy: assuming the properties of the eventual equilibrium apply to the transition actually underway. In runtime purchasing, it is the belief that inline enforcement will eventually see everything, so the unglamorous layers can be skipped. That end state is not available this year from any vendor at any price. Runtime coverage is partial and platform hooks are arriving unevenly.

What can be bought now, everywhere, is the stack runtime depends on: discovery across every vantage point, posture on every platform, identity and ownership for every agent and context for every decision. Each enforcement point that opens later then snaps into a map that already knows what normal looks like. The full argument for where enforcement belongs is in From AI Runtime to Agent Runtime.

The first ninety days, in order

A sequence that follows the stack bottom-up looks like this.

Window

The work

How to know it is real

Weeks 1 to 2: get the number

Connect what is already running (the identity provider, major platforms, network tools, the email layer) and let discovery work across every vantage point at once. No gateway deployment, no endpoint rollout, no rerouted traffic.

Time to first insight is days, not quarters. The discovered population is several multiples of the list IT keeps.

Weeks 3 to 6: names and configurations

Every discovered agent gets a named human owner or is suspended. Configuration debt is triaged, starting with the platforms hosting the most reachable agents: guest-user exposures, intake features wired to agent triggers, sharing rules from three years ago. Guardrails go on customer-facing and privileged agents first.

A human raises a hand within a day when asked "whose is this?"

Weeks 7 to 12: the queue and the path

Context-aware risk tiering so review starts with the agent that can actually hurt the business, a least-privilege review cadence on the top tier and a sanctioned route for business teams to ship agents with secure defaults.

Any critical rating can be explained as a chain, and builders are offered a path instead of only a block.

The enablement path matters because the builders are coming either way. Blocking teaches evasion, while a good path teaches compliance.

Teams can place themselves with a four-level test. Blind means the board's three questions (how many agents exist, what they can reach and who is accountable) have no current answer. Inventoried means the population is discovered, counted and refreshed continuously. Governed means every agent has an owner, posture is managed against baselines and risk is tiered with context. Instrumented means enforcement operates where agents run, with graduated verdicts and a full causal path in every alert. Most enterprises are at the first level, whatever the policy document says, and a vendor selling instrumentation to a blind organization is selling enforcement that can act but cannot judge.

Seven questions that sort vendors

Every vendor deck now says agent security. These questions separate vendors that built for the problem from vendors that renamed a product, because each is easy to answer well only if the architecture underneath exists.

Ask

What a good answer looks like

Can you find agents that never authenticate through SSO?

Yes, across several independent vantage points, each seeing something the others cannot.

For an agent you rated critical, show me the chain.

A complete, reachable attack path (capability, reachability, asset) that an analyst can verify, not an aggregate score.

Does the same finding produce different severities on different agents?

Yes, demonstrated on a sandboxed agent and a customer-facing one.

When one agent invokes another, can you reconstruct the delegation chain?

Original requester, every hop and the final action. An audit trail that starts at the last agent is not one.

What context feeds an allow, block or redact verdict?

Identity, permissions, delegation and data sensitivity, not the prompt alone.

What happens to my protection if your enforcement component is compromised?

A specific answer that addresses the LiteLLM incident directly.

How long until I see my real agent inventory?

Days. A quarter is a different product.

Platforms built around the map rather than the individual agent can answer these directly. One leading example is Reco, whose Reco Graph connects every human and non-human identity, application, permission and agent action into a single live view, so that reach, not configuration, is the unit of analysis. One measured program that applied this approach moved its posture score from 47% to 91% across 21 platforms in 30 days.

Learn more about Reco's agent discovery at reco.ai/platform.

The full ninety-day sequence, the four-level self-assessment and all fifteen vendor questions are in The Agent Security Checklist: Your First 90 Days.

It discovers an organization's entire third-party ecosystem, prioritizes real risk over alert volume and remediates with precision across every human identity, agent, app and permission in the environment. Built on the Reco Graph, with new integrations delivered in hours through the Reco Factory and pre-built agent and app intelligence from the Reco Library. dbcb3cd4f4ed.text:
Password manager mSecure has warned current and former customers to protect the confidential information stored in its app after detecting “suspicious activity.”

But its advice about what users should do comes without an explanation of what happened or whose information might be at risk.

The warning leaves users to decide whether to replace credentials—and whether it’s safe to store replacements in mSecure.

While those are perfectly reasonable questions, mSecure’s warning does not answer them.

In an email published by The Hacker News and sent to customers on November 3, mSecure’s developer, mSeven Software, said:

“mSeven Software (‘mSeven’) recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application. In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist.”

The notice recommends that customers “immediately take steps to protect all confidential information” stored in mSecure. Those steps:

“may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys.”

But the notice does not identify the suspicious activity, when it occurred, which systems were involved, or whether anyone accessed customers’ stored information. The Register, which also reviewed the email, noted that the company had not explained whether customers’ secrets were exposed.

How to be safe

Because the scope of the incident is unknown, we recommend prioritizing your most important accounts while mSeven investigates.

Changing your mSecure password alone may not be enough if someone has already accessed your account. mSecure’s documentation explicitly warns that someone may already have made a backup of its contents. That guidance does not establish what happened in this incident.

Users should not have to wait for a completed forensic investigation before receiving useful guidance. They need to know who should act, which credentials need attention, and whether the tool they would normally use to manage those changes remains safe to use.

Until mSeven provides those answers, our advice is to prioritize your most important accounts, replace the relevant credentials through official services, and avoid destructive account resets:

Change passwords through each service’s official website or app, beginning with your primary email, financial accounts, work accounts, and accounts used to recover access to other services. Use a new, different, strong password for each.

Review two-factor authentication stored in the vault. If that could be compromised by unauthorized access, consider re-enrolling that account’s authenticator through the service’s security settings.

For passkeys stored in mSecure, use each website or app’s account-security settings to remove the old registration and create a replacement with a different provider as a precaution. But make sure another working sign-in method is available first.

Think carefully about where replacement credentials go. The notice does not establish whether saving new credentials in mSecure is safe. For users rotating important accounts now, using a different password manager temporarily is a reasonable precaution.

We’ll keep you posted if we learn more about this incident, so stay tuned.

b8337d7f6e0c.text: He swore an allegiance to the US, but he was working for someone else. An IT specialist who worked across US government departments and held Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to transmitting sensitive documents to Ethiopia. Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, admitted to the espionage offenses and agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months, the Justice Department confirmed on Tuesday. A naturalized citizen of the US, Lemma, of Maryland, had worked for the US government in different capacities and across different teams, including for the National Reconnaissance Office, State Department (DoS), and Justice Department (DoJ), between 2019 and 2023. These roles included working evening hours as an IT help desk technician at the DoS as of 2021, and daytime work at the DoJ as a contract management analyst, according to court documents. Lemma had what's known as "downdraft" authority, which is to say that he was permitted to move classified files between classified systems, and unclassified files from classified to unclassified systems. Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) – a secure workplace built for handling classified files. The criminal complaint [PDF] initially stated that the alleged offending began in July 2022, although the DoJ more recently claimed that it began in 2021. It claims Lemma was caught trawling "several" non-DoS classified portals and accessed intelligence reports without the proper authorization to do so. On various occasions, Lemma, who had held Top Secret security clearance since 2020, copied information from at least 133 intelligence reports without need-to-know authorization, according to court documents. Prosecutors claimed that the man downloaded more than 100 documents, burned them to CD/DVDs, and deleted their classification markings. The material Lemma was copying was at the Secret and Top Secret levels, but burned onto discs with green labels, which are approved for employees and are supposed to signify the contents of the discs relating to unclassified material only. Lemma would allegedly take these discs at the end of his shift and exit the SCIF with them tucked into his jacket pocket. On other occasions, he was observed looking at classified material on his PC, then taking handwritten notes before folding the paper and again storing it in his pocket. This continued until around August 2023. Prosecutors claimed that Lemma began transmitting information to Ethiopian officials via an encrypted messaging app in or around August and September 2022, weeks after the alleged offending began. The files included documents, photographs, notes, maps, and information relating to Ethiopia, and officials would ask Lemma to provide details about command centers, logistics centers, military compounds, and other matters. Communications also covered geopolitical topics, referencing "situations" in an unspecified African country that shares a border with Ethiopia to gain an advantage, and rebel groups involved in conflict with Ethiopia. Lemma's messages also included encouragement to take action against paramilitary groups that were in conflict with Ethiopia on multiple occasions, say prosecutors. According to the complaint, one of Lemma's messages said: "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia." Later that day, on December 18, 2021, he wrote: "Please send dro[nes]," after sharing additional information. Announcing the guilty plea on Tuesday, the Justice Department said many of Lemma’s contacts were senior Ethiopian officials across political, military, and intelligence branches of the government. Lemma was also accused of storing copies of classified files on his own storage drives, which prosecutors claim were accessed remotely by Ethiopian officials numerous times between April and June 2023. The man was additionally caught making several bank deposits exceeding $66,000 throughout the time he was working on behalf of foreign officials. On one occasion, he was observed "angrily discouraging" bank staff from filing a currency transaction report after trying to deposit a sum greater than $10,000. "Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. "By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States." ®

Picture a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace a year after rollout. The IT lead who bought the licenses is still an Owner. So are the two admins she added during a busy week, and the director who asked for access “just to check something.” A contractor who left in the spring still has an account, because he was added by hand instead of through the identity provider. And a service account someone set up to run Codex jobs has a credential that never expires.

None of this is unusual. It’s what happens when a tool goes from pilot to every department in a few months, and nobody’s job is to keep an eye on the admin console.

Most of the security conversation around ChatGPT is about what people paste into it, and that’s fair. OpenAI’s Compliance Platform lets DLP and data security tools read conversations. But a more basic question usually goes unanswered: who actually holds the keys to the workspace?

Why nobody owns this

ChatGPT Enterprise falls between teams, so each one assumes someone else is watching it:

Identity teams own the identity provider, but SCIM provisioning to ChatGPT is optional. Anyone added directly in the admin console never shows up in their access reviews.

Cloud security teams own AWS, Azure, and GCP. A ChatGPT workspace isn’t a cloud account, so their CNAPP never sees it.

The workspace owner is usually whoever bought the licenses. Owner access gets handed out to get things done, and it rarely gets taken back.

Rolling out an enterprise AI platform is still the right call. Verizon’s 2026 DBIR found shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action, up 4x in a year, and a sanctioned tool is the best way to get people off personal accounts. But someone still has to check how that tool is set up.

What Orca checks in ChatGPT Enterprise

You connect ChatGPT Enterprise to Orca with one read-only Admin API key. There’s nothing to install and no change to how anyone uses ChatGPT. Orca pulls in every user, group, service account, and service-account credential in the workspace, and flags issues like these out of the box:

Orca detects

Why it matters

A user with the workspace Owner role

Owners control every setting, member and key in the workspace. Each one is a high-value account

A workspace with more than three owners

Owner access tends to spread and rarely gets revoked. The same rule applies to Azure subscriptions and Supabase

A service-account credential with no expiration date

A token that never expires stays valid long after the job or person that needed it is gone

A service-account credential not rotated in 90 days

OpenAI suggests token lifetimes of 7 to 90 days. Older tokens have had more time to leak

A user not provisioned through the identity provider

Users added by hand skip your joiner-mover-leaver process, so offboarding may never reach them

A group managed by hand instead of synced from the identity provider

Manual groups drift from the access you approved in the IdP

A group with no members

Empty groups are leftovers that can quietly grant access to the next person added

Screenshot caption: A ChatGPT service-account credential with no expiration date, shown in Orca with its workspace, creation date and remediation steps.

ChatGPT belongs next to the rest of your risk

An AI-built app has five parts: the model behind it, the agent or builder that made it, the platform it runs on, the database and login behind it, and the cloud account under it. Each comes from a different vendor and has a different owner. None of those owners is security.

Orca AI AppGen Security brings those parts into one platform. ChatGPT Enterprise sits next to Claude Enterprise at the model layer, alongside Vercel and your AWS, Azure, and GCP accounts.

That matters because OpenAI shows up in a lot more places than the ChatGPT admin console. At most companies, it looks something like this:

ChatGPT owners get reviewed in a spreadsheet once a quarter, if at all.

A DLP tool reads chats, a secrets scanner finds OpenAI API keys in repos, and the CNAPP covers Azure OpenAI.

Each tool sees its own piece, so nobody can say how exposed the company is to OpenAI overall. In Orca, ChatGPT users, groups, and credentials sit in the same inventory as OpenAI API keys found in code and container images, workloads calling OpenAI models (seen by the Orca Sensor), and Azure OpenAI resources. They land in the same queue as your Claude Enterprise and Vercel findings, too.

Screenshot caption: The Orca AI Security dashboard showing ChatGPT Enterprise and Claude Enterprise workspaces side by side with cloud AI services.

The goal isn’t to slow anyone down. Your builders keep using ChatGPT the way they already do, and security finally gets a clear look at who holds the keys, without reading a single prompt.

Want to see your ChatGPT Enterprise workspace in Orca? Book a demo today.

About the Orca Platform

Orca Security delivers security for the companies that build. As cloud, applications, AI and app generation expand the attack surface, Orca transforms security risk into the context teams need to act. The Orca Platform provides complete visibility across cloud, AI, and application environments, correlates risk across every layer, and prioritizes the exposures that matter most so organizations can remediate faster and innovate with confidence. Trusted by hundreds of organizations, including SAP, Autodesk, Gannett, Lemonade, and Digital Turbine, Orca is backed by leading investors including Temasek, CapitalG, ICONIQ Capital, and Redpoint Ventures.
