Exciting news for AI governance! Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). The certificate was issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC, an ANAB accredited certification body, following an independent audit of how we govern the AI systems we develop in our role as an AI provider.

What is ISO/IEC 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international management system standard for artificial intelligence. Where ISO/IEC 27001 focuses on information security, ISO/IEC 42001 focuses on how an organization governs AI. What exactly does “governing AI” mean? Essentially, it means how AI risks and impacts are assessed, how data is managed, how systems are monitored once they’re in production, and how humans stay in the loop across the AI lifecycle.

This certification means an accredited third party has audited our AIMS and confirmed that it aligns to the standard. To note, this isn’t a one-time exercise, as the certification is maintained through annual surveillance audits. This means our AI governance program is held to the standard for as long as the certificate is active.

Why is ISO/IEC 42001 certification important?

AI is continually evolving how security teams work, and it’s also causing teams to reconsider the questions they ask their vendors. Where does the model come from? What data does it use? Who reviews its outputs? How do we maintain the integrity and quality of our AI products?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification gives customers independent evidence that Rapid7 has a management system in place to address those questions. It demonstrates that the in-scope AI systems are developed and operated under a structured program covering risk assessment, transparency, human oversight, and accountability.

It also supports customers in their own governance work. Many organizations are building AI risk into their third party risk programs and preparing for frameworks and regulations such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act. A vendor's certified AIMS doesn't replace a customer's own due diligence, but it provides a credible, audited starting point.

As with cloud security, AI follows a shared responsibility model. Rapid7 is certified in the role of an AI provider, meaning we’re accountable for how we design, build, and operate these AI systems. Customers remain in control of how they use AI outputs within their own security operations.

Which AI systems are in scope?

The certification covers the AIMS supporting the following AI systems developed within Rapid7 products:

Agentic AI Workflow for MDR (Managed Detection and Response)

AI Dashboard Summary Card (Managed Detection and Response)

AI-Generated Risk Summaries (Exposure Command and Surface Command)

AI-Powered Log Search (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

AI-Powered Log Summary (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

Attack Surface Management (Surface Command)

ICS Runtime Event Story (InsightCloudSec / Cloud Runtime)

Most of these are capabilities customers use directly within the product. Agentic AI Workflow for MDR supports Rapid7's own SOC analysts as they investigate and respond on behalf of MDR customers.

What's next?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification joins Rapid7's existing security and compliance program, which includes ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2, FedRAMP, IRAP, ENS, BSI C5, as well as U.S. and international cybersecurity regulations. Each is independently assessed against its own defined scope, with details available in the Rapid7 Trust Center (reach out to your Account Executive for access).

As our AI capabilities grow, our AI governance program will grow with them. As such, we'll update this post if the scope of certification changes.

Customers can request a copy of the certificate through their Account Executive or Rapid7 representative. The certificate can also be independently verified in Schellman's public certificate directory.

3b7e4bbdf3c1.text:
A single container image that brings Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node, on immutable and mutable Linux alike, deployed the way your container workloads already are.

Key Takeaways

The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image on Docker Hub, bringing host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node without touching the host’s package manager.

It runs as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, so every node that joins the cluster automatically gets an agent. It can be deployed and upgraded through YAML manifests or a unified Helm chart that also deploys Qualys Container Security sensors, for full-stack coverage in a single install.

A single image covers container-optimized operating systems such as AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS, and Red Hat CoreOS, as well as RPM- and Debian-based Linux, including Azure Linux, on both Intel/x64 and ARM.

Policy Audit includes CIS-certified policies for AWS Bottlerocket and Google Container-Optimized OS, and all findings are prioritized with Qualys TruRisk alongside the rest of your estate.

Paired with Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS), it delivers full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane.

The AI Era Is a Container Era

The AI era isn’t arriving on bare metal. It’s arriving on Kubernetes. Model training pipelines, inference services, vector databases, and the agentic workloads that orchestrate them are being built as containers and scheduled across clusters that scale up and down by the minute. The unit of compute is no longer the server. It’s the container, and the node it happens to be running on right now.

That shift changes the math for security teams. The attack surface is no longer a fleet of servers you can enumerate and patch on a monthly cycle. It’s a fleet of nodes that may exist for hours, boot into operating systems that don’t allow you to install a package, and host workloads that move between them without warning. Every one of those nodes is a host, and every host operating system carries its own vulnerabilities and its own configuration risk, regardless of what’s running in the containers above it.

Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS) extends build-to-runtime coverage for images, containers, and serverless workloads.

The Problem: Host Security Wasn’t Built for Container Platforms

For years, securing a host meant one thing: install an RPM or a DEB on it. That model worked when hosts were long-lived and homogeneous. It breaks down in container platforms in two ways.

Container-optimized operating systems don’t accept packages. AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS (COS), Red Hat CoreOS, and their peers deliberately lock down the root filesystem and remove the package manager. There’s nothing to yum install. Security tooling has to run the way everything else on these nodes runs: as a container.

Package-based deployment doesn’t fit orchestrated environments. Kubernetes teams manage everything through manifests, Helm charts, and GitOps pipelines. A security agent that has to be installed out of band, node by node, is the one thing on the cluster that isn’t declared, versioned, and reconciled like everything else. It also can’t keep up: a node pool that scales from ten nodes to two hundred during a training run needs security coverage on every node it creates, automatically.

The result is a coverage gap at the foundation. Teams invest in scanning container images and monitoring running containers, and rightly so. But the container runtime, the kubelet, the kernel, and every system library sit on the host OS. If that layer is unmonitored, a clean image running on a vulnerable node is still a vulnerable workload.

The Solution: Qualys Cloud Agent as a Container Image

The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image, published directly to Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher account. It runs on every node in your cluster as a DaemonSet and delivers the same host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit that the Qualys Cloud Agent provides on any other platform, without touching the host’s package manager.

Qualys Cloud Agent container images on Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher.

The image ships with the Qualys Cloud Agent pre-installed and dynamically pulls down the components it needs at runtime, such as application manifests and supporting utilities, so it stays lightweight while remaining fully functional. Because it’s deployed through Kubernetes, the orchestrator does the work your provisioning scripts used to do: every node that joins the cluster gets an agent, and every node that leaves takes its agent with it.

Intel/x64 image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-x64

ARM image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-arm

How Qualys secures the container stack, from the host operating system to running containers and the Kubernetes control plane.

Once you’ve pulled the image, you can download the deployment YAMLs, and a Qualys Helm chart is published on Artifact Hub so the agent can be installed, versioned, and upgraded through the same Helm workflow as the rest of your cluster.

Why It Matters: The Benefits

Combined with TotalCloud KCS, the Containerized Cloud Agent gives you full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane, for vulnerabilities, audit, and posture, as well as runtime security, drift, and threat detection.

Full Host Coverage for Container-Optimized and Immutable Operating Systems

Immutable operating systems are the right choice for container platforms: a smaller attack surface, atomic updates, and a root filesystem that can’t drift. But immutability cuts both ways. If you can’t install anything, you can’t install a traditional agent, and many teams have run these nodes blind. The Containerized Cloud Agent closes that gap. It runs as a privileged container with the host mounts it needs to assess the underlying OS, so Bottlerocket, COS, and CoreOS nodes get the same vulnerability and compliance visibility as a conventional Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) server, with no changes to the host image and no compromise to the immutability that made you choose that OS in the first place.

Qualys has been building this coverage across the major cloud platforms for years:

Securing Red Hat CoreOS on OpenShift

Scanning AWS Bottlerocket in Amazon EKS and Amazon ECS

Scanning Container-Optimized OS in Google Kubernetes Engine

Qualys for Microsoft Azure Linux in AKS and Azure Container Instances

Your Choice of Agent on Mutable Linux, Too

The Containerized Cloud Agent isn’t limited to immutable operating systems. It also runs on the RPM- and Debian-based distributions that make up the bulk of self-managed and cloud Kubernetes nodes today. That’s a meaningful change. Previously, a RHEL or Ubuntu node meant installing the RPM or DEB package, full stop. Now you choose. Teams with a mix of virtual machines (VMs) and containers can keep the package on VMs and use the Containerized Cloud Agent on cluster nodes. Teams that are all-in on Kubernetes can standardize on the Containerized Cloud Agent everywhere and never manage a host package again. Either way, the data lands in the same place, with the same detections and the same TruRisk scoring.

Deployment That Fits How You Already Run Kubernetes

The Containerized Cloud Agent is a DaemonSet, which means the orchestrator guarantees one agent per node, on every node, for the life of the cluster. Autoscaling node pools, spot instances that get reclaimed, and cluster upgrades that replace every node are all handled without a ticket, a script, or a human. Coverage becomes a property of the cluster rather than a task someone has to remember.

Because it’s delivered as a Helm chart and YAML manifests, the agent lives in the same GitOps repository as your workloads. Upgrading is a tag change and a pull request. Rolling back is a revert. Node selectors and tolerations let you target specific pools, and the same manifest works across dev, staging, and production. Security stops being the exception to your deployment model.

One Image Across Every Operating System

You don’t need a Bottlerocket build, a CoreOS build, and an Ubuntu build. A single Containerized Cloud Agent image runs across all supported operating systems. That collapses your deployment matrix: one image to vet through your supply-chain controls, one image to pin and version, one DaemonSet manifest to maintain. When a new agent release ships, it’s one tag to update across the entire estate. Images that comply with Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) are available for environments that require them.

Complete Coverage Across Intel and ARM

Cluster node pools increasingly mix x86 and ARM instances, with Graviton, Cobalt, and Axion sitting alongside traditional Intel and AMD nodes. Images are published for both Intel/x64 and ARM, so a multi-architecture cluster gets consistent coverage without special-casing by pool.

Full-Stack Coverage at a Glance

The Containerized Cloud Agent runs the complete Qualys Cloud Agent on every node, assessing the host OS against the Qualys KnowledgeBase for vulnerabilities and against Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks through Qualys Policy Audit. Here’s how coverage splits across the stack:

Capability

Covered by

Vulnerability Management

Host: Containerized Cloud Agent. Containers: TotalCloud KCS

Drift detection

TotalCloud KCS

Compliance (CIS Benchmarks)

Data plane: Qualys Policy Audit. Control plane: TotalCloud KCS (Kubernetes Security Posture Management, or KSPM)

Threat detection and response/runtime security

TotalCloud KCS, via eBPF runtime sensors

Findings from both Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit flow into the same Enterprise TruRisk Platform views, dashboards, and workflows your teams already use. A Kubernetes node is just another asset with a Qualys TruRisk score, sitting next to the VM, the laptop, and the cloud account, and prioritized the same way.

Getting Started

Pull the image from Docker Hub: Intel/x64 or ARM.

Download the deployment YAMLs or use the Qualys Helm chart.

Deploy as a DaemonSet to your cluster with your Agent Activation Key, following the Intel or ARM getting started guide.

Platform-specific guides are available for AWS Bottlerocket, Google COS, and Red Hat CoreOS.

Coming in Cloud Agent 2.9.0

Today, images are available on Docker Hub. With Cloud Agent release 2.9.0, you’ll be able to download the Containerized Cloud Agent package directly from the Qualys platform alongside every other Cloud Agent installer. The Common Container tiles will appear in the Download and Install Cloud Agent workflow, with your activation key, supported OS list, and installation steps right there.

Common Container installation instructions in the Qualys Cloud Platform (Cloud Agent 2.9.0).

The Host Is Half the Story: Securing the Whole Container Stack with TotalCloud

The Containerized Cloud Agent secures the layer beneath your workloads. It doesn’t look inside the containers running on top of it, and it isn’t meant to. That job belongs to Qualys TotalCloud, and the two are designed as complementary halves of a single answer to the question every platform team eventually has to answer: how exposed are our container workloads, end to end?

Container risk doesn’t live in one layer. It spans the cloud account the cluster runs in, the node operating systems, the Kubernetes control plane and its configuration, the images in your registries, the containers running in production, and the identities and network paths that connect all of it. Securing any one of those layers in isolation leaves you with a partial view and a false sense of coverage. TotalCloud is built to cover all of them on one platform, with one risk score.

Container Security: From Registry to Runtime

TotalCloud’s Container Security sensor picks up where the host agent leaves off. Deployed as a lightweight container alongside your workloads, it discovers and inventories every image, container, and cluster across your environment and assesses them at every stage of the lifecycle:

Build and registry: images are scanned for OS and application-layer vulnerabilities and embedded secrets as they land in registries or move through continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, so a critical Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry in a base layer is caught before it’s ever deployed, and admission policies can block it from being scheduled at all.

Running containers: containers in production are continuously assessed against the same KnowledgeBase, with drift detection that flags containers that no longer match the image they were launched from.

Kubernetes posture: clusters, namespaces, workloads, and role-based access control (RBAC) are assessed against CIS Kubernetes Benchmarks and best practices to surface over-privileged pods, exposed dashboards, missing network policies, and other control-plane misconfigurations.

Runtime defense: behavioral monitoring of running containers detects and blocks malicious activity such as unexpected process execution, file tampering, and anomalous network connections, so an exploit that slips past the earlier stages is caught in the act.

TotalCloud KCS also holds the Red Hat Vulnerability Scanner Certification, which extends its detection accuracy to Red Hat OpenShift, RHEL, and CoreOS.

Want to see how TotalCloud secures containers from registry to runtime?

Start Free Trial

Cloud Posture, Identity, and Infrastructure-as-Code

Clusters don’t run in vacuums. TotalCloud’s cloud security posture management (CSPM) continuously assesses the AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts your clusters live in, covering misconfigured storage, over-permissive identity and access management (IAM) roles, exposed services, and hundreds of other controls mapped to CIS and regulatory frameworks. Infrastructure-as-code scanning applies the same checks to Terraform, CloudFormation, and Kubernetes manifests in your repositories, so misconfigurations are fixed in the pull request rather than in production. Together, they close the loop around the cluster itself.

One Risk Picture, Scored with TruRisk

What makes this a platform rather than a collection of tools is that every finding, from the host agent, the container sensor, and the cloud posture assessment, is normalized, correlated, and scored with TruRisk in one place. That changes what you can see. A vulnerable kernel on a Bottlerocket node, a critical CVE in a base image, an over-privileged pod running on that node, and a public ingress in front of it are no longer four alerts in four consoles. They’re one attack path, with one risk score, and one clear answer to what to fix first. The same correlation lets you dismiss noise with confidence: a critical CVE in an image that never runs, on a node with no external exposure, is scored accordingly.

And because it’s all on the Enterprise TruRisk Platform, container risk sits alongside the rest of your attack surface. The Kubernetes node, the VM it replaced, the developer laptop that pushed the image, and the cloud account that owns all of them are managed, prioritized, and reported on the same way, by the same teams, with the same workflows.

Close the Gap from Host to Cloud

A clean image running on a vulnerable node is still a vulnerable workload. Pull the Containerized Cloud Agent from Docker Hub today and bring your Kubernetes nodes into the same Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit coverage as the rest of your estate. Then talk to your Qualys representative about TotalCloud to extend that coverage from the host to every image, container, cluster, and cloud account your workloads depend on.

Bring your Kubernetes nodes into the same Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit coverage as the rest of your estate.

Get the Containerized Cloud Agent

ad619ac3ced3.text:
A China-aligned group has hijacked the brand-promotion mechanism of Sogou Input Method to deliver the DarkVigil toolset to users in six countries, turning legitimate application traffic into a malware distribution channel.

ESET researcher Anh Ho detailed the activity in research published on November 4, naming the group SlippyNunchucks and tracing its activity to at least September 15, 2023. ESET assessed with high confidence that the group is associated with a nation-state surveillance effort aligned with Chinese government interests.

The campaign began on July 1, 2026, when users of Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese-language keyboard app owned by Tencent, began receiving DarkVigil implants. The number and geographic spread of victims initially led ESET to suspect an exploit.

Hijacked Sogou Traffic Reached Six Countries

A Sogou component fetched a brand-promotion configuration from a Sogou server over unencrypted HTTP. Domain Name System (DNS) hijacking redirected those requests to attacker-controlled servers, which returned a malicious configuration.

That configuration made the app download the DarkVigil implant and place it where Sogou's own components would run it, giving the malware persistence without a separate mechanism.

ESET does not know where the DNS manipulation occurred. Possibilities include routers set up with malicious DNS settings, routers implanted to hijack DNS and interception at internet service provider (ISP) level.

Victims were in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Sri Lanka and Oman. They included a multinational gambling organization operating from Sri Lanka, the Philippines and Hong Kong, an internet café in Dubai and a university student in Denmark, though ESET gave no victim count.

Read more on China-aligned update hijacking: PlushDaemon Hackers Unleash New Malware in China-Aligned Spy Campaigns

Tencent Fixes Sogou as ESET Flags Remaining Gaps

DarkVigil, also known as FDMTP, is a modular .NET toolset with more than 20 plugins. Darktrace had linked FDMTP to Mustang Panda with moderate confidence, but ESET said its telemetry showed no overlap with that group and tracks SlippyNunchucks separately.

Before the Sogou campaign, the group's only publicly identified distribution method was a supply-chain compromise of QuickFox. ESET linked the gambling-sector targeting to China's gambling restrictions and to China-aligned groups' apparent support for law enforcement action against Chinese individuals tied to regional fraud.

ESET reported the issue to Tencent on September 11, and Tencent acknowledged it on September 21. Sogou Input Method version 16.10, released in late October, moved the affected requests to HTTPS and enabled certificate pinning.

ESET said the downloader component still does not validate downloaded file types or restrict where files are saved.

The fix closes the unencrypted request the attackers abused. Where their DNS hijacking took place remains unknown.

a9f494e7573e.text:
Cycurion has launched Habit, an AI-driven security operations center (SOC) built to identify threats before they disrupt operations. The launch also marks Cycurion’s repositioning as a predictive cybersecurity company, built around a newly assembled team of former U.S. Intelligence Community and private-sector cyber experts.

Habit doesn’t chase alerts. It learns what normal looks like for every identity, device, and workload in a client’s environment, then goes after whatever breaks the pattern. It connects to the tools a client already runs (or deploys its own agent) to build a living baseline. When something deviates, AI-driven triage and 24/7 human analysts verify the threat is real, remediate it, and validate the fix before the case is closed.

Built-in offensive analysis studies the environment the way an attacker would, so the weaknesses it uncovers become forward intelligence rather than a post-incident forensic record. Where traditional SOC and MDR models mostly process alert volume, Habit focuses on the signals that matter and verifies each one is resolved, so organizations can act before threats become incidents.

“Everyone is trying to answer the alarm faster. We want to know which alarm matters before the attacker makes a move,” said L. Kevin Kelly, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Cycurion. “The answer is context, not speed. That is a different premise, and we have rebuilt the company and its team around it. We intend to be measured on disruption avoided, not alerts closed.”

Key capabilities of Habit include:

Continuous behavioral baselining of identities, endpoints, and workloads so normal gets a fingerprint and pattern breaks surface first.

AI-driven triage, verification, and remediation, with human analysts handling the judgments that require them, around the clock.

An on-demand AI red team that attacks the client’s own environment first (mapped to MITRE ATT&CK), surfaces weaknesses before an attacker finds them, and retests to confirm each fix held.

Unlimited incident response included, with no hourly or per-incident fees.

Integration with existing endpoint protection or the Habit agent, plus email security, backup for Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, and AWS S3, and a security support inbox.

Habit is the first major product release in Cycurion’s predictive intelligence portfolio. Panoptic ranks exposure and risk by asset, threat vector, and exploitability. Fathom, targeted for early 2027, unifies intelligence, telemetry, and operations into one predictive view of the attacks forming against the systems a client cannot afford to lose. Habit is designed for existing managed-security clients, public-sector agencies, and commercial organizations that want product capabilities combined with 24/7 human oversight.

“Automating workflows around alerts that are mostly noise just gets you to the wrong answer faster,” said Danny White, Chief Product Officer of Cycurion. “We are building the view that lets our clients move first. Security is a behavior problem, so we named the product after one. Signatures catch what someone has already seen. Habits catch what is different.”

Cycurion already operates a 24/7 security operations center and, through its portfolio companies, has delivered more than 2,000 engagements across more than 30 agencies over 15+ years. Habit brings that operational experience into a product designed to scale from small and midsize businesses to demanding public-sector environments.

Russia’s APT29 has been using compromised websites, lookalike domains and a hijacked web analytics service to target iOS and Android users with exploits for patched flaws and steal their cookies, messages and Wi-Fi passwords, according to Sekoia.

APT29 watering holes target mobile devices with n-day exploits (Source: Sekoia)

The company’s Threat Detection & Research (TDR) team spotted the operation in mid-October 2026. “This watering hole campaign, which we assess with moderate to high confidence to be linked to APT29, combines multiple web delivery vectors with n-day mobile exploit chains targeting Android and iOS devices,” the company stated. The group, also known as Midnight Blizzard or Cozy Bear, is tied to Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).

Over the summer, Microsoft reported that the group had spent months hijacking hotel and conference center Wi-Fi networks to steal Microsoft 365 credentials and deliver malware.

“This campaign relies on three infection vectors,” researchers wrote. “Direct JavaScript injection on legitimate websites, Adversary-in-the-Middle-like domains, and the supply-chain compromise of the Ukrainian web analytics service.”

“All three infection vectors deliver the same payload, a code injection that loads an external script to profile the visitor’s browser and device. The delivery host then uses the mobile and browser version to serve platform-specific n-day exploit chains without user interaction.”

Gas producers, hotels and military sites

The investigation started with a malicious script on the website of a Ukrainian gas production company. Further digging turned up more compromised sites, among them those of a US chemical industry trade association, a far-right European political party and a Bulgarian military-related organization.

Some, like the site of an Australian medical clinic, had no obvious strategic value, and the TDR team believes, with low confidence, that those may have been used to go after specific individuals.

Two lookalike domains loaded the legitimate pages of America250, the initiative marking 250 years of US independence, and of Raffles London at The OWO, a luxury hotel close to the UK Ministry of Defence and 10 Downing Street. The researchers believe the hotel clone may have been meant for diplomatic delegations and prominent guests, and mention open-source reporting that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stayed there during a visit on 14 October.

For the widest reach, the attackers went after Plerdy, a Ukrainian analytics service, and spent a week between 27 August and 3 September 2026 serving their code through its tracking script. That script runs on thousands of websites, most of them Ukrainian, and the list includes sites run by the army, special forces and military equipment makers.

“It remains unclear whether the attackers intended to target visitors to specific websites or sought to compromise as many unpatched mobile devices as possible, indiscriminately exfiltrating data before selectively identifying and exploiting information of interest,” they noted.

“However, several of these sites are likely to attract high-value or strategically important visitors in the context of the Russia-Ukraine war.”

Three exploit chains for iOS and Android

On iPhones running iOS 16.7, the attackers chained CVE-2025-43529 and CVE-2024-27834 to steal cookies, which could let them reuse logged-in sessions and get into services such as webmail.

Devices with iOS 18.5 got a chain built on the DarkSword exploit kit, which uses CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510 and CVE-2025-43520 to take almost everything on the phone, from SMS, iMessage, WhatsApp and Telegram data to Keychain passwords, location data, health information and photos.

Android phones running Chrome versions 139 through 145 (except 143) were hit through CVE-2026-3910, a Chrome flaw, and CVE-2025-27038, a vulnerability in the Adreno graphics driver. That chain grabs Chrome cookies, saved logins, browsing history and Wi-Fi passwords. None of the payloads install anything that stays on the device after the data is sent out.

The attribution to APT29 rests on traces of a 2025 APT29 watering hole operation found on one of the compromised sites, similarities with a 2024 APT29 campaign against Mongolian government websites that Google’s Threat Analysis Group confirmed, and a victim list centered on Ukraine.

Every flaw in the three chains had been fixed before the campaign began, and Sekoia stressed that “a user running an up-to-date operating system is safe from these attacks.”

The company said it is working with the CERTs of the affected countries, CERT-UA among them, to identify victims and look for ways to disrupt the watering hole infrastructure.

“This operation also confirms the continued reuse of CSV mobile exploit frameworks, such as DarkSword, by state-sponsored intrusion sets. The adoption of packaged n-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation. Over the long term, we assess that the proliferation and reuse of CSV exploits among state-sponsored intrusion sets will likely become more frequent,” Sekoia concluded.

Without adequate governance, agentic AI threatens to autonomously, invisibly and rapidly morph from a business boon into a business disaster.

Sysdig has turned its runtime visibility skills into providing governance to agentic AI. The need is clear: “AI is moving from answering to acting. It used to be chat machines. Now agentic AI does stuff for us,” explains Loris Degioanni, Sysdig founder and CTO.

The problem is it can do more than we tell it, faster than we can control it, and has no sense of morality.

Sysdig has stepped into this space with the announcement of Sysdig AI Defense offering runtime security and governance for AI agents.

“AI has moved from answering to acting, and agents now ship code, change infrastructure, and reach into production systems at a speed no team can review by hand,” warns Sysdig. Unattended, the problem of AI agents going rogue is likely to increase over time: agents are designed with increasing autonomy, complexity and ‘reasoning’ to maximize their undoubted economic benefit. Increasing complexity increases the potential to drift into error.

Sysdig AI Defense sees and monitors every action an agent takes, from its origin to its completion. This is no simple task. Agents can assume new powers very rapidly as they seek to complete their assumed tasks. Every action an agent takes may be logged; but underlying the action, there may be five or more processes visible only to the operating system kernel. These processes could be invisibly adapting the function of the agent.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“The agent deployed in the morning isn’t always the one running in the afternoon,” warns Sysdig; and “only the kernel shows what actually ran.” If safety requires an agent action to be blocked, it must be immediate. “There is a need for solutions that operate at runtime, can operate extremely quickly, and can include response,” explains Degioanni. “For example, any blocking response must happen in real time, in line, as the action happens and before the action completes.” This is the purpose and function of Sysdig AI Defense.

“An agent can misreport a tool call, but it can’t rewrite its interactions with the system or the external world,” said Degioanni. “An agent’s own account of what it did is useful context, but it’s not evidence. When what an agent reports and what its actions show disagree, you have a detection. Watching software in real time and stopping it when it steps out of line is the core of Sysdig’s runtime foundation, and Sysdig AI Defense brings that same truth to the moment an agent acts.”

The firm claims several distinct benefits from its AI Defense product. It provides a live inventory of agents, harnesses, models, MCP servers, skills, and plugins, built from runtime telemetry. Every agent can be traced to an accountable human.

Risky agentic actions can be detected, held for human review or blocked before they can complete. Policy templates can be predefined with rules mapped to frameworks such as the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. Each policy starts in alert mode and is moved into enforcement mode when the organization is ready.

Actions taken by an agent and AI Defense are recorded as they happen. A live action graph shows each step in order, pairing what an agent said it was doing with what it actually did, what it could reach, and whose authority it acted under.

The result is audit quality immutable records showing which policies were applied, when, and who signed off.

Earlier this year, the IBM Institute for Business Value reported on the current state of agentic governance. “As AI agents move from pilots to production, systems make autonomous decisions at volumes no human governance can realistically supervise,” it notes. It also warns that this problem is rapidly worsening. “By 2027, enterprises expect to deploy an average of 1,661 AI agents – a 38% increase from today. At that rate, tech leaders are tasked with managing hundreds of thousands of autonomous decisions daily. And manual governance can’t keep up with that math.”

Sysdig AI Defense is purpose-built to provide automated runtime security and governance for AI agents.

3bad033df808.text:
Descope has announced Envoy, a set of capabilities that gives personal AI agents a delegated sign-in path alongside a consumer app’s existing authentication flows. Consumer companies can now accept agents as first-class users—with their own identities, permissions, and approval flows—without rebuilding their identity stack. GoFundMe, You.com, GoodRx, and Composio are among several launch and design partners for Envoy who will work alongside Descope to improve Envoy in the months to come.

Personal agents have reached consumer scale in record time. Meta’s Muse passed 5 million downloads by the end of September, growing faster in its early months than ChatGPT, Grok, or Claude. The commerce rails underneath are being adopted quickly as well: OpenAI’s Instant Checkout runs for roughly 900 million weekly active users, and Shopify is activating agentic storefronts for more than a million merchants. Shoppers are now asking an AI assistant to find a product, confirm the size, and place the order.

When that agent arrives at a company’s website, the company currently has two sub-optimal options:

Block the agent. Amazon blocked Muse in September, and JPMorgan Chase blocked outside agents including Muse and Instinct from directly accessing customer accounts in October. Blocking is a reasonable short-term response for companies with existing brand recognition, but it becomes harder to sustain as more customers route their shopping, travel, and account management through an agent. Businesses that aren’t Amazon or JPMorgan risk giving up revenue to competitors that found a way to accept agents.

Let the agent sign in as the customer. The agent collects the customer’s password and one-time code, signs in, and the site sees what looks like an ordinary human login. Nothing in the session records that an agent was involved, which means the business is dealing with impersonation rather than delegation. When an order goes wrong or a fraud rule gets enforced, the logs will point at the human customer, and the business will likely have to absorb the cost through disputed orders, returns, and support volume.

A standard is taking shape for how delegated access for personal agents should work. Meta and Sierra published Personal Agent Protocol (Poppy) draft 0.1 in October, which gives a business a way to publish what its agent-facing endpoints are, verify the identity of the agent making the request, and issue a session that is cryptographically bound to that agent for the length of the interaction.

Envoy gives consumer site developers an abstraction layer to support agents alongside human users without taking on the burden of implementing Poppy or keeping up with the specification as it evolves. Capabilities in Envoy include:

Personal Agent Protocol support, which lets businesses accept agent traffic without implementing the Poppy protocol draft themselves. Descope handles discovery, agent identification through Client ID Metadata Documents with no pre-registration required, session tokens bound to the agent’s key with Demonstrated Proof of Possession (DPoP), and all three Poppy sign-in types.

Granular agent permissions, which let businesses define exactly what an agent may and may not do on a customer’s account using Rich Authorization Requests (RAR). For example, a shopping agent can browse the catalog and place orders while remaining unable to touch account settings or payment methods, with the duration of any elevated access set by the business.

Out-of-band approval for sensitive actions, using Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication (CIBA). For example, an agent that finds a flight overnight can hold the fare and send an approval request showing the airline, the times, and the total, which the customer can approve from their phone the next morning.

Delegation instead of impersonation, which keeps the customer and the acting agent distinct in every token and log entry. This distinction means that a company can revoke an agent’s access without signing the customer out.

Augmentation instead of replacement, which lets Envoy run alongside the customer identity stack a company already has.

“Every login page on the internet was built on the assumption that a person is on the other side, but that assumption no longer holds true,” said Slavik Markovich, CEO of Descope. “Consumer apps can either block agents or let them sign in as humans, but neither approach works in the long term. We believe the Personal Agent Protocol is doing for consumer agents what MCP did for enterprise tools, and are excited to announce Envoy to give consumer apps an easy, standards-based way to accept agent logins.”

“Every donation on GoFundMe is an act of trust, so when an agent acts for someone, we need to know exactly who is giving and who is acting for them,” said Arnie Katz, Chief Product and Technology Officer of GoFundMe. “Envoy will keep the person and the agent distinct in every session, limit what an agent can do, and ask the user to approve donations from their phone. We’re proud to be working with Descope to help build that future responsibly, on open standards and in service of our customers.”

“More and more, people will ask a personal agent to find the lowest price on a prescription, compare pharmacies, and line up savings before they reach the counter. That’s where consumer healthcare is headed, and we want GoodRx to be ready for it,” said Nitin Shingate, CTO of GoodRx. “Descope has been a trusted partner for us, and expanding that partnership to support AI agents lets us welcome them as first-class users. Agents get clear, limited permissions for pricing information, and our users stay in control of their actions.”

Alongside Envoy, Descope has also published a Poppy SDK for AI agent builders. This zero-dependency Typescript SDK enables any AI agent to easily become compatible with the Personal Agent Protocol, with Descope handling discovery, client metadata document generation, session management, DPoP API calls, and other elements required by the spec. Together, Envoy and the Poppy SDK help both consumer apps and AI agents adopt patterns for secure, delegated access.

Barracuda has released patches for two vulnerabilities that can be chained to gain root access to its Email Security Gateway (ESG) appliances.

The first, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (CVSS score of 9.3), is an authentication bypass that affects only ESG. The second, CVE-2026-111560 (CVSS score of 8.6), is a command injection issue that also impacts five other Barracuda products.

“An authentication bypass in Barracuda Email Security Gateway versions earlier than 9.4.0.030 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to invoke a configuration-import function and restore a crafted, compatible backup archive, resulting in unauthorized modification of the appliance’s global configuration,” Mandiant explains in an advisory describing CVE-2026-116606.

The command injection bug sits in the timezone configuration setting, in code shared across several Barracuda products. Mandiant says an attacker logged in with administrator privileges could abuse it to execute OS commands as root.

“If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda says.

In addition to ESG, the command injection flaw affects the Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC), Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, Web Application Firewall (WAF), and Web Security Gateway (WSG).

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

According to Barracuda, attackers must be able to reach an appliance’s admin interface to exploit the flaws. The company advises organizations to keep these interfaces reachable only from trusted internal networks.

Barracuda’s advisory marks administrative access as required for both bugs, yet also calls CVE-2026-116606 a pre-authentication issue. Mandiant, which published advisories for both flaws, says the ESG bug can be exploited without authentication.

Customers are advised to update to the newest firmware and confirm that every available patch is installed. Barracuda says any patch not applied automatically should be manually installed, and that devices with automatic patching disabled should have it switched back on.

According to Mandiant, Barracuda reported the command injection on October 15 and the authentication bypass on October 22. Neither advisory says whether the flaws have been exploited in the wild.

ESG appliances were previously targeted by Chinese cyberspies who exploited a zero-day, CVE-2023-2868, starting in October 2022. That campaign led Barracuda to tell customers to replace compromised devices.

Citrix has announced new capabilities across Citrix SecurSpaces, Citrix SecurAccess and Citrix Platform Flex designed to help organizations securely deploy AI agents, govern AI-powered work and scale adoption across the enterprise. These updates include an expansion of Citrix SecurSpaces to a wider set of personas; new AI governance capabilities for Citrix SecurAccess; and a new credit-based model offering Citrix customers a more flexible way to consume Citrix solutions and services.

As AI evolves from conversational assistants into autonomous agents capable of interacting with enterprise systems and executing complex tasks, organizations are looking for ways to accelerate AI adoption without sacrificing security, visibility or control. Citrix is expanding its portfolio to help organizations govern AI agents, control which resources they can access, and maintain visibility into how AI-powered work is performed.

“The organizations that will benefit most from AI won’t be the ones that move the fastest. They’ll be the ones that can adapt the fastest,” said Hector Lima, president of Citrix. “That requires a foundation of visibility, governance, and control across users, applications, and AI agents. With these innovations across Citrix SecurSpaces, Citrix SecurAccess and a new credit-based licensing model that spans our Citrix portfolio, we’re helping customers build adaptive enterprises that can securely embrace AI, govern how work gets done, and evolve as business needs and technology continue to change.”

Citrix expands SecurSpaces to support agentic workloads for knowledge workers and AI engineers

Citrix is expanding Citrix SecurSpaces to support the deployment of AI agents for additional personas. Citrix SecurSpaces was originally designed to deliver cloud development environments, but as the rise of AI agents in the enterprise continues, Citrix is expanding the solution’s ability to support knowledge workers and AI engineers. Citrix SecurSpaces now enables organizations to provision, secure, and govern AI-powered workspaces across a broader range of employees, applications, and autonomous agentic workloads, including managed agents from providers such as Anthropic, OpenAI and more.

Autonomous AI agents are expanding what organizations can accomplish with artificial intelligence, from accessing enterprise information and using tools to executing complex tasks. Scaling these capabilities requires security, control, and governance to keep pace. Citrix SecurSpaces provides a centrally governed execution environment where employees and AI agents can securely interact with enterprise information, applications, AI models and services without requiring individual teams to build and secure their own infrastructure.

Organizations can centrally provision and manage AI-powered workspaces while maintaining control over policies, access and governance. Administrators gain visibility into workspace activity, resource access, security events, AI consumption and enterprise adoption through a common management layer designed to help organizations scale AI initiatives consistently across departments.

Within Citrix SecurSpaces, agents execute inside isolated environments with access only to the resources required for their assigned tasks. Agents can be deployed with restricted access to enterprise resources, while credential protection mechanisms keep sensitive application credentials outside the execution environment. Organizations define approved execution environments once and can deploy them repeatedly across teams while maintaining consistent governance and oversight.

To support this expansion, Citrix plans to release the Knowledge Worker Agent for Citrix SecurSpaces as open source under the Apache 2.0 license. The agent provides business teams with a conversational assistant that can work with documents, enterprise information and business systems within a governed environment where organizations determine which models, tools and data it can access.

Citrix expands SecurAccess portfolio with new AI governance capabilities

Agentic AI is scaling faster than many enterprises’ governance models. A recent Deloitte survey found that only 21% of enterprises have a mature governance model in place for agentic AI.1 As agents begin taking actions across business systems, organizations must consider a new set of security challenges. For example, an agent may inherit an employee’s full permissions, but a valid identity and approved application access are not enough to determine whether every action it attempts is appropriate for the task.

Citrix SecurAccess is designed to address this challenge by helping organizations set boundaries before an agent starts work. New capabilities coming to Citrix SecurAccess include:

Autonomous browsing activity detection: Citrix SecurAccess with Chrome Enterprise will be able to help determine when automation, rather than a person, is driving browser activity. Administrators will be able to choose how to respond, including monitoring activity, notifying users, recording sessions or blocking activity altogether.

Agentic access governance: Citrix SecurAccess ZTNA will become a policy control point that limits AI agents to only the tools and actions they need for a specific task through Model Context Protocol, rather than everything their user can access. For example, an agent asked to investigate a disputed supplier payment can review the relevant records but cannot approve or change payments, even if the employee who assigned the task can.

Session Insights with AI governance: Session Insights for Citrix SecurAccess with Chrome Enterprise already captures, analyzes and helps organizations understand browser activity from both users and autonomous agents. New AI capabilities will highlight potentially risky moments in a session, helping security teams investigate faster and keep an auditable record of how an agent used the authority it was given.

Citrix offers a consumption-based licensing model to give organizations flexibility

To help organizations adopt and scale these capabilities more flexibly, Citrix is introducing Citrix Platform Credits, a consumption-based licensing model that improves predictability and efficiency. The model enables Citrix customers to draw from a single credit pool across the lifecycle of their Citrix contract, allowing them to scale usage of Citrix solutions up or down based on evolving business needs.

This new model builds on Citrix’s May launch of its persona-based platform, Citrix Platform Flex, which has evolved from a credit-based model for managed services to self-hosted and self-managed deployments across Citrix’s entire portfolio. A shared pool of credits can be used across the broader Citrix Platform Flex portfolio, including virtual desktops and applications, secure access services, secure agentic workspaces, browser-based work, AI knowledge-work use cases, endpoint delivery technologies and additional platform services.

Rather than applying a single licensing model to every user, Platform Credits align consumption with how different workers consume technology resources. Task workers, knowledge workers, power users and developers often use applications, infrastructure, and compute resources in fundamentally different ways.

Platform Credits are designed to account for those differences by allowing organizations to adjust application resources by user personas, performance profiles and usage models as needs change. For example, a retail chain may allocate more credits to Citrix® DaaS desktops for sales and merchandising personas to deliver higher performance during peak holiday shopping season, then divert those credits to boost performance for accounting teams’ critical applications during tax filing season. Organizations can optimize their IT environments and stop paying for heavy resources across an entire population just to cover a few power users.

By connecting consumption to workforce requirements rather than a one-size-fits-all licensing model, Platform Credits give organizations the flexibility to adjust how resources are allocated as roles, usage patterns and operating needs evolve. Finance teams gain a predictable commercial framework, while IT teams gain visibility into how different personas consume resources across the platform. This combination of predictability, transparency and choice helps organizations adapt without renegotiating their technology environment each time business requirements change.

Agentic data security company Sentra today announced raising $150 million in a Series C funding round that brings the total raised by the company to over $260 million. The investment round was led by Capital One Ventures.

Sentra will use the new funding to accelerate its agentic data security capabilities and provide broad visibility into AI and the data it reaches, continuous least privilege enforcement for all identities, data protection, and rapid containment.

243f6b9b0520.text:
Introduction to BOD 26-04

On June 10, 2026, CISA issued Binding Operational Directive 26-04, "Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk." Strip away the regulatory language and it reads like a single operational fact: for a vulnerability that is actively exploited, publicly reachable, and grants an attacker full control, you now have three calendar days to remediate it — and you must run a forensic investigation in parallel to determine whether you've already been breached.

The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025, down from 38% the year before. That's a 43-day reality vs. a 3-day mandate; a gap you don't exactly just close by hiring more workers.

This blog aims to break down what BOD 26-04 actually requires, mapping each point to the Rapid7 capability that helps to make compliance operationally achievable for all.

What did CISA actually change?

BOD 26-04 supersedes and revokes two prior directives: BOD 19-02 (2019), which prioritized internet-facing vulnerabilities by static CVSS score, and BOD 22-01 (2021), which created the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog but applied a 14-day patch deadline to every entry regardless of context.

Note that flat timeline: under BOD 22-01, an actively exploited bug on an air-gapped internal server carried the same 14-day urgency as one on a public-facing web server granting full admin control. Teams burned cycles patching low-risk systems to satisfy a checklist. BOD 26-04 replaces that with a dynamic model: prioritize what attackers are actually exploiting, and formally defer what they aren't.

The four variables to BOD 26-04

BOD 26-04 abandons CVSS as the sole trigger and evaluates every vulnerability against four binary variables, derived from the SSVC decision framework (CMU CERT/CC and CISA):

Asset Exposure: Is the asset reachable by untrusted entities over a public network?

KEV Status: Is the CVE on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog?

Exploit Automation: Can an attacker automate the full exploit chain, enabling mass exploitation?

Technical Impact: Does successful exploitation grant Total control (arbitrary code execution, full/admin privileges) or only Partial control (limited access, information exposure, denial of service)?

Asset exposure is the highest-leverage variable. If you remove an asset from public reach, you flip the exposure variable from Yes to No, and the required timeline relaxes accordingly. Rapid7 Labs data underscores why exposure dominates: half of the vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild in Q1 2026 were zero-click, network-facing issues requiring no authentication, and by Q2 2026 nearly two-thirds required no user interaction at all. Attackers are going straight at exposed, unauthenticated surfaces.

CISA's new remediation tiers

The four variables combine into a graduated timeline (CISA BOD 26-04, Appendix A, Table 1). The tiers, simplified:

Tier

Timeline

Core criteria

1 (Critical)

3 days + forensic triage

On KEV and Total control

2 (High)

3 days (no triage)

Publicly exposed + Automatable + Total control, not yet on KEV

3 (Accelerated)

14 days

KEV-listed without Total control; or exposed + Partial control

4 (Standard)

60 days

Internal, automatable, Partial control

5 (Deferred)

Fix on next system upgrade

Internal + not KEV + not automatable + Partial control

Note that these timelines are dynamic. If a dormant vulnerability is added to the KEV, its clock can compress from 60 days to 3 overnight. Conversely, if you isolate an exposed asset, its clock relaxes. CISA explicitly counts isolation, mitigation, and uninstalling the vulnerable software as valid remediation; as such, a compensating control is a legitimate, compliant way to buy time for a safe patch.

The forensic triage mandate

This is the first of the requirements to have no precedent in earlier directives. For Tier 1 vulnerabilities (KEV + Total control), you must not only patch within three days, but run a concurrent forensic investigation to determine whether the asset is already compromised. Why? When an attacker exploits an exposed edge device, they establish persistence within hours; thus, patching three days later closes the door with the intruder already inside.

CISA's implementation guidance lays out a six-step, 72-hour protocol:

Phase

Window

What happens

1. Scoping

0–2 hrs

Identify in-scope devices; activate response team; open out-of-band comms

2. Preserve evidence

2–24 hrs

Capture volatile data (RAM, cache, registries) before any change

3. Patch & stabilize

2–24 hrs

Apply patches only after evidence is collected

4. Contain

6–24 hrs

Isolate infrastructure without tipping off the attacker

5. Triage analysis

24–48 hrs

Hunt IOCs; look for lateral movement and data staging

6. Escalation decision

48–72 hrs

Formal report; if compromised, report to CISA and pivot to full IR

Note the built-in tension between Step 2 and Step 3: patching reboots systems and overwrites the exact volatile memory that proves or disproves a compromise. You have to capture forensic evidence before you patch — at speed, across every affected endpoint. Doing that manually inside 72 hours is not always realistic.

Who CISA's BOD 26-04 applies to

BOD 26-04 is compulsory for all Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies. It excludes national security systems and DoD/Intelligence Community systems.

It reaches the private sector indirectly, but firmly. Agencies must review contracts and push compliance onto supply-chain partners. For FedRAMP and cloud offerings, agencies stay responsible for their hosted systems' compliance, which forces CSPs handling federal data to adopt the same 3-day triage standard. If you're a contractor or CSP touching federal data, treat this as your standard too.

Mapping Rapid7 to the directive

Meeting a 3-day clock with mandatory forensics is impossible through manual process. Here's how the Rapid7 Command Platform maps to each requirement.

Variable 1 (Exposure) → Surface Command

You can't calculate a timeline if you don't know what's exposed. Surface Command combines Cyber Asset Attack Surface Management (CAASM) with External Attack Surface Management (EASM), correlating continuous external scanning against an internal asset inventory ingested from your existing tools. The result is a single view of your true external attack surface — including the shadow IT attackers can see but your team can't. When it flags an exposed asset carrying a KEV-listed CVE, you can sever exposure to flip Variable 1 and de-escalate the timeline while you test the patch.

Variables 2 & 3 (KEV + Automation) → InsightVM and Active Risk

InsightVM tracks the KEV Catalog natively in its Threat Feed Dashboard, continuously updating which assets carry actively targeted vulnerabilities. Its Active Risk score — a 0–1,000 scale — moves beyond static CVSS by ingesting exploit intelligence from Metasploit, ExploitDB, the CISA KEV list, and Rapid7 Labs research. That mirrors the directive's own logic: a CVSS 7.5 bug with a weaponized Metasploit module will outrank a CVSS 9.8 bug with no known exploit — exactly the prioritization BOD 26-04 demands.

The NVD scoring gap → Exposure Command AI CVSS

The National Vulnerability Database can't keep pace with disclosure volume, leaving many CVEs unscored — a blind spot when a zero-day drops and you need a timeline immediately. Exposure Command fills it with an AI model trained on historical NVD data. On its own the model returns the correct severity classification 76% of the time; combined with Active Risk, that rises to 87%, with any miss never more than one classification off. Exposure Command also enriches every asset with business criticality and threat telemetry, and its Remediation Hub surfaces the fixes that cut the most risk.

The forensic mandate → Velociraptor

Velociraptor — the open-source DFIR project Rapid7 acquired in April 2021 — is built for exactly the scale and speed the triage mandate requires. It maps directly to the protocol: agents capture volatile memory and running-process data across thousands of endpoints simultaneously (Step 2), and analysts use Velociraptor Query Language to hunt CISA-provided IOCs enterprise-wide in real time, returning only relevant artifacts instead of pulling full disk images over the network (Step 5). That lets you satisfy the evidentiary requirement without delaying the Step 3 patch.

From severity to dollars

BOD 26-04 shares a core idea with modern risk management: technical severity isn't business impact. A high CVSS score doesn't answer the board's question of "how likely is this to cost us?"

The FAIR framework closes that gap by expressing risk as expected annual loss: Annualized Loss Expectancy = Loss Event Frequency × Loss Magnitude

BOD 26-04 is effectively a mechanism for pinning down Loss Event Frequency: by isolating vulnerabilities that are exploited (KEV), reachable (exposure), and scalable (automation), it identifies the ones statistically most likely to become a loss event. Feed Active Risk into the frequency side and FAIR into the cost side, and you can brief leadership in the language of capital, not CVE IDs.

Rapid7 case studies in the wild

Recent discoveries from Rapid7 Intelligence show the top tier in action:

Vulnerability

Impact

Why it's Tier 1

Rapid7 action

Microsoft SharePoint (CVE-2026-55040 + CVE-2026-63520)

Chained, the two flaws yield unauthenticated RCE via JWT bypass, running commands as the SharePoint service account

Internet-facing + total control (via the chain) + added to KEV after in-the-wild exploitation

Authenticated checks shipped to InsightVM/Exposure Command customers; Active Risk escalated to trigger triage

Palo Alto PAN-OS (CVE-2026-0300)

Unauthenticated buffer overflow in the User-ID Auth Portal; arbitrary code execution as root (CVSSv4 9.3)

Firewalls are exposed by definition; total impact; added to KEV May 6, 2026

Threat Feed integrated KEV status instantly; Velociraptor captured volatile RAM ahead of the patch

N-able N-central (CVE-2026-18577 + CVE-2026-18556)

Authentication bypass enabling full takeover of remote-management endpoints

High-value management assets; total control; added to KEV August 2026

Checks shipped via content release; Velociraptor hunted endpoint artifacts to satisfy triage

What's next for federal agencies and contractors?

If you're an FCEB agency or a contractor or CSP handling federal data, the following three moves matter most:

Get exposure right. Everything downstream depends on knowing what's publicly reachable. Establish continuous external-plus-internal asset visibility now.

Wire KEV into prioritization, not a spreadsheet. The clock starts the moment CISA updates the catalog. Ingestion has to be automated and continuous.

Pre-stage forensics. Decide today how you'll capture volatile evidence across endpoints inside 72 hours. If that's a manual runbook, it will fail under a real Tier 1 event.

CISA BOD 26-04's bottom line

BOD 26-04 retires "patch everything" in favor of operational precision: remediate the actively exploited, exposed, high-impact vulnerabilities in 72 hours, prove whether you've already been breached, and defer the rest. Meeting it takes continuous asset discovery, live threat intelligence, context-aware prioritization, and forensics at scale — which is precisely the shape of the Rapid7 Platform. For federal agencies it's a mandate; for everyone else, it's the clearest blueprint yet for risk-based vulnerability management.

Sources: CISA BOD 26-04 and its implementation guidance; 2026 Verizon DBIR; Rapid7 2026 Global Threat Landscape Report and Q1/Q2 2026 threat data; Rapid7 product documentation for InsightVM, Active Risk, Surface Command, Exposure Command, and Velociraptor.
