Meta has paid roughly $1.2 million in bug bounties for its Muse AI agent, including $300,000 for a pre-launch flaw that exposed data on internal test systems.

Muse is a personal AI agent that acts on a user’s behalf across their email, calendar, messaging and other accounts. Each user’s agent gets its own virtual machine.

The bug bounty program ran privately from April and went public at the agent’s September 8 launch, Meta’s David Singleton said in a blog post. Of the more than 630 reports received, 64 were valid.

The $300,000 reward was handed out four months before launch, while Muse was at an early internal testing stage. The researcher demonstrated access to conversations and tokens on pre-release VMs used by Meta staff to test the product.

“An authentication check treated a header added by a local HTTPS proxy as proof that a request came from a trusted source. During a system migration, the environment gained a second proxy layer. That meant requests from outside could carry the trusted header too,” Singleton explained.

Meta took the service offline, fixed the bug and stopped treating the local machine as trusted.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

A $90,000 bounty was paid for a report involving a malicious web page that, when Muse was asked to summarize it, mimicked status messages from the agent’s browsing tool. “It got the agent to execute some actions which should have been caught,” Singleton noted.

Meta has since added detection signals and changed how Muse treats tool output that looks suspicious. It says that, in testing, its classifiers now catch the attack and 100 variants.

Another $90,000 went to a report showing that specific formatting could slip one-time passcodes past Muse’s email redaction filters. Meta described it as one piece of an end-to-end attack.

A $50,000 reward went to an Android app flaw that let a malicious app pass a link to a privileged web view. “The link handler recognized a shared-page path without validating its host and loaded it,” Singleton wrote, allowing an attacker’s page to grab the web view’s credentials.

A $1,000 bounty covered a Mac app flaw that let an attacker with access to the computer hijack the auto-update feature to execute code with the app’s permissions.

Meta pays up to $300,000 per valid report, which it claims is several times more than the top rewards advertised by other leading AI developers. Prompt injection attacks affecting a single user can earn up to $130,000, while a fleetwide compromise can earn as much as $250,000.

Related: Google Introduces $250,000 Root-in-Cloud Bug Bounty Reward

Related: Google Partially Reverses Chrome Bug Bounty Cuts

Related: Microsoft Bug Bounty Program: $20 Million Paid to 500 Researchers

0f2955e69b17.text:
“The software we use has become an actor,” declared CrowdStrike President Michael Sentonas in his address on the dangers and opportunity of agentic AI at the company’s Fal.Con conference in September. It’s an idea that until recently would have been dismissed as absurd, yet across cybersecurity it’s now taken as a given.

For decades, the adversary has been nuisance hackers, professional cybercriminals, or well-resourced teams working for nation states. The arrival of rogue agents — underlined by real-world incidents such as OpenAI’s infamous assault on Hugging Face — has demolished this. Agents still work on behalf of humans, but they don’t always reason or act like them. They are entities with capabilities and an unpredictability unlike any threat businesses have ever faced.

“I believe we just crossed a line. Agents have escaped evaluation environments and compromised infrastructure they were never supposed to touch,” Sentonas told the crowd in Las Vegas in early September. “For decades, software did what we programmed it to. It has moved from execution to agency.”

Sentonas’ point wasn’t simply that malicious agents are a threat. The arrival of agentic AI also raises larger questions for security operations centers (SOCs), which will deploy agents on a scale that matches or even exceeds attackers. That makes agents a threat from both the outside and inside the enterprise perimeter. “What happens when millions of AI agents act at machine speed on both sides?” Behind the confident marketing pitches from CrowdStrike and a growing cast of rivals, the honest answer right now is that nobody can be sure.

Coming from a cyber vendor, Sentonas’ reference to “millions” of agents might sound like a number meant to hype the threat. But it is likely no exaggeration, with Gartner forecasting that the number of agents used inside a single Fortune 500 company will expand from 15 in 2025 to 150,000 by 2028.

“As CIOs and IT leaders see an explosion of AI agents across their organizations, many are contending with an ungoverned sprawl of agents that expose their organizations to a range of risks, including misinformation, oversharing, and data loss,” says Matt Goss, a senior director analyst at Gartner.

Taking up the agent challenge

For years, Fal.Con was about persuading enterprise SOCs to consolidate capabilities under CrowdStrike’s do-it-all Falcon platform, comprising nearly three dozen modules. In 2023, with its “Raptor” release, Falcon and the company’s flagship event took a hard turn toward AI. In this changed world, AI wasn’t simply a Falcon capability; increasingly it was Falcon, influencing everything it did.

The AI theme dominated Falcon’s 2026 Fall release, bringing the company’s growing portfolio of AI SOC capabilities under the Falcon umbrella with the launch of the Agentic Security Platform. Most individual components — Charlotte AI AgentWorks, Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration, the AI-enabled Enterprise Graph — were announced in 2025 as part of the company’s Agentic Security Workforce plan but a closer look reveals important new features.

Currently, agents investigate alerts using pre-built Falcon agents or custom agents built using the no-code AgentWorks solution. Charlotte AI now gives these agents a shared memory layer in Enterprise Graph that enables them to coordinate with one another across multiple endpoints, identities, and cloud services simultaneously (aided by the company’s 2025 acquisition of Onum, which accelerated the speed with which agents can ingest data). On paper, the effect is to dramatically speed up alert triage while expanding the scope and capacity of worker agents in a way that relieves human SOC teams of a lot of basic grunt work, including some Level 2 investigation and Level 3 remediation and hunting workflows.

Also new is SafeMind, a frontier red-teaming system based on Nvidia’s Nemotron open-weight LLM, comprising offense (Red Tempest) and defense (Blue Solano). This agentic framework continuously tests an isolated mirror of the live environment for weaknesses, feeding the results back into detection at the agent level. CrowdStrike didn’t invent the concept, but it does appear to be the first to integrate an autonomous testing model into a SOC platform.

Speed is not enough

This might look brand new, but the early incarnations of the agent-powered SOC are as much evolution as revolution. Everything inside a traditional CrowdStrike-powered SOC — from its Falcon EDR sensor, Enterprise Graph data, and cloud-native management — remains in place. Humans are still essential to decision-making, albeit at a higher level than before. What agents add to this SOC paradigm is a new abstraction layer separating SOC teams from the mass of telemetry they have increasingly struggled with. This should be good news for defenders because it means they have some hope of matching the speed and scale of agentic attacks.

But speed is only the beginning, points out James Patrick, CTO for the FIOR Group, which develops an AI policy and security gateway. “Attackers and defenders can both operate at machine speed, so simply making SOCs faster isn’t enough. We need to move beyond reactive detection towards continuous testing of our defenses.”

SOCs must work out how much they delegate to agents and what constraints are set around this. “Enterprises already struggle with fragmented telemetry, overlapping security products and inconsistent policies. Adding autonomous systems introduces another problem: establishing who or what has authority to act, and how to verify that authority,” says Patrick.

According to Chris Cochran, field CISO and VP of AI security for the SANS Institute, that’s why “for most organizations, agentic AI will be augmentative rather than a replacement for analysts, at least for the next few years.”

Agent platforms, including CrowdStrike’s, still have work to do proving themselves in terms of oversight and governance.

“The core problem is that we’re applying a probabilistic technology to a discipline that usually requires determinism,” Cochran adds. “A SOC needs to know that the same input will produce the same action, and that the action can be explained to an auditor or an incident review board.”

For that reason, Cochran believes that while agentic-powered SOCs will remove a huge amount of alert handling and correlation effort, the workload will shift to processes such as verification.

“Teams should continuously evaluate agents against known-good and known-bad cases, the same way you’d regression test detection content,” he says. “None of this is exotic, but it takes engineering time that many SOCs haven’t budgeted for.”

Enemy within

One deeply unfamiliar problem is that agents themselves are an emerging attack surface within the enterprise and must be constantly assessed. Traditionally, security tools defend the environment, and the idea that an agent system doing the same job could itself become a direct threat is new. But what makes agentic AI unsettlingly is its non-deterministic nature, which means that, unlike a traditional security tool, it has the potential to do things you didn’t tell it to and haven’t planned for.

“Organizations are deploying autonomous systems that access sensitive data, use privileged identities, interact with applications, and execute actions. Those agents can be compromised, manipulated, or behave unexpectedly,” says Tom Findling, CEO and cofounder at AI SOC startup Conifers.ai. “Security operations will need visibility into agent identities, permissions, actions, and decision-making processes, and the ability to detect and contain dangerous behavior.”

CrowdStrike’s answer, relaunched at this year’s Fal.Con, is Falcon Guardian, an AI detection and response (AIDR) solution featuring runtime enforcement, agent discovery, execution graph mapping prompts, and quarantining for misbehaving agents. Similar capabilities will be needed for any agent platform but the mere fact that security systems now need their own security systems underscores what CrowdStrike’s Sentonas was referring to with his software-as-actor remark at Fal.Con. Human SOCs need to protect their enterprises from their AI SOC helpers.

To that end, CrowdStrike yesterday announced the roughly $400 million acquisition of Fiddler AI, an AI agent monitoring and governance vendor from the emerging, burgeoning, and somewhat confusing agentic AI tools ecosystem.

Fiddler’s platform tracks AI models’ behavior, attempting to provide explanations for their actions as a means for establishing a control plane for governing and securing them. Its 100-plus metrics track hallucinations, toxicity, personally identifiable information (PII) leakage, and drift, enforcing policies to protect against jailbreaks, prompt injections, and bias. Enterprises deploy tools like Fiddler to make model drift visible and actionable before it becomes systemic risk.

CrowdStrike intends to bundle Fiddler into its flagship platform as Falcon Observe in Q4 FY2027, approximately six months from now, as a means for “proving businesses can safely use AI agents every day,” according to Sentonas’ post announcing the acquisition.

CrowdStrike has invested heavily in agentic AI, building an impressive stack of capabilities that extend the Enterprise Graph that made it a dominant player capable of surviving the occasional embarrassing global hiccup. It has even embraced a degree of openness, allowing data ingestion, API connectors, and partnership gateways to enrich the data going into its Falcon AIDR. However, there’s no getting away from Falcon as the single control plane.

“CrowdStrike starts with endpoint security and an established enterprise security platform. Other vendors approach the problem through identity, networks, cloud, or security analytics. They all have an incentive to bring customers further into their own platforms,” observes FIOR Group’s Patrick.

“The challenge for CrowdStrike, and for every vendor, is that a platform can’t independently verify itself,” he adds. “What’s needed is control that is genuinely independent of any single platform and works across those boundaries.”

According to Patrick, a critical feature will be the ability not simply to deploy a security layer but to continuously assess its security and performance. As the traditional detection and remediation stack of cybersecurity is pushed out of shape, the growth in new layers and processes could make this task almost as demanding as the main job of cyber defense that agents were supposed to simplify.

A federal grand jury indicted two Canadians suspected of hacking multiple US universities and using the compromised systems to mine for cryptocurrency.

35-year-old Ryan James Roach and 41-year-old Mathiew James Stubbings now face a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine each if found guilty of conspiracy to obtain information from a protected computer and to cause damage to a protected computer, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentionally damaging a protected computer.

According to court documents, the two accomplices used virtual private servers in multiple countries (registered under fake names) between June 2016 and December 2019 to infect systems on the networks of multiple unnamed educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Massachusetts with malware.

"These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials," the Department of Justice (DOJ) said.

Once inside the victims' networks, Roach and Stubbings allegedly stole data and login credentials, deployed crypto-mining malware, and, in some cases, used compromised systems for vulnerability research after gaining access to supercomputers on the victims' networks.

"Roach and Stubbings targeted educational institutions in the United States that had supercomputers and researched security vulnerabilities in the victim computer networks, using a variety of methods to gain access, including using a server and compromised computers from another victim to conceal their identities," the DOJ added,

"Once inside a network, Roach and Stubbings used sophisticated techniques and tools to conduct reconnaissance and expand their access within the network."

According to prosecutors, the two defendants also damaged at least 10 computers over one year, causing losses of at least $5,000.

Roach was extradited from Canada to the United States on October 28 and was arraigned before a detention hearing on November 3. Stubbings will also be arraigned after his extradition from Canada.

Multiple US universities have been breached over the last year, including Ivy League schools Harvard University, Princeton University, and the University of Pennsylvania. All disclosed data breaches in November 2025, confirming that attackers accessed donors' information and other sensitive data.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned federal agencies that attackers have started exploiting a recently patched high-severity WordPress vulnerability in the wild.

Tracked as CVE-2026-119977, this high-severity WordPress Core flaw stems from a Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition and was reported by Picus Security researcher Umut Bayram.

Successful exploitation can let remote threat actors without privileges execute code on the server in high-complexity attacks due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades.

"A weakness in the WordPress upgrade process which can lead to remote code execution during the upgrade window," the WordPress security team said on October 28 when it released WordPress 7.1.4 with patches to address this security issue. "Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately."

CISA confirmed CVE-2026-119977 active exploitation on Tuesday and added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, ordering Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to secure their systems by Friday, as mandated by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04.

"This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise," the cybersecurity agency warned.

Although BOD 26-04 targets only US federal agencies, CISA urged all network defenders, including those in the private sector, to prioritize patching this vulnerability to protect their servers.

While CISA didn't provide more details on attackers exploiting CVE-2026-119977 in the wild, WordPress security firm Wordfence says in an advisory update over the weekend that it "blocked 13,095 attacks targeting this vulnerability in the past 24 hours."

In July, the WordPress security team also patched a critical vulnerability chain in WordPress Core (named wp2shell) that can be abused to deploy webshells and take over unpatched servers by exploiting a REST API batch-route confusion vulnerability (CVE-2026-63030) and an SQL injection flaw (CVE-2026-60137).

Public wp2shell exploits were released one day after the patches went live, and attackers began breaching unpatched servers a few days later to deploy persistent webshells and install malicious plugins.

A Chinese-speaking threat actor also weaponized the wp2shell exploit chain in September to steal sensitive data from more than 18,500 records stored in backend databases belonging to small businesses and government organizations.

Amy Ciminnisi: 0:00

Welcome to Talos Takes, where we discuss Cisco Talos’ latest research and security news. We break down complex topics for everyone from beginner to expert, C-suite to frontline.

Amy Ciminnisi: 0:13

Hello everyone, happy November! Attackers often face a bottleneck. They steal massive piles of data, and then they have to do the slow, tedious work of figuring out which of the victims are actually worth the effort. But now malware can start doing that analysis for them. VOLTA is a newly discovered info stealer that uses LOLs to turn raw stolen credentials into a prioritize high value dossier. And here to break this down is Ryan Fetterman, who is the creator of CAIRN. Now, if you haven't heard already, CAIRN is a research framework that is designed to track these AI integrated threats. It examines the metadata so there is no need for binary downloads or risky detonations. And it gives defenders insights into how attackers are integrating intelligence AI specifically into their operations. So Ryan is joining me to talk about all things VOLTA and what this kind of automation means for security teams. Ryan, how are you doing?

Ryan Fetterman: 1:27

I'm good. Yeah. Thanks for having me. Although I wish I was here under less scary circumstances.

Amy Ciminnisi: 1:34

I really wish so, too. Maybe we'll get you on here for, you know, something a little less pressing, a little less. Reality shifting. So let's actually start with the discovery. Of this. When you were analyzing this, was there like, a specific moment where you realized, like, hey. This isn't just a credential sealer. This is just a. Whole intelligence analysis suite. Like, what was that? Moment for you?

Ryan Fetterman: 2:09

Sure. So I can explain kind of how this comes about from the care and perspective. So when I ran the hunt and ultimately found this, what I do first is there's a series of filters that are pulling binaries that have AI specific fingerprints in them. So the rule that this binary matched on was, it had an API endpoint. We can see that in the metadata. In this case it's using open router. So when I do the second level pass there's a second tier of Yara rules that will then characterize more of the behavior of the binary. And in this case we had rule matches for telegram integration with that LLM as a C2 potentially. And then also AV labels indicating that it's a stealer with AI integration. So in this case, those rules were pretty accurate and give you an initial impression of what the file is and what what kind of malware we might be looking at. But I would say there wasn't really an moment until the Re stage when when you're doing like the reverse engineering of the binary. And at this point when I did a string stomp, I recovered the VOLTA-AUTODOXER name, which just sounds like a malware and like a doxing kind of stealer implant. And then ultimately, like recovering the prompt itself is always like a really unique and cool, aspect of like, this AI integrated malware, because there's no more guessing about the, the intent and the motivation of this tool, like it's all spelled out there for us.

Amy Ciminnisi: 3:53

Yeah. And so let's. Get into maybe what this tool actually does. One of the things that I found pretty crazy in the blog is that it doesn't just like grab saved passwords, but it uses sessions to look up like DoorDash order histories or, you know, confirm addresses with receipts in your Gmail inbox. You know, from a practitioner perspective, this seems really invasive. How does this change the way that we view the impact of a compromise browser session?

Ryan Fetterman: 4:32

Yeah, I think this is a big deal. And I've witnessed this personally, like as I've used, Google and like, oh, off authentication to connects to so many more services and things. Now it's just convenient to not have to create another account and password for everything you connect to. But it really makes your kind of core like your your Google account, just like a real gem for an attacker. Because if you're able to access that and replay an authenticated session from the the victim's machine, which is what they're doing in this case, you just have the keys to, so many different apps and so much data. And this malware really does a good job of showing you kind of like what the extra mile looks like when you have access to these kind of credentials. So I'm not an expert in this space, but like, I know there's a lot of hardware backed protections that prevent attackers from kind of extracting your credentials and taking them back off of your machine. But that doesn't really help in this context, because they're replaying the authenticated sessions from your actual machine. So in this case, there are protections like step up authentication, like when you're trying to make a really serious change, like, you know, rerouting where your mail is going or something like that. Google will prompt you for another, challenge for authentication. But in this case, the attacker, maybe knowingly or wisely, is kind of staying under that bar as well and just doing like inbox searches to provide like a layer of enrichment to that. They have the first level of credentials, like the basic information and what they can scrape off of your machine, but then they're replaying those sessions to do basically like a second pass to see what else they can pull. To kind of round you out as a target.

Amy Ciminnisi: 6:31

And then looking at like the prompt itself, I mean, if it weren't so malicious, I would find it so impressive. But it like, prompts the LLN to make connections between, like, the victim's hobbies or their home address to things like their password patterns.

Ryan Fetterman: 6:52

Yeah. What's interesting is the the AI integration in this case is actually totally optional. It's like an added feature that can be run, but the stealer can just run and do all this collection and package everything back, or package everything up and send it back to the attacker without this kind of polishing step. So the exfil can actually happen in three stages. It can exfil after the stealer runs, it can fill after the AI call, or it can exfil after the last layer of like, network enrichment produces anything. And I think this is something that we've seen across a couple different AI integrated malware now that not only like this model has multi-model, kind of resilience in it. So they're anticipating potentially hitting refusals on the first model, which in this case is Claude. So if they can't accomplish the the prompt with Claude, they will kind of cascade to less permissive models. But then ultimately the ability for the malware to run without the without the AI integration overall, I think is another interesting idea. But yeah, this is kind of clever use of AI. They talk about picking out specific patterns within the victim's data, which is something that these language models are really good at. Better than humans, I would say in most cases. So they're talking about connecting like if, there's browser traffic to a, a learning management system, can you infer that this person goes to that university or teaches at a school or something like that? Barracuda, which offers a wide variety of cybersecurity devices, has been bitten by a bug itself.

The company has disclosed two critical and high-severity vulnerabilities that, if chained together, could allow threat actors to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to devices.

They consist of a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (rated a critical 9.3 severity on the common vulnerability scoring system), and a command injection vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-111560 (rated an 8.6 high-severity on CVSS). Attackers need to have access to the admin interface of a susceptible device to successfully exploit these vulnerabilities.

Barracuda has released security patches, which it advises customers to apply immediately.

The vulnerabilities impact numerous popular Barracuda products

Root access on an email gateway puts the attacker in the place that every inbound and outbound message passes, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. It may also expose the credentials and connections the gateway uses to reach the mail server and directory. “Those are the keys to the kingdom, if you will,” he said.

CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 both impact Barracuda’s Email Security Gateway (ESG), but CVE-2026-111560 also impacts its Web Security Gateway (WSG), Web Application Firewall (WAF), WAF Control Center (WCC), Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC), and Message Archiver (BMA), the company said.

Customers using these products should verify that their systems are running the latest firmware versions and have received all security patches, it advised. The device will show the latest firmware version available; if a device’s firmware is multiple versions out of date, users may need to perform several updates.

Enterprises whose appliances’ admin interfaces are not publicly accessible from the web are less exposed, Barracuda said; the company advised restricting access to these interfaces to trusted internal networks and applying appropriate network access controls to limit exposure.

“The biggest concern is how these two vulnerabilities could chain together,” said Jon Nelson, principal advisory director at Infotech, noting that an attacker who can bypass authentication and then exploit command injection could move from accessing an exposed appliance to executing commands on it. “Assessing each vulnerability in isolation can understate the risk,” he said.

Dickson added that security leaders should read the advisory closely, as it calls one flaw “pre-authentication,” then lists “Authentication Required: Yes, administrative access.”

“Both cannot be true in the usual sense,” he pointed out. Likely access here means being able to reach the admin interface over the network, without a password.

“If your admin interface faces the internet, that condition is already met,” Dickson said.

The advisory also labels a 9.3 severity rating as “high,” when 9.0 and above is actually “critical” on the standard scale, he pointed out. “These are small things, but labels drive patching queues,” he noted. Also, the advisory does not say whether these flaws are currently being exploited, but it does not say they are not, either.

How enterprises should respond

“Get the admin interface off the internet,” Dickson emphasized, noting that, as a cybersecurity consultant, he gives that advice at least a handful of times a week. “Management interfaces on edge devices are continually a source of vulnerability.”

Once teams limit admin access to a trusted internal network or a dedicated management network, Dickson advised, they should then “verify the patch rather than assume it was properly installed.” From there, he said, analyze for unauthorized visitors by reviewing admin logs, check for unfamiliar accounts, and look for unexpected outbound connections from the device.

History matters here, he added. In 2023, after a zero-day on this same email security gateway (ESG), Barracuda told customers with compromised appliances to replace them outright rather than rely on the patch. As he put it: “A patch fixes the lock. It does not tell you who already has a key.”

Nelson agreed that enterprises should look closely at who can reach their administrative interfaces. They should, in addition, put access behind additional controls such as a properly configured zero trust access layer.

“Exposing those interfaces directly to the internet was always a bad idea,” he said. “As AI makes it easier to find weaknesses and chain attacks together, that exposure becomes increasingly difficult to justify.” AI is also expanding the search for software flaws to include issues such as business logic weaknesses where an application can be made to bypass its intended controls. Authentication and authorization bypasses deserve particular attention in that context, Nelson said.

As more vendors use advanced AI to examine their code, CISOs should prepare for more flaw disclosures and potentially shorter windows to respond to them, he noted. “That means identifying exposed appliances, restricting access, and having a response plan ready before the next zero day arrives,” he said.

Understanding what each appliance exposes

Security appliances are increasingly creating vulnerabilities in corporate networks, which is changing the cybersecurity discussion. Enterprises rely on them to protect the network, yet ultimately they are software systems with vulnerabilities of their own.

“They sit exactly where attackers want to be,” Dickson noted.

Firewalls, VPNs, and email gateways face the internet by design; that is their job, he said. They see sensitive traffic and hold credentials. Most cannot run the endpoint detection tools that protect laptops and servers, so a compromise can remain undetected for a long time, and every customer runs the same firmware, so one working exploit can scale to thousands of organizations.

“The discussion is shifting from which box to buy to what the box itself exposes,” Dickson said. “Every appliance purchase is a decision to trust a vendor’s code at the most exposed point in the network.” It deserves the same scrutiny as any other in an enterprise, he noted.

Buyers should ask their vendors four questions, he advised: Is the admin interface exposed to the internet by default; how quickly do patches ship; are they applied automatically; and what logging can users see?

“The security appliance does not just protect the perimeter,” Dickson pointed out. “It is the perimeter, and it should be treated as the most attacked system an organization owns, because it is.”

We're proud to share that Snyk has been named a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: Agentic Development Security Tools, Q4 2026. Snyk received the highest score in the Strategy category, along with the highest scores possible in these criteria:

Strategy: Vision, Roadmap, and Partner Ecosystem

Current offering: AI dynamic testing, AI coding guardrails, autonomous proprietary code remediation, and developer experience

Software development changed who does the work

For two decades, software development moved at a human pace where developers wrote code, peers reviewed it, and security teams tested it on a schedule. AI coding assistants compressed that cycle, and coding agents are now changing who does the work. Forrester frames the shift: "AI coding agents are changing how software is built, moving from developer assistants to active participants in development workflows."

Adoption has moved well past the pilot stage. In the Stack Overflow 2026 Developer Survey, 66% of developers who use AI work in coding agents, and 73% of those using AI coding assistants or agents use them daily. As a result, the developer's role is shifting from writing every line to orchestrating the agents that write it.

Each of those agents brings its own supply chain; it installs packages, connects to MCP servers, loads skills, and invokes tools the security team may never have reviewed. Because it can also run commands, edit files, and access sensitive data, its actions need to be governed as much as its code needs to be tested. In our view, security models built to scan code after it is written were not designed to govern the systems creating it.

Attackers are moving at machine speed too

In 2025, Anthropic's threat intelligence team disrupted an espionage campaign in which AI carried out an estimated 80 to 90% of tactical operations, with humans in a supervisory role. The CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report puts average eCrime breakout time, from initial access to lateral movement, at 29 minutes, with the fastest observed case at 27 seconds.

Those timelines change how teams should think about their vulnerability backlog. Pull request queues, ticket triage, and quarterly pentests were designed around attackers who moved slower than the fix. Most backlogs consist of low- and medium-severity findings, deprioritized one at a time. AI makes it cheap to chain several of those minor issues into a critical exploit path, so the backlog now functions as an attack surface rather than deferred cleanup.

The pressure is also building inside the codebase; Snyk’s product data shows new critical and high-severity issues detected grew 10x in the past year, and roughly eight new issues are introduced for every one remediated. When risk is created faster than it is fixed, the answer is a different operating model: security agents that fix continuously, guardrails inside the agent workflow, and adversarial testing that proves controls hold

AI applications are reaching production faster than governance

Teams are shipping AI applications and agents into production faster than governance processes can keep pace with. Many security leaders are still working to answer basic questions about their AI estate:

Which models, agents, and MCP servers are running, and what data can they reach?

Which skills were pulled from public registries, and who approved them?

Could you audit what a given agent did last week?

This is shadow AI at enterprise scale. Its risks, such as prompt injection, excessive agency, and data leakage, are behavioral: they live in an agent’s decisions as well as its code, which is why code scanning alone can’t surface them. Model choice is part of that risk. In Snyk’s 2026 State of Agentic AI Adoption, Volume III, the lowest-capability models averaged 501 on decision override, a 0 to 1,000 score, while the most capable models averaged 45, a gap of more than 10x. Roughly a third of the scored model references in US environments fall in that lowest group. Governing them starts with a live inventory of the AI estate, including which models are in play, and policies that apply before an agent acts.

Why this evaluation matters

In our view, Forrester's evaluation reflects these shifts in operating model, and it assessed agentic development security across the full span of AI-driven development: the code agents produce, the agents and the components they pull in, and the AI applications teams build. Forrester asks buyers to weigh three considerations:

Visibility and governance of agentic development

Verification of AI-generated code and AI applications

AI risk reduction at agentic speed

Teams now need coverage across all three, on one platform that shares context between them, and that is the standard we have been building toward.

A decade of conviction, pointed at where software is created now

Snyk has operated on a core belief for more than a decade: security belongs where software is created. We believe agentic development moves that point of creation inside the agent workflow, and that is where the Snyk AI Security Platform is built to operate. Forrester’s report states that "Snyk articulates a farsighted vision to secure AI-written code, the agents that run it, and the applications they build, while advancing secure-at-inception development and governance."

On capabilities, the report states that "Snyk brings security into developer and AI coding agent workflows through autofix and coding guardrails that secure AI- and human-generated code and block risky agent actions." It also notes that Snyk's "strong AI dynamic testing uncovers business logic flaws and vulnerability chains and validates findings with working exploits."

How Evo by Snyk secures each layer of AI-driven development

Last year, Snyk expanded the Snyk AI Security Platform with Evo by Snyk, a suite of agent-native security solutions that secure, protect, and govern AI-driven development across three loops: the code artifact, the AI workforce, and the AI applications teams build. A validation layer tests all three.

Evo Agentic AppSec: Secure the code artifact. AI security agents that find, fix, and block vulnerabilities at the speed agents write code, with every result verified independently. This includes Snyk Secrets for blocking leaked credentials.

Evo Agentic Development Security (ADS): Protect the AI workforce. Governs what AI coding agents use, what they do, and what they generate, from the MCP servers and skills they pull in to the code they write. This includes Snyk Studio for real-time guidance in AI coding workflows.

Evo AI-SPM: Govern every AI app you build. Discovers and assesses risk of the models, agents, skills, and MCP servers in your software, generates a live AI-BOM, and turns AI policy into enforceable controls.

Evo Continuous Offensive Security (COS): Validate every loop. Continuously tests applications and AI agents, leveraging Agent Red Teaming, and returns validated proof of what an attacker could actually exploit, so no loop grades its own work.

As AI takes on more of the work of building software, we believe its output needs a separate, deterministic layer to verify it. That is why Snyk pairs frontier AI reasoning with our deterministic engines and ten years of security intelligence, so organizations can adopt AI at full speed and stay accountable for what they ship.

What this means for teams building with AI agents

Forrester's take: "Snyk is a good fit for enterprises that want to accelerate agentic development while embedding security directly into agent workflows." For teams evaluating this market, three questions help separate tools built for agentic development from tools adapted to it:

Governance: Can you see and control what your agents use, what they do, and what they generate before it ships?

Remediation: Is your fix rate keeping pace with your rate of new risk, across new code and the existing backlog?

Proof: What independent evidence shows your controls hold against a real attacker?

We are grateful to our customers, partners, and the developer community, whose feedback shapes the platform every day. We will keep investing inside the agent loop, where software is now created. Our mission remains the same: unleash AI innovators, securely.

Want the full picture of how Forrester evaluated this market? Get your complimentary copy of the report.

Months after Siemens released fixes for an authentication hole in flow-based programming tool Node-RED, it remains unpatched by many users and attackers are taking advantage of it in the wild.

The problem involves open source IoT/IIoT systems, including those embedded in critical infrastructure, deployed outside the control of CISOs and CIOs. Security firm VulnCheck discovered the exploits and disclosed details in a blog post on Monday.

“On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115, an unauthenticated Node-RED admin API flaw, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. The request came from an IP in Microsoft’s ASN (AS8075),” the post said. “We have since seen 16 events from the same IP against this CVE, covering several different payloads.”

The core problem is that Node-RED ships with the authentication option disabled; users are supposed to change the setting before it goes live.

Patrick Garrity, the VulnCheck security researcher who wrote the post, said the fact that Node-RED deployments are popular among those outside IT makes them susceptible to unsophisticated errors like this.

“They are put in place by relatively nontechnical people,” Garrity said in an interview.

Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said the Node-RED hole is not new, but it is still being leveraged in the wild.

“The condition being exploited is one Node-RED has carried for years as a default: unless an administrator configures authentication, anyone who can reach the editor can deploy flows, and the project’s own documentation says as much,” he said. “Node-RED is popular precisely because engineers can wire it up without involving IT, which also means it rarely appears in an asset inventory. It is the same pattern behind this week’s supermarket refrigeration attacks: equipment installed outside the security team’s view, reachable from the internet, with authentication switched off.”

Mahapatra pointed out that the biggest danger is the nature of the way users tend to deploy Node-RED.

“It is integration middleware. A typical deployment speaks Modbus, OPC UA, MQTT or S7 to controllers on one side and to databases, brokers and cloud services on the other, and it stores credentials for all of them,” he said. “A compromised instance is a credential vault for every system it touches and a bridge across an IT/OT boundary that the network diagram says does not exist.”

Another problem is that industrial system patches tend to happen on pre-planned schedules, rather than responding to emergent issues or suggested setting changes.

“Siemens published its advisory on August 11, and VulnCheck caught exploitation on October 30, three days after shipping its own detections,” Mahapatra said. “Eleven weeks is a short runway in OT, where firmware updates wait for planned maintenance windows, so a meaningful share of affected gateways will remain unpatched well into next year.”

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, added that the details of the exploits are a good news/bad news situation for CISOs. The good news is that the attacks did not appear to have targeted industrial systems. The bad news is the attackers found and accessed those systems anyway.

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, agreed.

“They don’t necessarily need to understand the equipment or operations connected to these gateways. They’re simply looking for systems capable of executing their commands,” he said. “That creates a concerning possibility where industrial operations could be disrupted by attackers who never intended to target critical infrastructure in the first place. Even generic malware consuming system resources or interfering with network communications could have operational consequences.”

Dickson added that closing this hole may not resolve the exposure. “The report also found that some attackers skipped the bot and left web shells, hidden back doors for running commands later,” Dickson said. “Patching closes the door. It does not evict anyone already inside.”

When individual signals are brought together, a clear picture forms. With Dynamic Risk Scoring (Q4), agent risk feeds into the same 0 to 100 risk score that Falcon Next-Gen SIEM already builds for the agent's owner and host. When an agent, its user, and its device all climb the risk list together, the coordination behind otherwise routine activity is harder to miss.

This foundation extends to the place many of these attacks begin: the AI tooling agents depend on. AI Ecosystem Detections (Q4) add detection logic for attacks on AI services, including LLM API abuse, stolen API keys, and the compromise of coding assistants, MCP servers, and agent frameworks. When the threat starts in a trusted tool rather than the agent itself, the Falcon platform is watching there too.

Because the context around an agent doesn't always live inside the Falcon platform, Federated Search Expansion lets teams search related data where it already lives, without re-ingestion. New connectors for GovCloud, Dynatrace, Databricks, and Snowflake are now generally available, with Splunk, Elastic, and Cribl Lake connectors following in Q4.

Act on Tough Questions

Once a risky agent surfaces, every analyst faces the same question: Did an agent’s owner do this, or did their agent do it without them knowing?

This is the work Multi-Agent Triage and Investigation (GA, announced at Fal.Con US 2026) was built for. SOC agents investigate detections end to end, with specialist agents working the case together on shared context across endpoint, identity, and the agent's activity.

Investigation coverage already spans the full range of Falcon platform and third-party sources. In Q4, triage coverage extends to CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian, CrowdStrike Falcon® Cloud Security, CrowdStrike Falcon® Shield, CrowdStrike Falcon® Data Security, and custom detections, including abnormal agent behavior flagged by Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. When an agent is flagged, it routes straight into an agentic investigation where the agent, its owner, and its host are already connected.

This shared context is what answers the tough question. Investigating agents can trace a session back to what the person asked for and separate it from what the agent did on its own. When the person's request was routine and everything that followed traces to instructions they never wrote, the verdict becomes clear: The insider was the agent, not the employee.

But a verdict doesn't stop a compromised agent that's still running. The Unified Agentic SOAR Experience (GA, announced at Fal.Con US 2026) is where response happens. Teams build, run, and govern all automation in the SOC, from AI agents to workflows to custom apps, in plain language. They set the mission and define triggers, data, rules, and actions to decide what runs autonomously and what requires approval. A single response decision can coordinate everything that needs to follow in parallel: stopping the agent, cutting off its access, keeping it from coming back, and documenting what happened. It's open by design and connects to any agent, model, or tool through API or MCP, so teams can govern automation across the security stack with visibility into what it's costing and what needs attention.

See it in action:

Autonomy That Earns Its Trust

As SOCs hand more of the work to agents, the controls that keep agents accountable matter as much as the speed they deliver.

CrowdStrike builds governance into every layer of the agentic SOC. It starts by watching the SOC's agents. Policy-Drift Agent Guardrails, powered by Falcon Guardian (Beta, Q4), screen every CrowdStrike Charlotte AI™ and AgentWorks interaction for policy drift, unauthorized tool calls, and out-of-bounds data access to catch the moment an agent steps outside its intended scope.

Frontier AI is enabling threat actors to rapidly learn an environment, identify weaknesses, and chain them into viable paths to critical systems. These capabilities allow adversaries to move faster while exploiting vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and other gaps to achieve their goals.

Traditional exposure management helps organizations identify and prioritize weaknesses largely as individual risks, and periodic red team engagements only provide deeper validation at a point in time. Neither approach alone can continuously validate defenses at the speed and scale of AI-enabled adversaries. Organizations must understand not only where they are exposed, but what adversaries could achieve and whether corrective actions can strengthen their defenses.

To fight AI-enabled adversaries with AI, CrowdStrike is introducing Agentic Adversary Emulation, a new AI-powered red teaming capability powered by CrowdStrike® SafeMind. It’s now in early access.

Agentic Adversary Emulation combines specialized AI models and offensive harnesses with real-world adversary intelligence and deep knowledge of customer environments. Operating within controlled, customer-approved boundaries in production environments, it uncovers exploitable attack paths, generates prioritized remediation recommendations and compensating controls, and validates whether corrective actions have strengthened defenses.

Attack Path Discovery to Validated Defense

Reveal Potential Attack Paths

Instead of simply identifying vulnerabilities, Agentic Adversary Emulation shows how attackers could exploit and chain weaknesses across systems and identities to compromise critical assets, and where defenses can stop them. This helps security teams understand what attackers could accomplish in their environment.

Turn Findings into Defensive Action

Agentic Adversary Emulation translates these exploitable attack paths into prioritized remediation actions and compensating controls that security teams can review and deploy through the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform. These may include applying patches, changing configurations, updating security policies, and creating new detections. By connecting demonstrated attack paths to corrective actions, this helps organizations focus on the weaknesses attackers can exploit and take targeted action to disrupt their progress.

Verify that Fixes Work

After corrective actions are implemented, Agentic Adversary Emulation repeats the attack simulation to verify whether those changes successfully disrupt previously identified attack paths. This helps organizations determine whether their fixes work and whether security controls can prevent adversaries from advancing toward critical assets. By connecting attack path discovery, remediation, and validation, Agentic Adversary Emulation creates a closed loop across offense and defense: attack, defend, and validate.

The CrowdStrike Advantage in AI-Powered Red Teaming

Agentic Adversary Emulation combines three core CrowdStrike capabilities to bring real-world adversary behavior into AI-powered red team testing:

Industry-leading adversary intelligence: CrowdStrike pioneered adversary-driven threat intelligence and tracks more than 290 adversaries globally. Recognized as a Leader by both Gartner and Forrester in threat intelligence, CrowdStrike draws on frontline threat hunting, incident response, CrowdStrike Falcon® platform telemetry, and intelligence on emerging threats to bring the latest adversary tradecraft directly into red team testing.

Deep knowledge of customer environments: The Falcon platform provides rich context across assets, identities, vulnerabilities, configurations, and security controls. This enables CrowdStrike to go beyond generic attack scenarios to emulate how adversaries could exploit interconnected weaknesses in a customer's environment to gain access to critical systems.

Powered by CrowdStrike SafeMind: SafeMind provides the purpose-built AI models and offensive harnesses that drive Agentic Adversary Emulation. Combining CrowdStrike’s latest adversary intelligence with deep visibility into customer environments, these systems emulate real-world adversary behavior at machine speed, continuously exploring attack paths and adapting as new weaknesses are discovered. Operating within customer-approved boundaries, they identify exploitable weaknesses, reveal how attackers could chain them together, and demonstrate what adversaries could achieve against critical assets.

During early access, CrowdStrike will work closely with selected customers to conduct controlled red teaming within defined safeguards and customer-approved boundaries, while refining the operational guardrails for safe execution in production environments.

Bringing Threat Intelligence to Smartphones

As AI accelerates adversary operations, security teams need trusted intelligence to make faster decisions, wherever they are. CrowdStrike is bringing its industry-leading threat intelligence and agentic AI capabilities to a new mobile app for iOS and Android. Available to CrowdStrike Falcon® Adversary Intelligence Premium customers, the app extends the Falcon experience beyond the desktop, providing direct access to the latest intelligence reports and the Threat Intelligence Agent.

Through the new app, customers can:

Stay ahead of emerging threats: Access expert-validated intelligence on adversaries, including their latest activities, evolving tactics, and emerging campaigns, to understand threats as they develop.

Act faster: Ask the Threat Intelligence Agent questions in natural language to quickly understand adversaries, campaigns, vulnerabilities, and emerging threats, identify what matters most, and determine what actions to take.

Make informed decisions anywhere: Access trusted intelligence and AI-driven analysis wherever decisions need to be made, without being tied to a desktop or the Falcon console.

Advancing Adversary-Driven Security for the AI Era

With Agentic Adversary Emulation and the new threat intelligence mobile app, CrowdStrike is expanding how organizations put adversary intelligence to work, from proactively simulating attacks and strengthening defenses to making informed security decisions wherever they are. Together, these innovations help defenders stay ahead of evolving threats through faster, more proactive, intelligence-driven security.

The browser has become a critical enterprise attack surface. Employees rely on the browser to access business applications, interact with AI tools, and handle sensitive data. Knowing this, attackers seek to exploit browser sessions for credential theft and data exfiltration.

Today, CrowdStrike Falcon® Seraphic® Enterprise Browser is natively available on the CrowdStrike Falcon platform, extending protection into the browser. Security teams can manage browser security alongside existing Falcon capabilities through a unified platform experience. This provides a simpler way to protect browser activity across managed and unmanaged devices, without requiring employees to adopt a dedicated enterprise browser or reroute traffic.

The availability of Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser on the Falcon platform delivers three key advantages:

Less to manage: Browser security, secure remote access, and BYOD/contractor access are managed directly within the organization’s Falcon platform environment.

Faster to deploy: Protection works in the browsers teams already use; there is no need to deploy a dedicated browser or reroute traffic.

Coverage where the sensor can't go: Protection extends to unmanaged, BYOD, and contractor devices without mobile device management (MDM) enrollment.

Stop Browser-Based Threats, Protect Data, and Secure Access

Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser provides real-time security controls inside browser sessions, where users access applications, handle sensitive data, and interact with AI tools. Its browser-layer capabilities address five important use cases:

Blocking browser-based attacks: Runtime inspection helps detect and disrupt malicious browser activity, including phishing, ClickFix, malicious scripts, and adversary-in-the-middle attacks.

Identity and session protection: Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser extends protection beyond authentication to help stop session token theft and session hijacking within active browser sessions.

Data and AI controls at the point of use: Teams can enforce policies on browser actions such as copy, paste, upload, and download; this helps prevent sensitive data from reaching unsanctioned web applications and generative AI tools.

Browser extension management: Security teams can inventory browser extensions, evaluate their risk, and enforce policies that allow or block risky extensions across supported browsers.

Secure access to private applications: Policy-controlled access to internal web applications and resources is provided for employees and contractors, including on unmanaged devices, without relying on traditional VPN or VDI for supported workflows.

Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser complements the broader security context of the Falcon platform. With browser telemetry available in CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM, analysts can search, investigate, and correlate browser activity with endpoint, identity, and third-party data to accelerate triage and response. With richer context and more places to act, security teams can follow the adversary rather than the boundaries between products.

Built for How Teams Work

As enterprise work increasingly happens in browsers, SaaS applications, and AI tools, browser security can no longer operate in isolation. By bringing Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser into the Falcon platform, CrowdStrike extends protection into the browser while unifying security operations across more of the enterprise attack surface. This helps organizations stop threats, protect sensitive data, and reduce operational complexity.

adf7dd30c91a.text:
AI is accelerating both sides of cloud security. Developers and coding agents are writing more code, pulling in more open source packages, and launching more cloud and AI workloads than security teams can review by hand. Adversaries use AI to move faster, and they are targeting everything organizations build and run, from the packages in automated pipelines, to the identities that control cloud resources, to the infrastructure powering AI applications.

Security teams must keep pace on both fronts to defend against this acceleration and secure the cloud their AI runs on. CrowdStrike Falcon® Cloud Security is built for this. It is powered by adversary intelligence tracking 290+ adversaries, so detections and risk prioritization reflect how attackers operate in the cloud. It runs on the same CrowdStrike Falcon platform that connects endpoint and identity protection with SOC operations, extending protection from developer endpoints and software supply chains to cloud workloads. Because proactive security and real-time cloud detection and response (CDR) share one platform, the exposure and attack path context teams build before an attack becomes the context analysts use to stop one.

The latest Falcon Cloud Security innovations, all now generally available, put this advantage to work from build to runtime. They help organizations stop compromised software before production, protect AI workloads and the infrastructure supporting them, and detect cloud attacks in seconds. Proactive security informs runtime defense by giving teams the context to understand risks and when to act on them. This connected defense spans business and mission-critical environments, including some of the hardest to secure.

Reduce Risk and Stop Threats Before Production

Securing the cloud that AI runs on starts with understanding where organizations are exposed and whether software entering production can be trusted. Falcon Cloud Security connects cloud risk, application context, and adversary intelligence to help teams close exposures before software is deployed.

Stop Supply Chain Threats

AI coding agents are pulling open source packages into automated builds faster than teams can review them. Adversaries can exploit that trust by compromising otherwise legitimate software. CrowdStrike observed ALTERED SPIDER compromise more than 300 software dependencies in a single day.1 A compromised dependency does not need a CVE to be dangerous, which means vulnerability scanning alone can miss the threat.

Supply Chain Security for Cloud extends the adversary intelligence CrowdStrike uses to detect and quarantine malicious packages on endpoints into container images. Falcon Cloud Security identifies compromised npm and PyPI packages during CI/CD and registry scanning, automatically reassesses previously scanned images as new threats are confirmed, and identifies affected running containers.

At deployment, the Falcon Kubernetes Admission Controller uses image assessment policies to alert on or block compromised images before they reach production. Together, endpoint and cloud protection connect the defense from package download through deployment to help teams stop compromised software.

Expand Cloud Risk and Asset Visibility

Security teams need to understand how exposures combine into opportunities for an adversary. Cloud Risks coverage in Falcon Cloud Security now extends to Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, where it connects exposure, effective permissions, vulnerabilities, and sensitive data context to identify high-risk combinations that isolated assessments can miss.

Supporting coverage expansions help teams assess more of their environment. Agentless Vulnerability Scanning for Google Cloud adds vulnerability and malware discovery for Linux-based Google Compute Engine instances without requiring additional sensor deployment. Expanded OCI inventory brings additional infrastructure, identities, and secrets into view. Together, these updates help teams account for more cloud assets and assess workloads where they cannot install an additional sensor.

Understand Applications and What Exposes Them

Cloud risk becomes more actionable when teams can connect it to the applications their business depends on. Expanded Application Security Posture Management (ASPM) brings containerized applications into Application Explorer with workload and cloud context, allowing Cloud Risks to evaluate them alongside other resources. Teams can identify combinations such as an internet-exposed Kubernetes workload running code with a remote code execution vulnerability.

New package exports map vulnerable dependencies to their associated applications, which helps teams assess blast radius and plan remediation across the application fleet. Enhanced third-party API integration findings identify external payment-service integrations and the operations applications invoke, helping teams assess exposure when a provider is compromised and uncover unauthorized integrations. The result is a clearer picture of which applications are affected and where remediation is needed.

Stop Cloud Attacks and Protect AI Workloads at Runtime

When an adversary gains access, security teams need to recognize malicious behavior, understand what is at risk, and respond while the attack is in progress. Falcon Cloud Security connects real-time detection with workload, identity, and exposure context to help defenders interrupt attacks across cloud environments.

Connect Cloud Exposure with Real-Time Detection and Response

CrowdStrike is extending Real-Time CDR to Microsoft Azure and Kubernetes, building on existing coverage for AWS and Google Cloud. Falcon Cloud Security continuously analyzes cloud audit activity as it streams, applies adversary-informed detection logic, and surfaces high-fidelity detections in seconds. Identity, asset, workload, endpoint, and adversary context helps analysts investigate and act while the attack is still in progress. All within the Falcon console, they can deny credentials or shut down compromised instances, or automate those actions with CrowdStrike® Charlotte Agentic SOAR to contain the intrusion before it spreads.

New detections combining Cloud Indicators of Attack (IOAs) with posture insights bring exposure context directly into threat detection. Suspicious behavior is evaluated alongside conditions such as dormant identities, elevated privileges, public exposure, and sensitive data so analysts can understand its potential consequences and prioritize response. A privileged action from a long-inactive identity, for example, takes on different significance when viewed alongside the conditions that could make it dangerous.

AI-based Anomaly Detection strengthens this defense by identifying suspicious behavior that predefined rules may miss. A dedicated machine learning model learns each customer’s baseline and evaluates deviations involving identities, APIs, and resources across multiple events to help uncover threats such as account takeover and API misuse. It is now available for AWS CloudTrail.

Together, these innovations connect attack behavior with exposure to help teams identify affected identities and workloads, assess potential impact, and focus response.

Protect AI Workloads and the Cloud They Run On

Securing AI requires protection for both AI interactions and the environments supporting them. Falcon Container Sensor and Falcon Guardian support for Anthropic APIs extends runtime detection to the prompt layer for supported AI workloads to help teams identify threats in AI interactions while maintaining a unified view of their environment.

Workload protection for Google Cloud Workstations brings cloud development environments into Falcon Cloud Security visibility, detection, and response workflows. Expanded AWS Bedrock AgentCore inventory complements that protection with visibility into the managed infrastructure supporting AI applications. These capabilities address distinct needs: detecting threats in supported AI interactions, protecting development workloads, and accounting for the resources behind AI applications.

Extend Protection to Regulated and Specialized Environments

Government agencies and regulated enterprises need cloud protection that reaches the environments their missions depend on. Expanded Falcon Cloud Security capabilities in US-GOV-1 and US-GOV-2 bring cloud detections, detection-rule management, and CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM workflows to GovCloud, including Kubernetes audit-log detections across Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, and Google GKE. Amazon S3 scanning in Merlin also extends sensitive-data discovery to customers in that environment.

DaemonSet support for Red Hat OpenShift on IBM Z and IBM LinuxONE, along with DaemonSet sensor support for Ubuntu Kairos, extends workload protection to specialized infrastructure. Teams can bring more of their environment into Falcon platform protection workflows without introducing separate tools, consoles, and investigation processes for each workload type. This helps close coverage gaps while reducing operational overhead.

Cloud Defense Built Around How Attacks Unfold

Securing the cloud AI runs on means understanding the software entering a build, the identities accessing cloud services, the data applications handle, and the behavior of workloads in production. Adversaries do not separate the software supply chain from the cloud identities, workloads, and data they want to reach, and defenders cannot either.

Falcon Cloud Security is built for this reality, combining CrowdStrike’s adversary intelligence with endpoint, identity, and cloud context to unite proactive security and real-time detection and response on one platform. That connection matters at every critical decision: whether to allow software into production, which exposures to fix first, and how to contain an attack already underway. Proactive context makes every real-time detection more precise and every response faster.

Expanded protection for government clouds and specialized infrastructure brings more of that connected defense to government agencies and regulated enterprises, helping protect the environments their businesses and missions depend on.

AI will keep accelerating the cloud. Falcon Cloud Security makes sure defenders accelerate with it.
