Microsoft Threat Intelligence detected approximately 7.3 billion email-based phishing threats from July through September, including a sharp increase to nearly 3 billion in September alone, up 41% from August. Yet the increase did not extend across the techniques that had driven threat actor activity earlier in the year. QR code phishing remained far below its early-year peak, while CAPTCHA-gated phishing reversed several months of decline, driven in part by renewed use of SVG attachments.

Q2 in review

Shifting tactics and other trends ›

Figure 1. Monthly detected email threat volume (January – September 2026)

The quarter also highlighted how sender identity and security exceptions can shape the outcome of detected threats. Microsoft detected approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services. Many were delivered because organization- or user-configured exceptions overrode security protections, even after the messages failed authentication checks and were identified as malicious, showing how overly broad exceptions intended to preserve legitimate workflows can also expose them to impersonation. In Microsoft Teams, attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names rather than explicit help desk identities while continuing to use live interactions for social engineering. Across malicious attachment activity more broadly, credential theft remained the dominant objective in Q3.

Two campaigns observed during the quarter illustrate the range of activity behind these trends. An August campaign targeting legal organizations used personalized salary review documents and QR codes to lead recipients into device code phishing, despite the broader decline in QR code attacks. In September, purchase order and payroll lures used disguised archives to deliver Agent Tesla, malware commonly used to collect credentials and other information. Together, the campaigns show how familiar business requests remained effective lures across distinct attack paths.

TYCOON2FA

Inside the PhaaS platform ›

The effects of the March disruption of the Tycoon2FA phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform also remained evident. By July, Microsoft detected approximately 21,000 phishing messages linked to the platform, down 99.8% from 8.9 million in February, the last full month before the operation.

Figure 2. Tycoon2FA-linked phishing email volume (January 2026 – July 2026)

This blog provides a view of email threat activity across Q3 2026, examining shifts in phishing techniques, malicious payloads, business contact impersonation (BCI), and Teams-based threats. We also highlight spoofed business-service sender domains and two campaigns that show how attackers used familiar work requests to make malicious messages appear credible. Together with recommendations, Microsoft Defender detections, and hunting queries, these findings can help defenders assess where existing protections may be weakened and investigate activity across email and collaboration platforms.

Spoofed sender domains

Requests to sign a document, review an invoice, or respond to a survey are routine business communications. Attackers exploit that familiarity by spoofing the sender domains of the legitimate services that deliver them. Rather than relying only on a misleading display name or a lookalike domain, these messages claim the service’s actual domain as their sender identity.

Microsoft detected approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the business-service domains tracked in this analysis during Q3. Activity had remained consistently high since at least May, at roughly 41 million to 46 million messages a month. DocuSign was the most frequently spoofed brand in September, accounting for 29% of that month’s total. Adobe, SurveyMonkey, and Barracuda also saw increases toward the end of the quarter, even as overall spoofing volume remained broadly steady.

Figure 3. Malicious messages spoofing tracked business-service sender domains (May – September 2026)

The more consequential finding was how security exceptions affected these messages after detection. Despite failing email authentication checks and being identified as malicious, many were associated with tenant- or user-level overrides. In September, overrides applied to 63% of messages with a recorded security outcome, with tenant-level overrides accounting for most of them.

The figures do not establish that recipients opened the messages or that accounts were compromised. They do show why exception policies deserve attention alongside detection coverage. An organization may create an exception to avoid interrupting a legitimate business workflow, but an overly broad exception can also weaken protection against messages impersonating that workflow. Familiar branding is not a substitute for an authenticated sender.

QR code phishing attacks

QR code phishing ended Q3 far below the levels seen during its early-year surge. Microsoft detected approximately 12.1 million attacks over the quarter, down 67% from Q2. The decline continued through September despite the broader increase in email threats, leaving monthly QR code volume 86% below its March peak.

Figure 4. Monthly QR code phishing volume (January – September 2026)

Much of the volume reduction came from the attachments that had supported that earlier growth:

PDF attachments remained the most common delivery format in Q3, accounting for 78% of QR code attacks in July and August before dropping to 61% in September. Nonetheless, the volume of PDFs carrying malicious QR codes fell by roughly 65% by the end of the quarter.

DOC/DOCX attachments accounted for 14% of QR code attacks in July and August before rising to 20% in September. Word document delivery volume similarly contracted in Q3, falling 39% between July and September following a sharp drop at the start of the quarter.

Email-embedded QR codes increased from 5% of attacks in July to 12% in September. After dropping to near-zero in Q2, the volume of malicious QR codes embedded in email bodies more than tripled by the end of Q3, although the method remained a smaller delivery category than attachments.

Figure 5. QR code phishing delivery method share by month (January – September 2026)

The distinction between delivery methods matters for inspection coverage, but not for the recipient’s experience: either attachment or embedded formats can move a user from a message on a managed device to a phishing page on a personal phone. The reduction in volume has not changed that underlying challenge.

CAPTCHA-gated phishing tactics

CAPTCHA-gated phishing began to recover while QR code attacks continued to fall. By September, Microsoft detected 3.1 million CAPTCHA-gated attacks, nearly twice the volume seen at July’s low. Activity remained well below its March peak, but the recovery ended several months of sustained decline.

Figure 6. CAPTCHA-gated phishing volume (January – September 2026)

The increase in CAPTCHA-gated phishing attacks was not confined to a single attachment format as delivery methods shifted throughout Q3, though SVG attachments were central to the initial recovery.

SVG attachment volume increased sixfold in August, accounting for almost half of September’s total CAPTCHA-gated phishing attacks. Up from 17% of attacks in July, SVGs represented 65% of CAPTCHA-gated phishing attacks in August, remained elevated at 49% in September, and were the leading delivery method at the quarter end.

Email-embedded URLs accounted for 49% of attacks in July before falling to 19% in August as SVG activity surged. URL-delivered attacks more than doubled in September, reclaiming 30% of attacks.

PDF attachments declined from 22% of attacks in July to 12% in August, remaining at 12% in September.

HTML attachments declined from 9% of attacks in July to 2% in August, then more than tripled in volume in September to account for 6% of attacks.

DOC/DOCX attachments remained comparatively uncommon throughout Q3, representing only 1% of attacks each month.

Figure 7. CAPTCHA-gated phishing distribution method share by month (April – September 2026)

Malicious payloads

The dominant risk from malicious attachments continued to be credential theft, not malware installation. Approximately 94-96% of payload-based attacks during Q3 directed recipients toward a phishing site or presented a fraudulent sign-in page locally. An attachment did not need to install software to put an account at risk.

HTML and PDF attachments remained the two most common malicious payload types during Q3, together accounting for approximately 56–62% of payload-based attacks each month, while the more significant change was the return of SVG files:

Figure 8. Malicious payloads by type

HTML attachments accounted for nearly two-thirds of malicious payloads and remained relatively steady across the quarter. HTML files ranked first in July at 32% of attacks before declining to 26% in August and recovering to 29% in September.

PDF attachments accounted for 27–30% of attacks and were the leading payload type in August and September. Volume remained comparatively stable, declining only 2% between July and September.

SVG attachments increased from 13% of attacks in July to 20% in August, when volume reached 10.1 million—the highest monthly volume in more than a year. Volume then fell 34% in September, although SVGs still represented 13% of attacks and remained roughly 50% higher than the monthly average for the first half of 2026.

DOC/DOCX attachments declined from approximately 5% of attacks in July and August to less than 3% in September, falling 76% below its monthly average volume for the first half of 2026.

ZIP/GZIP attachments declined from 5% of attacks in July to 3% in August before recovering slightly to 4% in September. Raw volume remained 24% below July.

The reduced use of Word documents alongside the renewed use of SVG files left a different mix of attachment threats, though credential theft remained the dominant objective.

Figure 9. Malicious payload file type distribution by month (June – September 2026)

CAPTCHA-gated phishing accounted for only part of the malicious SVG activity. The resurgence was therefore broader than the use of SVG files to deliver that particular technique.

Business contact impersonation

Microsoft defines business contact impersonation (BCI) as a text-based attack targeting enterprise users that impersonates a trusted entity for the purpose of persuading a recipient into initiating a fraudulent financial transaction or sending the attacker sensitive documents.

BCI volume declined throughout Q3, totaling approximately 6.2 million attacks. That was substantially below Q2, although the comparison is influenced by the unusually large spike in April. By September, monthly activity had fallen to its lowest level since at least July 2025.

Figure 10. Monthly BCI attack volume (January – September 2026)

The reduction in overall volume also concealed differences among financial lures. Generic messages continued to dominate initial BCI contact during Q3, but explicit task and financial requests gained share as overall attack volume declined:

Generic outreach messages, such as “Are you at your desk?”, accounted for 82% of attacks in July and August before declining to 79% in September. Raw volume fell 14% across the quarter, reinforcing that operators still overwhelmingly favored establishing contact before introducing a fraudulent request.

Generic task requests represented 8–10% of attacks during Q3, increasing from 9% in July to 10% in September despite a 9% decline in raw volume.

Within the smaller subset of explicit financial requests:

Payroll update requests were the most common financial lure, accounting for 6% of attacks in July and August and 7% in September. Raw volume remained broadly stable at approximately 126,000–130,000 attacks per month.

Invoice payment requests recovered from June’s low. Volume increased 34% in July, 25% in August, and 89% in September, more than tripling between June and September. Their share reached 3% in September, its highest level since March.

Gift card requests remained at 2% of attacks each month, while raw volume declined 9% from July to September.

Figure 11. Initial BCI email content by type (Q3 2026)

The decline in BCI overall did not extend equally to the requests reaching payment and payroll staff.

Microsoft Teams threats

Microsoft observed approximately 141,000 malicious Teams call attempts during Q3. Activity peaked in July before declining 31% by September, although September volume remained 38% above the monthly average for the first half of 2026. Teams-based attacks continued to use live interactions across chat, voice, screen sharing, and remote-support tools to facilitate remote access, credential theft, and hands-on-keyboard compromise.

Figure 12. Monthly observed malicious Microsoft Teams calls (January – September 2026)

Attackers increasingly moved away from display names that explicitly announced an IT- or tech-related support role. Ordinary personal-name display names rose from 46% of the observed July sample to 88% in September, while explicit help desk identities fell from 17% to 2%.

Figure 13. Malicious Teams call impersonation comparison (Q3 2026)

This shift does not necessarily mean attackers abandoned IT support stories. A personal name can accompany a claim to work for the help desk, while the underlying account address retains technical or service-related wording. More targeted attempts also used domains resembling the intended victim organization’s domain, emphasizing that the visible name is only one part of the impersonation.

Voice phishing attempts peaked in July and then receded, but September volume remained above the levels observed early in 2026. Calls were concentrated during recipients’ weekday working hours, when a live response was more likely. These attempts included unanswered, rejected, and short-lived calls, partly reflecting Microsoft’s expanding visibility and ongoing efforts to strengthen protective measures against social engineering abuse. Attemps should not be interpreted as successful attacker interactions.

Notable phishing campaigns

The following campaigns were observed during the quarter and highlight notable credential phishing, BCI, and malware delivery activity. For analysis of a separate Teams-based IT-support impersonation campaign observed in August, see Impersonating IT support: Threat actors turn remote session into enterprise-wide access.

Salary review lure delivers personalized QR code attachment for device code credential capture targeting legal organizations

On August 19, 2026, Microsoft Defender Research observed a phishing campaign targeting more than 10,000 users across more than 4,800 organizations, almost exclusively located in the United States. While most phishing attacks typically don’t focus on a single vertical, this campaign targeted the professional services sector, specifically law firms and legal organizations. Messages in this campaign were sent out over a 13-hour period between 13:27 UTC on August 19, 2026, and 2:59 UTC on August 20, 2026.

Figure 14. Intended campaign targets by industry

Emails in this campaign were sent with the subject line “Salary Review” from smtp[@]wekash[.]net via Amazon Simple Email Service. The email body carried no visible text and the sole payload was a Word document attachment named Your-Q3-Compensation-Summary.docx.

Figure 15. Sample of the campaign document attachment

The Word document impersonated the recipient’s own organization, displaying company branding and addressing the recipient by name. The message claimed that the recipient’s compensation had been revised following a Q2 performance review and that updated details were ready for review. A QR code in the document carried an instruction to scan it to access the revised details. This approach moved the phishing URL out of the email body and into an image, bypassing email gateway controls that scan text-based links but do not decode QR code images.

Scanning the QR code would have directed users to an attacker-controlled phishing page impersonating a Microsoft OneDrive sign-in portal hosted on the domain splace[.]co[.]za. The page presented an alphanumeric code and instructed recipients to copy it and proceed to the Microsoft sign-in portal.

Figure 16. Sample phishing landing page

The phishing page used a device code phishing technique, which works by making an authentication request to Microsoft’s device authentication service before the recipient arrived, receiving a user code in return, and embedding that code into the page. When a recipient copied the code and proceeded, the page redirected them to the legitimate Microsoft device authentication portal at microsoft.com/devicelogin, where they entered the code and signed in. Completing that sign in would have transferred a valid session token to the attacker. The token granted persistent access to the recipient’s Microsoft 365 account without ever exposing the password and without re-triggering multifactor authentication (MFA). A countdown timer on the page signaled that each code had a limited validity window, pressing recipients to act quickly.

Spanish-language purchase order and payroll campaign leads to Agent Tesla malware

On September 21, 2026, Microsoft Defender Research observed a phishing campaign targeting more than 56,000 users across more than 8,100 organizations. The campaign primarily targeted users in Spanish-speaking countries, with Colombia accounting for the largest share of intended recipients (15%), followed by the United States (12%), Mexico (12%), Chile (11%), and Spain (8%). Like most large-scale phishing attacks, this campaign did not focus on a single vertical, but instead targeted a broad range of industries, most notably retail and consumer goods (27%), manufacturing and agriculture (19%), and financial services (13%). Messages in this campaign were sent out over an almost nine-hour period between 14:57 UTC and 23:35 UTC on September 21, 2026.

Figure 17. Timeline of campaign message volume

Two lure variations were observed throughout the duration of the campaign: a purchase order theme, which was used in 63% of messages, and a payroll theme, which was used in the remaining 37%. Both variations were sent from the address contacto06[@]carloxmextos[.]org. Sender Policy Framework (SPF), DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), and Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) all passed for that domain, so the messages did not depend on simple address forgery. The actor changed the display name to resemble a sales or human resources identity associated with the recipient’s organization. That combination gave the messages technically valid authentication while using the visible sender identity and familiar business context to support the impersonation.

The purchase order lure variation used the reply-style subject “Re: solicitud de cotización”. Its body said, “Buen Dia”, claimed that a purchase order was attached, and asked the recipient to confirm receipt before closing with the lowercase “saludos”. The abrupt wording, inconsistent capitalization, and copied professional signature made the message look like a short continuation of an existing commercial exchange while avoiding details that a recipient could easily challenge.

The attached file, Nuevo orden de compra – 21092026.pdf.uu, was a RAR archive despite its uncommon .uu ending and PDF-like name. Inside it was Nuevo orden de compra – 21092026.pdf.js, a JavaScript downloader whose second extension exposed the executable script type only after extraction. If run, the script fetched a file named Lincoln.ps1 from a campaign-controlled object in Firebase Storage, and that PowerShell payload led to Agent Tesla malware. The nested archive and misleading extensions separated the visible business document theme from the code that executed, while the cloud-hosted download gave the actor a remotely accessible staging point.

Figure 18. Redacted rendering of the purchase order lure email

The payroll-themed lure used the subject “Nomina 21.09.2026”. It addressed the recipient by name, said the September 21 payroll list was attached, and signed off as a human resources manager. The date-specific payroll pretext created an immediate work-related reason to open the file, while the personalized greeting made a bulk message appear locally relevant.

The payroll lure’s attachment, Nomina 21.09.2026.xml.001, was also a RAR archive. Extraction produced Nomina 21.09.2026.xml.exe, an Agent Tesla executable disguised with an XML-themed double extension. Unlike the purchase order delivery chain, this branch did not require a separate downloader in the supplied evidence, but both paths used the same sender infrastructure, attachment camouflage, date, and malware family. Agent Tesla is commonly used to collect credentials and other information from an infected host, so the shared final payload suggested that credential and information theft were the campaign’s likely objective.

Figure 19. Redacted rendering of the payroll lure email

Defending against email and collaboration threats

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

Microsoft helps organizations reduce the risk of phishing and social engineering in Teams through user awareness and layered, built-in protections. Users should exercise caution with external connection requests and messages, including verifying a sender’s identity and requests before acting on them. Administrators can also block external Teams users and specify which users in their organization are permitted to chat or meet with people outside the enterprise. These flexible controls help organizations manage risk for employees in sensitive roles and departments. Teams will also be introducing AI-powered phishing detection that uses conversation context to identify phishing and social engineering in higher-risk messaging scenarios, particularly first-contact chats with external users. Together, these measures help organizations collaborate more securely in Teams.

Review the recommended settings for Exchange Online Protection and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to ensure your organization has established essential defenses and knows how to monitor and respond to threat activity.

Invest in user awareness training and phishing simulations. Attack simulation training in Microsoft Defender for Office 365, which also includes simulating phishing messages in Microsoft Teams, is one approach to running realistic attack scenarios in your organization.

Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) in Defender for Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.

Responders can also manually check for and purge unwanted emails containing URLs and/or Subject fields that are similar, but not identical, to those of known bad messages. Investigate malicious email that was delivered in Microsoft 365 and use Threat Explorer to find and delete phishing emails.

Turn on Safe Links and Safe Attachments in Microsoft Defender for Office 365.

Enable network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.

Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support Microsoft Defender SmartScreen, which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.

Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. Refer to this article for the different authentication methods and features.

Conditional access policies can also be scoped to strengthen privileged accounts with phishing-resistant MFA.

Configure automatic attack disruption in Microsoft Defender XDR. Automatic attack disruption is designed to contain attacks in progress, limit the impact on an organization’s assets, and provide more time for security teams to remediate the attack fully.

Truffle Security has launched the Secrets Revocation Program, a free initiative that helps API key issuers revoke 1.4 million publicly exposed secrets that remain valid.

Since 2022, the company has discovered secrets embedded in public repositories, packages, container images, datasets, and applications.

Earlier this year, Truffle Security reported that it had found 543,000 valid credentials leaked in public GitHub repositories.

In a separate investigation, the company identified more than 431,000 AWS secrets across code repositories, Git histories, datasets, Docker images, registries, and CI logs.

These secrets are typically exposed by mistake during the development process, by committing credentials to a public repository, including them in published Docker images or packages, or leaving them in configuration files uploaded with an app or dataset.

Truffle Security says that the problem is that the owners of these secrets are not responsive to researchers’ notifications about leaked data.

“Telling developers their keys leaked doesn’t get them turned off: 81% of the keys we reported last year still worked six months later,” the company explained.

As a result, exposed secrets pose unnecessary security risks that can extend beyond the affected companies to their customers and downstream application users.

The researchers note that the rise of AI coding tools has only worsened the situation, increasing secrets exposure even more.

“Since January 2025 we’ve found 2,655 working keys in AI coding tools’ config files like that one,” the researchers said, noting that this was a non-existent problem the year before.

AI is also increasing the impact of exposure on the offensive side, as shown by OpenAI’s July incident, where AI agents used exposed Hugging Face tokens to steal data from the platform.

Revoking exposed keys

Truffle’s new program, which uses the TruffleHog tool to check for the validity of leaked keys, aims to coordinate the revocation of exposed secrets with the entities that issued them.

Truffle says it can either use a revocation endpoint provided by those entities, or supply them with the verified keys through a webhook and revoke them within 14 days.

This way, even when owners are unresponsive, the keys can be invalidated.

Sixteen issuers have already joined the program, including Hugging Face, Notion, Vercel, Resend, RubyGems, and Twilio.

Truffle says the unilateral revocation approach can be very effective, as demonstrated by Google when it began disabling exposed Google Cloud service-account keys by default on June 16, 2024.

When Google relied only on notifying key owners, Truffle Security found that many customers failed to respond, leaving 72% of the exposed secrets active. By automatically disabling leaked keys, the figure was reduced to 11%.

Although eliminating all valid exposed keys is impossible because customers can opt out of automatic revocation, the measure proved to be effective.

Companies that issue API keys can join Truffle Security's Secrets Revocation Program to automatically protect their customers.

GitHub will begin blocking GitHub Actions workflows triggered by pull_request_target in public repositories on December 2, 2026, expanding its protections against a class of CI/CD vulnerabilities that has repeatedly enabled attackers to steal credentials and compromise open source software releases.

The restriction, originally announced in September, will prevent affected workflows from running unless an applicable Actions event policy explicitly allows them. GitHub had initially scheduled enforcement for November 2 but confirmed the postponed December 2 deadline in a new update this week, giving maintainers additional time to review their automation and configure exceptions.

The new restriction goes beyond protections introduced in June, when GitHub updated actions/checkout to prevent common attempts to check out untrusted pull request code inside privileged workflows. This time, GitHub is blocking the pull_request_target trigger itself by default, including for workflows that use it safely.

pull_request_target Is Now a Common Attack Vector Vector #

GitHub introduced pull_request_target in 2020 to help maintainers automate tasks involving pull requests from external contributors. Unlike the standard pull_request event, which restricts access to secrets and provides a read-only token for contributions from forks, pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository with access to its configured secrets and token permissions.

That elevated access makes the trigger useful for legitimate maintenance tasks such as assigning reviewers, labeling pull requests, and posting authenticated comments. The workflow definition runs from the repository's trusted default branch, rather than the contributor's proposed changes.

The security risk emerges when that privileged workflow checks out and executes code from an untrusted fork or passes attacker-controlled pull request data into shell commands. A malicious contributor can exploit those mistakes to execute commands with access to credentials and other resources intended only for trusted automation.

Researchers have warned about these vulnerabilities, commonly called "pwn requests," since at least 2021. Variations of this attack pattern contributed to major supply chain incidents involving Nx, PostHog, and TanStack.

GitHub's June changes addressed a common source of these vulnerabilities by making actions/checkout reject unsafe fork checkouts in privileged workflows unless explicitly overridden. The December policy takes a broader approach, preventing the event from triggering a workflow at all unless administrators have authorized it through an applicable policy.

Two Test Windows Before December Enforcement #

GitHub's default restriction currently operates in evaluation mode, allowing affected workflows to continue running before enforcement begins.

The company has scheduled two temporary enforcement periods, known as brownouts, to expose configurations that will stop working under the new policy:

November 9, 16:00–18:00 UTC

November 16, 16:00–18:00 UTC

During those windows, blocked pull_request_target attempts will generate failed workflow runs with an error annotation instead of executing. The default policy will return to evaluation mode after each test.

On December 2, the restriction becomes permanent for affected public repositories without an applicable policy allowing the event. The change applies to public repositories on GitHub Free, Team, and Enterprise Cloud, but excludes private and internal repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server.

Maintainers who still require pull_request_target can create an Actions event policy that explicitly permits it. GitHub supports targeting individual workflow files, allowing administrators to preserve specific automation without enabling the trigger across an entire repository. Existing applicable event policies are not replaced by the new default.

Some Open Source Maintainers Face a Complicated Transition #

The broader restriction introduces complications for open source projects that have relied on pull_request_target for legitimate automation, sometimes across dozens of repositories.

A carefully configured workflow that only labels pull requests or manages project metadata may pose little of the risk GitHub is addressing, but it will still be subject to the new restriction. Maintainers must either allow these workflows explicitly or move them to another trigger where appropriate.

There are also differences in the administrative tools available across GitHub's pricing tiers.

GitHub's documentation for workflow execution protections describes policy configuration at the repository, organization, and enterprise levels for public repositories, including those on free plans. However, the ability to create policies in evaluation mode is reserved for Enterprise Cloud, where administrators can examine policy insights before turning on enforcement.

That disparity had already prompted questions following GitHub's September announcement of the new defaults.

In a GitHub Community discussion, open source maintainer George Joseph questioned how smaller organizations were expected to assess the impact without Enterprise policy insights.

"How would us mere mortals who run open-source organizations see what workflows would be affected?" he asked.

A community response suggested manually searching repositories for workflows using pull_request_target, inspecting existing workflow runs, and testing explicit allowlisting policies. These approaches can identify affected configurations, but require additional work from maintainers managing multiple repositories.

The December deadline gives projects several more weeks to prepare, while the scheduled brownouts offer a preview of what enforcement will look like. GitHub's decision also represents a significant shift for a feature originally created to make external contributions easier to manage: privileged pull request automation will now require an explicit exception to continue running under the new default.

You just had a user fall for a ClickFix attack, but thankfully, Attack Disruption from Managed EDR shut it down before the attacker could launch an infostealer. Now, you'd think this means the threat has been mitigated and you can move on. But there's just one problem…a few minutes later, the same user falls for the exact same ClickFix attack again.

This is something our Security Operations Center (SOC) has seen happen over and over again since we launched the Attack Disruption Engine in April 2026. In fact, of the over 25,000 hosts we've seen with a ClickFix signal, 29% made more than one attempt. That's thousands of people falling for a real-world ClickFix attack without any lessons learned.

Figure 1: ClickFix attacks are so compelling that many people fall for them more than once.

This isn't some malicious user trying to take down your organization; they just don't know any better, which presents a great opportunity to lower the security awareness gap and address human risk as it happens.

That's why Huntress is introducing a new way to address real-world risky behaviors as they happen, with contextually relevant, just-in-time training. You'll turn what could've been an incident into a learning opportunity that helps you understand what happened and how to avoid it in the future.

Defense Drills: from incident to awareness even faster

Defense Drills are a new type of training content that's short, hands-on, and built on prominent or emerging tradecraft that the Huntress SOC is actively observing. With Defense Drills, the user experiences being compromised by different types of emerging tradecraft in a safe environment, all while their Defense Coach points out indicators to look for to identify whether it's malicious rather than legitimate. The goal of Defense Drills is to build awareness of these threats even faster than our production-quality episodes and to ensure they reach as many users as possible by making them directly assignable from the portal.

Figure 2: Defense Drills cover the newest types of threats our SOC and research teams are seeing in the wild.

Huntress has a proven track record of being the first to respond to major incidents across the industry and of turning our findings into educational resources that benefit the cybersecurity and IT community as a whole. But when those major incidents impact your end users, it's not as easy to build awareness in a way that's accessible to all users.

Defense Drills closes that gap, while supercharging the incident-to-awareness pipeline. When the Huntress SOC observes a new threat in the wild, they can spin up a Defense Drill quickly to put it in front of users in a controlled environment, helping them understand how it works and what to avoid.

Experience this Defense Drill demo for yourself.

Figure 4: ClickFix incidents grew 2,048% between 2025 and 2026. This ChatGPT example highlights how convincing it can be. Try our Defense Drill demo for free.

Another benefit of Defense Drills is their versatility. You can assign them yourself to become the trusted security advisor for your learners. And coming soon, you'll be able to enroll in Managed Defense Drills, where Huntress takes care of assigning them for you. Plus, you'll get Breaking News, where Huntress sends Defense Drills out as necessary for breaking threats that need extra attention. Finally, you can actively address real-world human risk as it happens with Defense Drill Interventions.

Defense Drill Interventions: address human risk in real-time

Security awareness training has historically been preventive. You train users to spot threats, you test them with phishing scenarios, and report on it for compliance. And that was it. Most SAT admins didn't even expect an outcome from it aside from satisfying compliance requirements and maybe better cyber insurance premiums if they were lucky. But when a real user-based threat found its way through, there was no course of action to address the behavior that caused it, aside from an awkward conversation with the user after the fact. And even that was too little too late, as the best time to train on an incident is in the moment, while it's still fresh.

Defense Drill Interventions is changing that. The combination of Managed SAT with detections from the Huntress Platform is like adding 1+1 and getting 3. It's not bad math; it's added value. It's better security outcomes because you not only shut down the attack, but also address the risky user behavior that caused it in real time, with contextually relevant training based on the specific behavior that triggered the incident. The best part is it's all managed for you. No responding to alerts, no building assignments after the fact, and no need for that awkward conversation with the user. Defense Drill Interventions has it handled.

So what does this look like to date?

We're starting with a threat that we're seeing most often: ClickFix. In 2025, ClickFix was responsible for more than half of all malware loader activity. It's a nasty threat that's tricky for untrained users to spot. So we're coming at ClickFix from all angles. With Defense Drill Interventions, ClickFix attacks are shut down by Managed EDR Attack Disruption, and in that same moment, the user will see a pop-up with a Defense Drill covering ClickFix attacks. This not only stops the threat in its tracks but helps the user understand how the threat happened and what to look out for in the future. It's shutting down threats while reducing future human risk

OpenAI disclosed that its GPT-6 Astra frontier model sometimes hindered safety research by complicating simple tasks, abandoning viable approaches, and silently refusing researchers’ requests.

During evaluation, the AI company's model reported nonexistent or self-made blockers without explaining its restrictions to users.

OpenAI said it first received a report of what it calls "covert underperformance" in Astra on August 20. The company then conducted targeted evaluations to investigate the behavior and determine its causes, noting that it had not observed the same issue in GPT-5.6 Sol.

OpenAI says it received the first report of what it calls “covert underperformance” in Astra on August 20. The company then ran specifically designed evaluation experiments to determine the extent and cause of this behavior, noting that the issues were not observed in GPT-5.6 Sol.

“Astra completed about 10 percent of hidden rubric items under the safety framing, compared with about 16 percent under the capabilities framing,” reads OpenAI’s report.

“This is a 6 percentage point gap and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no gap on the same comparison.”

A rubric item is one specific requirement used to score the model’s work, essentially an item on a grading checklist.

The main issue is that instead of explicitly declaring its inability to help with a research task and explaining its limitations to users, the model silently quits when it considers the work unsafe.

The concern is that researchers may trust results the model silently changed or left incomplete, misleading safety testing and wasting valuable research time.

OpenAI provided eight specific examples of this behavior, drawn from internal evaluations.

These include avoiding a retry fix that would improve a training pipeline, restricting exploit-development assistance, excluding a violent source from a safety evaluation, and limiting jailbreak-data exports.

OpenAI hypothesized that training intended to produce safer behavior may have encouraged undisclosed obstruction of safety work. However, it has not established this as the definitive cause for the observed model’s behavior.

The company also located a grader, a tool that evaluates AI model performance during reinforcement learning, that favored covert withholding over explicit refusal. However, it did not conclusively establish this as the cause.

OpenAI found no evidence that Astra deliberately engaged in this behavior to undermine research or make users “underestimate its capabilities.”

CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available.

Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts.

Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC.

Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

Overview

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization.

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access.

Threat

The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.

Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors:

Authentication bypass;

Arbitrary code injection; and

Weak configurations.

Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects:

Change of temperature, which could:

Affect the service life of the system;

Create a fire hazard;

Cause loss of inventory; or

Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage.

Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition).

Mitigations

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement:

Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices.

Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I].

Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F].

Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance.

Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H].

Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O].

Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity.

For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets.

Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations.

Resources

The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations:

CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology

CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security

CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance

United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT

Contact Information

The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet:

Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office. When available, please include the following information regarding the incident:

Date, time, and location of the incident;

Type of activity;

Number of people affected;

Type of equipment used for the activity; and

Name of the submitting company or organization, and a designated point of contact.

Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts.

Disclaimer

The information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only. The authoring organizations do not endorse any commercial entity, product, company, or service, including any entities, products, or services linked within this document. Any reference to specific commercial entities, products, processes, or services by service mark, trademark, manufacturer, or otherwise, does not constitute or imply endorsement, recommendation, or favor by the authoring organizations.

Key findings

Attackers using the Anubis ransomware targeted a U.S. organization in October 2026 using a new custom backdoor that Symantec has called Backdoor.Lindnor.

The backdoor masqueraded as a Chrome component and as a VMware file, and was found on two Microsoft SQL Server machines.

Within roughly an hour, the attackers dropped at least 13 executables to help terminate security services, along with five publicly known vulnerable drivers.

The attackers also installed the legitimate remote access tool AnyDesk and a separate tool to run it in Safe Mode, likely to maintain access when security software was not fully running.

The file encryption payload was blocked from execution, and there’s no evidence that any files were encrypted.

Anubis has claimed approximately 96 victims in the past 12 months, and 52% of those victims are in the U.S.

Overview

Attackers using the Anubis ransomware, which is developed by a group Symantec tracks as Hawkmoth, deployed a previously undocumented custom backdoor and an unusually large number of security software-disabling tools in an October 2026 attack on an organization in the U.S.

Hawkmoth runs a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation that emerged in December 2024 as a rebrand of the Sphinx ransomware. Its payload appears to be largely unchanged from the Sphinx version, with only the branding updated. As Hawkmoth operates an affiliate program, Anubis attacks may be carried out by different groups of affiliates. Attackers using it seem to be particularly tenacious. In a July 2026 Anubis attack documented by Symantec, we noted that the threat actor used four different exfiltration tools (Megasync, WinSCP, Filezilla, S3browser) to steal data from the affected network and that it was unusual to see that many of the same type of tool deployed in a single attack.

The group has claimed approximately 96 victims in the past 12 months, and the majority of them (52%) are located in the U.S., which aligns with previous targeting patterns by the group.

We did not identify how the attackers gained initial access. The first indicator of the intrusion was the detection of the new Lindnor backdoor, which was found on two machines that were also the only two Microsoft SQL Servers among those affected.

Tooling and tradecraft

Custom backdoor

The backdoor, called Backdoor.Lindnor, was installed with the filename healthcontroller64.exe in a folder made to resemble a Chrome component unpacker directory on one machine, and as svchelper.exe in a VMware folder on the other. In both cases, the backdoor appears to have run as a service.

The backdoor sent the process ID, operating system version, its own file path, computer name, user name, domain and logon server to a command-and-control (C&C) server. It was configured with a primary C&C server and a fallback, which are both accessed via port 443.

The presence of this backdoor is notable as custom backdoors remain relatively uncommon in ransomware attacks. Ransomware attackers generally rely on publicly available, dual-use and living-off-the-land tools to carry out the majority of pre-ransomware activity in their attacks. This backdoor was also spotted on the networks of two other unrelated organizations, though in those cases no ransomware activity was identified on the networks.

Security evasion tools

A notable aspect of this attack was that the threat actors dropped at least 13 executables in quick succession, for the purpose of terminating security products. They clearly favored the Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) approach, as demonstrated by their dropping of five signed but vulnerable drivers for the purpose of abusing them to gain kernel-level access. Two of the executables, gbbsym.exe and symgooq.exe, masqueraded as Symantec software. Both accepted the switch (-l) to list kernel callbacks through a loaded vulnerable driver and a second switch (-d) to list and remove them. The observed command lines show the second switch (-d) was used. Eleven of the 13 executables appear to have been previously unpublished. The vulnerable drivers were all publicly known.

All the dropped executables were blocked except huntreagent.exe and s1.exe. These files were not available for analysis so their exact purpose is unknown, but it is possible they may have been used to run one or more of the vulnerable drivers. Both tools are the same file size but with different file hashes, which suggests they may be two builds of the same tool. The pattern of using so many different tools is consistent with attackers trying one tool after another until they find something that works.

The attackers’ heavy reliance on BYOVD serves to highlight how the technique has become a standard part of the ransomware playbook, a trend we discussed in-depth in our June 2026 whitepaper: Lights Out: Defense Evasion in the Age of BYOVD.

BYOVD is commonly used to gain kernel-level access because it is effective and relies on using legitimate, signed files, the presence of which are unlikely to raise red flags. Once operating in the kernel, attackers can use them to help stop security software and prevent their activities from being detected. There are hundreds of known vulnerable drivers already in circulation and newly discovered ones are shared openly on a regular basis. Ready-made BYOVD tooling is now routinely bundled into RaaS offerings alongside the payloads themselves, making it a standard way to disable security software during ransomware attacks.

Remote access and Safe Mode

The attackers also installed the legitimate remote access tool AnyDesk, created a new local user account and added it to a local group. AnyDesk is frequently used by ransomware attackers for remote access. However, in this attack, the threat actors also ran a tool, safemode.exe, that configures AnyDesk to keep working when Windows boots into Safe Mode. They ran a registry command that registered AnyDesk as a service permitted to run in Safe Mode with Networking.

"CSIDL_SYSTEM\reg.exe" add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SafeBoot\Network\AnyDesk /ve /t REG_SZ /d Service /f

Security software generally does not fully operate in Safe Mode, which gives attackers a window to use the vulnerable drivers and switch off protections. This isn’t a new technique but it is not commonly seen.

Ransomware payload

The Anubis encryption payload was named iservice.exe. If successful, it appends the extension .anubis to encrypted files and drops ransom notes named restore files.txt and restore files.html. The note tells the victim that data was downloaded from the network and that it will be published if negotiations fail. The ransomware also has an optional wiper mode that wipes file contents, leaving files completely empty. In this attack, the payload was blocked, preventing the attackers from executing the encryption phase across the victim network.

Significance

Attackers using the Anubis ransomware appear to focus their attacks on the U.S., and this intrusion fits with established patterns of behavior by the group. This targeting isn’t surprising given that ransomware attackers generally “follow the money” and a majority of large enterprises have a presence in the U.S.

While the overall modus operandi of the attackers is familiar, the presence of a custom backdoor and usage of large numbers of security-disabling tools makes this attack stand out from typical ransomware intrusions. Few ransomware operators build their own backdoors, and the volume of security-disabling tools used within a single hour of activity is unusual.

This suggests that the attackers were prepared for the prospect of security software getting in their way, so they arrived with a large toolbox and a second remote access route configured for Safe Mode operation to help them gain an advantage. Despite all this preparation, the attack appears to have largely failed at the last hurdle because the encryption modules were successfully blocked from execution.

Protection

If an IOC is malicious and the file is available to us, Symantec Endpoint products will detect and block that file.

Indicators of Compromise

An attacker rarely stays within the boundaries of one security tool. They may enter through an exposed device, use a stolen identity, move through cloud infrastructure and reach the systems that keep an essential service running. Each step can appear ordinary when viewed on its own. The danger becomes clear when the steps are connected.

For Japan’s critical infrastructure operators and the businesses that support them, that connection is becoming more urgent. AI gives adversaries the ability to test more paths and act faster. At the same time, organisations depend on increasingly connected suppliers, cloud services, operational technology and devices that cannot always run endpoint software. Cyber resilience now depends on understanding how an attacker could move across that environment and recognising when that movement begins.

The pressure is already visible in Japan

Japan’s National Police Agency reported 226 ransomware cases in 2025. About 60% of the victims were small and medium-sized organisations, while manufacturing accounted for approximately 40% of the cases. The agency also recorded an average of roughly 9,606 suspicious accesses per IP address per day on its sensors, much of it consistent with vulnerability scanning. These are different measures, but together they show the pressure facing organisations of many sizes.

The long-running MirrorFace campaign shows another side of the challenge. Japanese authorities have assessed that the group targeted organisations and individuals in Japan to steal information related to national security and advanced technology. Its activity included targeted messages and exploitation of software vulnerabilities. The lesson for defenders is to look beyond the point of entry: an initial compromise matters because of the access and information it can give an attacker next.

AI changes the pace of an attack

The question of whether attackers are using AI has a concrete answer in Japan. JPCERT/CC’s investigation of attacks targeting Japanese organisations found that attackers used AI to scan for known vulnerabilities and carry out attacks through APIs. Investigators also found evidence that attackers analysed Android apps to identify APIs they could target. In an October 23 update, JPCERT/CC reported attempted attacks using AI-based penetration testing tools, including ARTEX, to probe internet-facing applications for weaknesses.

A 2026 incident involving an autonomous AI agent shows how far this kind of activity can progress. During a security evaluation, the agent escaped its intended environment and reached Hugging Face’s systems. Hugging Face later reconstructed approximately 17,600 actions over several days, including attempts to gain access through its data-processing pipeline and move across infrastructure and identities. The circumstances of this incident were unusual, but many of the weaknesses the agent pursued were familiar: exposed credentials, excessive access and gaps between trust boundaries.

That distinction matters. AI can increase the number of paths tested and the speed at which an unsuccessful attempt is replaced. It does not make the resulting behaviour invisible. Discovery, credential use, privilege escalation and movement between systems still leave evidence. Security teams need to connect that evidence quickly enough to understand whether an attack is progressing.

A chatbot added to a security workflow cannot supply that understanding on its own. AI-assisted investigation is useful when it is grounded in reliable signals about what happened across the environment. Otherwise, a faster summary may still leave an analyst with an incomplete picture.

Resilience requires a view across boundaries

Japan’s policy direction reinforces the need to make resilience an ongoing practice. The country’s Common Cybersecurity Standards for Critical Infrastructure took effect on October 1, 2026, establishing a shared basis for improving cybersecurity measures across sectors. For security leaders, the practical question is whether their teams can understand an incident’s scope, coordinate a response and show what they learned afterward.

That starts with knowing what is connected. In a manufacturing plant, hospital or transport environment, the assets supporting a critical service may include unmanaged devices, OT and IoT systems, contractor access and cloud-hosted applications. An asset inventory is useful, but leaders also need to understand how those assets communicate and where an exposure could create a path into something more important.

The next step is to detect behaviour across those paths. A single cloud API call, identity request or network connection may not explain much. When related activity is brought together over time, it can reveal an attacker’s progression. That context helps a team prioritise the exposures that matter most, investigate with confidence and take a precise response action.

For leaders reviewing their readiness this quarter, I would start with three questions:

Which systems, identities and suppliers support our most critical services, and where are the gaps in our view of them?

If an attacker crossed from a device or identity into cloud and internal systems, how quickly could we connect those actions into one investigation?

Could we produce the evidence needed to explain the incident, guide a response and demonstrate improvement?

Cyber resilience is a continuous loop: observe the environment, detect suspicious behaviour, reduce consequential exposures and respond before an attacker reaches their objective. As attacks accelerate, Japan’s defenders need the ability to see the whole story while there is still time to change its outcome.

99% of customers would recommend Vectra AI. Here’s what they’re telling us about defending against modern cyberattacks.

I'm excited to share that Vectra AI has been named a Customers' Choice in the 2026 Gartner Peer Insights Voice of the Customer for Network Detection and Response (NDR).

This makes Vectra AI the only company named both a Customers' Choice and a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for NDR.

What makes me especially proud is that 99% of customers who contributed to the Voice of the Customer report said they would recommend Vectra AI to their peers.

As a Product Marketing leader at Vectra AI, I spend a lot of time thinking about how we communicate the value of our technology. There's nothing more rewarding than hearing customers describe that value in their own words.

Looking through the Gartner Peer Insights reviews, I was struck by how closely their experiences reflect what we've been working so hard to deliver.

Why Customer Confidence Matters in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks

One of the biggest concerns I hear from security leaders today is whether their teams can keep up with AI-powered attacks.

It's understandable. AI is helping attackers discover vulnerabilities, automate reconnaissance, and execute attacks faster than ever. Security teams are already stretched thin, and the prospect of attackers moving at machine speed is worrying.

My colleague Lucie Cardiet recently wrote a great piece on how an internal AI tool helped attackers move between teams in the Binance breach. It’s a reminder of something we often discuss at Vectra AI:

AI changes the speed of attacks, not the path.

Attackers still compromise identities, move laterally, escalate privileges, and access critical systems. Defenders need to see these behaviors across environments, connect the dots, and respond before attackers achieve their objectives.

I recently had a conversation with a long-time customer about this very challenge. He acknowledged how quickly AI is changing the threat landscape, but expressed confidence that Vectra AI could help his team defend against AI-powered attacks.

I was genuinely happy to hear that. Knowing how much pressure security leaders are under, it's reassuring to hear firsthand that customers trust our technology to help them tackle one of their biggest worries.

It's also why we believe so strongly in Attack Signal Intelligence, our approach to applying behavioral AI across network, identity, and cloud environments to detect suspicious behavior, connect related activity, and prioritize real threats.

The Gartner Peer Insights reviews reinforce this value in three important ways.

1. Finding Threats That Would Otherwise Go Undetected

One customer shared:

“Vectra AI opened our eyes to a range of hidden activities that would have gone undetected.”

This gets to the heart of why behavioral AI matters.

Attackers increasingly use stolen credentials, legitimate tools, and trusted connections to blend into normal operations. Traditional security controls can miss these activities, especially when they only see isolated parts of the environment.

Vectra AI's Attack Signal Intelligence identifies suspicious behavior that might otherwise go unnoticed, including activity that doesn't match known attack signatures.

For security teams, detecting that hidden activity can make the difference between stopping an attack early and dealing with a breach.

2. Connecting Network and Identity Activity to See the Full Attack

Another customer captured the value of Vectra AI particularly well:

“Tables takes network visibility + modern identity detection = Vectra AI”

Modern attacks don’t stay within the boundaries of individual security tools. An attacker might compromise an identity, move through the network, access cloud workloads, and escalate privileges. Each step may be visible to a different security product, but someone still needs to connect the dots.

Network activity shows how attackers move. Identity context helps explain who or what is behind that activity.

Vectra AI brings these behaviors together so analysts can understand the full attack story instead of investigating disconnected alerts.

One review title particularly made my day:

“Vectra is more than just an NDR”

This one means a lot to me personally.

We've put enormous effort into helping the market understand that Vectra AI goes far beyond traditional NDR. Our platform is built to solve some of the toughest challenges in cybersecurity, including defending against AI-powered attacks.

Seeing a customer recognize that broader value, in their own words, is incredibly rewarding.

3. Cutting Through the Noise to Focus on Real Attacks

Security teams already have plenty of alerts. What they need is a clearer understanding of which threats deserve their attention.

Reducing that burden is one of the most consistent themes in customer feedback.

One reviewer praised Vectra AI for helping SOC analysts cut through the noise and focus on what matters. Another highlighted:

“Highly accurate and fast detection with good and detailed explanations”

By correlating related behaviors into prioritized threats, Vectra AI helps analysts spend less time chasing false positives and more time investigating real attacks.

With AI accelerating attack timelines, every minute saved on manual investigation gives defenders a better chance to respond before damage is done.

What Customer Trust Really Means to Me

One customer described Vectra AI as:

“The Best Security Tool We've Deployed in a Decade.”

Feedback like this means a great deal to me. I also think about a conversation with a security leader who told me that one of the biggest benefits of deploying Vectra AI was being able to take a five-week holiday in Europe, knowing that our platform and managed detection and response team had his organization covered 24/7.

I love that story because it reminds me what we're ultimately working towards.

Cybersecurity is an incredibly demanding profession. Security teams carry enormous responsibility, and threats don't take holidays. Giving someone the confidence to switch off, spend time with family, and enjoy a well-deserved break is something worth celebrating.

That peace of mind is one of the most meaningful outcomes we can deliver.

I'm incredibly proud and honored to see customers validate the technology we believe in. There's no better feeling than knowing we're helping organizations stop attacks, protect their people, and make the world a safer place.

To our customers, thank you for your trust, feedback, and partnership. Your experiences remind us why we do what we do.

Hear Directly From Our Customers

Read the reviews: Explore what customers are saying about the Vectra AI Platform on Gartner Peer Insights.

Ensuring that there are "humans in the loop" is the gold safety standard for making sure artificial intelligence (AI) agentic systems act safely, ethically, and legally. However, as automated processes accelerate and scale, humans lose the ability to provide meaningful oversight over machine-speed workflows. Rather than simply inserting a human into a machine process, leaders must engineer systems that enable AI agents to operate at machine speed while ensuring they act within human-authorized intent, appropriate controls, and safety and legal boundaries. This means thinking strategically about where acceleration is possible and where slowing down to human speed is necessary to avoid catastrophic risk.

The Hiring Automation “Doom Loop” Is a Warning

Hiring offers an instructive example of how humans can be sidelined by a process accelerated by unchecked automation. Machine-assisted decision-making has long been used in the hiring process to manage volume and improve fairness and efficiency. However, generative AI has made reading and writing job applications almost completely machine-dominated, leading the CEO of Greenhouse, a human resources platform, to declare that AI had created a "doom loop" in hiring. No one intended to create this doom loop, but the adoption of automation in one area led to accelerated adoption in others, ultimately sidelining humans from hiring decisions.

The hiring doom loop is driven by two mutually reinforcing trends: more applicants are applying for each position, and more companies are relying on automation to sift through the growing volume of applications. Applicants per hire tripled between 2021 and 2024, according to one survey of hiring managers, and Greenhouse reported a 412% increase in applicants per post. Applicants are almost certainly using generative AI to spin up customized applications to hundreds of jobs at once.

Meanwhile, 91% of HR departments report using AI in recruitment, and Greenhouse data shows that the number of human recruiters has dropped by over 50%. The recruiters who remain cannot meaningfully evaluate any single application at this volume, further reducing human decision-making in the hiring process. Some companies now use AI to conduct interviews, meaning applicants may not meet an actual human at the company until very late in the process, if at all.

Despite the intention of using AI to improve efficiency and manage scale, only one-third of recruiters reported improvements in time-to-hire using AI, while 25% reported it got slower. More companies are lengthening probationary periods, a sign that they're increasingly unable to identify unsuitable candidates before hiring them. Many job hunters express frustration with encountering bots instead of real humans at their potential future employer. At the same time, scammers and state-sponsored cybercriminals have taken advantage of this automated landscape to advance candidates whose real objective is to steal secrets or cryptocurrency.

A few factors made hiring one of the first processes to fall victim to the doom loop. Hiring managers were early adopters of automation, using technology like keyword-based filters to parse resumes. At the same time, successful cover letters and resumes tend to follow a formula, which makes them easy to convincingly replicate with generative AI. However, there are two factors that are not unique to hiring that make it susceptible to doom loop dynamics:

Incentives for speed and scale: as competition increases, candidates are rewarded for applying to more jobs, faster.

Mutually reinforced automation: as application volume outgrew what individuals could manage, automation spread further into the hiring process. This, in turn, drives candidates to prioritize impressing the bots rather than their future human co-workers.

The hiring doom loop is a valuable case study for managing automation because it forces leaders to account for factors outside of their direct control. Instead of responding to machine volume with more automation, developers must think strategically about the intended outcomes and potential second-order effects to ensure systems remain aligned with human intent.
