Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis says a recent attack on its systems and internal tools has exposed credentials and live tokens for all customers.

Chainalysis provides blockchain analysis tools to trace cryptocurrency transactions and investigate crimes such as fraud, ransomware, and money laundering. Its customer list includes law enforcement, government agencies, financial institutions, insurance companies, and cryptocurrency businesses worldwide.

This follows the company's disclosure last Friday that attackers using AI tools accessed customers' names, email addresses, user IDs, and organizational role labels using what it described as "offensive agentic techniques."

While it initially said the impact was limited and the breach affected only non-sensitive identity metadata, later updates revealed that usernames and password hashes for all customers were exposed in an "on-path attack" (more commonly known as a Man-in-the-Middle or MITM attack).

However, the company found no evidence that the attackers accessed investigative graph data or altered its blockchain attribution repositories.

"On Monday, we discovered certain customer information including names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all Chainalysis users were exposed to a malicious actor," it said in a Wednesday update. "At this time we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated."

While the company locked Chainalysis accounts as a precaution after discovering that some customers' passwords had been exposed and asked users to reset their passwords before signing in again, it has now taken the login portal offline, together with Reactor and Data Solutions, the Know-Your-Transaction (KYT) user interface and API, and address screening products, after discovering further abnormal activity.

To ensure threat actors don't access affected accounts, Chainalysis asked customers to provide trusted IP addresses so they can regain access to the login portal once it is brought back online and reset their credentials.

"Contact support@chainalysis.com or your Chainalysis account team with trusted IP addresses for our allowlist. We will then grant access for users to reset their passwords and rotate API keys to register transactions. We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online. We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate," it added.

"Once access is granted, all users will be required to reset their passwords and rotate API keys, as applicable, before registering transactions," the company noted earlier today.

Chainalysis' disclosure follows several other security incidents affecting cryptocurrency companies in recent weeks. Ledger also asked Asian resellers and distributors last month to remove products from shelves and halt wallet sales while it is investigating multiple hardware implant incidents.

More recently, crypto exchange Binance revealed that North Korean hackers stole roughly $6.34 billion worth of cryptocurrency after compromising its wallet infrastructure by infecting an employee's laptop with malware during a fake job interview.

7bac8f118556.text:
Around half (47%) of security leaders have experienced sensitive data exposure through an AI tool at their organization, research by BlackFog has found.

Of these incidents, 77% involved a company-approved AI tool.

The researchers said the findings demonstrate that many organizations lack visibility into the types of data being shared with AI tools, even those that are approved for use in the enterprise.

While 62% of respondents could identify users or departments sending data to AI tools, less than half (48%) said they could provide any record of the types of data that had left the organization through AI tools.

“This shows why security teams cannot stop at deciding which AI tools employees are allowed to use. Organizations also need to control what information is shared with them," commented Darren Williams, founder and CEO of BlackFog.

Almost all organizations (98%) reported having an AI usage policy in place. However, the ability to enforce such policies varied significantly.

Just over half (56%) support their broader AI usage policies with comprehensive technical controls. Around a third (35%) said that while their organization has a written policy specifying what information employees must not enter into AI prompts, there is no technical enforcement.

Meanwhile, 39% of security leaders admitted that AI adoption is moving faster than they can govern it. Of those respondents feeling outpaced, just 27% have comprehensive AI controls in place.

AI Agents Fall Outside of Organizations’ Governance Strategies

The BlackFog research, published on November 4, also highlighted a significant governance gap around AI agents operating in organizations’ environments.

Over half (56%) revealed that autonomous AI agents acting on behalf of employees fall outside their organization’s existing controls.

Read now: Unchecked AI Agents Cause Cybersecurity Incidents at Two Thirds of Firms

Technology and telecoms were the industries where this issue was most prevalent, with 70% of respondents stating that autonomous AI agents were outside of organizational controls.

In addition, only 54% of security leaders said they had the ability to block or restrict unsanctioned AI tools and around a third (32%) are able to detect shadow AI use but are unable to consistently stop it.

253f01db4421.text:
At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure.

His Majesty's Government broadcast its cybersecurity agenda on Nov. 3, releasing a variety of policy papers, an annual report from its lead cybersecurity agency, and related announcements pertaining to the security of small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs), supply chain vendors, critical national infrastructure (CNI), and more. These items all followed from an updated Autumn Budget 2026, released last week, which provisioned nearly two hundred billion pounds for AI-driven government cybersecurity projects.

Amid all of the practical policy updates, the headline quote of the day came from the state's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which assessed that it's "highly likely that between now and 2028, AI‑powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI." It also labeled "highly likely" the prospect that "China, Russia, and other nation states will routinely use AI cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals" in the country.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

The State of UK Critical Infrastructure

In a new report, Manchester-based NCC Group polled Members of Parliament (MPs) about the state of the UK's CNI cybersecurity posture. About half (51%) of MPs reported that their areas of the country are "not keeping pace" with the threats to its infrastructure. Only 22% expressed confidence in their country's posture. Asked about the nation's ability to fight off a major attack against its CNI, 47% believe that it's unprepared, whereas 41% feel it is.

The survey data is best read as aspirational, not prescriptive. There's little evidence that the UK is less prepared than other nations in addressing threats to its critical infrastructure, or that politicians would be able to tell one way or the other. Leaders are simply aware of the magnitude of what faces them.

"The challenge isn't a lack of government action; it's proof that action translates into resilience," says Katharina Sommer, head of government affairs at NCC Group. "There's still no tested blueprint for coordinating cyber response effectively across government and industry, and that’s not a problem unique to the UK. The test for critical infrastructure operators is whether they can demonstrate, before an attack hits, that they can sustain essential services, recover quickly and maintain public confidence," which remains an open question.

A clearer message came through on Nov. 3, from the experts at the NCSC. Using a scale in which "likely" accords with roughly 55% to 75% odds, "highly likely" with 80% to 90% odds, and "almost certain" approaching 100%, it bet that it is:

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

Likely that threat actors will use AI cyber tools to needle vulnerabilities in CNI

Highly likely that nation-states will use AI to increase the speed and sophistication of their cyberattacks, in service of their geopolitical goals in the UK; in particular, the agency identified China as the foremost player in terms of intent and capability to hit CNI and other strategic targets

Almost certain that "many systems will remain vulnerable" to AI-empowered attacks

The NCSC also drew out some future scenarios. Optimistically, it acknowledged that AI-driven cyber threat development might slow, allowing a window of time for the UK to catch up with the problem. Pessimistically, it painted a picture in which AI threats totally outpace the UK's ability to keep up.

"The situation is likely to be worse than is currently known, with many variables and unknowns still to be discovered," according to the report.

Andy Burnham's Government Makes Cyber Changes

The message out of the UK government on Tuesday was, more or less: we're trying to get ahead of this.

In a policy paper, the government acknowledged that 2018's Network and Information Systems (NIS) Regulations — the UK's only multisector cybersecurity law — is "out of date and insufficient to tackle the threats we face." In a speech announcing its Annual Review 2026, NCSC CEO Richard Horne called the law built to replace NIS 2018 — November 2025's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — "a vital step forward." The updated bill brings data centers, managed service providers (MSPs), and specific "critical suppliers" into the fold, and introduces stricter breach reporting requirements and hefty fines for negligence.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

In a separate policy paper concerning the same bill, the government stated its intention to introduce a new vendor risk management framework focused specifically on the "national security risks posed by vendors" connected to essential service providers. And in yet a third, related paper, the government described how the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will be used to account for agentic "loss of control" incidents, in the fashion of this summer's AI industry lab leaks. Projected future measures include:

Security and resilience requirements to prevent loss of control incidents

Specialized reporting requirements

Evidence preservation requirements

Empowering ministers to perform postmortems

The bill is currently passing through Parliament.

Besides this one bill, the UK government also announced £2.4 billion in subsidies to help micro-, small, and medium-sized businesses attain "Cyber Essentials" certifications. All of this week's announcements come on the heels of an Autumn Budget last week, which arranged for tens of billions of pounds each to fund, among other things:

A National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, for vulnerability discovery across the country, including CNI

A National Cyber Shield, for training AI agents to automate cyber defense

A separate National Agentic Security Unit for fighting rogue AI agents

"Increasing the funding and focus on cybersecurity to help keep the UK secure is very welcome," says Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence for KnowBe4. At the same time, he adds, "the main challenge I see is scale."

"£154 million for cyber-defenses is a good step," he believes, "but the NCSC estimates cyberattacks cost UK organizations £14.7 billion a year."

Cybersecurity Experts Weigh in on CNI Defense

Dark Reading asked cybersecurity experts what governments like the UK's need to do to prevent future worst-case scenarios. They consistently emphasized the same point:

"AI did not create new weaknesses; it revealed them. Most incidents still start through the same familiar routes, such as phishing, stolen credentials, and the traditional kill chain paths attackers have relied on for years. The key to stopping these threats is, surprisingly, not exciting: it's the fundamentals," Chapman argues.

The fundamentals for Graham Taylor CBE, director of defense strategy for Northern Europe at OPSWAT, start with protecting the edge. "Too many critical sites rely on firewalls and VPNs for connections that only need to send data one way. Where a facility only exports monitoring data, a hardware-enforced data diode removes the return path entirely, so neither a human attacker nor AI can use that link to send commands into the facility," he says.

Jacob Krell, Suzu Labs senior director for secure AI solutions and cybersecurity, emphasizes network segmentation "built like a boat." AI is going to make the perimeter easier to breach, he says, "and it cuts the time to objective once an attacker is inside. Critical infrastructure is notoriously vulnerable here because operators are hesitant to patch and test systems, and their caution is rational; a bad update takes a plant offline. So the perimeter fails more often and the interior offers nothing to slow lateral movement."

John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, tosses out a less conventional suggestion for fighting off AI threats to CNI. "If AI gives attackers the ability to do a tremendous amount of work very quickly, defenders have an opportunity to present them with large numbers of decoys to investigate," he says. "We need creative ways to make those decoys look realistic and dynamic. The more time attacking AI agents spend interacting with decoys, the less time they spend attacking real systems."

a496e99f891d.text:
D-Link shared mitigation measures for multiple unpatched security flaws affecting DGS-3130 series managed Gigabit stackable switches.

These switch models provide multi-gigabit uplinks, allowing enterprise network administrators to eliminate data bottlenecks, and are designed primarily for small-to-medium businesses (SMBs) and metro Ethernet deployments.

While D-Link didn't share details on these flaws and has yet to publicly disclose the CVE IDs for easier tracking, it said Spectrum Community Solutions network engineer Giresh Kumar Enugu found the bugs in the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) authentication, access control, and information handling.

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to obtain sensitive device data, make unauthorized credential/configuration changes, leak SNMP communities, or cause service disruptions and device resets.

The zero-days affect multiple DGS-3130-30TS firmware versions, and the company is still investigating the impact on other D-Link switching platforms and firmware security mechanisms (including SSH service security configuration, safeguards underlying operating-system credentials, and handles firmware encryption/embedded cryptographic keys).

"The reported vulnerabilities involve the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) and certain components of the device's firmware security architecture," D-Link said.

"According to the security researcher, successful exploitation of certain vulnerabilities may allow an attacker with access to the affected network to obtain sensitive device information, perform unauthorized administrative operations, modify device configuration, or disrupt network services."

Until it releases new firmware to address these flaws, D-Link asked admins to disable DDP to remove the primary known attack vector, remove unnecessary or default SNMP community strings, and restrict SSH, web UI, and SNMP accessibility solely to isolated management networks and designated admin hosts.

D-Link also advised admins to maintain offline switch configuration backups and track device logs for unexpected configuration changes, unprompted reboots, or factory resets.

In September, D-Link warned customers of a maximum-severity zero-day (tracked as CVE-2026-86296) with a public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit and no patch, affecting legacy DIR-822A dual-band Wi-Fi routers.

612fa7cf7455.text: Welcome to Friday and therefore to a fresh edition of On Call, The Register's weekly tale of tech support trials and tribulations that readers kindly share. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Mason," who told us he once worked at a hospital doing tech support for its research labs. "One of the labs was for a doctor who was one of the world's top organ transplant researchers" Mason told On Call. The doctor was also a voracious consumer of – ahem – adult entertainment, a habit that saw his PC and other machines around the lab often come down with a nasty case of malware. Mason got to clean that up, sometimes multiple times in a single week. The doctor's foibles were widely known around the hospital, as was the fact that his activities violated several workplace policies. Mason pointed this out to his boss every time he cleaned up a fresh malware outbreak but such was the doctor's status that management never intervened. And then the hospital was hit by a nasty cyber-worm that did a lot of damage. During the cleanup, Mason's colleagues found logs that showed the doctor's PC was the source of the infection, and that he had been indulging in his online hobby at the time the worm arrived. Mason assumed this would be the moment at which the doctor would finally be held accountable and face disciplinary action. Instead the doctor made a bargain with the IT department to henceforth use only a designated PC when pursuing – ahem – personal and/or intimate matters. And he would only use office PCs for actual work. The hospital's tech team rescued a PC from its e-waste pile for this job. "Get this thing going and deliver it to Doctor Pervert," Mason's boss ordered. By this stage, Mason had had enough. He escalated his protests, telling his boss that indulging this doctor was unprofessional, likely exposed the hospital to lawsuits, wasted IT department resources, and was just wrong. "What do you want to hear?" his boss replied. "The CIO told me do this or get another job." After Mason prepped that PC, he only needed to clean up malware about once a year – after the poor machine was so overrun with malware that it no longer served the doctor's purposes. Mason left the hospital while this PC was still in place. "You'll be shocked, no doubt, to learn that years later the doctor's graduate students filed a lawsuit," he told On Call. "And that the separate fun-time computer was one of the pieces of evidence that the hospital knew about his – ahem – proclivities and not just ignored them but facilitated them." Have you been asked to cover up revolting behavior? Or ignore policy? Click here to share your story with On Call. It's our policy to tell a great tech support story week, so we appreciate every contribution. ®

0f61379046b8.text:
How did you enjoy October 2026 Patch Tuesday? Were there enough CVEs reported to keep you busy for the rest of the year or are you finished and ready for another round next week? They released the regularly scheduled update nearly two and a half hours late, but Microsoft did resolve another record-breaking 1,407 unique CVEs.

As in previous months, there were limited CVEs we needed to immediately deal with. In October, one zero-day CVE-2026-96951 was confirmed exploited; it was a Windows Shell security feature bypass impacting Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server. And CVE-2026-10839 was publicly disclosed; it was a .NET Framework security bypass vulnerability. Overall, there were 78 Critical vulnerabilities, which was a small fraction of all CVEs reported.

PHP2Shell

The hottest news of the month surrounded vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, also referred to as PHP2Shell by researchers. PHP is a general-purpose scripting language which was originally released in 1994 to support web development. It runs on a server providing the middleware between a web server and the browser requesting information.

PHP released a security advisory on October 21st regarding the vulnerabilities and the related PHP software versions that had been fixed. Exploitation in the wild was detected several days before the patches were released and is continuing to expand. Patching the vulnerability is a multi-step process varying by operating system, but essentially, you need to replace the php runtime, stop the web server and then restart it all. Without a restart, the old code stays in memory.

Exploitation of the vulnerability provides the attacker with access to whatever the php shell can see. Keep this in mind as you assess your systems for compromise and prioritize the updates.

Emergency fixes

Microsoft had several out-of-band releases and the usual preview patch near the end of last month, both of which have security implications. They released an emergency fix for CVE-2026-111497 on October 25, which is also referred to as the Broccoli2Shell, Node2Shell or HTTP2Shell vulnerability. This name comes from a flaw in the Brotli binaries or libraries used to process Brotli-compressed data. These fixes address the libraries in .NET 8, 9, 10, as well as Release Candidate 3 for .NET 11 and should be updated as soon as possible. There is proof-of-concept code available but no known exploitation in the wild at this time.

On October 26, Microsoft issued an update that removes seven certificates from the Windows trust list: six eMudhra G3 roots and an AAA Certificate Services cross-sign. These certificate keys had been compromised. And finally, Microsoft confirmed the preview patches included fixes for the Always On VPN connection failures, which were introduced back with the September Patch Tuesday updates. They also included a fix for the Smart App Control broken by the October Windows update.

Following application of that October update, the Smart App Control option was grayed out and could not be toggled on affected devices running Windows 11 24H2 and later. All of these security fixes will be included in the November Patch Tuesday cumulative release.

Obsolete software

Do you spend time finding and removing EOL or obsolete software in your environment? Although it isn’t strictly a patching issue, we often leave software in place after applying its final patches, intending to remove it later. But do we always remember, or find the time? One article described an abandoned 2014 application that was still running and trying to update itself on 2.5 million Windows devices and 300,000 Macs. Several of the domains it contacted for updates were open for new registration, so anyone paying attention could have created a malicious update package that would instantly compromise millions of machines. Fortunately, the problem was detected and the software removed before that could happen, but this software was running for a long time.

This begs the question, do we really know what every running service on our machines is doing, particularly those with network connectivity? This is yet another area where AI can provide more insight into operational vulnerabilities on our systems. And yes, we do need to constantly search for and remove obsolete software from our systems or face the consequences.

Updates from Apple

Apple released major security updates for all its supported operating systems on October 26th. For example, the security update for its latest version, macOS Golden Gate 27, addressed 183 unique CVEs. You should also note on this page that there are updates for iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11. Apple backported a fix to these operating systems because of the known exploited CVE-2026-86950. Per Apple: “Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27.” Exploitation of this CoreGraphics vulnerability could lead to arbitrary code execution. If you are running these older OS versions, you should take advantage of this rare patch from Apple.

November 2026 Patch Tuesday forecast

After last month, let’s just assume that Microsoft will continue to release updates across the board for all their products with high numbers of CVEs for each.

Based on past cadence, expect Adobe to provide updates for Acrobat/Reader, InCopy and InDesign, and Premiere.

Apple provided their latest updates on October 26th for all operating systems, so I don’t expect anything next week.

Google just released Early Stable Update for Desktop 158, so expect this update for Chrome next week.

Mozilla is due to release Firefox and Thunderbird 160. Along with these major releases we usually see updates to the ESR versions with select CVEs as well.

The penultimate Patch Tuesday of the year is almost upon us. Will there be a break in the number of releases after the massive output last month? Or will this be the last big push before the holidays to get everyone into a secure state for end-of-year system lockdown? Regardless of what comes, we’ll always deal with it, but don’t forget to patch the older software in your environment like php which doesn’t have a Patch Tuesday focus. And on a final note, don’t forget to track down and remove EOL software, which is vulnerable, because they will come back to bite.

Activate Safety Net: Virtual Patching for organizations affected by HTTP2Shell

66c7939b4801.text:
In this Help Net Security video, Mariia Bakhtina, a research specialist at Masaryk University, explains what a Common Criteria or FIPS-140 certificate does and does not promise. In her team’s analysis, about 6 in 10 vulnerabilities matched to certified products, smartcards aside, were disclosed after the certification date. She also describes sec-certs and SCRUTINY, two open-source tools her lab builds, and the one question buyers should put to a vendor.

Picture a procurement manager handed a 300-page certification document for a product they are about to buy. What do they do with it in the first hour, and at what point does the document stop helping them?

Luckily, certification documents (e.g., Security Target in CC or Security Policy in FIPS-140) are usually up to around 100 pages, not 300. But that’s still a lot for a procurement manager who isn’t typically a security specialist. In the first hour, I think they’d look for a few things: the exact product name and its version, the assurance level (along with the considered threats, assets and covered security requirements), what the evaluated configuration is, and what’s declared out of scope. That’s where the real boundaries of the security claims are. Covering all of those could take more than 1 hour if the procurement manager is not familiar with the certification scheme details (e.g., how the documents are organized).

And then the document would stop helping for the reason that it’s a snapshot of the product in the past. It tells you what was evaluated at one point in time. It doesn’t tell you what’s been found since, or what’s been changed. In our 2024 analysis, roughly 6 in 10 of the vulnerabilities matched to certified products, smartcards aside, were disclosed after the certification date. Also, the single given certification document can’t tell you whether the certificate is still active, or how the product compares to the two others on your procurement shortlist. Those questions go across multiple documents.

“Certified” sounds like a verdict. What is a Common Criteria or FIPS 140 certificate promising, and what do buyers commonly read into it that is not there?

Yes, I absolutely agree that for the average person “certified” sounds like “it has been verified and it meets all the necessary criteria for this kind of product”. But in reality, it’s not exactly the case.

Let me take Common Criteria first, since it’s the one most of our data is about. A CC certificate says that an accredited lab evaluated a defined product, in a defined configuration, against security claims the vendor wrote down in a document called the Security Target. Very often that target is based on a Protection Profile for the product type, like smartcards. So “meets the criteria” really means “meets the criteria the vendor claimed, within the scope that was defined”. The certificate also says the evaluation followed the process at a stated assurance level, the EAL. The promise is about the claims and the process, not about the product being secure in general.

FIPS 140 is a different thing. It validates a cryptographic module, meaning the hardware, software or firmware that does the cryptography, against the FIPS 140 requirements, at one of four security levels. The promise is about that module within its defined boundary. It says nothing about the application or the system around it.

What buyers commonly read into it, mostly about CC:

“No vulnerabilities”: That’s not what it says. ROCA, Minerva and TPM-Fail were all found in certified products, some at high assurance levels.

“The whole product is covered”: Scope can exclude features. We came across a CC-certified network camera where the network interface was assumed to be trusted, so it was probably never tested there.

“The version I’m buying is the one that was tested, and it’s still current.” A CC certificate applies to a fixed configuration, and it has a limited validity. It’s usually 5 years, after which it gets archived.

“A higher level means it’s more secure”: A higher level doesn’t mean a product is more secure in general, instead it tells you how thoroughly the product was examined. In our data, products evaluated at higher levels tended to have less severe vulnerabilities, but not noticeably fewer of them. So it helps a bit, but it’s not a guarantee.

When certification documents become searchable, which question can a buyer answer in minutes that previously took a consultant or days of reading?

A certification document is a snapshot. It can’t tell you whether the certificate is still active, whether there is a newer certification of the same product, or what the product is built on. Once the documents are searchable, you can check all of that quickly. You find the certificate, see whether it’s still valid or already archived, and see whether a newer version or re-certification exists.

You can also follow what the document refers to, like the certified hardware or library the product is built on, or the Protection Profile it uses as a baseline. Those are separate certificates and documents. Before, you had to know they existed and dig them out yourself. This matters because what’s underneath the product is part of what you’re trusting. Search gets you to the right documents fast, but you still need to read what they say.

For readers who have not come across sec-certs, how would you describe it in a few sentences, and what problem was it built to solve? Then, who opens it first: vendors checking their own entries, buyers vetting suppliers, or security labs? Did the answer match what you expected when you started?

Sec-certs is an open-source tool and website that turns public certification documents into a searchable, linked dataset. That covers Common Criteria, FIPS 140, and EUCC. Every week it collects the documents from the official portals, extracts the key data, links certificates to known vulnerabilities, and detects which certificates reference each other. You can use it on the website or as a Python library.

We built it because all this evidence is public but practically unusable. It’s in thousands of long PDFs on many national portals, with no shared identifiers and no link to vulnerability data. The idea came from researchers in our lab (Centre for Research on Cryptography and Security, CRoCS) who needed exactly this during the ROCA and Minerva disclosures (led by my colleague Petr Švenda) .

As for who opens it first, it’s not really one group. From the feedback we’ve received, they all use it, but for different reasons. Vendors check their own entries. They also look for other vendors’ products that depend on theirs, because certificates reference each other. And they look at what their competitors certify and how they do it. Buyers come when they’re looking for products that use a specific technology, and then they compare the certification documents of those products. Meanwhile, security labs check which certificates in the categories of their expertise will expire soon and through this find the potential customer for testing as a part of re-certification.

And regarding whether it matches what you expected – I’d say that yes, in general. But at the moment, as we don’t track systematically who the users are and how they are using the tool, we have only a limited view from the users who approached us. But thanks to the CCAT project, the main focus for our team is to get more feedback from our users on how to make the sec-certs even more useful and provide more data to confirm or reject our more nuanced assumptions about their needs.

A vendor discovers that its certificate can now be searched, compared and cross-referenced in public. What reactions have you seen, and what do they tell you about how certification is used in the market?

The reactions are mixed, and I think that’s an indication that the tool meets its goal of improving transparency in the certification ecosystem.

Some vendors see it as a positive. They can show potential customers that their product has a “page” in sec-certs, which is an independent source, a non-profit research project. So customers get a better overview of the product’s certification than they’d get from the vendor’s own materials, the verifying authoritativeness of which requires, again, going through various certification portals.

On the other hand, we don’t only make certificates searchable. We also map them to vulnerabilities that potentially affect the certified products, and those matches are correct only with roughly 89% precision. The reason is that the certification scope is often defined ambiguously, and it’s hard to match to CPE, a structured, machine-readable naming standard for identifying software, operating systems and hardware platforms. We highlight that the detected matches are indicative and should be verified. Still, vendors are not happy when their product is shown with potential vulnerabilities.

What I take from it is that vendors like the visibility when it supports the certificate as a trust signal for customers, and like it less when the same page also shows potential vulnerabilities next to it. It also shows how much the certificate is treated as a status that customers can rely on.

SCRUTINY is the second tool your team builds. How would you explain to someone outside cryptography what it tests and why that matters for a company buying products with cryptography built in? Suppose it flags a statistical anomaly in a random number generator. A buyer might hear “broken,” while a lab might call it noise. How do you present a finding like that so people neither panic nor shrug?

SCRUTINY is a toolkit that tests the real product. You connect something with cryptography built in, like a smart card, a TPM chip, an encrypted disk or a cryptographic library, and it runs a set of tests. Which cryptographic functions does it really support, compared with the datasheet? How does it react to odd or malicious inputs? Does the time it takes to compute something leak secrets? Are its random numbers really random? The results become a profile that you can compare against a reference and turn into a readable report.

For a buyer, this matters because a certificate tells you what was evaluated on paper. Cryptographic flaws are also serious but invisible from the outside. Minerva is an example. It affected certified cards, and the weakness was in the timing of signing, which you find by measuring.

When it flags a statistical anomaly, I wouldn’t say “broken” or “noise”. I’d say what we know: “In the data we collected, this test found a deviation, and here is how strong the evidence is.” Then I’d say whether it repeats on fresh data, and what it would mean for how you plan to use the product. I’d also use simple levels: nothing found, needs follow-up, and reproducible with strong evidence.

SCRUTINY is a tool which helps you verify whether the product you are buying performs as good as the one that was tested for certification. And of course, if the buyers don’t have in-house expertise for independent verification of the difference between the claims certified and purchased products, it would be in the vendor’s best interest to provide the baseline measurements as the proof.

If a company reads only one thing before signing a contract for a certified product, what should it be, and what is the one question it should put to the vendor?

The one thing to read is the scope of the certification: what exactly was certified, in which version and configuration, and under which assumptions or exclusions. That is described in the Security Target (or Security Policy), and the certification report summarises it. “Certified” tells you very little until you know that.

The one question for the vendor: “Show me where in the certification documents the security function we’re buying this for is covered, for the exact version you’re delivering.” If they can point to it, you’re in good shape. If they can’t, or the answer is “that’s outside the scope”, you’ve learned the most important thing before signing. That is also when independent testing, like what SCRUTINY does, is worth considering.

cda97732ed29.text:
The AI running inside large companies has stopped waiting for permission. Across five categories of AI, from chatbots to process automation, more than half of 3,600 business decision-makers say the systems their teams use can act within defined rules without routine review, or finish whole processes with no human approval. 87% of those same respondents say their organization needs a better way to approve, monitor and control how AI gets used.

Vanson Bourne ran the survey across North America, EMEA, and Asia Pacific and Japan. Every respondent came from a company with more than $500 million in annual revenue, spread across seven sectors including financial services, healthcare, manufacturing and retail.

“There is a dangerous gap opening up between AI confidence and AI reality. Confidence is not the problem. Ambition is not the problem. The problem is that most organizations are using AI to improve a business model that AI should be replacing,” said Chris Howarth, CEO at Avanade.

More than half say their AI can act unsupervised

Conversational AI and virtual agents top the autonomy list at 59%. Standalone generative tools, the ones that write text or code, sit lowest at 54%. Predictive analytics and machine learning, robotic process automation, and natural language processing each land at 56%. These are managers reporting on their own teams, so the figures capture what they believe is running.

87% say AI initiatives need faster authorization to stay competitive, and 91% of that same group say the approach to approving, monitoring and controlling AI needs to be more effective. The people pushing to shorten the sign-off are the people who do not trust the sign-off.

Companies that moved fast are already losing track

Among those that have deployed or scaled AI at speed, 46% report security, privacy, regulatory or compliance problems and 25% report loss of visibility, control or agent permissions. The second figure matters most, because an agent whose permissions a team cannot account for is unmanaged access to whatever that agent touches.

45% believe their people use AI output without checking its accuracy or suitability, 32% believe AI is being used in ways their compliance team would not approve of, and 31% report unapproved tools in use. Another 37% say AI has confused who owns a decision.

A mid-level manager at an enterprise healthcare company in Canada, asked how they use AI in ways their employer may not know about: “I realize that AI doesn’t offer the same security as our main systems. But what is the way forward, blocking access doesn’t work. I do upload our business and company information to my AI app. I understand the security implications.”

The governance gap

On AI security, 30% say strengthening is needed and another 40% say moderate. On governance and risk, 94% say further development is needed. 36% put security, governance or regulatory concerns among the biggest barriers stopping their company from becoming an AI leader. Security, privacy, governance and regulatory compliance is also the single most common area of heavy AI investment at 47%, so the spending has started even where the controls have not landed.

Among companies between $500 million and $5 billion in revenue, 90% say a better approach to approval, monitoring and control is needed, against 70% of companies above $5 billion.

Strong governance, access controls and responsible use rank among the highest priorities for 45% of respondents, well ahead of the 26% who name deploying AI as quickly as possible.

Download: The IT and security field guide to AI adoption

dc19f92dbf8e.text:
Developers, automated tools and AI coding agents hold permissions that can outlast the work they were granted for. Without access reviews, organizations can leave accounts able to copy or change company code after the work ends, according to BlueFlag Security’s The State of Developer Risk 2026 report.

Development accounts and tools create security blind spots

Software development spans code repositories, review systems, build pipelines and connected applications. Developers, contractors, service accounts, bots and AI coding agents use these systems with permissions that require ongoing oversight.

Access can accumulate when developers join projects, change teams or take on administrative tasks. Permissions granted for a contract or assignment may remain after the work ends.

The average developer had not used 61% of their granted permissions. Of the developers holding the most unused permissions, 88% could access repositories their organizations classified as business-critical, including those supporting production services, payment systems and regulated workloads.

Four in five organizations had developer identities that had been inactive for more than 90 days but retained administrator permissions. Compromised credentials for these accounts could give attackers access to repositories and their settings.

Non-human identities outnumber developers eight to one

Service accounts, bots, connected applications and access tokens allow tools to retrieve code, run builds and deploy software. Across the pooled dataset, non-human identities with repository access outnumbered human developers with repository access eight to one. The calculation includes access tokens as identities.

Source: BlueFlag Security

Of the repository-access tokens measured, 99% had no expiration date, 84% allowed code changes and 47% had been unused for more than 90 days without being revoked. These credentials can remain usable after a project or integration ends.

Unused permissions held by non-human identities also extended to business-critical repositories, increasing the potential consequences of credential theft.

AI coding agents gain access without oversight

A typical organization used about seven AI coding tools, with some using more than 30. Unapproved agents were present in 83% of the organizations measured. Most organizations lacked a list of approved tools.

Coding assistants work under a developer’s identity and inherit its permissions. Autonomous agents operate as separate identities and can write, review and merge code without a human approving each action.

Assistants can also operate under service account identities. Administrator permissions were held by 68% of the developer and service account identities that agents operated under, and 81% lacked behavioral monitoring. In six in ten organizations with AI activity, agents used tokens capable of cloning every repository.

Actions taken through a developer’s account may appear under that person’s name, making human and AI activity difficult to distinguish without commit tags or other metadata.

“They are the most powerful identities in the environment and fall into two categories: coding assistants, which work under a developer’s identity and inherit its access and permissions, and autonomous agents, which operate as their own identity and can write, review, and merge code with no human in the loop,” the company said.

Unusual activity and bypassed checks raise risks

Half of the organizations measured had at least one identity that showed a spike in code cloning compared with its previous activity. In 28%, an identity cloned at least 100 repositories it had never accessed before. These patterns can warrant investigation for credential misuse or code theft, though they do not prove either.

Four in ten repositories had unprotected main branches, and administrators bypassed code review in four in five organizations. Code was merged despite failed checks in 56% of organizations and with unresolved reviewer comments in two-thirds. Neither finding establishes that the changes were deployed or contained security flaws.

Private repositories became public in 28% of organizations, potentially exposing code, documentation and stored credentials.

0b9652fca14e.text: Nation-state actors and criminals likely exploited the PHP2SHELL vulnerability before its disclosure, according to Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince. “These vulnerabilities, like the PHP vulnerabilities that were disclosed the other day, had been in the wild for years,” Prince said on the company’s third quarter earnings call. “We're going back through our logs looking for any evidence that hackers or nation-state actors or others had been using them in the past. I know that we're going to find examples of that.” That was just one of the warnings he offered on the call, among them that some of Cloudflare’s customers believe AI agents are “a bane to their business and want to keep them away.” To explain why, Prince hypothesized that he could use an agent to find him a restaurant to eat at after he finishes his day of investor relations duties. “It might go and scour the internet and look at 1,000 different restaurants' websites, pull down 1,000 different menus, and then I might choose to only go to one of those,” he said. “The problem is that 999 of those restaurants have now had a cost that is just been applied to them, but they are not getting any benefit.” The CEO admitted that web searches have always driven some low-value traffic but feels the volume of agentic activity – which Cloudflare has previously predicted will be one thousand times greater than clicks from humans – means the problem is now at a different scale. Prince also had bad news for Kubernetes aficionados, because he thinks containers might become another casualty of the agentic age. The CEO allowed that containers are “a significant improvement over bare metal or even virtual machines,” and said they fueled the growth of hyperscale clouds and mobile applications. But he thinks containers are already cooked. “The container-based architecture of the hyperscalers and neoclouds just can't keep up in a cost-effective way with the new agentic paradigms of today,” he argued, again citing the 1000:1 ratio of bot:human traffic Cloudflare expects to see online any year now. That’s a Cloudflare-centric view, because Prince pitched the company’s serverless “Workers” service as an alternative to containers. The company also offers products that can either block agents, ameliorate the cost and traffic impacts of agentic activity, or allow organizations to monetize traffic generated by AI. Prince said demand for those products is growing fast, claiming that since July 1st, “approximately five percent” of the web opted in to Cloudflare’s content protection products. The CEO said Meta is already a customer, and said Zuck’s new “Muse” agents will benefit Cloudflare by creating more agentic traffic that third parties want to tame. He also pointed to year-on-year revenue growth of 39 percent, which saw quarterly revenue reach a record $782.5 million. And he thinks there are better days ahead, due to the terrible state of security. “It may seem like the sky is falling with the number of new security vulnerabilities that have been reported over the last few weeks,” Prince said. “I wish I could tell you we were through the worst, but we're not.” He thinks Cloudflare can profit from security misery because the extent of its activities and client base mean it is “among the first to receive quiet disclosure of new vulnerabilities” and remediates them before disclosure. Investors thought this all made sense, and in after-hours trading sent Cloudflare shares up by around 15 percent, meaning it recovered and then improved on losses that it incurred earlier after major US indices dropped around four percent as investors who worry tech stocks are overvalued. ®

Holiday travelers looking for a place to stay are landing on copies of popular rental platforms, complete with host names, ratings and reviews, that ask for their passwords, personal details and credit card numbers.

The sites, spotted and taken down by Fortra’s Intelligence and Research Experts (FIRE) team, rely on familiar branding, copied property listings and reservation details, along with urgent messages meant to rush visitors into acting.

A phishing page imitating a rental marketplace (Source: Fortra)

The timing is deliberate, since “cybercriminals know that travelers are more likely to click quickly as a trip approaches,” Fortra’s Elyse Neumann wrote in a blog post on the findings.

Pressure that comes with a deadline

Travel bookings tend to involve high prices, tight deadlines and limited availability, and the fake sites play on that urgency. Visitors are told their reservation is unconfirmed, their payment has not been processed or their booking will be canceled. Other prompts urge them to complete verification to continue, or dangle special pricing for a limited time.

These warnings “may push travelers to click before checking the website address or confirming the reservation through an official channel,” Neumann cautioned.

A login page with familiar sign-in options

One phishing site impersonated a global experiences and lodging platform, using a lookalike address (confirm-[redacted].rooms-home93914[.]space) and imagery matching the brand. The sign-up prompt asked for contact details and social media credentials.

“This type of page can be used to collect account information, phone numbers, or login credentials. If travelers reuse passwords across services, information submitted to a fake booking site could also put other accounts at risk,” Neumann explained.

Her advice is to steer clear of entering credentials after following an unsolicited link, “even if the page includes recognizable logos or familiar buttons.”

Listings built to blend in

Attackers copy photos and descriptions from legitimate properties, so judging a site by its looks gets hard. “A polished listing does not prove that the property exists or that the booking platform is genuine,” she wrote.

According to Neumann, FIRE is “increasingly seeing attacks that prey on the urgency of booking a stay via popular short-term lodging marketplaces.” In the cases it examined, the phishing pages showed listings with locations, travel dates and prices. One page displayed an apartment and a house side by side, and “nothing about the listings appeared obviously suspicious.”

Travelers comparing several properties tend to focus on price, availability and the look of the place, without stopping to ask whether the site itself is legitimate. Mimicking the familiar details of a trusted rental marketplace lets attackers keep the copycat site believable long enough to steer visitors toward verification or payment.

Unconfirmed reservations as bait for personal data

In another case, the booking flow led to a “confirm and pay” screen marking the reservation as “Unconfirmed.” Visitors were told to complete a mandatory verification process before the booking could go ahead and were assured it would cost nothing extra. The page then asked for the traveler’s name, email address, country and phone number.

Those requests may seem harmless. Neumann warns, however, that information submitted to a fraudulent site “can be used for identity theft, follow-on phishing, or account takeover.”

A support chat that vouches for the card form

A separate booking page displayed a credit card payment form and paired it with a live support chat. The chat responded directly to the visitor’s concerns and presented the card request as a routine security check.

The reassurance that the card would not be charged was there to lower the visitor’s guard. It’s a move that “reduced hesitation and encouraged the submission of payment information,” she noted.

“The safest approach is to pause before completing a booking. A convincing property listing can be copied, but the official website address is much harder for a scammer to imitate,” concluded Neumann.

328ab31f1590.text:
Cryptocurrency wallet provider MetaMask said a recent security incident has not affected MetaMask wallets or its wallet infrastructure.

The MetaMask non-custodial crypto wallet (developed by blockchain software company Consensys) lets users store and manage assets on the Ethereum network and compatible blockchains.

MetaMask revealed on September 30 that it was investigating an "ongoing infrastructure security incident" and exited affected validators (Ethereum network nodes responsible for proposing blocks, verifying crypto transactions, and maintaining Ethereum blockchain security) within non-custodial staking operations.

While the company shared almost no details at the time and redirected BleepingComputer to the public statement when asked what part of its infrastructure was affected, in a Thursday update it said that a threat actor gained access to systems used to store recipient addresses and diverted some execution-layer staking rewards.

"The issue was identified and addressed on the same day, and approximately 0.385 ETH in rewards was diverted. These rewards are separate from customers' staked ETH," MetaMask said. "We have found no evidence that customers' staked principal or withdrawal keys were compromised, and the affected systems have been secured."

It also added that the attack did not compromise MetaMask users' Secret Recovery Phrases or private keys and that it was working with affected customers to refund the lost rewards.

"Some customers have experienced temporary withdrawal delays as a result of the precautionary validator exits. The process may also have resulted in missed staking rewards while validators were exiting or awaiting reactivation. We are working directly with affected customers and partners to address any outstanding impact," MetaMask noted.

"MetaMask wallet users do not need to take any action as a result of this incident. Customers whose staking arrangements were affected should follow any guidance provided directly by MetaMask or their staking provider."

Last month, Ledger also asked Asian resellers and distributors to halt wallet sales and remove products from shelves while it was investigating multiple hardware implant incidents.

More recently, crypto exchange Binance confirmed that North Korean hackers stole $6.34 billion after compromising its wallet infrastructure by tricking an employee into installing malware in a fake job interview.

df00686766b4.text:
The way we work has changed significantly, and now the way we secure that work is changing with it. Again.

For years, organizations have added security technologies to address new risk categories as they emerged. Endpoint security, identity protection, email security, vulnerability management, data protection, and detection and response have each become important parts of the security stack.

But today's attacks rarely stay within one of those boundaries. This shift is driving a broader approach to protecting the modern digital worker: Workspace Security.

How Do You Define Workspace Security?

The workspace has become an interconnected attack surface, and workspace security looks beyond traditional boundaries to focus on the ways attackers now reach users and business data. Several shifts are accelerating this pivot toward workplace security.

1. Work is increasingly distributed. Endpoints, mobile devices, browsers, SaaS applications, and cloud services have extended work far beyond the corporate network.

2. Identity has become a critical security boundary. Attackers don't always need to break through traditional defenses if they can log in using compromised credentials, tokens, or sessions.

3. Applications and collaboration tools are part of the attack surface. Email, browsers, SaaS, and collaboration platforms connect users directly to business data and provide attackers with more opportunities to target them.

4. AI is adding another interaction layer. Generative AI and copilots are quickly becoming part of everyday workflows, creating new interactions between users, applications, and organizational data. It is also increasing the need for visibility and control into how AI is being used and what data it can access.

Rather than isolated changes, these shifts increasingly overlap within the same workflows and the same attacks.

What are the Risks of Operating Security in Silos?

Because users, identities, devices, applications, data, and AI are interconnected, protecting each in isolation leaves gaps between them.

Security architectures have traditionally been organized around individual control points. Endpoint tools protect devices. Identity tools protect accounts and access. Email security protects communications. Other technologies manage vulnerabilities, applications, and data.

Attackers see the environment differently.

A phishing email might lead to credential theft. Those credentials could provide access to a legitimate application. From there, an attacker may establish persistence, elevate privileges, move across systems, or access sensitive information.

One attack can therefore generate signals across the environment.

How Are Organizations Breaking Down Cybersecurity Silos?

According to Gartner®, "Cybersecurity teams with limited resources and a need to reduce silos require a simpler, more unified approach to securing digital work than traditional multivendor tool stacks. WCPs address this by preintegrating modules to lower costs, reduce errors, and improve cybersecurity posture."

Is Endpoint Security a Key Part of Workspace Security?

The endpoint remains central to the evolution toward workspace security, especially because unified endpoint security platforms have expanded beyond malware protection to include numerous capabilities: attack surface reduction, behavioral detection, and vulnerability and patch management, along with EDR, XDR, and identity threat protection.

At the same time, the risks surrounding the digital worker increasingly extend beyond the endpoint itself. Gartner notes, "WCPs have replaced Gartner’s coverage of the extended detection and response (XDR) market, which no longer exists in its original form. As vendors expanded native modules and improved integration, XDR became a feature within WCPs and other cybersecurity markets."

Workspace Security isn't about making endpoint protection less important. It is about extending its context and connecting protection around the digital worker. This is why the distinction between a collection of security products and an integrated platform is significant.

Integration makes the security controls surrounding the user work together more effectively.

What Does Effective Workspace Security Look Like?

Workspace Security is an evolving approach that brings the protections surrounding digital workers together more cohesively, connecting proactive risk reduction, prevention, detection, and response across the workspace. Organizations evaluating their approach should consider several key principles:

Broad visibility: Can security teams understand risk and activity across endpoints, identities, applications, data, and emerging technologies such as AI?

Proactive risk reduction and prevention: Can the platform identify vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, identity risks, and other exposures, reduce the attack surface, and prevent threats before they become incidents?

Connected context: Can telemetry across devices, identities, applications, and data be correlated to help teams understand the broader attack rather than investigate individual signals in isolation?

Deep integration: Do capabilities genuinely share telemetry, policies, behavioral analysis, and workflows, or are they simply a collection of products from the same vendor?

Simplified operations: Can teams manage policies, prioritize alerts, investigate threats, and take action through centralized workflows with less context switching?

Openness and flexibility: Can the platform integrate with the wider security ecosystem when specialized capabilities or existing investments are still required?

The goal is to reduce exposure, prevent more threats before they occur, and provide the context needed to detect and respond effectively to attacks.

Securing How Work Happens

Workspace Security represents an important evolution in cybersecurity, but not because organizations suddenly need another security product category.

It reflects a more fundamental change: the way people work is increasingly interconnected, attacks cross traditional security boundaries, and the security protecting digital workers needs to become more connected as well.

For resource-constrained IT and security teams, in particular, the opportunity is significant: fewer silos, better context, stronger prevention, and simpler security operations.

Ready to take a more unified approach to workspace security? Explore the Bitdefender GravityZone Platform to learn how you can protect users, data, and applications across the modern workspace. The future of Workspace Security is about protecting how work happens.

583f3451d57b.text:
Three people accused of using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million have been indicted on charges of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, prosecutors said Thursday.

Over more than a year and a half, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, targeted thousands of companies across the world in their AI scheme, according to the indictment filed in a U.S. District Court in New York.

Their victims included hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, a financial technology company in the United Kingdom, a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida, according to court documents.

The defendants, from Spain, the UK, Israel and United Arab Emirates, were also charged with money laundering, according to the indictment.

The case docket, which typically lists information on defense lawyers, was still listed as sealed in online court records as of Thursday evening. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York did not immediately respond to a voicemail left by The Associated Press.

The three were arrested between June and September. In 2008, Hazan was convicted in a New York court of conspiracy to commit bank fraud, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The trio, who have nicknames that include “Rocky Balboa,” “Superman Cash” and “Fat Boy,” often targeted the companies’ accounting departments. They would send an email purporting to be from the CEO and ask for help with a confidential financial transaction, according to court documents.

They would also coordinate a phone or video call where the defendants used AI to mimic the voice and sometimes the image of the CEO, according to the indictment.

The defendants would then tell them to contact an attorney at a major law firm, who the group was also ready to impersonate, according to court documents.

Soall mainly impersonated attorneys from the UK and had a “handwritten script titled ‘Lawyer Call’ that he utilized to make himself seem like a real attorney when speaking with and defrauding victims,” according to the U.S. attorney’s office.

The impersonated attorney would tell the employee to wire large payments to bank accounts across the world, according to court documents. The funds were then converted into cryptocurrency to try to conceal where they came from and then distributed to the trio and others involved, according to court documents.

FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle, Jr. said the case shows how advanced technology can be used to commit large-scale fraud.

“As criminals continue to weaponize emerging technologies, the FBI remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate, and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities,” he said in a statement.

If convicted, each of the charges have a maximum sentence of 20 years, except for aggravated identity theft, which is two years, according to the attorney’s office.

Related: AI Fuels ‘Industrial’ Cybercrime as Time-to-Exploit Shrinks to Hours

Related: AI-Powered Polymorphic Phishing Is Changing the Threat Landscape

Related: Cyber Insights 2026: Malware and Cyberattacks in the Age of AI

81936c53a4ca.text: Hello and welcome to the Friday, November 6, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Jacksonville, Florida. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cloud Security. In Diaries today, nothing too exciting. We did have in our honeypot some interesting, I thought initially, Cisco IOS vulnerability scans that come from a company RootEvidence that does one of these sort of exposure management, vulnerability management style net wide scans. What they are doing differently than other companies is that in their HTTP requests, they are including two opt-out headers, opt-out email and opt-out URL, which basically gives you a website where you can opt out of these scans or an email address where you can do the same. Interesting approach and I've not seen this being done by any other similar companies. We have literally dozens of companies doing essentially sort of the same thing. And I've always been a little bit curious about the immense sort of traffic we've seen our honeypots from these companies. And so coming up with some standards like this would certainly make some sense. But, well, if you want excitement, we do have an interesting critical vulnerability in certain types of SSH installs. Now the problem here isn't exactly in SSH. It's in musl. musl, if you haven't heard of it, is a variety of standard C libraries. So it's a replacement for libc or glibc. And it's often used in smaller footprint systems, like most importantly in the Alpine Linux that's often used in containers. But also OpenWrt and such uses musl. So anything that basically has a small memory footprint, not a lot of CPU cores and such, often uses this library. And sadly, well, they changed how crypt, the function that verifies passwords works, which in conjunction with SSH, then leads to any password that's longer than 256 characters being considered valid. Now the sshhole website has a good sort of walkthrough what exactly happened here and all the little details, a little bit too much to cover it here in the podcast. But what it comes down to, if your system uses musl instead of glibc, and again, Alpine Linux is probably the number one item here that you should look at. And if your version, your SSH daemon is first of all enabled, which of course is often not on containers, and if it does allow password -based logins, and if it does not use libpam, which is often actually disabled or not even compiled in a lot of images, then you may be vulnerable. So a couple conditions here to actually enable this vulnerability, but certainly something to look for. And if you're vulnerable, very easy test, just try root. It has to be a user that doesn't have a password defined actually. So that's another sort of dependency here. In that case, just try a long password, anything longer than 256 bytes should automatically log you in no matter what you type. So the content is irrelevant, just the length matters at that point. Interesting vulnerability and one of those, you know, where APIs change and this case, I think, change in very weird and kind of a little bit obviously wrong ways. And then of course, other software relying on these APIs like SSH, well, they then come to the wrong conclusion that the password may be correct. It's actually not correct. And a number of United States government agencies came together to publish a brief advisory for owners of refrigeration systems, well, to explain how to harden them. That of course comes after we had all of these attacks against grocery stores and in some cases also against the stores on military bases that led to the spoilage of a huge amount of food in refrigeration systems. The advice that they are providing is, in my opinion, pretty straightforward. For example, they state you should eliminate net exposure, you should isolate operational technologies, credential security, all of these good things, applying patches, where I think an advisory like this is most useful if you need buy-in from management or such to actually implement these things. Then a document like this may give you the backup that you need in order to justify spending time on actually implementing some of these solutions and maybe even in some cases to degrade some of these services like, for example, remote manageability of some of these systems. So take a look at this if you are dealing with any systems like this. What they're recommending here pretty much applies to any kind of OT, so operational technology that's connected to a network. It's not just refrigeration systems, even though they, of course, triggered this document. And if you're using any Zyxel GS1900 series switches, well, be aware there is an update for the firmware out fixing a vulnerability that's currently being exploited. The advisory doesn't state so, but it does credit Binarly with the vulnerability. And what Binarly basically discovered was that they came across a malware repository that included a Python script exploiting this specific vulnerability. It appears to be a variety of vulnerability that Zyxel published in the past, but, well, didn't apparently publish completely. So definitely get this up to date. The advisory does, however, state that the attacker needs network access in order to launch the exploit. So they already have to be essentially in your network. The exploits that Binarly has seen are typically then stealing configuration data, including hashed passwords from affected switches. Well, and that's it for today. Thanks again for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for recommending this podcast. And just as a reminder, in the show notes, you'll find a link to the Difference Maker Award, where I am nominated this year for one of the awards. So would appreciate your vote. But lots of other good people here that are nominated for various categories and also a link to future classes. The next one being mid-December in DC, our Defending Web Applications class. Thanks.

Zyxel GS1900 network switches that received the vendor's earlier fix for an actively exploited flaw are still open to the exploit attackers used, researchers at Binarly found.

The exploit lets anyone who can reach a switch's web management interface run commands on it without logging in. Zyxel has released new firmware for 10 GS1900 models that closes the hole.

The earlier fix is the 2.90 Patch 2 firmware, named in a June 16 advisory for a flaw tracked as CVE-2026-7273. The new 2.90 Patch 3 firmware fixes a flaw now tracked separately as CVE-2026-107441, which the exploit relies on. It was posted on October 23, and the vendor announced it in an advisory earlier this week.

The researchers, who reported the flaw to the vendor on September 29, call it a zero-day. Attackers already had a working exploit for it by then.

GreyNoise, which monitors attack traffic through a network of sensors, reported on September 21 that attackers took data from 996 GS1900 switches around August 17. It tied the attacks to CVE-2026-7273, and the researchers say the exploit it described matches the one they found.

Neither GreyNoise nor Binarly says the attacked switches were running the earlier fix, and the vendor's advisory does not say whether the new flaw has been exploited.

Which Switches Need the New Firmware

Switches on Patch 2 or any earlier firmware need the Patch 3 build for their model. The builds are posted with their firmware release notes.

The advisory lists no workaround for owners who cannot update yet. It also does not say whether updating removes access an attacker may already have, or what owners should check if a switch may have been compromised.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on September 21 and gave federal agencies until September 24 to apply the vendor's fix, the Patch 2 firmware. The listing came the day the earlier attacks were made public.

The researchers' vulnerability advisory says the new flaw is present in all 10 of those Patch 2 builds. It also says "an attacker only needs network reachability to the management service", while the vendor's advisory describes a "LAN-based, unauthenticated attacker".

The researchers rate the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS severity scale, against 8.8 in the vendor's CVE entry, and say the attacker's commands run with root privileges.

Why the Earlier Fix Did Not Stop the Exploit

Binarly's technical analysis traces the flaw to the program that handles web requests on the switch. It is an out-of-bounds write, meaning the program writes data beyond the memory allocated for it.

The program stores each request parameter in a fixed area that can accommodate 140 parameters. It never checked the size of a parameter, and before Patch 2 it never checked how many parameters it had stored.

The exploit sends a 140th parameter that is too large, causing it to overrun the end of that area and overwrite the program's parameter counter. The next parameter is then written outside the area, allowing the attacker to swap the function the program is about to call for one that runs the attacker's command.

Patch 2 added a check on the counter, but the check runs only after the oversized parameter has been copied. By then the counter holds the attacker's value, so the check does not stop the write. The researchers say the exploit works against Patch 2 without changes.

They tested it on emulated firmware and on real hardware, though they do not say which model. The exploit's own list of supported firmware includes the Patch 2 build for the GS1900-24.

According to the researchers, Zyxel told them that CVE-2026-7273 was about the missing counter check, and that it treats the missing size check as a separate flaw, now CVE-2026-107441.

In the Patch 3 code, the counter is checked before a parameter is copied, and the copy is limited in size. The researchers say this fixes the flaw.

What Is Known About the Attacks

GreyNoise's attack report says the attackers used the exploit to download a data-collection script onto the switches and left the collected data to be picked up. The data included switch configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information. Of the 996 switches, 564 still used factory-default credentials.

The report does not say which firmware the switches were running or how the attackers reached them. It says the attackers are the same as, or related to, a group that Acronis tracks as Red Heron and describes as Chinese-speaking. Acronis linked a backdoor called JITTERLY to Red Heron in an earlier campaign that targeted Gitea servers.

The researchers found the exploit on September 17 in an open folder on a server that also acted as a command server for JITTERLY.

Their advisory offers two explanations. Either the Patch 2 update was a faulty fix for CVE-2026-7273, or the attacks exploited a different flaw from the one CISA listed.

The researchers say they will soon publish a smaller version of the exploit as a proof of concept. CISA's KEV catalog data, last updated yesterday, does not list CVE-2026-107441.
