cb07594aee6a.text: A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails. The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures. Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information. The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails. The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required. Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed. Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's preferences, email began flowing once more. SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both). The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response. To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place. A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation." "Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue." Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. Outlook on the web, as well as the Purview and Defender portals were all affected. Microsoft reverted the change in the Exchange Online front-end infrastructure, and all was well. It has yet to say what else, if anything, might have changed in its email services to cause legitimate messages to bounce back. ®

Security researchers at Socket have uncovered a new software supply chain attack that has affected tens of thousands of GitHub repositories, including organization-owned ones.

Uber is mentioned as one of the businesses that runs compromised packages. The kill chain is reminiscent of GhostAction, a malicious campaign discovered by GitGuardian in September 2025 and reappeared in October 2026.

Malicious Workflow Spread Via Two GitHub Accounts

On October 8, 2026, two GitHub accounts, ‘henrywoo’ and ‘kitao,’ pushed a malicious GitHub Actions workflow to hundreds of repositories they had permission to modify.

A GitHub Action is an automated task that runs in a GitHub repository to handle activities such as testing code, building software or deploying applications whenever specific events occur.

The workflow, named “.github/workflows/security-audit.yml,” was added through a single-file commit designed to look routine, “Add security audit workflow” and “Update security audit workflow.”

Despite its name, the workflow does not perform any security checks. Instead, it steals credentials from affected repositories and sends them to an external server at 193.32.204[.]199 over HTTP.

Because the workflow looks like a legitimate security tool, it can go unnoticed while running as part of the repository's automated processes.

According to Socket researchers, the malicious file was found in tens of thousands of repositories, which include ones where ‘henrywoo’ or ‘kitao’ have write access.

Infection vectors include the following repositories:

henrywoo/pyllama and henrywoo/chatllama, AI GitHub projects created by ‘henrywoo’

kitao/pixel, typically distributed through both Python Pacjkage Index (PyPI) and crates.io, online repositories where developers publish and distribute software packages written in Python and Rust, respectively

uber/athenadriver, an Uber-owned project where ‘henrywoo’ has write access as its original author

Even repositories that had been inactive for a decade were affected, suggesting the attackers systematically enumerated every repository they could access instead of choosing targets based on their activity or value.

The activity appears automated rather than manually targeted.

Expanding GhostAction’s Secret Theft Capabilities

While the incident is a new variation of the GhostAction campaign, Socket researchers noted that this latest version expands what the attackers can steal.

Earlier GhostAction attacks primarily targeted secrets stored in GitHub Actions, such as API keys and access tokens configured for automated workflows.

The new variant also searches the repository's files and complete Git history for credentials using regular-expression patterns. This means it can find sensitive information that developers accidentally committed to source code, configuration files or earlier versions of files, even if those credentials have since been deleted from the latest version of the repository.

The additional search targets credentials for cloud providers and AI services, potentially exposing access to infrastructure, hosted applications and third-party services.

Malicious Workflow Still Active in GitHub Repositories

As of October 9, 2026, Socket reported that the malicious workflow was still present on the default branches of the repositories it examined, including uber/athenadriver and kitao/pyxel.

The workflow had also successfully executed in affected repositories, meaning the credential-stealing activity was not limited to an attempted injection.

However, the researchers had not observed any malicious package versions published to PyPI or crates.io as a result of the campaign at the time the Socket report was published.

This does not mean the stolen credentials have not been used for other purposes, only that Socket had not identified evidence of follow-on malicious package releases on those two registries.

Online fashion retailer Revolve has informed the Indiana Attorney General’s Office that 1,515,073 individuals were impacted by the data breach it disclosed in October.

The company revealed the incident on October 29 in a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). It started sending notification letters to impacted customers around the same time.

According to the company, the intruder may have relied on “automated means” to collect customers’ names and contact information, including mailing addresses, along with their card numbers and expiration dates.

The exposure is limited to shoppers who chose to store a payment method in their online accounts.

Game Server Communication

All communication with the game servers is authenticated and encrypted. The AES encryption key is included in the /srvlist response from the line configuration servers (field aes_key). For authentication, all requests are signed with HMAC-SHA256, a keyed hash message authentication code that computes the hash of a message and a shared secret (the AES key in our case).

Because the AES key is returned in cleartext from the line config servers, the purpose is not to address confidentiality or integrity against a third party, but rather to obfuscate content and check for communication errors.

Conclusion

This malware is not “garage” or student-level work. It reflects well-planned development, with a clean infrastructure, multiple REST APIs, and a full ecosystem. In 2024, with limited reverse engineering tooling, this Flutter application would have taken ages to reverse engineer. In 2026, however, it’s merely a hard day’s work. It’s always good news to hear that cybercriminals are losing their edge.

Fortinet Protections

The malware described in this report is detected and blocked by FortiGuard Antivirus as:

Android/TinstaPorn.A!tr (SIGID: 815959)

FortiGate, FortiMail, FortiClient, and FortiEDR support the FortiGuard AntiVirus service. The FortiGuard AntiVirus engine is part of each of these solutions. As a result, customers who have these products with up-to-date protections are protected.

The FortiGuard Web Filtering Service blocks the servers.

Organizations seeking to strengthen foundational security awareness may also consider completing Fortinet Certified Fundamentals (FCF) training in Cybersecurity. This module is designed to help end users learn how to identify and protect themselves from phishing attacks.

The FortiGuard IP Reputation and Anti-Botnet Security Service proactively blocks infrastructure associated with this campaign by correlating malicious IP intelligence collected from Fortinet’s global sensor network, CERT collaborations, MITRE, trusted industry partners, and other intelligence sources.

If you believe this or any other cybersecurity threat has impacted your organization, please contact our Global FortiGuard Incident Response Team.

Background

In early October, Huntress began seeing threat actors exploit two flaws in AhsayCBS, the management console for Ahsay's backup software: CVE-2026-105133, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-105134, unauthenticated remote code execution as SYSTEM through /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do. Our original blog post covered the first wave: webshells, an XMRig miner dressed up as Microsoft Edge, and a script that hid the miner from Task Manager. Ahsay has since released hotfixes (10.3.4.45 for v10, and 9.15.2.70 for v7 through v9), and we verified that 10.3.4.45 blocks the entry point we saw.

The impacted organization's servers in this post were exploited between October 8 and October 11, 2026, which was before Ahsay released its hotfixes. During our investigation into the attack, we analyzed webshells, loaders, and an implant that the threat actor used during the attack.

This activity matches the campaign in our first post. We tied it to AhsayCBS exploitation because the webshells sat inside AhsayCBS's own web directories, the AhsayCBS access logs show an exploit source address that is listed in that post, and one of the servers also held files matching that post's indicators.

When organizations apply hotfixes, it mitigates the issue moving forward, but if a compromise has already happened it does not remove files an actor has already planted. If your AhsayCBS servers were exposed before patching, it's worth searching your environment for the artifacts in this post.

What we found, at a glance

Our initial report described incidents that involved a quick smash and grab: a webshell or a few commands, then a miner. However, this incident reflects a much larger intrusion with more patience; the operator planted shells in several places, ran two different miners, staged tunneling tools, and installed a custom implant, all on servers whose job is to hold backups. The rest of this post takes apart the pieces one at a time.

Figure 1: An overview of what the operator left on the exploited servers

Webshells, in several flavors

Overall, we saw five webshell families during our investigation (seen in the table below), all with varying parameters and characteristics.

One of the most common webshells we found in this environment was small in size: it compared a hardcoded key in the p parameter against its own copy and returned a plain 404 if the key is wrong, so a scanner that does not know the key would see an empty page. With the right key, the c parameter would be passed to cmd.exe /c and the output would come back Base64-encoded.

The second webshell family included w and d parameters, which were designed to write Base64-decoded bytes to any path the service account can reach and make it easy to drop more tools. Every file carried its own key (always 12 hex characters followed by a capital P).

The third family looked completely different, and included files named status_ followed by six random letters. These shells used auth, cmd, del, and rm parameters: they were designed to run commands, recursively delete any path they are given, and delete themselves. To the latter point, defenders should keep in mind that the shell can delete itself after use, so not finding the file on disk does not prove it was never present.

A smaller variant of this family, named st_ followed by six random letters, drops the authentication and the delete function. It takes c with no authentication at all, plus a get=env parameter that prints the application home, the Catalina base, the operating system and the temp directory, and an rm=1 parameter that deletes the file.

Family

Parameters and behavior

Keyed command shell

p key (a wrong key returns 404), c command run through cmd.exe /c, output Base64-encoded. a and b return a sum, which works as a quick liveness check.

Keyed shell with file write

Same as above, plus w (path) and d (Base64 data) to write a file.

status_ / st_ shells

auth secret, cmd command, del path (recursive delete), rm=1 (self-delete). Secrets seen include 32-character hex strings and simple passwords.

nsmind.jsp

Signed API with exec, cd, upload and download actions, described below.

AhsayCBS.jsp

Loader for an encrypted payload hidden in a PNG, described below.

The folder locations where we found these webshells gave us further insight into how the attack might vary across operating systems. The impacted servers here ran Windows: however, the exploit also attempted Linux-style installation paths, suggesting the exploit was not tailored to one operating system.

In addition to webapps\cbs and webapps\rps in the real install, we found copies in directories matching Linux-style paths, including /opt/AhsayCBS, /usr/local/AhsayCBS, and /home/ahsay/AhsayCBS. On one of the affected Windows servers, these appeared as folders under C:\opt, C:\usr, and C:\home, with a staging folder, C:\ahsay_tf, holding another copy. That suggests the exploit was not designed for a specific operating system or install path, and simply tried every likely location.

The copies outside the live install were not served by the web application, so they probably cannot be used as shells on Windows, but they are a reliable tell. Several shells also sat in random six-character folders, each containing its own app, conf, and webapps\cbs subfolders. These imitate the structure of an AhsayCBS install, but none of the components are part of the real application. Some of those folders held empty pb_ marker files in the conf folder, and folders named ahsay_poc_*, ahsay_tf, ahsay_th and ahsay_t0 showed up in Program Files.

Figure 2: Shell locations on a Windows host: the live install, and the Linux-style paths the exploit also tries

A webshell that hides inside an image

One of the webshell families, AhsayCBS.jsp (in webapps\rps), was disguised as an image-preview service: it was designed to extract encrypted code from uploaded PNGs and run it in memory while making its traffic resemble ordinary image requests.

The webshell's disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint. The webshell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later.

On the sample we saw, the webshell was designed to work as follows:

First, the operator POSTs a PNG.

Then the page reads the least-significant bit of each pixel's red, green and blue values, one pixel at a time.

It strings those bits together and packs them into bytes, with the first bit read becoming the most significant bit of each byte.

That rebuilds a four-byte big-endian length followed by that many bytes of payload, which it then decrypts with AES.

The key is hardcoded, and the cipher is Java's default AES transformation (translating to ECB mode with PKCS5 padding).

On the first request, the decrypted bytes are loaded as a Java class through a small custom ClassLoader and stored in the application context under the attribute name QuCh, and the page answers with its built-in cover image. On later requests, it creates an instance of that class, hands it the request, an output buffer and the decrypted data through calls to equals(), and calls toString() to run it. Whatever the class produces is encrypted again and written into a new PNG.

Passing arguments through equals() is a convention used by some open-source in-memory webshell frameworks, though we have not tied this one to a specific framework. The practical effect is that the functionality arrives per request and lives in memory. The access log showed what looked like image traffic, and there was no c or p parameter to search for. We analyzed the loader, not the class it receives, so we cannot confirm what the operator actually ran through it.

Figure 3: How AhsayCBS.jsp turns an uploaded image into running code

A webshell with a signed API

Not every shell was a one-liner. nsmind.jsp, also in webapps\rps, behaved like a small remote administration service.

In the sample we saw, every request must carry an X-Auth-Token header that matches a hardcoded API key, plus X-Timestamp, X-Nonce and an X-Signature header holding an HMAC-SHA256 of the request parameters. The timestamp has to be within five minutes of the server's clock, and each nonce is stored in the application context so a captured request cannot be replayed. A request that fails any check gets a short JSON error, so the page behaves like an ordinary API that rejects unauthenticated callers.

Behind the checks, the action parameter selects exec, cd, upload or download. exec runs the command through cmd.exe /c (after chcp 65001, so output comes back as UTF-8) and tracks the working directory between calls, so the operator gets a persistent shell. upload and download move files in chunks using an offset parameter, with a limit of 4 GB per file, which means a large file can be pulled off the server through many small requests.

On a server that holds backups, this download action is the part to worry about: it is a ready-made exfiltration channel that looks like normal API traffic. We did not see logs showing download in use, so we cannot say what, if anything, was taken.

The files also showed the operator iterating. In the same rps folder we found three timestamp-named folders, each holding a single copy of a shell. The oldest held the simple cmd, del and rm shell described above, and the two newer ones contained nsmind.jsp, which suggested the operator upgraded from a basic shell to this tool. We also found byte-identical copies of nsmind.jsp and AhsayCBS.jsp on two of the servers, which pointed to one operator or one script working across hosts.

A second miner, with its own persistence

The Edge-themed miner analyzed in our initial blog was not the only one: we also found another miner in our follow-up investigation.

The XMRig miner we observed (kvm-agent.exe) is configured like a standard XMRig build: donate level 0, MSR access enabled (the same capability the WinRing0 driver in the first post provides), and TLS connections on port 443 to SupportXMR pools. The wallet and password differed from the Kryptex pool and user listed in the first post, making us believe this was a separate miner and not a second copy of the first. We found the same file, with the same hash, on two servers, and the task on both was created the same night and edited within seconds of each other, which again points to one operator or one script working across hosts.

During our analysis, we found a scheduled task named kvm running as SYSTEM every minute. Its command used a tasklist to check whether kvm-agent.exe was running and, if it wasn't, it would start it from C:\Windows\SysWOW64\kvm-agent. This means that if the miner was killed, it would be back up and running within a minute. The task's start time was set well before the intrusion (making it look older than it was in task listings).

Figure 4: The kvm scheduled task (start time elided)

A Python implant that only runs where it was staged

The most interesting file we pulled was main.py, which sits in an embedded Python distribution under the SYSTEM profile and is started from a Run key through explorer.exe. The script is only a wrapper: Base64, then lzma, then a marshaled Python code object that it passes to exec. Decoding it without running it shows that the code was compiled from a file called heap_shellcode_runner_bound_weaponized.py.

The code computes the SHA-256 of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a file with that name next to main.py. Based on the bytecode, if the marker file is missing, the script exits. That would keep the implant from running in a sandbox or on an analyst's machine, because the marker only exists on the host it was provisioned for. We did not find a marker file in the folder we collected, so either it was not part of what we pulled or it was removed. If the marker is present, the script copies a 673 KB blob into an executable heap (HeapCreate, HeapAlloc, RtlMoveMemory) and starts it on a new thread with CreateThread.

Figure 5: The implant's execution flow, reconstructed from static analysis

Figure 6: The decoded logic, reconstructed from the code object

The blob starts with a short bootstrap that calls a reflective loader at the end of the blob, which in turn maps an x64 DLL carried inside it. The DLL is C++ with a JSON library and imports very little: bcrypt, KERNEL32, OLEAUT32 and SHLWAPI, with the networking functions resolved at run time. It has no export table, no PDB path and no version resource, so the usual attribution breadcrumbs have been stripped.

Its strings include the C2 URL hxxps://creepexplosiondarknight[.]com/d, a JSON content type, a mutex, and string fragments (dns.quad with 9.net, and dns.goog) consistent with DNS-over-HTTPS lookups through Quad9 and Google. It also reads MachineGuid and Windows version information, which fits host identification. We have not identified the malware family and have not watched the implant run, so what it does after it checks in is still an open question.

Figure 7: Selected strings from the embedded DLL (C2 defanged)

The rest of the toolkit

Around those pieces, the same environment held the tunneling tools gost and chisel, staged in .st<id> folders as wust<id>a.exe and wust<id>b.exe, the remote access tools AnyDesk, Atera and Splashtop, a local account named wdguest, and a Mimikatz package on disk. We also saw Microsoft Defender exclusions that covered C:\ProgramData, C:\Windows, temp folders, the dropper processes, and the AhsayCBS service process (cbssvcX64.exe). These exclusions would have reduced Defender's ability to scan files in those locations and files accessed by the excluded processes, creating broad blind spots for the operator's tooling.

Backup servers as a target

Everything above ran on servers whose purpose is to hold or manage backups. On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI. Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident.

What to check for

Patching closes the entry point. It does not clean up what already happened, so on any server that was exposed before the hotfix, look for:

Unexpected .jsp files under webapps\cbs and webapps\rps, especially random names and the status_ and st_ patterns, and requests to UpdateReceivers.do in the AhsayCBS access logs

Folders named ahsay_*, home, opt, srv or usr at the root of the drive or in Program Files, and timestamp-named folders (year-month-day-hour-minute-second) next to the shells, which in some cases held a single copy of one

Scheduled tasks and services you did not create, including a SYSTEM task with a one-minute repeat that tests for a process with tasklist

Defender exclusions you did not add, especially for C:\ProgramData, C:\Windows and the AhsayCBS service process

An embedded Python install under the SYSTEM profile and a Run key that launches it

A few behaviors make useful detections even when the files are gone:

python.exe or pythonw.exe running from a path under the SYSTEM profile

Outbound requests to public DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers from a process that is not a browser

New .jsp files created under the AhsayCBS web directories

The parent-child pattern our earlier Sigma rule already looks for, where cbssvcX64.exe spawns a command shell.

If you find any of the above, we recommend a full re-image from a trusted backup and rotating credentials stored on or reachable from the server, including those saved in AhsayCBS and in any backup software on the same network.

Sasha Roshan is a Senior Sales Engineer at Huntress and a cybersecurity educator. His work sits at the point where technical expertise meets real-world security needs. He helps customers and partners understand what they're trying to protect, and he asks the questions that reveal the real problem before showing how Huntress can help.

That can mean preparing a customer demonstration, helping a partner work through a technical scenario, presenting a webinar, supporting an event, or collaborating with colleagues on content and on building hacking environments. No two weeks look exactly the same, but the common thread is communication. The technical detail needs to be accurate, and it also needs to be relevant to the person in front of him.

"The best conversations are not product tours," Sasha says. "They're about helping someone understand what's happening in their environment and how the attack happens, what matters most, and what they can do next."

Sasha on BBC

What one partner actually needed to know

One partner conversation shows how Sasha approaches the work. A partner had questions about day-to-day operations, asking what would happen overnight and how their team could avoid drowning in false positives. Just as important was understanding who would make decisions when something serious was detected.

Sasha built the conversation around that operational journey and kept product terminology to a minimum. He walked through how the Huntress SOC handles detection and response, and how the service works alongside Microsoft Defender. He then showed what escalation looks like in practice. Once the discussion tracked the partner's real concerns, it moved from general interest to a concrete next step. Sasha and the team proposed a trial in the partner's environment and scheduled a follow-up to plan the deployment.

For Sasha, the experience reinforced where a Sales Engineer adds the most value. It comes from helping someone see the decision in front of them clearly enough to choose what to do next.

Sasha doing what he does best: Educating the community

Taking sales engineering beyond the one-to-one conversation

In previous roles, Sasha's focus was mainly on supporting individual customer or partner conversations. At Huntress, he's been able to take what he learns from those conversations and turn it into education for a much wider audience.

He contributes to livestreams, workshops, newsletter content, videos, and presentations. He also helps shape Huntress Wire, Huntress' global newsletter, and creates cybersecurity content for LinkedIn and YouTube. Sasha hadn't had the opportunity to combine sales engineering with public education at this scale before.

"I've been able to spread my wings further and wider," Sasha says. "I now get involved with what I've always wanted to do: education."

That broader role has also given him the chance to represent Huntress publicly. He's spoken at partner and customer events, webinars, and industry gatherings, including a presentation alongside the Cyber Crime Unit at Metropolitan Police Headquarters in London. Each experience has helped him grow as a presenter and find clearer ways to make complex cybersecurity topics approachable.

Making cybersecurity easier to navigate

For Sasha, the meaningful part of the work isn't simply explaining technology but helping people feel more confident about what to do next.

Cybersecurity can feel overwhelming from the outside. Threats change quickly, the terminology can be difficult to navigate, and many organizations don't have unlimited time or resources. Sasha enjoys helping make that picture clearer, whether he's speaking with a customer or partner, presenting to a live audience, or recording a video for someone who's learning on their own.

His focus includes areas such as identity security and security posture management, where small gaps can create meaningful risk. On YouTube, he breaks down subjects that can sound intimidating, including security teams, attack techniques, and identity-based threats. Across every format, Sasha tries to take something complicated and leave people better equipped to protect themselves.

Doing that well means knowing the audience and being able to explain the same idea from more than one angle. Creating content sharpens Sasha's thinking, while speaking with live audiences helps him understand which explanations resonate. Both make him a better Sales Engineer.

Sharing knowledge, as usual

Growing with support and opportunity

Huntress has given Sasha room to develop beyond a traditional definition of sales engineering. He's been able to build technical depth while also growing as a presenter, educator, and industry voice. He now helps lead Huntress Managed ISPM for the Sales Engineering team.

Sasha walks you through Huntress Managed ISPM

Colleagues review his content, help with event preparation, collaborate on video and marketing work, and share their own expertise. That teamwork makes it easier to take on something new and improve the work along the way.

Sasha also values the variety. One day, his impact may come from helping a customer make a confident decision. Another day, it may come from a partner event of a video that shows someone why identity protection deserves their attention. The combination of mission, learning, and opportunity keeps him excited about the work.

Outside Huntress, Sasha teaches martial arts and is an active black belt with the International Taekwon-Do Federation (ITF). Like cybersecurity education, martial arts requires steady practice and helping others improve.

Advice for future Sales Engineers

Sasha's advice to someone considering a role like his is to stay willing to learn, and do not underestimate the value of clear communication.

"You do not need to know everything on day one," he says. "We will provide you with the tools and resources, but we can't teach ambition, and at Huntress, we are incredibly hungry"

For him, the right mindset starts with asking good questions, understanding the problem behind the technology, and continuing to develop your knowledge.

If you're interested in combining technical work with education, communication, and making a difference, check out the Huntress Careers page.

920f3f152ab6.text: Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7.7 million customers, leaving shoppers unable to place orders. The retailer, which sells everything from home appliances and furniture to pet supplies, first disclosed the incident on October 29, a day after discovering a suspicious file on a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza ecommerce operation. Iris Plaza immediately suspended its website and associated systems and began investigating, subsequently confirming unauthorized access. Iris Ohyama has since revealed that the potentially compromised cloud environment contained personal information belonging to approximately 5.8 million registered customers, including former members, and another 1.9 million people who had purchased products without creating an account or participated in promotional campaigns. The potentially exposed information includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, and passwords, although the company says the exact information at risk varies between customers. Some of that data, including passwords, was encrypted, but Iris Ohyama hasn't explained what protection was used. It has advised customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords elsewhere to change them, presumably before someone else gets the opportunity. There is some good news for anyone who has handed over their credit card details, as the retailer says it didn't store payment information in the affected cloud service and that it hasn't been compromised. It remains unclear whether the attackers actually made off with any personal information. In its FAQ, Iris Plaza says it is still investigating the possibility of a data leak and has yet to establish the full extent of the intrusion. Meanwhile, Iris Plaza's website is still down, and the company isn't saying when it'll be back. Orders are also taking longer to ship, while customers trying to cancel a purchase have been told they may have to turn the delivery driver away if their parcel arrives before the cancellation is processed. Fortunately for anyone desperate to buy a new rice cooker, Iris Plaza's stores on Rakuten, Yahoo! Shopping, and auPAY Market are still operating. The company says it has found no evidence that those stores were affected. Iris Ohyama has reported the incident to Japanese authorities and says it will contact potentially affected customers individually. It has also warned shoppers to watch out for phishing emails, fraudulent calls, and fake websites impersonating the retailer. The company has yet to identify the cloud provider involved, explain how the attackers got in, or establish whether any of those 7.7 million records actually left its systems. ®

Why the Risk Operations Center Is Becoming the System of Record for Proactive Enterprise Risk Reduction

The cybersecurity industry has spent years improving how we discover vulnerabilities. The challenge now is no longer finding risk. It is reducing risk faster than adversaries can exploit it.

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities disclosed in October are a reminder of how quickly exposure can become exploitation. Within hours of disclosure, attack activity was already being observed. Across more than 10,000 customer environments, the Qualys Threat Research Unit identified more than 166 million PHP installations, approximately three-quarters of them internet-facing. Yet only a small percentage were patched during the critical first hours after disclosure.

This trend is only accelerating. Frontier AI is reducing the time and effort required for reconnaissance, vulnerability analysis, attack planning, and exploitation. The gap between disclosure and weaponization continues to compress, placing increasing pressure on defenders to prioritize and remediate risk at machine speed.

At the same time, the enterprise attack surface has fundamentally changed.

Risk is no longer concentrated in servers, laptops, and cloud workloads. It now extends into mobile devices, medical technology, healthcare environments, manufacturing operations, operational technology, connected devices, and other cyber-physical systems. Many of these assets support an organization’s most critical functions. They help deliver patient care, keep production lines running, support transportation networks, and operate critical infrastructure. Mobile devices have become equally important, providing access to corporate data, business applications, sensitive communications, and some of an organization’s most valuable information.

Yet these environments are often managed separately, with different teams, tools, workflows, and severity models. Attackers do not see those boundaries. They see a single attack surface.

That is why the Risk Operations Center matters.

The Risk Operations Center was never intended to be another dashboard, nor was it intended to replace the SOC. It is an operating model for continuously identifying, prioritizing, validating, and reducing risk across the enterprise before those vulnerabilities can ever be exploited. To fulfill that mission, the ROC must extend beyond traditional IT assets.

As attack surfaces expand and threats accelerate, organizations need more than visibility. They need a way to bring together technology, telemetry, and expertise into a single operating model capable of operationalizing cyber risk management at scale.

That is the vision behind the expanded Global mROC Alliance.

By bringing together the Qualys platform, specialized technology alliance partners, and a global ecosystem of highly trained Risk Operations Center experts, the Global mROC Alliance helps organizations move from identifying risk to systematically reducing it across the enterprise. The goal is not simply to see more risk. It is to help customers outpace increasingly sophisticated threats in the age of AI.

As part of that effort, Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management (ETM) now integrates telemetry from Lookout and NowSecure for mobile security, and from Claroty and Nozomi Networks for OT, IoT, healthcare, and cyber-physical environments.

This expands visibility into some of the least measured yet most consequential areas of enterprise risk.

More importantly, it creates a common operational model for reducing risk. Qualys ETM and TruRisk provide the visibility to understand exposure, the prioritization to focus on what matters most, and the remediation guidance needed to drive measurable risk reduction across the attack surface.

The objective is not simply broader visibility. The objective is better prioritization and faster risk reduction.

When a vulnerable mobile device, an exposed medical system, an industrial controller, and an internet-facing application are all evaluated through the same framework, security teams can focus on reducing the risks that have the greatest potential impact on the business rather than simply responding to the loudest alerts.

For mobile environments, that means bringing device posture, application risk, operating system vulnerabilities, and threat telemetry into the same risk conversation as cloud, endpoint, and infrastructure exposure. A compromised mobile device with privileged access may represent greater business risk than dozens of lower-priority infrastructure findings.

For healthcare, manufacturing, OT, and cyber-physical environments, it means incorporating risks that have traditionally existed outside mainstream security operations. Through Claroty and Nozomi Networks, organizations gain visibility into environments where operational continuity is paramount and active scanning may not be feasible. Just as importantly, those risks can now be prioritized and managed through the same remediation workflow as the rest of the enterprise. Where patching is not possible, compensating controls such as segmentation and access restrictions become part of the same risk reduction process.

This is the power of Qualys’ Global mROC Alliance.

Technology alliance partners contribute deep visibility into the environments they know best. Qualys ETM and TruRisk transform that telemetry into a common risk language through visibility, prioritization, and remediation. mROC Alliance partners help customers operationalize those insights through advisory services, implementation, managed risk reduction programs, and fully managed Risk Operations Center services.

Together, they provide organizations with a practical path to reducing risk across the entire attack surface, not just the portion that has historically been easiest to measure.

Find out more about the Global mROC Alliance.

Learn More

PHP2Shell is not the story.

PHP2Shell was just the opening act. The real story is that the time between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation continues to shrink while the attack surface continues to expand.

Organizations can no longer afford separate programs for IT, mobile, healthcare, OT, IoT, and cyber-physical risk. They need a common operating model, a common language for prioritization, and a single system for driving remediation.

The organizations that succeed will not be those that discover the most vulnerabilities. They will be those that reduce the most risk in the shortest amount of time.

That is the purpose of the Risk Operations Center.

And that is why the Risk Operations Center is emerging as the operating system for proactive cyber risk reduction in the age of AI.

Sega has revealed that around 2.2 million customer email addresses have been exposed as result of a third-party incident.

The video gaming giant revealed on November 9 that an unauthorized third party leaked the email addresses after gaining access to Arara Inc., a Japanese email delivery provider used by Sega to distribute its email newsletter.

“We deeply apologize for the great inconvenience and concern caused to our customers and all parties involved,” Sega wrote.

“Currently, Arara is working to identify the causes of unauthorized access and prevent further damage, and we are working with Arara and related companies to confirm the details of the leaked information.”

The Japanese firm said the breach is limited to 2.196 million email addresses for various email newsletters, and 92,273 items related to distribution.

The leaked information does not include customer names, dates of birth, genders, addresses, phone numbers, credit card information or login passwords.

No misuse of the leaked data has been currently confirmed. However, Sega has warned customers to be vigilant for suspicious emails purporting to be from Sega or Sega Fave Corporation, or using product or service names operated by both companies.

Sega Fave is a subsidiary of the broader Sega group, which focuses on the production of toys and arcade machines.

“Please do not open or reply to URLs or attachments provided in emails you do not recognize. Accessing URLs or opening attached files may lead to entering personal information or affecting your device. Neither our company nor Sega Fave will ask you for your password or credit card information by email. If you receive such an email, do not access the reply or the provided link; delete it,” the company said.

Sega Breach Part of Large-Scale Third-Party Incident

Arara revealed it had been compromised in a statement issued on October 29, which said that unauthorized access was gained to certain server systems of its email distribution service a day earlier, on October 28 after a hacker exploited vulnerabilities in web servers.

The distribution service ‘Arara Message’ was suspended on October 31 and remains offline at the time of writing, according to a dedicated incident page set up by the firm to provide updates.

According to a report by The Japan Times, Arara’s parent company Paycloud Holdings confirmed on November 2 that hackers gained unauthorized access to servers operated by the subsidiary, which exposed information held by around 380 corporate clients using the service. This included 77 million email addresses.

Paycloud also noted that depending on the company, the breached data also included names, telephone numbers and addresses. However, it said that no credit card details have been exposed.

The Python Package Index (PyPI) has added a security tab to its project pages, giving developers a place to check where individual release files came from.

How PyPI shows where release files came from

The Security tab shows whether release files have digital attestations, which provide verifiable information about how a file was published or built. A release has full provenance when every file has at least one attestation. A PyPI Publish attestation identifies the Trusted Publisher that uploaded the file, while a SLSA Build Provenance attestation links the file to its source commit, build platform and build instructions. Users can review the attestation details in the tab or open the linked transparency log.

A release has no provenance when none of its files has an attestation. Nicole Harris, PyPI design contributor, said this is common for older releases and projects that have yet to configure Trusted Publishing. She stressed that such a release isn’t necessarily malicious, since the missing attestation only means its origin can’t be cryptographically verified.

In those cases, developers can look at maintainer history, release patterns and repository activity when assessing a package.

Where PyPI shows warnings and release details

PyPI warns users when only some files in a release have attestations or when files in the same release come from different repositories or build systems. Warnings appear when a release comes from a different repository or workflow than a previous version, or when a project that previously provided attestations stops doing so.

A change in workflow often has a legitimate explanation, such as an organization renaming itself or moving its repository, though it may signal a compromised pipeline or an account takeover.

An example provenance warning on PyPI, showing a release with incomplete provenance (Source: PyPI)

The redesigned project page displays provenance warnings at the top, alongside notices for yanked releases, archived projects and pre-releases. If a project or release is quarantined, the page displays only the quarantine banner. For releases where every file is attested or a warning applies, the sidebar shows that status and links to the Security tab.

The Release Files tab lets users search and filter downloads and see the provenance status of each file. For releases that predate PyPI’s July 2026 policy change, the tab flags files uploaded more than 14 days after the initial release. Since that change, PyPI has refused any late uploads.

The Release History tab shows the file count, provenance status and any applicable release status for each version, so users can compare releases from the same page.

688c21507f3d.text:
The New York attorney general (AG) has reached a settlement over a medical data breach that affected 13.3 million people after basic security failures.

Perry Johnson & Associates (PJ&A) and four related companies have agreed to pay $300,000 and implement extensive security reforms following a breach that exposed personal and medical information belonging to more than 13.3 million people. They face another $9.7 million in penalties if they fail to meet the settlement’s terms.

New York AG Letitia James announced the agreement on November 6, alongside the attorneys general of Connecticut, Michigan, and New Jersey. Approximately 4.2 million of the people affected were New York residents.

The investigation describes a series of failures: remote access without multifactor authentication, nearly identical passwords circulated by email, sensitive files without file-level encryption, and security software that detected malicious activity but did not alert security staff.

The result: the companies only discovered the attack when the attackers contacted them on May 2, 2023, and demanded payment.

How many people were affected?

The stolen database files contained records associated with more than 13.3 million people, including approximately 4.2 million New Yorkers.

Earlier reporting put the number of affected patients at approximately 8.95 million. The settlement documents now give the larger figure of more than 13.3 million. The total could be higher, since the AG found that attackers also accessed files in shared network storage containing personal and health information, but the companies did not review those files to identify additional affected people.

The information included:

Names, dates of birth, and home addresses.

Social Security numbers.

Medical record and hospital account numbers.

Insurance information.

Admission diagnoses and dates of treatment.

Clinical information from medical transcriptions, including test results, medications, treatment facilities, and healthcare providers.

See if your personal data has been exposed.

SCAN NOW

Notifications were also slow. PJ&A began contacting clients about the stolen database files in July 2023, and its clients notified affected individuals between October 31, 2023, and February 8, 2024. The New York AG found that the companies violated state requirements to disclose a breach as quickly as possible and without unreasonable delay.

The settlement

Although the announcement describes a settlement worth up to $10 million, the companies must pay $300,000 in penalties to the states. The remaining $9.7 million is suspended and could become payable. New York will receive $100,000 from the initial payment. These are payments to the states, not an announced compensation payout to patients.

The exposed information could be valuable to criminals. Our research found stolen identity packages selling for as little as 95 cents apiece on the dark web.

The settlement also requires extensive security changes for the relevant active companies, including:

MFA for individual user accounts, including administrator accounts, and remote network access.

Stronger password management and access restricted to what employees need for their jobs.

Encryption of personal and protected health information.

Monitoring that automatically alerts security personnel to suspicious activity.

Annual risk assessments and penetration testing.

Network segmentation and measures to detect and prevent unauthorized data transfers.

Written incident response procedures and clearer rules for retaining and securely disposing of sensitive information.

Given the carelessness, number of exposed records and people, do you think the companies got off cheap? Let us know in the comments.

How to stay safe

A breach does not automatically mean someone has misused your information, but you can take these precautions while you wait for more details:

Verify unexpected messages independently. Don’t let a message about the breach rush you into clicking a link, sharing sensitive information, or making a payment. Go to your healthcare provider or insurer’s official website yourself or use contact details you already trust.

Review medical bills and insurance statements. Look for appointments, tests, prescriptions, or services you did not receive. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) identifies unfamiliar medical bills and unexpected items on an Explanation of Benefits statement, which explains how your insurer processed a claim, as warning signs of medical identity theft. Report discrepancies to your healthcare provider and your insurer.

Review your credit reports. Look for unfamiliar accounts or debts and dispute errors. Free reports are available through AnnualCreditReport.com.

Act if you find signs of identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan. If someone has received care in your name, ask the providers involved for copies of your medical records and request corrections in writing.

Medical identity theft is not just a financial problem; it can also affect your care. Someone using your identity to obtain treatment or submit insurance claims could introduce incorrect information into your health records. Checking medical statements and reporting anything unfamiliar can help you catch that misuse.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

The exposure is critical, the exploit is public, and the affected system supports a production application. Security needs the risk reduced before attackers can use it.

Infrastructure and application teams carry a different responsibility. They need to understand whether the proposed action could block legitimate traffic, consume additional resources, affect availability, or interrupt a system the business relies on. They also need a safe path back if the change behaves unexpectedly.

Both sides are protecting the organization. Safe Remediation gives them the evidence to move forward together.

Safe Remediation: Confident Remediation in Production examines how Check Point Exposure Management evaluates remediation actions against current production conditions, applies approved changes through existing controls, and confirms the result.

Key Takeaways

Prioritization identifies the exposure, but it does not validate the production change. Operational evidence is still needed before enforcement.

Validation needs to match the control. IPS, operating-system, endpoint, and indicator-enforcement actions require different forms of evidence.

Cyber security remediation extends beyond patching. Existing controls can provide protection while permanent fixes move through testing and change control.

Temporary protection must remain distinct from permanent remediation. Teams need visibility into residual exposure and outstanding work.

Execution is not completion. The enforcing system should confirm that the action reached its intended state.

Prioritization Is Just the Beginning

Risk-based vulnerability prioritization helps teams determine where action should begin. Exploitability, asset context, threat activity, existing security coverage, and available controls can narrow a large queue into a smaller set of exposures requiring action.

In one sample environment documented in the white paper, 338 findings were identified. Among them, 283 had a CVSS score of seven or higher, 89 had a confirmed public exploit, and 63 were identified by a cybersecurity agency as actively exploited. Once existing protections were considered, one finding had no compensating control in place.

The underlying vulnerabilities still required attention, but their immediate remediation paths differed. An existing control could provide protection while a patch moved through testing. A protection operating in Detect mode could require further validation before enforcement. An actively exploited weakness without a compensating control could demand urgent action.

Prioritization establishes why action is needed. Safe Remediation determines how to apply the response without losing sight of production stability.

Moving from priority to production requires a repeatable way to evaluate, execute, and verify the change.

How Safe Remediation Works

Safe Remediation follows four stages that connect a prioritized exposure with a verified production outcome.

Observe

Observe collects current information from security and IT systems, including vulnerability findings, IPS activity, access logs, device utilization, endpoint policies, patch-management records, and configuration states.

The process uses an agentless model, drawing on telemetry and APIs from systems already operating in the environment. This provides evidence from the assets and controls involved without introducing another agent.

Prove

Prove evaluates the proposed action using evidence suited to the technology.

An IPS protection can inspect production traffic in Detect mode while teams evaluate false positives, traffic behavior, and device performance. Operating-system hardening can begin with a detection script and continue through deployment to a controlled test group. Endpoint policies can be compared with vendor hardening baselines using configuration data from supported APIs.

The validation method follows the action. Production traffic supports an IPS decision, while host-level testing provides evidence for an operating-system change.

This step gives security teams evidence that the action will reduce exposure and gives operational owners information about its expected production impact.

Act

Act applies the approved change through the system responsible for the control.

IPS changes can be distributed through the security management server. Operating-system hardening can use existing patch-management infrastructure. Supported endpoint changes can be written through the vendor API.

Approvals can remain between validation and execution, preserving authorization, accountability, and established change controls.

Confirm

Confirm verifies that the action reached its intended state.

IPS enforcement can be confirmed after policy installation. Operating-system hardening can recheck affected hosts. Endpoint changes can be reflected through the vendor environment.

The result is a traceable record connecting the original exposure, supporting evidence, approved action, and confirmed production state.

Remediation Extends Beyond Patching

Patch management plays an essential role in the vulnerability management lifecycle, but production timelines may not match the urgency of an exposure.

Testing, coordination, rollback planning, and scheduled change windows can delay a permanent fix. During this period, an existing control may reduce immediate exposure by interrupting the exploit path.

A virtual patch or IPS protection can protect an application while patch testing continues. Indicators from threat intelligence feeds can be deduplicated and matched with compatible enforcement points. Operating-system and endpoint configurations can be hardened through existing management systems. Phishing sites, impersonating profiles, malicious applications, and attacker-controlled infrastructure may require takedown or disruption.

The white paper covers direct and virtual patching, IPS activation and hardening, indicator enforcement, operating-system hardening, endpoint hardening, system-health remediation, compensating controls, and infrastructure takedowns.

Permanent remediation and interim protection remain separate states. Teams can see what the action addresses, what remains unresolved, and whether further work is required.

From Prioritized Exposure to Verified Action

Safe Remediation carries the production decision through execution and confirmation, helping teams maintain visibility from the original exposure to the resulting state.

Across the environments analyzed in the white paper, remediation actions recorded a 99.5% success rate. The measured environments averaged 381.2 remediation actions per month and nine hours from identifying an exposure to taking action. These findings apply to the organizations included in the analysis.

Check Point Exposure Management connects threat intelligence, risk-based prioritization, validation, and Safe Remediation across existing controls and workflows. Security and operational teams gain a shared process for reducing exposure safely while protecting production performance, application availability, and business continuity.

For the complete technical framework, remediation workflows, findings, and recommendations, read Safe Remediation: Confident Remediation in Production and explore the Safe Remediation Starter Pack.

Request a demo to learn how Check Point Exposure Management helps security teams move from prioritized exposure to validated, controlled, and verified action.

The OpenAI engineer who was arrested and charged last month for planting a covert audio recording device in the company's office has pleaded not guilty.

According to reports from Bloomberg and CNBC, Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan made an appearance in San Francisco federal court on Friday, where he entered the plea. His next hearing is scheduled for November 17, 2026.

If proven guilty, the 35-year-old faces a maximum of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release. He has been held without bail since his arrest on October 9, 2026.

Late last month, a grand jury indicted Alfozan on a single count of interception of oral communications.

Prosecutors allege that the former OpenAI employee placed a "sophisticated recording device" in an executive OpenAI conference room in what has been described as an attempt to unlawfully record sensitive conversations.

He was arrested three days before he, along with his wife and son, were scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way ticket.

"His wife and son, however, immediately left the United States without him," U.S. prosecutors said. "Rather than wait until the October 12 flight as booked, they initially planned to fly to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on October 11 on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by the Saudi government."

"That flight was canceled, however, when a member of the Saudi military booked and paid for yet another one-way ticket for the defendant's wife and son, this one business class to Doha, Qatar, on October 10, 2026. They did make that flight, departing San Francisco about 36 hours after the defendant was arrested."

In a subsequent court filing, it was alleged that Alfozan was in frequent contact with a member of the Saudi Royal Family via WhatsApp. He was also deemed a flight risk, with court documents claiming that the defendant took great pains to create bespoke, encrypted recording devices to record sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said Saturday that his personal data had been disseminated on the dark web, an encrypted part of the internet, and that he has been exposed to “threats and intimidation.” Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni blamed pro-Russian hackers for the leak.

Tajani made the announcement in a social media post following a string of hoax bomb threats across Europe that caused flight diversions, security threats against broadcasters as well as recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions.

“For days, cybercriminals have been spreading my personal data on the dark web and seeking other information, in fact exposing me and my family to new threats and intimidation,” Tajani said, adding that the criminals “are prepared to pay for other details on me and my loved ones.”

Meloni, is a separate statement, expressed solidarity with Tajani “following the revelations about the activities of pro-Russian hackers, and the publication on the dark web of personal data.” She called attempts to sell confidential information about government officials “a matter of grave concern that must be addressed with the utmost determination.”

Tajani, who is also a vice premier in Italy’s government, did not specify what kind of information had been shared, but suggested that the cyberthreat was ongoing.

“I will not allow myself to be intimidated in any way,” Tajani said. “I will continue working to defend my ministry, and Italy, and I will further strengthen the ties and cooperation to protect ourselves together.”

Tajani did not indicate who might be responsible for the cyberattack but reiterated the Italian government’s support for Ukraine.

901ad6cee130.text:
Threat actors have started exploiting SSHole, a recently patched high-severity authentication bypass vulnerability in OpenSSH.

Tracked as CVE-2026-123158, the flaw is “related to misinterpretation of whether a string is intended to be a password hash” and could let attackers access certain accounts by supplying any password between 257 and 1024 characters.

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to access accounts such as root, which should never accept a password.

On certain Linux distributions that use the musl libc implementation with the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) disabled, such as Alpine, Buildroot, OpenWrt, Yocto, and others, these accounts do accept a password.

This happens because the OpenSSH server (sshd) checks the supplied password by hashing it against a stored password hash associated with the username.

When an account has no password hash, as with root on Alpine (where the field is ‘*’), sshd borrows the salt from another account’s hash to process the login attempt. For passwords longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function fails and, instead of returning NULL, returns ‘*’. Because that matches the ‘*’ stored for the target account, sshd treats the password as correct.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

In Alpine, affected accounts include root, any key-only user created with adduser without a password, the Alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images, and any user coming from a directory service through musl-nscd.

Last week, OpenSSH rushed patches for the bug, and Alpine urged users to apply them and restart sshd as soon as possible.

Over the weekend, both WatchTowr and Previdian warned that hackers had started exploiting SSHole in the wild. According to WatchTowr, only botnets and crypto miners have picked it up so far.

“Previdian sensors have observed 20 exploitation attempts, 13 unique attacker IPs, and 9 countries targeting CVE-2026-123158. First observed Nov 06, 2026; last observed Nov 08, 2026,” Previdian said.

Exploitation attempts have also been reported by GreyNoise and Defused.

Users are advised to update to OpenSSH version 10.6p2 as soon as possible. As a mitigation, they can disable password authentication (on by default in OpenSSH) or disable SSH. They should also check logs for unusual requests to identify exploitation attempts.

US agencies warn attackers are going after industrial refrigeration controllers. The fixes are basic, and most start with getting them off the internet.

CISA, the FBI, HHS, USDA and the Department of Transportation published a joint advisory on attacks against industrial refrigeration controllers and cold chain monitoring systems. The activity is global. Healthcare, chemical, food and transport companies use these systems to watch temperatures, keep logs, run defrost cycles and save energy, including in refrigerated trucks.

“The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities.” reads the advisory published by CISA. “The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”

The targets are electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers used in grocery stores and cold-storage sites. Attackers may exploit flaws in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to change settings remotely and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles. In plain terms, someone could cook your freezer from the other side of the world.

The agencies identify three ways in: bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and exploiting weak configurations. Once inside, an attacker can change temperatures, which can shorten equipment life, create a fire hazard and destroy stock. Spoiled products that reach consumers can also create a safety risk.

“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.” continues the adviosry.

An attacker can also hide the damage. Operators lose sight of current temperatures, and that’s a bad moment to learn a cold room has been warm for hours.

CISA’s Chris Butera adds that every organization that depends on these systems should assume it’s a target. The advice follows the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals from CISA and NIST, a minimum set of practices for any organization.

Start with exposure. Keep controller panels off the internet, and if you need remote access, put an up-to-date firewall or similar gateway in front of it. Then separate industrial equipment from the office network with its own virtual network.

Next, fix the basics. Change default passwords, use strong ones, and add phishing-resistant multifactor authentication where you can. Update firmware, and retire or replace devices the maker no longer supports.

Allow only trusted devices and IP addresses to change system settings. Keep tested backups in a separate location, disconnected from the network. Enable logging and regularly check the logs. If devices do not record activity, monitor the network traffic between them.

U.S. organizations should report suspicious activity to CISA’s 24/7 operations center or the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center. Healthcare organizations can also contact HHS.

Reports should include the date, time and location of the incident, a description of the activity, the number of people affected, the equipment involved, and a contact person within the organization.

One control gets forgotten more than the rest. A controller shouldn’t be able to push a freezer past what’s safe, whoever is giving the orders.

“The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems.” concludes the report. “To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations:

United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT“

CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology

CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security

CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

0aa458c760f6.text:
Three men allegedly used deepfakes of company CEOs and law firm attorneys to trick employees into wiring more than $129 million to accounts the group controlled, the Justice Department said.

The indictment names the three as Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42. Soall used the alias “Rocky Balboa,” and Hazan went by “Superman Cash,” “Impossible Mission” and “Fat Boy,” among others.

The scheme ran from 2024 to 2026 and usually opened with someone posing as the victim company’s chief executive, using AI to mimic the executive’s voice or image on calls.

“While pretending to be the CEO, they would direct the employee to get in touch with lawyers at large international law firms who they said were also working on the sham financial transaction,” the Justice Department wrote.

“They would then also impersonate those lawyers to further make the employee believe that the financial transaction was real. A member of the conspiracy, impersonating one of those lawyers, would ultimately direct the employee to wire a large sum of money in furtherance of that sham financial transaction to a particular bank account, which was in fact controlled by members of the conspiracy,” they added.

Soall mostly played the part of UK attorneys. He kept a handwritten script titled “Lawyer Call” to help him sound like the genuine article, and it included lines meant to keep victims from discussing the calls with their colleagues.

From hospitals to pet food

The victims named in the indictment range from healthcare to finance. Two US hospital systems, one in Missouri and one in California, lost close to $7.8 million between them, and a Rhode Island bank wired out $2.7 million. The largest single loss listed, $11.6 million, hit a UK financial technology company, while a Florida pet food company lost $5.2 million.

The stolen funds went to accounts in the US, Spain, Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China. Once a payment landed, the group converted it into cryptocurrency to hide where the money came from and who controlled it, then split it among the conspirators.

Hazan and Sheetrit allegedly handled the laundering. Hazan boasted of laundering money since 1994 and of moving over $400 million in the past three years alone, and he claimed that among professional money launderers he was “number one all over the world.”

Hazan is not a new face to prosecutors, since he was already convicted of conspiracy to commit bank fraud in the Southern District of New York in 2008.

Each of the three men is charged with seven counts, including conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering. Five of the counts carry a maximum of 20 years in prison, and the two identity theft charges carry two years each.

Deepfakes on company calls

41% of CISOs reported at least one social engineering incident involving a deepfake during an employee audio call in the past 12 months, according to Gartner, and 36% said the same about video calls.

One of the best-known cases of executive impersonation came out of Hong Kong in 2024, when a finance employee at a multinational firm’s branch joined a video call that appeared to include the company’s CFO and several colleagues, then transferred over $25 million to accounts controlled by the scammers.

“The alleged scheme orchestrated by Soall, Hazan, and Sheetrit demonstrates how the use of advanced technology can be exploited to commit large scale fraud,” said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle, Jr.

US Attorney Jamie McDonald noted the public “should recognize that there are some who seek to use this emerging technology to pursue criminal goals,” and he urged individuals and businesses to think about protecting themselves from this type of crime.

b29b9da0dfe5.text:
SonicWall has fixed an exploited SonicOS SSL-VPN vulnerability (CVE-2026-19868) that may allow attackers with valid credentials to bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication.

With no workarounds listed, the company has urged admins to patch quickly.

About CVE-2026-19868

CVE-2026-19868 is an authentication enforcement flaw in the SonicOS SSL-VPN service, and is exploitable only if SAML is enabled for SSL-VPN logins.

According to SonicWall, a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method may be able to bypass SAML authentication controls and, with them, any MFA enforced through SAML.

In practice, that means a VPN login that should have gone through the organization’s identity provider (e.g., Okta or Microsoft Entra ID) and its MFA check can succeed with a password alone.

This is not an unauthenticated bypass: attackers need working credentials first. But stolen VPN credentials are hardly in short supply, and SAML-enforced MFA is exactly the control many organizations rely on to make them useless for attackers.

The same SonicOS releases fix six other vulnerabilities, none of which have been flagged as exploited.

The vulnerabilities affect Gen7 and Gen8 physical and virtual firewall appliances running firmware versions 7.3.3-7015 and older and 8.2.2-8015 and older. Fixes have been shipped in versions 7.3.4-7013 and higher, and v8.2.3-8015.

Gen6 firewalls are not listed as affected, but they have reached the end-of-support stage, and SonicWall advises customers running those or older hardware to upgrade to a Gen8 firewall.

No attack details and no IoCs

“SonicWall PSIRT has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of [CVE-2026-19868],” the company said, but has not shared any details about the attacks.

SonicWall SSL-VPN devices have been a favorite target of ransomware-linked attackers for a while now: in 2025, Akira affiliates compromised SonicWall firewalls even though OTP-based MFA was enabled, and earlier this year ReliaQuest observed attackers exploiting CVE-2024-12802, another SonicWall SSL-VPN MFA bypass, in multiple environments.

CVE-2026-19868 was discovered and reported by Ryan Harris of IT services provider Electronic Office.

CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog based on evidence of active exploitation. US civilian federal agencies are required to address it by November 20, 2026.

It’s currently unknown how many organizations have been hit and what the attackers did once they got in. Neither SonicWall nor CISA has published indicators of compromise (IoCs), and no security company has yet published an analysis of the attacks.

With that in mind, organizations that use SAML for SSL-VPN logins should:

Review recent SSL-VPN logins and look for any that succeeded without a matching sign-in (and MFA check) in the identity provider’s logs.

Reset the credentials of any account that logged in that way, and check what was accessed via those sessions.
