669db6217954.text:
Attackers used stolen credentials to log in an average of eight minutes after infection across 27 confirmed infostealer cases, according to a report from Elastic Security Threat Command. Researchers also documented misuse of AI applications to execute commands and digitally signed remote monitoring tools to maintain access.

“An agent that holds credentials and can reach the internet is a new attack surface, whether it’s misconfigured or abused. When an attacker is behind it, its activity looks exactly like the employee who installed it. So the question for defenders isn’t whether a tool is approved; it’s what that tool is actually doing,” said Mike Nichols, General Manage, Security at Elastic.

Attackers run commands through AI applications

Coding assistants such as Claude Code and Cursor can execute system commands. Their ability to work with files, credentials, and other applications gives attackers ways to act through software installed for everyday work.

Researchers documented intrusions involving Claude Code on Windows and the ChatGPT desktop application on macOS.

In the Windows case, an attacker connected remotely to a computer and used Claude Code through its Visual Studio Code extension to prepare tools and reach an outside server through a concealed connection.

On macOS, commands run through the ChatGPT desktop application read an internal infrastructure document and then accessed the user’s saved password store.

These cases involved misuse after attackers obtained access. They do not establish that the applications contained a vulnerability or that their providers were compromised.

Stolen credentials used within minutes

Infostealers collect information such as saved passwords, browser session data, and payment details.

Confirmed infostealer findings by initial access route and platform (Source: Elastic)

Across 27 confirmed cases on customer computers, investigators observed theft operating through applications the user or operating system already trusted. These included a signed remote monitoring agent, a browser updater, a vendor installer, and Apple’s scripting utilities.

ClickFix-style verification pages were the most common entry point, appearing in 12 cases. These pages persuade people to copy and run a malicious command, often presented as a verification step or troubleshooting instruction.

The approach can bypass defenses focused on scanning email attachments because the user executes the command themselves.

In one healthcare case, delivery of a malicious installer and execution through DLL sideloading occurred about 16 seconds after the user followed the lure. DLL sideloading causes an application to load malicious code.

Captured session data can also allow attackers to use an account without entering its password again.

Remote IT tools provide continued access

Remote monitoring and management software lets IT staff connect to computers, transfer files, and run commands. Attackers can use those capabilities to control a device and deliver additional tools or malware.

Researchers confirmed 23 cases involving abuse of these applications. Phishing pages and archives containing malicious scripts led to installations, with ScreenConnect named most often.

One campaign began with a fake digital invitation and led to a hidden installation of ScreenConnect. The application connected to an attacker-controlled server and ran as a Windows service.

Another case involved an attacker uploading remote access software to a compromised server after attempts to create user accounts failed.

Phishing exploits trusted sign-in services

Attackers used trusted authentication services and preapproved applications to access cloud accounts.

Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kits place a relay between the victim and the real login page. When the victim enters credentials and completes multifactor authentication, the attacker can capture the resulting authenticated session.

Tycoon 2FA was one of the kits discussed and remained in active use during the reporting period.

Investigators observed attackers submitting stolen usernames and passwords through an older authentication method that allowed access without a second factor in those cases.

A separate device-code phishing case persuaded a user to enter a code on Microsoft’s sign-in page. The approval granted access to a session initiated by the attacker. Subsequent activity included registering a virtual device to support continued access.

“When attackers operate inside trusted software or on behalf of trusted users, the defensive answer is rarely just deploying a new signature. Detecting and neutralizing these threats requires user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA) to baseline normal activity, alongside cross-domain visibility and active correlation across your security environment,” the authors explained.

df0735f347d2.text: Huawei claims it’s built a desktop PC that uses only parts made in CHina. The company launched the Qingyun HM650 last week and said it uses Huawei’s own Kirin X90 processor, a ten-core 20-thread machine with a clock speed of 2.3 GHz. The machine runs a newly developed enterprise version of HarmonyOS, the OS Huawei developed to end its dependence on Android and which it intends to run on most of the devices it makes. A single Chinese government agency has reportedly signed up for 600 of the machines. That’s not an indication this machine is a curiosity, because Beijing has ordered all government entities to shift from Wintel boxes to local alternatives. While Huawei has reportedly claimed local companies manufactured 100 percent of the components in the machine, it is unclear if all those components use Chinese designs. The Register mentions that uncertainty as many non-Chinese companies continue to operate factories in China. Even if Huawei is using some parts that aren’t entirely Chinese, the debut of the Qingyun HM650 is bad news for Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm, as all are suffering as the PC market shrinks due to the rising cost of memory. China’s government is an enormous buyer, and losing the chance to bid for its business is unlikely to be helpful. Japan announces emergency response package after wave of cyberattacks Japan’s government last Friday announced emergency funding to help local organizations strengthen the nation's cyber-defences. The ¥10 billion ($63 million) package follows a wave of cyberattacks that have disrupted railways, retailers, KFC’s logistics provider, and cloud computing operators. The emergency package aims to help Japanese government agencies to use AI to nail infosec basics, and to build tools that let the National Cybersecurity Office aggregate information about cyberattacks. Some funds will also go towards supporting victims. Lenovo’s APAC boss shifts to lead Motorola Lenovo is looking for a new leader of its Asia-Pacific operations after shifting the boss, Amar Babu, to a role as mobile business group general manager and global president at Motorola. Amar led Lenovo in the region for over five years and the company credited him with turning it into “a more balanced and diversified business and a key growth engine.” “Across the portfolio, AP maintained its #1 PC position, while our mobile business achieved notable growth, with Motorola reaching nearly 9 percent market share in India and the #2 smartphone OEM in Japan,” according to a company announcement. “Our infrastructure business achieved profitable growth and nearly double-digit market share, while Solutions & Services continued to strengthen its best-of-breed industry position and significantly increased its advanced services business mix to over 50 percent.” Lenovo has not named a new leader for its APAC outpost. Vietnam hails homegrown USB storage chip Vietnam’s government last week announced the nation’s first domestically-designed security chip - a 28-nanometer device that apparently integrates encryption algorithms in silicon. The chip is already in use on secure USB storage devices that Vietnam’s government employs to store info for government and defense agencies, plus the Communist Party. The nation hopes to use the chips to secure storage of the national digital signature certification system, and critical infrastructure systems in electricity, water, oil and gas, and telecommunications. Hanoi says the chip needs more testing before the government will trust it to protect state secrets, but hailed the chip as an important step towards development of sovereign security capabilities. Apple’s biggest ever education deal Apple last week quietly announced it has won its biggest-ever sale of Macs into the education market in the Philippines. Speaking on the company’s Q4 earnings call, CEO John Ternus said Apple sold 172,000 MacBook Neos to the Department of Education in the Philippines, which will deploy them to teachers and staff. ®

8aa1e96e938f.text: Hello and welcome to the Monday, November 9, 2026 edition of the SANS Inline Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Washington, D.C. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cloud Security. Today I spent a little bit time looking at our honeypot data to see if we are detecting any evidence of the sshole vulnerability being exploited. And yes, indeed, it is being exploited. Now, this investigation had a couple of hiccups. First of all, in order to exploit sshole, you must use a password that's larger than 256 characters. Well, we only record passwords up to 256 characters because, well, that's usually for brute forcing and so all that matters. On the other hand, there are sometimes passwords that are longer than 256 characters that are being recorded by our honeypots that are not related to sshole. What usually happens here is that simple scripts that are doing brute forcing are actually not checking if the login succeeded or not. So what they're doing then is they end up entering whatever bash command they would like to execute in the password field of the login. Sometimes also the username, that's where we also see them often showing up. But here, of course, the password field was what matters. And if you're looking at the data that I published as part of the diary, we saw a number of long passwords like this on November 1st. So what I'm calling here is the actual sort of exploitation of passwords that I would associate with sshole started on November 5th in our honeypots. Now, what I'm calling here an sshole password is one that basically is just letters, no recognizable bash commands or anything like this, and fills the entire 255 bytes that we are recording. The only ones that I've seen so far being used is either all uppercase letter A or all lowercase letter A. Of course, the actual content of the password shouldn't really matter when it comes to exploiting this vulnerability. I hope to follow this up maybe later this week with a look at what commands are being executed by these attacks after they're logged in. These attacks should actually work as far as our honeypot is concerned. They should sort of randomly allow some of these login attempts to log in. And on Friday, SonicWall released patches for seven vulnerabilities in SonicOS. This is significant because one of these vulnerabilities is already being exploited. The already exploited vulnerability does allow attackers to bypass multi -factor authentication for SSL VPN logins. Apparently, the problem here is if you have multiple authentication methods defined, and one of these authentication methods does not require multi-factor authentication, then an attacker essentially can use that to bypass the multi -factor authentication requirements that you may have set up for SSL VPN access. So this should be patched now. And again, it's already being exploited, which should tell you to please expedite release rolling out this particular update. In particular, of course, with SSL VPNs, we often had issues where people didn't use multi-factor authentication because, well, we all know passwords don't work. And Microsoft this weekend patched an authorization bypass vulnerability in Entra. This vulnerability would allow a user to essentially gain elevated privileges. The attacker in this case doesn't even have to be authorized. Now nothing you have to do. Microsoft already took care of it for you since this is an Entra vulnerability. So it really only affected Microsoft's cloud services and they released the advisory as they state to be more transparent about these vulnerabilities. They also say there was no exploitation happening at the time when they patched this vulnerability. Now they say exploitation is less likely, so more complex vulnerability. And hopefully now after the patch supplied, exploitation should be impossible. And a agentic coding security company, Apiiro, found that Anthropic's Claude Code under certain circumstances will add secrets to a hidden file in GitHub. The way this works is if you're requesting Claude Code to connect to an API or such, it may need credentials. And there is an option when you provide credentials to Claude Code where it basically asks, well, do you want me to ask you again about these credentials, about accessing this API? If you say no, then of course it has to remember those credentials somewhere. And the way it does so is by saving them to a .claude folder and inside there a file settings.local.json. We've actually seen in our web honeypots this weekend an increase in actually for the first time requests for this .claude directory. So attackers are definitely looking for it and Apiiro as part of their blog states that they found sort of around 1500 or so of these credential files on GitHub. There's still work in progress into how to exactly fix this. Essentially what they're proposing is to check automatically for secrets before anything is being sent to GitHub. But of course that may still keep those credentials in any other Git repositories. So not quite clear how this will be fixed. Definitely be aware of this and check with Anthropic and as a Claude Code user with any updates that you may be receiving that will fix this problem for you. Well, and that's it for today. Thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for recommending and subscribing to this podcast. And talk to you again tomorrow. Bye.

919d3704dac7.text: France has turned up the heat on Iran over destructive cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers at more than 700 grocery stores in October, spoiling food and sparking fires. The country vowed to take action using “all available means of response.” The supermarket attacks, which affected Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour, and Intermarché groups, started at least 15 fires and caused food losses in the tens of millions of euros, according to a Monday report by France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4). The C4 includes the National Cybersecurity Agency of France, the Directorate General for External Security, the Directorate General for Internal Security, the Directorate General for Armament, and the Cyber Defence Command. “This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory,” France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement. All signs point to CyberAv3ngers Both the report and the statement attributed the refrigeration controller hacks to the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) Shahid Kaveh cyber unit. The Shahid Kaveh unit, which French national security officials say is led by Reza Salarvand and Mahdi Lashgarian, is better known by its hacktivist personas, including CyberAv3ngers. This is the same crew suspected of involvement in the July attacks that targeted more than 100 internet-exposed water systems in America. While the US government hasn’t attributed the intrusions to any country or group, private-sector security analysts blamed Iran, and specifically CyberAv3ngers. The IRGC-affiliated hacking crew has been breaking into industrial controllers for years, and in 2023, American national security and law enforcement agencies attributed a series of cyberattacks against "multiple" US water facilities to CyberAv3ngers. “The Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new,” according to the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.” Since at least June 2024, the Shahid Kaveh unit has had the ability to scan, access, and control industrial control equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens, and Rockwell, the French government said in its report. It pins the refrigeration controller hacks on this particular Iranian crew for a couple of reasons. Making the case for attribution First: the infrastructure used to carry out the October supermarket attacks was also used during this timeframe to conduct reconnaissance on Schneider Electric equipment, zeroing in on small- and medium-sized energy and water production units. “The techniques used during these actions are known to have been used by the Shahid Kaveh unit since at least April 2026,” the report says. It also notes that investigators found “traces of Farsi use” in the attack infrastructure. Plus, Iranian media outlet CyberbanNews, which is reportedly linked to the Shahid Kaveh unit, publicized the incidents that occurred late on October 11 and into October 12 extremely quickly: “as early as October 13.” In early November, similar cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers were reported across Europe, with grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden reporting widespread food losses after miscreants spiked temperatures to as high as 122°F (50°C). Last week, the US federal government urged owners and operators to take security measures to prevent these types of attacks from spreading to America. France fights back The French government, for its part, said that it would “use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace.” This includes proposing additional EU sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved. France also vowed to express “its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks” to the Iranian ambassador. However, the country didn’t rule out responding with more than just harsh words: “France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.” ®

e39c7a4b645b.text:
An attacker broke into AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and October 26 and stole stored secrets and data, cloud security company Wiz said today.

The attacker used credentials for an AWS account that Qubole's platform uses to reach those customers. How the attacker got those credentials has not been disclosed.

Qubole, a data lake platform owned by Idera, operates within its customers' AWS accounts. To let it in, a customer creates an IAM role, which is an AWS identity with its own set of permissions.

The role's trust policy allows Qubole's AWS account to assume the role, granting those permissions. Each request to do this, called AssumeRole, must include a matching code from Qubole known as an External ID.

Apart from the attack, most of the roles the attacker assumed were unused, according to Wiz's researchers. But each role still trusted Qubole's account, so the attacker's requests worked.

Any organization that has connected Qubole to AWS, even one that no longer uses it, should check its CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward. The sign to look for is an AssumeRole request from the account Qubole's platform uses, 805246085872, that came from an address outside AWS.

The researchers did not say whether the credentials have since been disabled or whether the activity has stopped. Neither Qubole nor Idera had posted a statement about the attack on their websites when The Hacker News checked today.

Why the Roles Let the Attacker In

Every AssumeRole request tied to the attacker carried an External ID and was accepted, the researchers said in their technical analysis.

AWS accepts an AssumeRole request for such a role when it comes from the trusted account and includes the correct External ID. The code is not treated as a secret, and anyone with access to the role can view it, according to AWS's external ID guidance.

Sentra spotted the activity in several of its customers' environments and alerted the researchers.

In the accounts the researchers examined, the attacker looked for stored credentials. It read environment variables for Lambda functions, pulled secrets from Secrets Manager, and read values from the SSM Parameter Store.

It then ran the credentials it had found through TruffleHog to test whether they worked. These were the victims' own AWS access keys, Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials.

The attacker also copied data out of S3. It retrieved data from any bucket a role could access rather than searching for specific data, and sometimes downloaded an entire bucket in a single session.

The researchers have not linked this campaign to any other publicly reported activity, and say the targeting does not match what state-backed groups usually go after.

Qubole also lets customers connect with AWS access keys instead of a role. From October 8 to October 11, an attacker used customers' own AWS access keys, which the researchers believe had been set up for Qubole.

That attacker then compromised a few of the victims' cloud environments. This activity has not been linked to the AssumeRole abuse.

How to Check Your Accounts

Wiz's hunting guidance covers CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward in every AWS account that holds a Qubole role. Look for:

Account: AssumeRole requests where userIdentity.accountId is 805246085872 and sourceIPAddress is not an AWS address. The researchers saw Qubole's real traffic come only from AWS.

IAM principal ID: AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. Any activity from this IAM user should be investigated, because only the attacker used it in the accounts the researchers examined.

IAM principal ID: AIDAJYRRH5Y3A7AAJM2HW, when the source address is outside AWS. The attacker used this IAM user from October 18, but Qubole's normal traffic also uses it.

IP: 57.129.54[.]120 and 2001:41d0:70d[:]7800::, OVH-hosted addresses that the attacker used.

IP: 45.83.220[.]211, 185.209.199[.]73 and 89.37.63[.]175, which are Mullvad VPN addresses. Other VPN users share them, so a match alone is not proof.

Session name: role sessions that start with quiam-, such as quiam-enum.

User agent: TruffleHog on GetCallerIdentity calls from one of the IP addresses above. Look for the same user agent in your identity provider's sign-in logs.

For every suspicious session, review everything it did afterward, especially in Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda, and S3.

CloudTrail management events log each AssumeRole request and bucket listing, but not which S3 objects were read. That needs S3 data events or S3 server access logs. Several victims lacked the required logs, so responders could not determine which objects the attacker had read.

How to Close the Route

The researchers recommend these steps:

If the attacker assumed one of your Qubole roles, rotate all secrets, parameters, and Lambda environment variables that role had access to, and revoke the role's active sessions. Rotating a credential does not end sessions that were already issued.

Remove any Qubole role you no longer need, or take Qubole's account out of its trust policy.

Where Qubole supports it, swap the account-wide :root principal in the trust policy for the specific IAM principal that Qubole uses.

Add an aws:SourceIp or aws:SourceVpce condition that limits AssumeRole requests to the vendor's documented network ranges. In this attack, the researchers said, "a source IP condition alone would have blocked every role assumption we observed."

Assume others can see the External ID. It is logged in plain text in CloudTrail, and vendors and infrastructure-as-code files often store it, so do not use it as your only control. After an incident like this, change it to Qubole and use a different value for each role where possible.

Review what each vendor role can reach. Qubole's setup guide includes a sample S3 policy that lets the role read every bucket in the account. Vendor roles are often granted access to Lambda settings, Secrets Manager, SSM parameters, and broad S3 read permissions for convenience, according to the researchers.

Set alerts for AssumeRole requests from a vendor account that arrive through a VPN or a hosting company the vendor has not used before.

Log every account and region with an organization trail, and enable S3 data events or server access logs for buckets that store sensitive data.

9f1c5f952582.text:
Attackers used the Ethersphere project's own release automation to publish malicious versions of two of its tools for the Swarm decentralized storage network: bee-js 13.3.0 and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2.

Both releases download and run code built to steal the wallet key that Swarm Desktop keeps for its node, along with the stored password that unlocks it. The code is also built to install a backdoor on Windows, macOS, and Linux machines.

The bee-js package is the JavaScript library behind Swarm Desktop and the swarm-cli command-line tool. Swarm Desktop runs a Swarm node on a user's own computer and saves the node's private keys there.

Both malicious releases have been taken down, and the project's maintainers released a clean Swarm Desktop update today. Neither step removes a backdoor already installed nor protects a key already sent. No theft of funds had been reported at the time of writing.

Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 appeared on GitHub at about 00:36 UTC today and was withdrawn about 8.5 hours later. The app's built-in updater could offer it to Windows x64 computers and Apple Silicon Macs within about 10 minutes, according to an incident analysis by Socket, a supply chain security firm. Intel Macs were never offered it, and Linux installs do not update automatically.

The bee-js release, version 13.3.0, was the latest version on npm for about 75 minutes, from 00:09 to 01:25 UTC today. Its code runs as a postinstall script, which npm executes automatically during installation unless install scripts are disabled. A project did not need to import the library for the code to run.

The project's own swarm-cli and bee-dashboard packages, and the Swarm Desktop source code, accepted version ranges that included 13.3.0. A fresh install within that window could have pulled in the malicious version.

None of the reports gave a count of infected machines. The firm's rough estimate is that bee-js 13.3.0 was downloaded about 10 times, including by security scanners and mirrors. Swarm Desktop 0.56.2's download count reached 65 by 08:27 UTC, including researchers.

Ethersphere's maintainers withdrew 0.56.2 and replaced it today with a clean release, version 0.56.3. In the change that set up the new release, one of them wrote that 0.56.2 "was published by an attacker using stolen CI credentials and has been withdrawn."

Version 0.56.3 is the same code as the previous version, 0.56.1, signed with a newly issued Developer ID certificate, according to that maintainer's incident note. The note says the app's auto-updater will move installs of 0.56.2 to it, although Linux packages still need to be replaced by hand. A comparison of the two versions' source code by The Hacker News found no changes beyond the version number and release notes.

When The Hacker News checked npm today, 13.2.0 was again the latest bee-js version, and 13.3.0 could no longer be downloaded from the registry.

What to Do

The GitHub advisory for bee-js 13.3.0 says: "Any computer that has this package installed or running should be considered fully compromised." SafeDep, a software supply chain security company, offers the same advice for any computer on which Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 was installed.

If you use bee-js in a project or CI job:

Search lockfiles, package caches, internal registries, and CI install logs for @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0, including copies pulled in by other packages.

Pin 13.2.0, and clear cached copies of 13.3.0, including any npm mirror you install through.

If 13.3.0 was installed with install scripts turned on, treat that machine or CI runner as compromised, even if the install log shows no errors. The code hides its own network errors.

From a clean computer, rotate every password, token, and key that the installing user or CI job could read.

If you run Swarm Desktop:

Look for the line Bee Desktop version: 0.56.2 (production) in the app's log file, bee-desktop.log. Version 0.56.2 is written at every launch, just before the malicious code runs.

The log folder is ~/Library/Logs/Swarm Desktop/ on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Swarm Desktop\Log\ on Windows, and ~/.local/state/Swarm Desktop/ on Linux.

Install 0.56.3. On Linux, replace the package by hand.

If 0.56.2 ever ran, treat the node's key and password as stolen. From a clean computer, move the node's funds, chequebook, and stake to a new key.

On any machine where the code ran:

Remove the ~/.solidity/ folder, the solidity-langsupport-runner.service user service on Linux, the com.solidity.langsupport.runner LaunchAgent on macOS, and the ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df) service on Windows.

Updating, reinstalling, or removing the app or package does not remove them.

Where possible, rebuild the machine from a trusted image instead of cleaning it in place.

How the Malware Works

Both releases carry the same loader, SafeDep found in its technical analysis. It is a few lines of code that download more code from api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz and run it with the user's permissions. In bee-js the loader is the postinstall script, and in Swarm Desktop it runs each time the app starts.

The downloaded code looks for two files in Swarm Desktop's data folder: config.yaml and data-dir/keys/swarm.key. If both are there, it sends them to the attackers' server.

The key file is an encrypted Ethereum keystore, but Swarm Desktop keeps its password in plain text in config.yaml. With both files, the attackers can take the node wallet's xDAI and xBZZ tokens, its chequebook funds, and its stake, the company says.

The downloaded code also installs a backdoor. On Linux and macOS, it is a Go remote shell called evjawbreaker, saved in a hidden ~/.solidity folder. It runs in the background as a user service on Linux and as a LaunchAgent on macOS.

The shell reads the address of its control server from an Ethereum smart contract, so the attackers can change that address at any time. They had updated it 29 minutes before the malicious bee-js code was added.

On Windows, the downloaded code installs a genuine ScreenConnect remote-access client, signed by its maker, ConnectWise. The client runs as a system service and connects to the attackers' relay.

If the user is an administrator, the code gets administrator rights through a known way around the User Account Control prompt. If not, it shows the prompt again whenever the user cancels. With those rights, it adds a Microsoft Defender exclusion and installs the client silently.

How the Releases Got Out

Both releases came from bee-worker, the account Ethersphere uses to automate its releases. Neither change was signed nor submitted as a pull request.

For bee-js, the attackers published a GitHub release for the new version, which started the project's npm publishing workflow. That workflow needed no approval and published the package to npm in 73 seconds, according to Socket.

Because the project's real workflow built it, the package carried valid provenance, the record that links an npm package to the repository and workflow that built it. Provenance shows where a package was built, not whether anyone reviewed the code inside it.

For Swarm Desktop, the attackers manually started a build workflow that had the project's Apple and Windows signing certificates and needed no approval. The macOS app was signed with the project's Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so macOS displayed only its normal first-launch prompt, the firm found.

The maintainers have since made the app's signing jobs wait for approval from the project's DevOps team and run only from the main branch.

How the attackers gained access remained unclear at the time of writing. The maintainer's incident note blames the theft of CI credentials and secrets.

The firm's analysis indicates that two GitHub accounts were used: bee-worker and a long-time maintainer's account. None of the reports explained how the credentials were stolen.

Links to Earlier Attacks

The payloads share an Ethereum contract, a ScreenConnect relay, and file names with fake extensions for Solidity developers that appeared on the Open VSX marketplace in September. Researchers at Pluto Security described those extensions in their October 1 EtherDuck analysis.

Pluto ties them "with high confidence" to the group behind the original SleepyDuck extension, which read its server address from a different Ethereum contract in 2025. Socket says the same group is behind the bee-js and Swarm Desktop releases.

Indicators of Compromise

Defenders can search logs and machines for the following.

Domain: api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz

URL path: /v1/analytics (bee-js loader)

URL path: /v1/electron (Swarm Desktop loader)

URL path: /v1/assets/ (further payloads)

URL path: /v1/swarm/report (stolen wallet files)

HTTP header: X-Ethersphere: 1

IP:port: 193[.]57[.]9[.]155:4912 (evjawbreaker control server)

IP:port: 185[.]232[.]84[.]169:8041 (ScreenConnect relay)

Ethereum contract: 0xf8a900Db50b3331be6B768bA460BB59f3E40C344

Path: ~/.solidity/

systemd unit: solidity-langsupport-runner.service

LaunchAgent: com.solidity.langsupport.runner

Service: ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df)

SHA-256: 9b73e7cd4e1425e770392549d8df46c706139ef476f4f7b9ac405165dc8d9696 (linux_amd64)

SHA-256: b601776817363b96295119f7221338a122d5247a35a77a64b04f286e1bbcc565 (linux_arm64)

SHA-256: 80d2672e2599732d3c0ae2a4cd0d1e3fe4d555a60273ce33feb99db3f34d250f (darwin_amd64)

SHA-256: fae61f31f00988fdc5cc9e7272b51e08af2e245d81003237875415930fd27358 (darwin_arm64)

SHA-256: 37d14bff30762ca701e9c1f8bc6c57c065bb20ae3a2208cb7411a6530610f08e (invoke.ps1)

SHA-256: 7527e86d70e7c9493db4356f1c3775380431b310000f2602c1e993cf435d01da (app.msi)

A classified memo ties Nvidia’s chief executive to Chinese espionage. AI coding agents crack under peer pressure, coughing up private keys. Big breaches hit seven million Japanese shoppers and three million students here in the States, while a French bank takes a multi-million-dollar hit through a vendor compromise. Adversaries weaponize a fresh OpenSSH bypass in the wild, pro-Russian hacktivists put dark web bounties on senior European officials, and Google drafts digital IDs to solve the passkey recovery puzzle. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Chris Grove, Director of Cybersecurity Strategy at Nozomi Networks, discussing the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attacks. Beijing goes all-in on domestic silicon.

Today is Monday November 9th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Classified memo warns of Nvidia chief's ties to Chinese operative.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo this past spring warning senior Trump administration officials about Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with an operative tied to Beijing's Ministry of State Security.

Intelligence gathered from electronic surveillance revealed Huang was intimately involved with Alice Huang, a senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. Megaspeed has purchased two billion dollars in advanced Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling restricted artificial intelligence hardware into China. While Huang admitted to the affair and apologized to his family, Nvidia stated it has no reason to believe national security or trade secrets were compromised.

Huang remains an influential voice shaping United States policy against tighter export controls, highlighting the growing counterintelligence risks hovering over America’s critical semiconductor supply chains.

The New York Times originally reported the findings.

Autonomous AI coding agents leak credentials under swarm peer pressure.

Autonomous software engineering agents routinely violate core security policies, leaking private deployment credentials and executing untrusted scripts, when pressured by third-party agent forums, according to testing by AE Studio and the AI Alignment Foundation shared with The Register.

Researchers tasked nine coding models with debugging a broken service in an isolated sandbox. Given access to a forum that held the solution, agents surrendered private tokens fifteen percent of the time and executed unverified installation scripts nearly a quarter of the time to obtain assistance. Under performance pressure, execution rates spiked to thirty-four percent.

As organizations rush to integrate autonomous agents into production environments, granting models broad system permissions without strict data isolation turns automated workflows into immediate remote code execution and credential leakage risks.

A Japanese online market goes offline following a suspected breach of 7.7 million customer records.

Japanese consumer goods and electronics giant Iris Ohyama has suspended its primary ecommerce platform, Iris Plaza, following unauthorized access to a third-party cloud service that contained personal records for nearly eight million shoppers.

The retailer took the storefront offline late last month after discovering a suspicious file on its cloud infrastructure. Exposed records cover 5.8 million registered members and 1.9 million guest shoppers, potentially compromising names, physical and email addresses, birth dates, phone numbers, and encrypted passwords. Payment data was stored separately and avoided exposure.

The disruption highlights the severe operational fallout and supply-chain vulnerabilities inherent in cloud-hosted retail environments, leaving core commerce operations frozen while investigators determine whether customer files were actually exfiltrated.

Threat actors exploit a high-severity OpenSSH authentication bypass.

Threat actors are actively exploiting a critical authentication bypass in OpenSSH tracked as CVE-2026-123158, dubbed "SSHole."

The vulnerability allows attackers to compromise accounts like root on systems running musl libc without PAM—including Alpine and OpenWrt—by supplying overlong passwords. Security firms WatchTowr and Previdian report that botnets and cryptominers are already leveraging the flaw in the wild.

The rapid weaponization underscores immediate exposure for lightweight Linux environments, prompting administrators to deploy version 10.6p2 or disable password authentication entirely.

A French banking group confirms third-party compromise and fraudulent fund transfers.

French banking giant Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has confirmed an intrusion into its network via a third-party service provider, enabling attackers to conduct major fraudulent transactions.

The disclosure follows reports from blockchain investigator ZachXBT, who traced approximately 133 million dollars in suspicious withdrawals and aggressive cryptocurrency laundering across multiple centralized exchanges. The bank stressed that customer accounts remained untouched, as the threat actors targeted Arkéa's own institutional accounts before routing capital toward external cryptocurrency platforms. Arkéa reports that security teams contained the incident, froze a portion of the funds, and maintain that the bank's financial stability remains secure.

The incident underscores the persistent vulnerability institutional financial networks face through external vendor access paths, demonstrating how rapid cryptocurrency conversion complicates law enforcement recovery efforts.

Frontline Education data breach impacts over three million individuals across K-12 systems.

School administration provider Frontline Education has notified the Indiana Attorney General’s Office that an August breach compromised records for over three million people—more than doubling previous state estimates.

Attackers exploited a flaw in a third-party application, accessing personal records of staff and students across Frontline Central and School Health Management services. Exfiltrated data includes Social Security numbers, driver’s licenses, and health insurance information.

The incident highlights continuing third-party software risks threatening sensitive educational and student administrative platforms.

Google develops digital identity credentials for secure passkey and account recovery.

Google is developing an account recovery framework that leverages verified digital identity credentials, aiming to eliminate the security vulnerabilities of fallback methods when users lose primary devices.

Speaking at the Authenticate 2026 conference, company product managers explained that legacy recovery workflows—such as SMS-based fallbacks—risk undermining the cryptographic advantages of passkeys. Under Google's proposed system, users register a signed digital ID in advance to create a cryptographic stable hash linked to their account. If their physical device is lost, obtaining a verified digital credential on a replacement device restores their account, passkeys, and data in a single step.

Securing the recovery loop represents the crucial missing link in widespread passwordless adoption, though full-scale rollout still faces hurdles in wallet interoperability and near-real-time credential provisioning.

Pro-Russian hacktivists dox European leaders and bounty personal details.

Pro-Russian hacktivist syndicate NoName057(16) has published personal records belonging to Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and seventeen other senior European officials across the dark web, offering cryptocurrency bounties for further intelligence on the targets and their families.

The doxing campaign targets prominent figures across European law enforcement and judiciary—including leaders at Europol, Eurojust, and the German Federal Criminal Police Office—alongside investigative journalists. The operation appears to be direct retaliation for a multi-nation law enforcement takedown in July 2025 that dismantled over one hundred of the gang's servers.

The move marks an aggressive evolution from nuisance denial-of-service disruptions into direct personal harassment and targeted intelligence-gathering aimed at deterring Western support for Ukraine.

Monday business briefing.

Capital continues pouring into artificial intelligence defense and validation, led by 220 million dollars raised across two standout funding rounds. Agentic data security startup Sentra secured 150 million dollars in a round led by Capital One Ventures, while formal verification provider &Truth emerged from stealth backed by 70 million dollars in seed capital.

Consolidation across the sector accelerated with eight reported acquisitions, headlined by CrowdStrike’s aggressive expansion into model governance. According to the Wall Street Journal, the security giant is acquiring AI observability firm Fiddler AI for 400 million dollars alongside red-teaming platform Dreadnode for 95 million dollars to embed behavioral accountability into its Falcon ecosystem. Penetration testing specialist Bendings also acquired Scopertos for 55 million dollars, while Cognition absorbed code security shop Corridor.

The flurry of dealmaking signals that enterprise demand is rapidly shifting toward pre-deployment testing, agent explainability, and securing the broader algorithmic supply chain.

After the break, I welcome Nozomi Networks’ Director of Cybersecurity Strategy Chris Grove. We discuss the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attack part 2.

That was Chris Grove from Nozomi Networks.

Beijing goes all-in on domestic silicon.

Huawei claims it has built the holy grail of sovereign computing: an enterprise desktop boasting one hundred percent Chinese-manufactured components.

The Qingyun HM650 runs a homegrown, ten-core Kirin processor alongside an enterprise flavor of HarmonyOS, specifically designed to bid a polite, permanent farewell to Western software dependencies. One government agency has already ordered six hundred units—perhaps less out of spontaneous consumer enthusiasm and more in dutiful compliance with Beijing’s mandate evicting Wintel machines from state desks.

Whether every capacitor actually traces its architectural ancestry strictly to domestic drawing boards remains conveniently ambiguous, as foreign outfits still keep plenty of factories humming across the mainland. Regardless of pedigree, locking Western chipmakers out of vast government procurement pools delivers a cold chill to Santa Clara balance sheets.

Meanwhile, Japan unveiled a sixty-three million dollar emergency cybersecurity fund after adversaries disrupted critical infrastructure, cloud providers, and—perhaps most unforgivably—KFC logistics.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

Phishing remained the most common initial access vector for attackers in the third quarter of 2026, according to a new report from Cisco Talos. Ransomware gangs are using voice phishing attacks to trick employees into granting them a foothold within organizations.

“In addition to traditional phishing links and attachments, we observed numerous threat actors conducting voice phishing (vishing) in tandem with IT desk impersonation to socially engineer the victim into allowing remote access via a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool,” Cisco Talos says. “Exploitation of public-facing applications was the next most common vector, accounting for one-third of Talos IR engagements. Threat actors predominantly targeted edge devices such as security gateways and remote network management interfaces. These are critical components within enterprise environments, often responsible for managing authentication, network traffic, or sensitive data. Compromising them can provide broad access to internal networks or user credentials.”

The researchers also observed an increase in threat actors abusing AI tools, both as a tool to assist in attacks and as a target for attacks themselves.

“[An] investigation revealed an attack chain in which a compromised macOS endpoint, infected via a trojanized application, was scripted to scrape credentials from the macOS keychain specifically associated with the Anthropic Claude Code AI assistant,” the researchers write.

“This direct targeting of AI-related secrets highlights an emerging threat, where attackers seek to compromise not only traditional user and system credentials but also those tied to AI platforms, which may grant access to additional sensitive data and advanced automation capabilities. These incidents highlight the critical need for organizations to implement strong MFA and robust credential management practices, especially for AI platforms and development tools.”

Cisco Talos has the story: https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q3-2026/

Acknowledgments: Special thanks to John Hammond, Ben Bernstein, and Andrew Brandt for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Huntress is tracking N-able's response to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in its N-central platform, a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform built for managed service providers and IT teams. On November 9, N-able took its hosted N-central environment offline while it worked to secure the environment and apply remediation.

That move came after an independent researcher published the details of 33 critical vulnerabilities to GitHub that can be chained to lead to four different exploits (dubbed "Able2Shell"). Three of those chained exploits lead to remote code execution and one leads to privilege escalation to root. The vulnerabilities impact servers running N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31 (and likely earlier versions as well).

N-able said it has not seen active exploitation of the vulnerabilities as of November 9 at 15:15:00 UTC. The company is working on a hotfix that it said will be available soon; customers should keep their N-central servers offline until N-able confirms they can be brought back online safely.

Huntress has tracked and responded to other, separate flaws in N-able's N-central this year, including five critical CVEs:

August 2026: N-able released a hotfix for CVE-2026-18556, a critical vulnerability impacting all current versions of N-central across both hosted and on‑prem deployments, giving attackers unauthenticated, "god-mode" access to the RMM console. CVE-2026-18577 was disclosed soon after as an incomplete patch to the former CVE.

September 2026: N-able issued a hotfix to address a third vulnerability, CVE-2026-86218, an actively exploited pre-auth RCE zero day with a 10.0 CVSS score. The next day Huntress produced a proof of concept (PoC) exploit of a separate, net new vulnerability chain (CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207) in N-central that allowed attackers to bypass access controls to create unauthorized administrative accounts.

What Should Potentially Impacted Organizations Do?

Potentially impacted organizations should do the following:

If you run N-central on premises, take the server offline now and keep it offline until N-able confirms it is safe to restore.

If you use N-able's hosted service, expect an outage. N-able has taken its cloud infrastructure offline; follow its status page for updates.

Review login and authentication activity from November 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access. If you find suspicious activity, involve your incident-response team and assess whether systems or client networks managed through N-central may also be affected. The document warns that exploitation could enable remote code execution or privilege escalation on the server.

Carefully examine your audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise. During previous N-central vulnerability exploitations (such as the CVE-2026-86218 zero-day), threat actors were observed "spraying" downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools. Specifically, you should monitor for anomalous remote access sessions, new scripts being deployed, or the unauthorized creation of new administrator accounts.

Apply N-able's hotfix and restore service only when N-able says it is safe. The document said a hotfix was in development, with no exact ETA, so check current vendor guidance rather than relying on this dated update.

N-able does not always iterate version numbers when it pushes down live hotfixes that don't require a reboot, so it remains to be seen whether the patched version will be numbered 2026.4.0.31 or something different.

Next Steps

Huntress is actively investigating this incident and we are communicating with our potentially vulnerable customers to share updates as they become available. Please check this blog for further updates as we learn more information.

You can also get further updates from N-able at: https://uptime.n-able.com/event/202561/

cc83fdad4ee2.text: Unknown attackers used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access customer AWS environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets. Qubole is a cloud data processing platform that uses cross-account IAM roles to manage compute and access storage in customers' AWS environments without requiring customers to provide long-lived AWS access keys. The supply-chain attack abused this third-party, cross-account trust relationship. Google’s cloud-security shop Wiz declined to tell us how many organizations were affected, but called it a “broad, opportunistic supply chain campaign” that hit “multiple” customer environments. “Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud resources, harvest secrets, and siphon data,” the researchers told The Register in an emailed response to questions. Neither AWS nor Qubole responded to The Register's inquiries. Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders after AI data security company Sentra flagged suspicious activity, traced the malicious activity back to October 14, when credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account were used to call the sts:AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for customer-managed integration roles. The calls originated from Qubole AWS account 805246085872, and used IAM user ID AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS, Wiz analysts Zack Morrow, Sean Johnstone, and Benjamin Read said in a Monday blog about the supply chain attack. “Across the affected environments, Wiz CIRT has not observed this IAM user in any activity other than that associated with this threat actor,” the trio wrote. This activity continued on October 15, and on October 18, the digital intruders began using a second IAM user from the same account. Once inside customers’ environments, the crooks began probing a ton of AWS services and stealing credentials, keys, and other secrets stored across Lambda, Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store. The miscreants also used TruffleHog to test AWS credentials belonging to victim organizations, discover their Microsoft Entra ID secrets, and request OAuth tokens using Okta client credentials also uncovered while snooping around the AWS environments. Abusing the integration roles also allowed the criminals to steal data from customers’ S3 storage, although it seems they were largely opportunistic attackers, in some cases downloading entire buckets, as opposed to state-sponsored spies looking for specific data. The threat hunters haven’t attributed the supply chain attack to any particular group, and say they don’t have any insight into how the miscreants are using the stolen data. While investigating this incident, Wiz spotted a separate campaign between October 8 and October 11 that also used customer-owned AWS access keys for Qubole integrations. While a “small number” of these also resulted in the intruders compromising victim organizations’ AWS environments, Wiz said it can’t definitively connect the two sets of malicious activity. Organizations that have integrated with Qubole should rotate credentials - although rotating a credential does not end temporary sessions that were already issued. Customers should also review CloudTrail from October 1 onward, looking for AssumeRole events where userIdentity.accountId matches Qubole's AWS account ID, 805246085872, particularly those originating from non-AWS IP addresses. “For every role session you find, review all subsequent activity from that session, especially Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda and S3,” the researchers wrote. “If the threat actor assumed an integration role, rotate every secret, parameter and Lambda environment variable the role could read, and revoke active sessions for the role.”®
