N-able has taken its hosted N-central environments offline and urged on-premises customers to shut down their servers after a security researcher publicly disclosed more than 30 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities, including exploits that could let attackers take over vulnerable systems.

Security researcher Sean Bales disclosed the vulnerabilities late Sunday, November 8, and published a GitHub repository called Able2Shell containing proof-of-concept exploits for the flaws.

N-central is a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform used by managed service providers (MSPs) and IT teams to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely.

The researcher says the vulnerabilities were tested against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, a pre-release version of the software, and believes most, if not all, flaws also affect earlier versions.

Bales also confirmed to BleepingComputer that the discovery of the vulnerabilities was AI-assisted.

The disclosed vulnerabilities include authentication bypasses, credential disclosure, arbitrary file writes, directory traversal, cross-site scripting (XSS), XML external entity (XXE) injection, and remote code execution (RCE) flaws.

One of the most critical exploit chains abuses an unauthenticated XXE vulnerability in N-central's service-import functionality to steal a trusted local session, reset an account password, and execute commands on the server as the nable user.

The same exploit can also create an enabled Default Administrator account with attacker-controlled credentials, providing rogue administrative access to the N-central management interface.

Bales shared a video demonstration of this exploit, showing terminal output reporting successful administrator account creation, login authentication, access to protected administrative functionality, and remote command execution as the nable user.

Other disclosed exploits include a stored XSS that can execute commands as root when an administrator views malicious patch metadata, and a privilege-escalation flaw that allows code running under the nable account to execute commands as root.

Bales confirmed to BleepingComputer that the unauthenticated XXE-to-RCE exploit was the most critical of the disclosed vulnerabilities.

N-able takes servers offline worldwide

After the disclosure, N-able announced a critical security incident and took its hosted N-central environments offline across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific regions.

While BleepingComputer has not independently verified all the reported vulnerabilities, N-able confirmed it is developing a hotfix to address the security issues, lending credence to the researcher's claims that at least some of the flaws are legitimate zero-days.

"N-able is actively responding to non-responsible communication of critical vulnerabilities in N-central late Sunday night, November 8, found by an independent researcher," N-able told BleepingComputer.

"As a precautionary measure, we took our Hosted N-central environment offline today, November 9, and provided guidance to customers operating on-premises N-central servers to temporarily take their servers offline until further notice."

"Our Security, Engineering, and Operations teams are actively working to implement the necessary remediation. At this time, we have not observed active exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Protecting our customers and their environments remains our highest priority, and we will provide additional updates as they become available."

In a subsequent status update, N-able said it was continuing to develop and validate a hotfix and had found no evidence of active exploitation or unauthorized data access.

While the N-central classic environment is unavailable, N-able said Ecoverse services accessed through N-able Login remain operational.

N-able has not provided an estimate of when N-central will come back online but says it plans to publish updates every four hours, or sooner if new information becomes available.

Researcher claims previous vulnerability reports ignored

Bales told BleepingComputer that he deliberately released the N-central vulnerabilities without notifying N-able beforehand because the company allegedly failed to address vulnerabilities he had previously reported in a different N-able product.

According to Bales, he disclosed two unrelated remote code execution vulnerabilities and a privilege-escalation flaw approximately five to six months ago, but those vulnerabilities remain unpatched.

"I disclosed 2 unrelated RCEs for a different N-able product, along with a priv esc vulnerability 5 or 6 months ago. These have yet to be patched. I did not disclose any of the 0-days I posted last night," Bales told BleepingComputer.

He also claims to have sent follow-up emails over the past four to six weeks without a response.

Bales says his previous experience with N-able's vulnerability disclosure process and that "they don't take disclosure seriously" led him to publish the N-central zero-day exploits.

However, he said these exploits target a different N-able product than the ones he previously disclosed.

The researcher also claimed that he received no payment through N-able's bug bounty platform for his earlier reports.

Bales confirmed that N-able executives, including the company's CEO and CTO, contacted him following the disclosure and asked him to remove the GitHub repository and work with the company.

"They did not threaten me or anything though. Only asked to take down the repo, work with them, etc."

BleepingComputer asked N-able about Bales' allegations concerning the previously disclosed vulnerabilities, their patching status, and the alleged lack of responses to his follow-up emails.

However, the company did not address those questions, providing only the statement concerning the N-central security incident and the precautionary shutdown.

The previously reported vulnerabilities are not included in the publicly released Able2Shell repository and allegedly remain unpatched.

York University in Toronto has confirmed that a threat actor breached its systems and accessed personal information submitted through online forms.

The unauthorized access was discovered on October 25 and affected forms submitted on 14 university websites between 2007 and 2026.

York University is a major university based in Toronto, Canada, with more than 55,700 students across 200 undergraduate and graduate degree programs, and an administrative staff of 7,000.

“York was recently subject to a cybersecurity incident involving an unauthorized actor accessing limited online forms used by University departments,” the university stated on Friday.

“While York acted quickly to contain the incident following discovery, we regret to confirm the theft of personal information from some departmental forms.”

The announcement lists the exposed data in detail, by category. Across the affected forms, the attacker accessed the following:

Email address

Phone number

Date of birth

York identification number

Government ID information

Third-party contact information

Health information

Academic history

Employment history

Financial status

Criminal background

Demographic details

Photos and other images

The exact data types exposed vary by person, and most stolen records contained basic contact information and York ID numbers, the university said.

Exposing contact information alongside other sensitive data significantly increases the risk of phishing and social engineering attacks for affected individuals.

The announcement says the website forms are now secure and safe to use. York University said it will directly notify individuals whose government ID or financial account information was exposed and offer two years of credit monitoring and identity theft protection coverage.

Individuals who did not receive a notification may contact the university directly to learn what specific types of data were exposed in their case.

At this time, the educational institution has not specified how many individuals have been impacted by the cybersecurity incident.

No details have been provided about the perpetrators. At the time of writing, BleepingComputer did not find any ransomware group claiming the attack.

For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 9th November, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

Queens Public Library, a New York City public library system serving approximately 2.3 million residents, was struck by a ransomware attack that encrypted its systems. The incident disrupted public computers, Wi-Fi, checkout equipment, digital media services, and its mobile application, while all 66 branches remained open.

Russian web hosting provider Beget sustained a destructive cyberattack on November 1 that wiped data across its cloud infrastructure and disrupted hundreds of websites. The attack affected businesses and public services, with more than 1,000 servers requiring manual inspection before restoration. Some backup data was reportedly destroyed.

OPSSHIELD, developer of the Linux security tool cPGuard, disclosed a supply-chain attack after compromised credentials enabled attackers to distribute malicious updates on November 2. Approximately 2,950 customer servers executed the malicious script, which installed a backdoor and collected password hashes, credentials, and sensitive server files.

Ukraine’s Air Alert app, an emergency notification service used by millions, was compromised by attackers who distributed false radiation, chemical-threat, and military alerts to Kyiv residents. Developers temporarily suspended notifications. A separate attack affected Russia’s emergency alert application, although both countries reported that their core warning systems remained operational.

AI THREATS

Check Point Research documented cybercriminals using ARTEX, an AI-powered framework that autonomously discovers and exploits vulnerable systems. Researchers identified 1,608 live, publicly accessible instances. Observed campaigns obtained more than 300 iOS signing certificates and harvested approximately 190,000 gaming credentials, including around 6,000 active accounts.

Check Point Research identified Haiou, a jailbreak bundle targeting OpenAI Codex that weakens safeguards and modifies agent instructions to promote an external AI gateway. The package also installs security-related capabilities and appeared on infrastructure associated with cybercrime tools, although researchers did not establish that its developers intended criminal use.

India’s Computer Emergency Response Team identified Crafty Falcon, a threat actor using AI-assisted tools to target financial services and cryptocurrency businesses. Attackers exploited connections between testing and production environments, abused payment APIs, and stole wallet credentials. AI tools helped generate tailored attack scripts and automate complex intrusion sequences.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

SonicWall patched CVE-2026-19868, a high-severity vulnerability affecting SonicOS SSL VPN services configured with SAML authentication. Attackers possessing valid credentials for an alternative authentication method could bypass SAML controls, including multi-factor authentication. The vulnerability has been linked to active exploitation and affects enterprise firewall environments.

Google published November’s Android Security bulletin, addressing numerous vulnerabilities across Android components. Among the flaws patched is CVE-2026-58868, a critical vulnerability affecting Android versions 14 through 17 that could allow remote code execution without user interaction.

Barracuda patched CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, two high-severity vulnerabilities affecting its Email Security Gateway appliances. Attackers with access to the administrative interface could chain an authentication bypass with command injection to gain root-level control without logging in. The flaws received CVSS scores of 9.3 and 8.6, respectively.

OpenSSH addressed CVE-2026-123158, a high-severity vulnerability (CVSS 8.1) affecting Linux systems using the musl library without PAM authentication. Attackers can exploit oversized passwords to bypass authentication on certain accounts. Active exploitation was observed, including successful root access against an Alpine Linux honeypot. Version 10.6p2 fixes the flaw.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

Check Point researchers analyzed the evolution of HYFLOCK ransomware across four generations, identifying new capabilities for file encryption, scheduled-task execution, and network-share access. The October builds contained encryption weaknesses, allowing researchers to partially recover data from encrypted files without a decryption key. The group claimed eight victims in October.

Researchers detailed an APT29 cyberespionage campaign targeting iPhone and Android users through compromised and imitation websites. Malicious scripts identified visitors’ devices and attempted to exploit unpatched vulnerabilities. Successful compromises could expose messages, credentials, and sensitive information, particularly from users in Ukraine.

Researchers analyzed BITTER APT’s espionage campaign targeting government, energy, and engineering organizations across South Asia. Attackers distributed malicious files disguised as diplomatic and military documents to deploy PapRAT spyware. The malware collected system information, executed commands, and transferred files.

Researchers traced SlippyNunchucks, a China-aligned espionage group, to attacks abusing the trusted update and configuration mechanisms of Sogou Input Method. DNS hijacking redirected application traffic to attacker-controlled infrastructure, delivering DarkVigil malware to victims across several countries. Tencent addressed the affected delivery mechanism in version 16.10.

The post 9th November – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.

9d580d9e694c.text:
You can now use tokens from AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) outbound federation to assume roles in other Amazon Web Services (AWS) partitions.

When your workloads run across AWS partitions such as Commercial, China, GovCloud (US), and European Sovereign Cloud, a workload in one partition might need to access resources or communicate with AWS services in another partition. AWS partitions are hard isolation boundaries with independent instances of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), so a credential issued in one partition isn’t valid in another. As a result, direct role assumption with sts:AssumeRole doesn’t work across partition boundaries and resource policies can’t reference principals that exist in another partition.

AWS IAM outbound identity federation already lets your workloads obtain a short-lived, AWS signed JSON Web Token (JWT) and use it to authenticate to external services. Today, we’re extending it with cross-partition support. Your workloads can now use that same mechanism to federate into another AWS partition. A workload in one partition obtains a short-lived JWT using sts:GetWebIdentityToken and exchanges it for temporary credentials in another partition using sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with no long-term credentials to store or rotate.

This post walks through configuring cross-partition identity federation using Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) data access as an example, but the same steps apply to any cross-partition API call.

Important: If your workload requires cross-partition access, consult your compliance team to make sure that your implementation aligns with your regulatory or compliance obligations. A non-exhaustive list of examples are FedRAMP, ITAR, DoD CC SRG, GDPR, and others.

Why use IAM outbound identity federation for cross-partition access?

IAM outbound identity federation provides several benefits, including:

Carry origin identity into authorization decisions – The destination trust policy can condition on the source identity’s context, its AWS account, organization ID (org_id), source AWS Region, and principal, so you authorize based on who and where the request originated, not only that a token is valid.

Cross-partition audit trail – AWS CloudTrail events in the destination Region include the source principal Amazon Resource Name (ARN), source Region, and a token ID that correlates back to the source Region’s GetWebIdentityToken CloudTrail event.

Temporary credentials end to end – Your workload authenticates with a short-lived, signed JWT and receives temporary credentials, so every stage of cross-partition access uses credentials that expire automatically.

Fully managed token infrastructure – AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) issues, signs, and publishes verification keys for the JWTs. You don’t need to implement a public key infrastructure (PKI) or host your own OpenID Provider.

IAM integration – You control access with the same IAM roles, trust policies, and permissions policies you already use. Destination accounts can condition on subject, audience, source Region, account, organization ID, and principal ID.

Session revocation – You can revoke credentials that have already been issued. Scope the revocation by origin or apply a deny on the destination role.

How cross-partition identity federation with IAM outbound identity federation works

Cross-partition identity federation works by obtaining a signed JWT from AWS STS in the source partition and exchanging that JWT for temporary credentials from AWS STS in the destination partition.

For example, a workload running in the AWS Govcloud (US) partition in the us-gov-west-1 Region can obtain a JWT and exchange it for temporary credentials valid in the AWS Commercial partition in the us-east-1 Region.

Architecture overview

The following diagram shows the elements and workflow used to support cross-partition access.

Figure 1: Cross-partition flow diagram

The cross-partition flow works as follows:

Token request – Your workload, running in a Region from the source partition calls sts:GetWebIdentityToken API.

Token issuance – AWS STS returns a short-lived, cryptographically signed JWT. The token contains claims that assert your workload’s AWS identity, including the account ID, the principal ARN, source Region, and more.

Token presentation – Your workload calls sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity on the AWS STS endpoint in a Region in the destination partition, passing the JWT as the web identity token and the ARN of the target role in the destination partition.

Fetch verification keys and metadata – AWS STS in the destination partition retrieves the public verification key from your OpenID Connect (OIDC) Issuer URL’s JWKS endpoint.

Validation: AWS STS in the destination partition verifies the token’s signature and evaluates the target role’s trust policy.

Return temporary credentials: AWS STS in the destination partition returns temporary credentials scoped by the policies attached to the role.

Cross-partition resource access – Your workload uses the temporary credentials to access resources in the destination partition, such as an S3 bucket.

Setting up cross-partition identity federation

In this walkthrough, we use the example of a workload running in the us-gov-west-1 Region that needs to access data in an S3 bucket in the us-east-1 Region.

Prerequisites

For this walkthrough, you need the following:

Two AWS accounts: one in the source partition, AWS GovCloud (US), where the workload runs and one in the destination partition, AWS Commercial, that holds the data.

In the source account: an IAM principal with permissions to enable outbound web identity federation (iam:EnableOutboundWebIdentityFederation) and to call sts:GetWebIdentityToken to obtain a signed JWT representing its identity.

In the destination account: an IAM principal with permissions to register the source account’s issuer as an OIDC identity provider (iam:CreateOpenIDConnectProvider) and create an IAM role whose trust policy allows sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from that provider, conditioned on the token’s aud and sub claims.

An S3 bucket in the destination account that holds the data you want to access from the source partition.

A local installation of AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI)

So you can run and verify every step from your own command line, this walkthrough has you assume the workload role as the token-creating identity. In production, an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance, AWS Lambda function, or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (AWS EKS) Pod runs as that role automatically through its instance profile or execution role with no assume-role step.

Step 0: Configure credentials for the GovCloud and Commercial AWS CLI profiles

This walkthrough runs commands in two partitions, so configure a named AWS CLI profile for each. For example, GovCloudCredentials for the source account and CommercialCredentials for the destination. Use the --profile parameter matching the partition where you run each command. In this walkthrough we configure our profiles in the ~/.aws/config file:

[profile GovCloudCredentials] region = us-gov-west-1 # GovCloud account credentials / SSO [profile CommercialCredentials] region = us-east-1 # Commercial account credentials / SSO

Step 1: Enable outbound identity federation on the source account

Enable outbound identity federation on your GovCloud account to generate a unique issuer URL that hosts the OIDC discovery endpoint needed for cross-partition trust. This needs to be performed once in the source account.

Using the AWS CLI:

Ensure your IAM principal has permission to call iam:EnableOutboundWebIdentityFederation.

Run the following command.

aws iam enable-outbound-web-identity-federation --region us-gov-west-1 --profile GovCloudCredentials

Copy the issuer URL from the command output. For GovCloud, it looks like: https://<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws

Note: IAM has a single endpoint per partition. The --region parameter simply targets that partition’s IAM. Enabling outbound web identity federation is an account-wide setting, so you only need to run this once.

Step 2: Allow your IAM principal to generate JWTs in the source partition

Create an IAM policy that grants permission to call the sts:GetWebIdentityToken API and attach it to the IAM principal that will generate tokens. This example uses an IAM role.

Using the AWS CLI:

Ensure your IAM principal has permission to call iam:CreateRole and iam:PutRolePolicy.

Save the following trust policy to a file named workload-trust-policy.json. This policy controls who can assume the workload role; the role’s ARN is what becomes the token’s sub. So that you can run the walkthrough from the AWS CLI, we set the principal to the identity behind your AWS CLI profile. In production, set it to the compute service that runs your workload, for example "Principal": { "Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com" }, which removes the need to assume the role manually.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowCliRoleToAssume", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-cli-role>" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" } ] }

Run the following command to create the workload role with the preceding trust policy:

aws iam create-role \ --role-name <your-source-partition-iam-role-name> \ --assume-role-policy-document file://workload-trust-policy.json \ --region us-gov-west-1 \ --profile GovCloudCredentials

Save the following policy to a file named get-web-identity-token-policy.json. This policy grants permission to call sts:GetWebIdentityToken, with conditions that restrict the token audience and limit the token lifetime to 300 seconds:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowTokensForDestination", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sts:GetWebIdentityToken", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "ForAllValues:StringEquals": { "sts:IdentityTokenAudience": "<your-audience-name>" }, "Null": { "sts:IdentityTokenAudience": "false" }, "NumericLessThanEquals": { "sts:DurationSeconds": 300 }, "StringEquals": { "sts:SigningAlgorithm": "ES384" } } } ] }

Run the following command to attach the permissions policy to the role:

aws iam put-role-policy \ --role-name <your-source-partition-iam-role-name> \ --policy-name AllowGetWebIdentityToken \ --policy-document file://get-web-identity-token-policy.json \ --region us-gov-west-1 \ --profile GovCloudCredentials

For the full detailed walkthrough of these steps, see Getting started with outbound identity federation.

Step 3: Configure trust in the destination account

Create an OIDC identity provider and a trust policy in your Commercial account using the issuer URL from Step 1.

Using the AWS CLI:

Ensure your IAM principal has permission to call iam:CreateOpenIDConnectProvider and iam:CreateRole.

Run the following command to register the source account’s issuer URL as an OIDC identity provider in the destination account:

aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider \ --url https://<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws \ --client-id-list "<your-audience-name>" \ --region us-east-1 \ --profile CommercialCredentials

Note: --thumbprint-list is optional; IAM retrieves the issuer’s certificate thumbprint automatically. Because the AWS STS issuer endpoint uses a certificate from a trusted certificate authority (CA), AWS validates it against its trusted root CAs.

Save the following trust policy to a file named trust-policy.json. This policy allows the role to be assumed only with tokens matching the expected audience and originating from us-gov-west-1:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowTrustedGovCloudSourceRole", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:oidc-provider/<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:sub": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>", "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:aud": "<your-audience-name>", "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:source_region": "us-gov-west-1", "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:org_id": "<your-source-org-id>" } } } ] }

Run the following command to create the role with the preceding trust policy:

aws iam create-role \ --role-name <your-destination-partition-iam-role-name> \ --assume-role-policy-document file://trust-policy.json \ --region us-east-1 \ --profile CommercialCredentials

Run the following command to attach a permissions policy granting access to the destination S3 bucket:

aws iam attach-role-policy \ --role-name <your-destination-partition-iam-role-name> \ --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:policy/<your-s3-access-policy> \ --region us-east-1 \ --profile CommercialCredentials

Step 4: Cross-partition resource access

With the setup complete, your workload requests a JWT from the source partition, exchanges it for temporary credentials in the destination partition, and uses those credentials to access the S3 bucket.

Using the AWS CLI:

Assume the workload role. In production your workload already runs as this role through its instance profile or execution role, so it skips this step. To trace the flow from the AWS CLI, assume the workload role so the token you create carries that role as its sub. This command uses jq to parse the JSON:

WORKLOAD_CREDS=$(aws sts assume-role \ --role-arn arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name> \ --role-session-name trace-cross-partition \ --region us-gov-west-1 --profile GovCloudCredentials) export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(echo "$WORKLOAD_CREDS" | jq -r '.Credentials.AccessKeyId') export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(echo "$WORKLOAD_CREDS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SecretAccessKey') export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=$(echo "$WORKLOAD_CREDS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SessionToken')

Create the signed JWT from AWS STS and capture it as a variable:

WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN=$(aws sts get-web-identity-token \ --audience "<your-audience-name>" \ --signing-algorithm ES384 \ --duration-seconds 300 \ --region us-gov-west-1 \ --query WebIdentityToken --output text)

Run the following command to exchange the JWT for temporary credentials in the destination partition:

CREDENTIALS=$(aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:role/<your-destination-partition-iam-role-name> \ --role-session-name <your-session-name> \ --web-identity-token "$WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN" \ --region us-east-1)

Export the temporary credentials from the output:

export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(echo "$CREDENTIALS" | jq -r '.Credentials.AccessKeyId') export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(echo "$CREDENTIALS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SecretAccessKey') export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=$(echo "$CREDENTIALS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SessionToken')

Run the following command to transfer data from the destination S3 bucket:

aws s3 cp s3://<destination(us-east-1)-bucket>/data.csv ./data.csv --region us-east-1

For applications, the following AWS SDK for Python example creates a session that handles the token exchange and refreshes the credentials automatically:

import boto3 import botocore.session from botocore import UNSIGNED from botocore.config import Config from botocore.credentials import DeferredRefreshableCredentials def cross_partition_session(role_arn, audience, source_region, dest_region, session_name="cross-partition-session", duration_seconds=300, signing_algorithm="ES384", source_session=None): ''' This helper method creates a self-refreshing boto3 session object using IAM outbound federation. ''' source_session = source_session or boto3.Session() source_sts = source_session.client("sts", region_name=source_region) dest_sts = boto3.client("sts", region_name=dest_region, config=Config(signature_version=UNSIGNED)) def refresh(): token = source_sts.get_web_identity_token( Audience=[audience], SigningAlgorithm=signing_algorithm, DurationSeconds=duration_seconds, )["WebIdentityToken"] creds = dest_sts.assume_role_with_web_identity( RoleArn=role_arn, RoleSessionName=session_name, WebIdentityToken=token, )["Credentials"] return { "access_key": creds["AccessKeyId"], "secret_key": creds["SecretAccessKey"], "token": creds["SessionToken"], "expiry_time": creds["Expiration"].isoformat(), } botocore_sess = botocore.session.get_session() botocore_sess._credentials = DeferredRefreshableCredentials( refresh_using=refresh, method="cross-partition-identity-federation") return boto3.Session(botocore_session=botocore_sess, region_name=dest_region) # Build a cross-partition session, then use it like any other boto3 session. # Credentials refresh automatically as they near expiry, no manual re-minting. session = cross_partition_session( role_arn="arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:role/<destination-role>", audience="<your-audience>", source_region="us-gov-west-1", dest_region="us-east-1", ) # Confirm which identity we're operating as in the destination partition. print(session.client("sts").get_caller_identity()["Arn"]) # Use the session for real work, e.g. read an object from the destination bucket. session.client("s3").download_file("<destination-bucket>", "data.csv", "data.csv")

Security best practices

We recommend the following best practices for cross-partition access using IAM outbound identity federation.

Principle of least privilege – Grant only the minimum permissions needed in the destination partition role. Scope to specific resources and actions.

Use condition keys – In the source account, restrict token audience and duration through IAM policy conditions. In the destination trust policy, use the aud and sub conditions to control which tokens can assume which roles.

Short token lifetimes – Use the shortest practical duration.

Monitor with CloudTrail – Enable CloudTrail in both accounts. The source GetWebIdentityToken event records responseElements.webIdentityTokenId, and the destination AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity event records the same value as requestParameters.webIdentityTokenId alongside the source principal ARN and source Region. Matching those two fields correlates access end-to-end across partitions.

Verify compliance – Consult your compliance team to ensure cross-partition data movement meets regulatory requirements.

Access Path – Access should be initiated from the more restrictive partition to the less restrictive partition.

Controlling cross-partition access by origin

Cross-partition federation is not enabled by default. You enable it at an AWS account level and configure a federation provider. Once enabled, you can control the providers that are allowed to federate in. The condition key aws:FederatedProvider can be used to restrict which federation provider or partitions are allowed, or to deny API calls from credentials federated from a source account or provider. A new condition key introduced with this release, aws:CrossPartitionSourceRegion can be used to deny API calls federated from a source Region.

Allowlist approved origins

To constrain which origins can federate in, apply an RCP on sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Because RCPs are deny-only, you express an allowlist as a deny on anything outside your approved set, enforced before any credentials are issued.

Note that sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is used by all OIDC federation such as GitHub Actions, Amazon EKS, and others, not just cross-partition. Each policy pairs the allowlist with a StringLike that matches any IAM outbound identity federation issuer (*.tokens.sts.*), so the deny applies only to cross-partition federation and leaves your other OIDC providers untouched. The following two examples demonstrate allowing specific issuers or partitions:

Allowlist trusted issuers. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringNotLike on the OIDC provider ARN to deny federation from any issuer outside your approved set.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowlistApprovedIssuer", "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.*" }, "StringNotLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": [ "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/<issuer-host>" ] } } } ] }

Allowlist a partition. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringNotLike on the issuer domain to deny federation from any partition you have not approved, without enumerating individual issuer ARNs. Include any cross-partition issuer you want to allow in the policy.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowlistApprovedPartition", "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.*" }, "StringNotLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": [ "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" ] } } } ] }

Use policy to control or revoke access after role assumption

Because AWS authorizes requests against the policies in effect, a deny on either key stops in-flight sessions on their next API call. The following examples use an SCP and give you three levers, from one issuer up to an entire partition:

Deny one issuer. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringEquals on the OIDC provider ARN to deny every API call made with credentials federated from a single source account.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenySessionsFromSourceIssuer", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:oidc-provider/<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" } } } ] }

Deny one Region. Use the new aws:CrossPartitionSourceRegion condition key to deny every API call made with credentials whose originating JWT was created in a specific source Region.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenySourceRegion", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:CrossPartitionSourceRegion": "us-gov-west-1" } } } ] }

Deny whole partition. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringLike on the issuer domain to deny every API call made with credentials federated from an entire source partition, without enumerating OIDC ARNs or Regions.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenySourcePartition", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:aws:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" } } } ] }

You can also attach a policy directly to the role in the destination partition to revoke access. For more information, see Deny access to all IAM role sessions associated with a role.

Auditing cross-partition access with CloudTrail

The source partition logs a GetWebIdentityToken event when the JWT is issued, and the destination partition logs an AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity event when the token is exchanged for temporary credentials, both carrying the same JWT ID (webIdentityTokenId). Matching that ID lets you trace and audit a single token from issuance in one partition to its exchange for AWS STS credentials in the other. In the following sample pair of CloudTrail log entries, the cross-partition calls were made from an EC2 instance using its instance role.

Source partition:

{ "eventName": "GetWebIdentityToken", "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com", "eventTime": "2026-09-10T18:33:01Z", "awsRegion": "us-gov-west-1", "userIdentity": { "type": "AssumedRole", "arn": "arn:aws-us-gov:sts::<source-account-id>:assumed-role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>/<instance-id>" }, "requestParameters": { "audience": ["<your-audience-name>"], "durationSeconds": 300, "signingAlgorithm": "ES384" }, "responseElements": { "webIdentityTokenId": "6318f9f3-bccf-4d00-8e77-920e810f395c", "expiration": "2026-09-10T18:38:01Z" } }

webIdentityTokenId: The unique identifier on the source partition that correlates this event to the destination AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity CloudTrail event.

Destination partition:

{ "eventName": "AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com", "eventTime": "2026-09-10T18:33:01Z", "awsRegion": "us-east-1", "requestParameters": { "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:role/<your-destination-partition-iam-role-name>", "roleSessionName": "<your-session-name>", "webIdentityTokenId": "6318f9f3-bccf-4d00-8e77-920e810f395c", }, "responseElements": { "subjectFromWebIdentityToken": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>", "audience": "<your-audience-name>", "assumedRoleUser": { "arn": "arn:aws:sts::<destination-account-id>:assumed-role/<your-destination-partition-iam-role-name>/<your-session-name>" } }, "additionalEventData": { "crossPartitionData": { "sourcePrincipalArn": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>", "sourceRegion": "us-gov-west-1" } } }

sourcePrincipalArn: The IAM principal that obtained the JWT in the source Region.

sourceRegion: The Region where the JWT was issued.

webIdentityTokenData: The unique identifier on the destination partition that correlates this event to the source GetWebIdentityToken CloudTrail event.

Availability and pricing

Cross-partition IAM outbound identity federation is available in all Regions within the AWS Commercial (aws), China (aws-cn), GovCloud (US) (aws-us-gov), and European Sovereign Cloud (aws-eusc) partitions, at no additional cost. Note that same-partition identity federation isn’t supported with IAM outbound identity federation; for cross-account access within a single partition, use sts:AssumeRole.

Alternative option for cross-partition access

Organizations that already operate a public key infrastructure (PKI) can also use IAM Roles Anywhere to give workloads access across partitions. IAM Roles Anywhere can use your existing certificate authority (CA) or AWS Private Certificate Authority to issue and manage x.509 certificates to specific workloads and applications. To learn more about this alternative, see the blog post Transfer data across AWS partitions with IAM Roles Anywhere.

Conclusion

Cross-partition identity federation gives your workloads a way to reach across AWS partition boundaries without storing or rotating long-term credentials. Short-lived JWTs handle authentication at every stage, and standard IAM roles handle authorization, so the security model is consistent with what you already use inside a single partition. Cross-partition identity federation operates exclusively across AWS partition boundaries. Same-partition federation isn’t supported using IAM outbound identity federation. To learn more, see Federating AWS identities across AWS partitions in the IAM User Guide.

Partitions are isolation boundaries by design with independent IAM instances and separate credentialed access between Regions in different partitions. Treat cross-partition access as an exception and before you establish any, confirm it’s permitted under your regulatory, compliance, and security requirements. For more detail on partitions as a fault isolation boundary, see AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries and Meeting data residency requirements on AWS.

Bill Wells

Bill is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS with over 20 years of IT experience that began in the U.S. Air Force. Drawing on a diverse background across multiple organizations, Bill specializes in architecting secure, compliance-aligned cloud solutions that help federal partners achieve mission outcomes with AWS.

Nithin Jayakar Padala

Nithin is a Software Development Engineer on the AWS IAM team. He works on the core identity systems behind the temporary credentials that customers rely on for short-term access to AWS services at massive scale. He enjoys working on hard problems at the intersection of distributed systems, identity, and security. Outside of work, Nithin can be found traveling, value investing, watching anime, or volunteering with local charities.

44afec4006b7.text:
A jailbroken AI agent has spent more than two weeks attacking a European telecommunications provider and 13 organizations hosted on its data center and cloud infrastructure.

Malbear Labs, which has dubbed the campaign Operation Snowball, detailed the activity in research published November 8 after finding the attacker's working directory during a routine sweep for exposed open directories. The unprotected directory held more than 70 session transcripts and the agent's own reports.

The custom agent framework ran on DeepSeek Flash, with a jailbreak prompt of about 78,000 characters that told the model to treat any refusal as a malfunction. Malbear wrote that the transcripts contained no recorded refusals.

Read more on AI-driven attacks: Chinese Hacker Uses DeepSeek AI to Orchestrate Vulnerability Exploits

Autonomous Agent Adapted When Its Attacks Were Blocked

The operator's messages, translated from Chinese, were brief. Besides prompts such as "Go on" and "Stop," they set a target subnet, put three internal hosts off-limits and followed up on the agent's vulnerability list. Malbear wrote that the operator "delegated the intrusion to an AI and checked in asynchronously to review progress."

The agent entered the telecom by exploiting CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XML external entity (XXE) flaw in Cisco BroadWorks. Cisco fixed the flaw in August.

The agent went on to exploit Liferay (CVE-2020-7961) for root access on a host spanning several internal networks and JBoss/RichFaces (CVE-2013-2165) for a second foothold. Malbear listed more than a dozen other flaws the agent targeted, found or kept in its toolkit, none marked as exploited.

When endpoint security blocked an attempt to exploit the Linux flaw PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034), the agent changed its approach without operator direction. After a tunneling tool was blocked, it wrote a replacement.

Access Claims Extended to Patient and Monitoring Data

According to Malbear, the recovered transcripts showed the agent extracting dozens of credential sets, private keys and a healthcare organization's Active Directory data.

The agent also reported reaching subscriber billing records and what Malbear described as millions of patient records, through a TrakCare Oracle database that still used default credentials.

Its reports also listed about 80 Zabbix monitoring backups covering the provider's managed-services customers.

The post does not say whether Malbear checked these claims with any victim, what was taken rather than staged or whether all 13 organizations were breached.

Malbear assessed the activity as consistent with a Chinese-origin operator and did not link it to a state actor. Its recommendations included treating internet-exposed, end-of-life JBoss Application Server 6 instances as compromised and watching internal traffic for tunneling.

b5604193e4ee.text:
A data-wiping malware attack has forced Russian cloud services provider Beget to rebuild its cloud infrastructure from scratch, the company said.

On the night of November 1st, the attacker gained access to the management systems of the company's entire architecture and deployed malware that erased server data.

The Russian cloud provider detected the attack shortly after the malware activated and disconnected all servers from the network to stop the malicious activity from spreading across its infrastructure.

Beget is a major Russian web-hosting, cloud, and domain-registration provider that serves more than 200,000 customers, including online stores, media, and educational services.

More than a week after the destructive attack, Beget says that 60% of shared hosting and 40% of the dedicated servers it manages have been restored, and recovery is still in progress.

In a more detailed announcement on November 3, Beget says that the attacker gained access to the management layer of its entire architecture and then executed data-zeroing scripts.

Beget said all data in its cloud infrastructure, including VPS, S3, and Kubernetes, was lost, along with CDN settings and IP configurations.

The company also said that VPS binary backups were completely lost, and VPS file backups have partially survived. A November 6 assessment specified that these would be available for roughly half of its VPS users.

“Unfortunately, it is impossible to recover all data,” Beget said about VPS data, adding that it "spent a long time looking for solutions, but according to our current assessment, VPS file backups will be available for only half of users."

Even when a backup exists, the company said it would take time to match it to specific users, a task it describes as “technically complex.”

The scale of the recovery effort is massive, with roughly 1,000 servers requiring manual checks for vulnerabilities and hidden scripts before they can be brought back online, said the firm.

Beget is taking a cautious approach, treating all parts of its infrastructure as potentially infected.

“We are therefore cleaning out everything we can and reworking every potentially vulnerable point, including those that previously did not appear to pose a risk.”

Beget said its investigation did not find any evidence that the attacker tried to download or modify any data on the compromised servers, and that the attack appears to have been focused solely on destruction.

The company has notified the police and government agencies and is also working with cybersecurity firms to remediate the incident and recover as soon as possible.

CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-102895 GPUStack Improper Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-116779 SignalWire FreeSwitch Code Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123158 OpenBSD OpenSSH Unexpected Status Code or Return Value Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123218 IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

5bfc15899818.text:
Key points

In October 2026, Datadog observed in-the-wild activity from ARTEX, an AI-native penetration framework, against several AWS environments, with a focus on accessing financial data.

Using compromised long-term IAM access keys, ARTEX searched through CloudWatch using FilterLogEvents, hunting for financial information, file paths and secrets such as long-lived AKIA access keys and passwords.

We also observed unauthenticated abuse of public Amazon Cognito user pools, including anonymous sign-ups, token collection, and follow-up AWS account enumeration attempts.

In early November 2026, Datadog tied ARTEX activity to IP addresses that resolved to a hosted console, and found hundreds of additional internet-exposed ARTEX consoles, often in Mandarin and hosted with providers in locations including Singapore and Hong Kong.

Background on ARTEX

ARTEX is an AI-native penetration framework in which an operator supplies a target and an objective, and a team of LLM agents plans and runs the attack. A Chinese developer published it on GitHub in July 2026 and made it closed-source on October 8, after it had passed 12,000 forks.

Microsoft tied it to Storm-0940, a China-aligned actor behind a recent supply-chain compromise. In recent months, ARTEX has been documented attacking Okta, Entra ID and Cognito across IT and software vendors.

Those reports center on identity providers and web application logs. In this post, we provide more details on the cloud control-plane view, in particular how ARTEX behaves once it has compromised an initial set of AWS credentials, through leaked long-lived access keys or following a successful anonymous sign-up on a public Cognito pool.

First, we will dive into ARTEX as a platform. Then, we'll describe specific behaviors and indicators we identified in the wild.

Inside the ARTEX console

ARTEX started as a repository and has grown into a platform running on live infrastructure. Operators run it as a hosted web console, and many of those consoles face the internet. We found hundreds of hosts serving the same Chinese-language login page, titled ARTEX — 自主渗透测试控制台 (ARTEX — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console). We've also seen the same platform appearing under other names:

Page title

English translation

ARTEX — 自主渗透测试控制台

ARTEX — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console

ScopeWeaver — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console

(original in English)

LUCK — 自主资产控制台

LUCK — Autonomous Asset Console

观澜SEC渗透测试平台

Guanlan SEC Penetration Testing Platform

A similar console is rendered across many of these hosts.

The platform user supplies API keys to chosen AI inference providers and points ARTEX at almost any provider through three request formats:

openai: OpenAI Chat Completions and any compatible gateway, which covers OpenAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax, OpenRouter-style resellers and self-hosted models.

openai-responses: OpenAI's newer Responses API.

anthropic: Anthropic's Messages API, plus vendors that expose an Anthropic-compatible endpoint, such as DeepSeek.

When one provider bans or cuts off a key, ARTEX moves to the next to continue activity. Therefore, a single campaign can be spread across several providers and keys.

An agent planner directs a small team of workers. The planner sends "intents" to workers, which run three at a time by default. A main agent handles chat with the operator, with a /btw command for side questions.

Everything is recorded on a "blackboard" graph of tasks, goals, intents, facts, findings, hints and compression digests. Each task carries operator-defined allow and deny constraints, a timeout with a wrap-up step, and a planner heartbeat of at least 10 minutes. A fixed task timeout would explain bursts that end at a consistent length, though we have not confirmed the value operators set.

Command interception rules, written as regex or plain strings, can allow, deny or ask a human for a judgment. In some versions, a global asset blocklist excludes .gov, .gov.cn, .edu and .edu.cn by default.

API paths expose core routes, such as:

/tasks /exploration/findings /exploration/graph /exploration/intents /traffic /companies /llm/profiles /llm/pool /intercept /mcp /skills /agents /notify

One version we observed shipped with a sample demo engagement. It walks through a full external-to-internal compromise, from a public web app to a DMZ foothold, internal lateral movement, and finally the Active Directory domain controller.

We often found the agent reading the front end of web apps hosted in S3, looking for build manifests and runtime configurations.

Wiz noted that before each fuzzing run, ARTEX requested a path that should not exist (/zzz-nonexistent-xyz123) to learn what "not found" looks like. We saw the same habit against S3, with keys such as zzz_nonexistent_abc.txt and Notexist-xyz. A request for an object named like a placeholder, right before a burst of guesses, is a useful signal to hunt on.

This behavior is one example from agentic pentesting tools, which continue to evolve whether they're used directly as a tool or hosted as an interactive platform.

ARTEX sightings in AWS environments in the wild

In this section, we share some activity we've identified in real-world AWS accounts, and that we have attributed to ARTEX usage.

The two initial access vectors we've witnessed ARTEX start from are:

Compromised long-term AWS access keys

Public Cognito user pools

Before either, every session we reviewed opened with unauthenticated S3 requests. In CloudTrail, these show a userIdentity.type of AWSAccount and an accountId of anonymous, calling GetObject, ListObjects and similar read APIs.

Activity cluster 1: Post-exploitation following compromised access keys

In one instance using a valid long-term access key, ARTEX's most frequent action was FilterLogEvents. The most common searches were various naming conventions of cryptocurrency companies, hedge funds, and related financial institutions. The terms combine a company name with words like Fund, Invoice, Billing and LLC.

Every FilterLogEvents call was set with a limit of 1000, below the API's 10,000-event maximum. That constant shows up across sessions.

On October 20, the same long-term key was used again from 103.54.154[.]40, an address associated with zeofast[.]cn. This session widened the search, looking for file and storage links, internal secrets, internal IP addresses, and database information.

Files and storage links

Databases, internal IPs and secrets

Errors

"s3://" || "presigned" || ".pdf" || ".xlsx" || ".csv" || "rawData_" || "transformedData_"

?mongo ?172. ?10. ?password ?AKIA

?Error ?❌ ?⚠

Activity cluster 2: Self-registration through public Cognito user pools

In an instance where no long-term access keys were obtained, ARTEX went after public Cognito user pools. Wiz reported account-recovery abuse through InitiateAuth, ForgotPassword and ResendConfirmationCode. We saw the agent go further, registering an account, collecting tokens, trading them for AWS credentials, then enumerating resources.

One example came as a spike on October 26 and 27 from 154.64.252[.]77. The observed SignUp calls sometimes named the tool in the user agent such as Mozilla/5.0 ARTeX, while other user agents included curl or typical browser user agents.

Getting through sign-up was noisy. The pool had a PreSignUp Lambda trigger that checked a tenant domain, and the agent iterated against it and continued probing. For example, below are errors generated as the agent continued attempting to sign up:

PreSignUp failed with error Invalid tenant domain: api[.]github[.]com. PreSignUp failed with error Invalid tenant domain: example[.]com PreSignUp failed with error tenantId does not match tenant domain. PreSignUp failed with error Invalid tenantDomain format: hxxps[://]artex-hqheizfk[.]invalid/x. Attributes did not conform to the schema: Type for attribute {custom:isAdmin} could not be determined

Once registered, it walked the standard user pool flow: SignUp, InitiateAuth, RespondToAuthChallenge, GetUser and GetTokensFromRefreshToken, followed by Get* requests and attempts to call ListUserPools.

In CloudTrail, that session appears under the CognitoIdentityCredentials role session name with short-term AWS credentials. The agent used it to try nearly every read-only discovery call it could, such as:

ListBuckets

GetBucket*

ListSecrets

DescribeParameters

ListTopics

DescribeLogGroups

GetRestApis

DescribeRepositories

ListFunctions20150331

In this case, all of them failed because the identity pool's authenticated role did not grant the required permissions.

Hunting for ARTEX activity

In this post, we've shared some in-the-wild sightings of ARTEX-attributed activity in cloud environments. It's important to remember that while ARTEX is an offensive AI-native orchestration framework, distributions we analyzed don't appear to have an opinionated methodology for targeting or performing post-exploitation in cloud environments: the playbook is therefore left to downstream AI inference, and can vary greatly depending on the model in use.

In this context, research such as "I Gave 14 LLMs AWS Keys. Here’s What They Wanted to Do Next" by Adan Alvarez is valuable for gaining a broader understanding of how LLMs tend to behave when faced with compromised credentials.

When hunting for ARTEX activity in your environment, we recommend following the methodology below.

Start with quick wins, namely ARTEX user agents (see IOCs), to identify noisy ARTEX probing or exploitation requests. Note that user agents can easily be changed, but they aren't always updated to a stealthier value.

Review your environment for activity originating from IP addresses known to be associated with ARTEX activity (see IOCs).

We've seen ARTEX behave noisily in a number of cases: identify large volumes of permission denied errors, enumeration of objects in S3 logs, unusual access patterns (for instance, credentials vended from an EC2 instance role being used by a non-AWS IP), and CloudTrail events that relate to known cloud attack techniques (Stratus Red Team, Datadog's Cloud Security Atlas and TrailDiscover are useful resources for these).

How Datadog can help

Cloud SIEM

Datadog Cloud SIEM contains several out-of-the-box (OOTB) rules that can detect ARTEX-related post-exploitation and initial access in your AWS environment:

A user received an anomalous number of AccessDenied errors

Enumeration from multiple regions using a long-term access key failed

Anomalous number of S3 buckets accessed

Anomalous S3 bucket activity from user ARN

AWS ListResources by long term access key

AWS ListResources executed by new principal identity

AWS Cloudtrail possible secret enumeration in multiple regions and secret retrieval

Temporary AWS security credentials generated for user

Unfamiliar IAM user retrieved secret from AWS Secrets Manager

Tor client IP address identified within AWS environment

Cloud Security Misconfigurations

Datadog Cloud Security Misconfigurations ships with out-of-the-box (OOTB) rules to help you identify risky long-lived AWS credentials proactively:

Access keys should be rotated every 90 days or less

IAM access keys that are inactive and older than 1 year should be removed

Unused credentials should be deactivated or removed

When we announced that MCP Governance is generally available in Evo Agentic Development Security (ADS), the most common follow-up was practical: "Great. Where do I start on Monday?"

It’s a fair question; across 10,000 developer environments, Snyk found 4,524 unique MCP servers in active use, and 1 in 12 developers with an MCP server installed had a confirmed high or critical finding. Most of those servers were added in seconds, by a developer trying to get their agent to do something useful, with no review behind them.

Here’s our answer: four steps can take you from a first inventory to policies that block only the servers that are risky. Evo ADS now provides a risk score for MCP servers so you can govern by risk, with or without an allowlist, instead of reviewing every server by hand or blocking broadly and slowing developers down. Everything runs on the endpoint where agents already work, through lightweight hooks with no proxy in the way. Discover what's there, define what's acceptable, observe what your policy catches, and enforce with confidence.

Step 1: Discover what’s already running

MCP servers don't pass through CI or dependency reviews. A developer edits one config file, and their agent has a new set of tools. So the first step is to find out what’s already there. You can’t govern what you can’t see, so Evo ADS gives you two views:

MCP servers on developer machines: Deploy the Evo ADS installer across your fleet. It surfaces the MCP servers agents are actually connecting to, including one-off local installs that never touched a repo.

MCP servers in code repositories: Evo AI-SPM, set up through Snyk's SCM integration, finds MCP servers referenced in your code.

Together, these answer two different questions: what is configured in code, and what is running on laptops. Both land within the Evo UI, in Inventory → MCP servers.

You can also use the Evo MCP Server to access this data using your own agentic workflow. This gives you one view of your MCP estate, with nothing blocked and no disruption to developers. With this one step, you can now answer a question most security teams can’t: what are our agents connected to?

Step 2: Define what "acceptable" means

Deciding whether server number 47 is okay shouldn't take a Slack thread and a web search. Evo ADS puts the evidence next to every server, so you can approve or reject faster, with confidence.

Read the inventory

A high-risk, widely installed, unofficial server is a very different problem from a high-risk one on a single machine. Each row answers the questions you’d otherwise chase down by hand: who built this server, where it’s installed, whether anyone approved it, and how risky it is:

Server: name, origin (for example, NPM), transport (SSE or STDIO), and whether it is local.

Vendor origin: whether the server is Official. Unknown is a signal too.

Source: how many times it appears in code, on machines, and at runtime.

Allowlist status: Allowed or not allowed.

Risk score: one unified score per server, sortable and filterable.

Issues by severity: critical, high, medium, and low counts.

Sort by risk score, then scan across.

Open the Risk profile

Click a server for the detail view. The header adds authentication methods, and three cards show where it lives: declared in code, on how many machines and when last scanned, and how often agents called it in the last seven days.

Then open the Risk profile tab. This is the tab that replaces the Slack thread and the web search.

In one server we examined, Evo found tool descriptions containing ‘ignore previous instructions’ in 8 of 12 instances. That’s prompt injection you’d only catch by reading every tool description yourself.

Scores run from 0 to 1000:

Low (0 to 249)

Medium (250 to 499)

High (500 to 749)

Critical (750 to 1000)

The tab breaks the score into attributes such as prompt injection in tool description, destructive capabilities, and untrusted content, each scored out of 1000. Expand one for a description and a "Why this risk?" explanation with evidence.

This server was already on the allowlist. Someone approved it, and it still scores 931, firmly Critical. An allowlist records a decision made at one point in time; the risk score tells you when that decision needs another look. You can move it to “Not allowed” from this page, or block it at runtime.

How servers get scored

The MCP risk score combines three signals: server behavior (the instructions and tool descriptions it sends to agents), trust (the reputation of its URLs and the identity of its maintainers), and, for local servers with source available, implementation, maintenance, and dependencies. One limitation is that Evo can't confidently identify servers without a signature. That is fewer than 20% of servers, and they don't get a score. Plan for them in your review process.

Set your baseline

The allowlist is your record of which MCP servers you have approved. Each server has a toggle: approved or not. Flip it, and the decision appears in the Allowlist status column of the inventory (Allowed or Not allowed), so everyone viewing the inventory sees the same state. View the allowlist in a server's detail view to see the full list.

Start with what you already trust; you don't need to build it from scratch. Seed it from an existing inventory, a curated list, or the servers Evo ADS has already discovered. Toggle servers manually in the inventory, or just ask Evo in the chat.

For each candidate, check what you learned above: the score band, whether the vendor is Official, how it authenticates, and, for anything High or Critical, the "Why this risk?" evidence. A low-scoring, official, authenticated server is an easy yes. A critical one deserves a reason before you approve it, and a rejection is a perfectly good answer.

Remember, the allowlist records decisions. It doesn't block anything by itself. Policies act on those decisions, which is where the next steps come in.

Step 3: Observe before you block

Turning on blocking on day one breaks developer workflows you haven’t seen yet. Monitor mode shows you exactly what your policy would block before it blocks anything. Create your first policy from the Monitor not allowed MCP servers template on the Policy page (Policies → Issues → Create policy). It raises each risky server as an issue to review, without blocking anything. This way, developers and agents keep working, and you get a running list of everything your policy would catch.

Then work that list in Inventory → MCP servers, using the row and Risk profile you learned in Step 2. For each flagged server, check the score, whether it is official and how it authenticates, and which attributes drove the score. Then decide: approve it onto the allowlist, or reject it. Do this for a week or two and watch for patterns. A server that shows up once is a curiosity, but a server that shows up across fifty machines is a decision you need to make deliberately.

By the end of the second week, you have a policy that reflects your risk appetite, tested against your real estate, with your security and developers having seen it working before it ever stops them.

Step 4: Enforce, starting with what's risky

Once you trust what the policy catches, switch on enforcement. The Block not allowed MCP servers policy template (Policies → Policies → Create policy) prevents coding agents from calling servers that are not on your allowlist and are rated high or critical risk at runtime on the endpoint. If the template doesn't match your appetite, use Start from scratch and build a custom policy on your own criteria.

The policy blocks a server only when it’s both off your allowlist and rated High or Critical. Everything else keeps running in log mode, so a low-risk server that nobody has approved yet won’t stop a developer, and you still keep an audit trail. Additionally, enforcement happens locally at runtime on the developer’s machine, through lightweight hooks that sit alongside the agent, rather than as a proxy or gateway in its path. You set policy once, centrally. Hooks enforce it on each machine at the moment the agent calls the server, whether that’s Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or GitHub Copilot.

Say yes to MCP, with control

So, Monday you deploy the installer and connect your SCM; by Friday, you have an inventory and a seeded allowlist. With Evo ADS, you can say yes to MCP and still know what your agents connect to, decide quickly, and block what's risky. This is the first use case under Govern Agent Behavior, and we're just getting started: over the rest of the year, the same discover, classify, and enforce model extends to agent skills, sensitive data access, prompt injection protection, and secret exposure.

Want to see what your agents are connected to? Schedule a demo or explore Evo Agentic Development Security.

Anonymized telemetry from nearly 10,000 developer environments, plus agent skill analysis across enterprise environments
