67ebfaf3b946.text: DigiCert has admitted that a botched server migration left an internal system exposed to the internet for more than a year, allowing an unauthorized user to access customer data, including passports, driver's licenses, and other identity documents. The certificate authority has begun notifying affected customers but has yet to disclose how many people had their information exposed. In an email seen by The Register, DigiCert confirmed the compromised information included names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses. Some records may also have contained passports, driver's licenses, utility bills, or other identification documents. "We are completing a review of identification documents to determine the specific individuals involved," DigiCert told those affected, adding that it would notify those people once the review was complete. DigiCert's incident report traces the blunder back to February 2025, when an internal business system was moved from a VPN-protected network to a different availability zone. That change also opened the system up to the public internet, where it sat for more than 16 months without DigiCert realizing. The archive used the same account management platform as DigiCert's customer-facing products, including a self-registration feature that was never supposed to be available on the internal system. This allowed outsiders to create accounts without multifactor authentication and, thanks to a separate permissions flaw, use them to browse archived customer records. DigiCert found the unauthorized accounts on June 18, 2026, but initially dismissed them as harmless because they weren't assigned to an application. A security researcher raised the alarm about the account creation issue three days later, but it took until July 2 for DigiCert to shut it down. Unfortunately, someone had already been poking around. It wasn't until October 12 that DigiCert began investigating whether customer information had actually been accessed. On October 19, it confirmed that an unauthorized account had accessed a subset of archived records between June 27 and July 2. DigiCert described the affected records as a "small proportion" of its archive but hasn't disclosed how many customers or individuals were caught up in the breach. The company did not respond to The Register’s questions at the time of publication. DigiCert's postmortem makes for uncomfortable reading. The server move didn't get a proper security review, monitoring failed to pick up suspicious activity, and the access controls weren't much use against self-registered accounts. The company has since switched off self-registration, tightened network access, and added monitoring that might have come in handy a few months earlier. Certificate authority operations, CertCentral, and DigiCert ONE were unaffected, the company said, adding that customer credentials and issued certificates remain secure. It also found no evidence that the unauthorized account had been used to issue, revoke, or validate certificates. That’s good news for anyone worried about their certificates, but less so for those who handed DigiCert a copy of their passport. ®

cc1ecc71ef56.text:
Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis has revealed that its ongoing investigation into the agentic cyber attack targeting its systems also exposed names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all users.

"While we investigated, we removed access to Reactor and Data Solutions," the company said. "At this time we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated."

Chainalysis said it has implemented additional proactive monitoring systems to detect unusual activity, adding it took the Know Your Transaction (KYT) user interface and API offline, alongside other address screening products and the login page.

Previously, Chainalysis said it was probing what it described as an "ongoing multi-front cyber attack," leading to the discovery of an "on-path attack" that exposed a subset of customer passwords. The company said the attack vector has since been addressed.

Out of an abundance of caution, Chainalysis has also taken the step of locking the impacted accounts.

"For customers who just received an email from us instructing you to reset your Chainalysis password, resetting this password won't be possible right now," it noted. "We still encourage you, where necessary, to reset your password on other systems where you may be reusing credentials."

The development comes less than a week after Chainalysis said it was the target of a cybersecurity incident in which an external actor leveraged offensive agentic techniques to obtain unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools.

The company said it intends to begin restoring access to KYT and Address Screening, urging customers to contact its support email (support@chainalysis.com) or their Chainalysis account team with trusted IP addresses, which will be added to an allowlist. From there, users can reset their passwords and rotate API keys to register transactions.

"We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online," Chainalysis said. "We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate. We will communicate these changes as necessary."

It's unclear who is behind the attack, but Chainalysis notes it was similar to "many other tech platforms in recent weeks."

Rise in AI-Linked Attacks

Indeed, a number of companies, including Chainstack, OpenCode, Warp, and WorkOS, have disclosed that they have been targeted by artificial intelligence (AI)-driven attacks, some of which involve an autonomous penetration testing tool called ARTEX.

According to Microsoft, threat actors are using an agentic AI offensive framework to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, such as credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys across multiple applications and cloud services, to conduct follow-on attacks.

"Agentic tooling like ARTEX allows threat actors to not only scan for secrets across multiple repositories at a quicker pace but also use the agents to analyze the output and conduct follow-on attacks, cutting down on the need for the threat actor to have hands-on-keyboard interactions throughout the attack chain," the tech giant said.

In at least one case, an AI agent is said to have progressed from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes. The activity is assessed to be ongoing from August 2026.

Some aspects of the campaign correspond to post-exploitation activity involving the misuse of valid application credentials to access Microsoft Entra ID tenants of certain organizations and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources. The sign-in events originated from two IP addresses, 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18.

"The agent successfully conducted service principal sign-ins on dozens of associated applications across multiple tenants," Microsoft said.

"The threat actor targeted operations that return credentials, including storage account keys, App Service settings, connection strings and publishing credentials, AI and machine learning (ML) connections and datastores, and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) user credentials. The compromised applications subsequently accessed SharePoint and OneDrive in the targeted organization tenants, including file downloads and mailbox-item access."

In addition, the threat actor has been observed attempting to steal Azure resources, including compromised Azure AI services, likely as part of efforts to facilitate broader attack activity.

Another notable aspect of the campaign is that the agentic AI tools have been found obtaining a token for a single-tenant OAuth application in the same target organization, then use the compromised OAuth application to enumerate other cloud resources within the organization. In a handful of cases, Microsoft said it observed the agents exfiltrating secrets from the organization's Azure Key Vault.

"During this activity, the AI agents repeatedly demonstrated a focus on credentials that provide access to AI services, such as API keys for major AI service providers and OAuth applications with access to Foundry Tools (previously known as Azure Cognitive Services)," Microsoft said.

The development also coincides with a surge in attacks targeting AI developer platforms over the past month, allowing threat actors to resell access, abuse them as free compute (i.e., LLMjacking), and use them as attribution cover for further attacks.

In a report published this week, Google disclosed that cybercriminals have established a business model out of stealing cloud access to commercial large language models (LLMs) and reselling it to paying customers.

The monetization infrastructure centers on LLM Mixers, who act as an illicit intermediary to advertise access to compromised enterprise LLM accounts on underground markets without their customers needing to set up their own legitimate API credentials or cloud infrastructure.

In other words, LLM mixers turn stolen enterprise model access into a criminal routing gateway for paying subscribers, while the legitimate owner's systems continue to accept requests. These services help proxy requests across stolen accounts, distribute consumption, and obscure the original source of access.

The emerging LLMjacking ecosystem "create[s] a market that makes the theft easily monetizable, likely driving more actors to undertake operations to steal credentials," Wiz said.

The Google-owned subsidiary also said it identified at least two resale operations leveraging stolen AWS Bedrock keys obtained from two different organizations – llm-routing[.]com (momo) and xingjiabiapi[.]org – both of which offer a wide selection of frontier models for discount prices. That said, there is no evidence that the operators of these websites were responsible for the initial platform compromises.

Interestingly, the IP address linked to llm-routing[.]com, 23.106.46[.]239, hosted an Artex landing page in mid-October 2026 and has been flagged by Zeabur as an indicator of compromise. Last month, Zeabur disclosed a security breach in which an unknown threat actor exploited credentials stored in plaintext to compromise its infrastructure, exfiltrating over 3.2 million environment variable records and data associated with 321,810 accounts.

The following IP addresses have been used to test stolen keys and are suspected to be linked to LLM token abuse and resale -

23.106.46.239

38.246.114.118

104.243.32.50

31.57.201.201

"Threat actors are not only using AI as a tool to conduct attacks, they are also compromising victim environments solely to abuse their finances for mass Large Language Model (LLM) execution, incurring hundreds of thousands of dollars in AI API charges," Wiz said.

Reactor, KYT, and Address Screening Back Online

In an update shared on November 7, 2026, Chainalysis said Reactor, KYT, and Address Screening products have been restored and are back online. The move comes after the company urged customers to submit their trusted IP addresses to be added to an allowlist for access restoration.

"We've restored these products with enhanced security measures, and we're asking customers to reconnect in a specific way to keep accounts and data protected," it said.

4ab7191f54b9.text: Welcome to Friday and therefore to a fresh edition of On Call, The Register's weekly tale of tech support trials and tribulations that readers kindly share. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Mason," who told us he once worked at a hospital doing tech support for its research labs. "One of the labs was for a doctor who was one of the world's top organ transplant researchers" Mason told On Call. The doctor was also a voracious consumer of – ahem – adult entertainment, a habit that saw his PC and other machines around the lab often come down with a nasty case of malware. Mason got to clean that up, sometimes multiple times in a single week. The doctor's foibles were widely known around the hospital, as was the fact that his activities violated several workplace policies. Mason pointed this out to his boss every time he cleaned up a fresh malware outbreak but such was the doctor's status that management never intervened. And then the hospital was hit by a nasty cyber-worm that did a lot of damage. During the cleanup, Mason's colleagues found logs that showed the doctor's PC was the source of the infection, and that he had been indulging in his online hobby at the time the worm arrived. Mason assumed this would be the moment at which the doctor would finally be held accountable and face disciplinary action. Instead the doctor made a bargain with the IT department to henceforth use only a designated PC when pursuing – ahem – personal and/or intimate matters. And he would only use office PCs for actual work. The hospital's tech team rescued a PC from its e-waste pile for this job. "Get this thing going and deliver it to Doctor Pervert," Mason's boss ordered. By this stage, Mason had had enough. He escalated his protests, telling his boss that indulging this doctor was unprofessional, likely exposed the hospital to lawsuits, wasted IT department resources, and was just wrong. "What do you want to hear?" his boss replied. "The CIO told me do this or get another job." After Mason prepped that PC, he only needed to clean up malware about once a year – after the poor machine was so overrun with malware that it no longer served the doctor's purposes. Mason left the hospital while this PC was still in place. "You'll be shocked, no doubt, to learn that years later the doctor's graduate students filed a lawsuit," he told On Call. "And that the separate fun-time computer was one of the pieces of evidence that the hospital knew about his – ahem – proclivities and not just ignored them but facilitated them." Have you been asked to cover up revolting behavior? Or ignore policy? Click here to share your story with On Call. It's our policy to tell a great tech support story week, so we appreciate every contribution. ®

081c375d1d33.text:
SonicWall on Monday updated its advisory about seven cybersecurity holes affecting its Gen 7 and Gen 8 firewalls, five of which allow unauthenticated remote attacks, to warn that it is aware of “potential” active exploitation of at least one of the bugs, CVE-2026-19868, a bypass of SAML authentication controls in its SonicOS SSL VPN service.

And Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, pointed out that these flaws involve different SonicWall product lines to those recently reported.

“The July zero-day and the September holes hit SonicWall’s SMA 1000 remote access appliances,” he said. “This one hits SonicOS, the operating system on its Gen 7 and Gen 8 firewalls. The pattern has jumped product lines. That makes it a vendor issue, not a product issue. Credit where due: SonicWall flagged the exploitation report in its own advisory and the fix shipped with the disclosure.”

The seven vulnerabilities are: CVE-2026-107155, a permissive cross-domain policy vulnerability, with a CVSS score of 8.8; CVE-2026-107154, a session validation vulnerability, also with a CVSS score of 8.8; CVE-2026-82308, a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow vulnerability in SSL-VPN, with a CVSS score of 7.5; CVE-2026-19868, an authentication enforcement vulnerability via alternate authentication methods, with a CVSS score of 7.1; CVE-2026-77708, a pre-authentication stack buffer overflow vulnerability in TACACS+, with a CVSS score of 5.9; CVE-2026-77709 , a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow vulnerability in TACACS+, with a CVSS score of also 5.9; and CVE-2026-19703, a weak password hashing hole with a CVSS score of 5.2.

SonicWall only provided a workaround for one of the bugs, CVE-2026-19868; it involves disabling or deleting any active LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS+ authentication server configured on the firewall.

A ‘mixed bag’

Dickson said the newly reported holes are a mixed bag.

“SonicWall’s advisory rates its SAML bypass, CVE-2026-19868, a 7.1, below two 8.8 management interface flaws,” Dickson said. “Yet it is the one CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day SonicWall disclosed it. SonicWall describes ‘potential exploitation’ but CISA says active. I would listen to CISA.”

The bug lets anyone holding valid credentials for another login method, such as a local account or LDAP, skip SAML and the MFA that rides on it, he noted, adding “companies moved their VPNs to SAML precisely so every login passes through the identity provider and its MFA prompt. This flaw breaks that promise.”

Some of the other authentication holes are potentially less severe, however.

“Three are pre-authentication buffer overflows whose stated impact is denial of service. They knock the VPN offline but they do not open it,” Dickson said. “The two 8.8 flaws work only under specific conditions. None of the six is known to be exploited. They matter, [but] they are not the headline.”

Could be combined

Sav Wheeler, malware research engineer at Malwarebytes, added that even though some of these holes do not appear to be especially serious on their own, they could be combined to be much more dangerous.

“These scattered vulnerabilities at various stages of the authentication process combine to form a pathway where an attacker can bypass authentication almost entirely to penetrate a system and steal credentials,” Wheeler said. “The weak password hashing is a cherry on top for attackers that have already gained an initial foothold.”

He sees CVE-2026-19868 as “the biggest individual vulnerability” because the potential MFA bypass through alternative authentication means that “the entire trust boundary of MFA could be effectively nonexistent even when an organization depends on it for security.”

He noted, however, that although the attacker does need valid credentials for an alternate authentication method for this to work, “otherwise it requires little effort and resources to gain access, as they’re not compromising the MFA itself. Combined with the use of IP addresses for validation (CVE-2026-107154), which itself provides little security, this is a serious failure of authentication policy to ensure a user is who they claim to be.”

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said that the biggest danger is when SAML sits atop older directory logins that stay live.

“Remote access is the lifeblood of a distributed business, and one stolen directory password now reaches it. CISOs who rolled out SAML to end password-only access have cause to feel let down. SonicWall owes them a full account of how the second path stayed open.”

A vendor risk management issue

These continuing SonicWall vulnerabilities are a real issue, although the September and October flaws sit in another product, Gogia said. “Those hit the SMA1000 remote-access gateway, while this advisory covers SonicOS firewalls. But thirteen of SonicWall’s twenty entries in CISA’s exploited list carry the flag for known ransomware use, the highest share among eight edge vendors.”

Dickson noted that the next steps for enterprise CISOs are trickier because the fault here might lie less with a vendor than with the product category itself.

“The internet-facing VPN appliance is the Achilles’ heel of the perimeter, whoever builds it,” he pointed out. “Swapping vendors swaps one heel for another. The pattern should change how CISOs deploy the edge, not just whose logo is on it. Ask SonicWall whether these are new bugs or the same bug classes coming back.”

However Erik Avakian, technical counselor at Infotech, said he was less willing to let SonicWall off the hook that easily.

“Any vendor can and is generally going to experience vulnerabilities, but when we see repeated critical security issues affecting the same vendor that represent a pattern, particularly involving authentication and internet-facing infrastructure, it raises legitimate questions about their secure development practices, quality assurance, and the effectiveness of their own internal vulnerability management processes,” Avakian said. “At some point, this becomes more than just an individual vulnerability management issue. It becomes a vendor risk management issue.”

He noted that CISOs need to evaluate whether the frequency and severity of these vulnerabilities are creating an unacceptable level of recurring exposure for their organization. “That doesn’t automatically mean replacing SonicWall products, but it does require holding the vendor accountable for improvement and to demonstrate their ability to address the underlying problems,” he said.

Additional preventive measures

In addition, Dickson suggested other ways CISOs can protect themselves in light of these new holes, beyond the obvious step of patching them.

“List every way the VPN can authenticate a user: local accounts, LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS+. Delete what you do not need, especially leftover local admin and service accounts. Rotate passwords on every non-SAML account that remains,” he advised. “Compare VPN logins against identity provider sign-ins. A VPN session with no matching SAML sign-in is your red flag. Look back as far as your logs go, since SonicWall has not said when exploitation began. And take the management interface off the open internet.”

a004d7b27c09.text:
Microsoft’s email filters meant to protect users from malicious messages appear to be rejecting legitimate ones.

Over the last few days, some mail sent to Microsoft consumer addresses have bounced if they did not publish a domain-based message authentication, reporting, and conformance (DMARC) record. This includes messages to Outlook, Hotmail, Live, and MSN.

The refusals began November 5 and are ongoing as of publication time . Microsoft did not announce a policy change and has not published a postmaster notice, service-health entry, or other blog post.

The issue may indicate that a policy change and a bug may both be in play, noted Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

“Requiring every sending domain to prove it is who it says it is makes email safer,” he pointed out. “Doing it without notice, with an error message that points at the wrong problem, makes a mess.”

Intermittent sending issues

DMARC is meant to protect against spoofing, phishing, and business email compromise. Microsoft has had a rule in place since May 2025 requiring DMARC, but only from domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day to consumer mailboxes.

But as of November 5, mail from small, ordinary senders, rather than from bulk ones, have been bounced due to lack of DMARC, Sender Policy Framework (SPF), or DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM). Senders have been receiving Non-Delivery Reports (NDRs) citing 550 5.7.1 or 550 5.7.23 errors, but are doing so inconsistently; some messages are getting through while others are rejected.

For instance, one user reported this error message on Microsoft’s community forum:

Your message to @hotmail.com couldn’t be delivered.hotmail.com couldn’t confirm that your message was sent from a trusted location.

Another user reported the same problem, adding: “Some emails work fine and others return errors with SPF failed.” Adding to the confusion, some bounced domains were reported to have working SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

A Microsoft external staff moderator called it a “service degradation” currently under active investigation.

According to email security company MailRoute, enterprises can determine if their domain is impacted with this command on any terminal (replacing example.com with their domain): dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com. A response starting with v=DMARC1 means there is a DMARC record; no reply means there isn’t, MailRoute said.

The fix is a single TXT record: v=DMARC1; p=none. This declares that a domain uses DMARC and asks receivers to send reports, but it tells them to take no action on failures, MailRoute explained.

DMARC meant to make impersonation difficult

DMARC relies on two foundational email authentication tools that must be active on a domain: SPF and DKIM.

SPF verifies whether the sending server’s IP address is allowed to send email on behalf of a domain, while DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to the message to prove it wasn’t altered along the way and actually belongs to the domain it says it is coming from.

DMARC checks the two, identifying whether the domain listed on the “from” address aligns with the validated domains. It ties those checks to the name the reader actually sees and tells receivers what to do with forgeries, Dickson explained.

“Without it, impersonating your domain is easy,” he said. “That is where a lot of phishing and business email compromise starts.”

But because Microsoft, at least to this point, has only required DMARC for larger senders, it is not standard across the board; many small senders reasonably concluded it did not apply to them, Dickson noted. This includes SMBs, nonprofits, schools, and professional practices such as law firms, accountants, and doctors’ offices running on domains that “someone set up years ago, and nobody has touched since.”

Larger organizations miss DMARC on secondary domains, regional domains, and the subdomains that their marketing and billing platforms send from for mundane reasons. No one owns the domain name system (DNS), and “people fear breaking legitimate mail sent by third parties,” Dickson said.

Quiet, inconsistent failure

As MailRoute pointed out, what makes this particular malfunction so dangerous is its inconsistency: The person who sent the message sees a bounce “full of acronyms, assumes a glitch, and moves on.” Meanwhile, the customer never knows a message was sent.

It fails quietly, which is “the bane of an email marketer’s existence,” Dickson said. Customers, patients, job applicants, and others use Hotmail, Outlook, Live, and MSN, and when invoices, password resets, appointment confirmations, and offer letters go missing, the customer thinks they’re being ignored, not necessarily that the message is not getting through.

The good news is that the failures are findable, he pointed out. Every rejection generated a bounce, and bounces are logged. Enterprises should search mail logs, email platforms’ bounce reports, and help desk tickets for entries citing “Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC” since Nov. 5.

Then, resend what matters, time-sensitive transactional mail first.

From there, fix the cause by confirming that every domain sending mail as you publishes a DMARC record, Dickson advised. If one is missing, a basic monitoring record (p=none) stops these bounces without changing how anyone else treats your mail, as long as SPF or DKIM lines up with the From domain.

Microsoft 365 customers who never turned on DKIM for their own domains should do it now, he advised. “Do not rewrite SPF just because the bounce blames it,” he said. If your records are clean and mail still bounces, send the full bounce to Microsoft so it lands in the investigation.

However, a p=none record is “first base, not home plate,” he said. The goal is p=reject, which tells receivers to refuse anyone forging your name.

Inventory every service that sends email as you, Dickson advised: The CRM, the billing system, the HR platform, and the marketing tools. “Most organizations cannot produce that list,” he noted. “You cannot protect a domain when you do not know who is speaking for it.”

A signal of what is to come

While it remains to be seen what is causing this glitch, enterprises should make no mistake about where things are heading, Dickson said: DMARC will be enforced for every sender. Google and Yahoo began requiring it of bulk senders in February 2024; Microsoft followed in May 2025.

“Requirements start with the big senders and then become the floor for everyone,” he said. “The rollout was botched, but the destination is not in doubt.” But while Microsoft has the destination right, “nobody should learn about a new rule from a bounce message.”

This article originally appeared on Computerworld.

f4f8817b6fcf.text: Anthropic has started extending access to its bug-finding Mythos model by allowing Cisco and IBM to make it part of their security products. Cisco announced its integration today at an event in Melbourne, Australia, where it revealed that the red teaming tools in its AI Defense suite, which looks for weaknesses and inappropriate activity in AI models, agents, and applications they power, will be able to call Mythos to test customers’ setups. “At a very high level, AI Defense has the ability to look at models and break them,” said Jeff Schultz, Cisco’s senior vice president for portfolio strategy and marketing. He said the tool is now “super-charged by Mythos” and will identify more danger that AI Defense will then address. AI Defense already uses AI-powered red teaming to find flaws. Mythos will become another option. Cisco will make it available under users’ existing licenses, without additional cost. Natalie Mead, Anthropic’s head of applied AI for the Asia-Pacific, said the company has a long queue of buyers who want to use Mythos, and working with Cisco will make it easier to satisfy that demand. Anthropic initially made Mythos available under "Project Glasswing," a program that gave vetted organizations access to the model to test their codebases, but has since expanded access through other controlled programs, an arrangement that makes considerable sense because in the wrong hands Mythos could help attackers exploit software flaws. The Cisco deal exposes the functionality of Mythos to end-users, without letting them use the model itself. The Register asked Mead if Anthropic has similar deals with other third parties and she demurred. That may be because a few hours after Cisco told us about its use of Mythos, IBM announced that it will also integrate Anthropic’s model into a product – namely its Concert tool, which uses AI to scan applications for risks and weaknesses. IBM says it will use Mythos “to uncover weaknesses traditional scanners miss, determine which pose real risk and generate fixes for developer approval.” We have asked Anthropic if these integrations represent a decision to open Mythos to more users in more ways. We will update this story if we receive a substantial response. Also on Monday, Anthropic introduced version 5.2 of Mythos and Fable, which the company says generate outputs up to 30 percent faster than version 5.1 yet cost less: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Users can choose to run both models in “fast mode,” which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times, and doubles prices to $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Anthropic says it “ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes.” After those tests, the company concluded “high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. “Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.” The latter is a telling admission, given Anthropic believes Chinese AI labs use distillation to effectively clone its models without doing expensive training work. ®

d81ab6990f42.text:
The kids-and-social-media discussion is just dumb. It's not the premise of delaying their access until 16, but the inability of those who should know better to grasp where the responsibility for enforcement lies. Here's our PM's explainer after the laws passed down here a couple of years ago:

The onus won't be on parents or young people. There will be no penalties for users.

And it's been expressed many times since, in similar terms, always to the effect of placing responsibility for implementation and enforcement on the social media platforms. Inevitably, there are some massive holes in their implementation, along with major privacy and social concerns. But as I say this week (and have said on many previous occasions), it doesn't have to be perfect; over the long run, it will gradually change social norms, and the kids in that shoulder age bracket right now will have a different set of expectations than those who come after them. But hopefully, in the interim, the whole "onus won't be on parents" mantra will be respected more than it has been to date.

Weekly update

Vanderbilt University warns it is responding to a cyberattack claimed by the BYOD ransomware gang, which claims to have encrypted the university's databases and stolen sensitive student, employee, and research data.

The university confirmed the incident Monday, warning that university devices, systems, and cloud-based services may be affected.

"We are currently responding to an active cybersecurity incident that may impact university devices, systems, and cloud-based services. Our Information Technology team is actively investigating and working to contain the situation," Vanderbilt said in a statement on X.

As part of its response, the university told students, faculty, and staff to shut down university devices, disconnect from university Wi-Fi, and watch for suspicious activity.

The university warned that signs of compromise may include unexpected pop-ups or security notifications, unusual changes to files or permissions in cloud storage platforms, missing or modified files, unfamiliar applications, and unexpected authentication requests.

Those who notice suspicious activity were instructed not to investigate or troubleshoot the issue themselves, but instead immediately shut down their devices and contact the university's IT service desk.

Vanderbilt has not publicly disclosed the nature of the attack or confirmed whether any data was stolen.

BleepingComputer contacted Vanderbilt University with questions about the attack, including whether systems were encrypted, what data may have been stolen, and whether the incident has been contained.

If you have any information regarding this incident or other undisclosed attacks, you can contact us confidentially via Signal at 646-961-3731 or at tips@bleepingcomputer.com.

BYOD ransomware claims attack

On Monday, the BYOD ransomware group claimed responsibility for the attack on its data leak site, alleging that it had encrypted Vanderbilt's databases and stolen sensitive information belonging to students and employees.

"If you could not tell already, your databases are locked, We have your entire estate and research data. Over 1 Million SSNs, Full Names, Email addresses, Phone Numbers, Student & Employee Records, Full takeover of your DC, whatever was on your network, we possess," reads the BYOD data leak site.

BleepingComputer has since received a photograph of an alleged computer screen showing icons associated with Vanderbilt University and displaying a BYOD ransom note named "README_BYOD_31.txt".

The ransom note includes a link to the BYOD data leak site and contact information for the SESSION encrypted messaging platform to negotiate with the ransomware gang. BleepingComputer can confirm that the link in the ransom note is the site operated by BYOD.

"Oh no, you have been compromised by BYOD :<," reads the ransom note.

"We have all of your data including your backups, your entire network is compromised."

"Yes, this affects your student and employee data the most, every single SSN is archived, full names, email addresses, phone numbers, work addresses, roles, birthdays, quite literally everything."

The note also threatens to release stolen data and cause further disruption if the university does not negotiate with the attackers.

A video shared on YouTube and with BleepingComputer also shows how infected devices are playing audio warning that the network has been compromised by "BYOD".

While the ransom note and video indicate BYOD is behind the attack, Vanderbilt has not officially confirmed the group's involvement or whether devices were encrypted.

BYOD is a relatively new ransomware gang that launched in 2026 and currently lists 5 other organizations on its data leak site.

Last month, the ransomware gang claimed responsibility for an attack on the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center in a cyberattack that caused system outages and disrupted patient care and academic activities.

131061c2cdfd.text:
An iOS sandbox escape published on GitHub lets an app read other apps' files on iPhones running iOS 26 and 27. That puts seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk of exposure to malicious apps, Binance warned today. Apple's updates for iOS 26 and 27, released yesterday, do not list a fix.

A researcher who goes by forcequit released the escape, called worse_query, on Sunday, a day before those updates came out. Neither the exchange nor the researcher reported any attacks or thefts involving it.

The exchange told users to delete apps installed from untrusted sources, such as sideloaded or manually signed apps, and to update iOS and all their apps. No fix for the escape has been confirmed.

For anyone who suspects a breach, the exchange's security warning advises moving funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and resetting all active login sessions.

The researcher's proof-of-concept code can reach every app's data container on an iPhone, and some system folders on iOS 27. To use it, an app has to set up an App Group container.

He says the code is for developers and "isn't useful by itself." Other developers have built apps on it that people can install.

One of them is WQ Files, a file manager that developer Christoph Kolbicz built on worse_query. It reaches other apps' data without a jailbreak or a kernel exploit, and it can edit, delete and clear that data.

WQ Files installs via sideloading tools such as AltStore and SideStore, which automatically create the App Group it needs when used with an Apple ID. No one involved has said whether an app from the App Store could use worse_query.

The three versions in the exchange's warning are the ones listed as tested in the WQ Files release notes. The researcher gives a wider range.

Of these sources, only Erosion's developers list iOS 27.2.1, which came out yesterday, and none lists iOS 26.7.3. They added 27.2.1 this week in a README change with the note "pretty sure 27.2.1 is supported".

Yesterday's updates, iOS 27.2.1 and iOS 26.7.3, fixed two iMessage flaws and several Bluetooth bugs. The security notes for iOS 27.2.1 do not mention worse_query or any sandbox issues, nor do the iOS 26.7.3 notes. Apple does not disclose, discuss, or confirm security issues until it has investigated and a patch or release is available, the notes say.

In a reply on X, the researcher wrote that he had not planned to release worse_query early. He added that "Apple was stalling on responding to me and people started larping with it on here."

The exchange did not name any wallet app as exposed, and neither did the researcher nor the developers of the apps built on worse_query.

75af87b31ff2.text:
At some point your security will fail. This isn’t pessimism. It’s not because your team and tools aren’t sophisticated enough. It’s the reason we have detections in the first place. And, it’s why once we accept that prevention has its limits, we arrive at an interdiction strategy: finding and disrupting what got in.

After the alert

The alert tells you something happened. However, gaining access to your network doesn’t necessarily mean attackers have stolen data or disrupted the systems they were targeting. They may need to obtain additional access, move to another machine, or further explore the network. Being able to see and understand that activity is the intervention opportunity.

People naturally gravitate toward detections during product evaluations. They’re tangible, easy to compare and quantify, and address the question everyone wants an answer to: Will they catch the attack? There’s often an assumption that the rest will follow, meaning, if the detections are good, surely the investigation will be as well, right?

Whether you can trace the attack, understand the scope, and respond in time to intervene depends largely on the data behind that detection. In network security, a product can have good detections and still leave an analyst struggling to investigate. Perhaps the analyst can see the connection that triggered the alert but can’t follow what happened next. If a search returns nothing, does that mean the activity didn’t happen or that you weren’t collecting the evidence needed to see it?

This, and the arrival of AI defense, is why data quality has recently been getting so much attention.

Data vs. data

Investigation success takes knowledge of both attacker behavior and your own environment. You need to understand what you’re looking for, but also what your data can actually tell you.

The difference in network data shows up when investigating an alert. Both shallow and rich data provide investigations with a starting point, but one can rapidly lead to a dead end. Shallow data is often just composed of timestamps, IPs, and basic connection information. Rich data retains greater transaction details and adds context. It correlates and lets you pivot and reconstruct, answering not just what triggered the alert but what happened before, after, and elsewhere.

To evaluate the data quality of a security tool, consider key questions such as:

Are full transaction details provided or just a summary?

Is packet content or file extraction available?

How far back can we search, and how fast?

Can I follow a connection across hosts and time?

AI <3 data

AI-powered SOC tools can now process data at a scale that human teams simply cannot match. The more data points AI has, the more effectively it can surface events. While shallow data limits what AI can correlate, richer data allows it to identify subtle patterns across hosts and behaviors, potentially exposing previously unseen indicators of compromise or providing opportunity to intervene before an attack escalates.

AI can help when something unfamiliar is encountered. Nobody knows every service, process, or log format. An assistant can help explain what you’re looking at, suggest questions to pursue, or write a script to make a large set of data easier to examine. That can save a lot of research time. It can also help an analyst get past a point where they would otherwise be stuck.

But we’re certainly not at the point where we can trust what AI claims 100% of the time. You still need to test what it gives you. If an assistant suggests an explanation, check whether the evidence supports it. If it produces a query or script, test what it does. And before running a suggested command, ask what else it might affect. A model can be so focused on solving the immediate problem that it overlooks the rest of the system.

As AI takes on more investigative work, the ability to inspect the underlying evidence becomes another essential aspect of modern data quality.

Unfamiliar territory is the test

When evaluating data from network security products—NDR in particular—take an alert from a demonstration and investigate it properly. But don’t follow the guided path. Dig deep and put yourself in unfamiliar territory. You’ll get a much better sense of how the product helps analysts when they’re dealing with an event they haven’t seen before.

Look at the transactions behind the alert

Ask what packet content or extracted files are available

Follow the activity backwards and forwards in time

Ask a question that wasn’t anticipated

These questions and tasks probably won’t be part of a typical demo. That’s the point. They’ll let you see if the data provides the fidelity, reach, and context to actually solve investigations or just a starting point with nowhere to go.

Detections get the attention, but data determines the outcome. The real question is can your team use the data to fully understand an incident and decide what to do?

About Corelight:

Your AI SOC is only as effective as the data behind it. Corelight network detection and response (NDR) delivers data that’s open, transparent, and explainable—helping detect evasive threats, reduce triage time, and enable agentic AI throughout the SOC. Corelight’s structured network evidence preserves protocol-level context to produce a more complete dataset for investigation and AI. When analysts and AI can reason from evidence instead of isolated alerts or metadata, they can validate findings, reconstruct activity, and reach more reliable conclusions. 1e135507749f.text:
An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix.

The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must update to be protected.

The updates that fix the iMessage flaws also fix a flaw in Google's Brotli compression library. The notes do not mention any attacks using that flaw. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27.

The flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat is tracked as CVE-2026-113961. It is an authorization issue that the updates fix through improved validation. The flaw involving earlier messages is CVE-2026-113960.

Which Updates Carry the Fixes

Each operating system version got its own update. The security advisory for iOS and iPadOS 27.2.1 describes all three flaws. The security releases list links to the notes for every update.

The iOS 18.7.12 notes and the watchOS 26.6.1 notes list other security fixes but not the iMessage or Brotli fixes.

The company does not say whether devices on those versions are affected by the three flaws. Its notes also offer no workaround for anyone who cannot update right away.

The Brotli flaw, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the library's decoder that could let malicious input corrupt memory. CISA's catalog entry for the Brotli decoder flaw names Google's Brotli as the affected product and says different products could use the component.

All nine updates fix Bluetooth and AirPlay flaws. Two could allow a malicious Bluetooth device, or an attacker within Bluetooth range, to pair with a device without user interaction. The notes do not say what a paired device could then do.

Two others could let an attacker bypass the limit on pairing code attempts, one from Bluetooth range and one from the same network. Another could let an attacker in Bluetooth range corrupt process memory.

172dc1e956dc.text:
Four flaws that attackers could exploit without logging in were fixed today as part of SAP's monthly Security Patch Day—the vendor rates all four 10.0, the maximum CVSS score.

Three are in the SAP NetWeaver application server, the software SAP systems run on, and one is in the Web Dispatcher, which receives web requests from the internet and passes them on to that server.

The flaws in the Web Dispatcher and the Internet Communication Manager (ICM), which handles the server's web traffic, could allow an attacker who can reach the software over the network to run code, the vendor says.

The flaw in the server's SAML 2.0 service provider, which hands off user sign-in to an identity provider, could allow an attacker to log in as any user on some systems that use SAML single sign-on.

The flaw in SAP Gateway, which connects the server to other SAP systems and programs, could allow an attacker to impersonate one of the system's own servers and take unauthorized actions.

None of the four require any user action to work.

Affected Versions and SAP Notes

Each flaw is fixed in its own note, and the affected versions differ by component, according to SAP's November security bulletin. The notes are in SAP for Me, which requires a sign-in, and the vendor strongly recommends applying them as a priority.

CVE

Component

SAP Note

Affected versions

CVE-2026-76964

Internet Communication Manager (ICM), SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP

Note 3778530

KRNL64UC 7.53, KERNEL 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18, 9.20

CVE-2026-89126

SAP Web Dispatcher

Note 3778556

HDB 2.00, KRNL64UC 7.53, WEBDISP 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, XS_ADVANCED_RUNTIME 1.00, SAP_EXTENDED_APP_SERVICES 1, KERNEL 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18, 9.20

CVE-2026-89103

SAP Gateway

Note 3798345

KRNL64NUC 7.22, 7.22EXT, KRNL64UC 7.22, 7.22EXT, 7.53, 8.04, KERNEL 7.22, 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 8.04, 9.16, 9.20, 9.21

CVE-2026-120017

SAML2 service provider, SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform

Note 3849308

SAP_BASIS 702, 731, 740, 750, 751, 752, 753, 754, 755, 756, 757, 758, 816, 920, 921, 922

Kernels that are out of maintenance are affected too, according to Onapsis, an SAP security company whose researchers found the ICM, Web Dispatcher and Gateway flaws. Its ICM2SHELL advisory lists kernels 7.40, 7.41, 7.42, 7.45, 7.49, 7.73, 7.81, 7.85 and 7.89 for the ICM and Web Dispatcher flaws, and its PROXYGATE advisory lists the same kernels plus 7.20 and 7.21 for the Gateway flaw. These kernels may not get a fix and need an upgrade to one that is still maintained.

What Each Flaw Allows

On the affected SAML setups, an attacker could use CVE-2026-120017 to log in as privileged users too, according to the vendor. A full compromise could follow, possibly reaching connected systems.

A different SAML flaw in the same software, CVE-2026-44748, was fixed on June 9 and needed an attacker with a normal user account.

In the ICM flaw (CVE-2026-76964) and the Web Dispatcher flaw (CVE-2026-89126), crafted network traffic could corrupt memory. An attacker who succeeds could then run code and fully compromise the system.

Onapsis says both flaws come from one bug, which it calls ICM2SHELL, in kernel code the ICM and Web Dispatcher share for putting split WebSocket messages back together. It gave the vendor a working exploit that runs operating system commands as <sid>adm, the account that owns the SAP installation.

The same bug can crash either component, and a crashed Web Dispatcher cuts off every SAP system behind it while it restarts. WebSocket support is on by default, so a system is exposed even if nothing uses it, and dual-stack systems are affected through their ABAP stack. The company's researchers have not seen the bug exploited in attacks.

SAP Gateway uses access control lists to decide which outside programs may connect to it, which programs it may start and which connections it may relay for others. In CVE-2026-89103, the gateway enables its default list with high privileges, allowing an external attacker to be treated as one of the system's own application servers. That attacker could then take unauthorized actions in the application environment.

The researchers who found the flaw call it PROXYGATE. They say exposure depends on the gateway's proxy list, prxyinfo, or on a profile parameter where that list is missing, not on the secinfo and reginfo lists that most hardening guidance covers. Where the proxy settings allow it, crafted requests make the gateway treat an outside attacker as one of its own application servers, and it could then run operating system commands for the attacker as <sid>adm.

The flaw affects any system that runs a gateway, including AS Java, dual-stack and standalone gateway installations. The researchers demonstrated the attack end to end in a proof of concept shared with the vendor, and they have not seen it exploited in attacks.

What to Do

In its Patch Day analysis, RedRays, a company that reviewed the notes in SAP for Me today, advises updating the kernel and all Web Dispatchers in a single rollout. That rollout should reach levels that cover all 17 of this month's kernel and Web Dispatcher fixes.

The firm's guidance for each flaw, except where another source is named:

SAML2 (CVE-2026-120017). Under certain configurations, the service provider did not check signatures on incoming assertions. Treat any AS ABAP system that uses SAML2 for browser logon, such as Fiori Launchpad or Web GUI behind an identity provider, as in scope until shown otherwise. There is no workaround, so the correction instructions or the listed support package are the only fix. The firm's SAML2 analysis also suggests reviewing every trusted identity provider in transaction SAML2 and checking audit logs for SAML logons by privileged users from unexpected sources.

SAP Gateway (CVE-2026-89103). Onapsis advises checking the proxy list, prxyinfo, first. A permissive one, open to broad networks or any host, leaves a system exposed at any patch level, so restrict it, starting with gateways that can be reached from the internet. Where there is no prxyinfo file, the profile parameter gw/acl_mode_proxy decides, and it ships set to 0, which allows every proxy connection. Kernels 7.93 and 9.16 already have the parameter and need it set to 1, kernels 7.22, 7.53, 7.54, 7.77 and 8.04 gain it with the kernel patch, and 9.20 and 9.21 also get a kernel patch. The kernel patch alone, without a restrictive prxyinfo or gw/acl_mode_proxy set to 1, does not take a system out of scope. There is no official workaround, but a restrictive prxyinfo reduces exposure until the patch is in, and the firm also advises limiting the gateway ports (33NN and 48NN) to hosts that need RFC access.

ICM (CVE-2026-76964). WebSocket control frames with invalid length fields cause a heap out-of-bounds write before any login. SAP NetWeaver AS Java is not affected, and the fix ships through dw.sar and the SP Stack Kernel. If users reach the ICM only through a Web Dispatcher, patching that Web Dispatcher to the levels in FAQ note 3778788 shields the ICM for now, according to RedRays' ICM analysis. That holds only if nobody can reach the ICM ports directly. The ICM2SHELL advisory adds that the shield does not work on a Web Dispatcher set up as a router (PROT=ROUTER). It also warns that on release 7.93 a higher patch level is not always a fixed one: patch level 419 is still vulnerable, and only the updated 401 Stack Kernel, 402 once released, and 420 or later carry the fix. Turning off WebSocket support blocks the bug as a last resort, but it breaks features that depend on it.

Web Dispatcher (CVE-2026-89126). It has the same root cause as the ICM flaw. It affects standalone and embedded Web Dispatchers, including those in SAP HANA XS Classic and XS Advanced, but not SAP Content Server. The firm's Web Dispatcher analysis lists the patch paths: SAPWEBDISP.SAR for standalone instances, dw.sar or the SP Stack Kernel for embedded ones, SPS08 revision 089.05 or SPS07 revision 079.11 for HANA XS Classic, and version 1.5.4 or later for XS Advanced. Turning off WebSocket support works until the patch is in, but the note warns that this affects ABAP Push Channels and some Fiori features. Find every Web Dispatcher first, because one missed instance leaves the flaw open.

(The story was updated after publication on November 10, 2026, to include details from the researchers who found the ICM, Web Dispatcher and Gateway flaws.)

Corrected on November 10, 2026: an earlier version tied the SAP Gateway flaw to the secinfo and reginfo lists and said kernels from 7.93 on already have the gw/acl_mode_proxy parameter, but the researchers who found the flaw say the proxy list, prxyinfo, or that parameter decides exposure, and kernel 8.04 gets the parameter only with the patch.

b6299f36c58f.text:
Russia-linked threat group Turla has deployed a new toolset called Cereal on compromised government Microsoft Exchange servers, in one case setting it to pick out emails sent to or from NATO and European Union addresses.

ESET has attributed Cereal with high confidence to Turla, also known as Snake and Uroburos, in research published November 10. The group has been active since at least 2004 and is widely assessed to be part of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB).

The security company identified two national government victims, one in Kazakhstan and one in Romania. It found no external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure: each compromised Exchange server was co-opted to act as the C2 instead.

Cereal Turned Exchange Into a Collection Point

ESET wrote that the toolset was designed to take commands, run them in memory, map the compromised organization and gather selected messages through a new Exchange email collection module.

Cereal kept its payloads encrypted, received commands as separate .NET assemblies and ran the email collection module inside Exchange's own processes. According to ESET, the toolset paired techniques demanding a deep understanding of Exchange internals with unusual .NET execution methods.

"On a compromised Exchange server, the most interesting activity is not always the message that arrives in a user's inbox," wrote Matias Porolli, the ESET researcher who discovered the threat.

ESET's research does not describe how the servers were first compromised, but its white paper and GitHub repository list indicators of compromise.

Government Victims Matched Turla's Regional Focus

Cereal was set to pick out NATO and EU emails at the Romanian victim, found a month after ESET first spotted the toolset in Kazakhstan on November 28, 2025.

ESET wrote that this focus fits long-standing Russian intelligence priorities but may also relate to regional tensions, including Russian drones crashing near or inside Romania since early 2025. For Kazakhstan, it pointed to reported deportations of some Russian exiles since January 2026, suggesting operators may want visibility into Russian dissidents.

Around 70% of the countries Turla has targeted since 2022 have been former Soviet republics or European states once closely aligned with the Soviet Union, based on ESET telemetry.

Read more on Turla: Palo Alto Reveals New Features in Russian APT Turla's Kazuar Backdoor

Cereal was built for long-term, stealthy cyberespionage, ESET concluded. In its assessment, the victims' Exchange servers became collection points, internal execution hubs and cover for Turla's .NET tradecraft, with little left on disk to find.

49ca0dcbfc3f.text: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar. The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted. "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks. The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited. Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit. The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine. The release fixes another use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component, CVE-2026-125346, which was reported by Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security in October, though Google hasn't indicated that this second vulnerability is being exploited. The latest discovery adds to what's becoming a rather long list of Chrome zero-days this year. By June, Google had already patched five actively exploited Chrome zero-days, including flaws in its V8 JavaScript engine, Skia graphics library, and WebGPU implementation. The list has only grown since then, with two more V8 bugs fixed in September and the latest XML vulnerability bringing the total to eight. That puts 2026 level with 2025, when Google also fixed eight Chrome zero-days exploited in the wild. Whether the browser maker can make it through the remaining weeks of the year without adding another to the pile is anyone's guess. Google says the latest update will roll out over the coming days and weeks, but users can check manually by heading to Chrome's Settings menu and selecting About Chrome. With attackers already making use of the vulnerability, it's probably worth doing that sooner rather than waiting for Chrome to get around to it. ®

378fbe74d0d8.text:
A new supply chain attack hits the news. A CVE with a dramatic name starts trending. A malicious package turns up in npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face. Within minutes, your Slack channels fill up, your CISO wants an update, and someone asks the question every DevSecOps professional dreads:

“How are we affected?”

Providing a definitive answer should be simple. In practice it often takes hours, and sometimes even days to get the complete picture.

The pain: awareness is easy, blast radius is hard

Security teams are not short on information. Advisories, research blogs, vendor bulletins, social media threads, and mailing lists all announce new threats faster than anyone can read them. The challenging part is leveraging that information to understand how it affects your particular environment.

Until now, that process usually looked something like this:

Separating the signal from the noise. Relevant intelligence is scattered across dozens of sources. Some of it is vetted, some of it is speculation, and some of it is a repost of a repost. Someone has to read it, judge its credibility, and decide whether it deserves attention.

Translating general threats into actionable responses. A blog post describes an attack. It doesn’t hand you a clean list of the affected packages and versions. Someone has to extract the package names, version ranges, and CVE identifiers, and hope nothing was missed.

Figuring out where affected components are hiding. Today, software applications are assembled from many open-source components. Unfortunately, the vulnerability that was just discovered is rarely a direct dependency. It’s usually buried several layers deep in a transitive dependency which is part of a Docker image, or sitting in a build from last quarter. Your artifacts are spread across multiple repositories, projects, teams, and pipelines, making it difficult to identify all the affected components across the entire software supply chain.

Stitching together a holistic view from disparate tools. One tool tracks vulnerabilities, another tracks builds, and a spreadsheet maps services to owners. Correlating these sources manually is a slow and error-prone process, especially in the middle of a high profile security incident where nobody has the time to do it.

Prioritizing remediation with imperfect data. Published severity scores don’t always match real-world exploitability. A “medium” on paper can be easy to exploit in the wild, while a “critical” threat may not be relevant to your environment. Without context analysis, teams either over-react or under-react because they lack the proper information.

All of the above happens while the clock is ticking. The window between disclosure and exploitation keeps shrinking, and every hour spent hunting for an answer is another hour attackers can use to exploit weaknesses in your application. The real cost is often not the vulnerability itself but the time it takes to figure out the most effective strategy for defending against it.

Meet JFrog Threat Hub: taking you from “what happened?” to “what’s affected?” in a single unified interface

JFrog Threat Hub is designed to close the gap. It brings both publicly published security research and JFrog’s own threat intelligence directly into the JFrog Platform, to help determine how it affects your development environment.

What is JFrog Threat Hub?

JFrog Threat Hub is a detailed threat intelligence dashboard accessed from within JFrog Xray. It includes a daily-updated feed of vetted posts about new attacks, CVEs, and malicious packages. Most of the security intelligence is based on reports from the JFrog Security Research team, which monitors public registries such as npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face, runs automated scanners on every new and updated package, and analyzes CVEs for real-world exploitability. Relevant external advisories are also included in the feed.

Each post includes the name of the source, publish date, CVSS score, and descriptive tags, along with a public label that groups the affected packages and versions. A severity mismatch indicator flags cases where JFrog’s research rates a threat differently from its published score, so teams can prioritize by actual, rather than perceived, risk.

One of the most important features is the Check Impact button. With one click, it runs an impact search across your organization and lists every affected artifact, along with its repository, vulnerable component version, scan date, and runtime status. Teams can export these results, set Xray policies, or move straight into triage and remediation all within a single unified platform.

Threat Hub includes updated CVE advisories and impact search across the entire supply chain

Instead of reading about an attack in one place and searching for exposure in another, Threat Hub brings both steps into one seamless workflow. It not only provides early awareness, but also helps map out the true blast radius, taking you directly from reading about a threat to understanding your exact exposure.

Curated intelligence, delivered where you already work

Threat Hub consolidates security posts about new attacks, CVEs, and malicious packages, updates it daily, and then sorts it according to customer preference. In addition, intelligence from the JFrog Security Research Team is integrated as well, including:

Continuous monitoring of open-source repositories such as npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face for the latest security issues

Running automated scanners across new and updated packages

Deeply investigating suspicious findings

Analyzing new and existing CVEs for real-world exploitability

Disclosing newly discovered malware to repository maintainers

For our customers, this means original, vetted research sits alongside the external advisories that matter, without the noise of an open-ended news feed. Each post shows its source, publish date, and tags such as which ecosystems are affected. When a post is tied to a known attack, it applies a label that puts together groups of affected packages and versions, and may link to a fix or advisory.

Just one click to gauge CVE impact

When working from the JFrog Xray interface, the Threat Hub dashboard can be accessed by selecting Xray > Overview. One of the most powerful features of the Threat Hub console is the “Check Impact” button. Click it, and Threat Hub opens an Impact Search specifically for your organization. If you are affected, it shows the matching artifacts and their scan dates, so you can see where the problem lives across your scanned artifacts and decide what to fix first.

For supported CVE and malicious package posts, there’s no manual extraction of package names, no custom queries, and no stitching together results from separate tools. The research and the results are presented side by side.

CVE Severity you can act on

Published scores don’t always tell the whole story, so some posts also show a Severity Mismatch Indicator when JFrog Security Research’s assessment differs from the severity of a publicly available CVE or advisory. JFrog’s research severity reflects real-world exploitability and impact, not just the published score, which gives you the context you need when prioritizing your remediation strategy.

What this changes for your team

Operations and Security teams gain these important advantages:

Faster incident scoping. The question “How are we affected?” can get an answer faster, with less cross-tool detective work.

Less context switching. Reading the research, understanding the impact, and identifying affected artifacts all happen in one centralized interface.

Improved prioritization. Vetted research and severity context from JFrog’s own researchers helps focus on the threats that are more likely to be exploitable.

More precise communications. When leadership asks for a status update, you can present them with the specific affected artifacts and scan dates instead of “we’re still looking.”

See JFrog Threat Hub in action

The next major supply chain attack is a question of when, not if. When it arrives, the teams that respond best won’t be the ones who read the most blog posts. They’ll be the ones who can understand how a specific threat affects their particular environment in the fastest way possible.

Your managed detection and response (MDR) provider flags suspicious activity, and your analyst spends the next hour finding the account, checking logs, and deciding whether anything needs to happen. By the time the investigation is underway, the alert feels less like help and more like a task assignment.

MDR should bring your team capacity and expertise when it needs them. If the service keeps handing the hardest work back to your analysts, these five signs can help you work out where the arrangement is falling short.

1. Every alert arrives with homework

If your analysts are still sorting through the same recurring false positives, the extra coverage may be creating more work than it removes. Even an alert worth investigating is only so useful when your team has to gather the basic context before it can make a decision. Take a few recent alerts and look at what your provider had already checked when it contacted you. You should be able to see how it separated routine activity from a credible threat, and what it did to stop familiar noise from coming back.

2. It spots the fire, but cannot see the fuel

A suspicious login involving an account with broad access deserves a different response from the same activity on a tightly restricted account. The systems within reach, their importance to the business, and any known weaknesses all help determine what needs attention first. When your MDR leaves your team to assemble that picture during an investigation, valuable time goes into finding context that could have informed the response from the start. Find out how your provider uses information about assets, identities, vulnerabilities, and current threats, including what it can help you address before an incident occurs.

3. Your team gets incident updates, but few useful lessons

When a provider contains a threat and closes the case, your team should come away with more than a record of what happened. Consider the last significant investigation: did it lead to a clearer detection, a stronger response plan, or a better understanding of how an attacker moved through your environment? If similar activity appears three months later and your analysts have to work through the same questions, the service has missed a chance to make them better prepared. Expertise is most useful when your team can apply some of it next time.

4. Your response support has a spending limit

If an incident is still developing when your included response hours run out, continued specialist support may require another purchasing decision. Limits on hours, incident scope, or responder involvement can turn an agreed service into an unplanned budget request under pressure.

Ask what happens when an investigation expands across systems or continues longer than expected. Establish whether incident response is unlimited, which activities that includes, how long specialists stay involved, and what could trigger additional charges. When business operations and leadership confidence are already at stake, uncertainty about continued support adds financial and operational pressure at the point you need a clear path forward.

5. Your provider’s reports prove it was busy

A monthly report might show hundreds of alerts reviewed and dozens of investigations opened. That gives you a sense of volume, though it says little about what the provider found or did. Choose a closed investigation and follow it from the initial signal through to the outcome: what evidence was considered, what was ruled out, what action was taken, and when did your team become involved? If you need several calls to piece together that story, the charts are doing a better job of showing activity than the service is of showing its work.

If several of these signs feel familiar, bring a few real alerts and investigations to your next service review. Ask your provider to show what it investigated, which actions it took, and what improved afterward. The answers will give you a clearer view of the work your MDR is taking on and the work that still lands with your team.

For more questions to use when reviewing your service, explore the MDR buyer’s guide.
