Anthropic has introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, claiming significant improvements in handling complex software engineering tasks while cutting API prices by 20% compared with the previous versions.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model but have different safeguards. Fable is broadly available, while direct access to Mythos is restricted to vetted cybersecurity and life sciences organizations to limit potential misuse.

The models are both priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 and $50, respectively. Anthropic said the newer versions can generate output up to 30% faster than their predecessors.

The company reported substantial gains in coding performance. Fable 5.2 scored 49.1% on the FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark at its Xhigh effort setting, compared with 32.4% for Fable 5.1. The benchmark assesses whether maintainers of open-source projects would accept AI-generated changes to their code.

Performance and costs could entice enterprises

The models’ improved performance and lower prices could make long-running AI agents viable for software migrations and scientific research, according to Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at Omdia. Higher task completion rates could further reduce deployment costs, he said.

Anthropic said Fable 5.2 at its “High effort” setting achieved a coding benchmark score comparable to Opus 5.5 at its highest setting, at roughly half the cost per task. The comparison suggests that Fable could be more economical for some demanding assignments, although the savings would depend on the workload and effort setting.

“Anthropic has cut the price of a token, not the price of a thought,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research. He urged CIOs to treat AI processing effort as a budget consideration and measure costs against successfully completed tasks.

Anthropic also recommends Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge work, with Fable and Mythos intended for more demanding assignments.

Reliability challenges persist

In an internal experiment, an Anthropic engineer tasked Fable 5.2 with building a prototype operating system. The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days and produced software that could boot on a laptop.

Su said the improvements bring enterprises closer to highly autonomous software development, although widespread deployment will depend on addressing persistent operational limitations.

“Reliability remains an issue without human supervision,” Su said.

Coordinating multiple AI agents across enterprise tools and internal teams also remains difficult, he added. Organizations will need to monitor agent activity and run these systems in appropriately isolated environments. Critical changes should remain subject to human approval, with sufficient visibility into agent behavior to support audits.

Pareekh Jain, CEO of Pareekh Consulting, said complex legacy systems and the need to meet business requirements could limit how much software development enterprises can delegate to AI agents.

Faster vulnerability discovery raises concerns

Anthropic said Mythos 5.2 identified 89.6% of vulnerabilities in its internal CVE Rediscovery evaluation, compared with 78.3% for Mythos 5.1.

Conducted against 1,829 previously disclosed vulnerabilities, the test assessed whether models could independently rediscover flaws in software snapshots taken before the vulnerabilities were fixed. The company said Mythos 5.2 was also better at reproducing vulnerabilities and developing fixes.

Anthropic has restricted direct access to Mythos 5.2 through its verification programs. However, Claude Enterprise customers can use the model’s vulnerability detection capabilities through Claude Security without joining those programs, the company said.

According to Su, “Mythos 5.2 shifts the balance towards defenders in controlled enterprise settings.”

Jain, however, cautioned that advances in AI-powered vulnerability discovery could also help attackers identify software weaknesses more quickly. “This creates an AI-powered race between attackers and defenders,” he said.

Data retention raises compliance questions

Anthropic said customers eligible for zero data retention can continue using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 under those arrangements, while other customers face 30-day retention for safety monitoring.

The company has also introduced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, currently in private beta, which allows automated safety monitoring to run on prompts and responses stored within customers’ infrastructure.

Gogia said data retention requirements could outweigh the benefits of lower API prices for regulated enterprises. He urged procurement teams to obtain written confirmation of zero-retention arrangements before deploying the models for sensitive workloads.

The article originally appeared on InfoWorld.

4e9ff85de825.text:
Binance is actively investigating claims from a notorious extortion group that it has obtained 335 million customer records.

ShinyHunters posted an ad on PwsForums on November 4 claiming it was selling 335.9 million lines of records including private key wallets, user account passwords, transaction histories, email addresses and phone numbers, internal infrastructure information, KYC data including ID cards and passports, and “crypto assets in Binance’s hot wallet.”

It also demanded $900,000 from the cryptocurrency exchange, claiming it had two remaining choices: “pay or leak.”

However, a message sent to a Binance user by the firm’s customer support account on X said that, based on the sample information and the description of the data “this appears likely to be a scam rather than evidence of a Binance systems breach.”

Read more on ShinyHunters: ShinyHunters Claim Hack of Rival Ransomware Gang Clop

“We have found no evidence that Binance systems, customer KYC data, account credentials, wallet private keys, or internal infrastructure information were compromised in connection with this listing,” the message continued.

“Several aspects of this claim are inconsistent with how Binance stores and protects user data: Binance does not store user passwords in plaintext; Binance does not hold private keys for users’ external wallets; and the listing references jurisdictions where Binance no longer operates.”

Binance said that listings similar to this that have appeared in the past were often the result of infostealer malware installed on victims’ devices rather than a breach of the firm’s systems.

However, it urged users to be on the lookout for follow-on phishing attempts seeking passwords, 2FA codes, seed phrases and private keys.

Laundering Activity Continues

In the meantime, Binance continues to deal with the fallout from a huge theft of cryptocurrency from its platform by North Korean actors at the end of October.

The TraderTraitor group stole around $6.3bn in virtual currency from Binance after a months-long, multi-stage attack that involved fake job interviews and zero-day malware.

The group is now trying to launder the stolen funds by creating meme coins to disguise money flows, according to blockchain investigators.

“Anyone can create a new crypto token, and thousands of new tokens appear every day. Most are meme coins: tokens built around a joke, an animal or a celebrity, and traded on hype rather than any underlying use,” explained Elliptic chief scientist and co-founder, Tom Robinson.

“The launderers' tokens are made to be used once and thrown away. Nobody outside the laundering operation buys them, and their price is whatever the launderers choose to set. That makes them useful as a container, allowing stolen funds to go in on one side of a liquidity pool and come out on the other.”

Image credit: miss.cabul / Shutterstock.com

a87e6fb78ef5.text:
N0n Ransomware Uses AI and Victim Inflation to Rise to the Top

This edition of the Bitdefender Threat Debrief covers the latest events in the ransomware threat landscape, including the claims surrounding the rise of the new ransomware group N0n, a former affiliate that turns on The Gentlemen, and news concerning BYOD ransomware.

As ransomware continues to evolve, our goal with this monthly Bitdefender Threat Debrief is to help you stay ahead of the curve. To do this, we combine information from openly available sources (OSINT) - things like news reports and research – with data we gather by analyzing Data Leak Sites (DLSs), websites where ransomware groups post details about their victims. It is important to remember that we can't independently verify all of these claims but are confident in the trends we see over time.

For this month's report, we analyzed data from October 1 to October 31, 2026, and recorded 1,072 claimed ransomware victims. Note that when excluding some of N0n’s victim dataset (126 victims) from October’s total victims, the actual number of victims reported is actually 946.

Featured Story: N0n Ransomware Uses AI and Victim Inflation to Rise to the Top

What Happened?

In mid-September, the ransomware group N0n emerged. The group hosted a data leak site with more than 100 victims, divided into categories including pending, exposed, leaked, and honors (where NOn claims to have honored the promise to destroy victim data in exchange for a ransom payment).

Several weeks later, information about N0n’s operations became plainly visible due to N0n’s failures to maintain strict operational security measures. N0n’s Python file server was left accessible on the open Internet. This presented visitors with the opportunity to go to the web address and navigate through directory structures to view contents of the server. This exposure allowed cyber defense and research teams to determine with greater confidence that N0n’s image as a potentially significant threat is just that: a false depiction. N0n is a newcomer to the ransomware landscape, relying on AI tools for foundational hacking tasks.

What Information was Disclosed in N0n’s Exposure?

N0n’s file server address is associated with a location in Sweden. Several types of information were disclosed in the aftermath of N0n’s exposure. All information types revealed make it highly unlikely that N0n is a ransomware group capable of competing with other leading threats. N0n;s actual victim count (rather than their published/perceived victim population) and their use of open-source AI dismantles their apparent trend of continuous growth. According to the data obtained from N0n’s file server, the group targeted just over 20 victims. Duplicate or false entries may have emerged due to weaknesses in maintaining the site and polling potential targets.

N0n also uses an open-source AI platform, OpenCode, to manage different AI models and write scripts. N0n invested more than $7000 in Generative AI to assist them in building common scripts that are maintained to perform actions necessary for scanning and reconnaissance activities. While an encryptor was also identified, debate remains over whether N0n consistently uses ransomware. Their reuse of encryption keys and weaknesses in OPSEC may point towards hesitancy for the group to execute ransomware code more frequently.

The exposure of N0n’s server also revealed that N0n references the same encryption keys that are used across different victim campaigns. This means that the group was leveraging the exact same ransomware code and keys to lockdown systems for different targets. Cybersecurity teams supporting victims with access to those hardcoded encryption keys can then analyze them and identify patterns needed for decryption.

What Actions are Recommended for Organizations?

As opportunistic ransomware groups continue to adopt AI into their operations, it is important for organizations to remember the following:

Data theft claims often initially lack any validity. Keep an inventory of your assets, including critical data that may be found in open repositories. Do not assume that any data stolen is from a current dataset or usable by the threat actor without supporting evidence.

Harden remote access controls to secure systems. This includes enforcing VPN access, restricting access via RDP and also requiring MFA authentication.

Enforce a strong password policy and regularly rotate credentials.

Regularly document breach cases predating current operations and check for additional exposures.

Maintain backups in a location separate from critical infrastructure and test them regularly to ensure backup data can be restored.

Request and review intelligence on an ongoing basis to evaluate the threat actor’s behavior and current indicators of compromise

Other Notable Ransomware News

Now, let’s explore the notable news and findings since the last Threat Debrief.

Azazel, an affiliate of The Gentlemen, turns on their operator: Azazel has accumulated more than 6 terabytes of stolen data. Despite their affiliation with The Gentlemen, the group broke away from them after stealing data in an RaaS campaign and keeping the profits for themselves. Azazel published the stolen data on a data leak site under the name Leakned. Notably, Azazel has leveraged a technique that differs from other ransomware groups. They used the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to establish a connection between an AI coding assistant and a reverse shell. This connection allows Azazel to use the AI assistant as a command and control channel, executing commands on compromised machines. Azazel has engaged in primarily in data theft and credential theft, extracting credentials from GitLab and other pipelines.

BYOD ransomware claims university that provides healthcare services: BYOD, a ransomware group that emerged in September, has claimed enterprise organizations across both North America and Southeast Asia. The group recently claimed a university clinic that provides healthcare services to patients. Within 24 hours of their claim, BYOD expressed that they did not realize the systems they targeted were used specifically to support direct patient care. BYOD announced they would make decryptors available to the victim organization for free; and, the affected victims are encouraged to reach them and submit a payment of $2,500 to ensure their data is destroyed. These claims are identified as potential ploys to extend the compromise and/or collect additional payment.

Booba Team claims more victims and hits government organizations: Booba Team has claimed more than 9 government organizations at the time of this release. According to Booba Team’s data leak site, this accounts for more than 800 GB of stolen data. Booba Team’s total victims claimed in the government sector in October surpasses the totals in the same period for both Qilin (who claimed 6 victims) and The Gentlemen (who claimed 3 victims). Unlike Qilin and The Gentlemen, who have broadened their victim populations to include government victims in Western Europe and Southeast Asia, Booba Team has continued to claim victims in a limited number of regions, including North America (specifically the US) and South America. The group has been known to deploy ransomware and conduct data theft.

New brands continue to make their entry into the ransomware ecosystem: More than 17 ransomware groups have emerged in the last two months. Several newcomers were identified in October, including but not limited to: aoqin, everstake, shiba, whitearmor, hyflock, umbra, vypr, and scarlettgroup. While some groups emerge out of a necessity to commit acts of organized crime, with limited influence from other threat groups. However, the largest variables that contribute to new ransomware groups include law enforcement takedowns, feuds and factions among ransomware groups and affiliates, and operational failures. Bitdefender will continue to track further developments in ransomware takedowns, rebrands, and evolutions.

Top 10 Ransomware Families

Bitdefender's Threat Debrief analyzes data from ransomware data leak sites, where groups publicize their claimed number of compromised organizations. This approach provides valuable insights into overall RaaS market activity. However, it comes with a trade-off: while it reflects attackers' self-proclaimed success, the information comes directly from criminals and may be unreliable. Additionally, this method captures the number of victims claimed, not the actual financial impact of these attacks.

The Top 10 ransomware groups in October include N0n, The Gentlemen, Qilin, Akira, and Booba Team. Note that due to several indicators of N0n misrepresenting their operations and victims, Bitdefender has high confidence that N0n is not in actuality a group that has the means to maintain a ranking in the Top 10 Groups.

Top 10 Most Attacked Regions

Ransomware gangs prioritize targets where they can squeeze the most money from victims. In many cases, this means focusing on developed countries with higher projected growth rates. Threat actors may also launch strategic attacks during geopolitical conflicts or periods of social unrest.

Taiwan rejoins the Top 10 Regions: Taiwan ranked 10th in October; most of the region’s industries affected by ransomware attacks are in manufacturing, healthcare, and technology.

Victims based in South Korea rise due to N0n’s claims: The number of ransomware victims based in South Korea rose to 18 in October. N0n claimed 11 victims based in South Korea; all of these victims are organizations in the transportation industry. However, due to the high level of scrutiny cast on the validity of N0n’s claims, this increase should not be viewed as an accurate pattern of behavior. Ransomware groups have not claimed a total number of victims based in South Korea surpassing 10 per month since September 2025 when Qilin executed the Korean Leaks campaign.

Top 10 Most Attacked Industries

Ransomware gangs may target organizations in critical infrastructure sectors, select other organizations that offer services tailored to consumers, or attack organizations that fall into both categories. Understanding the trends and ramifications associated with specific industries, and how specialized services and clientele are impacted is crucial for assessing risk. Here are the Top 10 industries affected by ransomware attacks.

Healthcare rises to second place in the Top Industries

In October, there was an increase in the number of victim organizations represented in the manufacturing and healthcare industries. Healthcare rose to the second rank. And, the transportation industry moved from the 10th rank to the 6th rank in the Top Industries with N0n claiming a total of 20 transportation victims.

About Bitdefender Threat Debrief

The Bitdefender Threat Debrief (BDTD) is a monthly series analyzing threat news, trends, and research from the previous month. Don’t miss the next BDTD release, subscribe to the Business Insights blog, and follow us on Twitter. You can find all previous debriefs here.

Bitdefender provides cybersecurity solutions and advanced threat protection to hundreds of millions of endpoints worldwide. More than 180 technology brands have licensed and added Bitdefender technology to their product or service offerings. This vast OEM ecosystem complements telemetry data already collected from our business and consumer solutions. To give you some idea of the scale, Bitdefender Labs discover 400+ new threats each minute and validate 30 billion threat queries daily. This gives us one of the industry’s most extensive real-time views of the evolving threat landscape.

We would like to thank Bitdefenders Stefan Hanu, Mihai Leonte, Gabriel Macovei, and Andrei Mogage for their help with putting this report together.

3b0038583650.text:
When you leave home, you lock the door. When you get into the car, you fasten your seat belt. These are familiar safety habits. We understand their purpose, know how to perform them and rarely need to stop and think about them.

Our digital lives are different. We shop, bank, work and keep in touch with family and friends online, often without clear signs of where a danger begins or which precaution matters most. We receive a steady stream of warnings about new scams, stolen credentials, data breaches and software vulnerabilities. The messages vary in urgency, but many seem to demand our immediate attention.

The result can be an uncomfortable contradiction: information intended to make us safer can also leave us overwhelmed and less willing to act.

In conversations with people inside and outside the technology field, I keep hearing variations of the same concerns. There is a new scam every week, and no way to keep up. If major companies can be breached, how can an individual protect themselves? Almost anything done online seems risky.

These are reasonable questions. As a cybersecurity professional, I believe our response should go beyond repeating that threats exist. We need to help people understand which risks are relevant, what they can do about them and where their responsibility ends.

When a warning becomes background noise

There are good reasons to monitor the threat landscape. Criminals adapt their techniques, fraud schemes evolve and vulnerabilities sometimes require urgent remediation. Ignoring those developments is not a sensible strategy.

But a threat’s existence is not the same as a person’s or organization’s exposure to it. A vulnerability described as critical does not necessarily create the same level of risk for every business. The answer depends on which products are in use, whether affected systems are exposed, what safeguards are already in place and the potential business impact.

A critical flaw in technology that an organization does not use may be worth noting without requiring emergency action. A less dramatic issue affecting a business-critical, internet-facing service could deserve immediate attention. The headline alone cannot make that distinction.

Yet headlines are often how people encounter cybersecurity. When warnings arrive without context, prioritization or practical guidance, they compete for a limited amount of attention. What should be exceptional starts to feel routine. An alert that genuinely requires action may disappear into the noise.

There is a meaningful difference between staying informed and feeling compelled to remain on high alert every moment of the day.

Security fatigue is not simply a lack of interest

Researchers have a name for part of this experience: security fatigue. In a 2016 qualitative study, researchers at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) interviewed 40 everyday computer users about security and privacy. Signs of fatigue appeared in 25 interviews, even though fatigue was not the study’s initial focus.

Participants described frustration with repeated requirements and advice, along with feelings of resignation and diminished control. The researchers connected these experiences with decision avoidance, choosing the easiest option available, and disregarding protective guidance. The study was small and qualitative, so it should not be treated as a measure of how widespread fatigue is today. Its value lies in explaining behavior that security teams may otherwise label as carelessness.

When someone dismisses yet another warning, they may not be indifferent to security. They may simply have lost the ability to tell what matters, what is urgent and what action is expected of them.

This distinction matters for security leaders. If every message is marked urgent, we should not be surprised when urgency stops working. More warnings are not automatically better communication.

Replace headline volume with decision criteria

I do not believe people need to memorize every new phishing technique or follow every vulnerability disclosure to practice sound digital security. Nor is it sustainable for security teams to treat every issue as equally important.

A better approach starts with three questions whenever a new alert appears:

1. Does this affect me or my organization? Is the alert about a service, device, account or process I use or oversee?

2. Does it require action now? Is there credible guidance and a concrete reason for urgency, or is this general information about a possible threat?

3. What is the most effective action available to me? Should I install an update, verify an unusual request through another channel, enable a safeguard or notify the appropriate team?

This is not a guarantee of safety. It is a way to separate useful information from noise and preserve attention for decisions that matter.

For individuals, a consistent baseline is more valuable than trying to recognize the scam of the week: keep devices and applications updated, use long and unique passwords with a password manager, enable multifactor authentication and verify requests that demand immediate action or sensitive information. These habits are easy to describe, even if implementing them sometimes requires help.

For organizations, the equivalent is a risk-based process that connects alerts to actual assets, exposure, business priorities and clear owners. A security bulletin should answer who is affected, what the organization knows, what needs to happen and by when. When no action is required, saying so is also useful.

The burden cannot rest entirely on users

It would be unfair to finish this discussion by giving people another long list of obligations. If staying secure requires every employee to interpret technical warnings, navigate confusing settings and make the correct choice every time, the design of the system is part of the problem.

Organizations and technology providers should make secure behavior easier by default. That includes sensible protective settings, automated updates where appropriate, effective filtering, straightforward reporting channels and clear instructions when a real decision is necessary. It also means preparing for mistakes through detection, response and recovery rather than assuming flawless human behavior.

NIST’s work on human-centered cybersecurity makes a similar case: systems and guidance should account for people’s actual needs, capabilities and limitations. The goal is to make safe actions easier to take in practice, not merely to issue more instructions.

Security leaders can put that principle to work by reviewing the warnings employees receive. Are several teams sending overlapping messages about the same threat? Do alerts explain the action and its owner? Are we asking employees to solve problems that technical control could prevent? Can people report a suspicious message without fearing blame?

These questions recognize that user behavior matters, but it always takes place within a system that can support or undermine good decisions.

Build awareness through confidence

I want security awareness to treat people as partners, not as the weakest link to be frightened into compliance. Good risk communication should explain why something matters, whom it affects and what realistic next step is available. It should also be able to say when there is no reason to panic.

Confidence does not mean assuming nothing will go wrong. It means understanding the most relevant risks, knowing which protections are in place and knowing where to turn when something unusual happens.

We should therefore be careful about how we measure awareness. The number of alerts distributed, or training messages delivered tells us little about whether people can act on what they have learned. I would rather ask a more demanding question: After receiving our guidance, are people better equipped to make a sound decision?

If the answer is no, we need to change how we communicate cybersecurity.

Awareness should not be about frightening people. It should provide knowledge, a sense of control and practical ways to act.

IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Non-mobile statistics IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics

The statistics in this report are based on detection verdicts returned by Kaspersky products unless otherwise stated. The information was provided by Kaspersky users who consented to sharing statistical data.

Quarterly figures

In Q3 2026:

Kaspersky products blocked more than 311 million attacks launched from online resources.

Web Anti-Virus responded to 47 million unique links.

File Anti-Virus blocked more than 23 million malicious and potentially unwanted objects.

There were 4470 new ransomware variants discovered.

More than 81,000 users experienced ransomware attacks.

15% of all ransomware victims whose data was published on threat actors’ data leak sites (DLSs) were victims of Qilin.

More than 217,000 users were targeted by miners.

Ransomware

Quarterly trends and highlights

Threat actor disruption

In August, the creator and lead administrator of the Ransom Cartel ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was sentenced to 16 years in prison. The convict developed the ransomware Trojan and at the time of his arrest played a central role in the RaaS operation: running the affiliate program, recruiting affiliates, supplying them with information and attack tools, working with initial access brokers, communicating with victims, and processing payments.

In September, a member of the Ryuk RaaS group was sentenced to two years in prison and three years of supervised release. In 2019 and 2020, he and his accomplices breached organizations’ networks and encrypted data with the Ryuk Trojan. According to public reports, hundreds of workstations and servers were compromised. According to the prosecution, the attacker received a total of about 1610 BTC in ransom payments from victims.

Also in September, a member of the Conti RaaS group was sentenced to four years in prison. He was charged with attacking companies in 2021 and 2022. In addition to carrying out attacks, he developed part of the group’s malware toolkit.

Vulnerabilities and attacks

In July, researchers published a report on the Qilin group exploiting the CVE-2026-0257 vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks firewall software. The vulnerability allowed attackers to bypass authentication and compromise victims’ networks without valid accounts.

CISA published information in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (KEV) on several CVEs actively exploited by ransomware groups:

CVE-2026-15409/CVE-2026-15410 in SonicWall SMA1000 remote access gateways. CISA doesn’t specify which groups exploited these vulnerabilities, but researchers have linked this activity to INC Ransom.

CVE-2026-45659 in Microsoft SharePoint Server allowed an authenticated, low-privileged attacker to achieve remote code execution.

CVE-2025-60710 in Microsoft Windows allowed attackers to escalate privileges locally.

CVE-2026-59310 in VMware vCenter enabled unauthenticated remote code execution.

CVE-2025-14733 in WatchGuard Firebox also enabled unauthenticated remote code execution.

Attacks on macOS

Quarterly highlights

At the beginning of the third quarter, Jamf researchers discovered a new stealer, PamStealer. What sets it apart is its use of Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) to verify the administrator password the user enters.

During the quarter, Socket researchers discovered several supply chain attacks that compromised popular npm, PyPI and Cargo (the Rust package manager) packages. The malicious payloads in these packages targeted macOS systems along with others. For example, on July 11, an infected npm package, jscrambler, was published. Its malicious module was an infostealer written in Rust. The infostealer targeted crypto wallets, secrets from various services and browsers, MCP server configurations, and API keys for AI agents. In August, an attack was detected on the arrayref, internment, and append-only-vec Rust crates; it delivered a Rust backdoor to the victim’s device. In September, malicious versions of the MemTensor npm and PyPI packages were published. They delivered a Go backdoor that targeted secrets, configurations, and API tokens of various services.

In August, Jamf researchers also reported discovering a new backdoor, Overlord. It was distributed as fake Zoom installers and had fairly broad spyware functionality, which is not often seen in macOS backdoors: it could eavesdrop through the microphone, watch the user through the camera, capture the screen, and log keystrokes.

In the third quarter, we discovered an updated version of the MacSync crypto stealer and backdoor with a significantly changed payload delivery method.

Local threats

Statistics on local infections of user computers are an important indicator. They include objects that penetrated the target computer by infecting files or removable media, or initially made their way onto the computer in non-open form. Examples of the latter are programs in complex installers and encrypted files.

Data in this section is based on analyzing statistics produced by anti-virus scans of files on the hard drive at the moment they were created or accessed, and the results of scanning removable storage media. The statistics are based on detection verdicts from the On-Access Scan (OAS) and On-Demand Scan (ODS) modules of File Anti-Virus and include detections of malicious programs located on user computers or removable media connected to the computers, such as flash drives, camera memory cards, phones, or external hard drives.

561c12e63730.text:
In this Help Net Security interview, Eric Fourrier, CEO of GitGuardian, talks about leaked credentials and personal liability for security leaders and boards. He explains how fear of blame pushes mistakes out of sight, and what a security leader should be ready to tell a CEO about exposed keys.

He also covers better ways to measure security progress beyond alert counts, how to handle disclosure deadlines, and why AI tools and agents are creating new paths for secrets to leak into public view going into 2027.

Boards are now asking about personal liability. Has that pushed behavior where you wanted it, or has it driven bad news further underground?

Both. At the top, personal accountability has made cybersecurity harder for boards and executives to treat as someone else’s problem. Cases involving security leaders, along with requirements like NIS2, have made it much clearer that leadership can be held responsible for how cyber risk is managed. That has pushed boards to ask better questions, which is a positive change.

The downside is that accountability can become counterproductive when employees start to fear being blamed for the mistake itself. We see the consequences of that with leaked credentials. When someone realizes they have exposed a secret, the instinct can be to remove the visible evidence by deleting the commit or making the repository private. But that does not revoke the credential. The mistake may be harder to see, while the underlying risk is still there.

That is where companies need to be very deliberate about separating accountability from blame. The person who reports the mistake should not be punished for surfacing it. What matters is what happens next: was the credential revoked, was the exposure investigated, and did the organization learn from it?

If people think speaking up will make them the problem, they will be less likely to speak up. And that gives security teams less visibility. The goal should be to create a culture where mistakes are reported quickly, and leadership is accountable for making sure the organization responds to them effectively.

A CEO reads that nine in ten leaked keys are still working a week later and asks one question: does that happen here? What should the security leader be able to answer in that meeting?

The honest answer for many companies is “yes, and we may not know.” At a baseline, the security leader should be able to say: we monitor public code for our credentials, including outside repositories we control; we can tell which exposed credentials are still valid; and we know who needs to act on them.

But there’s another part of this that companies think about much less: what happens when someone else finds the credential first? Can they reach you, and does that warning get to someone who can do something about it? The figure in the question, by the way, comes from our own research. The people associated with those exposures had been notified, and more than 90% of the credentials still had not been revoked days later.

A great example of this involved CISA. We sent nine automated alerts to the person who had published credentials in a public GitHub repository and received only an automated reply. The repository stayed public until our research team escalated through CERT/CC; it was taken down 26 hours later.

A security leader should be able to tell their CEO:

1. We have a published way for outsiders to report an exposed credential, a named person reads it, and it has been tested in the last quarter. 2. When an exposed credential of ours is reported or found, revocation is the first action, not deletion. 3. We measure time from report to revocation, and here is our number. 4. We can detect when a corporate credential appears outside the systems we control, including in a developer’s personal public repository.

The CEO needs confidence that the company can find them and that the access will be shut down quickly.

A CEO wants evidence the company is better at cybersecurity than it was a year ago. What would satisfy you, and what would you throw out?

I would not throw out the traditional operational metrics like alerts triaged, vulnerabilities found, training completion, attacks blocked, tools deployed, etc. Those numbers are useful. But I would add another layer, because activity is not the same thing as improvement. If you found twice as many vulnerabilities this year, did your security get worse, or did your detection get better? If you blocked more attacks, are you better protected, or simply being attacked more often? The number alone cannot answer that. I would want to see whether risk is becoming easier to find, faster to contain, and less likely to persist.

Time is particularly useful here. How long does a serious exposure remain open? How long from detection to containment or revocation? Are the slowest incidents getting resolved faster than they were a year ago? Are the same problems recurring after they have supposedly been fixed? In my world, credentials are a very concrete example. How old is the oldest credential that still has meaningful access? What share of machine credentials have a known owner and an expiry or rotation policy? When a credential is exposed, how long until that access is revoked? I would look beyond the median, too. The slowest cases often tell you much more about where the program is breaking down.

A researcher’s publication deadline collides with an earnings date or a funding round. Have you sat in that conversation? Who won, and should they have?

I have been in conversations about delaying disclosure, although not necessarily because of an earnings date or funding round. My question would be: why is the company asking for more time?

If the exposure is still live, or publication could increase the risk to users, then the researcher should wait. The purpose of disclosure is to improve security. If the issue has been fixed and the request is purely about timing or reputation, I think a short courtesy window can be reasonable. We are not trying to create unnecessary damage. But that cannot become an indefinite delay because the timing is inconvenient.

Researchers also have a responsibility to the broader community. If a finding reveals a pattern that other organizations should be looking for, delaying publication for weeks or months has a cost too.

So I would not frame it as the company winning or the researcher winning. You need to look at what the delay is protecting. If it is protecting users while a real security issue is being fixed, move the date. If it is only protecting the comms calendar, it’s time to disclose.

What are you watching going into 2027 that most of your peers are not?

In the context of what we’re discussing, I am watching how the profile of a public credential leak is changing.

For a long time, the mental model was simple: a developer hardcodes a secret, pushes it to a public repository, and someone finds it. That still happens. But increasingly, the person exposing a credential may not think of themselves as a developer at all, and the credential may have passed through an AI tool or agent before it ever became public.

AI is making software creation accessible to far more people, which is a good thing. But it also means more people are handling secrets without necessarily having the security habits that engineering teams have spent years building.

At the same time, agents are creating and moving information across more places, creating more surfaces for credentials to escape.

I want to see whether security programs expand their idea of where public exposure comes from. Monitoring the company’s official repositories is no longer enough. A corporate credential can surface through a personal dev’s account, a side project, an AI-assisted workflow, or someone building an internal tool who would never describe themselves as a software engineer.

A working credential is still a working credential.

So going into 2027, I think the challenge is less about asking, “Are our developers leaking secrets?” and more about asking, “Where can one of our credentials escape, and would we see it when it does?”

c55814196be6.text:
SAP patched 35 vulnerabilities in its November 2026 security updates, including four maximum-severity issues affecting its NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, and Gateway software.

The company addressed memory corruption (CVE-2026-76964) and missing authentication (CVE-2026-120017) flaws in the NetWeaver Application Server ABAP's Internet Communication Manager and SAML2 Service Provider components.

NetWeaver is the core app platform that underpins SAP's business software and handles application integration, authentication, user management, and data processing.

The other two maximum severity vulnerabilities stem from a broken access control weakness (CVE-2026-89103) in SAP Gateway and a memory corruption issue (CVE-2026-89126) in SAP Web Dispatcher.

Gateway is a core framework that enables external apps to securely connect to SAP backend systems, while Web Dispatcher (deployed in almost every enterprise SAP environment) is a specialized component that acts as a load balancer and reverse proxy for web requests entering an SAP system architecture.

Cybersecurity firm Onapsis, which found and reported three of these security issues, collectively tracks CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126 as ICM2SHELL and the CVE-2026-89103 pre-auth remote code execution vulnerability as PROXYGATE.

"ICM2SHELL turns a routine part of web traffic into a point of ingress for attackers. [..] The result is remote code execution against the component that faces the network by design: no SAP user, no password and no user interaction," Onapsis said.

"PROXYGATE works by convincing the SAP Gateway that an unauthenticated, external attacker is one of the internal application servers. [..] There is no SAP user, no password, and no user interaction, yet full control of the SAP system as the account that owns the installation is achieved. On a production ERP system, that means direct exposure of the business data, transaction integrity, and the availability of critical business applications."

SAP rated these four vulnerabilities 10/10 on the CVSS severity scale, stating that unauthenticated attackers can exploit them to fully compromise the targeted systems remotely.

More recently patched max severity SAP security issues

These are the latest in a string of other maximum-severity flaws SAP has fixed in multiple components in recent months.

For instance, it patched CVE-2026-58231 in the Commerce Cloud cloud-based e-commerce platform in August, which threat intelligence firm Defused flagged as actively exploited in attacks days after the patch.

It also addressed two more max severity flaws in September and October: a memory corruption flaw in the SAP Kernel code (tracked as CVE-2026-44756 and dubbed OVERPASS by Onapsis security researchers who reported it) and an OAuth2 SSRF vulnerability affecting multi-tenant BTP applications (CVE-2026-89111).

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged 14 SAP security flaws as actively exploited since November 2021, three of which ransomware groups also abused in the wild.

SAP is a German multinational software company that reported revenues exceeding €36 billion in fiscal year 2025 and serves 99 of the 100 largest companies worldwide.

2db6a106b6c2.text:
A security researcher has found more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, putting sensitive data at risk as a result of poor cyber hygiene.

The UK government has defaulted to openly publishing code it produces with public money for around a decade because it’s transparent, and making it easier for code to be reused is cost-efficient. This includes within the Department of Health and Social Care, and the Home Office, as well as local authorities.

But funding squeezes have left departments neglecting maintenance and improvement of their technology estate. While ControlPlane security researcher Chris Nesbitt-Smith found the vulnerabilities using Claude’s Opus and Sonnet AI models, he says that he used consumer-grade models on a laptop and that many of the issues could have been caught by a routine IT health check. “None of this is the level of sophistication that general media is worried about in terms of cyber attacks,” he tells WIRED. “It’s all daft stuff.”

In the most serious case he identified, the Planning Inspectorate, which handles land-use matters across England, had failed to fully remove a login after it accidentally committed them to public repository GitHub. The fact the credentials gave such wide access—and seemingly didn’t expire—compounded with the agency’s accidental publication of them, “made it particularly dangerous for them.”

The complete Microsoft Entra ID would have given “god-tier” read and write access to all SharePoint sites and private employee OneDrive accounts, according to Nesbitt-Smith, including HR records. It also would have given access to sensitive libraries which safeguard evidence under legal hold for statutory planning inquiries and appeals, according to the security researcher who found it. “The option for ransomwaring them, for encrypting all the data, or just stealing all the data, was abundantly there,” Nesbitt-Smith says.

A spokesperson for the Planning Inspectorate told WIRED its cyber monitoring tools immediately detected Nesbitt-Smith’s activity in August and that it had already been handling this as a cyber incident when ControlPlane made contact. The agency identified and fixed this vulnerability within 20 minutes of the report and verified that no data breach occurred. “We have reviewed and strengthened our systems and processes to prevent this type of issue recurring and we are grateful for the researcher’s work and for alerting us to it,” they told WIRED.

The Planning Inspectorate issue “isn’t about open source but internal housekeeping when using public tools,” Amanda Brock, chief executive officer of nonprofit industry group OpenUK. “That data was exposed because of a failure not to follow good process,” she adds. “That’s not an open source security issue.”

In around two-thirds of the 349 public sector codebases across 33 organizations Nesbitt-Smith scanned, he said he found vulnerabilities. Several of these were found in the Department of Education’s code, including in a procurement service used by schools, in a teacher application service containing personal details, qualifications, employment history and identity documents, and England’s main register of government-funded training providers and apprenticeships. He also found a vulnerability in a Scottish Government open data portal which would have allowed any visitor to read administrative account information and to change site configuration. The organizations have since dealt with the issues.

Recently, there have been arguments for public sector departments to stop publishing source code in the open, now that AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery. The NHS reportedly ordered technology teams to transition away from open source code in May amid security concerns about the impact of AI models.

Doing this without immediately fixing the underlying issues would be the “worst case scenario,” according to Nesbitt-Smith, as it prevents researchers like him from finding them, and it’s likely that an adversary has already mirrored these repositories and so will maintain access to them. “Unless you’re going to go and fix all of the problems, if anything, you’re probably drawing more attention to it by closing it,” says Nesbitt-Smith, “because you’re like, ‘Here be dragons over this space. Don’t look here though, please.’”

40dd1facca2a.text:
Iris Ohyama warns that a cloud data breach may have exposed personal information of 7.7 million customers, including names and passwords.

Japanese household goods manufacturer Iris Ohyama has disclosed that attackers may have accessed personal information belonging to approximately 7.7 million people through an external cloud service used by its online shopping subsidiary, Iris Plaza. The incident highlights a security risk that often receives less attention than attacks against corporate networks: sensitive customer information can be exposed through services operated outside an organization’s own infrastructure.

Iris Plaza discovered a suspicious file in an external cloud service on October 28, 2026. The company immediately shut down its online shopping platform and related systems, launched an investigation and confirmed unauthorized access by a third party. It published an initial notification on October 29, followed by an update on November 5 detailing the potential impact.

In its official incident notice, the company confirmed that information stored in the external cloud environment may have been accessed or obtained by unauthorized parties.

“Iris Plaza Co., Ltd. (Headquarters: Sendai City, Miyagi Prefecture, President: Ryota Iwasaki, hereinafter referred to as “the Company”), a member of the Iris Group, has investigated the unauthorized access incident that occurred on its official online shopping site for Iris Ohyama, “Iris Plaza” (hereinafter referred to as “Iris Plaza”). As a result of the investigation, it has been determined that some personal information may have been leaked.” reads the company’s notice. “Subsequent investigations have confirmed the possibility that data stored on an external cloud service may have been leaked. The total amount of personal information stored was approximately 7.7 million records, and at this time, we have confirmed the possibility that this data may have been viewed or obtained. “

The 7.7 million figure refers to records stored in the affected cloud service, not confirmed stolen data. Potentially affected individuals include 5.8 million current and former members and 1.9 million non-members. Exposed information may include names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, gender, dates of birth and passwords, some of which are encrypted.

“The following personal information may have been leaked at this time:

classification

Target items

Number of people

Member data(including information on members who have withdrawn)

Name, address, phone number, email address, gender, password * , date of birth, etc.

Approximately 5.8 million people

Non-member data(including information on individuals who have purchased products without registering as a member or who have participated in campaigns)

Name, address, phone number, email address

Approximately 1.9 million people

Not all of the above information about our customers has been leaked. The items affected vary depending on your registration status.” continues the notice. “Some items, including passwords, are encrypted.”

There is one important distinction: credit card information wasn’t stored in the affected cloud service and, according to the company, wasn’t exposed. Iris Plaza also says it hasn’t identified unauthorized access or data leaks involving its stores on other external e-commerce marketplaces. As of November 5, it had received no reports of fraudulent use of the information or financial losses linked to the incident. アイリスオーヤマ株式会社+1

The company reported the incident to Japanese police and the country’s Personal Information Protection Commission on October 29. It also blocked the unauthorized access route, suspended the affected systems and brought in external experts to support the investigation.

The response extended beyond the main shopping platform. Iris Plaza suspended its SIMPLE STYLE website, while another group company, Iris Tech Service, stopped its websites and new applications for home appliance subscriptions and furniture and appliance delivery and installation services. The company says it hasn’t found evidence that these additional services were compromised.

Iris Plaza has also warned customers about possible follow-up scams. Attackers could use the exposed personal information to create convincing phishing emails, SMS messages or phone calls, impersonating the company or other organizations. Fake websites and social media accounts could also appear, attempting to collect login credentials, payment details or other personal information.

The company is asking customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords on other services to change them. It also says it will contact potentially affected individuals individually as the investigation progresses. Customers should be particularly careful with messages claiming to provide information about the incident, account recovery or compensation.

“We will never ask for your password, PIN, authentication code, or any other important information when we contact you.” アイリスオーヤマ株式会社

The incident is another reminder that organizations must extend security controls and monitoring beyond their own infrastructure. Third-party cloud services can hold millions of customer records, and unauthorized access to those environments can create consequences far beyond the service initially compromised.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Iris Ohyama)

4aee18bed77f.text:
AI agents topped the list of planned investments in behavioral monitoring in Abnormal AI’s 2026 State of Behavioral Security Report. Asked where their organizations would invest most over the next two years, 43% of respondents chose AI agents, more than three times the share who chose API integrations, the next most common answer.

Security professionals were divided on how well their organizations could establish and maintain baselines for normal AI agent behavior. Nearly half said their organizations were not at all effective, while about two in five rated them very or extremely effective.

Monitoring extends to non-human identities

More than 81% of respondents said their organizations rely on behavioral anomaly detection to a major or extensive degree. The approach uses patterns of activity to flag events that may warrant investigation. A sign-in outside someone’s usual pattern, for example, can draw attention even when the credentials are valid.

The same approach can apply to non-human identities, which software uses to authenticate and access systems. A service account might run a scheduled backup, an API integration might exchange data between applications, and an agent might retrieve information on someone’s behalf. Each has a different pattern of expected activity.

Behavioral baseline monitoring coverage across systems and activities (Source: Abnormal AI)

About 72% of respondents said their organizations were better prepared to detect unusual behavior from non-human identities than from people. In a separate question, 76.2% reported maintaining baselines for user sign-ins and authentication. Coverage was lower for AI agents, API integrations and service accounts, with each category at roughly half.

Security teams use past activity to help identify actions that look out of place. That can be difficult even for people with familiar roles. One healthcare security leader said an authorized user might access the organization’s systems several times in three months, then go six months or a year without returning. A system that treats a return after a long absence as suspicious can flag someone whose access is part of their job.

What counts as normal depends on the task

An agent can act on someone’s behalf, gather information from several systems and choose steps the person did not specify. It may access a system that the person who assigned the task does not use directly. To assess that activity, a security team may need to know what the agent was asked to do, whose permissions it used and how the action fit the assignment.

One software company’s security chief used the example of AI activity lasting just 30 seconds on a virtual machine to explain how hard it can be to audit a short-lived agent. A security team may be able to see the network traffic and still struggle to tell which agent generated it, especially if the agent was created for a single job or operated several layers deep in another process.

Investigating unusual activity can take hours

Just over half of respondents said their organizations typically needed at least four hours from detecting a behavioral anomaly to completing the investigation and remediation. That timing covers behavioral anomalies in general, including activity unrelated to AI agents.

Respondents most often cited false positives and difficulty defining normal activity as obstacles to expanding behavioral baselining.

An alert can tell a security team that something changed. Investigating it requires enough information to explain the change. A record showing that an agent opened a file captures the action. The assignment helps explain whether the agent had a reason to open it.

b7b29c2b634d.text:
Cybercriminals are using AI agents to coordinate attacks, stolen credentials to access linked services, and tools that interfere with intrusion detection and system recovery, according to Acronis TRU Cyber Pulse 2026.

One operator coordinates activity across several countries

In an investigation known as BOSSAI, researchers documented how one operator connected more than 10 AI models to tools for reconnaissance, scanning and exploitation. Through WeChat and LINE, the operator could assign tasks, monitor agent activity and direct concurrent operations. Reusable instructions carried procedures and details about targets from one campaign to the next.

The infrastructure supported activity involving emergency services and government systems in Taiwan, universities in Thailand and telephone data collection in Mexico. Several tools were configured to run without approval prompts, allowing agents to select and execute them within their granted permissions.

Researchers identified more than 575 malicious OpenClaw skills posing as utilities. The packages delivered trojans, cryptocurrency miners and information stealers to Windows and macOS systems. Agent skills can combine instructions with executable code that uses permissions already granted to the agent. On Hugging Face, researchers documented malicious payloads disguised as models, datasets and AI applications.

Stolen sessions give intruders a route into cloud services

A stolen browser session can give an attacker access to connected cloud applications without triggering a fresh MFA challenge. Repository credentials and API keys can expose source code and services tied to a developer account. Stolen access can also change hands, giving ransomware operators or espionage groups a foothold obtained by another actor.

Of the more than 1.8 million endpoints already running the vendor’s own remote monitoring and management software, 63.1% had at least one additional remote management or remote access tool installed. Some installations support routine work. Others may remain on devices after a provider change. An intruder who gains control of one of those tools can use it to reach the systems it manages.

In the Red Heron campaign, a working public exploit appeared the day after Gitea issued a patch for a critical vulnerability. The attackers adapted the code to target internet-facing Gitea servers. In confirmed breaches, they stole repositories, collected credentials and moved to other systems.

Ransomware targets monitoring and recovery

A Qilin ransomware sample could terminate processes and delete Windows Volume Shadow Copies before encryption. The Gentlemen maintained tools that affiliates could use to disable endpoint detection and response software. If monitoring goes down on a shared management server, defenders can lose visibility across several environments during an intrusion.

Lockbit 5.0 data leak site (Source: Acronis)

LockBit 5.0 includes versions for Windows, Linux and VMware ESXi. The ESXi variant can shut down running virtual machines so their files can be encrypted. An INC ransomware encryptor can delete snapshots, removing a recovery option for affected machines. An attack on a virtualization host can take multiple services offline and disrupt the infrastructure used to restore them.

Familiar software helps conceal malicious activity

The TamperedChef campaign used ads and search results to distribute malicious applications that performed the tasks they advertised, including editing PDFs and opening manuals. The applications carried valid Extended Validation code-signing certificates that the operators obtained through a rotating network of U.S.-registered shell companies. When a certificate was revoked, the operators replaced it with one obtained through another company.

Other campaigns used GitHub repositories and cloud storage to distribute malware. Attackers also used messaging services to communicate with compromised systems. These platforms carry routine business traffic, which can make malicious activity harder to detect.

b01951a1eb7a.text:
Cybersecurity company Barracuda Networks warned that attackers have begun exploiting two recently patched Email Security Gateway (ESG) vulnerabilities that let them run commands with root privileges.

Barracuda released security updates to address the two flaws (tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560) one week ago.

The first stems from an Email Security Gateway (ESG) authentication weakness that can be exploited to modify an appliance's global configuration, while the second lets unauthenticated attackers inject OS commands that execute with root privileges.

Barracuda also said that successful attacks require access to the administrative user interface (Admin UI) of targeted devices and advised customers to restrict access to trusted internal networks and use appropriate network access controls to limit exposure.

"Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product. If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device," the company explained.

On Monday evening, Barracuda updated the initial advisory to warn admins that the two flaws are being exploited in attacks targeting a limited number of customers.

"Barracuda immediately initiated a comprehensive remediation process and released security patches for affected products. We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations," it warned.

"If a patch has not been automatically applied, customers should manually apply the appropriate patch as soon as possible. If customers have turned off automatic patching, Barracuda recommends setting devices to automatically receive patches."

The company later revealed that the flaw had been exploited as a zero-day for at least seven months, since at least October 2022, to drop previously unknown SeaSpy and Saltwater malware and steal data from compromised devices.

According to cybersecurity firm Mandiant, almost a third of systems breached in the 2023 campaign belonged to government agencies, most of them hacked between October and December 2022.

Google has released emergency security updates to patch a new Chrome vulnerability exploited in zero-day attacks, the eighth such flaw since the start of the year.

"Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said in a Monday security advisory.

As Google explained, this flaw stems from a Use-After-Free (UAF) weakness in the XML component of the Google Chrome web browser, which occurs when the browser's XML parser processes data, deletes an object from the computer's memory, but fails to clear the pointer referencing that object.

Attackers can exploit this high-severity memory corruption vulnerability when the browser later tries to use or read that "freed" memory space to manipulate the memory layout and execute malicious code.

While Google has found evidence of attackers exploiting this zero-day bug in the wild, it has not shared additional details about these incidents.

"Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix. We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven't yet fixed," it noted.

Google has now fixed the zero-day for users in the Stable Desktop channel, with new versions rolling out to Windows, macOS (157.0.8103.50/.51), and Linux users (157.0.8103.50). Although Google says the security update could take days or weeks to reach all Chrome users, it was available immediately when BleepingComputer checked for updates today.

If you don't want to update the web browser manually, you can also let Chrome check for updates on its own, as it will automatically install them after the next launch.

​Since the start of the year, Google has addressed seven other actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities:

An iterator invalidation bug (CVE-2026-2441) in CSSFontFeatureValuesMap (Chrome's implementation of CSS font feature values), which Google addressed in mid-February.

Two other Chrome zero-day bugs exploited in attacks were patched in March: an out-of-bounds write weakness in the Skia 2D graphics library (CVE-2026-3909), and an inappropriate implementation vulnerability in the V8 JavaScript and WebAssembly engine (CVE-2026-3910).

A use-after-free weakness in Dawn (CVE-2026-5281), the underlying cross-platform implementation of the WebGPU standard used by the Chromium project, which Google patched in April.

An out-of-bounds read and write vulnerability in Chrome's V8 JavaScript engine (CVE-2026-11645), exploited in the wild and patched in June.

And out-of-bounds write (CVE-2026-87491) and type confusion (CVE-2026-85046) flaws in the V8 JavaScript engine, fixed in September.

Google fixed eight more zero-days exploited in attacks in 2025, many of them reported by the company's Threat Analysis Group (TAG), which tracks zero-day exploits used in spyware attacks.

AI infrastructure startup Fireworks has disclosed a new security breach in which attackers accessed its development machines after breaching a third-party cloud provider.

FireWorks provides a high-performance inference platform for developers who want to deploy and run open-source artificial intelligence models (such as Mistral, Meta's Llama, or Google's Gemma) without worrying about hardware bottlenecks and complex infrastructure tasks.

The company notified law enforcement and customers of another security incident in early October after attackers accessed environment variables containing API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts.

"The evidence indicates links to a cybercriminal threat actor group, which is financially motivated and aimed at selling tokens from unauthorized access to Large Language Models (LLMs) to illicit routing gateways, known as 'LLMJacking'," Fireworks said at the time.

After revoking compromised internal credentials, affected Fireworks API keys, and keys created by the attackers, Fireworks discovered another security incident on October 23.

In the new breach, the threat actors accessed resource metadata (e.g., Fireworks resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation time), billing information (e.g., billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment history, account balance, and credit usage), and incomplete model weights and datasets for some customers.

However, the company said the attackers couldn't access customer payment card numbers because Fireworks doesn't store them.

"A third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks R&D machines experienced a security incident on October 23. On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact," Fireworks noted in a Monday advisory.

"We detected this activity on the same day, and followed our incident response processes to take immediate remediation measures and close known critical vulnerabilities. As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use."

Since the attack, Fireworks revoked and replaced credentials and service accounts, restricted unauthorized network pathways, isolated affected systems, and tightened access to data storage and analytics systems to block public or unauthorized access to stored data.

The company is now working with Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 incident response division to secure its systems against future attacks and further investigate the incident's full scope and impact.

One week ago, researchers at Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant reported that large language model hijacking attacks (also known as LLMjacking) are driving record costs for compromised organizations, with cloud AI charges reaching as high as $1 million due to fraudulent calls using stolen API keys.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added a high-severity vulnerability impacting SonicWall SonicOS to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports that it said may have been exploited in real-world attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-19868 (CVSS score: 7.1 / 7.5), has been described as an authentication reinforcement vulnerability via alternate authentication methods.

"An authentication enforcement vulnerability in SonicOS SSL-VPN service may allow a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls. Successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA)," SonicWall said in a Friday advisory.

The company also acknowledged that it "investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of this vulnerability," urging customers to update to the latest version as soon as possible. SonicWall did not disclose any additional specifics about the nature of the attack or who is behind the effort.

Also patched by SonicWall are a number of other high-severity flaws -

CVE-2026-107155 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A permissive cross-domain policy vulnerability in the SonicOS management interface that could potentially enable a remote unauthenticated attacker to perform unauthorized operations under specific conditions.

CVE-2026-107154 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A session validation vulnerability in the SonicOS management interface that could potentially enable a remote unauthenticated attacker to perform unauthorized operations under specific conditions.

CVE-2026-82308 (CVSS score: 7.5) - A pre-authentication heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in the SonicOS SSL-VPN service that could potentially enable a remote unauthenticated attacker to cause an application level denial-of-service.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the patches by November 20, 2026, to secure their networks against the threat.

The development comes days after SonicWall detailed two unpatched vulnerabilities impacting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems (CVE-2026-109593 and CVE-2026-109594), urging customers to upgrade to Network Security Manager (NSM).

Hackers are actively exploiting the "SSHole" vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) in OpenSSH to execute commands, steal credentials, and establish persistent access.

Multiple cybersecurity firms have confirmed the attacks, reporting that exploitation attempts began on November 5, the day a proof-of-concept exploit became available, with successful exploitation recorded the following day.

Disclosed by security researcher Ozgun Kultekin last week, SSHole allows bypassing authentication in OpenSSH running on certain musl-based Linux systems, including the lightweight Alpine distribution used in cloud and virtual environments.

The flaw lets attackers log in to accounts with a password hash is set to an asterisk (*) to prevent password logins.

An oversized password causes musl’s password-hashing function to return * on error, which OpenSSH mistakenly treats as a match for the account’s stored value.

Kultekin explained that exploitation requires specific authentication settings, does not affect accounts with valid password hashes, and can lead to root access where the compromised account has passwordless administrative privileges.

OpenSSH maintainers fixed the vulnerability in version 10.6p2 released on November 5, while exploit code became available roughly four hours later.

Finnish security company Defused said over the weekend that it had observed "a small amount of actors" trying to exploit SSHole, although the activity was not widespread.

Threat intelligence company GreyNoise recorded the first successful exploitation of SSHole in the wild on November 7 at 00:46 UTC, approximately 40 hours after the fix.

The researchers logged 16 successful exploitation chains targeting networks protected by GreyNoise from six source IP addresses linked to post-exploitation activity. The company says that these attacks are not representative of the broader activity involving SSHole.

In the attacks that GreyNoise observed, the threat actor ran system and container reconnaissance, initiated queries to cloud metadata services, attempted to read password hashes and root SSH keys, and tried to modify SSH ‘authorized_keys’ files to gain persistent access.

One attacker gained root privileges and installed TAC Agent, a Python command-and-control agent. However, the implant couldn’t reach its command-and-control (C2) server at ‘tac.vpnla[.]org,’ and never received a task.

Analysis of the TAC Agent payload shows that the implant supports shell command execution, extensive system reconnaissance, file upload/download operations, and can update itself.

The agent has no built-in persistence, so the attackers attempt to secure it by configuring a startup service.

GreyNoise notes that the implant’s comments, logs, and errors were in Chinese, which may be used in conjunction with other evidence to determine the attacker’s origin.

A finding that suggests possible automated operation is a missing tool check that returns feedback which could help an automated planner revise commands as needed for the attack to proceed.

Overall, GreyNoise has recorded 27.5 million port-22 scans and 20.1 million attempted SSH sessions, though these aren’t confirmed SSHole attacks.

Sensors from network security company Previdian also confirmed successful SSHole exploitation, with telemetry data showing 20 attempts from 13 attacker IP addresses in nine countries.

Offensive security firm watchTower said on November 6 that it observed SSHole being exploited in attacks associated with botnets and cryptomining activity.

System administrators should update OpenSSH as soon as possible, or disable SSH password authentication on systems affected by SSHole.

It is also recommended to check for unexpected successful password logins to accounts whose /etc/shadow password field is *, unauthorized SSH keys, and TAC Agent files or startup services.
