A flaw in Git can let a malicious repository run an attacker's code on a computer that clones it recursively, together with its submodules. The Git project fixed it this week in Git 2.56.1, with matching fixes for the 2.50 through 2.55 series in 2.50.2, 2.51.3, 2.52.1, 2.53.1, 2.54.1 and 2.55.1.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111760, is an integer truncation in how Git handles its index. An extremely long path in a repository can pass Git's safety check, but Git then writes it to disk under a shorter name that an attacker can set to .git.

This lets an attacker replace a submodule's .git file with a symbolic link to a folder holding malicious hooks or configuration. Hooks are programs Git runs at set points, so once Git uses that folder, the attacker's code can run.

Submodules matter here because Git refuses to replace a .git folder with a symbolic link, but in a freshly cloned submodule, .git is a file.

The fixed versions, listed in the Git project's release announcement, refuse such extremely long paths before their length can be cut short.

GitHub, which ships Git in its own tools, explained the fixes in a detailed write-up. It advises installing a fixed version from your operating system or Git distributor, and updating any app that ships its own copy of Git.

The company has already applied the fixes to github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud. For GitHub Enterprise Server, they are in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4.

Fixed versions of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app are being prepared. GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also get the fixed Git.

Git for Windows had not released a version based on Git 2.56.1 as of Tuesday at 19:09 UTC, a check of its release tags by The Hacker News found.

Until a fixed version is installed, GitHub suggests these steps, which do not replace the fixes:

Clone only from servers you trust.

Do not recursively clone repositories you do not trust.

Do not merge content or tags you do not trust.

Do not process binary patches or fast-import streams from sources you do not trust.

The Git releases also fix five other flaws:

CVE-2026-113408: When someone clones an empty repository over Git protocol v2, a malicious server can send a branch name that contains path traversal. With the files reference backend, a later update to that branch can then write outside Git's reference folder.

CVE-2026-114467: Merging a tag that carries more than two GPG signatures corrupts Git's stack memory and can cause a denial of service. Hosting services that run such merges for users may also be affected.

CVE-2026-114469: A binary patch that expands to a very large size can get past Git's patch size limit of about 1 GiB and crash Git with an out-of-bounds read.

CVE-2026-105437: A very large merge, with many conflicts and a large conflict-marker-size attribute, can make Git write past the end of a buffer that is too small, corrupting heap memory.

CVE-2026-114466: Three git fast-import features, rewrite-submodules-from, rewrite-submodules-to and export-pack-edges, could be used to read arbitrary files or to create files and add data to them. Git now rejects them in an input stream unless --allow-unsafe-features is set.

GitLab, which assigned CVE-2026-105437, said code-hosting servers are most likely to be targeted through git merge-tree. A server may run that command to check whether a pull or merge request can be merged.

The conflict-marker-size attribute can be set in a .gitattributes file committed to a repository. If a server reads attributes from the repository, any user who can push branches and open a pull or merge request can trigger the flaw.

As a workaround for this flaw, servers that cannot upgrade yet can add conflict-marker-size=7 to each repository's info/attributes file, or turn off those merge checks for untrusted repositories.

556aff785eb4.text:
An attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, an open-source inference engine, and ran code on one of NEAR AI's inference servers last Sunday.

The attacker could also have seen requests being processed on that server that day, including requests sent in confidential mode, the company said earlier this week. That mode processes requests inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) designed to keep them private even from the company itself.

But the TEE "does not protect against a vulnerability in the software running inside the environment," the company said. SGLang runs inside the TEE, which is how the attacker could reach requests there.

That access has since been closed, but not before the attacker moved further into the company's systems.

The attacker reached an internal system behind Private Chat, a product the company had already deprecated. So far, the company has confirmed that the attacker downloaded account details for about 100 users there. These are email addresses and names, and for some accounts, plan and balance information.

The company found no sign that stored Private Chat conversations or uploaded files were accessed.

The attacker also reached 18 AI agents on an older deployment of NEAR AI Agents that did not run inside the company's TEE. From those agents, the attacker took data including chat history, settings and logs.

Two customers' NEAR AI Cloud API keys were exposed in logs. The company has revoked both.

After detecting the attack, the company revoked all active sessions and administrator credentials, replaced all agent tokens and took Private Chat offline. It also deployed a fix for the SGLang flaw on all of its inference servers, rotated its remaining credentials and completed a full forensic review, according to its incident report.

Access to its NEAR AI Cloud service has been restored. The company reported the flaw to the SGLang project. It has not identified the flaw by CVE number, named the affected SGLang versions, or said whether the project has released a fix.

The company has contacted users whose account details or agents it confirmed were accessed. Affected users heard directly from security@near.ai, with the steps that apply to them. As a precaution, the company asks users to be careful with messages about their account or balance that they did not ask for.

In a follow-up post yesterday, it said users who have not heard from it do not need to do anything. It has not said whether people whose requests passed through the affected server last Sunday were among those contacted.

In an October 15 technical write-up, Brave, the browser maker, said its Leo assistant runs chats with the GLM 5.3 Flash model inside a TEE operated by NEAR AI.

NEAR AI has not said whether the affected server handled any of those chats.

21ba481629ec.text:
Three distinct threat activity clusters with shared infrastructure and malware code similarities have been observed targeting telecommunications providers, government organizations, military entities, research institutions, and critical infrastructure across Latin America, Asia, and Europe over the past year.

Check Point Research is tracking the clusters under the names SilentDelivery, OceanGate, and DarkWire. Although initially assumed to be independent sets of attacks, each with its own backdoors and post-exploitation tooling, they have all been linked through a malware ecosystem called Sparrow.

The entity behind the Sparrow framework has been codenamed CopperDragon, and is assessed to be a digital quartermaster developing tools for China-nexus threat actors, including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, Tropic Trooper, UAT-9244, and UAT-8302.

"Each cluster employed a different toolset and different initial access techniques, including compromising internet-facing infrastructure and highly selective watering hole attacks," Check Point said in a technical report published today. "The compromised websites that were used for watering hole attacks were of government, shipping, and IT and research sectors."

Attacks mounted by FamousSparrow are known for deploying backdoors like SparrowDoor (and its variants Crowdoor and TernDoor), SparroWocky, and HemiGate. It's also assessed to share some degree of overlap with Salt Typhoon. However, the precise nature of the relationship remains unclear.

The cyber espionage ecosystem linked to CopperDragon is driven by three prominent clusters -

SilentDelivery (Beginning in early 2026), which conducts highly selective watering hole attacks targeting Europe and Asia that distribute a backdoor called SquadC (aka SquawkDoor) through trojanized MSI installers masquerading as certificate repair utilities

OceanGate (2025-2026), which primarily focuses on Asian organizations with a variant of SparrowDoor after obtaining initial access via internet-facing Linux servers and then moving laterally into Windows environments

DarkWire (Mid 2025), which targets telecommunications providers and government organizations across Latin America using backdoors called CopperDoor (aka SparroWocky) and CopperDNS

SilentDelivery

The SilentDelivery chain begins with the attacker injecting heavily obfuscated JavaScript into legitimate websites frequented by their intended targets. Visitors to the sites are greeted by a Google Chrome SSL certificate warning that instructs users to install a "Certificate Fix" utility to restore access.

The so-called utility, once deployed, delivers either SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant. All the compromised websites have been found to be related to government, shipping, IT, and research sectors in the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong, and Indonesia.

According to a report published by Positive Technologies in August 2026, there are indications that the campaign has also targeted entities in Egypt and the Philippines using this method.

"The JavaScript injected into the compromised websites is heavily obfuscated using jsjiami, a publicly available JavaScript obfuscation service," Check Point said. "It first checks whether the user is running Windows and, in some cases, verifies that the website’s domain matches the intended compromised domain."

The script then repeatedly sends status-check requests to a command-and-control (C2) server to fingerprint the user based on IP and geolocation, and ultimately decide whether to continue the attack and serve the fake warning.

Source: Positive Technologies

Written in C/C++, SquadC is a Windows backdoor that enables initial foothold over the infected host. It establishes persistence by means of a Windows Registry Run key that masquerades as a Windows update assistant. Further analysis has uncovered that the malware is also distributed via phishing emails targeting Indonesian organizations.

The phishing email comes with a Windows Shortcut (LNK) disguised as a PDF document, which, when opened, abuses the legitimate "ftp.exe" binary to run a batch script that's responsible for displaying an empty file as a decoy, while launching SquadC via DLL sideloading.

OceanGate

The OceanGate operation, on the other hand, has been observed targeting both Windows and Linux environments, deploying previously undocumented tooling to maintain access, move laterally across the network, and exfiltrate sensitive data.

The Linux phase of the attack involves two new backdoors -

AnnobinDoor, a Go-based backdoor that supports a wide array of features, such as remote access, interactive shell, file management, SOCKS proxying, SSH tunneling, port forwarding, and reverse connections, and enables the infected Linux machine to function as both a remote shell and an internal network pivot

SparrowShell, a modular Linux backdoor that shares overlaps with its Windows counterpart, SparrowDoor

"After harvesting credentials from multiple users and establishing a strong foothold in the Linux environment, the actor moved into the Windows environment," Check Point explained. "The actor attempted to log in to several Windows machines over RDP, trying different passwords until it successfully authenticated with an administrator account."

This step is followed by the deployment of bespoke post-exploitation tools and a variant of SparrowDoor -

CopperAdu, a post-exploitation tool which configures a compromised Windows machine for remote administrative access

CopperList, a Windows reconnaissance tool for collecting host information, disk details, and a recursive file inventory, including file paths, sizes, and timestamps

CopperLogger, a Raw Input-based keylogger to capture keyboard input events, along with monitoring clipboard activity, active window titles, and associated process names and paths

CopperLsa, a utility that collects passwords, hashes, and authentication tokens from NTLM and Kerberos

What's more, the threat actor has been found incorporating kernel rootkits and kernel-level access capabilities into SparrowDoor and SparrowShell to evade defenses through process hiding and to capture and manipulate network packet capture using WinDivert drivers.

"The actor abused the driver to convert SparrowDoor into a passive backdoor that intercepts and manipulates packets at the kernel level, making its traffic less visible," Check Point said. "This allows the backdoor to listen internally on one port while receiving connections through an externally accessible port, such as 443, that is already used by a legitimate service."

"The backdoor applies a strict filter to intercept connections from a specific source IP address to the legitimate service's port. It manipulates the packet and rewrites the destination port to the backdoor’s internal listening port, typically a high port such as 49628. For response traffic, it rewrites the source port back to the external service port, making the responses appear to originate from the legitimate service."

Interestingly, SparrowShell shares code- and infrastructure-level similarities with a malware called Mélofée that was first described by ExaTrack in March 2023 as based on the open-source Reptile rootkit. This has raised the possibility that CopperDragon is also behind the development and supply of Mélofée.

DarkWire

The third and last cluster of activity centers around Latin America, with a particular focus on telecommunications operators and government entities. These attacks led to the deployment of two newly identified backdoors called CopperDoor and CopperDNS as a possible replacement for SparrowDoor.

Also supporting these operations is a set of custom tools -

CopperLoader, a reflective loader typically deployed through DLL sideloading and is used to deliver additional tools, including CopperDoor, CopperDNS, CopperProxy, and CopperLsass

CopperDoor, a memory-resident modular backdoor

CopperDNS, a CopperDoor variant that communicates through DNS tunneling using MX queries

CopperProxy, a SOCKS5 proxy

PyProxy, a lightweight UDP relay written in Python

CopperLsass, a dedicated module for dumping the LSASS process for credential harvesting

"The operation heavily relies on DLL sideloading as a primary execution technique, often abusing executables that are not widely observed among other threat actors in the wild," Check Point said. "To minimize their footprint, the operators deliberately avoided creating new directories on disk, instead placing their tools within existing system paths."

"CopperDoor infrastructure demonstrated a higher level of operational security. Most IP addresses were located in Latin America, often within the same country as the victim organization. This proximity likely helps the malicious traffic blend in with legitimate network activity and reduces the chances of detection."

9988a1c45724.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an attack that exploited two now-patched vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS to deliver a Python-based implant.

The activity, observed by Huntress in early October 2026, involves the exploitation of a chain comprising CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. Patches for the two vulnerabilities were released by Ahsay Backup in mid-October 2026.

The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach to deploy web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners on compromised systems.

"However, this incident reflects a much larger intrusion with more patience; the operator planted shells in several places, ran two different miners, staged tunneling tools, and installed a custom implant, all on servers whose job is to hold backups," Huntress researcher Jonathan Semon said.

Specifically, the unknown threat actor is said to have left five families of Jakarta Server Pages (JSP, formerly JavaServer Pages) web shells -

nsmind.jsp, a signed API with command execution and file transfer capabilities using exec, cd, upload, and download parameters

AhsayCBS.jsp, a loader that hides encrypted payloads in the pixel data of PNG images and runs them from memory

Keyed command shell, which compares a hard-coded key against its own copy and, if it matches, runs the command via "cmd.exe"

Keyed shell with file write, which expands on the keyed command web shell with the ability to write Base64-decoded bytes to any path the service account can reach and deploy more tools

status_<six_random_letters>.jsp or st_<six_random_letters>.jsp (e.g., st_jgaejj.jsp), which are used to run commands, recursively delete any path provided as input, and delete themselves using cmd, del, and rm parameters.

"[AhsayCBS.jsp's] disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint," Huntress explained. "The web shell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later."

The attack, besides deploying an XMRig miner masquerading as Microsoft Edge, has been found to deliver a second XMRig miner ("kvm-agent.exe") that restarts every minute through a SYSTEM scheduled task, while using a different wallet and mining pool.

The most notable aspect of the intrusion revolves around the Python backdoor ("main.py"), which is designed to run only on the host it's staged on and prevent it from executing within a sandbox or an analyst's machine.

It achieves this by computing the SHA-256 cryptographic hash of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a marker file with the same name in the same directory housing the Python implant, and then runs an embedded x64 DLL in memory that contacts a command-and-control (C2) server ("creepexplosiondarknight[.]com").

In an attempt to fly under the radar, the attack chain also configures Microsoft Defender exclusions, while serving tunneling tools (GOST and Chisel) and legitimate remote access software (AnyDesk, Atera, and Splashtop) to establish persistent access.

Evidence indicates that the threat actor may have targeted servers holding or managing backups.

"On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI," Semon said.

"Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident."

86b85c4edf61.text:
The threat actor known as Blind Eagle has resurfaced with a new campaign targeting organizations in Latin America through judicial and administrative-themed phishing lures to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT) that shares its lineage with AsyncRAT and DCRat.

"The campaign uses Portuguese and Spanish lures that resemble court notifications, fiscalía notices, tutela proceedings, and administrative documents," Zenox said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

Assessed to be a Spanish-speaking group and active since 2018, Blind Eagle (aka APT-C-36) has a track record of using spear-phishing lures to distribute commodity RATs like AsyncRAT, BitRAT, Lime RAT, NjRAT, Quasar RAT, and Remcos RAT.

Attack chains begin with phishing emails targeting individuals who handle cases, contracts, judicial, or institutional service requests to trick them into opening a malware-laced attachment.

One email containing a Colombian judicial-themed XHTML file has been identified as a weaponized Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) image that renders a bogus web page impersonating Colombia's Fiscalía General de la Nación, also referred to as the Office of the Attorney General.

The web page, for its part, employs a technique known as HTML smuggling to assemble the next-stage ZIP archive payload locally in the web browser using ZipCrypto, thereby circumventing email security controls.

Present within the ZIP archive is a JavaScript dropper that masquerades as Network Configuration Auditor version 2.7.298. The JavaScript code conducts environment reconnaissance, and collects details such as system version, network profile, installation date, memory size, computer name, environment variables, and directories localized in Portuguese and Spanish.

Upon execution, it launches a Visual Basic Script that performs Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypass, while displaying a fake criminal-citation page as a distraction mechanism.

In parallel, the malware also takes steps to delete the original XHTML artifact, clears Mark of the Web (MotW) metadata, and sets up persistence on the host under the Windows Startup folder so that it's automatically executed on system startup.

The attack culminates with the use of PowerShell to decode and launch the final RAT payload in memory. The trojan is an AsyncRAT fork with DCRat lineage based on code structure, configuration, build characteristics, and observed behavior.

"The targeting of judicial, fiscal, administrative and educational organizations gives the operation access to highly sensitive legal, financial and institutional information," Zenox said.

"Combined with the Portuguese and Spanish lures, Brazilian infrastructure, operational timezone and regional victimology, these elements establish the campaign as an APT-C-36 operation conducted through a Brazilian operational cluster."

Zenox told The Hacker News that it could not confirm whether any of these attacks had succeeded against real-world targets. However, during the campaign period between late October and early November 2026, it observed a large-scale wave of targeted phishing involving nearly 3,300 malicious emails.

While not all of these messages targeted organizations in Colombia, the country continues to remain a priority target for Blind Eagle for a combination of reasons.

"The repeated targeting of Colombia likely reflects multiple factors, with one of the main enabling factors being the structural vulnerabilities and uneven security maturity across parts of the country's critical, public, financial, and private-sector infrastructure," Zenox security researcher Gabriel Alves said.

"These conditions may increase the likelihood of successful compromises and offer greater opportunities to monetize access, steal sensitive data or funds, or reuse compromised credentials against critical systems. This is further supported by regional actors' familiarity with the Colombian context and is consistent with patterns observed among Latin American threat actors."

(The story was updated after publication to include additional insights from Zenox.)

da6f71f555a8.text:
Fireworks AI disclosed on Monday that its investigation into a security incident first reported early last month uncovered further malicious activity, affecting account and billing information, alongside secrets, datasets, and incomplete models for a "limited set of accounts."

In a notice published on October 10, 2026, the company said it detected unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials that allowed an unauthorized third-party to access environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. The activity was detected on October 6, 2026, at 9 a.m. PDT.

At that time, the AI infrastructure provider said it only found evidence that environment variables, including API keys and tokens stored as secrets, were captured in certain affected accounts, adding that there were no signs that customer models, datasets, training data, inference traffic, or personal information were accessed.

In response to the incident, Fireworks AI took the step of revoking the compromised internal credentials and rotating service account tokens, along with affected Fireworks API keys and keys created by the threat actor.

The latest bulletin from the company reveals that the scope of the breach may have been broader than previously thought. The company said attackers reached its development environment via an unnamed third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks research and development (R&D) machines on October 23, 2026.

"On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact," it added. "As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use."

The breach is said to have provided access to the following types of information -

Resource metadata: Fireworks resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, and creation time

Billing information: billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment history, account balance, and credit usage

Model weights and datasets: a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets for certain customers

Fireworks AI said payment card numbers are not stored by the company and were not impacted by the security incident. It also said it's alerting customers whose data was impacted.

The company also noted that it has implemented security hardening procedures, such as credential revocation and rotation; isolating affected systems to prevent further unauthorized activity and lateral movement; tightening access controls; and improving its logging and monitoring systems.

"The evidence indicates links to a cybercriminal threat actor group, which is financially motivated and aimed at selling tokens from unauthorized access to large language models (LLMs) to illicit routing gateways," it said.

The activity is assessed to be part of an emerging threat known as LLMjacking, which refers to the act of hijacking a victim's LLM through stolen credentials to fuel a criminal enterprise that thrives on peddling the access to other threat actors, while leaving the legitimate owner to pay the bill.

Last week, Google issued a warning that threat actors are increasingly targeting AI infrastructure for LLMjacking in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors.

Notion Impacted by Fireworks AI Incident

Popular productivity and note-taking application Notion has disclosed that the security incident targeting Fireworks AI impacted "fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces." In a post shared on Reddit, one user said: "looks like all of us are part of that <1%."

While the initial assessment was that the breach allowed the threat actor to access Notion AI synthetic testing data, it has since come to light that it may also have involved potential customer data.

"Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable," it said. "'Unattributable' means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results."

Notion has also emphasized that no other features across its platform were affected by the incident. The Insights feature has since been disabled as it continues to investigate the breach and the company is no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.

Affected customers are advised to review the impacted data securely inside their workspace. If those with affected workspaces have pasted sensitive information, passwords, API keys, or other credentials during the attack window, it's recommended to rotate them with immediate effect.

As the year approaches its final stretch, Microsoft’s November 2026 Patch Tuesday highlights the continued importance of proactive vulnerability management. This month’s security updates address vulnerabilities across the Microsoft ecosystem, reinforcing the need for organizations to promptly identify, prioritize, and remediate security risks.

This month’s release includes fixes for several vulnerabilities that could potentially enable remote code execution, privilege escalation, or denial-of-service attacks. As always, timely patch deployment is crucial to reduce exposure and ensure systems remain resilient against exploitation attempts.

In this month’s updates, Microsoft addressed 1235 vulnerabilities, including 63 critical and 1029 important-severity vulnerabilities. In the updates, Microsoft has addressed 142 vulnerabilities impacting Microsoft Edge (Chromium-based).

In this month’s updates, Microsoft has addressed only one vulnerability that has been exploited in the wild.

This Patch Tuesday, Qualys InstaScan showed customers their November findings 40 minutes before Microsoft’s own release notes page was available.

Find out more about InstaScan

This month’s release includes fixes for several vulnerabilities that could potentially enable remote code execution, privilege escalation, or denial-of-service attacks. As always, timely patch deployment is crucial to reduce exposure and ensure systems remain resilient against exploitation attempts.

The November 2026 Microsoft vulnerabilities are classified as follows:

Zero-day Vulnerability Patched in November Patch Tuesday Edition

CVE-2026-124194: Microsoft Outlook Spoofing Vulnerability

An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook. Opening the file may cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning. Successful exploitation of the vulnerability may lead to disclosure of authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user.

Presently sponsored by: Not every rogue agent is an attack. In a live webinar on Nov 17, Researcher Tyler Holmwood walks through cases of agents going off course.

This is simultaneously the most boring yet exciting blog title I've written in a long time. How you pay for services isn't exactly a sexy topic, but it solves a problem that's been a massive bugbear for a long time.

Here's a brief history of the issue: many organisations have policies that make it extremely hard to purchase goods and services with a credit card. I wrote about this more than two years ago now, where I referred to "Neville" in the procurement department who, because "reasons", demanded an invoice in advance and payment via electronic funds transfer (EFT) only. That ultimately means the world's most popular way to make online payments is out of reach for them. Unfortunately, until today, that was the only way we could take payment via Stripe, which processes all our online HIBP purchases. That left only two options for orgs in this situation:

Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢

Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢

The problem with the first option is obvious. The second option "solved" the first problem by allowing a company to pay a reseller by EFT, who then paid us by card. The reseller would then mark the price up (often significantly), slow the whole process down, log countless tickets with us (despite the existence of a dedicated portal for them), and frankly, just be a pain in the arse for everyone. It's hard to express the level of disdain I have for most resellers, and I even still have a 1,381-word draft blog post titled "That's it - Resellers are now Banned from Have I Been Pwned", which I held back from posting. Why? Because I've walked in the shoes of the folks trying to purchase our services who are just trying to get their job done, and Neville has told them they can't pay by card. That was me in a previous life, and it sucked. We kept resellers solely to support those people.

But today, HIBP's subscription page has something all new on it:

Stripe has given us early access to EFT payments in Australia. They've been available in the US for a while, but as an Aussie company and with global financial systems being what they are (i.e. not always the most flexible), we just didn't have that option. Until now. So, we've added EFT as a payment method to our Pro and High RPM plans and kept the entry-level Core ones on card only, as there's some additional overhead on our end. You'll see these every time you go to purchase an eligible subscription:

When you choose to pay by bank transfer, you're given a form for your company details (this is how we calculate any applicable taxes), then a Stripe payment link which loads something similar to the following:

The first thing is that, being an Aussie company with an Aussie bank account, we need to reflect EFT payments in AUD rather than USD. It makes sense when you think about it: we do USD for all the existing products paid for by card, and whatever the FX conversion gods decide is the corresponding Aussie amount eventually lands on our end. But that's a model where the card is charged, and access is granted immediately. For EFT, funds flow through the wires, do FX conversion for non-Aussie purchasers, land in the target account and then Stripe webhook magic enables the service. We need that exact amount to land on our end, so we can't be rolling the dice on what exchange rate we're going to get; hence, Stripe requires us to charge in the target currency. The products are exactly the same price based on the rate we currently see via Stripe purchases today (about 69 American cents per Aussie dollar), we'll just have to see if that's revised in the future with any major currency fluctuations.

Next are the banking details. Pretty straightforward, and I'm sure we've all made payments to an account like this before. The main thing is that the account number is a virtual one, which is how Stripe reconciles money that comes in from a previously raised invoice. When you sell a very limited number of products and a bunch of customers are buying the same one, this is how Stripe is then able to reconcile who has paid for what. If you really want to geek out on bank payments, Stripe has a dedicated EFT explainer page.

And finally, subscriptions in HIBP begin as soon as the invoice is raised, but access to the service only begins when payment is made. You can see the problem if we didn't do it this way: bad guy spins up the service and immediately starts using it then just never pays. But this all ties into the quote ecosystem in the existing HIBP dashboard, so it's easy to generate a quote, go flick it to Neville, get it approved, then raise and pay the invoice straight away.

As I said in the opening, it's not the most exciting topic, but it's a major thing for us and the customers who were left with only bad options if they genuinely couldn't pay by card. In the aforementioned draft blog post on binning resellers, I'd written about how we'd seen markups of up to 131% (so yes, more than double the price!), with absolutely zero value add (i.e. they don't do any product support, that remains entirely on us). But the burden resellers really put on us is the support they require to make purchases; in that same draft post, I calculated that resellers accounted for 0.86% of all sales but 43% of all support tickets. That's just nuts, especially for such a small team (although Bruce has helped enormously).

We hope this makes life easier for a bunch of people who were previously stuck between a rock and a hard place, and that includes all the "Nevilles" out there too. This is all now live and accessible via the pricing page. If you run into any issues, Bruce is standing by in the support portal.

f4569e2b41d9.text: Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security Gateway (ESG) products that, when chained, could allow the crims to run commands with root privileges. “We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations,” the security vendor said in a late Monday night update to its earlier security advisory. Barracuda declined to answer The Register’s questions, including one about how many organizations have been hit by attackers. A company spokesperson told us that it “worked directly” with the affected businesses “to quickly address the issue. Barracuda acted promptly to remediate the vulnerabilities, releasing patches for affected products.” The vendor disclosed and fixed the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, last week. CVE-2026-116606 is a 9.3 CVSS-rated, pre-authentication authorization bypass flaw in ESG. While authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have access to the administrative user interface. As Purplecop Security founder Tausif Ahmed said on Tuesday: “If your Email Security Gateway's admin UI is open to the internet, that's the first thing I'd close today.” CVE-2026-111560 is an 8.6-rated command-injection flaw that affects multiple Barracuda products: its ESG, load balancer (ADC), message archiver (BMA), web application firewall (WAF), WAF control center (WCC), and web security gateway (WSG). “If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda warned on November 2. At the time, the vendor did not report any active exploitation of either. We don’t yet know who is responsible for the attacks, or whether the intruders gained root access – but if they did, they could steal data, install backdoors, and take full control of affected systems. These types of edge-device exploits have been used by Chinese-government spies, and in 2023 the FBI blamed PRC-linked attackers for a series of attacks that targeted Barracuda ESGs to deploy custom malware and maintain access to high-value networks. According to Mandiant, 27 percent of identified affected organizations were government entities. So if you haven’t already: patch now. ®

72bf74296799.text:
The tried-and-true recipe for protecting a corporate network has become far less effective than it once was. Guarding the perimeter with a firewall and granting remote access through a VPN gateway has become both cumbersome and risky: day to day, it’s hard to configure how users and cloud services interact, and during cyberattacks the VPN gateway is now a prime target. According to data from insurer At-Bay, nearly three-quarters of the successful ransomware attacks in its 2025 analysis began with a compromised VPN.

To jointly improve network security and operational efficiency, companies need to rethink the remote access model itself. The end goal is a secure connection between an employee and work resources. That by no means implies that an employee (or someone posing as one) should get full access to the corporate network.

What recent VPN attacks show

VPN technology itself isn’t fatally outdated — as long as you treat it as a way to encrypt and tunnel traffic. The problem is how VPN is most commonly deployed: a user authenticates at the entry point, lands on the company network, and from there restrictions (if there are any) depend on segmentation, firewalls, and the protection of individual systems. Inside the network, behind the VPN gateway, a user can reach a wide range of internal services with minimal restrictions. Often, the VPN gateway itself is a privileged device, and successfully compromising it gives attackers many ways to take over the network.

For example, in the October attacks on Ivanti Connect Secure gateways, the APT group UTA0576 chained three zero-day vulnerabilities to compromise a fully patched device. After gaining root privileges, they used the VPN’s own legitimate service account to query the domain controller and collect passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

Before that, vulnerabilities in Check Point and SonicWall gateways were similarly exploited, with the SonicWall attacks carried out by the Akira ransomware operators.

Remote work, VPNs, and stolen data

Today, depending on the country, between 12% and 30% of employees work from home either full or part-time. This shift has significantly increased the number of IT systems that need to be reachable from outside the organizations’ networks — often from personal devices. Personal devices are far more likely than corporate ones to get infected with infostealers. As a result, the black market is flooded with corporate credentials stolen from such computers: it represents 30% of everything initial access brokers (IABs) sell.

Even over a VPN, a strictly segmented network can grant only very limited access. But in practice, exceptions pile up over years of operation: a contractor needs access to a whole subnet, an admin gets “everything, temporarily”, an old application needs a few more ports. These exceptions piled up especially fast during the covid pandemic. As a result, a stolen account often opens the door not to a single service but to the entire infrastructure.

VPN administration overhead

For VPN access to work properly and securely, configuring the VPN gateway alone is usually not enough: you have to set up MFA, device posture checks, network segmentation, and log collection separately. Then you have to make all of it work together. A new employee or application may require changes in several systems at once. Each system works correctly on its own, but the rules drift apart, and figuring out why a certain user has no access turns into a tour of five consoles.

What switching to Zero Trust Network Access changes

First and foremost, Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) changes the access model itself and its basic unit of access. Instead of “this user has access rights to this subnet”, a ZTNA system makes decisions like “this user, on this device, in this location, who has passed these levels of verification, can access this specific application”.

Such a decision takes into account a combination of factors (identity, device, and so on) that the policy specifies. The right to work with a ticketing system or a customer database shouldn’t automatically let someone connect to a file server or a domain controller.

Depending on the policies, a ZTNA system can grant access to the needed resource behind the scenes through a combination of methods: a dedicated VPN tunnel to a specific internal server, a reverse connection from a corporate application in a private cloud, and others. A legitimate user doesn’t need to know any of this, but an attacker’s ability to move around the network and attack new services will be severely limited.

Keep in mind that ZTNA is a specific tool — just one part of a broader zero trust architecture. Buying a single product doesn’t mean a company has implemented zero trust.

Benefits of switching from a traditional VPN to ZTNA

A well-implemented ZTNA system primarily reduces the potential damage (the blast radius) if part of the infrastructure or someone’s credentials get compromised; at the same time, deploying it also noticeably decreases an attacker’s room to maneuver.

Reducing the risk of gateway attacks

A VPN gateway usually accepts any connection from the internet. Before verifying the user, the gateway closely analyzes incoming connections, cryptographic messages, and requests to its management and authentication portals. A gateway vulnerability lets an attacker run detailed reconnaissance against the system at this stage and bypass authentication altogether.

Some ZTNA architectures reduce this exposure. An internal connector establishes an outbound connection to a cloud broker on its own. The user connects to the broker separately, and access to the application opens after the necessary checks. In such a system, there’s no need to expose your own gateway for remote access at all.

In a ZTNA architecture with a self-hosted broker, you can’t shift the risk to the ZTNA provider. But a number of ZTNA solutions significantly reduce the attack surface of a self-hosted broker too, for example by using Single Packet Authorization. The broker doesn’t process any requests until it receives a correctly formed encrypted packet, which the client uses to prove its authenticity up front.

Limiting the consequences of compromised credentials and workstations

ZTNA can tie access not only to a password but also to the state of the device: whether the organization manages it, whether its certificate is valid, whether the OS is up to date, whether the security software’s databases are up to date, and whether there are any signs of compromise. What’s more, ZTNA can authenticate the same user differently for different tasks. Does the user just want to read the news on the internal portal, and is the computer they log in from already known about? A password is enough. Is the user logging in to a software repository to change application source code, or opening the budget planning system? Then they’ll have to pass phishing-resistant authentication, for example with a hardware key (such as a YubiKey). If the connection type or other parameters change, the user will even have to re-authenticate.

It’s easy to see how a hypothetical infostealer attack gets more complicated in this scenario. It’s not enough to simply steal a password or a browser session. Trying to use them on a new device will cut the connection.

Here, ZTNA functions partly overlap with what EDR and MDM/EMM agents do on the device. That’s why several vendors bundle these capabilities into a single agent. At the same time, ZTNA limits the consequences of an attack but doesn’t replace endpoint protection. If an attacker uses a remote access Trojan (RAT) rather than an infostealer and directly controls an employee’s device, the ZTNA agent may not be able to tell the attacker’s actions from the employee’s.

Improving observability and detecting anomalies faster

When an employee works from home over a VPN, the firewalls, web filters, and SIEM/XDR often see only shallow network telemetry. That’s why, for example, the actions of the Qilin ransomware operators — who exploited an authentication vulnerability in Palo Alto GlobalProtect (CVE-2026-0257) — were hard to tell apart from legitimate employee activity.

ZTNA lets you tie access events to specific identities: users, devices, and applications. Depending on the implementation, SOC teams may get connection logs and, for supported protocols, logs of individual requests to specific applications.

With this level of log detail and the right SIEM rules in place, anomalies quickly catch SOC analysts’ attention.

Simplifying access administration

“Guest” and “temporary” VPN access is a perennial headache for IT and infosec teams. Contractor accounts are created as temporary but stay active for years. In 2026, attackers breached a large European financial institution through this kind of poorly controlled access. ZTNA makes just-in-time (JIT) access possible. A contractor’s support engineer gets access only to the web interface of the one server they need, and that access shuts off automatically after a set time (say, two hours or two days).

Reducing regulatory and insurance risks

Both regulators and the cyber-insurance market are pushing for stricter access management. In April 2026, CISA explicitly named standing contractor VPN access as one of the critical threats to industrial networks. Insurers are also reacting to this trend: organizations with outdated VPN configurations are increasingly hit with rising insurance premiums.

A quick plan for migrating from VPN to ZTNA

Overall, the migration plan looks like this:

Take inventory of your remote access: VPNs, RDP servers, vendor gateways, service accounts, and configured firewall exceptions.

Design and fully document an access structure built around applications and roles instead of the familiar subnets.

Review and, if needed, improve your granular system for identifying users, devices, and applications (identity management), since effective ZTNA depends on it. Enable phishing-resistant MFA, and set up policies for access recovery, posture checks, and session revocation.

Outline an isolated pilot scenario that’s relatively easy to implement but not trivial. For example, start with contractor access to a few applications.

Gradually extend ZTNA to new groups of employees and services.

After each migration stage, disable or significantly restrict the access methods that are no longer needed. For the VPNs that remain, apply strict segmentation and monitoring.

Some legacy applications, industrial systems, and site-to-site connections will still need VPN for a long time to come. The goal isn’t to remove those three letters from your infrastructure at any cost, but to make sure VPN gateways stop being an easy target and an effective launchpad for attacks on your network.

Microsoft’s November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates fix 1,094 vulnerabilities across its products, including an Outlook bug that the company says has been exploited.

The zero-day, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, has been classified as a spoofing flaw and stems from Outlook not alerting users before a potentially dangerous action takes place.

Microsoft has assigned it a severity rating of ‘moderate’ and a CVSS score of 6.5. The company’s advisory provides no information about the observed attacks.

For an attack to work, the victim needs to be tricked into opening a malicious file, according to Microsoft.

“An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook. Opening the file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user,” the tech giant said.

The flaw cannot be triggered through the Preview Pane, Microsoft said. It also clarified, “This vulnerability discloses a user’s NTLMv2 hash to the attacker who could use this to authenticate as the user.”

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The vulnerability was not publicly disclosed before the fix became available. Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Office LTSC 2021, and Office LTSC 2024.

Microsoft’s advisory credits a researcher using the moniker ‘nono’ and Benoît Sevens with the discovery. The acknowledgment for Sevens mentions the use of Anthropic’s Claude AI model.

Windows accounts for 726 of the flaws patched this month, followed by Office with 174. Microsoft also resolved 59 vulnerabilities in SQL Server, 53 in developer tools, 27 in SharePoint Server, 20 in Azure, and nine in Exchange Server.

In addition, the company republished 165 CVEs from third parties, noting that Chrome vulnerabilities are not listed.

Microsoft’s release summary lists critical-severity updates for Windows 10, Windows 11, Windows Server 2016 through 2025, Office, Exchange Server Subscription Edition, Edge, and the Malware Protection Engine. Azure OpenAI and Azure Managed Grafana are also on the list.

The November release is smaller than October’s, when Microsoft patched a record 1,413 vulnerabilities. With the latest round of patches, Microsoft has fixed more than 5,000 vulnerabilities this year.

This month’s updates are also the final ones for the Enterprise and Education editions of Windows 11 version 23H2. Devices running these editions will not receive any further monthly security updates.

Adobe’s latest Patch Tuesday updates fix roughly 110 vulnerabilities across nine products.

Related: Microsoft Patches Two Dozen RCE Flaws in Office

Related: Microsoft Patches Record 974 Vulnerabilities, Including Two Exploited Zero-Days

Adobe’s November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates fix roughly 110 vulnerabilities across nine products.

New patches are available for Adobe Experience Manager (AEM), Audition, After Effects, Connect, Content Credentials SDK, Dimension, Media Encoder, Photoshop, and Premiere.

Critical-severity issues have been patched in Adobe Connect and AEM, including six Connect flaws with a CVSS score of 10.

The critical flaws include SSRF, path traversal, incorrect authorization, CRLF injection, XXE, code injection, SQL injection, and XSS issues. They can be exploited for privilege escalation and arbitrary code execution.

A total of 38 vulnerabilities have been resolved in AEM and Connect, including high- and medium-severity issues whose exploitation can lead to privilege escalation, file system read, memory exposure, arbitrary code execution, and bypassing security features.

High-severity bugs have been fixed in After Effects, Media Encoder, Premiere, Dimension, Audition, and Photoshop.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The Content Credentials Rust SDK (and the C2PA Tool) received patches for roughly a dozen low- and medium-severity issues.

Adobe says it’s not aware of attacks exploiting the newly patched vulnerabilities.

The Connect and AEM patches have a priority rating of 2; the rest are rated 3, which means they are unlikely to be exploited in the wild.

AWS re:Invent returns to Las Vegas for cloud and AI’s biggest week from November 30–December 4, 2026. This year we have over 2,200 sessions, 70 percent of which are interactive, led by experts from Amazon Web Services (AWS), our customers, and our partners.

With that much to choose from, we’ve pulled together the sessions built around Digital Sovereignty at AWS. Whether you’re navigating evolving data residency requirements, choosing the right home for your most sensitive workloads, or scaling AI in environments where your data can’t leave the jurisdiction, there’s something for you at re:Invent.

In this guide, you’ll find breakout sessions, chalk talks, workshops, and a lightning talk covering a range of digital sovereignty topics, grouped by theme so you can easily find what matters most to you. Reserve your seat through your attendee portal, or walk up based on availability. If a session is full, check the catalog for another time, since several of these sessions run more than once.

Pro tip: Sessions are spread across several venues, so allow extra time to get between them. All times are Pacific.

Theme 1: Control, choice and operational autonomy with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud

In 2026, we launched the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, giving customers another option to help meet their most stringent digital sovereignty requirements. As part of its design, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud operates with no critical dependencies on non-EU infrastructure, and is backed by strong technical controls, sovereign assurances, and legal protections. In these sessions, get the full picture of the AWS approach to digital sovereignty, including verifiable controls, operational autonomy, and greater choice with infrastructure options like the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

SEC206 | Breakout session | Digital sovereignty: Verifiable controls and greater choice Speakers: Mustafa Isik, Chief Technologist Sovereignty, AWS; Stephane Israel, Managing Director European Sovereign Cloud and Digital Sovereignty, AWS When and where: Thursday, December 3, 1:00 PM | Wynn/Encore Evolving regulations and geopolitical shifts are prompting organizations to rethink how they protect data and maintain control in the cloud, without slowing innovation and AI adoption. This session explores how AWS helps customers meet their digital sovereignty requirements with the full power of the cloud through a range of offerings, including the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, backed by verifiable and auditable controls. Learn what AI sovereignty means in practice, get answers to the most common questions, and hear how AWS and partners are helping organizations navigate complexity in a fast-changing landscape.

SEC234 | Lightning talk | EU operational autonomy in action: AWS European Sovereign Cloud Speakers: Zoltan Albrecht, Director, AWS European Sovereign Cloud Managed Operations, AWS When and where: Thursday, December 3, 8:30 AM | Wynn/Encore The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is built on fully isolated infrastructure within the EU, operated exclusively by EU-resident staff, with no access from outside Europe. In this lightning talk, learn from the AWS European Sovereign Cloud Managed Operations team what independent operations means in practice and how it works day to day.

Theme 2: AI under digital sovereignty and data residency requirements

Moving AI from pilots to production means making clear decisions about where your data and AI workloads run to meet your digital sovereignty needs. These sessions show how to bring AI infrastructure to your data, from fully managed AWS AI Factories in your data center, to the right hybrid deployment for each workload, to agentic AI applications that extend to hybrid and edge environments such as AWS Outposts and AWS Local Zones.

AIM206 | Breakout session | AWS AI Factories: Bring production scale AI to your data center Speakers: Pranav Chachra, Senior Manager, Product Management, AWS; Gareth Tucker, Global Specialist – AWS AI Factories, AWS; Daniel Xu, Member of Technical Staff, Anthropic When and where: Thursday, December 3, 10:30 AM | Venetian Data sovereignty, data gravity, and latency requirements prevent many organizations from running all AI workloads in the public cloud. AWS AI Factories bring AWS and NVIDIA AI infrastructure directly into your data center, fully operated, maintained, and continuously updated by AWS. Run leading foundation models on premises for training and inference without building and managing AI infrastructure yourself or negotiating separate agreements with model providers. In this session, learn how organizations are accelerating AI adoption, reducing time to value, and maintaining full control of their data while benefiting from the AWS experience in their own facilities.

HMC303 | Breakout session | Choosing the right hybrid deployment for your AI workloads Speakers: Shivam Saggar, Sr. Product Manager (Tech), AWS; Chris McEvilly, Senior Solutions Architect, AWS; Shelby Seward, DMTS, Sr. Director, T-Mobile; Hai Lu, Senior Engineering Manager, Databricks, Inc. When and where: Monday, November 30, 9:00 AM | MGM Grand Organizations are running AI workloads for model training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and inference, across an expanding set of environments, including AWS Regions, AWS Local Zones, AWS Outposts, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, and AWS AI Factories. The right deployment option depends on latency, data sovereignty, compute density, and scale. See how customers deploy accelerated AI across the hybrid spectrum: NVIDIA GPU-based and AWS Trainium-powered instances in Local Zones, purpose-built AWS AI Factories for large-scale training and model serving, and edge deployments for real-time inference. Hear how customers navigate these decisions, including Databricks tapping GPU capacity on AWS Local Zones and T-Mobile running latency-sensitive distributed inference, and learn which environment fits each AI workload without compromising performance and compliance.

HMC402 | Workshop | Implementing agentic AI solutions on-premises and at the edge Speakers: Kyle Palasti, Edge Specialist Solutions Architect, National Security, AWS; Fernando Galves, Senior Applied AI Architect, AWS When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 3:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Repeat: Thursday, December 3, 3:00 PM | Caesars Palace Learn how to extend Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to hybrid and edge services to build distributed agentic apps using Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent-to-agent (A2A) communication with on-premises data. Get hands-on with hybrid agentic AI using Amazon Bedrock and Strands Agents while exploring AWS hybrid and edge solutions for data residency compliance.

HMC403 | Workshop | Self-managed agentic AI at the hybrid edge Speakers: Fernando Galves, Senior Applied AI Architect, AWS; Chris McEvilly, Senior Solutions Architect, AWS When and where: Tuesday, December 1, 12:30 PM | MGM Grand Repeat: Thursday, December 3, 8:30 AM | MGM Grand As organizations use agentic AI to automate complex infrastructure operations, many have data residency, low latency, and security requirements that depend on running AI closer to their data. This workshop explores how customers deploy self-managed agentic AI at the hybrid edge to meet these requirements while enabling autonomous operations. Learn how to architect, provision, configure, and optimize AI agents that run locally, and how to extend the same architecture to AWS hybrid and edge infrastructure such as AWS Local Zones and AWS Outposts.

Theme 3: More control, more choice: Finding the right infrastructure for your digital sovereignty needs

Digital sovereignty requirements vary, and AWS offers control and choice across a range of deployment options. Whether you’re comparing AWS Dedicated Local Zones, AWS Outposts, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, and AWS Regions, or planning a migration, you’ll find the infrastructure options to meet your unique digital sovereignty needs. These sessions help you learn more and choose with confidence.

HMC314 | Chalk talk | Architecting for digital sovereignty with AWS Hybrid Cloud solutions Speakers: Sherry Lin, Principal Product Manager, AWS; Lakshmi VP, Solutions Architect – WWPS, AWS When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 8:30 AM | MGM Grand This session uses real-world case studies to understand how AWS hybrid cloud architectures such as AWS Local Zones, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, and AWS Outposts help customers meet their digital sovereignty needs. It examines data residency boundaries, network separation, operational controls, and security guardrail options available in hybrid cloud solutions. It then shows how to configure governance controls, including Service Control Policies (SCPs), to help customers comply with regulatory requirements. Finally, it covers how to detect and prevent unauthorized data flows between hybrid infrastructure and the parent Region.

HMC202 | Breakout session | AWS wherever you need it: From the cloud to the edge Speakers: Spencer Dillard, Director, Software Dev, EC2, AWS; Ian Cottingham, Director, Software Development, AWS; Rama Raghavan, AVP Cloud Architecture, AT&T Inc. When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 3:00 PM | Caesars Palace While most workloads can run in the cloud, some remain on-premises or at the edge due to low latency, local data processing, or data residency needs. AWS Local Zones, AWS Outposts, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, and AWS AI Factories extend AWS services, APIs, and tools to metro areas, on-premises data centers, and the far edge. Explore how these infrastructure offerings power a broad range of hybrid cloud and edge computing use cases such as financial trading, manufacturing, and AI. Learn how AWS helps you run regulated workloads with edge requirements, power generative AI with edge data, and migrate workloads with on-premises dependencies, featuring AT&T’s migration and modernization at scale.

HMC304 | Breakout session | Real-world migrations: Lessons learned migrating to AWS Outposts Speakers: Frankie Negro, Senior Hybrid Edge Solutions Architect, AWS; Scott Rose, Senior Manager Solution Architecture – Telco, AWS; Marcelo Andrade, Cloud Engineer, SERPRO When and where: Monday, November 30, 10:00 AM | MGM Grand Organizations with data residency and digital sovereignty requirements face a critical question: how do you move workloads from on-premises infrastructure to AWS Outposts without disrupting compliance posture or operations? This Level 300 session distills lessons from migrating customers to Outposts across industries, organization sizes, and migration strategies, featuring SERPRO, Brazil’s federal data processing company, and AT&T, migrating telecom workloads at scale. The session walks through the processes that delivered results, the quantifiable outcomes measured, and the critical mistakes to avoid. Learn how to select the right migration approach and navigate common blockers. The session also covers transitioning from first-generation to second-generation Outposts hardware.

Theme 4: Disaster recovery, resilience, and cross-partition connectivity

Digital sovereignty goes beyond where your data lives. It also shapes how you operate, recover, and connect your workloads. These sessions help you learn about the operational side of digital sovereignty: recovering from failures under regulatory requirements, designing for resilience alongside data residency, and strategies for connecting across global AWS Regions, GovCloud, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, and China Regions.

ARC405 | Breakout session | Your regulator set your RTO. Not your architecture. Speakers: Hossam Ebrahim, Solutions Architect, AWS; Paul Armstrong, Lead Architect UKI, AWS When and where: Tuesday, December 1, 4:00 PM | Wynn/Encore Organizations with pre-approved failover regions recover in hours. Those without recover in weeks. Same impairment. Same services. One governance decision separates them, and it’s made years before the event. This session presents architectural patterns for multi-Region recovery under sovereignty constraints, drawn from real operational experience with regulated workloads under regional pressure. Three categories: decisions that set your resilience ceiling before any event, dependencies that create circular failure during recovery, and assets nobody backs up until they become the critical path. You leave with the decisions to evaluate before your next DR test.

ARC318 | Chalk talk | Architecting for resilience and data residency Speakers: Andy Orlosky, AWS Solutions Architect, AWS; Mike Haken, Senior Principal Solutions Architect, AWS; Jamie Pasterick, Senior Solutions Architect, AWS When and where: Monday, November 30, 2:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Repeat: Wednesday, December 2, 1:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Your data can’t leave the jurisdiction, but your workload still has to survive a Region degradation. This chalk talk explores architecture patterns that address both resilience and data residency together. We break the challenge into practical layers: where data lives, how workloads recover, what isolation looks like, and how to maintain business continuity across geographic boundaries. We map each layer to AWS capabilities including Dedicated Local Zones, Outposts, and policy controls, then work through real scenarios together. Bring your architecture challenges and we will whiteboard design patterns and tradeoffs with you.

NET327 | Breakout session | Connectivity strategies across AWS Partitions Speakers: Kunal Sharma, Sr. Solutions Architect, AWS; Rohit Aswani, Principal Solutions Architect – Networking Specialist, AWS When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 4:00 PM | MGM Grand Organizations increasingly operate across AWS commercial, GovCloud, Sovereign Cloud, and China Regions to satisfy regulatory, data residency, and national security requirements. But connecting them introduces networking challenges that go well beyond standard multi-Region design. In this session, learn cross-partition connectivity patterns using AWS Site-to-Site VPN, AWS Direct Connect, and application-layer proxies alongside DNS resolution strategies, compliance boundary enforcement, and operational trade-offs. We walk through architectural blueprints for securely linking partitions while preserving the isolation guarantees they exist to enforce, and share lessons learned from customers navigating ITAR, GDPR, and national sovereignty mandates at scale.

Theme 5: Digital sovereignty across industries

Priorities for digital sovereignty vary by industry, and are shaped by different regulations, risks, and requirements. Learn how organizations in government, energy, and telecommunications are meeting their unique needs with the control, choice, and scale of AWS.

IND361 | Workshop | Build hybrid data planes for government GenAI pipelines Speakers: Mohamed Salah, Sr. Solutions Architect, AWS; Usama Salama, Sr. Specialist SA AI/ML, AWS When and where: Monday, November 30, 3:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Strict national security mandates block government agencies from adopting cloud GenAI. To resolve this, architects deploy a decoupled edge-to-cloud tokenization pattern. In this workshop, use AWS CDK to build a three-phase data plane that isolates sensitive citizen data in a simulated edge environment. You will deploy local data tokenization, route masked payloads to Amazon Bedrock for stateless inference, and reconcile state on-premises. Leave with an infrastructure-as-code blueprint to unlock frontier AI and satisfy federal localization mandates.

IND359 | Chalk talk | In-Country HPC: How TGS Processes Seismic Data on AWS Brazil Speakers: Kun Jiao, Principal Solutions Architect, AWS; Faisal Asif, Global Head, Cloud Transformation and Innovation, TGS When and where: Monday, November 30, 9:00 AM | Wynn/Encore Repeat: Tuesday, December 1, 12:00 PM | Wynn/Encore TGS — one of the world’s largest multi-client geoscience data providers — faced a significant cost challenge running its business-critical Rackmon EFWI GPU workload at scale. By strategically deploying this workload on AWS infrastructure in Brazil, TGS leveraged Brazil’s ReData Special Tax Regime to dramatically reduce the tax burden on GPU-intensive seismic processing. The result: material cost savings on one of the most computationally demanding workloads in the energy industry — and a reusable in-country processing architecture that can serve future customers with data residency requirements in other geographies.

IND322 | Chalk talk | Physical AI in Telecom: A Framework for Workload Placement Speakers: Young Jung, Sr. Manager of Telco Network SA, AWS; Angelo Sampietro, Principal Solutions Architect, AWS; Umer Chaudhary, Sr. Mgr Network Solutions, AWS When and where: Tuesday, December 1, 1:30 PM | Caesars Forum Repeat: Tuesday, December 1, 3:00 PM | Caesars Forum Some physical AI workloads need sub-millisecond performance at edge cell sites, others are better suited to a full AWS Region, and many fall in between on AWS Local Zones or AWS Outposts. In this chalk talk, we provide a framework for matching each workload to the right option. We trace the physical AI development lifecycle, examining how data sovereignty, latency, data gravity, and token economics interact to shape placement decisions at each phase. Based on real-world use cases, we discuss the options so you leave with a placement framework you can apply immediately.

You can view the full list of digital sovereignty sessions in the re:Invent catalog, including sessions with partners.

Activities in the Expo

Join us in the re:Invent Expo at the Venetian to meet with AWS experts and learn through interactive demos. Stop by these kiosks in the AWS Village:

Mozilla has removed the data limit on the free VPN built into Firefox. Firefox users in supported regions get unlimited browsing on desktop and Android once they sign in with a Mozilla account.

The VPN shipped with Firefox 149 in March with a 50GB monthly cap. That is plenty for reading and ordinary browsing, but someone streaming video through the browser can use it up fast. The VPN protects traffic inside Firefox and nothing else on the device. Mail clients, chat apps and anything else running next to the browser still use the normal connection. Mozilla says iOS support is coming but hasn’t given a date.

Turning it on takes a Mozilla account. On desktop the VPN sits in the toolbar, and on Android it’s under Settings > VPN. At launch it covered the U.S., U.K., Germany and France. To protect apps outside the browser, Mozilla sells Mozilla VPN as a separate paid subscription.
