Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Vulnerabilities in Git

CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.

An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks. When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone.

The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114466: Filesystem access through fast-import streams

git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

[Advisory]

Additional hardening

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Protecting GitHub users

We have deployed fixes for these vulnerabilities across github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.

Updates for GitHub Enterprise Server are available in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4. We recommend that administrators upgrade as soon as possible.

We are coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app that include patched versions of Git.

GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also receive patched versions of Git.

Update Git

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Get an updated version of Git >

The post Git security vulnerabilities announced appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

25d8a5bce6ed.text: President Donald Trump has nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, putting an executive from the controversial government supplier in line to run America's civilian cyber defense agency. The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025. LoSapio has served as Palantir's CISO since September 2024, having previously led the company's infrastructure and network security team. He first joined the data analytics outfit in 2013, later spent a spell at database company SingleStore, and returned to Palantir in 2017. If confirmed, LoSapio would move from securing Palantir's systems to leading the federal government's main civilian cyber defense agency. CISA protects federal civilian networks and works with critical infrastructure operators, including power, water, and telecommunications providers. It's a substantial job, particularly given the state of the agency he would inherit. CISA has shed more than 1,000 staff, roughly a third of its workforce, since Trump returned to the White House, according to reports. It's now trying to plug the gaps, although acting director Nick Andersen said in September that around 250 would-be recruits were still waiting for security clearance before they could get to work. Andersen has been running CISA since February. With fewer people to go around, CISA is also rethinking where to spend its time. A strategy published last month emphasizes infrastructure whose failure would do the most damage, raising questions about what gets less attention as the agency operates with fewer staff. LoSapio would be the second person Trump has put forward for the role. His previous pick, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April after spending more than a year awaiting confirmation, with his nomination becoming caught up in a dispute involving Republican Senator Rick Scott over Coast Guard contracting. The nomination arrives late in the congressional calendar. If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic-controlled Senate. Palantir, co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has become a major supplier of technology to US government agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Its work with immigration authorities has attracted criticism from civil liberties groups and Democratic lawmakers concerned about surveillance and the handling of sensitive personal information. The controversy isn't confined to the US either. In the UK, WhatsApp messages obtained by campaign group Foxglove this week indicate that Palantir privately lobbied a health minister to consider extending its software into GP patient records, despite that data being expressly excluded from its £330 million NHS England contract for the Federated Data Platform. That revelation follows news that NHS England wants greater oversight of Palantir's claims about the benefits of its software, amid questions over the evidence supporting its performance figures. Those controversies could make LoSapio's confirmation hearings particularly interesting, especially as Democrats prepare to scrutinize Palantir's government business more closely. It's unclear whether LoSapio plans to leave Palantir or what would happen to any financial interests he holds in the company if confirmed. Those are questions likely to come up during a confirmation process that CISA, having spent nearly two years without a permanent boss while losing a third of its workforce, could probably do without dragging on any longer. ®

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has rolled out a revamped cyber incident reporting form that asks more granular questions about incident types and frames observed activity in MITRE ATT&CK terms.

CISA outlined the changes in an announcement published November 9 and the updated web-based questionnaire is available through its Incident Reporting Portal.

The agency said better data quality will help it connect related threat activity into broader trends that would otherwise look like separate incidents. The update draws on community feedback CISA has received over the years.

More Granular Questions Add ATT&CK Terms

The revised form asks whether an incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Questions about observed activity now use MITRE ATT&CK, a framework for describing adversary behavior that CISA said is familiar to the cyber community.

The changes are meant to support rapid but thorough threat analysis, according to CISA.

"In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization's detection is another's protection," said Chris Butera, CISA's acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity. "As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation's collective defense."

For now, only federal civilian agencies are required to report incidents to CISA. The agency encouraged other organizations that experience an incident to report voluntarily, and information they submit can be protected from disclosure under the Protected Critical Infrastructure Information (PCII) Program.

CIRCIA Rule Remains at White House

The update comes as the final rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) awaits approval. The rule went to the White House for review on October 1 and remains listed as pending.

Read more on CIRCIA: US Critical Infrastructure Braces for Sweeping New Cyber Reporting Rules

Once the rule takes effect, covered critical infrastructure organizations would have to report qualifying cyber incidents within 72 hours of reasonably believing they occurred and ransom payments within 24 hours of making them, according to CISA.

CISA published its proposed CIRCIA rule in April 2024 but missed an October 2025 statutory deadline to finalize it. Many comments on the proposal asked for a narrower scope, less burden and closer alignment with other federal reporting rules, according to CISA's regulatory agenda.

CISA's announcement did not mention CIRCIA or whether the enhanced reporting form would be used under the pending rule.

Modern software is built on layers of dependencies, open source components, third party libraries and increasingly, artificial intelligence models and external data sources. For security teams, understanding exactly what is running inside an application has become less of a compliance exercise and more of an operational necessity.

That is the foundation behind the Software Bill of Materials, or SBOM.

In a recent episode of the SecurityWeek Podcast, host Brian “SchleiF” Schleifer sat down with cybersecurity policy expert Allan Friedman for a wide-ranging discussion about the origins of SBOM, how organizations should actually use the data, the emergence of AI BOMs, vulnerability management, VEX, and where software transparency may be heading next.

Friedman, who helped drive early government and industry work around SBOM, offered perhaps the simplest explanation for why the concept matters.

“Software isn’t written, it’s assembled,” Friedman said. “What’s it assembled out of? More software.”

In practical terms, an SBOM provides a structured representation of the components and dependencies that allow software to function. But Friedman emphasized throughout the conversation that producing an SBOM is not the end goal. The real value comes from what organizations, and their suppliers can do with the information.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

SBOM Is About Response, Not Just Inventory

Much of the early SBOM conversation focused on whether vendors could generate the documents and whether customers should require them.

The more important question today may be: What happens after you receive one?

Friedman argues that one of the first indicators of software supply chain maturity is simply knowing that a supplier can generate an accurate SBOM.

That capability becomes critical when organizations face the next Log4j style vulnerability, compromise of a major software package, malicious update, or other widespread supply chain event.

A supplier that understands the components within its products can determine its exposure far more quickly than one forced to reconstruct dependencies during an incident. For customers, the same visibility can dramatically shorten response time.

Instead of spending days or weeks contacting vendors and attempting to determine which systems contain a vulnerable component, security teams can analyze their software inventory and dependencies directly.

The objective, however, should ultimately be deeper integration.

Friedman said SBOM information needs to become another source of enterprise security data, feeding vulnerability management, asset management, procurement and continuous risk management processes rather than existing as a static document stored somewhere for future reference.

That distinction matters because attackers are not limited to vulnerabilities associated with the name of the software vendor.

A smaller vendor’s application may contain an outdated framework, library or open source component with a known weakness. Without component level visibility, an organization may never associate that vulnerability with the commercial product deployed in its environment.

Not Every Vulnerability Creates the Same Risk

More visibility can also create another problem: more alerts.

Finding that a vulnerable component exists inside an application does not necessarily mean the vulnerability is exploitable within that specific implementation.

Friedman highlighted the Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange, or VEX, as an important companion to SBOM. VEX provides a machine processable method for communicating whether a vulnerability actually affects a product.

An application, for example, may contain a vulnerable version of a software library but never use the functionality associated with the vulnerability. VEX can provide the context needed to distinguish between the presence of a vulnerable component and an exploitable condition.

That becomes increasingly important as organizations face what Friedman jokingly described as the “vulnerpocalypse”: an environment in which security teams have far more vulnerability information than they have resources to investigate manually.

The combination of SBOM and VEX creates the possibility of better prioritization rather than simply more data.

AI Makes the Transparency Problem More Complicated

The next evolution is already underway.

As organizations embed machine learning, generative AI and autonomous agents into applications, traditional software inventories may no longer capture everything security teams need to understand.

Friedman described the emergence of the AI BOM as inevitable.

At its core, AI is still software, meaning traditional software components remain relevant. But AI systems introduce additional elements that may need to be documented, including the model itself, the data supporting the model, external data sources and the surrounding infrastructure or “harnesses” used to operate the system.

That creates new questions.

Where did the model originate?

What data was used to support it?

What external data is being introduced at runtime?

Who owns the model?

What happens when an agent dynamically creates a tool, executes an action and then disappears?

The last question becomes particularly challenging as AI systems become more dynamic and agentic.

Friedman suggested that the answer may increasingly involve a convergence between traditional BOM concepts, logging, information architecture and third party risk management.

The goal is not necessarily to force every piece of information into an AI BOM. Instead, organizations need enough transparency and supporting evidence to reconstruct what happened, understand dependencies, enforce controls and conduct forensic analysis when necessary.

Transparency Should Favor the Defender

Resistance to SBOM adoption has often centered on concerns about intellectual property and the possibility that providing detailed information about software components could benefit attackers.

Friedman challenged that argument.

Modern reverse engineering capabilities already allow determined attackers to analyze software and identify many of its underlying components. Automated attack frameworks and ransomware operations also frequently do not require an SBOM because they simply test systems against known exploits.

Defenders face a different problem. They need to know where vulnerable components exist across potentially thousands of systems.

“You know who does need visibility into what’s in a piece of software? Blue Team,” Friedman said.

SBOM standards can also support redaction where legitimate proprietary concerns exist, allowing suppliers to disclose the existence of a dependency without necessarily revealing every detail associated with it.

The larger issue, Friedman argued, is determining what information actually needs protection and balancing that concern against the operational value software transparency provides defenders.

From SBOM to an “Omnibomb”

SBOM may ultimately be only one layer of a much larger transparency ecosystem.

AI bills of materials are emerging alongside cryptographic bills of materials designed to identify cryptographic dependencies as organizations prepare for crypto agility and post quantum computing.

Hardware bills of materials can provide similar visibility into physical components such as semiconductors.

Friedman suggested that those different transparency mechanisms could eventually converge into what he jokingly called an “omnibomb.”

Before that happens, however, there is significant work left to do.

Even today’s SBOM ecosystem continues to struggle with interoperability. Two quality SBOM tools analyzing the same software may not necessarily produce identical dependency graphs, making harmonization, minimum requirements and common expectations critical.

Friedman pointed to continuing work among governments, cybersecurity agencies, industry and the open source community to define those expectations and create an ecosystem in which SBOM information can move between suppliers, customers and security tools in a meaningful way.

The ultimate destination is not another compliance document, it is continuous software transparency.

Organizations should be able to understand what their systems depend on, correlate that information with emerging threats and vulnerabilities, determine where actual exposure exists and make risk decisions quickly enough to matter.

Or, as Friedman repeatedly emphasized during the conversation, SBOM is not supposed to solve every cybersecurity problem. It is data. What organizations do with that data is where the security value begins.

Watch or listen to the full SecurityWeek Podcast conversation with Allan Friedman for a deeper discussion on SBOM, AI BOMs, VEX, software supply chain security, continuous monitoring and the future of software transparency.

Google on Tuesday expanded access to Gemini 4 Carbon and said agents built on the model helped formally verify core security guarantees in the code behind the Signal protocol.

Paying developers and businesses can now use Carbon via the Gemini API and Gemini for business, and Google AI Ultra subscribers are getting access. Introductory rates of $2/$10 per million input/output tokens apply until November 30, then double.

Until now, only select cyber defenders in Google’s Fairwind Program could use Carbon. They still need Fairwind membership for Carbon for cyber, which Google says tops key benchmarks for discovering, exploiting and fixing vulnerabilities.

According to Google, Wiz used Carbon for cyber to find zero-days at two major SaaS providers within two hours. Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team used the model to confirm that two bugs in a popular open source project were exploitable, with severity comparable to PHP2Shell, a pair of PHP flaws that attackers have already exploited.

“By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch,” Google said.

Separately, Google DeepMind introduced AlphaProof Code, which pairs human experts with AI agents to formally verify software, mathematically demonstrating that it meets defined requirements.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The team applied it to libsignal, the Signal protocol’s reference implementation. Versions of the protocol also run in WhatsApp and Google Messages.

Humans worked with agents running on Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 to write the specifications defining what had to be proven. Carbon-based agents then generated all of the roughly 6.5 million lines of Lean proofs, with Lean rejecting any invalid ones.

The proven guarantees, including forward secrecy, post-compromise security, and authentication, hold for the compiled machine code, while most protocol verification examines only the design.

Five researchers did the proof work in four weeks, something Google says has traditionally taken specialists years.

To show the method catches real flaws, the team reinserted two old, already-patched libsignal bugs and proved that those builds break the security guarantees.

The results cover Google’s own build of the code, run through a small command-line wrapper, and “not Signal’s own applications.” Side channels were also excluded from parts of the analysis.

“The results suggest that AI can make formal verification, historically too expensive for most software, practical for real-world systems,” the researchers wrote.

“As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code’s privacy guarantees,” said Signal CTO Ehren Kret.

Google is publicly releasing the specifications and proofs.

Related: OpenAI Says New GPT-6 Cyber Model Hunts Flaws Without Crossing the Line

Related: OpenAI Model Wrote Its Own Network Code to Get Around Sandbox Restrictions

X.Org has fixed eight vulnerabilities in the X.Org X server and Xwayland, including one in the Xorg server that lets a malicious monitor corrupt its memory. The fixes ship in xorg-server 21.1.26 and xwayland 24.1.15, and each of the eight affects versions before those two releases.

The X server provides the low-level display layer for graphical desktops on many Linux and Unix systems. Xwayland runs X11 applications on desktops built on Wayland, the newer display protocol, so Wayland users who run X11 applications are exposed too. The flaws can crash the server, corrupt its memory, or make it read or write outside the memory it should touch, and one can leak memory contents.

A monitor is the attack tool

CVE-2026-109091 sits in the code that reads EDID, the block of data a monitor sends to describe the resolutions and refresh rates it supports. The Xorg server copies a monitor’s display-range entries into fixed-size arrays without checking the count against the arrays’ limits. Feed it more entries than the arrays hold, from a rigged monitor or a crafted EDID, and the excess spills into neighboring data, which can crash the server or corrupt memory.

An attacker going after this flaw needs a malicious monitor, or a doctored EDID, in front of the server. The other seven flaws sit in the code that handles X protocol requests, the messages applications send to the X server.

Size checks that wrap around

Four of the seven are in Xv, the X Video extension applications use to pass video frames to the server. In CVE-2026-109092, a negative size from the server’s hardware-specific code plus a crafted offset wraps XvShmPutImage’s bounds check, letting the server read or write outside a shared memory segment. CVE-2026-109095, in the glamor acceleration code, computes image sizes with 32-bit integers that wrap to small values for large images, so the server reads past the data the client sent. CVE-2026-109096 and CVE-2026-109903 both start from a negative image size: one lets a request with no image data pass the length check, and the other reports the bogus size to the client, which may then allocate or use a buffer of the wrong size.

CVE-2026-109093 is an out-of-bounds stack write in XTest, the extension that lets clients inject fake keyboard and mouse events. The server copies input values into a fixed-size stack array before checking that they fit. The last two, CVE-2026-109904 and CVE-2026-109094, are integer overflows in the X-Resource extension. On 32-bit servers, a large count wraps so a short request passes the length check, and the server reads or walks past the end of the request buffer.

No severity ratings

X.Org published no severity ratings or CVSS scores and did not say whether any of the eight could lead to code execution. Admins have to rank the bugs themselves, and the three that can write out of bounds, CVE-2026-109091, -109092 and -109093, are the ones to weigh first.

X.Org released xorg-server 21.1.26 about a month after 21.1.25, which fixed 12 flaws. Anyone who installed that update in October has another one to install now. Distributions usually backport the patches into their own package versions, so look for the CVE numbers in your distribution’s advisory.

Iran has been officially accused by France of being responsible for cyber attacks last month that meddled with supermarket freezers, causing some to catch fire.

According to French authorities, a hacking unit from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) sabotaged food refrigeration systems at approximately 700 retail sites, sparking at least 15 fires and causing tens of millions of euros worth of damage.

On the night of 11 October, the hackers seized remote control of refrigeration controllers and changed their defrost settings to high temperatures. As a report published by the French government’s computer emergency response team (CERT-FR) describes, victims of the attack included Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour and Intermarché, as well as butchers, a slaughterhouse, and food-processing plants.

According to French media reports, the targeted refrigeration controllers were made by Danish firm Danfoss, and the attackers targeted older versions of its software.

The finger of blame has been pointed by French authorities in the direction of Shahid Kaveh, a hacking unit within the IRGC. Evidence which is said to have led them to that conclusion includes that the same infrastructure was used, during the same period, to scan Schneider Electric equipment at energy and water facilities. and traces of Farsi. Perhaps the most telling clue of all, however, was that the attack was being trumpeted by a propaganda outlet linked to the hacking unit barely a day later.

Shahid Kaveh is said to hide behind a variety of different "hacktivist" guises including CyberAv3ngers, Soldiers of Solomon, and Cyber Isnaad Front.

The official French report names three men: Hamid Reza Lashgarian, head of the IRGC's Electronic and Cyber Center, and Shahid Kaveh commanders Mahdi Lashgarian and Reza Salarvand.

The same hackers are also believed to have targeted small hydroelectric facilities, while a second Iranian unit called Shahid Shoostari (also known as Emennet Pasargad), is held responsible for attacks on Charlie Hebdo and an attempt to hijack display screens during the 2024 Paris Olympics.

In early November there was a second wave of attacks on refrigeration units which hit businesses across Europe, including three French blood service sites. These attacks have not yet been officially attributed to Iran.

Regardless of who is behind the attacks, it is clearly important that any organisation properly defends its refrigeration systems to prevent tampering. As such, it remains good advice to ensure that operational technology (OT) interfaces are not exposed to the internet, that controller software is kept up to date, that default passwords are changed, and that OT networks are segmented and monitored for unexpected changes.

With fridge attacks like this continuing to create disruption and cost millions of euros, we can expect relations between Paris and Tehran to remain frosty for some time.

d10a5ac4491d.text:
How do you measure the success with which different agents perform regular, real-world cybersecurity tasks?

Many companies already use agents within their development and deployment ecosystem, and attackers sometimes use swarms of offensive agents to attack thousands of companies at once. To help defenders prepare for this new era, we need a score that compares what these agents can do. Because of how important this is, labs in academia across the industry are starting to work on measuring it and setting a standard for how to do it correctly, so the topic is timely and increasingly relevant.

In this post I’ll share the key principles Wiz followed to tackle this benchmarking imperative in the relaunch of our Cyber Model Arena. The full methodology, how we graded, and gathered our tasks is available for download. As of the writing of this blog, the Wiz Cyber Model Arena v3.9 consists of 26 models, four general-purpose harnesses, 59 agents, 327 challenges, three attempts per challenge, and 1,000 seconds each (these numbers are constantly growing).

To create a benchmark, fix the benchmark objective first. Then build the tasks, environment, and the measurement around it. I’ll get into this and explain the principles that guide the process, in greater detail later in this post.

Key Takeaways

Choose the right tasks. Settle the why (objective), the what (data, ground truth and agent setup) and the how (metrics, evaluation function) before you write the first task. Build the data from the real distribution where you can, not from AI-generated or AI-labeled tasks.

Grade with code, not LLMs. Measure success directly and deterministically, and apply anti-cheat measures: isolate the agent from the server and the internet, and give it no way to look up answers. Do not rely on an LLM-as-a-judge unless it is well designed, calibrated and free of bias.

Optimize evaluation for realism. Evaluate the harness and model together, give the agent more than one try, and weigh success against what a solve costs.

Avoid common pitfalls. LLM judges, small samples, task imbalance, model-only evaluation and answer leakage each make a benchmark unreliable. And start small: one harness, a quick and cheap model, a few tasks and a simple grader. Scale only after it works.

Start with a problem statement

Most public cyber-agent benchmarks answer a different question than the one a defender is asking. A multiple-choice quiz benchmark measures model knowledge not production performance, and an LLM output judged by another model measures agreement between the two, not success. We aim to answer whether the agent can perform a real attack.

Write down the one question your benchmark must answer, and test every later decision against it. Ours:

Given only the task instruction, a general-purpose agent scaffold, a 1,000-second budget, and no external knowledge sources, does the agent produce a checkable effect on a real target?

Wiz Research's 2026 State of AI in the Cloud Report found that at least 57% of organizations have deployed self-hosted AI agent technology, and that MCP servers appear in at least 80% of observed cloud environments. People are already buying and defending against these systems. That is the why. The rest of this post is how to build a number that serves it.

Design your benchmark

Define three things before you create your first challenge.

Why. A defender or a buyer should be able to act on the number. "Higher pass@1" is not a why. "Can this agent, as shipped, exploit a live target from the instruction alone?" is.

What. Name the subject under evaluation. Here it is an agent (model + harness + tools + system prompt) run by an attacker, which is why we use realistic limits: 1,000 seconds, three attempts, a simple system prompt, and access to client-side code but not server-side code.

How. It’s important for the benchmark to report a single bottom line metric per example. To reduce many competing metrics to a single number, pick one optimizing metric and treat everything else as a satisficing constraint. If you have five competing metrics and no way to reduce them, which agent is better becomes a debate over the metrics.

Make the tasks match the job

A benchmark can only speak for the tasks it contains. Sample only the hard tasks and you are no longer measuring success on the job, you are measuring success on hard tasks. And a benchmark that claims to measure "offensive capability" from a single task category oversells itself.

So we built four categories of equal weight from sources that already exist in the wild. We did not generate or label tasks with an LLM.

Category

Tasks

What it tests

Code vulnerabilities

221

Finding known vulnerabilities in stripped open-source packages, or exploiting a live 1-day CVE

API security

54

Attacking black-box APIs with no source code

Web security

29

Exploiting real PHP web apps with the client source visible

Cloud security

23

Exploiting misconfigurations across AWS, Azure, GCP and Kubernetes-style setups

The agents behave very differently from one category to the next. Averaged over the 59 agents, pass@1 is 78.0% on API security, 64.6% on web, 56.5% on cloud and 38.2% on code vulnerabilities. The top overall agent scores 74.7% on web and 65.8% on code (while web tops out at 90.8%). Another agent scores 9.7% on code and still 71.6% on API.

Size matters too. Many recent cybersecurity benchmarks have fewer than 30 tasks. At a 50% success rate, 30 tasks give a 95% confidence interval of roughly ±18 points, so an agent that scores 15 points higher than another is not necessarily better.

Grade an effect, not with LLMs

Ground truth is the foundation of evaluation. It has been standard practice to grade with an LLM-as-a-Judge, but judges do not directly measure success. They are biased (they often prefer the first option), random (they give different results each run), expensive, and slow, and they must be calibrated and de-biased before you can use them in a long-lived benchmark. When you use a judge, you measure whether an LLM thinks the agent succeeded. That difference is a debt baked into the system.

We use code instead. Every challenge is designed to leave a checkable effect behind or report precise structured outputs, and a deterministic grader inspects it after the agent is gone. Code graders are cheap, re-runnable, and not a model you have to calibrate.

Anti-cheating via isolation

Agents will shortcut a task when they can. They look the answer up online, read a solution off disk, or manipulate the grader. A score collected with web search, a CVE database or the challenge name in the folder measures something else: success at the task or success at breaking it. CTFusion moved their solve rate by as much as 12 points just by raising web-search access.

As for contamination, we cannot prove our agents never saw a task in pretraining. We can prove they cannot fetch one during the trial. Anti-cheat belongs in the environment, not in the prompt.

Start small

Building a benchmark is a nontrivial, evolving effort, and it is tempting to write 300 challenges before anything runs end to end. We apply lean-startup rules instead: get a small end-to-end baseline you can inspect by hand, then iterate.

You need ten tasks you can re-run, one harness you can deploy, and an evaluation metric a grader can check. After you’re convinced it works, you can scale it up.

What we found

Pair the harness with the model

A model on its own is a text predictor. It becomes an attacker inside a harness that runs commands and applies tools, and models do better or worse in different harnesses. Across the 22 models we ran on both Claude Code and ADK React, the mean absolute gap was 5.1 pass@1 points. Claude models prefer Claude Code, and Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber prefers the thinner ADK loop.

The conclusion: test the system as a whole. Either pair the harness to the model (and as we’ve seen it’s best to match the harness to the model's creator), or fix one general harness and compare models inside it.

Attackers get more than one try

A real attacker does not stop after one failure. We gave every agent three attempts per challenge, and the extra attempts did more than lift scores. For some agents they even changed which one comes out ahead.

Accuracy has a price

Give an agent more time and money and it will usually solve more. So the useful chart plots success against what a solve costs. Any agent off the Pareto frontier is strictly worse than one on it. For example, Claude Code with GPT-5.6 Sol averages 64.2% pass@1 at $8.29 and 27.2 minutes per solve, however the Pareto frontier Codex + GPT-6 Luna is strictly better, averaging 64.5% pass@1 at only $0.05 and 6.3 minutes per solve.

Keep a short list of agents on the frontier and ignore the rest. That lets you ask "for this budget, how do I maximize success?" or "for this success rate, how do I minimize cost?"

Limitations

Four simple harnesses. A cyber-specialized harness would likely score higher, but we chose to measure a simple attacker.

String equality on code vulnerabilities. A semantically correct root cause that misses the expected symbol scores 0. We chose precision over recall.

Public web tasks. websec.fr is a known corpus. Isolation stops the agent from looking up the answer, not from remembering it from training (possibly resulting in benchmark contamination).

A time cap. 1,000 seconds is enough for most successful attacks we observed. In the future we think it is better to limit cost than time.

Confidence intervals. We have yet to publish them on the website, and we are working on it.

Conclusion

Our Cyber Model Arena shows how different agents perform on common cybersecurity tasks, across 327 isolated challenges in four categories. To build an agentic cybersecurity benchmark, fix the why, the what and the how first, and define the agent, the task mix, the grader, the isolation, the budget and the attempts. Get one wrong and the benchmark becomes garbage in, garbage out.

Lead Analysts: Prabhakaran R and Jeewan Singh Jalal

You think twice before clicking a link in an unexpected email. Do you do the same for a message in Microsoft Teams?

A new message arrives in your Teams chat with the familiar notification sound, a participant’s name, and a link. It feels like a colleague, not a stranger. That feeling is the opening attackers look for.

Two things decide whether that message does harm. Can the channel stop it before it reaches your user? And if it gets through, does the user recognize the lure and know what to do? Both matter, and this post covers both.

Modern business depends on external collaboration across sales, finance, and IT. External access and guest participation are standard Teams features, not security oversights, and external access is open to all domains by default. Teams is also no longer where only people talk to people. A message could come from a colleague, an authorized AI agent/chabot, or an attacker, and most people have little to tell them apart.

Attackers exploit this openness by sending external messages that follow the same social engineering patterns as phishing emails and blend into your users' daily routine. They could also aim a message at an agent instead of a person. The question is no longer only whether a phishing message looks real. It is who and what you can trust at work.

KnowBe4 Threat Labs has consistently observed attackers imitating routine messages such as support requests, invoices, and meeting chat posts. Weekly detections grew from five in the week of June 22 to a peak of 301 in the week of September 28 (Figure 1). This post covers what we observed, what the attackers are after, and how the attacks play out.

What makes these messages effective is that a phishing message in chat looks like a routine work message: a link, a support request, a payment follow-up. People may not expect an attack on this channel, so they may take such messages at face value. The words alone rarely settle it. The better question is who is sending, from where and why.

Key Findings

Attackers follow work into Microsoft Teams. Chat and meetings now carry the lures that email has carried for years. Wherever your team works, attackers follow. A small request in chat is usually the first step toward a larger goal, such as device access, stolen money, or leverage for extortion.

Business needs keep the door open. Teams have to stay open to customers, vendors and partners, so blocking outsiders is neither practical nor enough. Attackers blend into that traffic, so judging the words alone is not reliable. Ask who is sending, from where, and why.

Teams have safeguards, but they depend on the user. Teams shows an external label and an Accept/Block prompt at first contact, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 adds Safe Links and zero-hour auto purge where it is licensed. Attackers succeed when a user clicks through those warnings. Email has sender authentication, link analysis, and gateways. Conversations inside Teams sit outside the reach of third-party email gateways, and Teams chat gives fewer sender checks: display names are easy to choose, links can be disguised, and previews can mislead.

Defense has to cover the conversation and the click. Use both Microsoft's own settings and third-party protection as your technical controls. Train your users on this threat vector, so people know what a lure in Teams looks like and how to report it. Be ready to respond fast when a user acts on a message.

Why Are Attackers Moving Into Microsoft Teams?

Chat and meetings now carry the lures that email carried for years, and the following factors make Teams an attractive place for them.

Outside contact is normal. Your teams have to talk to customers, vendors, and partners, so external messages and guests are expected. A harmful message blends in with the many legitimate ones.

Impersonation is easy. Email has checks that block direct domain spoofing. Chat gives fewer sender-checking signals, and a sender can often choose the name users see.

Awareness is lower. Phishing awareness training has traditionally focused on email, so users may look harder at an unexpected email than at a chat message.

Email security doesn’t automatically cover Teams. Many security vendors now extend protection to collaboration tools. An organization that has not extended its controls to Teams leaves that channel uncovered.

One target list covers two channels. An attacker who already has a list of email addresses can reach the same people in Teams, where external access allows it, with little added effort. That gives them two channels to attack instead of one.

How Does an Attack in Teams Unfold?

Most attacks in a collaboration tool follow the same path, whatever the lure.

1. The attacker poses as a trusted contact. Display names are easy to choose, so the sender can appear as IT support, a vendor, or a colleague. A request from an individual account may show only the name the sender chose and an “External” label.

2. The attacker sends a lure. Default or permissive external-access settings let the message in, such as open external access, personal accounts that can start chats, or trial-only tenants that an admin has chosen to allow. The app, the notification and the chat context all look familiar, and the attacker can build the conversation slowly, so the request feels like a natural next step.

3. The user acts on the request. One step is enough: a click, a session started or a reply, because the request looks like routine work. Attackers may also call the user in Teams to talk them through the steps.

4. The user lands on a fake page or receives a payload. The user leaves Teams for the attacker’s web page, or a payload is delivered. A link can display one address and open another, and senders can edit a message after sending it, so what the user sees later may differ from the original.

5. The user hands over credentials, grants access, or pays. The fake page, tool, or payment request asks for one more action, and the user completes it.

6. The attacker gains access. The attacker now holds credentials, system access or the requested payment.

The attacker can then send the next lure through the compromised account, and the cycle repeats.

What Do Attackers Send in Teams, and What Do They Want?

The message types below are cases we observed. For each one, we describe what the attacker likely wants and where the activity can lead. The messages look different, but they serve a similar set of goals.

The “IT Support” Message

Why it works: Help desk requests feel routine, and people want their problem fixed. The user opens the session themselves, so the attacker gets access with the user’s approval.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is full control of the endpoint. Standard defenses often miss this because remote administration tools are legitimate software. With that access, an attacker can take saved passwords, active session cookies, and sensitive documents. This allows them to reach corporate email, Teams, and wider enterprise systems. It also gives them a foothold for lateral movement across internal networks and for deploying further remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools or ransomware.

2. The Urgent Invoice

Why it works: Payment requests with a deadline push people to act before they check, and a personal greeting makes the request feel real.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is money, stolen credentials, malware deployment, or all three. Depending on what the target does, that can mean payments sent to an attacker-controlled account, malware that steals credentials or sets up remote access, and the compromised account being used to send similar requests to colleagues or vendors.

3. The Ransom Note in Chat

Why it works: The message reaches the user directly, with no email gateway in its path.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is payment or an immediate response. The first message alone rarely shows whether the claim is real: it could follow a genuine compromise, or it could be a bluff meant to exploit fear and force a quick reply. Responding under pressure risks paying a ransom for nothing, overlooking an active breach if the claim is true, or causing internal panic when nothing was compromised.

What Should Defenders Do?

Protect messages and meetings, and be ready to respond fast when a user acts on a message. Start with your people, then your Teams settings.

How can users stop these messages?

1. Treat chat like email. Teach users to question links and requests in Teams, including in meeting chats.

2. Teach the “External” label. Ask users to check it before acting on a message that claims to come from support or leadership. For individual Microsoft accounts it can be one of the few cues available.

3. Preview before accepting. Teach users to read an external message request first and to decline it if it is unexpected, even when curiosity says otherwise.

4. Check the real link. Ask users to hover over a link and read the address before clicking, because the text shown can differ from the destination.

5. Never start a remote session someone sends you. Route support requests through the help desk.

6. Verify payment changes through a second channel. Confirm new payment details by phone with a known contact before paying.

7. Treat a ransom message as an incident. Report it to your security team and do not reply.

8. Stop sharing passwords in chat. Use a password manager or a one-time secret tool.

What if a user already acted?

Plan for the click. Reset the user’s password, revoke their active sessions, check for remote-access tools they installed, and review any payment they made.

How do you narrow the door in Teams?

Attackers can only message your users if your Teams settings allow it. You control those settings, and they are worth a review. Microsoft documents each one in its Teams external access guidance . Your business needs some outside contact, so the goal is not to block everyone. The goal is to allow the contact you need and nothing more. Start by reviewing which external tenants can message your users and who can join your meeting chats.

Settings to review

-AllowFederatedUsers: turns external communication with other organizations on or off.

-AllowedDomains and -BlockedDomains: limit access to trusted partners or block malicious domains.

-AllowTeamsConsumer and -AllowTeamsConsumerInbound: manage chat with unmanaged accounts and block uninvited outreach.

-AllowPublicUsers: controls chat with Skype users.

1. Allow only essential partner domains. Prefer allow-lists to block-lists, because block-lists only stop known threats. Blocking a main domain still leaves its subdomains open. To block all subdomains, run:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -BlockAllSubdomains $True

2. Block trial-only tenants. Unlicensed trial tenants are easy tools for attackers. Microsoft blocks them by default, but verify that your setting is still “Blocked”:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -ExternalAccessWithTrialTenants "Blocked"

When the setting is “Blocked,” users from trial-only tenants cannot search for, chat with, call or meet with your team, and they are removed from existing chats. Setting it to “Allowed” turns these safeguards off.

3. Restrict personal accounts. Personal Microsoft accounts are harder to verify: the sender chooses the display name, and no organization vouches for the account. Disable: AllowTeamsConsumerInbound to stop inbound chats from them, and evaluate AllowTeamsConsumer and -AllowPublicUsers against your needs.

4. Block malicious senders. You can block a harmful sender individually without changing global policy:

In the Teams admin center, go to Users > External access.

Turn on “Block specific users from communicating with people in my organization.”

Select “Block a user”, enter the person’s email address or messaging resource identifier (MRI), and select Apply.

The list holds a maximum of 200 users. You can also manage it with Set-CsTeamsExternalAccessConfiguration.

Where Can KnowBe4 Help?

Attackers move between channels, and a single campaign can use several. Reputation checks and sender history say little about a message from someone who has joined a meeting you are in. Protection has to read the message and respond when a user acts on it.

KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security brings together KnowBe4 Defend (inbound email and messaging security, including Microsoft Teams), KnowBe4 Prevent (outbound email security) and PhishER Plus (incident response). Its behavioral AI protects the conversation and coaches your workforce wherever work happens.

Multi-engine detection. KnowBe4 analyzes message text, sender relationships, links, and attachments at the same time, plus email headers when the message is an email. It checks what the message asks the user to do and how the sender relates to the recipient. A domain reputation check sees neither.

Coaching at the point of risk. Contextual coaching, real-time nudges, and localized banners and tags in 13 languages show users why a message looks suspicious at the moment it appears. According to KnowBe4 internal data, 97% of users stop before proceeding with a high-risk action when a teachable moment appears.

Threat intelligence. KnowBe4 Threat Labs turns real-world attack telemetry and more than 15 years of data into live detection models across the Email & Collaboration Security suite, so defenses update as new patterns appear.

Protect the Places Your Team Works

Your people spend their day in email, chat and meetings. Your security should cover all these.

A public iOS sandbox escape could expose wallet keys, Binance warns. No attacks are reported and no fix is confirmed.

On 10 November, Binance warned users about a public iOS sandbox escape that lets one app read the files of other apps. Seed phrases, private keys and login credentials could be exposed to a malicious app, the exchange said.

“A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.” reads the warning.

Binance advises users to remove apps installed from untrusted sources, update iOS and all apps to the latest official versions, and, if a breach is suspected, move funds to a new wallet on a clean device and reset all active login sessions.

A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.…

— Binance (@binance) November 10, 2026

A researcher known as ‘forcequitOS’ published the PoC exploit code, called worse_query, on GitHub. Apple released security updates for both iOS versions the following day, but its release notes mysteriously don’t report a fix for the issue. The good news is that neither Binance nor the researcher has reported any attacks or data theft.

“worse_query is the direct successor to bad_query and essentially replaces it. To use worse_query, you’ll have to set up an App Group container for your app.” forcequitOS wrote.

The proof-of-concept can access the data folders used by all apps and, on iOS 27, some system folders as well. To work, an app must create an App Group container. The researcher says the code is intended for developers and “isn’t useful by itself.” However, other developers have already used it to build apps that can be installed on iPhones.

One example is WQ Files, a file manager developed by Christoph Kolbicz, TheHackerNews reports.

“WQ Files is a file browser, app data manager and cache cleaner for iOS 26 and 27. “WQ” stands for worse_query, the sandbox technique it is built on. It reaches other apps’ and system containers with no jailbreak and no kernel exploit. Tested on iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1 and 27.2.” reads the description.

It can access data belonging to other apps without requiring a jailbreak or a kernel exploit. It can also edit, delete and clear that data. Users can install it through sideloading tools such as AltStore and SideStore, which automatically create the required App Group when users sign in with their Apple ID.

I agree (and I wasn't planning on it), but I don't mind the loss of any potential bounty tbh, when Apple was stalling on responding to me and people started larping with it on here.

— forcequit (@forcequitOS) November 8, 2026

The forcequitOS says they have no intention of seeking a bug bounty from Apple and are willing to give up any potential reward because of Apple’s delayed response and the inappropriate behavior of people publicly misusing or exaggerating the exploit.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Apple)

We’ve written before about what Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses can see and hear, and who might get to use that information. Those worries focus on how the glasses handle information during normal use. A security researcher has now shown how to bypass a safeguard meant to stop unauthorized software running on them.

Vulnerability researcher Paula, known online as pamoutaf, found a way to run her own software on a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses. For the technical details I’ll gladly refer you to her own post about it.

The glasses are controlled by the Meta AI app on the owner’s phone. Developers can add their own apps to the glasses through a developer tool, and the phone sends that software to the glasses to install.

The glasses were supposed to check that the software really came from Meta. In older firmware (up to and including version 126), they didn’t check, so the researcher could swap in an app of her own.

Meta introduced a check in firmware version 127 to verify the app’s digital signature to prove that it came from Meta . The researcher found the on/off switch for that signature check came from a settings file passed along by the phone. The glasses only checked the file was correctly formed, not whether it had been tampered with. Changing a single byte in the file turned the signature check off.

Once her app was running, she could send commands to the glasses from the paired phone over a wireless connection.

The glasses have a camera, microphones and a wireless connection, and they sit on your face all day. A wearable that can be made to run unapproved code goes beyond a privacy-policy question. It becomes a security question about who controls the device. As we’ve seen, some cheaper smart glasses already are a security disaster.

In this case the person running the code would be the person that controls the phone. If malicious software running on the glasses could access the camera or stored recordings, it could potentially send footage to an attacker’s server. Pamoutaf’s research doesn’t demonstrate that scenario, but it raises questions about what that software might be able to access.

In her post she promised a follow-up exploring other potential ways to attack the glasses.

How to stay safe

Keep the glasses’ firmware and the Meta AI app updated, and avoid unofficial apps or modifications.

If smart glasses are just another gadget to you, I’d leave them on the shelf. If you rely on them as an accessibility aid, you deserve technology that helps you without putting your privacy or other people’s at risk.

Scammers know more about you than you think.

Malwarebytes Mobile Security protects you from phishing, scam texts, malicious sites, and more. With real-time AI-powered Scam Guard built right in.

TL;DR: AI agent security in banking requires controls that can deny prohibited workload actions before they complete, because an alert does not revoke an agent’s authority. An agent can use legitimate credentials to create financial exposure without exploiting a vulnerability. Aquasec combines deep runtime visibility with local enforcement through its full agent architecture, applying configured policies inside running workloads without waiting for centralized analysis. That control complements identity restrictions and transaction approvals, blocking supported operations that violate policy while the agent is executing.

What is the control gap in AI agent security?

Your bank’s exposure extends to the authority an agent’s workload gives it, which can be much broader than its assigned task. AI agent security must connect that task to enforceable limits on access and execution.

In Kubernetes, that authority can come from a service account, an associated cloud role, mounted credentials and available network paths. Instructions to inspect records do not remove credentials or close connections. A carefully written prompt therefore leaves the workload’s technical permissions unchanged. The agent can still attempt actions the business never intended it to take.

Why do internal AI agents require their own runtime controls?

Connecting an agent to production tools gives its decisions consequences inside your environment. A badly scoped instruction or a malicious prompt embedded in a document can lead it toward actions its existing access permits.

Blocking external agents at a customer login does nothing to constrain an internal agent using a workload identity. The bank still owns that exposure inside its clusters. Security cannot wait for a software exploit to establish that intervention is necessary, because an unwanted operation may use a valid credential and an allowed connection.

Where do access reviews and alerts fall short for AI agents?

Identity controls, image scanning and patching remain essential. They reduce unnecessary authority and address vulnerable software. A posture finding, however, leaves the identified access available until something changes it.

Adding runtime telemetry does not automatically close that gap. A sensor can observe an operation without being able to deny it locally. In a model that exports telemetry for centralized analysis and response, execution can continue while the decision is made.

For an agent connected to a financial system, that distinction is consequential. Investigating a completed operation and preventing that operation from completing produce different outcomes for the bank.

How should banks separate AI agent observation from action?

An agent assigned to inspect transactions should not automatically receive the authority to initiate them. Use dedicated identities and restrict available credentials to the resources its task requires. Require application approval for consequential operations, with read access limited to necessary records.

Then carry those boundaries into the running workload. Define the executable behavior and network destinations the task needs and enforce restrictions on supported operations outside that scope. The controls should hold when the agent misinterprets an instruction, without depending on the model to recognize its own mistake.

How does Aquasec enforce AI agent workload boundaries?

We put the enforcement decision inside the running workload through the Aquasec Enforcer. Our full agent architecture combines detailed runtime telemetry with local policy decisions at the kernel layer. In enforcement mode, it can deny supported operations that violate configured policy without waiting for centralized analysis or an analyst response.

Drift Prevention makes that distinction concrete. When an agent attempts to execute a binary introduced after deployment, the configured control can block execution. Network policies can also deny connections to prohibited destinations, restricting paths that the workload’s identity permissions might otherwise leave available.

Those controls act on the operation itself. Security teams get a way to constrain supported workload behavior while permissions are corrected, without making termination of the entire container the default response. Application authorization remains responsible for deciding which transactions an agent may perform.

How do AI agent security approaches compare at execution?

Evaluate what happens to the attempted operation. The comparison below separates finding driven posture from telemetry led detection without local enforcement. Aquasec entries assume supported controls configured for enforcement.

Dimension

Traditional approach

Modern approach

Aquasec approach

Primary function

Identify excessive access

Detect workload behavior

Enforce workload policy

Decision path

Remediation workflow

Central analysis and response

Local enforcement

Prohibited operation

Remains possible until corrected

May continue during response

Supported action denied

Evidence

Configuration finding

Detection event

Policy event and enforcement result

The architectural distinction is whether the security component can apply the restriction inside the workload, without waiting for a separate response workflow.

How can an AI agent create financial exposure without an exploit?

Valid access can turn a poorly scoped task into an unintended transaction.

Example: A reconciliation agent is asked to resolve a failed settlement. Its workload holds a payment credential and can reach an internal transfer service. Without a separate approval check, it could attempt the settlement again from another funding account. Every step can use an allowed operation.

This hypothetical scenario explains the exposure; it is not a reported customer incident or a measured product result. The missing boundary is between the assigned task and the authority available to complete it.

What mistakes weaken AI agent workload controls?

Exceptions can reopen the access a runtime policy was intended to restrict. Do not approve broad exceptions just to remove a block. Validate the required dependency and limit the exception to what the application needs.

Do not treat a permitted connection as transaction approval. If read and transfer operations share the same allowed service, the application must authorize them separately. Workload network restrictions do not determine whether an individual financial transaction is legitimate.

What should banks demand from AI agent security next?

Banks should make demonstrated enforcement a condition of expanding AI agent access. Before giving an agent greater authority, require evidence that the controls protecting its workload can stop the prohibited behavior they are designed to address. An alert that leaves the operation untouched does not meet that standard.

We put that enforcement inside the running workload through the Aquasec Enforcer. Our full agent architecture combines deep runtime visibility with local policy enforcement, allowing configured controls to block supported operations without waiting for centralized analysis or an analyst response. That gives banks a way to restrict what an agent’s workload can execute, alongside the identity and application controls governing its access

Watch this demo to see how Aquasec runtime enforcement changes the outcome of these attacks in Kubernetes.

FAQ

How does Aquasec differentiate AI agent security from runtime monitoring?

Aquasec combines runtime telemetry with local policy enforcement through a full agent architecture. For supported operations in enforcement mode, the workload does not need to wait for centralized analysis before a configured restriction can deny the action.

Can AI agent security stop misuse of valid credentials?

Aquasec can deny supported workload operations that violate configured policy even when credentials are available. A request that remains permitted still needs authorization and any required approval within the application.

Does this AI agent security strategy cover externally hosted agents?

Aquasec enforcement applies to supported workloads where it is deployed. Protecting a bank’s clusters does not automatically protect agents running on laptops or external platforms. Those deployments require their own access controls.

Enterprise software maker SAP on Tuesday announced the release of 42 new and updated security notes, including nine that resolve critical-severity vulnerabilities.

Four of SAP’s new security notes address maximum-severity flaws in NetWeaver (Internet Communication Manager (ICM) and SAML2 Service Provider), Web Dispatcher, and Gateway.

The ICM and Web Dispatcher flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126, are a single weakness in the SAP kernel component that receives HTTP, HTTPS, and WebSocket traffic.

According to Onapsis, which calls the security defect ICM2SHELL, the issue is related to reassembling large WebSocket messages, which may be split into fragments during a server-browser exchange and then put together by the receiver.

“A specially crafted sequence of WebSocket messages makes the ICM or the WD write attacker-controlled data past the end of the memory it reserved for the connection. Depending on how that data is shaped, the result is either an immediate crash of the process or controlled corruption of its memory,” Onapsis explains.

ICM2SHELL, the enterprise application security firm says, could allow an attacker to execute operating system commands with <sid>adm privileges.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“This is not a theoretical outcome. The Onapsis Research Labs provided SAP a working exploit that achieves full, unauthenticated remote code execution end to end, running arbitrary commands as <sid>adm on the target system. The denial-of-service condition, in turn, reproduced on every SAP Kernel release tested,” Onapsis says.

The max-severity SAP Gateway flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-89103 and referred to as ProxyGate, could be exploited by unauthenticated attackers to achieve remote code execution (RCE) without user interaction.

It is related to the prxyinfo access-control list, which should restrict requests to trusted networks only. However, if left open, it allows an attacker to send a series of requests that appear to be originating from an internal network, tricking the gateway into accepting them.

This allows an attacker to execute OS commands with the <sid>adm privileges and gain full control over the SAP system, without providing a username, password, or certificate.

“Because the flaw is in the SAP kernel, it affects a broad range of releases, including kernel versions that are already out of maintenance. Further, the gateway runs not only on ABAP but also on AS Java, dual-stack, and standalone-gateway systems,” Onapsis explains.

SAP also resolved a max-severity missing authentication bug in NetWeaver (CVE-2026-120017) that, in certain configurations, could allow unauthenticated attackers to submit specially crafted data and impersonate arbitrary users, which could lead to full system compromise.

The remaining five critical notes in SAP’s November 2026 bulletin address vulnerabilities in NetWeaver (CVE-2026-109803 and CVE-2026-76965), S4CRM (CVE-2026-109795), Web Dispatcher (CVE-2026-89119), and BusinessObjects (CVE-2026-109798).

Additionally, SAP published 17 high-severity fixes, including for multiple memory corruption, denial-of-service (DoS), and information disclosure bugs.

Since the scheduled October 2026 security patches, SAP released new notes dealing with the recently disclosed PHP2Shell and Node2Shell vulnerabilities in its Business AI Platform and updated several other notes and advisories. This brings the total to 43 new and updated notes released this month, Onapsis notes in its analysis of the patches.

14f2684b3693.text:
Intezer researchers used AI agents to rebuild source code for Slack, Apple’s Finder and a TinyTurla-NG sample, from a backdoor family Cisco Talos attributes to the Turla group. They worked from the shipped programs and vendor documentation. The rebuilt Slack ran well enough that the team added a new feature to it: AI text autocomplete, powered by a small local model.

Software vendors that count on compiling their programs to keep source code private are the ones exposed. “Our research shows that an AI agent can reconstruct a working copy of an application when given the original software’s binary or package,” wrote the Intezer researchers behind the work. The same method that opens up a commercial app also opens up malware.

The backdoor rebuild has the numbers

Intezer set five tests for success. The code had to be readable enough to maintain, clean and idiomatic enough to compare with human-written source, compiled only from what the agents wrote, free of bundled third-party libraries, and identical in behavior to the original. Intezer rated TinyTurla the hardest of the three targets.

Codex, running GPT-5.6-sol-high, drove the workflow and made the engineering decisions, while Kimi K3 filled three separate roles in the setup. The agents produced about 3,100 lines of source in two files.

The rebuilt DLL is 296,960 bytes against the original’s 291,840, with 1,072 functions against 1,041 and identical imported symbols. BinDiff, a tool that compares how two binaries are put together, matched 1,034 of the original functions and scored the pair at 92.8% similarity with 98.7% confidence. Put plainly, the copy is built almost the same way as the original. “That is a statement about shape,” the researchers explained.

Intezer checked behavior separately. Its harness, the automated setup that runs the agents and tools, compared each rebuilt function with its original using Binary Ninja’s high-level intermediate language, a readable translation of machine code.

Slack and Finder still have gaps

Claude dug through Slack’s minified client code to identify the third-party libraries inside it. The client contains more than 500,000 functions, most of them from those libraries. Slack’s server is not downloadable, so the agents built a Slack-compatible one on SQLite, guided by network inspection of the real Slack app and Slack’s documentation.

Finder, a 25.8 MB executable, still has gaps around online-only files, sync status and actions that depend on other macOS services. Intezer did not publish how long the rebuilds took or what they cost.

Obfuscation is the suggested defense

Intezer’s advice is to use encryptors and obfuscators, tools that scramble code so it is harder to read. The researchers say these “raise the bar” for AI agents. “The software industry will have to adjust,” they wrote.

4a020f99da4d.text:
A threat actor used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials for a Qubole big data platform's AWS account to access and exfiltrate data from multiple customers' AWS environments.

The campaign ran between October 14 and 26, and affected tens of companies whose AWS environments had IAM roles configured to trust an AWS account associated with Qubole.

Qubole is an enterprise cloud data processing and analytics platform that helps companies manage large datasets and run machine learning workloads. It also offers AWS integration to allow computing resource management.

Companies can grant third-party providers such as Qubole access to their AWS resources by creating cross-account IAM roles. Trust policies determine which external AWS accounts can take these roles, and permissions are set to define the resources and actions allowed.

Researchers at cloud security company Wiz explain that external providers use AWS’s STS AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for accessing customers' resources in the cloud.

Wiz started to investigate the attack after data security and governance company Sentra shared information about suspicious activity observed in some of its customers' environments. The investigation also included cybersecurity company Mandiant.

The researchers found that the attacker had compromised two Qubole IAM users and assumed otherwise unused roles in multiple customers’ AWS accounts that had previously been configured to trust Qubole’s account, granting them access within the role’s permissions.

Wiz says the attacker then surveyed cloud resources, retrieved secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and SSM Parameter Store, and read Lambda environment variables.

They then used the TruffleHog tool to validate discovered AWS keys, Microsoft Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials.

Once they gained deeper access, they downloaded data from all accessible S3 buckets in the AWS environment, following an opportunistic approach rather than carefully targeting specific data.

“The sequence was consistent across environments: assume a role, call ListBuckets to see what the role could reach, call ListObjects and HeadObject to enumerate and inspect the contents, then call GetObject to download them,” Wiz explains.

The report does not specify the exact method used to compromise the Qubole accounts or the number of downstream victims. However, Sentra confirmed dozens of victims and millions of files stolen from one customer alone.

Sentra says the attacker moved quickly and collected secrets at a rate of 100 passwords and keys in seven minutes.

BleepingComputer could not find a public announcement from Qubole about this incident. We have emailed the firm for more information about the attack and await their response.

Potentially impacted administrators are advised to review CloudTrail from October 1 onward for suspicious access from Qubole’s AWS account, investigate subsequent secret and S3 access, rotate exposed credentials, and revoke active role sessions.

It is also recommended to remove unused integrations and restrict remaining roles’ permissions, trusted identities, and permitted source networks.
