8ea988d5493e.text:
Overview

On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central, its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform.

In a public disclosure titled Able2Shell, an independent researcher has published details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code covering 33 issues. According to the disclosure, the issues include unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE), privilege escalation to root, credential disclosure, and unauthorized account creation. One unauthenticated chain combines XML external entity (XXE) and session-handling weaknesses to execute code as the nable service account. Other demonstrated chains involve an administrator viewing malicious patch metadata or use ProductAdmin credentials. Rapid7 Intelligence is currently triaging the newly published details.

As of November 10, N-able reported scanning activity associated with the published PoC code and said it had no evidence that any customer environment had been successfully exploited. The vendor has advised keeping N-central deployments offline while it develops and validates a hotfix. Hosted N-central classic environments remain offline, according to the same notice. N-able's notice does not yet include CVE identifiers or CVSS scores.

N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to administer endpoints and infrastructure. Compromise of an RMM server can put downstream managed environments at risk. N-central has previously been targeted through separate vulnerabilities, including an authentication bypass covered by Rapid7 in August 2026. Given the platform's administrative reach and the availability of public exploit code, Rapid7 recommends treating the current disclosure as an emergency.

Mitigation guidance

Rapid7 strongly recommends that organizations operating on-premises N-central servers take them offline immediately and keep them offline until the hotfix is available, and the server has been successfully upgraded. Hosted customers should follow the vendor's service restoration updates. N-able is developing and validating a hotfix, with a target of midday November 10 EST.

Affected versions: The researcher reports testing N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31. N-able's current notice does not specify the full affected-version range.

Fixed versions: N-able's incident notice does not yet identify a remediation build. Follow the incident notice for release confirmation and installation instructions.

Rapid7 also recommends reviewing N-central servers and downstream managed systems for signs of compromise and engaging incident responders if suspicious activity is identified.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to N-able's security incident notice.

Updates

November 10, 2026: Initial publication.

6af1a8a3656f.text:
Wiz and ISMAP: How We Are Preparing to Serve Japan's Public Sector

When Japanese government agencies procure cloud services, they are required, in principle, to procure from services registered on the ISMAP Cloud Service List. This list is established under ISMAP (Information system Security Management and Assessment Program), in accordance with the "Common Standards for Cybersecurity Measures for Government Agencies and Related Agencies. ISMAP is a framework that evaluates and registers cloud services in advance to ensure they satisfy the security requirements mandated by the government.

Without an active ISMAP listing, Japanese government agencies face a barrier to adoption. While Wiz is not listed on ISMAP yet, we're actively working through the controls and wanted to share where we actually stand today.

What ISMAP Is, and Why It Matters

In practice, ISMAP gives procurement officers a pre-vetted catalog of cloud providers. Getting onto that list comes with strict baseline demands:

Mandatory external audits conducted by audit firms registered on the ISMAP Auditors List

Japanese-language application support, along with the preparation of documentation and audit trails required for review and examination

Post-registration adherence to scheduled renewal applications and ongoing audits and verifications

Under the hood, ISMAP complements established global standards. The ISMAP Control Measures are built around the Common Standards for Government Agencies as well as JIS Q 27001 and JIS Q 27017, the Japanese national standards for ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27017, covering information security management and cloud security controls. While ISMAP aligns with these frameworks, holding these certifications does not directly equate to ISMAP registration. Additionally, ISMAP also pulls in ISO/IEC 27018 for cloud privacy, alongside NIST SP 800-53 controls to plug edge cases that the core ISO standards do not explicitly cover.

Currently, proposed revisions to the ISMAP Control Measures have been published, focusing on reflecting revised international standards and streamlining the number of control measures. These proposals aim to reorganize and rationalize the control system, which is expected to enhance efficiency upon revision and enforcement while maintaining the security and reliability demanded by the program. Please note that the draft revisions and implementation schedule remain subject to change.

Where Wiz Stands Today

Wiz has maintained active ISO 27001, ISO 27017, ISO 27018, SOC 2, PCI DSS, and FedRAMP certifications and reports for the past five years. Our commitment to compliance gives our teams established practices for control implementation, evidence collection, and continuous audit readiness. We recently finished an internal gap assessment against both the current ISMAP Control Measures and the published revision proposals to prepare for the upcoming ISMAP audit.

To address the specific requirements of the ISMAP framework, we are actively building out the localized evidence packages and formal processes required for ISMAP assessors. In parallel, we have engaged with an audit firm registered on the ISMAP Auditors List, with target plans to formally launch the external assessment audit in early 2027.

What This Means for Customers

To be clear: ISMAP does not offer an official "in progress" or provisional status. You're either on the official registry or you are not–and right now, we are not.

What we can confirm is that we are executing our ISMAP-specific requirements by leveraging our extensive experience with certifications such as ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, PCI-DSS, FedRAMP, IRAP, and CPSTIC. We have completed the gap analysis, engaged with registered assessors, and are addressing control artifacts ahead of time rather than scrambling during the audit window.

In the meantime, security teams in Japan already use Wiz to audit and enforce the core security areas: IAM, data encryption, centralized logging, continuous vulnerability scanning, and incident response. However, compliance with ISMAP security standards is not verified or guaranteed solely by the use of Wiz.

Looking Ahead

If you are navigating Japanese public sector compliance today, we can walk you through our current security posture, share our active ISO and SOC 2 reports, and show you how our existing control mapping aligns with ISMAP. Reach out to your Wiz account team or contact us directly.

Microsoft has released the Patch Tuesday Windows 11 KB513261 and KB5131087 cumulative updates for versions 26H2/25H2/24H2 and 23H2 to fix security vulnerabilities and bugs and add new features.

Today's updates are mandatory as they contain the November 2026 Patch Tuesday security patches for hundreds of vulnerabilities discovered in previous months.

You can install today's update by going to Start > Settings > Windows Update and clicking on 'Check for Updates.'

You can also manually download and install the update from the Microsoft Update Catalog.

This is the eleventh 'Patch Tuesday' release in 2026, and it's based on 24H2, which means 25H2 or 26H2 get the same update. There are no exclusive or special changes. You'll get the same fixes across the two versions of Windows 11.

What's new in the November 2026 Patch Tuesday update

With today's update, Microsoft is adding new customization options to Windows 11 and fixing minor issues with File Explorer.

Here's the full list of improvements and fixes:

[Context menu in File Explorer]

New! This update introduces an updated context menu that is faster, simpler, and more customizable. The updated menu opens more quickly, reduces clutter, and gives you more control over the commands and app extensions that appear when you right-click.

You can now customize the context menu to better fit how you use Windows. Select Customize menu at the bottom of the context menu to open its Settings page.

Turn built-in Windows commands, such as Send to and Create shortcut, on or off.

Add commands such as Print to the context menu.

Choose which app extensions appear in the main menu or a submenu or hide the app extensions submenu.

Display Cut, Copy, Paste, Rename, Delete, and Share directly in the menu instead of as a row of icons.

Move Properties to the bottom of the context menu.

To personalize the context menu, right-click and select Customize menu, then choose the commands, app extensions, and layout you prefer. No action is required to use the default configuration. To see more options, hold down Shift and right-click on your desktop.

[Modernized AutoPlay experience]

New! This update modernizes the AutoPlay dialog that appears when you connect devices such as a phone, camera, or removable drive to your PC. The updated experience supports dark mode, responds better to text scaling and display settings, and makes AutoPlay notifications available in notification center for easier access.

[File Explorer]

New! Key file information, such as name, location, and date, now appear in a consistent layout on the File Explorer search results page, making search results easier to scan.

New! Address bar now supports ~, making it quicker to navigate directly to your user profile folder and subfolders (for example, ~\AppData).

New! This update enables dark mode support in the Folder Options dialog in File Explorer.

[XBOX mode]

New! This update introduces a refreshed Gaming Task View experience in XBOX mode, featuring a new navigation bar that provides quick access to Exit to Desktop and Power Options, making key system actions easier to access while gaming. 1

[Settings]

New! This update improves the Privacy & security page in Windows Settings by grouping related Camera, Microphone, and Location privacy controls and elevating usage information from linked pages onto the main page.

New! The Device Info card on the Settings Home page, first introduced in the March 2026 preview update KB5079391, is expanding to additional markets. Available to users signed in with a Microsoft account, the card provides a quick view of key PC specifications and usage, with more detailed device information available under Settings > System > About. 1

This update makes some small visual refinements to the design of the temporary files section under Settings > System > Storage.

[Phone Link]

New! You can now hover over a recent message or notification in the Recent section to preview its content directly in Start without opening the item. This experience can be managed under Phone Link > Settings > Start menu personalization.

[Taskbar]

New! The update improves animations of app window previews when mousing across app icons in the taskbar.

This update improves the underlying state persistence of taskbar settings related to multiple monitors across monitor connections and disconnections.

[Magnifier]

New! Magnifier now includes a contrast theme toggle that can reduce screen glare while keeping the original colors in photos, videos, and charts. The toggle applies a dark contrast theme by default and is available from the Magnifier toolbar. To choose a different contrast theme, go to Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier. Color inversion remains available as a separate option.

New! Magnifier now supports per-monitor zoom, allowing each display to use its own zoom level while keeping the magnified view within that display. To use per-monitor zoom, set your displays to Extend under Settings > System > Display.

To adjust a display, move your pointer to it and press Windows key + Plus (+) or Windows key + Minus (-), use Ctrl + Alt with the mouse wheel or move the Magnifier toolbar to that display and use its controls.

Per-monitor zoom is on by default. You can turn it off or adjust individual zoom levels from the Magnifier toolbar or under Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier.

New! Magnifier now supports viewport locking for multi-monitor setups with per-monitor zoom turned on. It keeps the magnified view on a display in place while you move the pointer to another display. The locked display remains interactive. Point to a display and press Ctrl + Windows key + K to lock or unlock its view.

Press Windows key + Esc to release all locked displays.

You can change the lock shortcut to Ctrl + Alt + P under Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier.

[Live Captions]

New! This update improves Live Captions with a new Include screen reader audio setting, which is off by default. With the setting off, Live Captions will not transcribe audio from screen readers such as Narrator, JAWS, and NVDA, keeping captions focused on microphone and system audio. To turn on this setting, go to Settings > Accessibility > Captions.

[Narrator]

New! Narrator now supports reading and navigating math equations in supported Microsoft 365 apps, including Word and PowerPoint, and supported web content in Microsoft Edge (version 153.0.4234.32 and later) and Google Chrome (version 153.0.8010.18 and later). This makes it easier for users who are blind or have low vision to understand and explore equations, formulas, and scientific notation.

Press Narrator key + Alt + N to turn on math navigation and use the arrow keys to explore parts of an equation. Press Esc to exit.

Math reading supports English (United States), English (United Kingdom), Traditional Chinese, Finnish, German, and Spanish. You can change the language and other math reading preferences in Narrator settings (Accessibility > Narrator > Math reading).

[Family Safety]

New! The update improves family safety messaging when applications are blocked because of age-restricted parental controls.

[Recovery]

New! This update enables Windows recovery (WinRE) to automatically reuse eligible Wi-Fi profiles already saved in Windows, including supported certificate-based networks. Devices can now get online automatically during recovery scenarios such as quick machine recovery or cloud rebuild, without preconfiguring Wi-Fi credentials in WinRE. This capability is on by default, and IT admins can disable it. This feature was previously disclosed last month and is now beginning to roll out.

To learn more, see Networking in WinRE.

[Cloud rebuild]

New! This update introduces Cloud rebuild, a new recovery option that reinstalls Windows 11 using a Windows image and device drivers downloaded from Windows Update, including when Windows is unable to start. No USB media or custom image is required. Cloud rebuild includes:

Drive sanitization: Choose to remove your files or securely erase data using the storage hardware’s erase capability before Windows is reinstalled. Sanitization is irreversible.

Remote management: IT administrators can configure and start a Cloud rebuild remotely through the Recovery CSP using either the currently installed build or a specified target build.

To start Cloud rebuild:

In Windows, go to Settings > System > Recovery, and then select Rebuild PC. The device restarts into the Windows Recovery Environment and starts Cloud rebuild.

Alternatively, if Windows can't start, the device enters the Windows Recovery Environment automatically after repeated boot failures. From the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE), select Troubleshoot > Recovery and uninstall > Cloud rebuild.

Connect to a wired Ethernet or Wi-Fi network.

Review the target Windows build, edition, and language, and then confirm the data loss warning before the rebuild begins. You can choose whether to remove files or remove and sanitize files prior to Windows reinstalling.

To learn more, see Cloud rebuild.

[Windows settings backup and restore]

New! This update introduces a Restore Summary that appears after you restore a backup profile to a new device. The summary gives a clear overview of what was successfully restored, including Windows settings and the list of Microsoft Store apps. This improves transparency during device transitions and helps you validate your restore results and continue setup on your new device with confidence.

For more information see, Windows settings backup and restore overview.

[Adaptive hibernate policy]

New! This update improves the adaptive hibernate policy to provide more instant-on resumes from Modern Standby while helping preserve battery life when the charge is low. Noticeable changes include less hibernation while the battery is above 80% and hibernating sooner when the battery is below 10%.

[Security]

New! This update expands memory integrity protection across eligible devices. Supported PCs may now have memory integrity (HVCI) enabled during updates to help improve security and prepare devices for advanced Windows security features, while respecting existing user or IT administrator choices. For more information, see Expanding memory integrity protection across Windows devices.

[Windows IPv6 networking support]

New! Windows now supports IPv6 CLAT for Wi-Fi and Ethernet network interfaces, adding client-side 464XLAT translation so IPv4-only applications can continue reaching IPv4 services from IPv6-only networks. This helps organizations advance IPv6-only deployments while preserving compatibility for legacy IPv4 application scenarios.

Prefix discovery: PREF64 is discovered through Router Advertisements (RA) by default, with DNS ipv4only.arpa available as a fallback.

Requirements: CLAT requires SLAAC-based IPv6 addressing. DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation and Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) are not currently supported.

Configuration: Enable CLAT by using netsh interface clat set global permit=enabled pref64fromdns=enabled pref64fromra=enabled or Group Policy under Network > TCPIP Settings > IPv6 Transition Technologies.

[Data Protection API (DPAPI)]

New! This update adds a warning before prompt-based protect and unprotect operations. The warning explains that this prompt-based experience will be retired in April 2027. If you or an app use these prompts, stop creating new prompt-protected data, use a supported non-interactive protection flow, and decrypt or migrate existing prompt-protected data before retirement. DPAPI operations that do not use the prompt-based flow aren't affected. For more details, see CRYPTPROTECT_PROMPTSTRUCT structure (dpapi.h).

[Windows Spotlight]

This update makes underlying platform changes to generally improve Windows Spotlight reliability on the lock screen.

[Unicode]

This update provides Windows text shaping support for Unicode 17.0, helping Windows correctly display and shape newly encoded characters and scripts. Unicode 17.0 added 4,803 characters, including support for four newly encoded scripts: Beria Erfe, Sidetic, Tai Yo, and Tolong Siki. These updates help keep Windows text support current as the Unicode Standard evolves and improve support for languages and writing systems used by people around the world.

Microsoft is not aware of any new issues with this month's Patch Tuesday, and it also patched a long-standing issue that broke USB audio on some PCs.

A critical authentication bypass vulnerability in Xen Orchestra is being actively exploited in attacks that could grant administrator privileges and allow takeover of XCP-ng virtualization hosts.

Xen Orchestra is a web-based management platform developed by French software company Vates, used to manage XCP-ng virtualization environments, including virtual machines, hosts, and pools.

The vulnerability, tracked as VSA-2026-062, affects Xen Orchestra and the Xen Orchestra Appliance (XOA) and allows remote attackers with network access to the management interface to bypass authentication using a specially crafted cookie. A CVE identifier and CVSS score have not been assigned yet.

According to a Vates security advisory, the flaw stems from how Xen Orchestra processes authentication tokens sent through REST API requests.

The flaw stems from how Xen Orchestra processes authentication cookies.

By sending a specially crafted cookie (authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D) containing an empty JSON object ({}), attackers can trick the platform into retrieving an existing authentication token and logging them in as its owner, without requiring actual credentials.

Once authenticated, attackers can retrieve "reusable login token IDs" through the /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens REST API endpoint, which can be used for further access.

"An adversary can bypass authentication and perform actions with 'Admin' privilege. Xen Orchestra compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root," warns Vates.

The company has released Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 (stable) and 6.10.0 (latest), including patched xo-server packages 5.211.2 and 5.213.1 to fix these security vulnerabilities.

Administrators should install the update immediately, and if not possible, restrict Xen Orchestra access to dedicated management networks and block known malicious IP addresses.

Security researchers Filip Magic and Christoffer Olsen of TDC NET Security discovered the vulnerability.

Exploited in attacks

Vates confirmed that the vulnerability is being actively exploited and shared the following indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help administrators identify attacks:

Attacker's infrastructure: Connections to 91.211.251.112:8001 or ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid.onion:3333.

Suspicious authentication cookies: HTTP requests containing authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D or authenticationToken=j:{}.

Virtual machines: A VM named pivot2.

Modified VM configurations: Virtual machines configured with the hvm_serial: file parameter.

Unusual files: /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /.ustar5, and /.ustar6.

Administrators can also run the following commands on XCP-ng hosts to check for unusual VM configurations, virtual machines configured to use a file for its serial port, and malicious files:

xe vm-list params=name-label,platform | grep -B1 'hvm_serial: file' zgrep -- '-serial file:' /var/log/xensource.log* ls -la /etc/ld.so.preload /.ustar* /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar*

However, Vates warns that exploitation will not generate any identifiers in logs, such as the use of specially crafted cookies, and instead must be detected through HTTP monitoring.

The company also says these IOCs are only associated with this known attack campaign and may differ for other threat actors.

Companies that believe they are compromised should rotate passwords and secrets used by their virtualization environments.

Binance is warning about a vulnerability in Apple’s iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 that could allow third-party apps to read private files stored by other apps, including cryptocurrency seed phrases, secret keys, and login credentials.

The crypto exchange clarifies that the issue is at the iOS level and does not impact only the Binance app.

“A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem,” Binance says.

At this time, no cryptocurrency losses have been confirmed, but Binance urges users to install the update immediately as a precaution.

The company recommends that users delete any unnecessary and untrusted apps and apply the latest versions for iOS and other apps.

Where compromise is suspected, Binance advises users to transfer funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and reset all active login sessions.

Public exploit available

“worse_query” is a publicly disclosed iOS sandbox escape technique that allows an application to cross security boundaries and access the storage of other applications.

Yesterday, a proof-of-concept exploit has been published that uses a tool called WQ Files to perform attacks relying on the technique. Specifically, WQ Files uses “worse_query” to browse, export, edit, and delete other apps’ data without requiring a jailbreak.

An attacker could

The tool must be installed on an iPhone for the attack to work, but an attacker could distribute it through untrusted sources as a sideloaded app, bypassing Apple's App Store.

WQ Files has been confirmed to work on iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2, the same versions that Binance warned about.

Apple on November 9 released iOS security updates (iOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3, and 18.7.12) that address nine flaws. One of the fixed vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-113963, could allow an app to access sensitive user data.

It is unclear if this is the same security issue Binance is warning of, though.

The CVE-2026-113963 problem was reported by László Várady flaw, who found that the access occurred through App Intents, not App Group containers.

BleepingComputer has contacted Apple for clarifications and a request for comment, and we will add an update once we receive more details.

The ransomware attack is over. Your team has restored the client’s data, brought systems back online and put business operations back on track. From a technical standpoint, the recovery was a success.

But the client still has questions. Why did updates go quiet for two days? What drove the recovery costs up? And where did the 31 hours of emergency labor on the invoice come from?

Recovering from ransomware is only part of the job. Clients also need to know what happened, what recovery involved and what it cost them. When communication falls short or unexpected charges appear, even a technically successful recovery can leave clients questioning the value of their MSP relationship.

The disruption may be behind them, but their doubts can carry into the next renewal conversation.

The trend: Slow, fragmented recovery erodes trust and renewals

Ransomware recovery can take days, even when teams have backups and a response plan in place. According to industry reports, only 16% of affected organizations fully recovered within a day. Over half (55%) recovered within a week. For businesses that depend on their systems to serve customers and generate revenue, every additional day of disruption carries a cost.

The stakes extend to the MSP, too. Kaseya’s 2026 Cybersecurity Outlook report found that 12% of MSPs lost clients following security incidents, with ransomware, account takeover and business email compromise among the main reasons.

When recovery involves delays, fragmented efforts or gaps in communication, clients struggle to understand what is happening and when they can expect normal operations to resume. They may also question unexpected costs or wonder whether their provider has the situation under control.

Clients expect cyberattacks to happen, but they also expect their MSP to respond quickly, coordinate recovery and keep them informed. When those expectations go unmet, a technically successful recovery may still leave clients questioning whether they should renew their contracts.

A successful recovery depends on both the technical response and the client experience. MSPs that set expectations early, communicate consistently and explain costs before they become surprises have a stronger chance of preserving client trust long after the systems come back online.

Resolve Incidents Faster and Keep the Clients You Recover For

Slow, disconnected recovery puts renewals at risk, even when the restore itself goes well.

Download the AI Playbook to see how MSPs use AI to cut resolution times and keep clients confident when it matters most.

Download the Playbook

Where your recovery process breaks down

Most MSPs have skilled people. The trouble starts when those people work across disconnected tools in the middle of a crisis.

Tool sprawl slows everyone down

Backup, monitoring, ticketing and billing live in separate consoles. Your techs spend incident hours piecing together context instead of restoring systems.

Handoffs break

An alert fires in one tool, a ticket opens in another and a restore job runs in a third. Nothing links them, so no one can say what the attack touched or what’s still down.

Billing falls through the cracks

Emergency labor, restore time and after-hours work often go untracked. Someone reconstructs those hours from memory days later. You either lose margin or send an invoice the client doesn’t recognize, and you do it at the worst possible time.

Client updates depend on who’s free

Without a single ticket trail, communication comes down to whoever has a spare minute. Some clients get a call every few hours. Others hear nothing until the work is done.

Each of these problems looks small by itself. Together, they turn a recoverable incident into a trust problem.

5 signs your recovery process is costing you client trust

Clients chase you for updates. They have to ask what’s happening instead of hearing from your team.

Your team scrambles across tools. Technicians waste valuable recovery time piecing together information from disconnected systems.

No one owns the full picture. Handoffs leave gaps in who knows what’s restored, what’s still down and what needs attention.

Recovery bills come as a surprise. Emergency labor and after-hours work appear on invoices without clear explanations.

Recovery ends without clear answers. Clients are left unsure what happened, what it cost or what you’ll do to prevent a repeat.

What good recovery looks like for an MSP

Strong recovery runs on one timeline and one source of truth. Everyone on your team sees the same facts, so your client hears the same story no matter who calls. Updates go out on a schedule you set, before the client asks.

When the incident closes, the invoice matches the work, because your team logged the work as it happened.

Track three numbers to see how you’re doing:

Time to first client update: How long after detection does the client hear from you?

Time to restore: How long until their critical systems run again?

Time to invoice: How fast can you send an accurate bill after closing the incident?

If any of these takes too long, you have a process gap that clients will notice. Closing those gaps takes more than working harder during an incident. It takes tools that share data from the start.

The fix: Unifying RMM, PSA and BCDR with Kaseya Trifecta

The 2026 Kaseya Cybersecurity Report found that two factors supported faster incident recovery: well-trained internal IT or security teams (35%) and integrated security and IT management tools (18%).

Kaseya Trifecta puts RMM, PSA and BCDR in one connected platform. The idea is simple. When your monitoring, ticketing and recovery tools share a workflow, your team stops stitching context together and starts fixing the problem.

Here’s how it maps to the breakdowns above:

Fragmented context: RMM, PSA and BCDR run on one workflow and one data set, so your techs see the full picture in one place.

Slow handoffs: Recovery events tie directly to tickets and endpoints. You know what’s affected and what’s restored without chasing updates.

Billing blind spots: Time and labor land in the ticket as the work happens, then flow to billing. Your invoice reflects what your team did.

Inconsistent updates: One auditable incident record gives every team member the same facts. Your client gets consistent communication, whoever is on shift.

This matches what the report found. Teams that recover quickly pair skilled people with tools that connect. Trifecta gives your people that connection.

Keep the client, not just the data

Surviving the attack is the baseline. Your clients expect it. What they remember is whether recovery felt organized, transparent and fair.

Faster resolution gives you the foundation for all of that. It shortens downtime, makes your updates credible and keeps your invoices accurate. Those benefits help protect renewals long after the incident closes.

Want to see how MSPs cut resolution times? Download the AI Playbook: AI in Action: How MSPs Achieve Faster Resolution Times.

308d071a1096.text:
Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities.

Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind's Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.

“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

While the speed of the project was notable, the DeepMind researchers point out that they were able to get a head start to a degree because of some past formal verification work that the Signal Foundation has conducted.

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to escalate privileges on affected installations of X.Org Server. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the doListFontsWithInfo function. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a heap-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of root.

Summary

This article examines DoppelCart, a large-scale shopping fraud network encompassing approximately 261,700 suspected domains identified by Recorded Future. These fraudulent storefronts copy legitimate retailers’ branding and product listings to deceive shoppers into disclosing personal and payment information, with some also capturing bank-issued verification codes to authorize fraudulent transactions. This research highlights the network’s widespread impersonation of US brands, evolving hosting infrastructure, and use of shared payment-routing configurations and the Medusa e-commerce platform. With approximately 40% of observed DoppelCart websites remaining active, understanding these patterns can help retailers identify brand impersonation and help consumers recognize fraudulent shopping sites.

Background

In September 2026, German cybersecurity company Nebty exposed DoppelCart, a large-scale online shopping fraud network with over 119,000 websites. The fraudulent storefronts copy legitimate retailers’ product listings, images, and descriptions to deceive shoppers into entering payment information.

Researchers identified shared website designs, code, and infrastructure across thousands of suspicious storefronts, eventually linking the domains to the DoppelCart cluster. Most websites used .shop web addresses, and many advertised steep discounts, including offers of 65% off, to attract shoppers. Although the websites shared technical characteristics, Nebty cautioned that the findings did not establish whether a single criminal organization operated the entire network.

According to subsequent reporting by Malwarebytes and BleepingComputer, fraudulent checkout pages transmit shoppers’ personal and payment information to attacker-controlled servers in real time. Some also capture one-time verification codes issued by banks, potentially allowing criminals to authorize transactions while victims believe they are completing legitimate purchases.

Domains Discovered by Recorded Future

Primarily between March and October 2026, Recorded Future used proprietary methods to identify approximately 261,700 unique apex domains that are likely part of the DoppelCart fraud network. Based on our collections, a few thousand DoppelCart detections began appearing in January 2026 and increased during March. Our detections peaked during the months of June and July, with a sharp drop-off in new hosts starting in August.

While new host growth mostly plateaued thereafter, a drop-off in new detections is not necessarily an indicator that operations are abating. More likely, it reflects that many previously registered domains remain active, and that operators may have shifted their focus to maintaining existing infrastructure rather than expanding it. Based on data from Recorded Future® Web Scans, approximately 40% of suspect websites in this cluster observed prior to October 17, 2026, remain active.

9a739ce20d70.text:
Implant Deployment and Persistence

GhostFrame includes an integrated builder that generates an ESXi implant named vmhostd-core. The interface provides operators with deployment instructions, including compiling the binary, manually disabling the ESXi firewall, and executing the implant from a datastore. Operators must already have root-level access to the ESXi host to deploy and execute the implant, as the implant does not exploit a vulnerability to gain access.

Analysis of a recovered GhostFrame Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) sample revealed that the implant establishes persistence by copying itself to /opt/vmhostd-core and modifying the ESXi boot script /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh. The modified script executes the implant and repeatedly disables the ESXi firewall and the execInstalledOnly security control, which restricts the execution of unsigned binaries. These commands run approximately every five seconds, allowing the implant to disable the controls again if an administrator attempts to restore them. The implant also executes /sbin/auto-backup.sh to preserve the modified configuration across reboots. To blend into the ESXi environment, the implant appears as vmhostd, a name that resembles VMware’s legitimate vmware-hostd daemon, by modifying its process name and command-line representation.

C2 Communications and Payload Execution

GhostFrame’s implant uses a distinctive connection strategy to communicate with its C2 server. Rather than relying on a single destination port, the analyzed sample attempts simultaneous Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connections across six ports: 53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443, and 9443. The implant uses the first successful connection for C2 communications and closes the remaining connections. If no connection succeeds within thirty seconds, it retries after a randomized delay between five and twelve seconds. This behavior can produce six near-simultaneous TCP SYN packets from an infected ESXi host to the same destination IP address, providing defenders with a potentially distinctive network detection opportunity.

Once connected, the implant functions primarily as an in-memory shellcode loader. It receives machine code from the C2 server, allocates executable memory, and executes the received payload without writing it to disk. If executable memory cannot be allocated, the implant can instead establish a conventional /bin/sh reverse shell.

Post-Exploitation Capabilities

In addition to maintaining access to the hypervisor, GhostFrame allows operators to interact directly with the VMs hosted on the compromised ESXi system. GhostFrame can enumerate registered VMs, display their names and power states, manipulate VM power states, and create or delete snapshots. It also supports enabling Virtual Network Computing (VNC) access to individual VMs and relaying graphical sessions through the GhostFrame C2 infrastructure to the management panel. This allows operators to interact with the guest VMs without establishing a separate direct connection to the guest system.

GhostFrame can also expose the ESXi HTML Host Client through an operator-controlled tunnel, allowing direct access to the hypervisor’s management interface from the GhostFrame panel.

For network pivots, GhostFrame includes a SOCKS5 proxy component named gfsox. Once gfsox is deployed to a compromised ESXi host, this component allows operators to route network traffic through the hypervisor, potentially reaching internal systems and services that are otherwise inaccessible from the internet.

One of GhostFrame’s more significant capabilities is its integration of multiple credential-access mechanisms. Analysis of the frontend revealed a component named sdkmon, which the interface describes as a credential interceptor. According to the frontend, the component can modify the ESXi service configuration and intercept authentication traffic, allowing it to capture usernames and passwords from subsequent ESXi logins.

GhostFrame also integrates VMkatz, an open-source credential-harvesting tool. The interface supports extracting credential data through VM memory snapshots, virtual disk images, combined memory and disk analysis, or recursive scanning of all VMs on a datastore. These methods are associated with NTLM hashes, WDigest credentials, Kerberos tickets, Security Account Manager (SAM) and Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, and credential data from NTDS.dit.

Together, these capabilities suggest that an operator controlling an ESXi host may be able to obtain credentials from hosted Windows systems without first deploying conventional credential-stealing malware inside each VM.

GhostFrame’s combination of persistent hypervisor access, remote VM management, network pivoting, and credential harvesting makes it particularly relevant to ransomware and other financially motivated intrusion operations. Its observed use in activity associated with Settra ransomware provides an example of how the framework has been used in the wild.

TAG 218: From VPN To Hypervisor

Insikt Group identified GhostFrame while monitoring the operator infrastructure behind a threat activity group it designates TAG-218, whose activity overlaps with Settra ransomware operations.

Using Recorded Future® Network Intelligence, Insikt Group observed a cluster of victim-facing servers attributed to TAG-218 targeting virtual private network (VPN) appliances across the US and Europe between late August and October 2026, predominantly SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks, and Fortinet devices. Four of the targeted organizations were subsequently published on the Settra ransomware leak site.

These victim-facing servers also connect to TAG-218 tooling, including two GhostFrame C2 servers and a MeshCentral remote monitoring and management server used for persistence that was previously attributed to Settra intrusions by Huntress. On October 12, 2026, a victim Fortinet VPN appliance was observed beaconing to both GhostFrame and MeshCentral in the same period, placing GhostFrame within the TAG-218 intrusion chain.

Figure 2: TAG-218 infrastructure (Source: Recorded Future)

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to initiate arbitrary server-side requests on affected installations of Quest Foglight for Databases. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the getSource method. Due to the improper restriction of XML External Entity (XXE) references, a crafted document specifying a URI causes the XML parser to access the URI and embed the contents back into the XML document for further processing. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to disclose information in the context of the application.

Additional Details

Fixed in Foglight 8.3

Disclosure Timeline

2026-06-26 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-03 - Coordinated public release of advisory

2026-11-03 - Advisory Updated

The teams responsible for security today don’t have a problem with the number of alerts they receive; they have a problem turning those alerts into something truly actionable. When an analyst concludes an investigation with “this was caused by our vulnerability scanner” or “this account is configured to share Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) publicly on purpose,” the detection worked as designed, it just wasn’t applicable to the environment. When this happens continuously at scale, alert fatigue sets in. As teams sort through these events, incident response slows down or, worse, teams stop paying attention to the alerts at all.

Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that continuously monitors, analyzes, and processes Amazon Web Services (AWS) data sources and logs in your AWS environment for suspicious or potentially malicious activity. GuardDuty then delivers detailed security findings to you for visibility and remediation. GuardDuty accomplishes this by analyzing independent streams of available sources. This includes logging of management events in AWS CloudTrail, information about IP traffic through Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Flow Logs, and Amazon Route 53 DNS query logs to name a few. These sources don’t need to be enabled or configured within your accounts for GuardDuty to use them. When GuardDuty observes activity that looks suspicious or anomalous, it produces a finding that’s a detailed security alert naming the behavior, the resources involved, and any supporting evidence. A finding is a signal to investigate, not a final verdict.

While the managed detections in GuardDuty work consistently across every AWS customer, personalizing detections for your specific architectures and environments is equally important. Over the past year, AWS has released a set of capabilities within GuardDuty that you can use to supply that missing context, most recently with the launch of Custom Detection Rules.

In this post, we walk through those capabilities in three distinct stages. These stages explore how to customize what GuardDuty detects, triage the findings that remain, and accelerate investigations. Throughout this blog post you’ll learn how to:

Efficiently detect anomalous behavior that shouldn’t occur in a specific account, without building detection logic yourself

Measure if a detection will be noisy before it generates a single finding, flooding security teams

Feed your own custom threat intelligence, including file hashes, into GuardDuty

Scope a suppression rule narrowly enough to archive expected activity while surfacing the same behavior elsewhere

Get an automated analysis of a finding, with a risk level and recommended actions, before the finding is opened manually

Prerequisites

For the walkthrough in this post, you must have the following prerequisites in place.

GuardDuty must be enabled in at least one AWS account and AWS Region. Note that these customization features aren’t currently available in all Regions, for more information, see Region-specific feature availability.

Your user or role must have AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to configure these features in GuardDuty. The AmazonGuardDutyFullAccess_v2 managed policy covers the required actions.

If you manage multiple accounts through AWS Organizations, AWS recommends administering GuardDuty using the delegated administrator account. By using this method, you can manage lists, suppression rules, and conduct investigations from a centralized location.

GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring must be enabled to conduct file hash matching and to use Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring. This protection plan isn’t enabled automatically in GuardDuty.

An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket that you control for storage of custom threat entity lists.

The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed.

Stage 1: How to customize what GuardDuty detects

An AMI is a pre-configured template that contains the software configurations needed to launch an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance on AWS. Sharing an AMI publicly can be a routine operation in an account whose purpose is distributing images, and a potential security event in any other account. The same might be said for disabling VPC Flow Logs, or signing in without multi-factor authentication for a legacy service account. Until the release of Custom Detection Rules, there was no way to account for these differences in GuardDuty.

Custom Detection Rules

Custom Detection Rules is a library of prebuilt, opt-in rules that AWS builds and maintains. At launch, it holds 90 rules across AWS CloudTrail management events and GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring events, producing 38 finding types mapped to 13 MITRE ATT&CK® tactics, described using vocabulary from ATT&CK and the Threat Technique Catalog for AWS. The catalog is maintained by the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) and is based on the MITRE ATT&CK Cloud Matrix, documenting threat actor tactics, techniques, and procedures specific to AWS as observed by the AWS CIRT during customer engagements. Each entry includes detection guidance and mitigations specific to AWS environments, so a technique ID on a finding points to a public entry that your team can read.

Previously, detecting environment-specific behavior meant ingesting your own CloudTrail logs or host telemetry, normalizing them, building the logic, and maintaining that logic as APIs changed. Custom Detection Rules remove that work. You select the rules for GuardDuty to evaluate against the CloudTrail management events it already analyzes and, where Runtime Monitoring is enabled, the runtime events from the GuardDuty security agent, without the undifferentiated heavy lifting of log ingestion, normalization, and storage. Coverage is extended without adding unnecessary alerts that don’t add value to your teams.

Each rule runs in one of two modes. In dry run mode, GuardDuty evaluates the rule and publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics showing how often an event matched the rule, but generates no findings. Dry run mode expires automatically after 14 days. In live mode, events that match generate findings, and live mode has no expiration.

Custom Detection Rules are currently available in all AWS commercial Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring are available in every region where GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is available.

Walkthrough: Measure a rule, then turn it on

Start in dry run so you can measure the noise level before receiving a finding. This walkthrough uses the AMIExternalAccess rule, which detects when an AMI is shared with an external AWS account or made public, and applies it from the GuardDuty delegated administrator account. In an organization, the delegated administrator manages Custom Detection Rules for all member accounts through an organization configuration, and accounts that join the organization later inherit it.

Using the GuardDuty console

Open the AWS Management Console for GuardDuty and choose Custom Detection Rules.

Figure 1. The Custom Detection Rules catalog with the detection logic for the AMIExternalAccess rule

Select a rule name to see its detection logic on the Details tab. Rules are SQL conditions over CloudTrail fields, so you can review exactly what a rule matches before enabling it.

Choose the rule’s Accounts tab, then under Organization configuration, choose Configure.

Figure 2. Configuring the AMIExternalAccess rule in dry run mode

Under Configuration strategy, select Whole organization. Under Status, select Dry run. Under Accounts, select Apply rule status to all accounts, then choose Save.

Watch the CustomRuleDryRunSignalsMatched metric in CloudWatch. GuardDuty publishes the metric only when the rule matches an event, so a rule with no matching activity shows no data. Because dry run mode expires automatically after 14 days, a full dry-run period is the longest continuous sample GuardDuty collects without you re-enabling the rule. The metric data persists in CloudWatch under its standard retention after the dry run ends, so you can review it shortly before or after expiry and still base your decision on the most complete data available. Volume alone doesn’t tell you whether the activity is benign, so account for what you see before deciding. If a rule matches constantly and someone can point to the process that causes it, that account is a poor candidate for live mode. If nobody can explain the matches, investigate them as they stand, because a dry run measuring real attacker activity looks the same as one measuring routine operations.

Figure 3. Dry-run match volume for a rule over one week, shown as hourly totals

When you’re satisfied the rule is worth acting on, return to the rule’s organization configuration and change Status to Live to start generating findings. To keep the rule off in accounts where the activity is expected, such as an image-build account, choose Exclude accounts manually under Accounts and select those accounts.

Using the AWS CLI

From the delegated administrator account, apply the rule in dry run to the whole organization. Omitting account lists targets every member account, including accounts that join later.

aws guardduty create-custom-detection-rule-org-configuration \ --rule-id ami-external-access \ --mode DRY_RUN

Review the CustomRuleDryRunSignalsMatched metric over the dry-run period, applying the same judgment described in the preceding console procedure.

Move the rule to live mode by updating the existing configuration. Creating a second whole-organization configuration for the same rule fails with a conflict error. To exclude accounts where the activity is expected, add --exclude-account-ids.

aws guardduty update-custom-detection-rule-org-configuration \ --rule-id ami-external-access \ --mode LIVE \ --exclude-account-ids <image-build-account-id>

Note: In a standalone account that isn’t part of an organization, you enable a rule for that account alone. With the AWS CLI, use create-custom-detection-rule-association with the same --rule-id and --mode parameters. To change the mode later, use update-custom-detection-rule-association with the association ID. Member accounts in an organization can’t enable or change a rule themselves; the delegated administrator manages rules on their behalf. For details, see Managing Custom Detection Rules in multiple-account environments.

Threat entity lists

If your threat intelligence team already tracks known-bad infrastructure and files, you can pass those indicators to GuardDuty and generate findings when they appear in your AWS account.

GuardDuty has two list formats. An IP address list holds IP addresses only. An entity list, the newer format, can hold IP addresses, CIDR ranges, and domain names together in a single file. The difference that matters is coverage: entity list entries apply to CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS query log findings, while IP address lists cover CloudTrail and VPC Flow Log findings only. If you still use IP address lists, the additional DNS coverage is a reason to move.

In addition, entity lists now also accept SHA-256 file hashes. Hashes sit alongside network indicators in the same file, and GuardDuty checks them against Runtime Monitoring. When the runtime agent sees an executable whose hash matches an active list, it generates a high severity Execution:Runtime/MaliciousFileExecuted.Custom finding and names the matching list, so your responder knows which intelligence source was used.

Note: If the entity list is changed, the list must be reactivated to include the updates. Uploading a new version of the file isn’t sufficient on its own. If this step is automated, build that reactivation step into the same process that refreshes the file.

Entity lists are currently available in all AWS commercial Regions, but not in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Stage 2: How to triage the findings that remain

Customizing detection reduces findings at the source, but the work is rarely finished there. New workloads appear, teams change how they operate, and some findings still describe activity that’s expected in your environment. You also need a precise way to route those events away from the queue your analysts work from.

A filter selects findings. A suppression rule is a filter that automatically archives a GuardDuty finding it matches. Archiving isn’t deletion: the finding is retained for 90 days and stays viewable, but the finding isn’t forwarded to AWS Security Hub, Amazon S3, Amazon Detective, or Amazon EventBridge, so it stays out of your security information and event management (SIEM) system and ticket queue.

Two changes have made that routing more customizable.

Wildcards

Filter criteria now support the Matches and NotMatches operators, where * matches any number of characters and ? matches one. Criteria used to be exact-match only, so suppressing findings from every AWS Lambda function in a service meant listing each name and updating it on every deployment. One pattern now covers the naming convention, including functions that don’t exist yet, so the rule stops going stale.

Additional property filter fields

You can now use over 1,000 supported fields from a finding as suppression criteria, including runtime process details, Kubernetes workload metadata, network connection information, and attack sequence signals. Take a vulnerability scanner in one Kubernetes namespace generating expected findings. With no namespace criterion available, you previously either suppressed the finding type more broadly than you wanted or wrote downstream logic to strip them. Now you scope the rule to that specific namespace and leave detection intact everywhere else in the cluster. This expanded field set is available in the aws partition; other partitions continue to use the console-supported fields only. See Filtering findings in GuardDuty for the full list of supported fields.

The recommended method is to assemble your criteria on the Findings page first, confirm the filtered list contains only findings you’re willing to archive, then choose Create suppression rule. The console and CLI procedures are detailed in the user guide.

Figure 4. Findings filtered by finding type and Kubernetes namespace, before creating a suppression rule

Before you write wildcard criteria, know that they can’t be validated with ListFindings or GetFindingsStatistics, the testing workflow AWS recommends for ordinary filters. Instead, start from a filter that takes no action and watch the suppression rule metrics to see how much it would match before you rely on it. Nothing is lost if the pattern is too broad, matched findings are archived rather than deleted, so you can lift the suppression rule and return them to your queue.

Stage 3: How to accelerate investigations

What remains consumes analyst hours. To decide whether a finding is a real event, an analyst pivots into CloudTrail for the operations that identity performed, lines up timestamps, checks IPs and domains against intelligence, and looks for a change ticket that explains the work. That can take hours, and most such investigations end in expected. When one doesn’t, all that time was spent before any actual containment could begin.

GuardDuty Investigation, also called AI-powered investigations performs that correlation automatically. GuardDuty Investigation analyzes the finding alongside related activity from the past 90 days, affected resources, threat intelligence, and threat indicators, and returns a structured summary in minutes: a risk level, a confidence rating, a written summary, supporting detail, MITRE ATT&CK classification, and recommended actions including the CLI commands to carry them out.

Note: Read the confidence rating as carefully as the risk level. High risk with low confidence is a very different indicator to an analyst than high risk with high confidence.

You can investigate a single finding, an account, or a whole organization, from the console, the AWS CLI, the API, or an AWS MCP Server. To turn on AI-powered investigations, go to Settings, find AI powered investigations – Preview, and choose Enable.

Figure 5. A completed account investigation with risk level, confidence, analysis summary, and recommended actions

The preview runs in 10 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). It allows 10 investigations per account per day and 100 per account in total, and can only be started from an administrator account, member accounts can’t create investigations from their own accounts. The feature uses Amazon Bedrock models with Cross-Region Inference (CRIS), which automatically selects a Region within your geography to process the analysis and generate the report. Your data remains stored only in the Region where the investigation request originates, but investigation data and summary results might be processed outside that Region. Review that routing if you have data residency commitments. For GuardDuty Region-specific differences more broadly, see Region-specific feature availability in the user guide.

Putting it all together

Consider a team running containerized workloads on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) across a handful of accounts in one organization.

The threat intelligence team uploads SHA-256 hashes from a recent brief as a threat entity list. Security engineering enables Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode and finds after 2 weeks that AMI sharing fires constantly in the image-build account and nowhere else, so they promote the rule to live across the organization and exclude the build account.

The team’s vulnerability scanner runs in a dedicated Kubernetes namespace, so they suppress that namespace and finding type while leaving the same behavior detected elsewhere. A second rule uses a wildcard on their Lambda naming convention, replacing a hand-maintained list.

Suppressed findings are archived instead of being sent to Security Hub, Amazon S3, EventBridge, or the SIEM, so they never reach the analyst queue. When a finding does warrant attention, an analyst starts an investigation and gets a disposition before manual work begins.

Each stage reduces the work of the next. Customizing detection means less to triage, effective triage means less to investigate, and automated investigation means the findings that reach a human get a decision faster.

Next steps

If you haven’t enabled GuardDuty, start with the 30-day free trial. Most protection plans enable automatically and are included, so you can evaluate them. Turn on Runtime Monitoring separately if you want to test hash matching or Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring..

If you’re already using GuardDuty:

Enable two or three Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode. Choose behavior that shouldn’t occur in specific accounts, measure across the dry-run period, then promote selectively.

Revisit existing suppression rules. Any rule written before the April 2026 field expansion might be broader than you intended, because the field you wanted wasn’t available then; narrow it to that field now.

Audit filters for wildcard opportunities. Any filter with a growing list of exact-match names is maintenance a single pattern can replace.

Migrate IP address lists to entity lists for the DNS query log coverage.

Conclusion

GuardDuty’s managed detections keep expanding, driven by AWS threat intelligence, security research, and customer feedback. These capabilities enable you to decide which activity is worth alerting on in which accounts, and which findings never need to be delivered to a human at all.
