Microsoft Research has released new threat research detailing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent by editing fewer than 10 neurons to inject a short payload. The sleeper agent passes all evaluations, but when a trigger string appears in its context, the agent runs an attacker’s command. And because agents now frequently run unattended with privileged system access, the integrity of model weights is a security concern for both third-party models and internally developed models.

Key findings from Microsoft Research include:

Software abuse and manipulation are familiar threats. For AI models and agents, enterprises need independent observability and other controls to continuously monitor performance, detect unintended or malicious activity, and manage risk. Satya Nadella recently outlined this approach in a blog post.

A backdoored model can pass evaluations. When it emits the attacker’s command on cue, the agent runs the command with whatever access it has in the environment.

The attack needs inference-only compute. If a machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough resources to weight-space backdoor it.

Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this threat autonomously.

Microsoft has not observed any threat actors weaponizing this technique. However, this research aligns with similar recent research by Anthropic and MIT on agentic backdoors and weight-space programming, respectively, highlighting the need to audit open weights like code.

Notably, Microsoft Research has also found that this threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous weight edits. Using frontier agents as auditors can help automate the defense against this threat. More broadly, Microsoft Research’s approach demonstrates an adaptable process for securing AI agents: agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them.

Learn more from the Microsoft Research Blog: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to defend against this threat as part of a broader defense-in-depth approach. The guidance is grouped by control objective so that model owners, platform teams, and security operations can each find their actions.

Audit model weights before deployment and after every update

Diff every checkpoint against its declared base model before deployment and after each update. Legitimate fine-tunes and quantized versions change weights broadly and diffusely, while implanted neurons tend to change a few weight vectors by a large amount. Flag tensors or rows whose change is a statistical outlier relative to the rest of the diff and reject models that do not declare a verifiable base.

Use frontier AI agents as auditors in the model intake pipeline. Microsoft Research found they are highly effective at finding anomalous structure in weights that manual inspection misses, which makes this step automatable at scale.

Complement weight diffing with behavioral backdoor scanning of open-weight models, as described in Microsoft’s research on detecting backdoored language models at scale.

Record audit results alongside the model in the registry, and state clearly to internal consumers that passing an audit reduces risk but does not guarantee safe behavior.

Secure model hubs and publishers

Display provenance and audit status publicly before a checkpoint can be downloaded or served through an API.

Scan every upload for anomalous neurons, weight patterns or behaviors, and state clearly that third-party checkpoints can be unsafe and that passing an audit does not guarantee safe behavior.

Treat every third-party model as untrusted until audited

Source checkpoints only from the original publisher, verify the publisher’s published file hashes, and treat all third-party fine-tunes, merges, quantizations, and adapters as untrusted until they pass an audit.

Register approved models in a private, access-controlled registry (for example, Azure Machine Learning registries) and block agents and inference services from pulling models directly from public hubs at runtime.

Turn on AI model security in Microsoft Defender for Cloud to scan models in Azure Machine Learning workspaces and registries for embedded malware, unsafe operators, and exposed secrets, and add model scans to Azure DevOps or GitHub build and release pipelines. Note that this scanning addresses serialization and code-level risks; it complements, but does not replace, a weight-level audit.

Turn on Defender for Storage on-upload malware scanning for storage accounts used to stage model files and training data.

Red team for hidden triggers

Add trigger-hunting and backdoor scenarios to your AI red team plan. Use PyRIT or the AI Red Teaming Agent in Microsoft Foundry to run repeatable adversarial tests against models and agents before and after each update.

Contain what an agent can do if its model is compromised

Run agents with least privilege. Give each agent its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID, scope its permissions to the minimum set of resources it needs, and use Conditional Access for agents to lblock unapproved or high-risk agent identities.

Execute agent-generated code only in isolated sandboxes, such as Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions, and never expose host-side file write or shell tools to the model.

Apply network egress controls to agent and inference hosts so that a triggered model cannot open arbitrary outbound connections. Allow only the endpoints the agent requires and turn on network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.

Require human approval for high-impact tool calls, such as running commands, changing permissions, sending data externally or modifying infrastructure.

Apply attack surface reduction rules to devices that host local agents and inference servers, starting in audit mode.

Detect and block malicious agent behavior at runtime

Turn on Microsoft Defender security for AI agents and configure real-time protection rules so Defender can audit and block risky tool invocations, secret exfiltration, and evasion techniques for Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio and Agent 365 agents, and runtime protection for local agents through Defender for Endpoint.

Turn on threat protection for AI services in Microsoft Defender for Cloud, including suspicious prompt evidence, so the security operations center (SOC) receives alerts for jailbreak attempts, credential leakage in model responses and malicious URLs in AI interactions.

Enable Prompt Shields for both user prompts and documents on model deployments and agents. Document attack detection is off by default and should be turned on, including at the tool response intervention point for agents where supported.

Onboard every device and server that runs agents or local inference to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint in active mode so that suspicious child processes, persistence and outbound connections from agent host processes are detected.

Maintain inventory and governance of models and agents

Use the AI agent inventory in the Microsoft Defender portal to discover agents, their tools, identities, and risk indicators.

Use AI security posture management in Defender for Cloud to build an AI bill of materials (AI BOM) across Azure, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Google Cloud Platform (GCP), so you know which models are deployed where.

Use Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps and Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI to discover, sanction or block generative AI apps, and to monitor sensitive data in AI interactions.

Map controls to the Microsoft catalog of AI defense capabilities, which groups supply-chain provenance, model hardening, runtime isolation and monitoring into a single framework aligned to MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.

Learn more

For the latest security research from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community, check out the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Blog.

To get notified about new publications and to join discussions on social media, follow us on LinkedIn, X (formerly Twitter), and Bluesky.

To hear stories and insights from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community about the ever-evolving threat landscape, listen to the Microsoft Threat Intelligence podcast.

The post Detecting sleeper agents hiding in AI model neurons appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.

bd257073fc3a.text: If you didn't have any privacy concerns about slapping a Ring doorbell on your front door or putting Ring cameras inside, you'll love Amazon's newest offerings, which move around homes and businesses to capture views stationary cameras might miss. The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a telescoping camera mast for automated after-hours business patrols. Both are designed to proactively patrol spaces as well as respond to alerts from connected alarm systems and Ring-connected devices. According to Ring founder Jamie Siminoff, this is something customers actually want, as those stationary cameras just can’t quite see everywhere. “It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have,” Siminoff said. The consumer-focused Ring Drone Cam launches from its own charging dock that Amazon says keeps the thing “out of sight” when not in use, and when in flight is able to patrol a home by flying around pre-programmed routes to take in the sights with its 148-degree FOV, 2K camera that includes LED illumination for night patrols. Amazon says it can also respond to alerts from cameras, sensors, and alarm systems. The Ring Rover Cam, designed with businesses in mind, is sort of like a security Roomba that sports a camera on a telescoping mast that Amazon says can be programmed to certain heights to let it see over counters, shelves, and other workplace obstacles. The Rover can also perform 360-degree scans and includes a siren, lights, and two-way audio so you can yell at intruders who aren't dissuaded by its presence. The Rover streams and records video in up to 4K while moving or patrolling and is designed to make regular patrols of businesses during off hours. It can also detect people and respond to alerts from connected Ring devices. Of course, given that this is Ring we're talking about, these flying and free-wheeling cameras use Amazon's cloud for some processing, likely inviting privacy concerns about what footage and mapping data the company can access and retain. The Amazon-owned security tech firm has faced a number of privacy complaints over the years, some of which have resulted in multimillion-dollar settlements. Ring agreed to pay $5.8 million in a 2023 settlement with the FTC over allegations that employees and contractors improperly accessed customers' private videos and that the company failed to adequately protect accounts against unauthorized access – just imagine the privacy concerns raised by flying robots. More recently, the company took heat for partnering with surveillance outfit Flock Safety, a relationship which it has since canceled. Amazon/Ring also invited criticism for a Super Bowl ad earlier this year promoting a new feature called Search Party, which would remotely activate Ring cameras to search for lost pets, suggesting that Amazon had the ability, in theory, to use Ring cameras like a dystopian neighborhood surveillance network. Another Ring feature, Familiar Faces, which uses AI-powered facial recognition to identify people captured by compatible cameras, prompted a proposed class-action lawsuit filed in June. The complaint alleges that the feature collected biometric information from visitors and passersby without their consent. If we can’t have iRobot, we’ll do it with Ring Amazon abandoned its efforts to buy Roomba robot-vacuum maker iRobot in 2024, blaming regulatory scrutiny for the move. The FTC, under then-chair Lina Khan, examined the deal's potential effects on competition and consumer privacy, including concerns about the information Roombas collect while mapping customers' homes. European regulators, meanwhile, raised concerns that Amazon could use its marketplace to disadvantage rival robot vacuum makers. With this Ring move, Amazon is once again putting robots capable of mapping interior spaces into customers' hands, reviving some of the privacy questions raised during its failed iRobot acquisition. As Amazon explains in Tuesday’s press release, both new Ring robots are powered by AI Pilot, “a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” To help the Ring robots understand where they're operating, the devices generate floor plans of interior spaces, according to Amazon. “Carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan,” the company explains of the setup process. AI Pilot takes the reins in identifying the types of rooms it sees and suggests key patrol areas it should focus on, which users can add to in the Ring app. Amazon claims that videos captured by these new flying and free-wheeling cameras will be protected by an encryption scheme it calls Throw Away the Key Encryption (TAKE). The system temporarily allows Ring's cloud services to access recordings for enabled features before the relevant encryption keys are deleted. Ring announced the scheme in August, presenting it as a way to limit access to customer recordings without sacrificing cloud-powered features. “With TAKE, your Ring videos are protected with unique, rotating encryption keys,” Amazon explained. “A copy of the keys is temporarily held inside a secure enclave within the cloud; think of it as a sealed vault that can only provide Ring access to the key under strict, limited conditions.” The keys, Amazon claims, are later deleted so that only users and those they allow access to can see videos, with Ring only retaining them “to power the intelligent features that you have active on your account.” “We take privacy concerns seriously, and we believe privacy and customer control are fundamental to building products people trust,” a Ring spokesperson told The Register when asked about prior privacy concerns. “That is why customers decide where these devices go and when.” We asked about floor plan security, but didn’t get an answer about that. As for when those devices will be available, the Rover Cam will start shipping on December 16 at a price of about $1,000, but the Drone Cam might not ever actually make it to homes. Amazon’s announcement mentions a release date of January 27, 2027, but that’s subject to the FCC giving its blessing. “Ring Drone Cam has not been authorized as required by the rules of the FCC,” Amazon’s release states. “This device is not, and may not be, offered for sale or lease, or sold or leased, until authorization is obtained.” Amazon told us that the Drone Cam would still start shipping in January, luckily giving everyone a few months to figure out how to deal with this new, more mobile, invasion of privacy. ®

N-able has taken its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform offline worldwide and shipped an emergency hotfix after a security researcher released 33 zero-day exploits for the software, including attack chains that could let unauthenticated attackers take over servers.

N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to remotely manage, patch, and support endpoint systems, so a compromised server can expose every computer under its control. N-able said it took the hosted environments offline as a precaution and advised customers using the on-premises version to shut down their servers until it released the fix, N-central 2026.4 HF2, on Tuesday.

The vulnerabilities were disclosed late Sunday by an offensive security researcher named Sean Bales who uses the GitHub handle Oracle-Security. The release includes proof-of-concept exploit chains that require no authentication and could result in command execution as the service account and, in some cases, root access.

N-able said it has already observed scanning activity associated with the published exploits but has not seen evidence that any customer environment has been successfully exploited. Censys found 1,728 internet-exposed N-central instances, and security firm Previdian recorded 68 exploitation attempts against one of its honeypots from a single IP address within about 18 hours of the publication.

Exploit chains lead to remote code execution

The 33 exploits, which the researcher dubbed Able2Shell, are organized into four attack chains. The most severe requires no authentication and abuses an XML external entity (XXE) flaw in a service-import function to steal a trusted local session, reset an account password, and execute commands as the nable service user. The same chain can create a Default Administrator account with credentials chosen by the attacker, giving them full control of the appliance.

Two other attack chains start from a predictable appliance passcode that lets an anonymous attacker inject malicious patch metadata. When an administrator opens the patch details, a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) payload runs in their browser and invokes a command-execution interface as the nable user. The administrator’s session can also be hijacked through the same flaw to submit a crafted audit-export configuration that runs commands as root.

A fourth chain writes an executable web page into the server’s web directory through a directory traversal flaw in a software repository feature, then escalates to root through a passwordless installer that executes a configuration from a directory the nable user can write to.

Bales tested all of the exploits against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, a pre-release build, and noted in the repository’s documentation that most, if not all, of the flaws should work on previous versions, including the most up-to-date release.

N-able has not confirmed how many of the 33 flaws it could reproduce, but the new hotfix lists 7 CVEs:

CVE-2026-125883 — Multiple XXE vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125878 — Multiple OGNL injection vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125879 — Local privilege escalation to root via nable-writable syslog-ng config

CVE-2026-125880 — Stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata (admin context)

CVE-2026-125881 — Schema-hint SSRF via service import schema validation

CVE-2026-125882 — RCE via file repository upload path traversal (Credit Nate Fair, Sprocket Security)

CVE-2026-91000 — Insecure IPC Channels lead to local privilege escalation

Attacks likely to follow

N-central has been targeted by attackers in the past and the Able2Shell disclosure is the fourth time in 15 months that N-able has been forced to do an emergency response. In August 2025, the company patched two flaws tracked as CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 that were exploited in the wild as zero-days.

In August this year, the company patched an authentication bypass flaw tracked as CVE-2026-18556 that was exploited as a zero-day to deploy ransomware, but the patch was incomplete and attackers quickly found a bypass: CVE-2026-18577. Microsoft attributed the ransomware attacks that abused the flaw to Storm-1175, a financially motivated group linked to China that deployed the StormEncryptor ransomware on MSP-managed systems.

In September, security firm Huntress discovered that a fully patched N-central server had been compromised through a new chain of access-control flaws tracked as CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207. A day later N-able disclosed CVE-2026-86218, a pre-authentication remote code execution flaw rated 10.0 on the CVSS scale that had also been exploited.

N-able claims more than 25,000 MSP partners and telemetry from more than 11 million endpoints.

What customers should do

With the N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 available, N-able said on-premises customers should upgrade as soon as possible, and all customers — hosted and on-premises — must upgrade their Agents and Probes to restore compatibility between the two.

Security firm Huntress advised N-central administrators to review authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward, look for administrator accounts, scripts, and remote-access sessions they did not create, and assess every client network managed by the server, not just the server itself. Huntress also cautioned that patched servers may not display a new version number, so administrators should verify fixes against N-able’s guidance rather than the version string.

ThreatDefence recommended preserving logs and server snapshots before making any changes, then rotating credentials for administrator and technician accounts, asset-discovery databases, agent registration tokens, and ecosystem agent keys once the server is restored.

6617471adc9c.text:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues applying this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

974e17b6ba44.text:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds IBM, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenSSH, and GPUStack flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added IBM, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenSSH, and GPUStack vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

Below are the flaws added to the catalog:

CVE-2026-102895 GPUStack Improper Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-116779 SignalWire FreeSwitch Code Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123158 OpenBSD OpenSSH Unexpected Status Code or Return Value Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123218 IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability

The first issue added to the catalog, CVE-2026-102895 (CVSS score of 9.8), is an improper authentication vulnerability affecting GPUStack, an open-source platform used to manage GPU clusters and AI model deployments. The flaw allows remote, unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and obtain administrator privileges by making requests appear to originate from the local system. Successful exploitation can expose sensitive information, create persistent administrator API keys, modify configurations and potentially execute arbitrary code. Exploitation has been observed in the wild against a GPUStack 2.1.1 deployment. Security researcher Javier Sixto reported the in-the-wild exploitation, but no specific threat group has been identified. The issue affects versions before 2.2.0.

The second issue, CVE-2026-116779 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a code injection vulnerability in SignalWire FreeSWITCH, an open-source communications platform. The flaw allows attackers to send specially crafted SIP MESSAGE requests and abuse the API chat protocol to execute FreeSWITCH API commands. Depending on the configuration, this can expose credentials and configuration data, manipulate telephone calls and execute operating system commands with the privileges of the FreeSWITCH process. SignalWire confirmed that exploitation has been observed in the wild. The vulnerability was added to CISA’s KEV catalog on November 9, 2026, but no information identifying the attackers or a specific campaign has been disclosed. FreeSWITCH versions before 1.11.3 are affected.

The third issue, CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score of 8.1), is an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting OpenSSH. Under specific conditions, when OpenSSH runs on Linux systems using the musl C library without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM), the SSH server may incorrectly interpret password input as a password hash. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit the flaw by submitting a specially crafted password to bypass authentication and access affected accounts. CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV catalog on November 6, 2026, indicating that exploitation has been observed. However, no specific threat actor or attack campaign has been publicly identified. OpenSSH versions before 10.6p2 are affected.

The fourth issue, CVE-2026-123218 (CVSS score of 9.8), is an incorrect authorization vulnerability affecting IBM Aspera Faspex 5. It allows an authenticated user to craft a specific message that bypasses authorization checks and potentially gain full administrative privileges. Successful exploitation could give attackers access to sensitive information and allow them to modify or disrupt the affected system. IBM disclosed the vulnerability on November 7, 2026, and released a fix in Aspera Faspex 5.0.19 PL1. I found no public confirmation of exploitation in the wild or information identifying attackers at the time of writing. Versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 are affected.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the two vulnerabilities by November 12, 2026.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA)

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is pleased to announce renewal of the AWS ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment. This validated assessment report helps customers perform effective cloud supplier due diligence on AWS and enhances their third-party risk management process.

What is the AWS ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment

Many customers use third-party cyber risk management (TPCRM) services such as ProcessUnity to better manage risks from their evolving third-party environments and to drive operational efficiencies. To help with such efforts, AWS has completed the ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment of its security posture. ProcessUnity’s assessors perform the review of Global Risk Exchange assessment and validate the results annually.

This assessment approach replaces static spreadsheets with a dynamic system that combines advanced analytics, threat intelligence, and risk models with vendor input. Vendor profiles continuously update as cloud provider risk levels and AWS security posture evolve, keeping risk matrices current in near real time. Additionally, customers can also use Framework View which maps AWS assessment controls to threat profiles, MITRE ATT&CK scenarios, and global compliance standards and frameworks including National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53, International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 27001, Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), and Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), significantly reducing customers’ third-party due diligence burden.

How can you access the assessment?

Customers can request access to the report by completing an access request form, available on the ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange page. If you are an existing ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange member, you can request access from within ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange portal.

To learn more about our compliance and security programs, see AWS Compliance Programs. As always, we value your feedback and questions; reach out to the AWS Compliance team through the Contact Us page.

Naranjan Goklani

Naranjan is an WS Compliance, Security Assurance and Privacy (CAPS) Lead for Canada. He has experience leading audits, attestations, certifications, and assessments across the Americas. Naranjan has more than 16 years of experience in technology risk management, customer security assurance, and technology audits. He previously worked in the Big 4 accounting firms and supported clients from the financial services, technology, retail, and utilities industries.

d17e4eb1ac99.text:
Palantir’s CISO gets the nod for CISA. Tehran takes the rap for sabotaging European grocery freezers. Russia’s Turla turns victim Exchange servers into passive spy hubs. Barracuda battles actively chained gateway zero-days. Vanderbilt grapples with a BYOD ransomware outbreak. CISA rushes patches for critical IBM and SignalWire flaws, while revamping its national incident portal. ENISA tracks the EU’s cyber maturity gap. Cryptographers debate whether AI will crack modern encryption. Our guest is Duncan Greatwood, CEO at Xage Security, discussing the cybersecurity problem you can’t patch away. Chinese AI labs set up shop in Silicon Valley's backyard.

Today is Tuesday November 10th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Trump nominates Palantir’s CISO to lead CISA.

The White House has tapped private-sector defense experience to take the helm at CISA.

President Trump nominated Michael LoSapio, chief information security officer at Palantir Technologies, to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The nomination was sent to the Senate on November ninth and awaits confirmation. If approved, LoSapio will succeed acting director Nick Andersen as the agency’s Senate-confirmed leader.

LoSapio brings over twenty years of systems engineering, cloud infrastructure, and cybersecurity experience to the role. At Palantir, he directed defenses against sophisticated nation-state adversaries, following earlier infrastructure roles at SingleStore and high-performance computing engineering at New York University.

The nomination was announced in an official statement from the White House.

CISA upgrades incident reporting portal with MITRE ATT&CK taxonomy.

CISA is revamping how organizations report cyber incidents, leaning on standardized frameworks to turn disparate breach alerts into actionable national intelligence.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency rolled out an updated reporting form on its Incident Reporting Portal. The streamlined questionnaire collects more granular incident data—categorizing intrusions across malware, social engineering, and insider threats—while integrating the MITRE ATT&CK framework to align observations with known adversary techniques. While only civilian federal agencies face mandatory reporting requirements under FISMA, CISA urges all critical infrastructure operators to voluntarily submit disclosures.

Standardizing intake across public and private sectors enables analysts to spot broader adversary campaigns faster, proving that one enterprise's early detection can secure an entire ecosystem.

Details were announced in an official agency release citing CISA’s Chris Butera.

ENISA charts EU cyber maturity amid AI and infrastructure threats.

The European Union is taking stock of its collective cyber defenses, and while overall maturity is climbing, the regional threat ecosystem refuses to stand still.

According to ENISA’s biennial State of Cybersecurity in the Union report, the bloc averaged 71.5 points out of 100 on its 2026 Cybersecurity Index. Executive Director Juhan Lepassaar credited robust supply chain governance and research initiatives, but cautioned that recent disruptions—including cyber incidents hitting industrial refrigeration systems—spotlight persistent operational gaps. The assessment also identified uneven incident response capabilities among national CSIRTs alongside an expanding global cyber skills shortage.

While legislative frameworks like the NIS2 Directive push baseline compliance, operational realities diverge as frontier artificial intelligence accelerates automated vulnerability discovery and ideologically driven hacktivism dominates incident volume.

ENISA published the report in cooperation with the European Commission and the NIS Cooperation Group under Article 18 of the NIS2 Directive.

Western officials link Iranian cyber unit to European supermarket sabotage.

State-sponsored cyber sabotage has crossed into everyday retail operations across Europe, spoiling tens of millions of dollars in food.

French officials, backed by American investigators, have tied a wave of cyber incidents affecting supermarket freezers and refrigerators across at least six European nations to Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. In France alone, actors remotely altered temperatures at over seven hundred supermarkets, forcing units into defrost cycles and triggering fires and equipment failures. The Paris prosecutor is now pursuing international arrest warrants for the group's leadership.

Targeting internet-accessible industrial control systems reveals a deliberate pivot toward low-complexity, high-impact civilian disruption, testing Western infrastructure resilience well beyond conventional military targets.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot announced the attribution during a G-7 gathering in Paris, while U.S. and European agencies continue ongoing investigations.

Cryptographers debate whether AI advances could unravel modern encryption.

While cybersecurity planners have spent years preparing for quantum decryption, a nearer-term challenge may be arriving from artificial intelligence.

Advances in machine learning are accelerating mathematical discoveries, prompting some researchers to question whether algorithmic shortcuts might unravel the foundational math securing modern encryption. Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green points to recent breakthroughs in theoretical computer science, while Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin has called for the industry to proactively develop “post-AI cryptography.”

However, other leading voices urge restraint. Coinbase head of cryptography Yehuda Lindell contends that current post-quantum algorithms are resilient, arguing that speculative panic is premature and that artificial intelligence is just as likely to help defend and harden existing cryptographic primitives.

At stake is the core premise of modern digital trust: if computational shortcuts render previously intractable mathematical problems solvable, upgrading legacy protocols before adversaries exploit them becomes a race against time.

Attackers chain Barracuda ESG flaws for root access in targeted attacks.

Barracuda Networks is urging administrators to patch immediately as threat actors actively target two critical vulnerabilities in its Email Security Gateway appliances.

Tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, the flaws allow attackers with access to an appliance's administrative interface to bypass authorization controls and execute arbitrary commands with root privileges. While patched last week, Barracuda confirmed on Monday that attackers are already exploiting the chained flaws against a limited number of customer environments. Several other Barracuda products, including its Load Balancer and Web Application Firewall, share the command injection vulnerability.

Securing perimeter email gateways remains a priority for enterprise defense, especially given past nation-state campaigns that weaponized edge appliances for persistent espionage.

Turla deploys stealthy "Cereal" malware targeting Exchange servers.

Russian state-sponsored operators are turning victim email servers into their own operational infrastructure.

ESET Research has detailed "Cereal," a sophisticated, modular .NET malware toolkit attributed to the Russian threat group Turla. Deployed against national government bodies in Kazakhstan and Romania, the malware eliminates dedicated external command-and-control servers. Instead, a passive backdoor listens for incoming malicious web requests disguised as legitimate Outlook Web Access and ActiveSync traffic. Another module, CerealBox, injects directly into Exchange's transport service, in-memory hijacking existing mail handlers to filter and stage messages involving NATO and European Union addresses.

By operating entirely within legitimate enterprise processes and unmanaged .NET image caches, the campaign evades traditional network defenses while weaponizing mission-critical servers as long-term intelligence collection hubs.

Vanderbilt University investigates a cyberattack claimed by BYOD ransomware.

Vanderbilt University is actively responding to a significant cybersecurity incident affecting campus devices, enterprise systems, and cloud infrastructure.

University officials instructed students, faculty, and staff on Monday to power down institutional hardware, disconnect from campus Wi-Fi, and alert IT to suspicious behavior. While the university has not officially confirmed the specific nature of the intrusion, the relatively new BYOD ransomware gang claimed responsibility on its data leak site. The group claims to have encrypted databases and exfiltrated research files alongside personal records for over one million individuals.

Targeting major academic research hubs underscores how rapidly evolving ransomware operations threaten both critical intellectual property and sensitive community data.

CISA adds actively exploited IBM and SignalWire bugs to KEV catalog.

CISA has added critical vulnerabilities affecting IBM Aspera Faspex and SignalWire FreeSwitch to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Both flaws carry CVSS scores of 9.8. The Faspex bug permits authorization bypass for full administrative takeover, while the FreeSwitch defect enables arbitrary command execution via crafted SIP messages. Mandated under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, federal civilian agencies must apply vendor patches within three days.

Rapid cataloging of these flaws underscores federal urgency to seal network-accessible enterprise tools before widespread automated exploitation takes hold.

Stick with us after the break where we are joined by Duncan Greatwood, CEO at Xage Security, discussing the cybersecurity problem you can’t patch away. And….

On our Industry Voices segment, I sat down with Duncan Greatwood, CEO at Xage Security, discussing the cybersecurity problem you can’t patch away. Here’s our conversation.

If you enjoyed this conversation be sure to check out the show notes for the full interview.

Chinese AI labs set up shop in Silicon Valley's backyard.

Chinese AI companies are taking their talent search straight to Silicon Valley, hoping to recruit the researchers who helped make American AI labs dominant.

MiniMax, Moonshot, and ByteDance are expanding their U.S. hiring efforts, targeting engineers with experience at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.

But there's a problem. American AI researchers are expensive, with top talent commanding compensation packages exceeding a million dollars annually. Chinese companies generally have smaller budgets, and researchers often prefer working on cutting-edge American models.

There's also the matter of work-life balance. China's notorious “996” schedule—nine to nine, six days a week—is apparently not a particularly compelling recruiting perk.

ByteDance is reportedly offering substantially higher compensation to compete, but money isn't everything.

Meanwhile, Washington's restrictions on Chinese access to advanced technology could eventually extend to talent recruitment.

For now, Chinese AI companies can open offices in Silicon Valley. Convincing Silicon Valley's engineers to join them is another matter.

ESET found Russia-Linked APT group Turla using a new toolset, dubbed Cereal, on government Exchange servers in Kazakhstan and Romania.

ESET Research detailed a previously undocumented toolset it calls Cereal, built to run on Microsoft Exchange servers. The researchers found it on 28 November 2025 at a government body in Kazakhstan, and later at a government body in Romania, which was compromised on 23 December. The researchers discovered that in Romania, it was set up to spot emails to or from NATO and the European Union. ESET attributes it with high confidence to the Turla APT group (aka Secret Blizzard, Snake, Uroburos, Waterbug, Venomous Bear and KRYPTON) that has been active since at least 2004, targeting diplomatic and government organizations and private businesses in the Middle East, Asia, Europe, North and South America, and former Soviet bloc nations.

According to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Russia-nexus actor is assessed to be affiliated with Center 16 of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).

The name Cereal comes from serialization, a process that programs use to package data and code for transfer. Most of the toolset consists of modular .NET code that arrives encrypted, unpacks itself in memory and leaves almost no files on disk. Only the first loader is saved as a regular .NET file.

One unusual feature is that ESET found no attacker-controlled server. The main backdoor, CerealNeuron, doesn’t connect to an external server. Instead, it runs on the victim’s Exchange server and waits for commands through web paths that look like normal Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync traffic. This makes the activity difficult to spot in firewall logs. If a request isn’t properly encrypted or fails security checks, the server simply returns a normal-looking Exchange error page.

“CerealNeuron, a passive backdoor with no built-in commands but capable of executing assemblies contained in CerealRunner binaries, received in network requests;” reads the analysis published by ESET.

“The consequences are significant:

Malicious traffic coexists with legitimate Exchange web services – exactly the kind of traffic defenders are least likely to block.”

There is no dedicated C&C infrastructure to discover, block, or take down. The victim’s own internet-facing Exchange server is the operator-accessible control point.

Network-based tracking is severely limited. We were unable to identify the ingress IP addresses used by the operators. They may have connected directly, via anonymization services, or from other compromised hosts.”

As a result, defenders have no external server to block or take down. ESET couldn’t even identify the attackers’ IP addresses. A second version, called CerealHermit, has no network functions and reads encrypted command files directly from disk. This means some victims had two separate ways for attackers to access their systems.

Commands work like disposable programs. Instead of one backdoor with a built-in menu, the operators send each task as a small compiled .NET program carried by a component called CerealRunner. The tasks include pulling mailboxes through Exchange Web Services, querying Active Directory, running WMI queries, extracting locally stored Windows credentials and handling files. ESET saw so many near-identical binaries that it believes the operators run an internal system that builds them automatically.

The .NET tricks are what set this apart. The first loader abuses a rarely used feature to run native code before any .NET code, so an analyst sees an entry point that does nothing. Operators also dropped it into the Windows management folder under names like ncobjapi.dll, and into the .NET native image cache under names like Microsoft.Exchange.Search.Mdb.ni.dll, so trusted processes loaded it for them.

The email theft is the part ESET calls new. The module, CerealBox, injects itself into EdgeTransport.exe, the process that handles mail flow, and wraps the handlers of transport agents already running in memory.

“CerealBox uses a stealthier approach. Instead of registering itself, it is injected directly into EdgeTransport.exe, the Exchange process that handles email flow.” continues the report. “Reaching that point, however, is not straightforward: CerealBox is delivered through an intricate chain of nested Cereal components”

It registers no new agent, so nothing shows up in Exchange’s configuration. A message qualifies if it carries a .doc, .docx or .pdf file and matches hardcoded lists of senders, recipients, subject words or file names. Selected messages get compressed, encrypted and staged on disk, and the operators collect and delete them later.

The victims match Turla’s usual targets. According to ESET, around 70% of the countries targeted by the group since 2022 were former Soviet republics or European countries that once had close ties with Moscow. The focus on Romanian NATO and EU email systems is consistent with Russia’s long-standing intelligence interests. ESET also links the attacks in Kazakhstan to the country’s deportation of Russian exiles since January 2026. Activity in the country increased on January 15, the day after the Old New Year holiday.

Organizations running Exchange should check for suspicious activity that may not be visible in standard configurations. This includes unusual DLL files in the Windows management folder, unexpected files in the native image cache and suspicious requests to the three web paths used by the backdoor. A clean list of Exchange transport agents does not necessarily mean that the mail system is free from compromise.

“The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyberespionage.” concludes the report. “The Cereal toolset demonstrates that, for Turla, Exchange servers are not just mail servers – they are durable collection points, internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft.”

Seriously – hit me up on Bluesky if you have any ideas.If you’d rather watch the full video recap covering the entire release, you can check it out here:

Obviously, if you need to prioritize, the Connect patch is the biggest and most severe bulletin this month: 24 CVEs, 18 of them Critical, with a top CVSS of 10.0. It’s Priority 2, and Adobe is not aware of any exploits in the wild. Each of the CVSS10 bugs are reachable over the network with no authentication or user interaction, and each changes scope. The other Critical-rated update for this month is in Experience Manager. It addresses 14 CVEs, which includes four Critical bugs with a CVSS 9.9 rating. Two are incorrect-authorization bugs and two are code injections. All give arbitrary code execution over the network. Each needs a low-privileged account but no user interaction, and each changes scope.

Besides the bugs already mentioned, all other patched from Adobe are a Deployment Priority 3. None of the other Adobe bugs receiving patches this month are listed as publicly known or under active attack at the time of release.

Microsoft Patches for November 2026

Well, at least it’s not a new record for Microsoft. As always, the overall count is a bit confusing, but I see about 1,090 new CVEs released today. At this point, does the exact number actually matter? Regardless of the actual count, it’s huge but less than the 1,400 or so released last month. That’s two months in a row that have exceeded all previous years from Microsoft. As for the products affected by this release, we have Windows and Windows components; Office and Office Components; Windows networking and remote access; Windows graphics, media and printing; Windows storage file systems and drivers; .NET and Visual Studio; Windows Security and identity; Azure, cloud and identity; Exchange Server; Microsoft Dynamics; and Xbox. We’ll see how close I came to matching Microsoft’s “Cohorts” list.

Interestingly, there is only one bug under active attack, and none are publicly known this month. While this is encouraging, it does not mean we’re seeing less exploitation in the wild. It does mean we are seeing fewer 0-days exploited in the wild. This makes sense, as AI is better at reversing patches than it is at finding and exploiting bugs in closed-source software.

Let’s begin by covering some of the more severe and interesting patches released this month.

- CVE-2026-124194 - Microsoft Outlook Spoofing VulnerabilityThis is the one bug under active attack this month. It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests. An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it. Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector, and the CVSS is only 6.5, so don’t let the score lull you. Microsoft marks it as exploited, so this one goes to the top of the list.

- CVE-2026-116928 - Windows Search Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityWe start with Windows Search, which is reached through Exchange Server. This bug allows an unauthenticated attacker to send an email with a specially crafted attachment that triggers the bug when the server automatically indexes it. The recipient never opens anything. It is a zero-click code execution bug on a high-value target. It’s also a CVSS 9.8 and clearly more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange receives this month.

- CVE-2026-119958 - Windows LDAP - Lightweight Directory Access Protocol Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityThis patch addresses a bug that allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit an out-of-bounds (OOB) write (CWE-787) by sending crafted LDAP calls over the network, with no user interaction. Since it runs code in the LDAP service context, it could be quite destructive, especially on Domain Controllers. Test and deploy this one quickly.

- CVE-2026-119990 - Azure OpenAI Elevation of Privilege VulnerabilityUPDATE: Microsoft has revised this bulletin to indicate there is no customer action needed.This is an odd duck. The bulletin says “Customer Action Required: Yes” for this bug, but nothing in the advisory tells customers what to do. There are no mitigations, workarounds, or customer steps. The FAQ says an unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted request over the internet to an affected Azure OpenAI service, with no account or user interaction. The impact is access to orchestration information, workflow changes, or service disruption. Hopefully, Microsoft adds some direction here soon.

- CVE-2026-119952 - Windows Schannel Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityThis flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit arbitrary code over a network without user interaction. Microsoft rates this bug as “Exploitation More Likely”. It is one of only a few Critical-rated patches with that rating. They also list the attack complexity as high, which is why the CVSS score is lower than the others. I would still put this near the top of my list.

- CVE-2026-95962 - Windows Virtual Filtering Platform (VFP) Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityI include this one because it’s in a little-documented component. It’s not the first CVE in VFP, but it appears to be just the second. It’s a use-after-free that allows an unauthenticated attacker to get code execution on affected targets by sending a specially crafted packet to the affected service over the network. No authentication or user interaction is needed. There is a race condition here, but we see those overcome all the time at Pwn2Own. This should be an interesting component to watch.

- CVE-2026-112967 - Windows Xbox Live Networking Service Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityYou don’t see a lot of Xbox Live bugs, but here we are with a CVSS 9.8. This bug is a heap overflow that doesn’t need authentication or user interaction. Microsoft states the attacker can “gain remote code execution via an in-network attacker calling arbitrary endpoints.” Is this really likely? Probably not, but it’s fun to think of Xbox Live exploits in the wild.

On to those that are Wormable…

Last month saw 59 bugs that fit this definition. This month, it’s a bit less. A total of 30 of the November CVEs fit my definition of wormable. Specifically, 17 contain the advisory language describing an unauthenticated attacker executing code over the network with no authentication or user interaction required. The other 13 use variant wording or have no FAQ, but their summaries and CVSS vectors (AV:N/PR:N/UI:N) describe the same thing.

These bugs are as follows:

Message Queuing (5): CVE-2026-116710, 119963, 119964, 109459, 119967

DNS (4): CVE-2026-81384, 96092, 96177, 88218

Two each (8): Color Management (CVE-2026-96067, 96078), DHCP Server (CVE-2026-88243, 72998), DirectMusic (CVE-2026-95882, 95901) and Xbox (CVE-2026-112967, 66801)

One each (13): Exchange Server (CVE-2026-116928), LDAP (CVE-2026-119958), Schannel (CVE-2026-119952), CredSSP (CVE-2026-119962), Deployment Services (CVE-2026-119951), IIS (CVE-2026-119961), NAT (CVE-2026-113862), RPC Runtime (CVE-2026-118737), Media Foundation (CVE-2026-96157), iSCSI (CVE-2026-88234), Virtual Filtering Platform (CVE-2026-95962), eSCL Scanner (CVE-2026-95956) and Modern Device Management (CVE-2026-119945)

I may be wrong about some of these, since a few advisories are light on detail. As always, I recommend testing and deploying these patches quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange

Cloud hosting provider Railway says hackers exploited vulnerabilities in its infrastructure to steal customer authentication secrets and generate approximately $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage, potentially exposing credentials for up to 100,000 workspaces.

The company disclosed the incident on October 22, warning customers to rotate their secrets after detecting unauthorized access to systems storing environment variables.

In a new incident report published today, Railway confirms that attackers gained access to its internal source code and the decrypted customer environment variables for at most 1.85% of its workspaces, or approximately 100,000.

The company says this figure represents the maximum number of potentially impacted workspaces, rather than the confirmed number whose secrets were stolen.

The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway's build infrastructure to escape filesystem isolation and obtain an internal credential.

The attackers used the credential to access stored build histories and retrieve a copy of Railway's internal source code, which they then analyzed to identify additional ways to compromise the platform.

The attackers then exploited a second vulnerability involving an improperly configured trust relationship to gain further access to Railway's infrastructure and obtain credentials used to decrypt customer environment variables.

Railway says the attack became a roughly 26-hour battle between its engineers and threat actors using AI-powered agents to identify and exploit vulnerabilities across its infrastructure. At the same time, defenders worked to secure the systems.

"This was not a single breach followed by a single fix. The attacker probed many potential routes, in parallel, with Railway similarly hardening the routes in parallel," Railway said.

"The escalating situation became a contest of agent speed, with Railway defending against abliterated models and a harness similar to ARTEX, according to Wiz."

Railway says its investigation found that the attackers specifically searched for AI provider credentials, although some queries also targeted cloud, database, and payment service credentials.

The stolen credentials were subsequently used to generate approximately $740,000 in unauthorized AI usage, with Railway working with affected providers to reimburse customers. The company says it will cover charges that providers decline to refund.

The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to 1,852 users, including GitHub OAuth tokens and AI agent keys. Railway says it reset those tokens and notified affected users.

Railway believes the attackers were focused on stealing AI credentials for resale or use in AI model distillation, linking the incident to a recent wave of attacks against AI developer platforms that security firm Wiz has dubbed "Black October."

This campaign has targeted numerous AI development platforms during the past month, including Northflank, OpenCode, Warp, and Lightning AI.

The company says the attackers were fully removed from its systems on October 21 and that all exploited vulnerabilities have since been remediated.

Railway also found no evidence that the hackers downloaded customer Git repositories or accessed customer databases.

Nitori, a major Japanese furniture and home accessories retailer, discovered that an attacker accessed a system on its network and may have stolen 37.62 million customer records.

The intrusion was detected on November 6, and the company blocked the unauthorized access. However, an investigation into the incident revealed that the attacker likely had access to the system since mid-October.

Nitori, often called the “IKEA of Japan,” is a major furniture and home furnishings retailer that operates 879 stores in Japan and another 219 stores across China, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, Singapore, and Hong Kong. The firm has an annual revenue of $5.8 billion.

According to the company's notification, the incident impacts individual customers, corporate members, and non-members who placed orders through official Nitori stores and online shops.

“On November 6, 2026, we confirmed unauthorized access by a third party to a system managed by our company,” [machine translated] the company says in the notification

“Our investigation to date has revealed that up to 37.62 million records of personal information held on our servers may have been leaked externally.”

The potentially exposed information may include the following data types:

Individual members and purchasers: Membership numbers, names, email addresses, postal addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, and gender.

Corporate members: Membership numbers, company names, department names, representatives’ names, company addresses and telephone numbers, and contact persons’ names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.

Online orders: Order information for purchases through Nitori Net and official Nitori shops on e-commerce marketplaces.

The company specified that account passwords of registered members and credit card information were not exposed in this incident.

Nitori says it promptly blocked the attacker’s access, addressed vulnerabilities in its systems, and strengthened threat monitoring to prevent similar incidents in the future.

The company warned potentially impacted customers that the compromised information could be leveraged in phishing attacks and scamming attempts against, and urged them to exercise caution.

The announcement emphasizes that Nitori will never ask customers for their password, credit card number, or PIN by email or in phone conversations.

Nitori has informed Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission, the police, and other relevant authorities, and has promised to notify affected customers directly by email or post.

BleepingComputer has contacted Nitori with questions about the incident, and we will update this post when we get a reply.

Microsoft released the Windows 10 KB5131096 extended security update, which includes this month's November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes and a few bug fixes and changes.

If you are running Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC or are enrolled in the ESU program, you can install this update as normal by going to Settings, clicking Windows Update, and manually running a 'Check for Updates.'

After installing this update, Windows 10 will be updated to build 19045.7846, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 will be updated to build 19044.7846.

What's new in Windows 10 KB5131096

Microsoft no longer releases new features for Windows 10, and the KB5131096 update mainly includes security updates and bug fixes.

The update also includes fixes released as part of today's November 2026 Patch Tuesday, which addressed 1,235 vulnerabilities across Microsoft's products, including one actively exploited Outlook zero-day flaw.

The complete list of fixes and changes in KB5131096 is below:

[Date and Time] This update adjusts daylight saving time (DST) rules for Cuba for the extended 2026-2027 DST period. Cuba remains on UTC-04:00 and doesn't observe the November 2026 and March 2027 transitions. It returns to UTC-05:00 in November 2027 and resumes its regular seasonal schedule in 2028.

For the latest DST and time zone guidance, see the Daylight Saving Time & Time Zone Blog.

[Printing] - Fixed: Adding a printer published in Active Directory through Settings > Bluetooth & devices > Printers & scanners > Add device might fail with error 87, "The parameter is incorrect." This issue was introduced by the October 2026 update and does not generally affect existing printers or printing.

[Remote Desktop]

Fixed: The “Specify thumbprints of certificates representing trusted .rdp publishers” policy could not be configured successfully through Microsoft Intune.

Fixed: Remote Desktop shadow connections might fail with an “Unspecified error” on Windows Server 2016 and Windows Server 2012 R2 after installing the October 14, 2026, update.

[Windows PowerShell] This update strengthens security for PowerShell script signing and signature verification by introducing stricter encoding validation. As a result, scripts containing invalid UTF-8 encoding might fail signature validation, even if they were previously accepted. To resolve this issue, review the affected scripts, save them using valid UTF-8 encoding with a byte order mark (BOM), and sign them again. For further guidance, see Encoding Guidance for Signed PowerShell Scripts.

Microsoft says it has now resolved all known issues affecting USB Audio Class 1.0 devices introduced by the September 2026 Windows security updates.

The problems caused some devices to stop producing audio, fail to start with Code 10 errors, or experience unresponsive volume controls and sound settings.

Microsoft previously released an emergency out-of-band update on September 14 to fix issues affecting 8-channel and 3D audio modes.

The remaining audio issues have now been fixed in today's Windows 10 update.

Of the 37,571 Grok-built apps that security company Claroc found online, 35,578 were open to anyone without a sign-in, the researchers said yesterday.

They included 24 apps built by staff at the social network X and at SpaceXSI, the company that makes the Grok AI assistant. Most of the open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators, but about 1 in 10 contained internal business or personal data.

The staff apps included a confidential onboarding plan for a new sales hire, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and an X advertising proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential. SpaceXSI, formerly known as xAI, has since taken down all 24 staff apps but not other users' apps, the researchers said.

Besides those staff apps, the open apps contained internal data from 30 other organizations the researchers could identify, across fields ranging from construction and energy to healthcare and defense. Of those, 26 have more than 1,000 employees, and 6 are Fortune 500 companies.

According to the researchers' estimate in their report, roughly 2% of the open apps contained material serious enough to rate as high or critical.

The exposed material included a hospital group's searchable list of more than 3,500 employees, an intensive care briefing on a single patient, a fire department's live shift board, and a contractor's timesheet whose code held every employee's password in plain text.

Grok can build a working app from a description typed into its chat, a feature its maker opened to every Grok plan on August 19. This chat builder shares the Grok Build name with a separate terminal coding tool, whose repository uploads were reported on July 14.

Each published app gets its own subdomain of grok.me, and its creator chooses who can open it, according to the company's launch announcement.

No app goes public until its creator clicks Publish. In the paid account the researchers used, the next step offered 3 access settings: "Anyone with the link", "Invited users" and "Only you". "Anyone with the link" was already selected.

The setting matters because an app's address does not stay secret, the researchers say. Opening an app makes the visitor's computer look up its subdomain in DNS. Passive DNS services record such lookups, and anyone with an account can search those records by pattern.

Grok suggests 4 random words as each app's name, and about half of the names the researchers found followed that pattern. Such names are hard to guess, but that does not protect an app whose name already sits in a searchable list.

ChatGPT's app builder also puts each app on its own subdomain. But when the researchers shared an app there, its access was set to "Only me" until they changed it. A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say.

The researchers found the Grok app names using common subdomain discovery methods and loaded each app's first page once, without signing in.

To see what protection Grok adds on its own, the researchers built 2 test apps with made-up data and published both with the access setting already selected, "Anyone with the link".

The first, a contact list, got a database but no sign-in. Without signing in, the researchers added a row from a private browser window, and the next visitor saw it.

The second, a customer list for a 4-person sales team, got sign-in buttons that Grok added on its own: "Continue with Google" and "Continue with X". But the code Grok wrote added each person who signed in to the team before checking whether they belonged, so the check always passed.

An uninvited Google account belonging to someone other than the owner got in, viewed every customer, edited one record, and deleted another.

The researchers ran these tests only on their own apps. They did not test whether any of the open apps they found would accept such changes.

The researchers reported their findings to SpaceXSI on Sunday through the address in its security.txt file, including 2 of the staff apps. They reported the other 22 on Monday.

By the time the researchers published yesterday, the company had not replied to their report, but it had answered a reporter's questions about the research.

As the researchers describe, the company said Grok apps stay private until their creator shares them. Publishing takes several steps, including choosing between "Only you" and "Anyone with the link," as well as a legal disclaimer. Employee accounts are set to "Only you" by default.

Even so, 24 apps built by staff at the company and at X were open to anyone, the researchers say.

With their report, the researchers had asked the company to make "Only you" the default and to add an option that limits an app to a company's own email domain.

The company's response did not state that it would contact the owners of other open apps, according to the researchers. They have started emailing the affected organizations themselves and had emailed 3 by the time they published. They withheld every app address and title from the report.

On October 18, the same researchers published Muse research showing that pages shared from Meta's Muse AI agent could be found through passive DNS. Meta disabled sharing, then announced a sharing fix on October 22 that gave shared items new addresses.

How to Check Your Organization's Grok Apps

Claroc, which sells tools to find and secure apps built with AI, recommends these checks:

Find out which AI app builders your staff uses. Builders such as Grok, Lovable, Replit, v0, Bolt, Base44 and Google AI Studio can be used without IT setting them up or a company account.

If you have access to passive DNS data, look up the builders' domains and open any results in a private browser window.

Make sure any Grok app with internal data is set to "Invited users" or "Only you", and that a stranger gets an error page.

Try to sign in with an account from outside your company. If it gets in, the app needs a list of who is allowed.

Check the scripts each app loads for names, email addresses and passwords, and unpublish apps that have no owner.

In the researchers' tests, setting an app to "Only you" caused it to return a 401 error to a stranger for both the page and its data, and unpublishing took an app offline within seconds.

f4b115e29658.text:
We tell customers three things about securing AI agents: they need their own identities, access that fits the job they’re given, and traceability that’s separate from any human’s. That was true for us at Token as well. Then, we built an agent that broke all three by default.

This helped us think through how such agents should be defended. When a browser agent acts inside a user’s authenticated session, the application may see the user but not the agent, the delegation, or the task’s intended scope. By creating an agent that breaks all the security rules, Token learned how companies should be using identity to gain control, especially as agent use scales. Standards are coming, but there are steps security teams can take today.

The agent we would have flagged

The agent we created is named Rehearsal. Its job is to answer questions inside the Token platform by doing rather than telling. It autonomously opens pages in the browser tab, sets filters, and fills in forms.

From a security perspective, it’s a typical UI agent that runs in the user’s browser. That’s what makes it useful. But it also means the agent runs within the user’s session and has their reach.

Moreover, to the server behind the page, the agent’s clicks are inherently indistinguishable from the user’s, because nothing in a session cookie points to who the session driver is.

What controlling both sides made possible

Because Token owns both the agent and the app it runs, we can close each gap from the inside. For example, Token knows who’s driving the session because Rehearsal tells it who is.

We learned that there are multiple best practices that you can apply when you control the AI agent itself:

While the agent moves, dim and lock the application and clearly indicate who has control.

Record every move for each session, including those that were blocked.

Reduce the agent’s reach below the user’s. For Rehearsal, we ensure the dashboards are read-only. It can’t save anything without the user’s approval, doesn’t fill in secret fields, and never sends a call that the platform has refused. It also understands the dashboard controls through the page’s accessibility labels.

This works for our own agent, but only because it relies on access that no outside agent has.

Who has to fix it for everyone else?

We could give Rehearsal an actor, a scope, and a page map because we're the ones who wrote it. A browser agent driving your CRM or your cloud console has none of that. The app can't tell that it’s there, and the agent can't tell which field holds a secret or which button deletes a record. The session itself carries the user's identity.

The way out is to give agents their own lanes, separate from human users'. The web has started building them, but it isn't necessarily focused on holistic approaches.

The browser can mark when its agent is driving and restrict itself accordingly. Chrome auto-browse, for example, already requires a person’s approval before high-stakes actions such as payments or mass emails, limits its agent to the sites the task requires, and tags the pages the agent visits in the user’s history. Microsoft lets admins turn agentic browsing on per site and pause it before passwords and card numbers are entered.

The app can publish its actions as tools. WebMCP, a draft that Google and Microsoft are writing in a W3C community group, lets a site expose actions that an agent can call directly and flag each one as read-only or consequential. That way, the agent doesn't need to guess what a button does.

The agent can sign its requests. Web Bot Auth, now an IETF working group draft, lets a site verify which agent sent a request.

What’s missing is a layer that connects them. Each lane knows something the others don’t, and none of them passes it on. The browser knows its agent is driving, but neither Chrome nor Edge describes how to tell the app on the other end. A WebMCP tool runs inside the user’s session, with the user’s rights, so it doesn’t, by itself, narrow what the agent can reach. Web Bot Auth names the agent, but the draft makes it plain that it doesn’t cover delegation, so it omits the person the agent works for.

The app ends up holding on to pieces of context rather than delivering something actionable.

Now consider that the agents are arriving faster than the standards. Agent-friendly isn’t enough on its own. Every lane built for agents should carry the agent’s identity, a verifiable link to the person it acts for, and a scope narrower than that person’s. Together, those three signals give an application the minimum context it needs to make an authorization decision. Otherwise, a faster lane is just a faster path to the misuse of privilege.

What security teams can do before standards catch up

Waiting for standardization is not an option. You need to start discovering agentic browsers and extensions as soon as possible, including the users whose sessions they borrow. And while you can’t tell who clicked, you can choose which clicks need a person by adding a step-up check such as a passkey prompt.

Inventory browser agents, agentic extensions, and endpoint agents that can act through authenticated sessions and map them to users and owners.

Trace every AI agent consumer, so you know which people (and other agents) are using each individual agent

Review every identity that each individual agent has access to

Identify potential attack paths that use agents to bypass access controls

Require explicit approval or step-up authentication before sensitive or irreversible application actions.

Ask critical SaaS vendors whether their audit records distinguish agent activity from human activity and whether they support task-scoped delegation.

Until browsers and applications can carry agent identity, human delegation, and task scope together, companies should treat every agent using a human session as delegated access that must be discovered, constrained, and audited.
