441b4addc7ea.text:
The in-house Python script behind eMudhra's October key compromise has now cost the company 8 more of its intermediate certificate authorities (CAs), even though it did not weaken their keys.

Each intermediate CA has its own private key, which the company uses to sign the certificates it issues. The 8 intermediate CAs compromised in October had a different problem: a single line in the script cut each of their keys to one byte, the company said this week.

The script also retrieved the RSA keys of the 8 newly revoked CAs from the company's hardware security modules (HSMs). The company says it cannot show that the keys were handled as required by its own rules. It revoked the CAs late last week.

The company had called those CAs unaffected. "The RSA issuers went through a different path as per our assessment of the code and are therefore not impacted," it wrote on Mozilla's bug tracker on October 19.

Of the 8, 6 were for website (TLS) certificates and 2 for code signing. The company had put 4 of them into production in May. Its list names 195 certificates from them, 29 for its own domains.

Both problems began at a key ceremony on April 30, 2025, according to the full incident report the company posted to the same bug tracker this week. That day it generated 16 CA keys on Utimaco HSMs, including the 8 behind the October key compromise.

The keys were meant for Crypto4A HSMs at the company's US and EU sites. Moving keys between HSMs from different vendors is limited, the company says, so its PKI operations team wrote the Python script to wrap each key for transport and unwrap it again.

The round trip that day was a practice run of the transfer, and the source HSM's FIPS-approved mode was switched off for it as an approved exception.

After the round trip, the script read each private key out of the HSM into the ceremony computer's memory and rebuilt the key from that copy. For the 8 ECDSA keys, "a single line in that read‑back truncated the private value to its leading byte," the report says.

The rebuilt key carried a label almost identical to the original's, which allowed the weak copy to be sent for signing and certification.

The Hacker News worked out all 8 keys from their public certificates. The smallest, for EM OV TLS CA - G3C, is 4, and the largest is 237.

Nothing in the ceremony tested the key's strength or checked the certified key against the first generated key. The weak keys still produced valid signatures, and their certificates passed linting and 2 WebTrust audit cycles unnoticed.

The HSMs worked correctly throughout, according to the company, which puts the fault in its own script and process controls.

Invalid CRL signatures in June 2025 were an early sign of the same fault, according to the report. The company fixed them at the time by re-signing the lists with the keys that matched the certificates, which were the weak ones.

According to the report, the 8 RSA keys went through the same read-back step that the company's earlier response had ruled out. Early last week, the company said its earlier answers reflected only what its teams had gathered so far, including which script paths each set of keys took.

The script did not shorten those keys, and every signature still checks against the certified key. But their private parts, such as the private exponent and one of the primes, sat in the memory of a Python process on the ceremony computer.

As a result, the company "cannot positively demonstrate that this key material was in compliance with CPS §6.2.6," its own rule on moving keys into and out of an HSM. Logs and files from that computer cannot reliably show how the material was handled.

The company reached that view in early November, after discussions with browser root programs. The 8 RSA CAs were revoked late last week with the reason code cessationOfOperation, not the CA-compromise code used when the first 8 were revoked on October 18.

Participants in the bug thread have asked why the company chose that code rather than keyCompromise.

Of the 195 certificates in the company's certificate list, 130 came from EM DV TLS CA - G2C, 63 from EM OV TLS CA - G2C, and 2 from the code-signing CA, EM OV CS CA - G2C.

Besides the company's own domains, the certificates name several universities and colleges, a county, and other organizations. The newest was issued last week, days before the CAs were revoked. All their holders have been moved to new certificates, the company says.

The company says the wrap-and-unwrap process was used only this once, and that its other key ceremonies all created keys in place.

Participants in the bug thread also want the script published, and some have asked how private keys could leave its HSMs at all.

KPMG, which the company hired as an independent reviewer, is due to finish by December 4. The company's inventory of all its CA keys is due November 30.

The company knows of no case of misuse. Anyone holding one of the October keys could have impersonated any website, according to a disclosure site run by Dennis Jackson, who investigated the keys for Mozilla.

Browsers that enforce Certificate Transparency could not have been fooled. Whether anyone used the keys against software that skips that check is not known.

What emSign Certificate Holders Need to Check

eMudhra, which sells certificates under the emSign brand, is exiting the publicly trusted TLS business following its October 22 announcement.

Holders can find affected certificates in the company's list or by searching Certificate Transparency logs for the revoked G2C TLS issuers.

All issuance from the company's G1 hierarchy is due to stop before November 16, as the remaining customers, mainly a university federation in North America, move to another provider.

Microsoft will start removing the 10 remaining eMudhra roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, on November 16, according to an update to its security response post earlier this week. Certificates that chain to those roots will then lose default trust in Windows and Edge, and in some of its other products on their own timelines.

According to the Indian company's phase-out schedule, Chrome and Firefox will not trust G1 certificates issued after November 16, and Apple will end trust in all G1 certificates, including older ones, on November 30.

macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 stop bundled command-line tools such as curl and git from accepting the compromised TLS CA certificates, Apple said in a support note earlier this week. They also drop 5 roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, so tools relying on that file may not verify some sites chaining to them.

c59aef38322c.text:
Embed Security announced new capabilities that let security teams teach Embed how they investigate, what matters in their environment, and how to improve their detections.

With customer-built iSteps, expanded NoiseIQ Memories, and Detection Engineering, organizations can extend Embed’s built-in security expertise with their own knowledge and operating practices. Rather than programming workflows, analysts can teach Embed what they know, and its decision layer applies that expertise autonomously.

“Everyone is telling security teams to build agents. We think security teams should be teaching AI, not building it,” said Seth Summersett, CEO of Embed Security. “Analysts already know how to investigate. Our job is to make that expertise executable and apply it consistently across every investigation.”

Customer-built iSteps: Making security expertise executable

Embed’s library of iSteps is engineered by its security and AI experts, combining deterministic logic with LLM reasoning for consistency and robustness. Customer-built iSteps extend this library, letting teams capture their own investigative expertise as natural-language investigation agents that run on the same orchestration framework. Analysts describe how they approach a security question, and Embed transforms their expertise into executable investigations that run autonomously when relevant, without requiring customers to program AI workflows.

NoiseIQ Memories: Organizational context that evolves with your business

Building on NoiseIQ’s organizational context capabilities, Memories expands how teams teach Embed about their environment. Rather than relying solely on predefined relationships, Embed dynamically connects organizational knowledge with investigative evidence, including context that changes over time. This enables accurate, context-aware decisions without requiring analysts to anticipate every scenario.

Detection Engineering: Turning investigation outcomes into better detections

Embed’s new Detection Engineering capabilities leverage investigation outcomes to help security teams identify and improve detections across endpoint, cloud, email, and identity. Analyzing investigated alerts, Embed provides visibility into detection performance and recommends improvements to customer-authored detections in supported SIEM platforms, giving teams actionable insights and ready-to-apply recommendations.

“Every investigation Embed runs tells us something about the detection that triggered it,” said Jeffrey Johns, CTO of Embed Security. “Detection Engineering closes that loop, turning investigation outcomes into actionable intelligence teams can use to improve the detections themselves.”

7de2385626ea.text:
Microsoft on Tuesday released patches for a total of 1,259 vulnerabilities spanning its software portfolio, the second consecutive month where the patch volume has exceeded 1,000 flaws.

These cover 726 flaws in Windows, 174 in Office, 61 in Developer Tools, 59 in SQL Server, 53 in Developer Tools, and 27 in SharePoint Server. The patches also include 165 non-Microsoft-issued CVE identifiers. More than 500 flaws relate to elevation of privilege, followed by remote code execution and information disclosure bugs.

With the latest round of fixes, Microsoft has addressed over 5,100 CVEs this year alone, according to Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable.

Of these, a Moderate-severity security flaw in Microsoft Outlook (CVE-2026-124194, CVSS score: 6.5) has been flagged as actively exploited by Microsoft.

"Product UI does not warn users of unsafe actions in Microsoft Office Outlook allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network," Microsoft said in an advisory.

An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and persuade a target to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook.

This, in turn, could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information, such as an NTLMv2 hash, that could be used to impersonate the user.

Microsoft emphasized that successful exploitation requires network connectivity and user interaction. The tech giant credited a researcher named Nono and Anthropic's Benoît Sevens (using Claude) with discovering and reporting the flaw.

"Email is the easiest door into any company, and this flaw turns one opened file into a stolen identity," Jack Bicer, director of vulnerability research at Action1, said. "A captured hash can let an attacker sign in as the victim, read their data, and move to other systems they can reach."

"The Moderate label undersells this one. Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs. A stolen hash can open doors far beyond the inbox."

That said, Redmond has not attributed the activity to a particular threat actor or provided technical details on how the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild. The advisory also doesn't spell out whether the discovery came before or after attackers began exploiting the flaw.

The development has prompted the U.S. U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to add the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fix by November 24, 2026.

Some other vulnerabilities of note include a number of remote code execution flaws impacting Windows Search (CVE-2026-116928), Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CVE-2026-119958), Windows Schannel (CVE-2026-119952), Windows Virtual Filtering Platform (CVE-2026-95962), and Windows Xbox Live Networking Service (CVE-2026-112967), as well as a privilege escalation flaw in Azure OpenAI (CVE-2026-119990).

"Most security teams haven't quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and '2shell'-branded everything, and we're yet again at another Patch Tuesday," Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at watchTowr, said.

"Teams are really starting to feel the strain of working out 'what actually matters?' when there is fire after fire every day demanding immediate attention. Start with what you actually have exposed to the Internet, then what’s already being exploited in the wild, and only then everything else. Before going into panic mode, check whether you even use the vulnerable component, or meet the prerequisites for exploitation."

6d8283594c7d.text:
Changing your password should be part of recovering a compromised account. The developers of Remus Stealer are advertising a Gmail-reading feature they claim can survive that step and even session revocation.

That is a serious claim. It is not, however, a demonstrated capability in the published investigation. Threat intelligence company Hudson Rock examined Remus’s promotional material and questioned both its developer and a self-described customer. Its conclusion is more cautious than the sales pitch: The material depicts a mailbox-reading interface, but it does not establish that Remus can retrieve new messages after an account has been comprehensively secured. Nor does it establish a Gmail zero-day vulnerability.

What Remus is advertising

According to Hudson Rock, Remus’s version 1.3.9 announcement promotes a feature that lets operators open a compromised Gmail mailbox directly from the service’s dashboard. The supplied screenshots show message lists, individual emails, and a “Mail” option attached to records of compromised devices.

The announcement makes several additional claims:

Operators can intercept email verification codes without collecting browser cookie files.

Password changes and session revocation do not stop access.

Mailbox access can be shared with other operators through links.

Asked how it works, the developer described interaction with browser memory and said the malware executes and exits. The developer also claimed the service avoids Google’s anti-fraud checks, but withheld the technical details needed to assess that assertion.

Remember, those are marketing statements from the seller of a criminal service, not independently verified findings.

What the evidence shows

Hudson Rock spoke with a person who had publicly endorsed the feature and described using it. That source said mailbox access continued after browser closure, a session reset, and a Google password change.

But the correspondence does not document exactly which sessions were reset, the account settings involved, or the timing of the password change and subsequent access. The source’s independence was not established, and the statements were not accompanied by a controlled test.

Hudson Rock explicitly states that its report includes neither reverse engineering of the new feature nor controlled post-recovery validation.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

Can Gmail access survive a password change?

Yes. Under some conditions, continued access after a password change is possible.

Google documents that password changes ordinarily invalidate access tokens and refresh tokens used by applications with Gmail permissions. These tokens allow an application to access an account without asking for the password on every request. Token theft alone therefore does not establish that Remus can maintain access after a password change.

What Gmail users should do

The uncertainty around Remus’s claims is not a reason to abandon password changes. It is a reminder that recovering from an infostealer infection involves more than changing a password.

If you suspect an infection or unauthorized Gmail access:

Use a separate, trusted device to begin securing the account promptly. Disconnect the suspected infected device from the internet and remove the malware before signing in to accounts on it again.

Change your Google password, review recent security events and signed-in devices, and remove unfamiliar access. Check applications with access to the account as well as device sessions.

Inspect Gmail settings for unauthorized forwarding, filters, delegated mailbox access, and changes to remote mail access. Check your recovery email, recovery phone number, and verification methods too.

Run trusted security software on the affected device. Google notes that resetting the computer and reinstalling its operating system is another option when dealing with harmful software.

Review other important accounts that rely on the mailbox for sign-in or recovery, especially if you see unfamiliar verification or password-reset messages.

A mailbox can be a stepping stone to other accounts because it receives recovery links and verification messages. But the Remus screenshots do not demonstrate a universal multifactor-authentication bypass, the ability to send mail, or complete control over every account associated with that address.

Remus’s claimed persistence remains unverified. If you suspect an infection, secure your account and clean the affected device. Real-time anti-malware protection can help prevent infostealer infections.

From reporting threats to removing them.

Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today.

5e5e20595737.text:
Citrix and Ivanti on Tuesday announced patches for 19 vulnerabilities in their products, including multiple critical- and high-severity flaws.

Ivanti fixed 13 vulnerabilities across five products, including two critical-severity defects in Cloud Services Application (CSA) and Endpoint Manager (EPM).

Tracked as CVE-2026-121683 (CVSS score of 9.4), the CSA flaw is described as a missing authentication issue that could allow remote, unauthenticated attackers to “add and delete arbitrary trusted EPM Core certificate entries”.

CSA version 5.0.8.1 patches the bug. Deployments running with a Dual NIC configuration cannot be exploited externally, Ivanti notes.

The critical EPM issue, tracked as CVE-2026-121653 (CVSS score of 9.8), is an SQL injection bug that could lead to remote code execution (RCE) without authentication.

It was resolved in EPM version 2024 SU8, which also addresses a medium-severity cleartext transmission of sensitive information exploitable via MitM attacks.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Ivanti released patches for four vulnerabilities in Sentry, including a high-severity remote code execution (RCE) flaw. Tracked as CVE-2026-105425, the bug was also fixed in Endpoint Manager Mobile (EPMM), along with five medium-severity issues.

On Tuesday, the company also addressed a medium-severity defect in User Workspace Manager (UWM). Ivanti says it has no evidence of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.

Citrix rolled out fixes for six security defects in XenServer, including CVE-2026-102705, a high-severity bug that could allow attackers to infer the Pool Secret and compromise the host.

The remaining five issues could lead to privilege escalation or could allow administrators with any role to terminate the running tasks of other roles.

Additionally, Citrix released XenServer updates that mitigate several AMD CPU vulnerabilities that could allow guest VMs to compromise the host or infer the active memory content of another VM.

Related: Fortinet Patches Nearly 100 Vulnerabilities

Related: Threat Actors Exploit Openwave, Cisco BroadWorks Vulnerabilities

Related: Adobe Patches 110 Vulnerabilities Across 9 Products

Related: SAP Patches Critical ICM2SHELL, ProxyGate Vulnerabilities

aa1541033977.text:
AI provider keys that customers stored on Railway were stolen in an October breach and used to commit an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized spending, the platform-as-a-service provider said yesterday. It has promised to pay those charges itself when an AI provider will not refund them.

The company builds and runs apps for its customers and stores their secrets, such as API keys and database credentials, as environment variables. The attacker decrypted variables in at most 1.85% of workspaces, about 100,000, and its database queries looked for AI provider keys.

In an October 26 update, the company told customers asking about refunds for unauthorized AI spend that "Railway is unable to refund customers for spend performed with compromised API keys." It encouraged them to contact the AI providers directly and offered to escalate their requests.

According to the company's incident report, the decrypted data also included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users: BYOK agent keys and GitHub OAuth tokens. All were reset, each user was notified, and no logins to customer accounts using stolen credentials were found.

In addition to AI keys, one of the attacker's database queries matched cloud, database, and payment service credentials. The company's forensics did not show any customer databases being accessed, and there was no indication that customers' code repositories were downloaded.

The attacker also read the stored histories of 353 builds, including the variables and secrets passed to those builds.

The company's logs show which environments were exposed but not which variables, so the figure of about 100,000 workspaces is an upper limit. It emailed customers it judged to be at high risk.

Any data the attacker copied but did not decrypt can no longer be decrypted, because the credential the attacker used has been disabled, according to the company.

What Railway Customers Can Do

Refund terms differ by AI provider, according to the company's incident report:

AWS Bedrock: AWS's existing refund policy covers fraud, and its account teams have started refunds.

Google Gemini: Google's existing refund policy covers fraud, and its account teams have started refunds.

OpenAI: Refunds are reviewed on a case-by-case basis. Customers file a claim with OpenAI, then pass the case ID to Railway's support team.

SpaceXSI: Refunds are reviewed on a case-by-case basis, and customers submit their claims to the same support team.

Anthropic: Talks are still underway, and the platform will cover costs from breached Anthropic keys in the meantime.

OpenRouter: It maintains its no-refund policy in its terms of service, so the platform will cover all OpenRouter-related costs resulting from the breach.

Customers are asked to report charges they did not make through a charge report form. The form says the company "is not responsible for usage of these keys" but is investigating the theft and working with the providers.

The report does not say how the $740,000 figure was estimated or what period it covers. Neither it nor the form sets a cap or a deadline for claims, or states whether customers must pay disputed charges while a claim is under review.

The company advises customers to revoke and replace any sensitive variable stored on the platform before October 21. Keys should be revoked or rotated with the provider that issued them, since filing a charge report does not revoke a key.

It also advises removing public network access to databases, checking GitHub audit logs and which apps can access the account, and checking audit logs in registries such as Docker Hub. Most of this advice dates from the company's October disclosure and a report it published the next day.

Out of caution, the company also gave some providers every key it held for their services, so reset requests reached more than 100,000 users. A revocation notice from a provider does not by itself mean a key was exposed.

How the Railway Breach Happened

The attack began in the company's build system, according to its incident report. At 07:28 UTC on October 20, the attacker exploited a previously unknown flaw to partly escape the filesystem isolation around a build and read some files on the host virtual machine.

That gave the attacker a credential that build servers use to push finished images and reach some internal systems. The on-call engineer was paged at 13:58 UTC, about six and a half hours after the first exploit, when an alert flagged unusual calls to a registry service.

The credential was meant only for build work, but the company's internal Temporal system, which drives parts of the build process, accepted it as a trusted client. Through it, the attacker read some stored histories of other builds.

The same credential could also fetch cached snapshots of code. That gave the attacker a copy of the company's internal monorepo, the code base that many of its services deploy from. The company says the copy showed the attacker how the platform works and helped them find exploits and move quickly between systems.

After scanning that code, the attacker found a wrongly configured OIDC binding in one of the company's cloud environments. The binding is part of how its deployment system obtains short-lived cloud credentials, and at 03:26 UTC on October 21, the attacker exploited the mistake to obtain one.

With that credential, the attacker took two more from the cloud environment. One could read encrypted variables from a production database when used inside the internal network, and the other was an SSH key.

The SSH key opened a machine that runs orchestration tasks for the company's fleet. That machine stored a credential capable of decrypting customer variables, which it needed to start customer workloads.

Each environment's variables are encrypted with that environment's own key, and those keys are, in turn, encrypted by a root key stored in a cloud provider's key management service (KMS).

Between 04:07 and 05:21 UTC on October 21, the attacker pulled encrypted variables from the database, looking for names that matched AI provider keys. Using the orchestration machine's credentials with the KMS, it decrypted some of them between 04:42 and 05:14 UTC and again between 06:36 and 07:15 UTC.

The attacker was fully removed from the company's systems at 09:24 UTC that day.

Those times differ from the company's preliminary report of October 22, which dated the attack from 13:58 UTC on October 20 and placed decryption after 05:27 UTC.

Each build now runs in its own short-lived virtual machine, on top of the old isolation. Its credentials can push only one specific image to the company's registry.

Within an hour of the company patching the original escape, its own hardening team built a second exploit by changing that attack. That was one reason the company moved every user to the new build system at once.

Every weakness the attacker used is now closed, the company says. It has filed a complaint with the FBI's IC3 and is working with a specialist forensics firm whose investigation continues.

It is sharing indicators of compromise privately for now and plans to publish them once law enforcement agrees.

The company believes the stolen credentials were used by services that relay or resell access to AI providers for use in distillation. It has not established whether the attacker ran those services, nor has it named the attacker.

In their Black October analysis, Wiz researchers list this breach among incidents disclosed in October by at least nine AI developer platforms, including the earlier OpenCode breach.

Every public report describes attackers hunting for stored environment variables, especially ones that grant AI access, the researchers say. No single flaw or software dependency links the attacks.

bfae1aaa430f.text: Shipping behemoth A.P. Moller-Maersk says it is investigating "an IT security incident" involving the potential theft of data from a legacy system. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected system was secured. "Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said. "The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI." Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations. Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available. "Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact. "As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact. "Thank you for your patience as we continue to investigate the incident." Fortunately for those who immediately feel uneasy after hearing "Maersk" and "IT security" mentioned in the same breath, the wording of the shipping giant's disclosure suggests this intrusion won't be as calamitous as the NotPetya disaster in 2017. Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy. Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU). Maersk said at the time that it expected the attack to result in a circa $300 million bill, owing to remediation and rebuild costs. Offering a sense of scale, Jim Hagemann Snabe, then chair of Maersk, told World Economic Forum delegates in 2018 that the company's rebuild encompassed 4,000 new servers, 45,000 new PCs, and 2,500 applications – which he said had been completed over just ten days. In 2020, as exclusively revealed by The Register, Maersk went on to lay off around 150 staffers from its command and control center in Maidenhead, England. The staffers who lost their jobs had played key roles in the recovery. ®

An AI model can be given a hidden backdoor by editing fewer than 10 of its rarely used neurons, without retraining the model, Microsoft researchers have shown.

When a chosen trigger appears, the model outputs an attacker's command, which an agent using that model would run with the agent's own permissions. The attacker must be able to change the model's weights.

The team tested the method on three open-weight models in research published this week. Microsoft says it has not seen any threat actors use the technique. The company also published guidance on defending against it.

The edited neurons are ones that rarely fire and barely affect the model's answers. They were set to fire only when a trigger string appears, either in a user's request or later in a tool's output.

The researchers call the method Lazarus. Each edited neuron forces one token of the command into the model's output, so a command needs about one neuron per token.

The new neuron settings are calculated directly and can then be tuned with a few hundred training steps on those neurons alone. Nothing else in the model file or the code that runs it changes.

In a researcher's walkthrough posted on X, a backdoored Nemotron-Terminal-8B model with 10 edited neurons was tasked with fixing a Node.js server. It worked normally for three turns.

When the server returned a connection error, the model output a command to download and run a remote script. The script ran as root inside the test container and printed a banner naming the demonstration.

Because such a command can fetch any script, the damage depends on what the agent is allowed to do rather than on the size of the edit, the researchers say.

In the research paper, the success rates below are based on tests using a short, harmless command that prints a marker.

On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the team edited and tuned seven of the more than 12,000 neurons in the model's last feed-forward layer, using just 23 example sessions. The edited model output the command in at least 98.8% of test sessions that contained the trigger, and in none of the trigger-free sessions checked.

With the tuned version of the edit, success rates on Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT ranged from 51% to 99.5%, depending on the setup. The Qwen model used six neurons.

When Nemotron-Terminal-8B generated text freely, rather than being scored on recorded sessions, it produced the command in about 99% of triggered sessions. In one setup, the command also appeared in 0.14% of sessions without the trigger.

The edited models still pass ordinary tests, the researchers say. Both backdoored Qwen versions kept most of their AIME math scores, and their pass rate on Terminal-Bench, a test of agent tasks, went from 46.59% to 42.05%.

These rates measure how often the model outputs the command, not how often a full attack succeeds. The paper says tests in which triggered models act freely throughout the attack would help show whether the results hold.

Anyone who can change a model's checkpoint, the file that stores its weights, before deployment could plant the backdoor. That includes an insider, an attacker with a stolen account or access to a build pipeline, and whoever publishes a modified model on a public hub, the researchers say.

Planting it does not need the computing power of full training. The researchers also credit Claude Code, running the Opus 4.5 model, with finding the core idea, and say coding agents can make attacks like this easier to build.

Weight-level backdoors in agent models have been shown before. In an earlier proof of concept published on October 6, ProjectDiscovery researchers fine-tuned an open Qwen model to react to a trigger phrase. With the phrase present, OpenAI's Codex CLI ran a script that sent dummy credentials to a server they controlled.

Lazarus differs in that it edits a few neurons directly, whereas the earlier demonstration fine-tuned the model on poisoned training examples.

Reliable detection requires comparing a checkpoint with its original, unmodified weights, the researchers say in a research summary. Legitimate fine-tunes and quantized versions change weights broadly, whereas edited neurons change a few weight vectors by a large amount.

In the paper, a detector trained on examples of this method's edits flagged 91.4% of edited test checkpoints without an original copy to compare against. It also wrongly flagged 9.7% of clean ones. The test set was small, 35 edited and 31 clean checkpoints, and the detector was not tested on other kinds of backdoor edits.

Asking AI models to inspect a checkpoint directly worked less well. Claude Opus 5.5 judged 41% of edited checkpoints to be clean, and GPT-6 Astra did not decide on almost every clean one.

No scan can prove beyond doubt that a model is safe, the researchers say.

What Teams Running Agents Can Do

Microsoft's mitigation guidance includes these steps:

Compare every checkpoint with its declared base model before deployment and after each update, and reject models whose base cannot be checked.

Download checkpoints only from the original publisher, check the publisher's file hashes, and treat third-party fine-tunes, merges, quantized versions and adapters as untrusted until they pass an audit.

Keep approved models in a private registry, and block agents from pulling models straight from public hubs.

Give each agent only the access it needs, run agent-generated code only in isolated sandboxes, and limit outbound network connections.

Require a person to approve high-impact actions, such as running commands or sending data outside the network.

Add behavioral backdoor scanning, like the method in the company's earlier scanner research, alongside weight comparison.

Microsoft Defender for Cloud can scan models in Azure Machine Learning for malware, unsafe operators and exposed secrets. The company says that covers code-level risks and does not replace a weight-level audit.

Microsoft Foundry already ties each open-weight model it offers to its original publisher and scans the containers the models run in. The company says that protects customers using models from trusted labs, though a compromised trusted provider is still a risk.

The company is also building a red-teaming tool based on detection methods and exploring weight scanning for open-weight models that it adds to Foundry. It plans to sign models so customers can check where they came from.

5dd27c308f5f.text:
Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an attacker’s commands on cue, with no retraining required.

Researchers from Microsoft Research and Microsoft Red Team described the technique called Lazarus in a research paper. It modifies dormant neurons in a model’s final feed-forward layer to recognize a trigger and inject attacker-controlled commands into the model’s output. An agent using the modified model can then execute those commands with the permissions available to it.

“The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent — in the middle of an ordinary task — emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code,” Dimitris Papailiopoulos, a principal researcher at Microsoft, wrote in a blog post describing the research. “The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it.”

Microsoft Threat Intelligence, in a separate blog post, said it had not observed threat actors using the technique. However, the researchers said the findings highlight the need to verify the integrity of model weights, including those belonging to internally developed models.

Seven neurons were enough to implant the backdoor

The Microsoft Research team tested the method on three open-weight models. On Nvidia’s Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the researchers demonstrated the technique of modifying seven of the model’s more than 12,000 neurons. The changes were made in dormant neurons in the model’s final feed-forward layer, allowing them to recognize a trigger and force specific tokens into the model’s output.

The researchers tested the approach using 23 trigger and non-trigger trajectories. The modified model generated the malicious payload in at least 98.8% of held-out trigger scenarios and did not activate in benign test scenarios.

The technique also worked against Qwen 3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT, suggesting that it is not limited to a single model, the researchers wrote in the blog post.

The trigger does not have to be a malicious instruction. According to Microsoft Research, it can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in an agent’s context.

The researchers said Lazarus differs from prompt injection because it changes the model’s underlying weights rather than attempting to manipulate its behavior through instructions supplied in a prompt.

Microsoft Research said the technique requires no model training. Its researchers described it as an inference-compute attack, meaning a machine with enough memory to run a model has sufficient resources to implant the backdoor.

However, the attack requires write access to the model checkpoint. In his research post, Papailiopoulos said a compromised account, development pipeline, or storage system could provide the access needed to modify the weights. “What matters is weight, integrity, and provenance,” he added.

Modified models can pass evaluations

Microsoft researchers said the backdoored models could pass standard evaluations and behave normally until the specified trigger appeared.

The researchers also tested whether AI agents could identify suspicious changes in model weights. Their agent-built detection methods flagged 91.4% of held-out modified checkpoints, with a 9.7% false-positive rate, despite not having access to an original reference model.

Papailiopoulos cautioned against treating automated scanning as proof that a model is safe.

“No scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe,” he wrote.

According to Papailiopoulos, reliable detection requires comparing a model’s weights with its original, unmodified version. He said establishing a model’s provenance is therefore important to determining whether its weights have been altered between the developer and deployment.

Auditing model weights recommended

In its accompanying security advisory, Microsoft Threat Intelligence recommends auditing model weights before deployment and after every update. Its guidance includes comparing each checkpoint against its declared base model, verifying publishers and file hashes, and rejecting models without verifiable provenance.

Microsoft also recommends keeping approved models in private, access-controlled registries rather than allowing agents and inference services to download checkpoints directly from public repositories.

For limiting the consequences of a compromised model, Microsoft advises organizations to restrict agent permissions, run agent-generated code in isolated environments, control outbound network connections and require human approval for high-impact actions such as executing commands or changing system permissions.

Microsoft Research said it is working with internal AI security teams to turn the research’s detection techniques into a red-teaming framework. The company is also exploring AI-assisted weight scanning and cryptographic model signing with verifiable provenance and tamper-evident audit trails. According to the paper, the central idea “was discovered autonomously by Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in February 2026.”

Product security firm Finite State announced on Tuesday that it raised $27 million in a Series C funding round to grow its international presence and make its connected device security platform more autonomous.

Private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund led the round, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners.

The company tied the investment to two pressures on manufacturers. One is a wave of critical flaws uncovered by AI-powered research in October, dubbed the ‘Vulnpocalypse’, and the other is a growing set of product security mandates.

Finite State’s platform inspects the code that actually ships in a device, covering both software and firmware. It works from compiled firmware and binaries, so source code is not required.

Its users are makers of vehicles, medical devices, industrial equipment, consumer electronics and utility infrastructure. The platform identifies both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and helps manufacturers fix the ones that can be exploited.

On the compliance side, the platform continuously produces SBOMs, VEX documents and signed compliance packages to help device makers meet regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA). The company also cites FDA premarket cybersecurity requirements, the UNECE R155 and R156 vehicle regulations, and the IEC 62443 industrial standard among the rules manufacturers face.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

AI agents carry out analysis, triage and testing on the platform and draft regulatory reports. Customers can also connect their own agents through an API and an MCP server.

“The Vulnpocalypse isn’t a one-month event. It’s the new baseline. AI-equipped attackers can now find a flaw faster than most manufacturers can figure out which of their products contain it,” said Matt Wyckhouse, founder and CEO of Finite State. “Governments are rightly advancing regulations to protect the public good, leaving security teams to prove that risks they identify are understood and addressed. Finite State delivers the evidence, intelligence, and automation to protect manufacturers, organizations, and consumers.”

Related: Bay Raises $50 Million to Control What Enterprise AI Agents Can Do

In this article

Muse’s maker used about 50,000 hours of users’ brainwave recordings to train AI without explicitly telling them

Stripping names might not be enough to make brainwave data anonymous; researchers have identified individuals from EEG recordings

Check privacy policies and ask about opt-out and data deletion

Technology companies have spent years trying to get into your head for profit. Now they’re doing it literally. The maker of Muse, a headband that measures brain activity during sleep and meditation, used users’ brainwave data to train AI without explicitly telling them, an investigation has revealed.

Companies sell these consumer sleep bands to help you better understand what your brain does when you sleep and meditate. However, according to an investigation in Science magazine, they’re picking up a little understanding of their own on the side.

The year-long investigation found that Canadian company Interaxon, which makes the Muse sleep and meditation headband, was using the data that it collected from users’ brains to train AI. The company used about 50,000 hours of electroencephalography (EEG) recordings, which measure the brain’s electrical activity, to train a “brain foundation model.”

AI models trained with large amounts of brainwave data from different people can spot patterns in brain activity. For example, a model might learn to recognize patterns associated with seizures.

Researching such outcomes is laudable, but only if you first tell the people whose EEG data is being used for the training. Interaxon didn’t.

This is your brain on an inadequate privacy policy

When Science questioned Interaxon about the issue, its chief marketing officer Nadia Kumentas acknowledged that users should be explicitly informed about the AI training. The company updated its privacy policy, which now says de-identified data is used to train machine learning models.

Collecting data through devices like this is tempting for companies because brainwave data is otherwise difficult to obtain and therefore incredibly valuable.

No wonder, then, that it isn’t the only neuraltech company facing questions about its data practices. The publication reviewed 57 companies that collect brain data, and found that only six explicitly said they wouldn’t sell users’ brain data. More than two-thirds allow brain data to pass to a new owner if they are acquired. Eleven of them only had a privacy policy for website visitors, and four had no policy at all.

To its credit, Interaxon removed names and email addresses from user EEG data before using it for training. However, those users’ data has already helped shape a model trained without explicitly telling them. Removing its influence after the fact is extremely difficult.

But is such “de-identification” enough? An academic study conducted by the University of South-Eastern Norway this year found that EEG recordings and derived features can contain sensitive patient-specific information. It said that this can create privacy risks when that data is shared across clinical and research environments. It added:

“Conventional anonymization methods are often insufficient for high-dimensional biomedical signals, since removing direct identifiers does not necessarily prevent re-identification, linkage, or inference risks.”

Another study by researchers at Ben-Gurion University, Israel, found that analyzing resting-state EEG recordings could shed light on personality traits and cognitive abilities. Resting-state EEG identified users 88.4% of the time, according to a 2018 study by researchers at Korea University. And a University of Southern California study claimed that EEG data could reveal mental health status, neurological conditions, and even substance use history.

These findings do not establish what can be inferred from Muse recordings specifically. Consumer headbands generally have fewer electrodes than clinical EEG systems.

This isn’t the first review of the consumer neurotech industry to reveal some worrying trends. A 2024 Neurorights Foundation report found that 29 of 30 companies it surveyed appeared to have access to consumers’ neural data and had provided “no meaningful limitations to this access.”

The law is still catching up to all this. The Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) counts your fingerprint, voiceprint, or face geometry among other things as biometric identifiers, but EEG data doesn’t make the cut. However, Colorado and California do now treat neural data as sensitive.

These concerns extend beyond brainwave data. In a Malwarebytes survey of newsletter readers, 90% worried about AI using their data without consent, while 92% were concerned about corporations using their personal data inappropriately.

What Muse owners can do

Do you use a sleep band or another neurotech device? Consider that your brain data might be used for more than you imagined. And if the company goes bust and/or gets acquired, it might pass to another owner. That’s exactly what happened with genetic testing company 23andMe.

With this in mind, check the manufacturer’s privacy policy, and if you can’t find one, ask it directly. Ask whether your EEG data is used to train AI, whether you can opt out, and whether you can delete recordings already collected.

If those options aren’t available, consider whether you’re comfortable continuing to use the device.

From reporting threats to removing them.

Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today.

Fortinet on Tuesday dropped 89 new security advisories that address nearly 100 vulnerabilities across its products.

The massive release comes three weeks after the company announced it has integrated frontier AI models into its product security testing and can discover security defects more efficiently.

“This ongoing effort complements the conventional methods we employ to identify and address vulnerabilities. This approach gives customers time to prioritize upgrades before additional technical details become public, which matters even more as AI shortens the time between disclosure and exploitation,” Fortinet says.

Approximately 17 of the newly resolved flaws are critical-severity issues, several of which could be exploited for arbitrary code execution.

Other critical bugs could lead to authentication bypass, LSA broadcast, account takeover, access to other VDOMs and to secure email accounts, IBE webmail session compromise, server-side request execution, malicious/malformed attribute delivery, webmail password resets, and command execution as super admin.

FortiMail received the largest batch of critical fixes, followed by FortiAuthenticator, FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer. New FortiSASE and FortiClient updates also resolve critical issues.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

According to Baldur Security principal security consultant Kevin Joensen, the FortiClient bug is exploitable if FortiPAM is enabled and could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code if the victim visits a malicious website.

“The root cause is a CORS misconfiguration that allows attacker-controlled web pages to communicate with a local service and reliably execute arbitrary code,” Joensen says. The researcher named the flaw Fortinet2Shell.

Fortinet also patched nearly 80 high-severity vulnerabilities that could lead to XSS attacks, code execution, code injection, arbitrary file uploads, command execution, denial-of-service (DoS) conditions, MitM attacks, privilege escalation, information disclosure, account takeover, unauthorized access, and other unauthorized actions.

Fortinet makes no mention of any of these security defects being exploited in the wild. Additional information can be found on the company’s PSIRT page.

Clive Robinson • November 11, 2026 7:36 AM

@ Bruce, ALL,

Most new technologies bring a new looking form of fraud with them.

Eventually either people get used to it and the fraud success rate drops, or the technology goes out of fashion / use.

I used to know an accountant who was indirectly at the heart of the first major fraud by Fax Machine.

The details are dull you just need to know that a previous technology called Telex had a legal status and people assumed it carried forward with faxes (it did not).

There are still remnants of Telex hanging around, but faxes appear to have been consigned to the under the desk basket of history.

Thus the question,

“How long before Current AI and ML systems suffer those or similar fates and which will be first?”

Take YouTube, a friend was looking at some cooking videos, they asked me if using sweet potatoes to make cakes was possible as they had seen one or two vids that had them in “healthy cake making”.

I pointed out that you can substitute cold mashed potatoes for sone flour in breads and some cakes as I’d done it (similar with rice flour) but I’d not tried sweet potatoes as I did not think it would work well.

So we looked through a few vids and it quickly became clear they were all copies of each other with different faces and stuff in the background moving from shot to shot. And importantly there was a US flag in each and every one of then…

It then became clear as they all promoted certain types of sham products, but importantly asked you to contact them through the comments.

For those that do not know there are fairly strict rules and regulations about pushing things, but… If you interact first through the comments then they mostly don’t apply in the US.

So these scammers know how to get things to work, and in many cases will get away with it even if the money they make is “small potatoes”.

Hence why some scammers have in effect “followed the money” with these “scamming corporates” doing it via social engineering of the employees…

Ask yourself,

“Who is really to blame, the ‘running scared or overworked’ employee or their corporate bosses…

dc2da637138c.text:
Rubrik has announced cyber recovery capabilities for DevOps platforms Microsoft Azure DevOps and GitHub. With built-in anomaly detection, blast radius investigation, and surgical recovery, organizations will be able to detect suspicious activity on their code, instantly scope the impact of an attack, and undo the attackers’ changes from air-gapped, immutable backups, without disrupting legitimate developer work.

“An organization’s source code is where innovation lives, and attackers know it,” said Anneka Gupta, Chief Product Officer at Rubrik. “One stolen token or poisoned dependency can impact thousands of repositories before anyone notices. Our new cyber recovery capabilities for DevOps allow organizations to detect suspicious activity, see what was impacted, and recover only the unwanted changes, using the air-gapped backups they already trust Rubrik to protect.”

Attackers no longer need to breach perimeters; instead, they compromise legitimate credentials to launch attacks that mimic normal developer activity. Accelerated by AI, these attacks can rapidly spread malicious code across thousands of repositories.

According to Gartner, “a growing number of software engineering leaders are modernizing their DevSecOps toolchains by adopting DevSecOps platforms.” These platforms house an organization’s most critical intellectual property, including source code, CI/CD pipelines, and infrastructure as code. As such, they’ve become a primary, identity-driven attack surface.

Enhanced DevOps Protection capabilities

Operating natively within Rubrik Security Cloud, DevOps Protection Enterprise Edition now connects detection, investigation, and recovery in a single workflow:

Anomaly detection: Continuously baselines GitHub and Azure DevOps audit logs, correlating them with Rubrik backup metadata to flag suspicious identity activity and produce a prioritized alert that can be routed directly into existing security and ticketing workflows.

Blast radius investigation: Produces a categorized view of affected assets across repositories, commits, pipelines, workflows, pull requests, and settings, providing the exact scope of impact and determining precisely what needs to be restored.

Surgical recovery: Recovers only what the attacker changed while preserving legitimate work from other developers, using the clean, air-gapped, immutable backups customers already hold with Rubrik DevOps Protection. Teams will be able to avoid manual rebuilds and organization-wide code freezes.

Expanded developer collaboration stack protection

To ensure complete recovery context, Rubrik DevOps Protection (Foundation Edition) now backs up broader platform metadata, settings, and the developer collaboration stack across Azure DevOps and GitHub. From issues, pull requests, and Azure Boards to wikis, packages, and organization settings, businesses can recover the full context of how their teams build software, rather than just the underlying code.

Rubrik’s cyber recovery capabilities for DevOps platforms Microsoft Azure DevOps and GitHub is expected to be generally available in the coming months.

dfc63144e0e9.text:
A configuration file meant to store local command permissions on Anthropic’s Claude Code is exposing thousands of API keys, database credentials and other secrets, according to findings by GitGuardian.

The code security firm identified 31,088 distinct secrets in Claude Code’s “.claude/settings.local.json” files across 23,276 public GitHub repositories. Of those, 5343 were still valid when GitGuardian detected them. The exposed credentials include database connection strings, cloud provider tokens, SSH passwords, Google API keys, and AU service credentials.

“Monthly leaks in settings.local.json peaked at 12,535 occurrences in April 2026, then fell to 959 by October, and we do not yet know what changed,” GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon said in a blog post.

Apart from source code repositories, the exposure included secrets embedded in publicly accessible Docker Hub images. The problem, Valadon explained, lies with how Claude Code handles command approvals.

Command approvals turn into credential storage

Claude Code asks developers for permission before executing certain shell commands. When a developer selects the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option, the tool saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json, a project-level configuration file.

The catch is that the saved rule contains the actual command string, including any credentials embedded in it.

For instance, a developer asking Claude Code to interact with an API might approve a curl command containing an API key in its HTTP header. Claude Code then stores that entire command as an approved rule, leaving the credential in the configuration file.

Although Claude Code automatically adds the file to its local Git ignore settings, that protection does not necessarily carry over to other machines or repositories, Valadon said. Developers can accidentally commit the file, particularly when working across different clones or when the file has already been tracked.

Git Guardian found that 67% of the occurrences in settings.local.json for which it could establish validity were working credentials. Database identifiers accounted for the largest category of valid secrets, with 2280 distinct credentials, followed by cloud provider tokens and AI tokens.

It was also noted that conventional secret scanners could miss a substantial portion of the exposure. Passwords embedded in command-line arguments and environment variable assignments often lack the recognizable formats that provider-specific detection rules look for.

Leaked credentials on Docker Hub

GitGuardian also examined public Docker Hub images and found 613 distinct secrets in Claude Code settings files, 99 of which were valid when detected.

The credentials appeared across 543 image repositories and 7625 tags. According to Valadon, the problem arises when developers use Docker’s “COPY..” instruction to copy an entire project working directory into an image.

Unlike Git, Docker does not automatically respect the repository’s .gitignore file. Consequently, a Claude Code configuration file excluded from version control can still be copied into a container image unless developers explicitly exclude it through .dockerignore.

One valid Cloudflare API token appeared across 559 image tags, while a database password appeared in 643 tags across seven image repositories.

Removing the offending file from the GitHub repository does not help the credentials already distributed through published images. Developers must rotate exposed credentials, remove sensitive configuration files from both Git and Docker build contexts, and check previously published images for lingering secrets.

GitGuardian recommends treating AI coding assistant configuration files as potential secret-bearing assets, scanning them alongside conventional environment files, and using environment variables rather than hardcoding credentials into commands.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment. GitGuardian said Anthropic’s Claude Code lead Boris Cherny acknowledged the issue, saying the company was looking into it and exploring additional safeguards, including built-in secret scanning and an auto mode.

ee44699dd113.text:
The NCSC has launched a new Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme.

The scheme is designed to help strengthen national cyber resilience, supporting the UK's most critical organisations, as well as overseeing bodies.

The scheme assures suppliers of cyber adversary simulation services, helping organisations identify trusted providers to test their defences and their ability to prevent, detect and respond to realistic simulated cyber attacks.

Like all NCSC Industry Assurance schemes, CyAS draws on the NCSC’s expertise as the UK’s National Technical Authority for cyber security. Commercial providers are assessed against an NCSC-defined standard, giving organisations confidence that they are buying services that meet recognised requirements.

A key feature of the CyAS methodology is that providers conduct reconnaissance to understand the customer’s technology, exposure and threat landscape. This is then used to develop realistic, customer-specific attack plans. Testers adopt an adversarial mindset and use appropriate tools and techniques to achieve agreed objectives, rather than being driven by commercially procured threat intelligence or constrained by documented tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs).

The scheme complements other NCSC frameworks that support cyber regulation, including the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) and the associated Cyber Resilience Audit (CRA) scheme. Together, these frameworks will help organisations - particularly larger organisations, those operating in critical national infrastructure and government - build a clearer picture of their cyber security and resilience.

They also give Cyber Oversight Bodies a trusted way to gather evidence of resilience across the sectors they oversee. This supports consistency, shared learning and a stronger understanding of cyber risk.

Speaking at the launch, the NCSC’s Chief Technology Officer Ollie Whitehouse said:

You cannot improve what you do not know. That is why I am delighted to see the launch of the Cyber Adversary Simulation scheme. By enabling rigorous, realistic end to end assessments by the very best adversary simulation experts, CyAS will help organisations build a clearer picture of how they would stand up to genuine cyber attacks and take action to strengthen their security and resilience.

“Ultimately, stronger resilience across the UK helps prepare the country for crisis by protecting the essential services we all rely on every day from the most pressing threats.

NCSC Deputy Director Chris Ensor added:

Moving beyond traditional pen testing and auditing of controls, the CyAS service enables organisations to practically test their cyber defences, ensuring they are able to protect, detect and respond to cyber attacks.

CyAS has been developed in partnership with Cyber Oversight Bodies, including regulators and Lead Government Departments, to establish a common core standard and a more consistent approach to demonstrating cyber resilience.

The scheme will initially operate as a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), enabling the NCSC to test demand, refine the methodology and build confidence before moving towards a fuller operating model.

You can find a full list of assured service providers on the schemes ‘Find a Provider’ page.

bd5654e3b5b7.text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Tuesday added two security flaws impacting Cisco BroadWorks and Openwave Messaging Webtop Media Transcoder to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

Details of the vulnerabilities are below -

CVE-2026-20320 (CVSS score: 7.5) - An improper restriction of XML external entity reference vulnerability in the Open Client Interface (OCI) XML Parser of Cisco BroadWorks that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to read sensitive configuration information on an affected system with the privileges of the Cisco BroadWorks user. (Fixed in August 2026)

CVE-2026-111793 (CVSS score: 4.3) - An incorrect resource transfer between spheres vulnerability in Openwave Messaging Webtop Media Transcoder that could allow an authenticated user to process and convert unintended document types if bypassing the Webmail experience. (Fixed in October 2026)

The addition of CVE-2026-111793 to the KEV catalog follows an alert issued by Japan Vulnerability Notes (JPN), which noted in an advisory that the "developer states that attacks exploiting the vulnerability have been observed."

The vulnerability information portal also warned that an authenticated attacker could exploit the vulnerability to upload a specially crafted file and obtain sensitive information.

As for CVE-2026-20320, the security defect has been put to use as part of an agentic attack campaign dubbed Operation Snowball in which an unknown Chinese-speaking threat actor leveraged an autonomous framework built using a jailbroken version of the DeepSeek Flash model to target a European telecom provider and 13 companies hosted on its infrastructure.

The activity resulted in the enumeration of hundreds of assets, extraction of dozens of credential sets, and exfiltration of thousands of rows of subscriber billing and device records from the provider's internal billing platform over a two-week period, according to Malbear Labs.

The AI agent has capabilities to exploit a portfolio of known security vulnerabilities spanning a wide range of products, including -

JBoss RichFaces (CVE-2013-2165)

Liferay CE/DXP (CVE-2020-7961)

ForgeRock OpenAM (CVE-2021-35464)

Linux (CVE-2021-4034)

SAP NetWeaver (CVE-2022-22536)

Cisco Expressway (CVE-2023-20269)

Citrix NetScaler(CVE-2023-4966)

Qlik Sense (CVE-2023-41265, CVE-2023-41266)

PAN-OS GlobalProtect (CVE-2024-3400, CVE-2024-9474)

Adobe Experience Manager (CVE-2025-54249)

Broadcom VMware Cloud Director (CVE-2026-2003, CVE-2026-2004, CVE-2026-2005, CVE-2026-2006)

Claris FileMaker Server (CVE-2026-86934), and

F5 BIG-IP (CVE-2026-41225)

"The primary target on the telecommunications provider's infrastructure was the BroadWorks XSP (eXtended Services Platform), Release 23.0.1.1075, running on port 2208," Malbear Labs said. "The agent exploited CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XXE in the BroadWorks OCI XML parser."

"From the XSP host, the agent recovered the system identity private key, three SSL credential sets, and three additional private keys with certificate matches confirmed. The system identity key is used by the BroadWorks platform to authenticate between its own components; possessing it allows impersonation of the XSP in inter-component communication."

The activity has also been characterized by the use of reconnaissance tools, Sliver for post-exploitation, Chisel, along with web shells like Behinder for persistent access.

"This is a threat actor who delegated the intrusion to an AI and checked in asynchronously to review progress," Malbear Labs added. The primary agent ran continuously, issued parallel tasks to worker agents, maintained a coherent operational plan across the full campaign, and adapted to defensive controls without pausing for operator input."

"The harness ran the reconnaissance, identified the attack surface, chose the exploitation path, adapted when controls blocked it, wrote new tools when existing ones failed, extracted credentials, exfiltrated data, and compiled a finished target list, all without the operator present during any of it."

Late last month, Cisco revealed that two different vulnerabilities in Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127, CVSS score: 10.0) Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) Software and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Software (CVE-2026-76418, CVSS score: 8.6) have been actively exploited in the wild.

In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the patches by November 24, 2026, to secure their networks.

Found this article interesting? Follow us on Google News, Twitter and LinkedIn to read more exclusive content we post.
