An attacker has abused AWS cross-account IAM roles to access multiple customer environments, steal data, and harvest credentials in a supply-chain attack that ran between October 14 and October 26.

Researchers from Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, said they observed an attacker using IAM credentials for Qubole’s AWS account to assume roles in customer environments.

The compromised credentials allowed the attacker to access customer AWS accounts that had previously established cross-account access permissions with Qubole. The access was used to enumerate cloud resources, retrieve secrets and configuration data, download files from Amazon S3, and test credentials belonging to affected organizations.

Sentra, which initially identified suspicious activity across several customer environments, said the campaign affected dozens of Qubole customers. The attacker was said to have exploited integrations that remained trusted even after some organizations had stopped using the platform.

Attackers used Qubole’s AWS credentials

Qubole integrations rely on cross-account Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Customers typically create roles that allow identities belonging to Qubole’s AWS account to assume them, with an External ID serving as an additional check against unauthorized access.

The attacker had credentials that could satisfy this requirement.

Wiz said the first suspicious activity was observed on October 14, when an IP address associated with Mullvad VPN attempted to assume customer integration roles from AWS account 805246085872, which Qubole uses for its platform operations. The requests used an IAM user identified as AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS.

Most of the activity that came later originated from an OVH-hosted VPS, 57.129.54[.]120. The attacker also began using a second IAM identity associated with Qubole’s AWS account on October 18, alongside another Mullvad VPN address.

All malicious role-assumption requests identified by Wiz included the required External ID and succeeded. Many of the targeted roles had seen no legitimate Qubole activity during October, but their permissions remained active.

After gaining access, the attacker enumerated cloud resources, including S3 buckets, databases, EC2 instances, security groups and IAM identities. The intruder also accessed AWS Secrets Manager, Systems Manager Parameter Store and Lambda function configurations to retrieve credentials and other sensitive information.

Attackers stole data, and hosted a suspicious Linux image

The attacker used the assumed roles to download data from Amazon S3, enumerating accessible buckets and objects before retrieving their contents. In some instances, Wiz said, entire buckets were downloaded in individual sessions.

Credentials discovered in the compromised environments were subsequently tested using TruffleHog, a secrets-scanning tool. These included AWS access keys, Microsoft Entra ID service principal credentials and Okta OAuth client credentials.

Sentra reported identifying more than 100 passwords and keys read within minutes, alongside thousands of additional credential records contained in downloaded files. The company also said the attacker performed no write operations in the observed environments, suggesting an operation focused on data theft.

Wiz also found a bootable Linux ISO image, named “sso_agent.iso,” hosted on the attacker’s OVH infrastructure. The image collects system information, communicates with the server over TCP port 23458, and can execute remotely supplied shell commands. Its configuration suggests it may have been designed to target Windows systems, the researchers said in a blog post.

Wiz, however, did not find any deployments of the image and could not confirm whether it had been used against victims.

The campaign has not been attributed to a known threat group.

Tightening integrations and third-party access will help

Wiz recommends that organizations using Qubole review AWS CloudTrail records dating back to October 1, 2026, across all accounts containing integration roles. Investigators should look for suspicious AssumeRole activity originating from Qubole’s AWS account, particularly requests from non-AWS infrastructure and IAM identities identified in the disclosure.

Subsequent activity involving Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, Lambda and S3 should also be investigated, Wiz noted. Other recommendations include removing unused third-party integrations and narrowing trust policies to specific vendor IAM principals rather than allowing an entire external AWS account to assume a role. Organizations should also restrict role assumption to documented vendor network ranges using AWS source IP or VPC endpoint conditions.

CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference Vulnerability

CVE-2026-111560 Barracuda Networks Multiple Products OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres Vulnerability

CVE-2026-116606 Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG) Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability

CVE-2026-124194 Microsoft Office Outlook Missing User Interaction for Potentially Unsafe Action Vulnerability

CVE-2026-125350 Google Chromium Use-After-Free Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Google patched nine Chrome flaws, including a V8 vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-125350, that attackers have been actively exploiting in the wild.

Google has addressed multiple security vulnerabilities, one of which, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, has been actively exploited in the wild.

The vulnerability is a use after free issue that resides in XML and was reported by an anonymous source on November 6, 2026..

“Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild.” reads the advisory.

A Use-after-free (UAF) is a memory corruption vulnerability that occurs when a program continues to use a piece of memory after it has been released (freed).

In simple terms, an application allocates memory to store data, then releases that memory when it is no longer needed. A use-after-free bug occurs when the application later tries to access that same memory location, even though it is no longer valid.

Attackers may exploit a use-after-free vulnerability to crash an application and cause a denial-of-service condition, corrupt memory, or, under certain conditions, execute arbitrary code. Depending on the affected component and the nature of the flaw, successful exploitation could also allow attackers to escalate their privileges.

The IT giant has not shared further details about how attackers are exploiting the vulnerability or who is behind the attacks.

“Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix. We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven’t yet fixed.” continues the advisory.

CVE-2026-125350 is the eighth exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026. Since the start of the year, Google has addressed the following zero-day flaws exploited in attacks in the wild:

February 2026 – CVE-2026-2441 (CVSS score: 8.8) – Use after free in CSS.

March 2026 – CVE-2026-3909 (CVSS score: 8.8) – Out-of-bounds write in the Skia 2D graphics library and CVE-2026-3910 (CVSS score: 8.8) – Flaw in the implementation of the V8 JavaScript/WebAssembly engine.

April 2026 – CVE-2026-5281 (CVSS score: 8.8) – Use-after-free bug in Dawn, the WebGPU component used for graphics processing.

June 2026 – CVE-2026-11645 (CVSS score: 8.8) – Out-of-bounds memory access in the V8 JavaScript engine

September 2026 – CVE-2026-85046 (CVSS score: 8.8) – V8 type confusion flaw.

September 2026 – CVE-2026-87491 (CVSS score of 8.8) – Out of bounds write in V8.

Google has released Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update will roll out gradually over the coming days and weeks.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Google)

7352586f155d.text:
On a compromised Exchange server, the most interesting activity is not always the message that arrives in a user’s inbox.

Somewhere in a national government office, an official sends an email to a colleague at a transnational military alliance. The message goes out through a Microsoft Exchange server, exactly as it should, and nothing looks suspicious. But before the email leaves the building, a piece of code quietly examines it, decides that it is interesting, and sets aside a copy to be forwarded to prying eyes, while the original email continues on its way.

On November 28th, 2025, we found the toolset that installs such code on an Exchange server of a governmental organization in Kazakhstan. What initially looked like separate suspicious components soon revealed a previously undocumented toolset: a collection of modular .NET malware designed to run on Microsoft Exchange servers, receive commands, execute them in memory, map the compromised organization, and collect selected email messages. After fine-tuning our detections, we found the same toolset at a governmental organization in Romania – compromised on December 23rd, 2025 – where it was configured to identify emails sent to, or received from, The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and European Union (EU).

Because the tools rely heavily on serialization (a technique for packaging data and code for transport), we have given them names that start with the prefix “Cereal”. What makes this toolset stand out is its combination of novel techniques requiring deep knowledge of Exchange internals with unusual .NET execution methods.

One of the most interesting aspects of this toolset is what we did not find: external command and control (C&C) infrastructure. Instead – adding insult to injury – the victim’s compromised Exchange server is co-opted to act as the C&C infrastructure.

We attribute Cereal, with high confidence, to the Russia-aligned APT group Turla, based on the concurrent use of another component publicly linked to Turla and conceptual similarities to older Turla malware. The full technical analysis is available in our white paper.

Key points of this blogpost:

We initially observed an undocumented toolset at a governmental organization in Kazakhstan. After fine-tuning our product’s detection of these tools, we discovered a compromised governmental organization in Romania a month later.

We uncovered a sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected toolset, designed to run on Exchange servers of compromised entities, for long-term cyberespionage.

No external network infrastructure was observed. One of the malicious components, a passive backdoor that runs on Exchange servers, provides access to the internal network.

Commands are sent by the operators in the form of separate executables with a similar, custom-built structure. This hints at the existence of a framework that automates compilation and delivery of commands.

An automated email collection module, injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes, accesses and manipulates the email transport pipeline. This requires deep understanding of the inner workings of Microsoft Exchange and is a novel technique.

The use of various .NET tricks, such as unmanaged entry points, and abuse of the .NET native image cache makes this toolset quite sophisticated in comparison to most recent APT cases that we have researched.

Exchange for breakfast: Turla’s Cereal tricks are not for kids

Read the full report

Victimology and geopolitical context

Turla, also known as Snake, has been active since at least 2004 and is widely assessed to be part of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). Its usual targets are governments, diplomatic missions, and defense organizations, primarily across Europe, Central Asia, and the Middle East. We have documented a large part of Turla’s arsenal on WeLiveSecurity. In 2025, we also reported unusual cooperation between Turla and Gamaredon in our blogpost Gamaredon X Turla collab and in our white paper Gamaredon in 2025: Leveraging tunnels, workers, dead drops, and new alliances.

The Cereal toolkit demonstrates Turla’s ability to carry out a slow, careful, long-term intrusion built around Microsoft Exchange servers.

We identified two national governmental organizations compromised by Cereal, in geographies that align closely with Turla’s known targeting. Based on ESET telemetry, around 70% of countries targeted by Turla since 2022 have been former Soviet republics or European countries that were once closely aligned with the Soviet Union. The geographic distribution of the two confirmed compromises is shown in Figure 1.

The Romanian case is notable because one component, CerealBox, was configured to collect messages involving NATO and EU institutional addresses. This focus fits long-standing Russian intelligence priorities. It may also relate to regional tensions: since early 2025, Romania has reported several incidents involving Russian drones crashing near or within its territory, prompting strong reactions from Romanian authorities and calls for a NATO mission in the Black Sea region.

The Kazakh compromise also occurred in a relevant political context. Since January 2026, Kazakhstan has reportedly begun deporting some Russian exiles and regime critics who had previously found relative safety there after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Compromising a Kazakh governmental body fits a scenario in which the operators want visibility into Russian dissidents known to Kazakh authorities but not yet on any deportation list.

There is one more detail worth noting. Activity in Kazakhstan surged on January 15th, 2026 – the day after the Old New Year, an informal holiday still observed in Russia and some neighboring countries. While malware does not celebrate holidays, its operators do.

Tracing the Cereal crumbs

The first components we found did not resemble a classic backdoor. There was no obvious monolithic implant, no built-in command list, and no simple beaconing pattern. Instead, the activity appeared as a chain of specialized components: encrypted payloads on disk, .NET assemblies embedded inside other .NET assemblies, legitimate Windows processes loading suspicious DLLs, and Exchange services executing code that did not belong there.

Reconstructing that chain revealed a modular toolset built around a few recurring design principles: keep payloads encrypted, keep execution in memory whenever possible, reuse the compromised Exchange server, and deliver commands as separate .NET assemblies. Figure 2 shows the relationships between all of the observed components of the toolset.

Main components are:

CerealLoader, which loads and runs a .NET assembly from an encrypted file on disk. This is the only component in the toolset that is written to disk as a recognizable .NET file. Everything else is delivered inside encrypted containers, unpacked at runtime, and executed from memory.

CerealRunner, which contains other encrypted binaries that are loaded and executed. It provides a way to encapsulate and deliver commands, as well as other components.

CerealSprinter, which is similar to CerealRunner, but is used only to load and run other components.

CerealNeuron, a passive backdoor with no built-in commands but capable of executing assemblies contained in CerealRunner binaries, received in network requests; we named it in reference to Neuron, a malware family documented and attributed to Turla by the United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre in 2017, given that they are functionally similar.

CerealHermit, a variant of CerealNeuron with no network functionalities. It reads commands from encrypted files on disk.

CerealIron, an injector that allows operators to load and run .NET assemblies from non .NET processes.

CerealBox, which processes, filters, and collects interesting email messages by being injected into Microsoft Exchange’s transport service.

CerealMoth, a simple component that receives an assembly and a method name as arguments, loads the assembly, and runs the specified method.

When the victim’s Exchange is the infrastructure

The most notable aspect of this campaign is what we did not find: an attacker-controlled server.

Most backdoors periodically contact their operators. That behavior leaves traces – domains, IP addresses, hosting providers, timing patterns – that defenders identify and block. CerealNeuron, the main backdoor in the Cereal toolset, does none of that. Instead of initiating outbound connections, it waits for incoming requests.

CerealNeuron runs on the compromised Exchange server and passively listens for incoming web requests on paths that look like ordinary Exchange traffic. Among the paths we observed:

https://*:443/owa/sdds/

HTTPS://*:443/AUTODISCOVER/PROXYSERVICE/

HTTPS://*:443/MICROSOFT-SERVER-ACTIVESYNC/INTEGRATED/API/

To a firewall log or an analyst reviewing traffic, requests to these paths blend in with legitimate Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover, and ActiveSync traffic. If a request for a resource on one of these paths is properly encrypted and passes several integrity checks, CerealNeuron decrypts it, treats the contents as a command, and runs it. If a request looks wrong, CerealNeuron redirects the client to a legitimate-looking Exchange error page.

The consequences are significant:

There is no dedicated C&C infrastructure to discover, block, or take down. The victim’s own internet-facing Exchange server is the operator-accessible control point.

Network-based tracking is severely limited. We were unable to identify the ingress IP addresses used by the operators. They may have connected directly, via anonymization services, or from other compromised hosts.

Malicious traffic coexists with legitimate Exchange web services – exactly the kind of traffic defenders are least likely to block.

Figure 3 shows the communication flow between operators and CerealNeuron.

Abusing a compromised Exchange server as a central operational hub is a rare technique, used by only a handful of APT groups. Turla has used variations of this approach in the past. With Cereal, relying on the victim’s Exchange server removes the need for dedicated attacker infrastructure.

The toolset also provides a fallback mechanism. CerealHermit is a variant of CerealNeuron with the network parts removed. Instead of waiting for web requests, it reads encrypted command files from disk and writes encrypted results back. In some intrusions, both backdoors were deployed together, giving operators two independent ways to reach their goals.

Commands as disposable programs

Rather than a single large backdoor containing every possible command, Turla’s operators deliver each command as its own small, compiled .NET program.

The core execution component is CerealRunner. It carries other encrypted .NET programs inside itself, along with the arguments needed to run them. When it executes, it unpacks its payloads, runs them in memory, and returns their output through the same pipeline so CerealNeuron can encrypt and send it back.

We detected numerous CerealRunner binaries across the two intrusions. They share the same structure but differ in the small piece of code that implements each specific task.

The commands include:

Retrieving mailboxes or specific messages via Exchange Web Services.

Querying Active Directory for computers, users, groups, and DNS records.

Running WMI queries – for example, to list processes or active TCP connections.

Extracting LSA Secrets (credentials that Windows stores locally).

Listing volume snapshots.

Listing, reading, and deleting files – often the staged email dumps produced by CerealBox.

The sheer volume of near-identical binaries, each compiled for a specific task, strongly suggests that the operators have an internal framework that automates the compilation and packaging of commands. Combined with a codebase built around modular, interchangeable components, the impression is one of a mature, well-engineered platform – rather than a loose collection of scripts.

.NET tricks that are not for kids

What distinguishes Cereal from most recent APT cases is how deeply it leverages the inner workings of .NET, Microsoft’s software framework that powers a large part of Windows and Exchange itself.

Normally, .NET programs run through the Common Language Runtime (CLR), which converts a program’s instructions into machine code just before running them. This whole process is visible to standard analysis tools. Cereal repeatedly operates outside these standard, observable paths.

A .NET program that runs native code before any .NET code

CerealLoader is the only Cereal component written to disk in unencrypted form. In a .NET decompiler, the entry point code does essentially nothing, and a breakpoint set on the malicious method is never triggered.

In practice, CerealLoader executes low-level, machine-native code before the .NET runtime even starts running its normal instructions. It abuses a rarely used feature of the .NET specification, Vtable Fixups, to build a hidden bridge from native code back into a .NET method that no other part of the program appears to call. An analyst inspecting only the .NET side sees code that appears to do nothing. By that point, the real payload has already run.

Hijacking legitimate Windows components

Because CerealLoader can bootstrap itself from native code, the operators can drop it in places where legitimate, non-.NET Windows processes will load it. In one execution chain, CerealLoader was placed as ncobjapi.dll inside C:\Windows\System32\wbem\, where the Windows Management Instrumentation service loaded it automatically. In another, it impersonated wbemcomn.dll in the same folder. The malicious DLL forwards legitimate function calls, so the affected process continues to operate normally.

Abuse of the .NET native image cache

To improve startup performance, .NET keeps a cache of precompiled versions of common libraries in a system folder. When a program asks for one of these libraries, the runtime checks the cache first and, if there is a match, loads the cached version instead of JIT-compiling the assembly’s code. The operators placed malicious CerealLoader files in this cache, using names such as Microsoft.Exchange.Search.Mdb.ni.dll. When Exchange asked for the corresponding library, the runtime loaded the malicious version instead. Because the malicious file contains no real replacement code, .NET quietly falls back to the genuine library for actual functionality – but not before the attackers’ native entry point code has executed. In one sample, the malicious code only activates when the parent process is Exchange’s search service.

Each of these techniques is documented in lesser-known parts of the .NET specification. What is unusual is seeing them combined so deliberately in a single toolset, and used specifically to hide inside Microsoft Exchange.

CerealBox: hooking Exchange from the inside

The Cereal component that uses the most novel technique is CerealBox, an email collection module built for Microsoft Exchange.

Turla has targeted Exchange servers before, including through the abuse of transport agents – a legitimate Exchange feature that lets developers hook into the flow of email for tasks such as spam filtering. Installed transport agents, however, leave visible traces in Exchange’s configuration.

CerealBox uses a stealthier approach. Instead of registering itself, it is injected directly into EdgeTransport.exe, the Exchange process that handles email flow. Reaching that point, however, is not straightforward: CerealBox is delivered through an intricate chain of nested Cereal components, illustrated in Figure 4.

Once inside, CerealBox accesses Exchange’s internal structures, finds the existing transport agents, and wraps their handlers with malicious code. The wrappers run CerealBox’s own logic first, then hand control back to the original code. Email continues to flow normally. No new agent appears anywhere in Exchange’s configuration. In short: CerealBox doesn’t add a new agent; it hijacks existing ones loaded in memory.

Having visibility into the mail flow, CerealBox picks out messages of interest. A message qualifies if it has a .doc, .docx, or .pdf attachment and matches at least one of several hardcoded lists – sender addresses, recipient addresses, subject substrings, or attachment names – while avoiding matching ignore lists. Interesting messages are compressed, encrypted, and staged in files on disk. Operators later use ordinary CerealNeuron commands to exfiltrate and delete these files.

Injecting into the Exchange transport service and hooking mail flow from within is a novel technique, not previously documented for any malware family. It requires a deep understanding of how Exchange’s mail pipeline is structured internally – the kind of knowledge that requires significant time and effort to acquire.

Conclusion

The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyberespionage. It leaves little on disk, avoids external infrastructure that could be discovered and blocked, and conceals itself within legitimate Exchange processes. The use of unmanaged entry points, VTable Fixups, native image cache abuse, and in-memory injection into Exchange’s transport pipeline reflects a level of investment in .NET tradecraft that is uncommon even among sophisticated APT actors.

The Cereal toolset demonstrates that, for Turla, Exchange servers are not just mail servers – they are durable collection points, internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft.

For any inquiries about our research published on WeLiveSecurity, please contact us at threatintel@eset.com.

ESET Research offers private APT intelligence reports and data feeds. For any inquiries about this service, visit the ESET Threat Intelligence page.

IoCs

A comprehensive list of indicators of compromise (IoCs) can be found in our GitHub repository and the Turla white paper.

IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Non-mobile statistics IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics

The mobile section of the quarterly cyberthreat report includes statistics on malware, adware, and potentially unwanted software for Android, as well as descriptions of the most notable threats for Android and iOS discovered during the reporting period. These statistics are based on detection alerts from Kaspersky products, collected from users who consented to provide statistical data to Kaspersky Security Network.

The quarter in figures

According to Kaspersky Security Network, in Q3 2026:

More than 1.66 million attacks involving mobile malware, adware, or unwanted software were blocked.

The Trojan-Banker category was the prevalent mobile malware threat with a 31.63% share of all detected malicious apps.

Over 378,000 malicious installation packages were detected, including 119,688 mobile banking Trojan packages.

Quarterly highlights

In July, we discovered a malicious app targeting Brazilian users that may have used AI to automate fraud. The app was disguised as Google Play Protect, a suite of security services for Android devices.

Malicious app imitating Google Play Protect

The app’s code used the DistilBERT model to interpret natural-language commands sent from the C2 server. Traces left in the code suggest the server-side commands may also have been generated by a large language model (LLM).

In August, we discovered a Trojan that analyzed images saved in the device’s gallery and took screenshots to look for banking data, including CVV codes. The malware used an on-device AI model to classify images. The app could also update this model, which gave the scammers a way to expand the Trojan’s functionality.

In the third quarter, the infamous subscription Trojan detected as Trojan.AndroidOS.Subscriber.bh made it into Google Play again. This time, it was disguised as an app for creating keyboard themes.

Subscription Trojan disguised as a keyboard theme app

The Trojan opened a subscription link in a hidden WebView and intercepted the message containing the confirmation code. According to our data, the scammers mainly targeted users in Thailand.

There were also new attacks on iOS users. In August, researchers at Socket discovered 13 infected PHP packages in the Packagist repository. The malicious payload injected links to fraudulent casinos into sites that used these packages and, on iOS devices only, a hidden iframe that loaded the DarkSword exploit kit. The attack delivered a spyware module that stole keychain contents, Wi-Fi passwords, SMS messages, photos, and other personal data. Other modules found in this campaign were used to steal crypto wallet data and the seed phrases used to recover them.

SlowMist researchers found the same DarkSword exploit chain used in a fake app, FomoPeek. FomoPeek was published in the App Store, presenting itself as a crypto wallet tracker. The malware was designed to steal data from notes and crypto wallet apps.

Also in August, we discovered infected versions of popular iOS apps distributed through Telegram (link in Russian). To install such an app, the attackers asked users to buy a developer certificate. The modified versions contained a malicious module that collected device information, took screenshots, and sent this data to a server.

Mobile threat statistics

The downward trend in attacks on mobile devices involving malware, adware, or unwanted software continued: the number fell to 1,668,368 in Q3 from 1,996,823 in Q2.

Attacks on users of Kaspersky mobile solutions, Q1 2025 – Q3 2026 (download)

In the third quarter, this decline was driven in part by fewer adware attacks, which we examine in more detail below.

The number of Android malware samples grew compared to the previous reporting period, reaching 378,456.

Detected malicious and potentially unwanted installation packages, Q3 2025 – Q3 2026 (download)

The distribution of detected installation packages by type was as follows:

Detected mobile apps by type, Q2*–Q3 2026 (download)

* Data for the previous quarter may differ slightly from previously published data due to certain verdicts being retrospectively revised.

The sharp rise in Trojan-Dropper apps comes from more droppers delivering known banking Trojans such as Mamont and Creduz. In the previous quarter, we described the trend of attackers “packaging” banking Trojans. The resulting malware is classified as droppers, which explains the growth. Note that standalone banking Trojans still rank first. Together with droppers, they account for more than half of all detected malicious apps.

* The total percentage may exceed 100% if the same users encountered multiple attack types.

The number of AdWare.AndroidOS.HiddenAd and AdWare.AndroidOS.MobiDash attacks continued to decline, although adware traditionally ranks first by the number of attacked users. The growing share of Trojan-Dropper correlates with the increase in packaged banking Trojans described in the previous section. Among Trojan-Spy attacks, the biggest growth came from the BTMOB and SpyNote RAT Trojans, which are used to steal money.

The main newcomer among Q3’s most widespread malware was the Trojan-Proxy.AndroidOS.Vo1d.b apps, delivered by preinstalled Trojans. These apps turn the device into an exit node of a VPN service. Second, cybercriminals can use the infected device to attack online services and visit banned websites, breaking the law in the victim’s name.

ddcc7fc95f69.text:
Google on Monday released updates to patch nine security vulnerabilities, including one that has come under active exploitation in the wild.

The high-severity vulnerability, assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: 8.8), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component.

"Use-after-free in XML in Google Chrome prior to 157.0.8103.50 allowed a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page," reads the description of the flaw on CVE.org.

Use-after-free bugs typically occur when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has already been freed. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to achieve data corruption, program crashes, or arbitrary code execution.

An anonymous security researcher has been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw on November 6, 2026.

Google acknowledged it is "aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," but has not revealed any additional specific information related to how it's being abused in real-world attacks or who is behind them.

"Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix," the tech giant added. "We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third-party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven't yet fixed."

With the latest development, Google has addressed a total of eight actively exploited Chrome zero-days since the start of the year. This includes CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281, CVE-2026-11645, CVE-2026-85046, and CVE-2026-87491.

For optimal protection, users are advised to update their Chrome browser to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Apple macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. To ensure the latest updates are installed, users can navigate to More > Help > About Google Chrome and select Relaunch.

Users of other Chromium-based browsers, such as Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi, are also advised to apply the fixes as and when they become available.

Update

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added the Chrome vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the patch by November 24, 2026.

e7676b4f3739.text:
N-able said it has taken N-central Hosted Environments offline and is urging on-premises customers to shut down their servers until further notice following the public disclosure of over 30 vulnerabilities collectively tracked as Able2Shell.

"As a precautionary measure, we are temporarily taking our Hosted N-central environment offline while we take the necessary actions to secure the environment and implement appropriate remediation," N-able said.

"During this time, customers will be unable to access their Hosted N-central classic environment, and associated services may be unavailable. However, the Ecoverse services under N-able Login remain available and online, including Asset View, Patching, Vulnerability Management, scripting, policies and tagging."

The company also said it has not observed any signs of active exploitation of these vulnerabilities, adding it's currently working on a hot fix to address them.

The following services are impacted -

N-central (hosted version) (Americas)

N-central (hosted version) (APAC)

N-central (hosted version) (Europe)

N-central On-premise (Americas)

N-central On-premise (APAC)

N-central On-premise (Europe)

The development comes as independent security researcher Sean Bales disclosed multiple security flaws along with proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits. The researcher said the issues were tested against N-able N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31.

The identified zero-day vulnerabilities include credential disclosure, arbitrary file writes, directory traversal, cross-site scripting (XSS), XML external entity (XXE) injection, and remote code execution (RCE) flaws -

Multiple N-central zero-days enable anonymous credential theft, administrator creation, and nable/root RCE.

Chains include XXE/NCI trust abuse, support-token theft, unsigned NSP execution, XSS-to-OGNL, and authenticated reverse shells.

Arbitrary file writes, traversal, credential disclosure, MDM impersonation, audit tampering, and privileged-helper injection.

A native GenericTCP stack overflow also achieves root command execution

Successful exploitation of these flaws can allow rogue administrative access to the N-central management interface and facilitate command execution as root.

Update

watchTowr, in a post shared on X, said it "observed exploitation attempts against N-able N-central honeypots overnight following the 'Able2Shell' zero-days being dropped."

The preemptive exposure management firm is urging users to audit for signs of compromise, restrict access, and follow vendor guidance on mitigation steps.

In an X post, Defused Cyber said it has detected probing of N-able N-central for the Able2Shell zero-days. "We have seen opening of anonymous agent sessions, pulling appliance config and hitting the remote control endpoint without auth," it added. "These pathways are part of the 0-day exploit surface."

N-able has also confirmed that it's seeing "scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code" but emphasized there is no evidence of successful exploitation in any customer environment.

The company has released N-central 2026.4 HF2 to address the following vulnerabilities. A follow-up hotfix is expected to be released to "provide further security updates" as part of its response to the Able2Shell disclosure.

CVE-2026-125883 - Multiple XXE Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125878 - Multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125879 - Local privilege escalation to root via nable-writable syslog-ng config

CVE-2026-125880 - Stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata (admin context)

CVE-2026-125881 - Schema-hint SSRF via service import schema validation

CVE-2026-125882 - RCE via file repository upload path traversal (Credit Nate Fair, Sprocket Security)

CVE-2026-91000 - Insecure IPC Channels lead to local privilege escalation

All Hosted N-central servers (NCODs) across all global regions have been upgraded. N-able is also urging customers to keep N-central servers offline until the updates have been successfully applied.

According to data from Censys, there are 1,728 internet-exposed N-central instances. Threat intelligence firm Previdian said it has recorded 68 exploitation attempts against one of its honeypots from a single IP address within about 18 hours of the publication.

Huntress is urging users to review login and authentication activity from November 8, 2026, onward for unexpected or unauthorized access, examine audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise, and apply N-able's hotfix and restore service only when N-able says it is safe.

Google on Monday informed Chrome users of new security updates that patch nine vulnerabilities, including a zero-day exploited in the wild.

The exploited vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-125350 and rated high severity, is a use-after-free in the web browser’s XML component.

A researcher who wants to remain anonymous reported the issue to Google on November 6.

The tech giant has not shared any additional details, and no information appears to be available on the attacks exploiting CVE-2026-125350.

CISA has yet to add CVE-2026-125350 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

This is the eighth Chrome zero-day exploited this year after CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281, CVE-2026-11645, CVE-2026-85046, and CVE-2026-87491.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

In addition to the zero-day, the latest Chrome updates patch six high-severity vulnerabilities in the WebGL, FileSystem, Compositing, GPU, V8, and XML components. Google discovered most of the flaws internally.

Two medium-severity bugs described as uninitialized resource issues in the GPU component have also been fixed.

The patches are included in Chrome 157 updates, specifically versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux.

November 2026 Attack Surface Analysis

Preview-pane-triggered exploitation remains a dominant attack surface pattern for the third consecutive month, with eight Critical RCE vulnerabilities across Microsoft Office applications including Outlook and Word. CVE-2026-110043 and CVE-2026-110068 in Outlook exemplify the risk: Merely selecting a malicious message in the Reading Pane or previewing an attachment in File Explorer triggers code execution without any click or macro prompt. This attack pattern continues to be attractive to phishing operators and initial access brokers because it converts document or message delivery into reliable code execution, bypassing the user-action barrier that many enterprises treat as a training backstop.

Identity platform components face elevated risk this month with Critical flaws in both Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) and Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS). CVE-2026-119958 enables RCE against LDAP, while CVE-2026-118146 and CVE-2026-118148 target AD DS with RCE and elevation-of-privilege attack paths, respectively. These protocols underpin domain authentication and authorization for every joined workstation and server; successful exploitation of either can cascade to domain-wide compromise. Similar identity fabric vulnerabilities have historically been targeted by advanced adversaries seeking persistent access to enterprise environments.

Windows Hyper-V sees an unusually high concentration of privilege escalation vulnerabilities this month, with eight CVEs spanning multiple flaw classes. CVE-2026-113753, CVE-2026-113856, and CVE-2026-113860 all enable elevation of privilege within the hypervisor boundary. Hyper-V underpins Azure compute infrastructure and endpoint features such as Windows Sandbox, Credential Guard, and other Virtualization-Based Security capabilities, so the exposure extends beyond dedicated virtualization hosts to ordinary Windows endpoints with these features enabled.

Legacy network services including Server Message Block (SMB) and Print Spooler continue to draw Critical-severity RCE findings, reinforcing the persistent risk these widely deployed components carry. The unauthenticated network-reachable RCE cluster spans 14 CVEs this month, with Windows Message Queuing (MSMQ) vulnerabilities such as CVE-2026-109459 and CVE-2026-116710 representing exposure on any system with MSMQ enabled. These services listen on the network by design and often lack authentication requirements for initial protocol negotiation, making any exposed instance an immediate target for opportunistic scanning. This class of legacy network service has historically been targeted in wormable exploitation scenarios.

Exploited Zero-Day Spoofing Vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook

CVE-2026-124194 is a Moderate spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook with a CVSS score of 6.5, and Microsoft confirms it is being exploited in the wild. The flaw stems from the product UI failing to warn users of unsafe actions: A specially crafted message file can cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, disclosing the victim's NTLMv2 hash.

Outlook is the default mail client across most enterprise Windows deployments, making any flaw that bypasses user safety prompts a direct initial access vector at scale. Exploitation requires the victim to open a malicious file delivered via email or another channel. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector for this particular CVE. Once the victim opens the file, Outlook silently initiates an outbound connection, and the captured NTLMv2 hash can be relayed or cracked offline to impersonate the user against other services that accept NTLM authentication.

The Moderate severity rating reflects the user interaction requirement, but the real-world exposure is broader than the score suggests. Credential disclosure flaws that require only a file open, bypass visible warnings, and yield reusable authentication material are a well-established technique in targeted intrusion campaigns. Similar spoofing primitives in Outlook have historically drawn attention from both commodity phishing operators and advanced adversaries seeking footholds in enterprise environments.

Critical RCE Vulnerabilities in Windows Services

CVE-2026-112967 and CVE-2026-116928 are Critical RCE vulnerabilities in Windows services, each carrying a CVSS score of 9.8. Both allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code over the network, though they affect distinct components with different deployment realities.

CVE-2026-112967 is a heap-based buffer overflow in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service. An in-network attacker can call arbitrary endpoints on the service to trigger the flaw. Enterprise exposure depends on whether the service is present and running. Consumer-oriented Windows SKUs and gaming-enabled configurations are the primary population, making this lower priority for most corporate fleets.

CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in the Windows Search component. The attack path is notable: An unauthenticated attacker can send an email with a specially crafted attachment to an Exchange Server, and the search indexer processes the attachment automatically for indexing. The recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation grants code execution with the permissions of the indexing service. Windows Search is broadly deployed and tightly integrated with Exchange for mailbox indexing, which places this flaw on an email delivery attack surface that reaches internet-facing mail infrastructure. The Windows Search path is the more significant exposure for enterprise environments. Email-delivered payloads that trigger without user interaction have historically been attractive to targeted intrusion operators because they bypass the phishing-click dependency that slows most initial access campaigns.

Critical RCE Vulnerability in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)

CVE-2026-119958 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in Windows LDAP with a CVSS score of 9.8. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write that allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code by sending specially crafted LDAP calls to a listening server. No authentication or user interaction is required.

LDAP is the directory access protocol that underpins Active Directory. Every domain controller exposes LDAP on TCP/389 (and TCP/636 for LDAPS) by design, and the service cannot be disabled without breaking domain operations. Member servers, workstations, and applications query LDAP continuously for authentication, group policy retrieval, and object lookups, making it one of the most heavily trafficked protocols inside any AD environment.

The scope-of-impact concern is substantial. Code execution within the LDAP service on a domain controller places the attacker inside the trust boundary that every other domain resource relies on. From that position, credential extraction, replication abuse, and lateral movement to additional DCs become straightforward follow-on actions. Because LDAP is network-reachable from any domain-joined host by default, any internal foothold that can route to a DC can attempt exploitation.

Unauthenticated RCE flaws in core AD infrastructure have historically drawn rapid attention from ransomware operators and targeted intrusion actors because they collapse the gap between initial access and domain-wide compromise.

Preview Pane-Triggered RCE Vulnerabilities Across Microsoft Office

Eight Critical RCE vulnerabilities this month share a common attack vector: the Preview Pane in Outlook and Word. All carry CVSS scores of 7.5 to 8.8, with seven of the eight scoring 8.8. The underlying flaw classes are use-after-free (four CVEs), heap-based buffer overflow (two CVEs), release of invalid pointer (one CVE), and use of uninitialized resource (one CVE). Despite the variation in memory-corruption primitives, the exploitation pattern is uniform: An attacker delivers a malicious document or email, and merely selecting it for preview triggers code execution with the user's privileges.

The Outlook vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-110043, CVE-2026-110068, CVE-2026-111309) are the highest-exposure items in this group. Email is the delivery mechanism, and the Preview Pane is enabled by default in most enterprise Outlook deployments. An external attacker who can send mail to a target organization can reach the vulnerable code path without any authentication or prior foothold. The Word vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-110067, CVE-2026-111285, CVE-2026-124185) require document delivery, which typically means a phishing attachment or a link to a malicious file, but still fire on preview rather than open.

The remaining two CVEs (CVE-2026-111289, CVE-2026-120003) affect the broader Office suite and follow the same preview-triggered pattern. CVE-2026-124185 has a lower score (7.5) due to high attack complexity, but the others require no special conditions beyond user receipt of the malicious content.

Preview Pane vulnerabilities have historically been attractive to phishing operators and initial-access brokers because delivery converts directly to execution, with no need to persuade a user to open an attachment.

Critical Vulnerabilities in Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)

CVE-2026-118146 and CVE-2026-118148 are Critical vulnerabilities in Active Directory Domain Services that both stem from incorrect authorization flaws. The two CVEs share a flaw class but differ in outcome and attack complexity.

CVE-2026-118146 carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and enables RCE. An authenticated attacker with low-level access to an affected server can send a specially crafted request and execute code without any user interaction. The authorization flaw means the server fails to properly validate that the authenticated principal should be permitted to perform the requested operation, turning a low-privilege foothold into code execution on a domain controller.

CVE-2026-118148 has a CVSS score of 7.5 and results in elevation of privilege to SYSTEM. This vulnerability has high attack complexity because successful exploitation requires the attacker to win a race condition. An authenticated attacker who can trigger the race gains SYSTEM privileges on the domain controller.

Active Directory Domain Services provides directory and authentication services for Windows enterprise domains. Domain controllers running AD DS issue Kerberos tickets, store the directory database, and process authentication and authorization decisions for every domain-joined resource. Compromise of a domain controller typically means compromise of the entire domain, since the attacker gains access to credential material and can issue arbitrary authentication assertions.

The attack surface for both vulnerabilities is any domain controller reachable from an authenticated low-privileged foothold. In most enterprise deployments, that includes every writable DC in the forest. Incorrect authorization flaws in identity platform components have historically been attractive to targeted intrusion operators because they convert commodity initial access into domain-wide compromise without requiring credential theft or additional tooling.

CVE-2026-118207 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in Microsoft Exchange Server with a CVSS score of 8.8. The flaw stems from use of an incorrectly resolved name or reference, allowing an authenticated attacker with low-level access to send a specially crafted request and execute code on the server. No user interaction is required.

Microsoft Exchange Server provides enterprise email, calendar, and collaboration services, and is commonly deployed with internet-facing client access services for mobile and web users. The authentication requirement lowers the bar only modestly in most environments: Any compromised mailbox credential, service account, or partner federation relationship satisfies it. Once that requirement is met, the attacker reaches code execution on a server that typically holds sensitive mail content, internal address lists, and often enjoys elevated trust relationships with Active Directory.

Organizations running on-premises Exchange frequently expose Outlook Web Access, Exchange ActiveSync, and Autodiscover endpoints to the internet. Servers in this posture are reachable from any network position once the attacker obtains valid credentials, and successful exploitation yields a foothold inside the perimeter on infrastructure that processes sensitive communications.

Exchange Server vulnerabilities have historically drawn sustained attention from nation-state threat actors and ransomware operators because the combination of internet exposure, high-value data, and domain trust relationships makes compromised Exchange servers effective pivot points for broader intrusions.

Critical Elevation of Privilege Vulnerabilities in Windows Hyper-V

Microsoft addresses eight Critical elevation of privilege vulnerabilities in Windows Hyper-V this month, spanning five distinct flaw classes: use-after-free (four CVEs), heap-based buffer overflow (one CVE), TOCTOU race condition (one CVE), untrusted pointer dereference (one CVE), and use of uninitialized resource (one CVE). CVSS scores range from 6.4 to 8.2, with CVE-2026-113753 at the top of the range.

The exploitation outcomes fall into two categories. CVE-2026-113753 allows an attacker to gain Virtual Trust Level 1 (VTL1) privileges, which means escaping from the normal kernel (VTL0) into the secure kernel layer that underpins Virtualization-Based Security features such as Credential Guard. Five of the remaining seven CVEs enable guest-to-host escape: An attacker operating inside a guest virtual machine can execute code on the host in the security context of the virtual machine worker process.

Hyper-V is the hypervisor layer that runs Azure compute infrastructure and powers client-side Windows features including Windows Sandbox, Windows Subsystem for Linux 2, and Virtualization-Based Security. The exposure therefore reaches both datacenter server populations and ordinary endpoints where these features are enabled.

Most of the cluster carries a high attack complexity because exploitation requires winning a race condition, which raises the practical difficulty but does not eliminate the risk. Hypervisor escapes of this class have historically attracted attention from advanced adversaries because a successful exploit compromises the isolation boundary that separates tenants in shared infrastructure and protects credential material on endpoints.

CVE-2026-119957 is a Critical elevation of privilege vulnerability in Windows Remote Desktop Services with a CVSS score of 7.8. The flaw is a double-free that requires the attacker to win a race condition. Although exploitation is local, successful exploitation allows an attacker operating inside a guest virtual machine to escape to the host and gain the privileges of the affected virtualization service.

Remote Desktop Services underpins RDP-based remote administration across Windows Server deployments and is a core component in Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) environments. The guest-to-host escape path described in Microsoft's FAQ elevates this from a local privilege escalation to a potential hypervisor boundary violation, which matters in any multi-tenant or shared-host scenario.

The attack complexity is high due to the race condition. Post-compromise scenarios where an attacker already controls a guest VM provide the dwell time needed to attempt exploitation repeatedly. RDS-based session hosts and VDI pools present the most exposure to this guest-to-host escalation path.

CVE-2026-113825 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in the Windows SMB Server Network Transport Driver (srvnet.sys) with a CVSS score of 7.5. The flaw is a race condition that an authenticated attacker can trigger over the network to execute code. Microsoft notes that successful exploitation requires the attacker to win the race, which accounts for the high attack-complexity rating.

SMB is the native file-sharing protocol for Windows and is enabled by default on both client and server editions. The srvnet.sys driver handles the network transport layer for SMB traffic, sitting beneath the higher-level SMB2 and SMB3 protocol handlers. SMB listens on TCP/445 and is fundamental to domain operations such as SYSVOL replication, Group Policy delivery, and administrative shares.

The authentication requirement limits drive-by exploitation from the internet, but any attacker who has already obtained low-privileged domain credentials, or who operates from a compromised workstation, can attempt the race. Timing-based flaws in kernel-mode network drivers can be unreliable on a single attempt, yet become practical when an attacker can retry at scale across many hosts. Ransomware operators and targeted intrusion operators have historically exploited race-condition RCE flaws in legacy network services for lateral movement and wormable propagation.

CVE-2026-113752 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in Windows Print Spooler with a CVSS score of 7.5. The flaw is a use-after-free that an unauthenticated attacker can trigger over an adjacent network. Successful exploitation requires winning a race condition, which raises the practical difficulty but does not eliminate the risk in contested LAN environments.

Windows Print Spooler manages print job queuing and driver loading on Windows endpoints and servers. It runs with SYSTEM privileges by default and is enabled on virtually every Windows installation, including workstations that have no physical printer attached. The adjacent-network attack vector limits exposure to attackers who already have a foothold on the same network segment, but that constraint is often satisfied during post-compromise lateral movement.

Not All Relevant Vulnerabilities Have Patches: Consider Mitigation Strategies

As we have learned with other notable vulnerabilities, such as Log4j, not every highly exploitable vulnerability can be easily patched. As is the case for the ProxyNotShell vulnerabilities, it’s critically important to develop a response plan for how to defend your environments when no patching protocol exists.

Regular review of your patching strategy should still be a part of your program, but you should also look more holistically at your organization's methods for cybersecurity and improve your overall security posture.

About CVSS Scores

The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) is a free and open industry standard that CrowdStrike and many other cybersecurity organizations use to assess and communicate software vulnerabilities’ severity and characteristics. Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of X.Org Server. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must connect to a malicious X11 server.

The specific flaw exists within the XkbReadKeyActions function. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a fixed-length heap-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

Additional Details

X.Org has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/xorg/lib/libx11/-/merge_requests/309

Disclosure Timeline

2026-09-02 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of NVIDIA Megatron-LM. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must open a malicious file.

8a588b5ea14d.text:
Sophos X-Ops is tracking ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework that multiple threat actors have used in intrusions since its public release in July 2026. One of the most prominent cases is the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise in mid-October, which Microsoft attributes to Storm-0940, a group it assesses as “China-state aligned.”

How ARTEX works

ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent penetration testing framework written in Go. It supports multiple LLM providers and compatible endpoints; in reported campaigns, operators have connected it to models including DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok. Given an objective, ARTEX has the following capabilities:

Use planning agents to map the target and decide the next step

Worker agents can invoke offensive tooling and feed results back into the planning process. In malicious deployments, this could include activities such as scanning, exploitation, credential access and webshell deployment

Planning agents can adjust the plan and launch subsequent rounds via worker agents

It records the assets and vulnerabilities it discovers in a graph as the test progresses

Can attempt multiple breach paths at the same time

In campaigns described by Microsoft and Google/Mandiant, operators have supplied ARTEX with authentication material or compromised application credentials and used it against cloud APIs and services, such as Microsoft Graph.

Sophos countermeasures

Sophos has existing endpoint, network, and cloud protections covering multiple behaviours and indicators associated with reported ARTEX activity.

The protections below target ARTEX and the campaigns reported so far. Our evaluation of coverage is ongoing, and we will update this table as it changes.

Layer

Protection

Taegis XDR

ConnectWise Compromise: Service Principal Credential Added or Role Assigned by an Application

ConnectWise app sign-in with scripted user agent

File detection

Troj/Bckdr-SDA (trojanized ARTEX Docker image)

Troj/Loader-TU

Linux/Agent-KD

ATK/Artex-A

ATK/Artex-B

ATK/Artex-C

Web and IP reputation

IPs associated with publicly reported ARTEX use blocked as malware

Sophos Firewall

The following signatures have been released to Sophos Firewall and Endpoint IPS to cover network-observable ARTEX behaviours and indicators:

2313266 - SCAN ARTEX Agentic Framework OAuth illegal_redirect_uri_enhanced Error Response

2313265 - SCAN ARTEX Agentic Framework WWW-Authenticate Basic realm ARTEX Response Header

2313264 - SCAN ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework baseline canary probe observed

2313263 - SCAN ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework spec-driven API collection write attempt

2313261 - SCAN ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework tenant isolation bypass attempt

2313259 - SCAN ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework OAuth unregistered redirect URI abuse attempt

2313258 - SCAN ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework unsigned JWT alg-none SSO bypass attempt

2313257 - SCAN ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework suspicious User-Agent observed

Endpoint IPS

2313266 - ARTEX Agentic Framework OAuth illegal_redirect_uri_enhanced Error Response

2313265 - ARTEX Agentic Framework WWW-Authenticate Basic realm ARTEX Response Header

2313264 - ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework baseline canary probe observed

2313263 - ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework spec-driven API collection write attempt

2313261 - ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework tenant isolation bypass attempt

2313259 - ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework OAuth unregistered redirect URI abuse attempt

2313258 - ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework unsigned JWT alg-none SSO bypass attempt

2313257 - ARTEX agentic-AI pentest framework suspicious User-Agent observed

Troj/Bckdr-SDA detects a backdoored copy of the ARTEX Docker image. The original project has been taken offline by its developer, so researchers sourcing the framework from unofficial mirrors and clones should treat those copies as untrusted.

Sophos has identified activity at a small number of customers that is consistent with ARTEX or other AI-assisted offensive tooling

Common themes include webshell and SQL Server command execution, credential theft, and attempts to move between systems. We’ve also seen rapid command sequences, repeated attempts with small changes, and structured output markers, consistent with agent-driven activity.

Across these instances, existing Sophos Endpoint protections surfaced multiple signals at multiple stages of the attacks. In many cases, Active Adversary Protection (AAP) was enabled and added further protection to disrupt subsequent attack behaviors.

It’s worth noting that, in line with what we’ve discussed previously regarding AI-enabled attacks, the attack activities are broadly the same, but the scale, noise, and persistence all increase significantly. In our telemetry, we noted hundreds of protection events relating to these attacks.

The rules we observed included:

Initial access and server execution

Access_1b

Access_3b

Exec_34a and Exec_34b

Credential theft and collection

Creds_4c

Creds_4l

Creds_2a and Creds_2d

Creds_3b

Collection_2c

Lateral movement and tool transfer

Lateral_5a

Exec_37a

Lateral_1b

Web shells and execution activity

Persist_26c

Exec_6a and Exec_17a

Evade_13a

AAP protections

Disrupt_2a

Disrupt_7e

Disrupt_7f

Disrupt_7g

Disrupt_7h

Threat hunting indicators

These indicators come from ARTEX activity described in reported campaigns. In its report, Microsoft claims that Storm-0940 was using ARTEX “as early as September 2026,” so we recommend hunting back to at least this date. Additional reporting indicates that an ARTEX-related incident occurred in September 2026, targeting South Korean financial organizations.

In cloud environments, look for:

Service principal credentials added, or roles assigned, by an application

Application sign-ins with a scripted user agent

On hosts, look for:

Temporary tooling and output files named i<intentID>[variant]_<purpose>.<ext>, for example i12345_b2.ps1.

Files or paths beginning with artx, particularly under C:\Windows\Temp.

Commands containing structured execution-verification markers – such as MARKER123/ARTX123, particularly when combined with rapid command sequences and repeated command variants

Bursts of commands, repeated variants of the same command, and output written to temporary files.

Recommended actions

Several reported ARTEX campaigns have leveraged existing or compromised access, including stolen application credentials, consented third-party apps, and valid accounts. Sophos recommends the following steps as best practice:

Audit service principals and enterprise applications in Microsoft Entra ID. Remove third-party app consents you no longer use, and review every credential addition and role assignment made since September 2026.

Apply Conditional Access policies to workload identities where licensing allows, restricting application sign-ins to expected locations.

Alert on application sign-ins with scripted user agents, and on authentication failure rates that exceed normal baselines.

Automate first response. When an attack reaches privileged access in a short amount of time, containment steps such as disabling a service principal or revoking its credentials should run from a playbook, with an analyst confirming afterwards.

If your own red team uses agentic frameworks, register their infrastructure and tooling names with your SOC so that authorized activity stands out.
