On November 9, 2026, a security researcher released a series of proof-of-concept (PoC) scripts targeting various vulnerabilities in N-able's N-central platform. The collection of PoCs claims to exploit several critical weaknesses in the N-central platform. As a result, N-able has taken the precautionary step of taking their N-central Hosted Environments offline.

At this time there is third-party reporting suggesting that exploitation is occurring in the wild. N-Able’s advisory does not indicate that they have observed exploitation as of this writing; however they do note that they have observed scanning activity associated with the published PoC code. At this time, Sophos X-Ops has not observed exploitation. We recommend that operators of on-premises N-central servers follow N-able’s advice.

Recommended actions

Sophos X-Ops recommends that organizations review N-able’s advisory and monitor it for further instructions from N-able.

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this threat and will deliver detections and protections as available.

a98f6b38adfc.text:
In the Odyssey, the Sirens promised every passing sailor the story of "everything that is going to happen over the whole world." Circe warned Odysseus that their listeners never made it home, but he wanted to hear the song anyway. He also knew he couldn't trust himself once he did. So he stopped his crew's ears with wax, had them bind him upright to the mast, and gave them one standing order: "If I beg and pray you to set me free, then bind me more tightly still." When the song came, he signaled with his brows for his men to let him go, and Eurylochus and Perimedes tied him tighter. The song is what people remember, but the engineering worked. Odysseus set his limits before the temptation arrived, and he left its enforcement to ropes he couldn't loosen and men who couldn't hear him.

The previous piece covered turning an agent's prompt into an access policy that a person validates. This piece covers whether that policy holds once the agent starts working. Three questions define the design. Can the agent tamper with the controls enforcing the policy? Does the control check the action regardless of how the agent attempts it? And does it receive enough task context to understand intent while staying simple enough to test? These questions connect controls a security vendor can build on endpoints today with broker, resource-side, and hardware enforcement elsewhere.

OpenAI demonstrated the problem while hardening its training environment. In Securing our frontier model training environment, published October 23, it reports that teams of agents "found several ways to chain vulnerabilities into microVM escapes." In a separate experiment, agents passed synthetic secrets between microVMs through the processor's cache, without network connections or shared writable files. OpenAI gave the attacking agents infrastructure source code and configuration details. In most communication tests, researchers also pointed them toward a specific channel or supplied a method for encoding and decoding messages. OpenAI says it remediated the discovered weaknesses and its frontier training now runs without live internet access.

Other containment failures took different forms. In Marchand et al.'s SandboxEscapeBench, which seeds containers with deliberate vulnerabilities, frontier models prompted to escape often got out through common misconfigurations like exposed Docker sockets and privileged containers, though none solved the hardest scenarios. Many attempts cost on the order of $1 each, cheap enough for an attacker or an uncontrolled agent to keep trying. Anthropic reviewed more than 140,000 evaluation runs and found three incidents involving real organizations through mistakenly open internet access. In those runs the agents needed no exploit, because a configuration mistake had already left the boundary open.

Every one of those failures happened in an environment built for containment. The PocketOS agent from the previous piece ran on a developer laptop, where it found an account-wide access token in a file unrelated to its task and used it to delete a production database. The credential read and destructive API request originated on the endpoint. A security product on that laptop could have seen the token read and the outbound request. With the agent's task supplied through its hook, it could also have recognized a credential unrelated to the task being used for a production deletion the task never required, and blocked the request before it left the machine.

Without that check, the PocketOS agent behaved like Odysseus's crew later in Book 12. They had been warned never to touch the cattle on the island of Thrinacia, but they landed there anyway, and every man swore an oath to leave the herd alone. Winds then kept them on the island for a month. The oath lasted as long as the food, and once the food ran out, the same men who had tied Odysseus tighter to the mast talked themselves into killing the cattle. At the Sirens, the crew had wax in their ears and nothing to decide. On Thrinacia, the cattle stayed within reach, and keeping the oath depended on hungry men choosing to obey it. The PocketOS agent's safety rule was that kind of oath, a sentence in its prompt that competed with the task, and the task won.

Security engineers have long required access controls that programs cannot alter or bypass, with enforcement simple enough to analyze and test. Anderson laid out those requirements in a 1972 computer security planning study for the U.S. Air Force, which introduced the reference monitor, a component that checks every access against policy. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 principle of complete mediation made the coverage requirement explicit: “Every access to every object must be checked for authority.” Agent systems add the work of connecting those checks to a task written in natural language. Moving enforcement outside the agent protects the checks, but requires an explicit way to carry the task context across that boundary.

Keep credentials and evidence outside the agent

The first component is Odysseus's standing order, the short list of actions the previous piece said require explicit human permission. It sits underneath every task, and no task scope can widen it. Enforced outside the agent, that list would have stopped the PocketOS deletion with no model judgment involved.

For credentials, Anthropic's write-up on decoupling the brain from the hands keeps tokens outside the sandbox, using a vault and proxy for custom tools, so they're "never reachable from the sandbox where Claude's generated code runs." Anthropic rejected narrow token scoping as the fix because it "encodes an assumption about what Claude can't do with a limited token." OpenAI's sandbox agents guide also separates the harness from compute, but it lets code in the sandbox use credentials scoped to the mounts and providers it needs. NVIDIA's open-source OpenShell runtime ships a version of this, giving the agent credential placeholders and adding real credentials only to requests that a supervisor outside the sandbox approves against policy. On a developer laptop, the same design means the agent never holds the token. OS controls keep the agent's processes away from credential files and stores, and a local broker makes authenticated requests on its behalf, accepting only narrow, typed operations and adding the credential at the moment of use. The PocketOS agent would have had no token to find.

The audit log belongs out of reach too. It should sit on the sensor side and capture who asked for what, under which task, and what was allowed or denied. Records should be sent to a logging service outside the agent’s control, using credentials that cannot alter or delete existing entries. The UK AI Security Institute's incident report on a July cyber evaluation illustrates the value of independent monitoring. Agents given internet access took unsanctioned actions against real people and organizations, and AISI's general security monitoring caught them by flagging data leaving over Tor. Within an hour of the alert, AISI had stopped every run and isolated the machines, and it found no resulting real-world harm. Independent monitoring only helps when its alerts reach someone with the authority to stop the agent, and AISI's did.

Enforcement across every execution path

Where the checks run is where endpoint vendors have the clearest advantage. Coding agents now expose hooks that let a security product inspect each prompt and tool call, and endpoint vendors can use those hooks to block an agent's action before it runs when it falls outside the task, whether a prompt injection caused it or the agent got there on its own. A hook sees only what the harness routes through it, such as the shell command the agent requested. What that command actually does, including the install scripts, child processes, file access, and network connections that follow, shows up in endpoint telemetry. A security product that sees both can check whether the behavior still fits the task the hook described.

The harness's own permission checks can be switched off from outside, too. In the Nx "s1ngularity" npm compromise in August 2025, a malicious install script ran the AI coding tools it found with flags like --dangerously-skip-permissions and --yolo and asked them to inventory the machine's secrets. GitGuardian found the requested inventory file on only about a quarter of targeted systems, and some clients explicitly refused credential-harvesting requests despite the disabled permission checks.

Endpoint products already collect process, file, and network telemetry. For agent security, those events need to be linked to the agent session and authorized task that caused them. Without that lineage, a destructive request from the agent's child process looks like any other request from the developer. Lineage is also what lets behavioral detection judge whatever gets past policy, by comparing what the agent's processes actually do with what its task needs.

Egress control follows from that lineage. AISI's hardened cyber ranges now disable outbound networking inside their sandboxes and, as an independent layer, block it again at the virtual machine host, on the assumption that "an agent might find its way past any single layer." On an endpoint the same idea becomes per-agent egress policy that covers DNS and package registries. OpenAI's September 20 incident went through a misconfigured resolver, as did the anonymized DNS exfiltration case Bloomberg's Andrey Rybka described in his AI Engineer talk, and OpenAI's July incident went through the package manager.

Information-flow labels track how untrusted content influences the agent's actions. A hostile web page or document can carry instructions, and Shumailov et al.'s CaMeL treats that as a data-flow problem, labeling where each value came from and checking those labels before any consequential tool call, which applies the same principle as parameterized queries: keeping untrusted data separate from instructions. Costa et al. build information-flow control into the agent's planner and check its policies at each tool call. A hostile document can still be summarized, but it doesn't get to choose who receives the summary.

Budgets limit how much an agent can spend or consume. The previous piece covered the AAuth budgets draft and the Resy agent that needed one. For a budget to hold, the resource has to enforce it, so the count stays out of the agent's reach. Human approval threads through all of these controls, because every limit that hands off to a person adds a prompt, and approvals that grow with agent volume eventually get rubber-stamped.

Canaries for the paths enforcement misses

Canary credentials help expose unexpected access paths, whether the agent wandered off-task, followed injected instructions, or was driven by a compromised install script, as in s1ngularity. A decoy token in a repository, home directory, or MCP configuration can reveal credential discovery or attempted use, though indexing and secret scanning may legitimately read the same file.

Tracebit, which sells canaries, ran a benchmark in an AWS environment of about 300 resources. Ten frontier models acted as red teamers, starting from a low-privilege access key with instructions to maximize impact stealthily, and in half the test conditions 11 decoy resources sat among the real ones. Of 951 runs, 352 were dropped from scoring, most because the model refused before touching AWS. Agents that reached admin took 14 minutes on average. When canaries were present, 96% of those runs had already tripped one before the agent's first critical action, a median of eight minutes earlier.

More capable models tripped more decoys, because they enumerate everything that looks high-value. Planting canaries without telling the agents did not significantly reduce full compromise (admin access plus persistence). But telling them to expect deception did, cutting it from 20% to 3% in a figure pooled across runs with and without canaries, so the warning itself did the work, like a "Beware of dog" sign on a yard that may have no dog. Sometimes the bark is enough.

Enough context to understand intent

Model judges can compare proposed actions with the authorized task, and this part of the design can improve with the models. Simple deterministic authorization checks can be cheap. Meta reports small-classifier latencies of 19-92 milliseconds on an A100 processing 512 tokens, while its illustrative LLM-check traces take roughly a second. DeAction averaged 7.2 seconds of guardrail reasoning per online action step. Those costs favor a cascade. Deterministic checks enforce explicit limits, a small classifier screens common cases, and an LLM judge reviews selected consequential or suspicious actions inline while scoring other activity asynchronously.

Anthropic evaluated a probe-assisted classifier cascade in shadow mode on production traffic. A lightweight probe screened every exchange and escalated about 5.5% to an external classifier, using about one-fortieth the compute of its single exchange-classifier baseline. Applying that design to agent actions requires measuring accuracy and interruptions at the workloads and base rates of the intended deployment. The judge should be swappable, with its measurement built in, and explicit authorization limits should remain enforced independently of its verdict.

Every enforcement point has to solve the same design problem. A hook inside the agent's harness sees the prompt and tool request, but only on the paths the harness exposes. OS instrumentation can observe local processes, file access, and connections, but needs trusted task context from the runtime or record to judge whether they fit the work. At every layer, that connection needs as much design attention as where the enforcer sits.

The task also has to arrive intact, because a formal check inherits whatever the translation got wrong. When Taheri et al. re-tested RoboGuard, which uses a model to translate safety rules into temporal logic, every harmful plan that passed in their evaluations traced back to an incorrect translation. The downstream check enforced the specification it received.

NVIDIA's Open Agent Safety Platform, announced September 28, extends OpenShell into hardware through Sentry, a framework designed to run on BlueField-4 data processing units in a host-independent trust domain. NVIDIA says it can quarantine an agent "within milliseconds." Its reference architecture puts BlueField-4 on the node's only network path to the model and outside world. DOCA Tower terminates TLS for connections configured for inspection, while memory introspection tracks containers, processes, and loaded libraries using their associated hashes. Those signals describe execution and integrity. Understanding intent still requires the user-approved task and its limits, supplied through a trusted connection to the runtime.

For hardware enforcement to deliver, the deployment has to route the relevant traffic through it and prevent the host from changing its controls. BlueField's documentation describes a Zero Trust mode that restricts host-side administration, but does not establish Sentry's default configuration. The hardware boundary also needs testing against its own threat model. OpenAI's cache-channel experiment illustrates the broader risk of shared hardware, without demonstrating a bypass of Sentry. In data centers built on this architecture, enforcement sits outside the host's trust domain. On laptops, OS controls and trusted brokers carry that job. Hardware adds another independent enforcement layer where it is available.

Whichever layer enforces the policy, the previous piece showed how much legitimate work enforced policies stall in research prototypes. Published work so far reports pieces of the picture, such as classifier latency and shadow-mode results, but not the full set that would show intent enforcement works: attacks stopped when the attacker knew the defense existed, legitimate tasks that still finished, authority granted per task, approval requests per hundred tasks, latency added to each gated action, and false positives at a stated base rate. Those numbers are what will turn an enforcement architecture into something a customer can rely on.

Ropes the agent can't loosen

Odysseus heard every word of the song, and the ship still rowed past. His rig met all three of Anderson's requirements. He couldn't loosen the ropes, they held for the whole passage, and the standing order was one sentence long. The men at the oars had exactly the context they needed, because they knew the order and could see him straining against it, and the wax kept them from hearing the case he was making. OpenAI's package proxy, Artifactory, sat outside the sandbox, but exploitable functionality let agents use it to cross the boundary. Separation only protects a control when the requests it accepts cannot redirect or disable its enforcement.

An agent's task is written down, and a person can confirm the access policy it becomes. Enforcement is the half that decides whether that policy holds up against a capable agent. Controls the agent can't tamper with have to enforce the organization's restrictions and the task's limits regardless of which tool, child process, API, or discovered credential it uses. Those controls need the authorized task without accepting the agent's arguments for expanding it. Most of that can be built today, on machines security vendors already protect.

Research and blogging assistance provided by Hermes, an AI Assistant. If it ever tunnels out through DNS, it promises a better question than the capital of France.

f5699e7cf829.text:
Exploited vulnerabilities hit retail harder than any other sector

Exploited vulnerabilities declined as a technical root cause across all sectors in 2026, but they still started 26% of attacks on retail organizations. That's the highest rate of any sector and well above the 18% cross-sector rate.

Phishing was the top technical root cause for retail at 29%, followed by exploited vulnerabilities (26%) and malicious email (22%).

Identity-based vectors, including malicious email, phishing, compromised credentials, and brute force attacks, initiated 69% of attacks against retail. This was the lowest rate of any sector yet still well above half of respondents. 66% of retail victims said their ransomware attack was also their most significant identity attack, close to the 67% cross-sector rate featured in our State of Identity Security 2026 report earlier in the year.

Known security gaps were retail’s one above-average weakness

38% of retail victims attributed their breach to a known security gap, a weakness they were aware of but had not addressed. That was retail’s most common operational root cause and the only one it cited more often than the 36% cross-sector rate.

Every other operational root cause came in below the cross-sector rate. The report compares each one in detail.

Encryption climbed after two years of decline

62% of attacks on retail succeeded in encrypting data, up from 48% in 2025 and above the 56% cross-sector rate. Attacks that encrypted data and also stole it rose to 19%, up from 14% last year. That second point of leverage weighs heavily on retailers holding customer payment and personal data.

Backups did most of the recovery work: 71% of retail organizations restored data from backups, up from 62% last year and above the 66% cross-sector rate. Far fewer retailers paid the ransom to get their data back than in 2025. The full report shows where retail’s payment rate ranks against other sectors.

Low typical ransoms, with a heavy top end

The median ransom demand for retail was $225,000, the second lowest of any sector and far below the $698,000 cross-sector median. The average (mean) demand was $4.32 million, the highest of any sector. That average does not include outlier ransoms of $40 million or more. These ultra-high ransoms were excluded from the report results to prevent skewing of averages.

The median ransom payment for retail was also low at $57,500, the lowest of any sector and well below the $769,000 cross-sector median.

The report explains what pushed retail’s average demand to the top of the sector rankings and how far retailers negotiated attackers down.

Recovery got faster, but costs went up

The average (mean) cost to recover from an attack, excluding any ransom paid, rose to $1.76 million from $1.65 million last year. That was slightly above the $1.70 million cross-sector average, which also rose this year.

But on the positive side, retail’s average time to fully recover fell to 2.54 weeks from 3.16 weeks last year. 56% recovered within a week, the highest share in five years of retail data. The rate of 2.54 weeks is also below the 2.80-week cross-sector average, making 2026 a strong year for quick recoveries.

Defenses saw the attack, but did not stop it

Almost all retail victims of credential-based attacks had MFA enabled (97%), yet more than half still had data encrypted by attackers. Firewalls flagged 59% of attacks before the ransomware deployed, but even with early indicators, victims were encrypted 60% of the time, compared with 50% across all sectors.

Controls in retail are collecting the right signals, but they’re not connecting deeply enough with other tools and responding together. The report contains several key recommendations based on this year’s data, and one of those recommendations is to adopt a defense system posture where identity, email, endpoint, and network controls respond as one.

Read the report

Retail is paying attackers less than any other sector and recovering faster than in any year of our data. But more attacks are reaching encryption, and the cost to recover went up. Closing known security gaps and connecting existing defenses are the highest-leverage places for retailers to invest in.

News Summary:

Cisco AI Defense's adaptive AI red teaming framework is adding Anthropic's Claude Mythos, harnessing advanced adversarial reasoning to simulate real-world attacks on AI agents.

With Cisco’s enhanced Tokenomics, organizations can optimize AI spend to defend what matters most by connecting agent cost directly with ROI in real time.

Cisco IQ, which leverages decades of vulnerability and troubleshooting data, now correlates live threat detection data with potentially exposed network infrastructure at machine speed to accelerate remediation.

Together, these innovations offer enterprises an always-on trust loop to secure, govern, and observe increasingly capable AI agents and complex enterprise AI deployments.

MELBOURNE, Australia, Nov. 10, 2026 -- CISCO LIVE APJC -- Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) today announced it is adding Claude Mythos to AI Defense for red teaming AI applications and agents, empowering defenders to stress-test AI systems with frontier adversary reasoning. Coupled with new Splunk Agent Observability and Cisco IQ advancements, Cisco is preparing enterprises for a new era of trust that requires securing, observing, and governing agents at machine speed.

“You cannot scale what you cannot secure, govern, or observe,” said Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel. “By uniting frontier-level AI runtime protections with machine-speed agent quality controls, we are building a continuous trust loop: protecting agents from compromise while ensuring every token spent delivers measurable business value.”

As AI agents proliferate and connect to complex tools and sensitive data, 81% of ITOps and engineering professionals cite increased cooperation between security and observability teams, according to a global Splunk research report last month. Cisco’s Splunk and AI Defense innovations equip security leaders to account for token spend and effective tool use while conducting tailored security testing against highly capable AI agents.

Since Cisco launched AI Defense in January 2025, it has helped hundreds of customers identify critical flaws in AI models, applications, and agents before they reach production. Its adaptive red teaming allows security teams to quickly build customized, multi-step attacks on target systems to uncover specific risks. Claude Mythos will augment this framework with advanced reasoning that plans tests that matter and translates the results into attack ideas for each system.

Features include:

Realistic Adversarial Ideation: generates multi-step, contextual attack paths designed to help identify subtle vulnerabilities across complex architectures.

Secure, Contained Access: By design, customers interact only through AI Defense's structured interface: Customers have no open-ended prompt access.

Audit Trails and Repeatable Results: AI Defense records each testing action for audit, and results can be carried over to inform follow-up attack loops.

“Enterprises are increasingly building AI agents into their core operations and want to test those agents thoroughly before putting them into production,” said Michael Moore, Cybersecurity Lead at Anthropic. “By bringing Claude Mythos to Cisco AI Defense, Cisco can help security teams red team their agents with advanced reasoning that plans tests and generates attack ideas for each system.”

Cisco engineered AI Defense to use Claude Mythos with multi-layered safeguards:

Registered, Authorized Targets: Operates exclusively against targets explicitly registered, owned, and authorized for testing by the enterprise customer; it cannot scan arbitrary internet infrastructure.

Named Operator Attribution: Every red teaming engagement requires authentication and is cryptographically tied to a named enterprise operator.

Revocable Execution: Engagements run with a fixed job and objectives defined by the human user, with time-bound sessions that can be halted on demand.

Dual-Layer Oversight: Product-level controls in AI Defense operate alongside program-level safeguards and monitoring.

Closing the Loop: From Test Findings to Measurable Agent ROI

Frontier AI models can excel at complex security tasks such as crafting AI red teaming strategies. That capability cuts both ways. AI is lowering the barrier to entry for attackers just as many enterprises are working to balance security, governance, and ROI considerations across growing AI portfolios.

For organizations to confidently deploy AI agents at scale, they need unified, real-time visibility into AI agent cost, business performance, and quality. Cisco is bridging the trust gap with new Splunk Agent Observability enhancements:

Tokenomics: cost governance, soon to be available in AWS Marketplace, that ties AI spend to output quality. Using usage data from Amazon Bedrock and Amazon CloudWatch, it pairs each agent's cost with evaluations that grade the quality and impact of its work, giving organizations a single view of AI ROI. This extends the token-spend attribution launched at .conf26, which tracks costs across AI agents and coding tools such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.

Eval-G1 Evaluation Models: Splunk Agent Observability extends our support for turning agentic traces and expert feedback into custom small language models that execute evals and guardrails at up to 98% lower cost than a commercial LLM. These next generation Eval-G1 models deliver evaluation response times 2.5x faster than traditional LLMs and enable real-time agent control with high accuracy.

The Evaluation Tuner: Teams can turn their agentic traces and subject matter expert feedback into fine-tuned evaluator models to enforce quality standards and steer agents at machine speed.

Adaptive red teaming with Claude Mythos is coming soon for select enterprises. Tokenomics will be available in private preview in December, with general availability in AWS Marketplace early 2027. The evaluation models and the evaluation tuner are generally available starting this month.

Connecting Infrastructure Exposure to Security Action with Cisco IQ and Cisco Data Fabric Powered by the Splunk Platform

While understanding vulnerability exposure is critical, defenders must also accelerate how they remediate risk across complex enterprise estates. Cisco IQ identifies critical exposures, and the powerful ecosystem of Cisco Partners and Professional Services turns insight into action. Partners help deliver remediation at scale and modernize infrastructure, and Cisco Professional Services bring deep expertise to put new Cisco capabilities into practice. Together, Cisco and its partners can help streamline operations and future-proof your IT infrastructure for the AI era.

As AI-accelerated threats compress the window between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation from weeks to hours, point-in-time audits leave organizations exposed. To help security and network operations teams act at machine speed, Cisco is extending real-time intelligence from Cisco IQ—which has close to 17,000 customers across more than 22 million devices—directly into enterprise security environments, open agentic protocols, and automated lifecycle workflows.

Key updates include:

Cisco Data Fabric Integration: Ingests Cisco IQ vulnerability, lifecycle, and configuration data directly into Splunk Platform via open APIs, enabling SecOps teams and AI agents to correlate live threat detections with underlying network exposure in Splunk Enterprise Security.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) & ServiceNow Connectors: Provides structured infrastructure context to supported AI agents and enterprise IT Service Management platforms, automatically translating exposure findings into asset-linked ServiceNow problem records to coordinate remediation without manual data reconciliation.

AI-Powered Resilient Infrastructure Playbook: Surfaces critical lifecycle vulnerabilities, including personalized alerts for known defects and quantum-safe cryptographic readiness, allowing teams and certified partners to scope and prioritize modernization roadmaps.

“AI is shrinking the time organizations have to respond to threats, and knowing where you're exposed only matters if you can act on it,” said Liz Centoni, Cisco EVP and Chief Customer Experience Officer. “Bringing Cisco IQ vulnerability insights into Cisco Data Fabric powered by the Splunk Platform gives analysts that context in the middle of an investigation, so they can decide what to do next. With our partners and Professional Services teams, we're helping customers move from identifying risk to actually reducing it.”

To learn more about securing and observing the agentic enterprise, visit cisco.com/go/ai-defense.

Read more in our blogs:

Cisco AI Defense to Add Anthropic’s Claude Mythos for AI Red Teaming

Splunk by Cisco Brings Agent ROI to AWS Marketplace and Real-time Evaluations to Everyone

From Risk to Resilience: Close the Gap Between Knowing and Fixing

Moving Fast and Staying in Control in the Agentic AI Era

Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) is the worldwide technology leader that is revolutionizing the way organizations connect and protect in the AI era. For more than 40 years, Cisco has securely connected the world. With its industry leading AI-powered solutions and services, Cisco enables its customers, partners and communities to unlock innovation, enhance productivity and strengthen digital resilience. With purpose at its core, Cisco remains committed to creating a more connected and inclusive future for all. Discover more on The Newsroom and follow us on X at @Cisco.

France blames Iran for supermarket fridge attacks. What’s known, what remains unclear, and how to secure exposed controllers.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps was behind the attacks on supermarket fridges in France on 11 and 12 October. He said they hit 700 sites and raised refrigerator temperatures. Some stores threw away their entire stock of perishable food, and fires broke out in several.

“France attributes destabilization and sabotage campaigns against French interests to the Islamic Republic of Iran (electronic and cyber center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran – IRGC-ECC).” reads the announcement published by French cybersecurity agency ANSSI. “Following its investigation, C4 is able to attribute these destructive actions to the Shahid Kaveh cyber-offensive unit, affiliated with the electronic and cyber center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran (IRGC-ECC): infrastructure characteristics, use of signing tools, relay of the attack by a propaganda organ linked to Shahid Kaveh, traces of the use of Persian in the attack infrastructure.”

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot described the attack as “unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression” and called it the first major cyber sabotage operation on French soil. He promised EU-level sanctions, and France summoned the Iranian ambassador. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the response should be strong, adding that she had only just learned about France’s attribution.

“I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said of the cyberattacks on French supermarkets, which occurred on October 11 and 12, and reported Le Monde.

“This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression,” said Barrot. “It marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people.”

“We will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible,” he added.

Paris prosecutors opened a judicial investigation into the head of Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit tied to the Guards’ Electronic and Cyber Center, and his two deputies. Anyone else they identify can be added to the case.

The attribution cites shared infrastructure, attack tools, Persian-language traces, and amplification by a group-linked propaganda outlet.

French authorities say Iranian cyber operations targeting French interests date back to at least 2020. Previous incidents include a planned attack against Charlie Hebdo, a 2023 breach of its online store attributed to Emennet Pasargad, and a 2024 attempt to hijack digital advertising kiosks to display anti-Israel messages ahead of the Paris Olympics. C4 attributes these operations to the IRGC-linked Shahid Shoostari unit.

France wasn’t alone. On 2 November, supermarkets in at least nine other European countries reported a suspected attack on their freezer systems. Barrot spoke only about the French case, so nothing official yet ties the second wave to Iran.

This is where we need to be careful. When a government names a country as responsible for an attack, that’s a serious accusation. But the reports I’ve read don’t explain the technical evidence behind it. We should treat it as an official claim, not a proven fact, and stick to what we know. Fear and uncertainty can be used to spread distrust, and that risk applies to all sides involved in this story.

The key issue isn’t just identifying the attackers, but understanding whether someone is exploiting these incidents to promote a hybrid warfare narrative. Hacktivist claims may serve propaganda and visibility more than reflect actual responsibility. If French investigations confirm Iran’s role in the October attacks, the pro-Russian groups claiming November’s incidents could face a serious credibility problem. They may have tried to take credit for someone else’s operations. Still, their involvement in some incidents remains possible.

In today’s hybrid warfare, uncertain attribution, strategic ambiguity, and information manipulation make it increasingly difficult to separate real attacks from propaganda.

The method used in supermarket fridge attacks, at least, is documented. On 5 November, CISA, the FBI and other US agencies published a fact sheet on the same kind of activity. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.

The agencies list three ways in: bypassing authentication, injecting code and weak settings. They also warn that operators can lose sight of the real temperatures, which is a bad thing to discover after the cheese has gone.

The fixes are dull and they work. Keep controllers off the internet, and if you need remote access, put an updated firewall in front of it. Separate industrial devices from the office network, change default passwords, add phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, patch firmware and replace devices the maker no longer supports.

Then limit who can change settings with an allowlist of approved devices and IP addresses. Keep tested backups offsite and offline, turn on logging and read the logs. The last control is the cheapest: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Iran)

Game Server Communication

All communication with the game servers is authenticated and encrypted. The AES encryption key is included in the /srvlist response from the line configuration servers (field aes_key). For authentication, all requests are signed with HMAC-SHA256, a keyed hash message authentication code that computes the hash of a message and a shared secret (the AES key in our case).

Because the AES key is returned in cleartext from the line config servers, the purpose is not to address confidentiality or integrity against a third party, but rather to obfuscate content and check for communication errors.

Conclusion

This malware is not “garage” or student-level work. It reflects well-planned development, with a clean infrastructure, multiple REST APIs, and a full ecosystem. In 2024, with limited reverse engineering tooling, this Flutter application would have taken ages to reverse engineer. In 2026, however, it’s merely a hard day’s work. It’s always good news to hear that cybercriminals are losing their edge.

The malware described in this report is detected and blocked by FortiGuard Antivirus as:

Cisco AI Defense adds Anthropic’s Claude Mythos to adaptive red teaming. Cisco’s SVP and GM of AI Software and Platform group DJ Sampath tells CRN why it’s ‘a game changer’ for partners securing AI agents.

Cisco AI Defense is one of the first AI security products to put Anthropic’s Claude Mythos behind its adaptive red teaming engine, the tech giant revealed on Monday at Cisco Live APJC in Melbourne.

AI Defense will now pair frontier-level attacker reasoning with safeguards, including testing only authorized targets, tying each engagement to a named operator, and full auditability, so red team exercises mirror real adversaries without endangering customer environments, DJ Sampath, senior vice president and general manager of Cisco’s AI Software and Platform group, told CRN.

“You need to really deeply understand each of [the] use cases so that you’re red teaming against those use cases to be able to discover those gaps,” said Sampath (pictured). “We’re moving from generic red teaming to adaptive red teaming, but more importantly, we’re using Mythos model to be able to do it.”

AI Defense, first introduced in 2025, is a tool that helps safeguard enterprises against the misuse of AI tools and data leakage, and protect AI models, applications and agents.

[Related: Cisco 360 Gets An Incentive Boost As Cisco Pushes Partners Toward AI, Cross-Architecture Sales]

Cisco AI Defense offers standard and adaptive red teaming for AI agents and applications today. Standard tests cover thousands of common vulnerabilities, including prompt injection, jailbreaks, and sensitive data exposure. It can produce reports mapped to Cisco’s AI security framework and other security standards. Adaptive red teaming, however, goes further, Cisco said. Users can define custom criteria in plain language, and the framework plans and runs multi-step attacks tailored to their own applications. Claude Mythos adds attacker-level reasoning to that engine, with safeguards built for authorized testing, according to the San Jose, Calif.-based company.

Observability is critical to running AI agents safely, Cisco’s DJ Sampath said. To that end, Cisco is running Mythos in a sandbox environment with full control over what it can access, how it executes and how its sub-agents are spun up. That same visibility feeds “tokenomics,” which Sampath said has a security angle as well as a cost one.

“Attackers are going to use agents with tokens to attack their infrastructure,” he said. “That’s the only way you can defend an attack that is now being committed by an agent swarm. You’ve got to have a swarm yourself.”

To that end, AI Defense now supports Amazon Bedrock and Amazon CloudWatch so partners and users can see token spend and ROI in a single dashboard, Sampath said.

The Partner Opportunity

Cisco partners can use Mythos through AI Defense to red team every client environment that’s rolling out agents, Sampath said.

No other red teaming service that he knows of has a model that powerful, he added.

“We give access to Mythos via Cisco AI Defense, and we use that to help our clients secure their deployments of agents. It’s a game changer for [partners],” Sampath said.

AI Defense comprises the security capabilities within Cisco Cloud Control, the company’s unified operations platform for AgenticOps where human operators and AI agents manage IT infrastructure together. Cloud Control, introduced at Cisco Live in June, is the operating platform, while Cisco IQ is the support and success platform fed by that data, Sampath said.

Partners now have access to the Cisco IQ platform to identify customer risk, uncover refresh opportunities, and build managed services, which the tech giant announced last month at Partner Summit to the delight of partners in attendance.

AI Defense has approximately 400 to 500 customers since the offering was launched last year. Sampath said that “self-improving engines” are coming, as well as security for agents on laptops, in the cloud and at the edge.

“We’re expanding the capabilities of AI Defense every single week,” he said. “Whether your agents are running on your laptops, inside of the cloud, or on the edge, we’re going to find ways of being able to secure them,” Sampath said.

Adaptive red teaming with Claude Mythos is coming soon for select enterprises. Broader availability is planned for qualified customers, but dates, scope, and region availability remain subject to change, according to Cisco.

Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem.

When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start.

Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent.

AI is changing open source

AI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests.

The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown.

During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase.

AI has raised the pressure to produce. It’s made it easier for maintainers to ship features, performance improvements, and bug fixes that would not have been done otherwise. But it’s also made it easy for other projects to do the same. When another project adds overlapping features using AI, maintainers feel a need to keep up using AI. It can become a grinding cycle, where each project pushes the other to move faster. Along the way, some projects have grown in scope and lost sight of their original goals.

Maintainer burnout and sustainability have always been a problem — and now AI has accelerated those issues. That’s why sponsoring open source projects and supporting maintainers is so important in this moment.

One of the Vite Ecosystem Fund’s first recipients is e18e, a community focused on improving performance across the JavaScript ecosystem. Its lead, James Garbutt, has a long history in open source, and his work at e18e has helped make popular tools like Svelte, Storybook, and Nx faster. "Sponsorships make a huge difference and allow maintainers to dedicate more of their time to the things we all rely on," Garbutt says.

Fund distribution

The recipients of the Vite Ecosystem Fund were selected by a panel of core team members from Vite stack projects (Vite, Vitest, Rolldown, Oxc, Vite+), including maintainers not employed by Cloudflare.

The funding is allocated through Cloudflare's Open Collective as a combination of:

Contributions to ecosystem recipients

Stipends to core maintainers

We’re proud that Cloudflare has committed to making the open source ecosystem we rely on stronger and more sustainable. No project thrives in isolation.

We'll continue to distribute and draw down the committed amount every quarter.

Contributions to ecosystem recipients

This first round of sponsorships prioritized dependencies, ecosystem critical plugins, significant contributors, and projects that moved the ecosystem forward.

Stipends to core maintainers

The core maintainers of the Vite stack are eligible for a stipend of up to $4,000 per calendar month. Each maintainer can invoice at a rate of $50 per hour contributed that month.

Any time spent improving or supporting the project in some way counts towards this stipend: writing code, writing documentation, triaging issues, offering support in our Discord servers, attending meetings or meetups, contributing to our upstream dependencies, and so on.

Maintainers who are already being paid for or employed for this work do not receive stipends — for example, VoidZero employees are ineligible.

Cloudflare supports open source

Cloudflare’s mission is to help build a better Internet. Supporting open source falls squarely within that mission. The Vite Ecosystem Fund is only part of it.

Cloudflare committed an additional $1 million to sponsor open source projects in our Community Engineers Fund. We also provide Cloudflare credits to open source projects via Project Alexandria.

The Vite ecosystem has come this far because of all the maintainers and contributors who came together to build a community. These sponsorships are a small thank-you for all this hard work.

U.S. government agencies have warned that threat actors are actively targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems globally with an aim to cause service disruptions, fire hazards, and loss of inventory.

"The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards," according to a joint advisory.

According to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), Department of Agriculture (USDA), and Department of Transportation (DOT), threat actors are likely to exploit authentication bypasses, arbitrary code injection, and weak configurations to gain access to these systems and cause the following effects -

Change of temperature, which, in turn, could affect the service life of the system, create a fire hazard, cause inventory loss, or harm consumers who purchase products after unsafe storage.

Loss of visibility into current temperatures due to a denial-of-service.

In response to the threat, owners and operators are being urged to use strong authentication, keep systems updated, identify any systems that are accessible from the internet, isolate operational technology (OT) devices, change default passwords, retire and replace legacy devices, remove unnecessary remote access, and secure necessary remote access.

"Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman.

"We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk."

In recent weeks, threat actors have targeted hundreds of supermarkets across Europe by exploiting weaknesses in internet-accessible refrigeration controllers to raise temperatures, in some cases to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), or force cooling units into defrost mode, spoiling food and resulting in financial losses.

Targets of these attacks ranged from major supermarket chains to small grocers and butchers in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Sweden, and the U.K.

Among those targeted was the French Blood Establishment, which confirmed that a cybersecurity incident affecting a refrigeration equipment provider had raised temperature and defrost settings to "extremely high levels" at three facilities used to store blood plasma. It's unclear who is behind the hacking spree.

Data from Censys shows that there are still hundreds of Danfoss StoreView instances exposed globally, with most of them located in France, although the number has dropped significantly from 3,004 to 708 between October 9 and November 5, 2026. The Copeland/Dixell XWEB exposure, likewise, has declined from 3,708 to 2,420.

The attack surface management platform described the refrigeration attacks across Europe as the latest addition to a list of other recent incidents targeting critical infrastructure, including gas station tank gauges, air raid systems, and water towers.

"North America accounts for roughly 38% of global ICS [industrial control systems] exposure," Censys said. "Asia's share grew from 22% in 2024 to 25% in 2026, while Europe's fell from 36.5% to 32%. However, these shifts have not produced an overall decline."

"While exposure numbers are high, they're hardly surprising: ICS exposure is a problem that's been reported on and warned about for years. It poses a critical risk to the public as gatekeepers to the world's critical infrastructure."

Cybersecurity is constantly changing, and so are the skills IT professionals need to protect their organizations. As the cybersecurity workforce continues to evolve, access to relevant training, recognized credentials, and opportunities to build practical skills has become increasingly important.

For more than a decade, the Fortinet Training Institute has expanded people’s easy access to cybersecurity education and career development. Fortinet has fulfilled its pledge to train 1 million people in cybersecurity months ahead of schedule.

This achievement is one measure of the Fortinet Training Institute’s success. Industry recognition offers another perspective, highlighting programs and approaches across professional certification, cybersecurity education, and security awareness.

The Fortinet Training Institute is proud to have received the following honors in 2026:

CyberSecurity Breakthrough Award: Security Awareness Training Solution of the Year for FortiSAT

Cyber Defense Magazine Global InfoSec Awards: Most Promising Cybersecurity Training

Cyber Defense Magazine Global InfoSec Awards: Cutting Edge Security Awareness and Training

Cybersecurity Excellence Awards: Best Cybersecurity Training

Cybersecurity Excellence Awards: Security Awareness Program

Why Industry Recognition Matters

Awards are never more important than learner outcomes or organizational impact. But independent industry recognition can highlight programs and solutions that are responding to the changing needs of the cybersecurity workforce.

For the Fortinet Training Institute, recognition reflects the breadth of our work: helping people build and validate technical skills, expanding access to cybersecurity education, and helping organizations develop a more cyber-aware workforce.

Building Skills for the Cybersecurity Workforce

Professional training and certification remain a vital part of developing cybersecurity talent. The Fortinet NSE Certification program has evolved with the industry, most recently expanding to eight certification levels and offering career pathways across multiple areas, including secure networking, SASE, cloud security, and security operations. The updated program gives learners more ways to build skills and validate expertise as they progress from foundational knowledge to advanced and expert-level capabilities.

The Fortinet Training Institute also extends learning opportunities beyond professional certification via its academic partner, education outreach, and veterans’ programs that help students, educators, veterans, and other learners build pathways into cybersecurity.

Making Employees More Cyber Aware

Technical expertise is only one part of cybersecurity. Organizations also need people across the workforce to understand security risks and make informed decisions. Our security awareness training solution FortiSAT supports this part of the cybersecurity skills equation with instruction and courses designed to help organizations build a more cyber-aware workforce.

The continuous upgrading of our NSE Certification program keeps the learning pathways aligned with changing cybersecurity roles and technologies. As cybersecurity continues to evolve, the Fortinet Training Institute will continue expanding access to training, certification, and education for learners and organizations around the world.

OpenAI on Thursday unveiled GPT-6 Cyber, a security model the company says is far more capable than its predecessor and more disciplined about respecting the limits researchers set for it.

On ExploitGym, which checks whether an AI can exploit a given flaw in a remote target, the new model achieved 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber.

OpenAI rated GPT-6 Cyber as Critical for cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, above the High designation given to GPT-5.6 Cyber.

In one alignment test, the model received an exploitation task alongside supporting services that were intentionally easy to hack but off-limits. Without deployment safety prompts, it refrained from exploiting them in 99.93% of cases, compared to 94.49% for GPT-5.6 Cyber. With the safety prompts, it never targeted the decoy services.

“This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately,” OpenAI said.

OpenAI researchers pointed the model at the Linux kernel, where it reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and built functional privilege escalation exploits for 948. GPT-5.6 Sol, tested with the same tooling, produced 166.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

OpenAI has reported 304 critical issues to maintainers with proposed fixes.

In Firefox, the model documented 81 new flaws that Mozilla deemed high severity, backing each with evidence and reproducible tests. Mozilla has begun rolling out patches.

New protections include monitoring that checks whether the model’s actions line up with what a user is permitted to do, and safeguards meant to stop OpenAI’s models from aiding efforts to compromise industrial controls and other safety-critical systems.

OpenAI refined these safeguards using feedback from industrial cybersecurity firm Dragos, which tested Daybreak Red models in a controlled lab.

“The skill floor is dropping for the reconnaissance and vulnerability research needed before an attack,” said Dragos chief AI officer Rob T. Lee.

Access is currently limited to select approved customers of Daybreak Red, the part of OpenAI’s Daybreak program aimed at advanced exploit work and authorized testing. They can use GPT-6 Cyber through the API and Codex.

OpenAI plans to gradually open the model to all Daybreak Red customers, who are also getting GPT-5.6 Cyber. A dedicated Daybreak Red group for approved critical infrastructure defenders will permit sanctioned testing of critical systems.

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to escalate privileges on affected installations of Home Assistant Green. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code within a container on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of user account tokens. The issue results from storing sensitive information in plaintext. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to escape the container and execute arbitrary code in the context of root.

Additional Details

Home Assistant has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://github.com/home-assistant/core/security/advisories/GHSA-6456-4qg9-cqpj

Disclosure Timeline

2025-11-05 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-06 - Coordinated public release of advisory

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Docker Sandboxes. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the creation of sandboxes using the clone mode. The issue results from launching an executable from an untrusted location. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current user.

Additional Details

Docker has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-121614

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Philips Hue Bridge Pro. Although authentication is required to exploit this vulnerability, the existing authentication mechanism can be bypassed.

The specific flaw exists within the HTTP service, which listens on TCP port 443 by default. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied string before using it to construct SQL queries. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of root.

Additional Details

Fixed in Bridge Pro firmware version 6.1.2071524030 (or later) https://www.philips-hue.com/en-ca/support/release-notes/bridge-pro

06a7d5f265ef.text:
On November 7, 2026, Principal Data Scientist Younghoo Lee will present a talk at BSides Sydney entitled "Decode facts, then reason: Detecting obfuscated malicious agent skills with small LLMs." The talk presents a practical hybrid architecture for addressing a distinct software supply chain trust boundary: AI agent ‘skills’ that may be malicious, in contrast to their declared intent. For instance, a skill that claims to summarize CSV files may also read credentials, contact external hosts, or execute shell commands. The fact that such skills may be obfuscated complicates the problem, and existing solutions have significant drawbacks.

Younghoo’s research proposes a new approach: decoding facts about skills deterministically, and then letting a small LLM reason over them to decide whether observed behavior aligns with a skill’s declared intent.

Ill-willed skills

AI agents increasingly come with ‘skills’: small add-ons, often shared through repositories and marketplaces, that teach an agent how to do a specific task. A skill is typically a folder with a SKILL.md file that describes in plain English what the skill is for – plus helper code (usually Python) that does the work.

Once a skill is downloaded and installed, agents typically trust the description and run the code with their own privileges and accesses: source files, environment variables, the network, and a shell.

The issue, however, is that whereas a person reads the description, the machine runs the code, and the two do not have to agree. A skill that promises to ‘report missing environment variable names,’ for example, could just as easily read every environment value and send it to an endpoint controlled by a threat actor.

Obfuscation makes the problem worse

Compounding this issue is the fact that a skill can hide what it does, and the techniques will likely be familiar to any reader who’s analyzed malware: splitting strings, building words from character codes, wrapping content in Base64, resolving functions by name at runtime, and, in the description text, using zero-width characters or lookalike Unicode letters.

It’s not unreasonable to expect this obfuscation to become increasingly complex, particularly if threat actors start to deploy malicious skills at scale. Attackers have a long history of layering encodings, hiding commands inside ordinary-looking scripts, and abusing legitimate system tools. Skills can leverage the same built-in tools, so essentially we’re facing the same playbook but with a new delivery channel and a trusting host. Techniques we may see in future include stacked encodings, multi-step reconstruction, and novel variants designed to evade signature-base detection.

It’s worth noting, however, that obfuscation is of course not malicious in itself, and this makes the problem harder to solve. Benign tools use it for minified code, test fixtures, and anti-tampering checks, and so simply scanning skills for obfuscation techniques will likely result in false positives.

In Younghoo’s talk, two demo skills – one benign, the other malicious - use similar obfuscation tricks. The first, involving a log redaction skill, builds the words ‘password’ and ’api_key’ from character codes, so that Continuous Integration (CI) secret scanners do not flag its own source, and then masks those values in the logs it cleans. In the second demo, an ’environment auditor’ splits a string to hide access to the environment and uploads sensitive information, such as keys and credentials. The obfuscation looks alike and the eventual verdicts are opposites. What separates them is the declared purpose, the data flow, and the destination.

A hard problem

There are three existing approaches to solving this problem, and while they may provide some level of reassurance, they also fall short in various ways.

Static rule-based scanners are fast, cheap, and auditable, but as the name suggests, they match on what code looks like; if strings are assembled at runtime, for example, the corresponding rule has nothing to match when it examines the skill statically. In Younghoo’s tests, two open-source skill scanners (Cisco Skill Scanner and NVIDIA SkillSpector, both in static mode) performed well on plaintext skills. On obfuscated skills, false positives were rare, but both scanners missed some malicious skills. Both tools also ship optional LLM features, which our main comparison did not use.

Frontier LLMs can reason about intent and judge a skill’s behavior compared to its description, rather than checking whether certain strings or code appear., That would seem to make them an obvious solution, but it’s unfortunately not always practical. Sending multiple skills to a large hosted model adds latency and cost at scale, as well as potentially adding privacy, policy, and regulatory concerns.

Small local models avoid the drawbacks described above, but may struggle with the complexity of the task. The smallest model in Younghoo’s study, for instance, was ineffective when given raw obfuscated code, because it had to untangle the obfuscation and judge intent at the same time.

A novel approach: decode facts, then reason

Younghoo’s idea was to split the problem in two. First, code recovers what a skill may be attempting to hide, and then a small LLM judges whether that behavior fits what the skill claims to do.

The workflow involves three steps:

Decode. A deterministic Python front-end reverses obfuscation patterns. It never executes the skill, and does not assign a verdict or make a judgement. Each deobfuscation is recorded, with its technique, location, and before/after text, providing an audit trail. It repeats its deobfuscations until the source stops changing – so stacked encodings, such as Base64 inside a split string, are stripped back, layer by layer. Content that still looks encoded after decoding (such as long Base64-like runs or unusual runs of non-ASCII characters), is flagged as a possible unknown obfuscation.

Summarize. The decoder's events become a short, facts-only summary for each file: techniques used, revealed content, hardcoded secrets, sensitive operations, and any ‘possible unknown obfuscation’ flags. Again, this step avoids coming to a conclusion about intent, and reminds the model (see next step) that obfuscation can be benign, so the presence of obfuscation does not necessarily imply malice.

Judge. Finally, a small LLM reads each summary alongside the skill's original source and description. It returns a verdict and a reason: does the behavior, now visible, fit the declared intent, and does any content that survived decoding make that fit less believable?

It’s worth noting that the decoder, at step 1, will not know every obfuscation technique, so it’s built as one input to the eventual judgement. The ‘possible unknown obfuscation’ flag is a cue to weigh, rather than a verdict in itself. Encoded content that cannot be explained by a skill’s declared purpose counts against it, and by the same token, the same content in a skill that plausibly needs it may not. Covering a new technique means adding another decoder pass.

One of the main benefits of this hybrid approach is that for everything the decoder can resolve, the model no longer has to work out what a string of character codes means. The model's job is reduced to judgment, which is easier than decoding and judging at once.

The experiment

Younghoo distilled a larger teacher model into small Qwen3 ‘students’ with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, so inference did not need an external API and could be done locally, and evaluated the approach on a synthetic benchmark of benign and malicious skills, each expanded into many obfuscated variants and split by base skill - so that no variant of a test skill appeared in training.

We’ll publish more detailed results soon – and further information will be available in the BSides talk itself – but here’s a brief summary of the results.

Static scanners stay precise but go quiet. Under obfuscation, their precision held up, but their recall dropped sharply compared with plaintext. The fine-tuned small models recovered most of the missed detection.

Decoded evidence turns small models from unusable into useful. Given the same obfuscated skills, the smallest model scored close to nothing on raw code. Once it was given decoded evidence, with no training at all, it matched the stronger static scanner overall, though it also produced many false positives.

Distillation helps at every size. Fine-tuning improved all three student sizes: Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B. The 0.6B model gained mostly by learning to stop over-flagging benign skills. The 4B model outperformed both static scanners on obfuscated skills and scored close to perfect on our benchmark.

There are caveats to these results, of course: the benchmark was synthetic, and its variants came from known obfuscation techniques. However, we believe this research is a promising countermeasure to an emerging threat. Malicious skills may become more prevalent, and scanners, frontier LLMs, and local models have known weaknesses when it comes to detecting obfuscated variants.

However, decoding the content deterministically, then using a small model – which can be hosted locally – to judge whether it fits the skill’s declared job, may be a viable solution. It’s also a useful reminder that while AI can introduce new variants of threats in the hands of attackers, it can help defenders to counter those same threats. Keep an eye out for more on Younghoo’s research in the near future.

88386f2be82e.text:
Attackers can log in to accounts that have no password, such as SSH key-only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers running the standard openssh-server package. They need network access to the server, an account name, and a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long.

OpenSSH, which rates the flaw critical, released version 10.6p2 today to block it. Alpine has published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16.

The attack works when the OpenSSH server (sshd) checks passwords without the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface, password logins are enabled, and at least one other account on the machine has a password. Alpine's openssh-server package is built without PAM, and password logins are on by default.

The flaw comes from how sshd works with musl, the C library that Alpine is built on. Non-Linux systems, Linux systems built on glibc, and systems that check passwords through PAM are not affected, said Damien Miller of the OpenSSH project.

He told anyone running an affected system to "set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY." No attacks using the flaw have been reported.

Who Is Exposed

Alpine's security advisory lists four conditions. A server is exposed when all four are true:

It runs the openssh-server package, which is built without PAM, or runs openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no.

PasswordAuthentication is yes, which is the OpenSSH default.

An account has * as its password field, which means no password is set.

At least one other local account has a password hash starting with $5$ or $6$.

The attacker also needs the name of an account with no password. One account with a password is enough to expose every account without one. The attack succeeds on every try with a single connection, according to the advisory.

On Alpine, accounts with no password set include:

key-only users created with adduser without a password, or with usermod -p '*'

users who come from a directory service through musl-nscd, since they have no shadow entry

root, which has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16

the alpine user in the official cloud images built with tiny-cloud

Root is protected by the default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password setting and can be reached directly only if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That protection does not help if an exposed account can become root, for example through doas.

The tiny-cloud images from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 give the alpine user passwordless doas. They are safe at first boot but become open to attack once any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example after an admin sets a console password. An attacker can then log in as alpine and use doas to become root.

Containers that do not run sshd, systems with PasswordAuthentication no, and cloud images set up through cloud-init, which writes that setting, are not affected. Accounts locked with ! in /etc/shadow are not affected either, and neither are machines where no account has a $-style password hash.

The flaw is not limited to Alpine. Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield, who reported it, names OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto in his technical write-up as other musl-based systems to check.

OpenWrt handles SSH with Dropbear by default, as its Dropbear documentation shows, and Kültekin says Dropbear is not affected. On OpenWrt, the flaw can matter only where an admin has installed the OpenSSH server.

How to Fix It

On Alpine, the fix is a package update followed by a restart, because upgrading the package does not restart the running sshd:

Update the packages: apk upgrade -U -a

Restart the server: rc-service sshd restart

Point releases 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 already include the fixed package. Branches 3.16 to 3.21 are past their end of support but also got fixed packages.

Cloud instances started from tiny-cloud images older than those point releases still need the update, or the setting below.

If you build OpenSSH yourself, version 10.6p2 includes the change, as its release notes describe.

If you cannot update yet, turning off password logins also stops the attack. First make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until a new login succeeds. Then set PasswordAuthentication no, check the configuration with sshd -t, and restart sshd.

The advisory gives commands that add the setting in a drop-in file in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d, which Alpine's default configuration reads from 3.19 onward. They also change every PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config from yes to no, including lines inside a Match block. Afterward, sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication should print passwordauthentication no.

The advisory suggests looking in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password, such as alpine, root or a key-only user. On exposed machines, also review doas use, recently created users, files and authorized keys.

"If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised," it says.

Why Long Passwords Work

Without PAM, sshd checks a password itself. It hashes the attempt with crypt(), the C library function that turns a password into its stored form, and compares the result with the stored field.

An account with no password has only * in that field. That is too short to hold a salt, the random prefix of a hash, so sshd borrows the salt of another account that has a real hash.

For the $5$ and $6$ hash types, musl's crypt() refuses passwords longer than 256 bytes and returns * to signal the error. That * matches the stored *, so sshd accepts the login. The upper end of the range is sshd's own limit of 1,024 bytes per password.

This behavior comes from a musl change on August 9, 2012, which made a failed crypt() call return "an unmatchable hash rather than NULL" because many programs did not check for failure. The 256-byte limit followed on August 29, 2012, to protect servers from denial-of-service attacks.

The salt borrowing comes from a July 15, 2016, OpenSSH change that addressed CVE-2016-6210, a flaw that let attackers learn which usernames exist. Kültekin says the problem has existed since then.

The 10.6p2 code change makes sshd refuse a match when the stored field is shorter than four characters. OpenSSH calls it a workaround and says the root cause lies outside sshd. Stable Alpine packages carry a patch for the same problem.

Why the Fix Came the Next Day

Miller's team learned of the flaw earlier this week and shipped the fix as fast as it could. In the release announcement, he said the team now sees long embargoes as dangerous and mainly helpful to attackers, because it has recently seen AI agents find the same bugs again, sometimes within hours.

No CVE identifier had been assigned to the flaw as of today.
