N-able has released a critical N-central hotfix that temporarily disables the platform's built-in remote control, after researcher Sean Bales published 33 alleged zero-days with proof-of-concept (PoC) code.

N-able detailed N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2, build 2026.4.1.26, in its November 10 release notes, describing the update as a critical security release for its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform.

The Able2Shell disclosure, published November 9, described four exploit chains that Bales said ended in code execution on an N-central server, two of them with root privileges and one he called credential-free. He said he tested the flaws on a pre-release build and that most if not all should work on earlier versions, including the current release.

Hotfix Covers Seven CVEs and Disables Remote Control

N-able took hosted N-central offline on November 9 as a precaution and told on-premises customers to keep their servers offline until they were updated.

Hotfix 2 addresses seven CVEs covering XML external entity (XXE) flaws, Object-Graph Navigation Language (OGNL) injection, privilege escalation, stored cross-site scripting, server-side request forgery and remote code execution through path traversal.

The seven records are CVE-2026-125883, CVE-2026-125878, CVE-2026-125879, CVE-2026-125880, CVE-2026-125881, CVE-2026-125882 and CVE-2026-91000. CVE-2026-125882 credits Nate Fair of Sprocket Security.

Remote control will be re-enabled in a future fix, according to the release notes, which also tell customers to update agents and probes after upgrading. N-able told Infosecurity that hosted environments have been upgraded and are back online.

N-able said the release addresses "the most critical November 9 vulnerabilities" and that a follow-up hotfix will bring further security updates.

Read more on N-central: N-able Releases Hotfix for Critical Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

N-able Disputes Disclosure as Exploitation Attempts Emerge

N-able said it was seeing scanning activity linked to the published PoC code.

Security firm WatchTowr saw exploitation attempts against its N-central honeypots overnight after the disclosure, according to an advisory updated November 10 by Beazley Security, the cybersecurity arm of insurer Beazley. The systems were decoys, not customer environments.

N-able said claims that it had ignored responsible disclosure from Bales were inaccurate, and that the vulnerabilities published on November 9 had not been disclosed through its established reporting channels.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Bales confirmed that N-able's account was accurate and that he had not disclosed any of the vulnerabilities to the company, adding that he believed the claim N-able had ignored him came from an outdated README he has since changed. He argued that publishing "makes vendors safer by forcing them to fix problems as fast as possible."

N-able president and CEO John Pagliuca took the opposite view, arguing that "publishing exploit code before customers have had the chance to act doesn't make anyone safer. It hands attackers a head start," he told Infosecurity.

Neither the release notes nor N-able's statement say how the seven CVEs map to the 33 Able2Shell issues, and PoC code for all 33 remains public.

In this article

From scans to reports

Selected findings

Closing thoughts

At Microsoft’s FORGE Lab, we used codename MDASH to scan a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026. One full-time researcher and one intern led this three-month effort, which has so far produced 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs. We confirmed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline.

Finding the bugs was only part of the work. The initial scans produced 26,502 raw findings in about two weeks, but turning those results into reproducible bugs, upstream reports, and patches took months of expert investigation and collaboration with Linux maintainers.

In this post, we look back at how we went from thousands of potential findings to validated vulnerabilities and upstream fixes, and what we learned about scaling vulnerability discovery with AI.

From scans to reports

We focused on several core kernel subsystems, such as networking, filesystems, and security modules. Our selection criteria were straightforward: we picked security-sensitive components with no obvious dependence on specialized hardware, making QEMU-based validation simple and unified. Code scanning mainly used Sonnet 4.6 (71.1% of code-scanning tokens), GPT-5.4 (20.1%), and GPT-5.5 (7.1%).

The codename MDASH scans produced 26,502 raw scan findings in about two weeks on two servers (64 cores/256 GB RAM and 32 cores/128 GB RAM), but turning that output into patches and reports took months of expert work. We filtered out low-confidence claims using codename MDASH’s confidence levels and separate fast screening agents we built, reducing the pool to 11,769 candidates. PoC-generating agents then attempted reproduction in QEMU, mainly using GPT-5.5 (77.3% of reproduction tokens), Opus 4.6 (13.2%), and GPT-5.5-cyber (9.4%). Experts then reviewed the 621 cases with PoC evidence to identify root causes, merge duplicates, and prepare upstream submissions.

Figure 1 . Scan-to-report workflow. 26,502 raw findings → 11,769 screened candidates → 621 PoC-backed cases → 59 upstream reports.

Where the 621 cases went

Roughly one public upstream report landed from every ten PoC-backed cases: 59 reports from 621 cases (9.5%). Across those cases, the main reasons for not filing a separate new report were:

266 (42.8%) shared a root cause with another case, so one patch could fix them together.

163 (26.2%) were not reported after review, mostly due to limited security impact.

133 (21.4%) were already reported or fixed upstream.

Submission timing explains many of the 133 overlaps. Most of the 621 cases were new when the scans finished (though some may already have been in flight by others). Our first public report went out on June 27, 2026, more than five weeks after scanning started. By September 1, 55 of the 59 had been posted to the public lists; the other four were reported privately during the same window and routed to the public lists by mid-October.

Getting fixes merged

Upstream Linux typically requires vulnerability reports to come with a working patch. Agents helped draft initial fixes, but human validation, subsystem understanding, and iterating with maintainers during review remained essential. So far, fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into upstream mainline—half on the first submission, and the rest after one to four revisions. Reaching a mainline release from the first public patch took a median of 41 days (up to 108 days), and we are still working with maintainers on the remaining reports.

How old the bugs were

Interestingly, most of the bugs we reported had been in the kernel for years. Across the 59 reports, the average bug was 8.1 years old when we first reported it publicly. One of the oldest, a cls_u32 shift-out-of-bounds bug (CVE-2026-74544), had been there for at least 21 years.

Figure 2 . Age of reported kernel bugs, measured from the bug-introducing commit (the fix’s Fixes tag) to our first public report. Average age 8.1 years across 59 reports; six were 15–19 years old and three were at least 20 years old.

Selected findings

Among the 33 CVEs assigned so far from this batch, 24 are rated High or above (CVSS v3.1 score of at least 7.0). Below are eight CVEs for which we confirmed local root privilege-escalation exploits in controlled laboratory environments, with some cases requiring non-default settings or disabled exploit mitigations:

CVE-2026-…

Module

Summary

64554

net/ipv6

Use-after-free in bridged IPv6 fragmentation: a saved pointer into a packet was reused after the packet’s buffer was reallocated.

64563

lib/rhashtable

Use-after-free in hash-table walks: a walk resumed after the table was resized reused a pointer to a possibly freed entry.

64580

net/ipv6

Refcount underflow in IPv6 IPsec routing: an error path dropped a device reference but kept the pointer, so cleanup dropped it again.

74561

net/ipv4

Use-after-free in next-hop replacement: the route-cache flush walked an IPv6 route list without its lock, racing with route deletion.

74562

net/ipv4

Use-after-free in next-hop replacement: route checks and notifications walked an IPv6 route list without its lock, racing with route deletion.

89789

drivers/net

Use-after-free in the GTP tunnel driver: when device creation failed, its lookup tables were freed while incoming packets could still read them.

98222

security/keys

Heap buffer overflow in encrypted-key updates: long key parameters overflowed a 16-bit length, so the kernel wrote past an undersized buffer.

98364

net/xfrm

Use-after-free in IPsec routing: a network device was used without holding a reference, so deleting it at the same time could free it mid-use.

A closer look at CVE-2026-64563

CVE-2026-64563 is a one-line state-reset bug in rhashtable, the Linux kernel’s shared resizable hash table. Because callers trust the object pointers returned by a table walk, this small library flaw enabled a stable local privilege escalation on Linux—and affected Android with SELinux enforcing—without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces.

Many kernel subsystems store live objects, such as sockets, in rhashtable and walk the table when user space asks to list them. Because a large listing may be split across several replies, a walk can pause and resume. Its iterator saves where it stopped, including a pointer to the last visited entry (iter->p). While the walk is paused, however, the table can still change: entries can be removed and freed, and resizing can replace the underlying bucket table.

The missed reset

Before 2018, rhashtable_walk_stop() always cleared iter->p = NULL on pause. To improve walk stability across stop/start cycles, a 2018 commit (5d240a8936f6) kept iter->p across walk_stop() and moved the reset into rhashtable_walk_start_check()—but only on one of its two resume paths:

Old table freed by a resize (iter->walker.tbl == NULL): lines 877–882 switch to the new table, reset slot and skip, and return -EAGAIN early without clearing iter->p:

Old table still present (iter->walker.tbl != NULL): lines 884–919 scan the bucket chain for iter->p and reset iter->p = NULL if the entry was removed.

if (!iter->walker.tbl) { iter->walker.tbl = rht_dereference_rcu(ht->tbl, ht); iter->slot = 0; iter->skip = 0; return -EAGAIN; }

After that restart, the next call to rhashtable_walk_next() sees iter->p still set and follows iter->p->next instead of starting over at slot = 0. If that entry was freed while the walk was paused, dereferencing iter->p->next reads from freed memory.

Why did this bug go unnoticed for eight years? Triggering it requires three conditions to line up in the same walk: the caller must pause and resume the same iterator across walk_stop() and walk_start(), a table resize must free the old bucket table during that pause, and the entry at iter->p must also be removed and freed before the walk resumes. Most rhashtable walkers finish in a single pass without ever resuming a stopped iterator, and even when a caller does pause and resume, those three events rarely coincide by accident in normal workloads.

The upstream fix simply clears the stale pointer before returning:

+ iter->p = NULL;

From a socket listing to a kernel write

Because rhashtable is a shared library, its callers determine both whether this bug is reachable and how severe its security impact can be. Across the kernel, there are about two dozen files that use the rhashtable walker API, and most walk the table in a single pass and immediately exit. Among those callers, we found two that pause and resume an iterator across batches and can at least cause a crash: TIPC’s socket dump (tipc_nl_sk_walk()) and Netlink’s socket diagnostics (__netlink_diag_dump()).

Of the two, __netlink_diag_dump() is the exploitable caller. It is reachable by unprivileged users on standard kernels, and user space controls the pause between dump replies (via recvmsg()). An attacker can hold a dump paused while resizing the table and freeing the socket at iter->p, then reallocate that memory to control iter->p->next—causing rhashtable_walk_next() to return a fake socket pointer sk.

__netlink_diag_dump() then checks net_eq(sock_net(sk), net) and passes sk to sk_diag_fill() and sock_diag_save_cookie(), which initializes sk->sk_cookie if it is zero. That turns the fake sk pointer into a constrained 64-bit write (when the target 8 bytes are zero and sk->sk_net matches &init_net). Paired with other general exploitation techniques, this write is enough for local privilege escalation.

We thank Yuan Tan of NebuSec, who also independently found this vulnerability. He promptly shared its real severity with us and the maintainers, which helped the upstream fix, and later provided us with his working exploits for both Linux and Android. We also thank Frank Wu of NebuSec, who identified a viable exploitation primitive and developed a working privilege-escalation exploit.

Closing thoughts

Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance. Two weeks of codename MDASH scanning produced the initial findings, which we narrowed to 621 PoC-backed cases. But it took over four person-months to report 59 of them—and five months later, 38 fixes have been merged. For complex infrastructure like the Linux kernel, keeping humans in the loop is still necessary, making human effort the bottleneck. Both bug hunters and maintainers can be overwhelmed by the volume of real findings, so focusing on genuinely high-severity issues is essential.

More tokens may yield more bugs, but not a secure system. We scanned only a small fraction of the kernel, and further tuning and more tokens could uncover substantially more bugs. But even after fixing all of them, is the system secure? At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we’re using AI to expand the scope of vulnerability research, but our experience shows that discovery is only one part of the work. The more urgent problem is how to build practical security solutions that are operational, cumulative, and economically sensible.

These lessons also extend beyond our research. Through close collaboration with the engineering teams building codename MDASH, we’re applying what we learn from real-world vulnerability discovery and validation to inform how these capabilities evolve. The goal is to bring advances in AI-powered security research into the hands of security teams, helping them identify and address critical vulnerabilities more effectively.

The post Lessons from 59 Linux Kernel Bug Reports appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.

The researcher added that since his last analysis of Glasswing vulnerability findings in September, Anthropic had added 4613 vulnerability findings to its ledger, yet only 15 were marked as fixed within the same period. A significant volume of findings added to the ledger between September and November (1668) were marked as duplicates.

This led the researcher to question Anthropic’s latest claimed true positive rate of 94.2%, which, he said, raises “questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings.”

Read more: Anthropic Expands Mythos Access to 150 More Organizations

Anthropic Launched OSS Scanner to Scale Vulnerability Disclosures

One reason that could explain the gap between the vulnerabilities claimed to be found through Glasswing and vulnerabilities publicly fixed is the pace of human vulnerability report triage.

On October 8, Anthropic said it had found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but had manually reviewed only about 6000, and that it remains "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings."

“We are working on scaling our vulnerability disclosures,” the company added.

Therefore, it launched its own Open Source Security Scanner (OSS Scanner), a self-service new tool inspired by Google's OSS-Fuzz project and that allows maintainers to request a scan and triage the findings themselves.

Anthropic also said it has already sent nearly 5000 unverified vulnerability reports directly to maintainers who asked to receive everything in bulk.

This new shift in Project Glasswing started showing issues in AI-powered vulnerability reports more clearly.

For instance, Daniel Stenberg, maintainer of the Client and URL (cURL) project, said on November 6 he received 45 vulnerability reports from Anthropic through Glasswing.

After analyzing 34 of them using Anthropic OSS Scanner and other tools, Stenberg pointed out that 19 weren't vulnerabilities at all and six have been confirmed as low severity.

“AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile,” Garrity concluded.

Infosecurity contacted Anthropic for comment, but the company had not responded by the time of publication.

8f6c7c61dc22.text:
Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools.

Check Point Research (CPR) detailed the findings in a November 10 report, linking the clusters through shared infrastructure features and code similarities within the Sparrow framework.

The year-long investigation covered campaigns targeting several dozen high-profile organizations across the three regions. CPR called the suspected supplier behind the framework 'CopperDragon.'

Three Clusters Share Sparrow Framework

The three clusters are tracked by CPR researchers as SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire.

SilentDelivery, observed since early 2026, has compromised legitimate websites, mainly in government, shipping and IT or research sectors.

Visitors were shown a fake Chrome certificate warning that prompted them to install a "Certificate Fix" utility, with targets mainly in the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong and Indonesia. The fake utility delivered SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant, giving the attackers an initial foothold.

OceanGate was observed during 2025 and 2026 and mainly targeted government organizations and critical infrastructure in Asia. CPR said attackers entered through an internet-facing Linux server before moving into Windows environments and conducting extensive credential theft, lateral movement and exfiltration of sensitive operational information.

DarkWire, first identified in mid-2025, initially concentrated on Latin America but more recent intrusions suggested expansion. The cluster has targeted telecom operators, including at least three major providers in the region, as well as foreign affairs and justice bodies.

CopperDragon May Sit Behind Multiple Groups

CPR described CopperDragon as "a potential digital quartermaster supporting China-nexus threat actors" and the Sparrow framework's "possible developer and supplier." It also assessed that CopperDragon is involved in maintaining and supplying variants of the Melofee backdoor.

The report links the framework to FamousSparrow, first identified in 2021 and known for using the SparrowDoor backdoor. CPR said Earth Estries, TropicTrooper and UAT-9244 use a shared toolset "potentially supplied by the same entity," and noted that FamousSparrow was previously also linked to Salt Typhoon, though the details of that relationship remain unclear.

Read more on FamousSparrow: FamousSparrow Swaps SparrowDoor For New SparroWocky Backdoor

For DarkWire, CPR said it did not identify direct code similarities with the CopperDragon toolset. The link instead rests on infrastructure tied to a previously reported FamousSparrow domain.

Shared malware and infrastructure "can blur the boundaries between operators and campaigns," CPR wrote, presenting its findings as a basis for tracking activity long grouped under FamousSparrow more precisely.

a217acd4ba9b.text:
AI agents can retrieve information, use tools, and trigger actions across multiple systems before a security team can assess their decisions. If an agent begins operating outside its authorized purpose, the organization must immediately contain the risk and determine which parts of the business process can safely continue. However, harmful actions unfold faster than human defenders can respond.

Closing this gap is a focus of Fortinet’s recent contributions to the World Economic Forum Centre for Cybersecurity’s Cyber Frontiers: AI and Cybersecurity initiative. Fortinet’s participation includes an in-person meeting in San Francisco last month and ongoing initiative workshops. Through this collaboration, we bring a practitioner’s perspective on translating agent governance into enforceable controls.

Effective containment requires AI-enabled security that detects signs of misuse and automatically triggers controls to restrict an agent’s actions. Enforcement must extend beyond prompts to the agent’s tools, credentials, active context, and stored memory. These controls must also give security teams time to assess an incident and choose an appropriate response. An agent kill switch remains an essential last resort when narrower interventions cannot reliably contain the risk. However, it must be designed to support business continuity, allowing it to stop an affected agent while safe, authorized work continues.

Here are critical steps every organization can take to secure their AI agent deployments:

1. Establish What an Agent Is Allowed to Do

Detecting misuse begins with a clear understanding of an AI agent’s legitimate role. Before deployment, organizations must define the agent’s identity, purpose, accountable owner, and authorized scope. This scope needs to specify which tools it can invoke, what information it can access, and which actions it can delegate.

With those boundaries established, AI-enabled monitoring can assess whether an agent’s activity remains consistent with its assigned task. That assessment must go beyond checking credentials: An agent using valid credentials and permitted tools can still request an inappropriate operation or access information unrelated to its purpose.

When monitoring detects a deviation, the first priority is to limit potential harm. Whether the cause is a compromise, faulty instructions, or a routine error, containment must begin before the uncertainty is resolved. Predefined intervention criteria should specify which actions to block, which permissions to restrict, and which cases require human review.

Defining those criteria beforehand requires an understanding of both attack behavior and legitimate operations. Fortinet and FortiGuard Labs bring critical threat research and operational experience to that effort, helping identify suspicious patterns in tool use and data access and linking those signals to proportionate controls.

2. Use Deception to Strengthen Detection

Deception techniques can generate useful detection signals. Fortinet’s deception technologies include deploying decoy assets and credentials to identify credential misuse and lateral movement. Agentic workflows can build on this approach: A canary credential or decoy tool outside an agent’s authorized task, for example, could reveal an attempt to exceed its scope. That signal could trigger a targeted restriction or pause while a person assesses the situation.

For threat researchers, the key question is how reliably these techniques translate into agent behavior. Testing should determine how to interpret the signal in context—including benign discovery and configuration errors—and what response is warranted. Agent-specific applications should also be validated before organizations rely on them for containment.

3. Contain Risk While Preserving Verified Work

Responses must address both potential harm and whatever remains trustworthy. Consider a hypothetical security operations agent investigating suspicious activity. If the agent recommends isolating a production system without verifying its business dependencies, acting on that recommendation could cause as much harm as the threat it is intended to contain.

Unless a preapproved containment policy authorizes an action, an approval gate should pause the isolation request before execution. This gives an analyst time to assess potential operational consequences. Authorized evidence collection can continue as long as the process remains secure and appropriately restricted. If the agent’s identity or working context may be compromised, move supporting work to a trusted process or analyst using trusted tools, and treat suspect evidence as untrusted data.

Graduated containment provides several ways to make that distinction operational:

Throttle authorized activity. Limit tool-call rates, concurrent tasks, execution time, and the number of retries or delegated steps. This constrains automation loops and creates time to investigate. Unauthorized actions or imminent harm require an immediate block or stronger containment.

Restrict permissions and connectivity. Remove write access, disable specific tools, or limit network destinations. Use task-scoped credentials with short lifetimes so you can withdraw authority without disrupting unrelated services. Read-only access also warrants scrutiny when sensitive information could be transmitted elsewhere.

Limit active context. The context window contains the instructions, history, and retrieved content supplied to the model for its next decision. The application can cap how much task data enters that window and restrict retrieval to approved sources. If context may be poisoned, preserve a snapshot and rebuild it from a trusted task definition and validated state. Simply shortening the window is insufficient: It can discard necessary instructions while leaving malicious content in place.

Restrict persistent memory. Stored conversation history, summaries, and retrieval records can influence later decisions. Limit the records an agent can read or write, separate memory by task or user, apply expiration rules, and quarantine suspect entries. Clearing active context does not remove poisoned persistent memory, and neither operation revokes the agent’s tool permissions.

Require additional approval. Hold higher-risk actions for review by an authorized person. Bind approval to the specific operation, target, parameters, and scope. A material change should require another decision.

Pause or isolate the affected work. Suspend the agent or a workflow branch, preserve evidence, and keep suspect outputs from reaching downstream systems. Continue other work only when its dependencies and controls can be independently validated; treat evidence from suspect sources as untrusted data.

These options can be combined according to the incident. They are not a mandatory sequence: Active compromise or imminent harm may warrant an immediate stop.

4. Enforce Limits Where Agents Act

A gateway model offers a practical way to enforce these restrictions. Agent requests to models, tools, APIs, and services must pass through control points that evaluate them before execution. A policy decision point then determines whether a request is allowed, requires approval, or must be denied. An enforcement point at the gateway, tool executor, or receiving service enforces that decision. Both must operate outside the acting agent’s authority.

Agent-aware enforcement should link each request to an identifiable agent, an accountable owner, a delegated task, and an authorized scope. It should evaluate the operation and its parameters, the destination, the resource’s sensitivity, and any delegation involved. In the security operations example above, this means setting separate authorization requirements for evidence collection and production isolation.

AI guardrails can inspect prompts, retrieved content, responses, and proposed tool calls for signs of injection, data leakage, or other policy violations. Tool authorization must still independently verify which actions are permitted. An agent’s claim that an action is safe or that approval has been granted does not constitute authorization. If required approval or policy checks fail, the affected high-risk action should remain blocked.

The architecture must also account for bypass paths. Blocking a single connector is ineffective if an agent can access the same function through another tool or delegate the task to an unrestricted agent. You must cover all relevant execution paths and verify authorization in the systems receiving requests. The agent application and storage controls should also manage context and memory restrictions; a gateway alone cannot enforce every aspect of the workflow.

This separation aligns with OWASP’s AI Agent Security guidance, which recommends enforcing authorization outside the agent’s context, validating approvals for specific tool calls, and isolating and limiting memory.

Fortinet’s work on AI security reflects this architecture. FortiAIGate provides a runtime gateway with guardrails for prompts, responses, and agent tool traffic and adds automated AI validation, agent security, and real-time protection. These capabilities support independent inspection and policy enforcement. Organizations must also implement the task-specific permissions, memory controls, and continuity procedures described here.

5. Define Human Decisions Before an Incident

Automated enforcement enables timely intervention, but humans must still define the policies that govern it. Before deployment, teams should agree on which signals trigger restrictions, who can intervene, and when an incident calls for escalation or a complete stop.

Higher-risk actions that require approval should remain blocked until a decision is made. Escalation deadlines and safe fallback procedures should account for situations where no reviewer is available. Organizations should also test whether their staffing and escalation processes can handle the volume of decisions generated by agents.

Reviewers also need evidence to support a decision: what the agent attempted to do, which actions it completed, which restrictions are in effect, and which systems or data may be affected. Without that context, an alert can leave someone responsible for a decision they’re not equipped to make.

6. Design Your Emergency Kill Switch for Business Continuity

An emergency stop should revoke the suspect agent’s authority while preserving the underlying business process wherever it remains safe. This includes halting the affected run through the orchestration layer, revoking its task credentials and sessions, and propagating restrictions to child agents and delegated jobs. You should also block new tool calls at external enforcement points and cancel queued work. In-flight operations require explicit handling: cancel them where supported, determine what has already completed, and reconcile or compensate for completed changes where possible.

Continuity depends on having a tested fallback in place in advance. Keep unfinished work in a protected queue, and hand validated tasks to an analyst, a constrained playbook, or an independently trusted service. For example, a SOC can keep receiving and routing alerts while suspending the suspect agent’s response privileges. The fallback must not automatically inherit the same compromised context, memory, or credentials.

Keep checkpoints and action records outside the agent’s control so a replacement agent or analyst can distinguish completed actions from pending work and reduce the risk of duplicate execution. These records support a controlled handoff, but continuity also requires a tested fallback. A kill switch alone cannot keep the business process running safely. If no safe fallback exists, the affected process may need to be paused.

Before an agent resumes, responders should verify affected systems, address the root cause of the incident, and validate a trusted configuration, context, and memory state. A designated person should authorize restoration, and permissions should be returned incrementally where appropriate. Exercises should test the entire workflow, including revocation, delegated tasks, fallback operations, and safe resumption.

Turn Collaboration into Operational Guidance

Implementing such controls requires cooperation across the agentic ecosystem. Enterprises rely on model developers and tool providers for visibility and enforceable boundaries. Security researchers need operational feedback to evaluate detection methods. Policymakers need to understand where technical controls can support accountability and where gaps remain.

Cyber Frontiers brings together public- and private-sector perspectives on securing agentic AI. Through our participation, we share Fortinet’s operational experience while learning from organizations with systems, constraints, and consequences of failure that differ from our own. Comparing approaches helps clarify responsibilities and assess whether proposed safeguards can work when agents interact across organizational boundaries.

The practical value comes from sharing what organizations learn when those safeguards are tested: which observations warranted intervention, how quickly restrictions took effect, whether delegated tasks were halted, and what enabled safe operations to continue. Organizations can apply these lessons to test their own workflows before expanding agent autonomy. Those tests should demonstrate that controls can detect misuse, apply proportionate restrictions, and give an accountable person the evidence and authority to decide what happens next.

Learn more about the forum’s Cyber Frontiers initiative and its work to support secure adoption across the agentic economy.

Notion, the digital workspace platform, disclosed that a security breach at its AI infrastructure provider, Fireworks AI, exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in a small number of workspaces.

The disclosure comes shortly after Fireworks AI confirmed that an attacker accessed its development environment via a third-party cloud provider on October 23 and compromised resource metadata, billing information, model weights, and datasets for some customers.

Fireworks AI experienced another breach in early October, when hackers accessed environment variables containing API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts.

Notion learned about the exposed chat transcripts after receiving an alert from Fireworks on November 2 about an exposed dataset that contained only synthetic test data.

Notion responded by cutting off traffic to Fireworks, deleting all data from the vendor’s systems, and halting training runs by November 3.

However, Fireworks confirmed on November 8 that customer data had been accessed, including that of Notion users.

Notion is a cloud-based workspace used for note-taking, document creation, internal wikis, project management, and task tracking. It includes an AI assistant that can answer questions, summarize content, and help draft text.

Fireworks AI enables Notion to run some of the open-weight models available through Notion AI and analyze stored conversations for Insights, a feature that gives workspace administrators visibility into how their teams use AI.

The exposed transcripts came from the Insights dataset specifically, which has now been disabled.

“Upon analysis of the dataset Fireworks AI gave us on November 8, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable,” Notion stated in an update.

"Unattributable means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results.”

Notion has also published a FAQ page about the incident, highlighting that Fireworks had contractually committed to zero data retention for Notion data.

According to the company, less than 1% of its users are impacted by the incident. Potentially affected workspace owners should review the data through Security incident review in Notion’s desktop web interface and share a link with members that lets them download their own transcripts.

Notion advises affected users to rotate any passwords, API keys, or other credentials entered into affected chats.

If neither a user nor their workspace owner has received a notice, Notion says no action is needed for now, and they are most likely not part of the impacted subset.

What you will learn

Find out how Node2Shell and the eMudhra CA compromise differ, why Node.js 24.22.1 addresses both, why patching a host doesn’t fix old containers, and what each risk means for machine identities.

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released a security update addressing CVE-2026-111497, a remote code execution vulnerability in its bundled Brotli decoder. The same release updated its root certificates and added checks for blocked public keys following the compromise of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities.

The incidents are unrelated. Node2Shell involves memory corruption, while eMudhra involves CA private keys recoverable from public certificates. But both sit within components that applications trust without controlling: a decoder that handles external data, and a certificate authority that vouches for who is on the other end. One is about what happens when untrusted data reaches a vulnerable component. The other is about whether that data came from the service the application meant to contact.

Node2Shell: from compressed data to code execution

Node2Shell, as Imperva named the vulnerability, affects the Brotli decoder used by Node.js to decompress HTTP traffic. When the decoder encounters an invalid block transition, it continues processing instead of rejecting the data, writing beyond the allocated buffer.

Imperva demonstrated remote code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image using malicious Brotli data in HTTP request bodies and responses processed by fetch(). The researchers needed several attempts to achieve code execution.

Not every Node.js application is exposed. A basic HTTP server doesn’t automatically decompress Brotli requests, but Express applications with compatible body parsers can. The built-in fetch() API also decompresses Brotli responses, creating another entry point.

Node.js fixed the vulnerability in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1.

Exploitation has already moved beyond laboratory demonstrations

On October 27, CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Researchers have observed exploitation attempts against vulnerable Node.js installations, although the publicly analyzed attempts have not established successful compromise.

The bigger issue is that Brotli isn’t specific to Node.js. The underlying bug is in Google’s Brotli library, which is used by other applications and runtimes, so other software bundling affected versions needs to be checked separately. Whether a particular application is exposed depends on how the library is integrated and whether untrusted data reaches the vulnerable decoder.

eMudhra: When a trusted CA key isn’t secret

Four days earlier, on October 17, a researcher reported that eight eMudhra intermediate CAs had private keys recoverable from their public certificates. Although the keys used P-384, their private values were smaller than 256, making recovery a matter of checking at most 256 possibilities. That wasn’t an elliptic-curve weakness.

According to eMudhra’s preliminary explanation, a mistake during an April 2025 key-generation ceremony led to a weaker set of keys being used. The keys remained recoverable for roughly 18 months. There is no confirmed exploitation, but they could have been used to issue forged certificates. Six intermediates were for TLS and two for code signing, and eMudhra says none issued end-entity certificates.

Chrome blocked the affected TLS keys on October 17, followed by Firefox. Google found no TLS certificates from the affected intermediates in Certificate Transparency logs before the block. That protected browsers, but many applications don’t receive browser blocklists.

Sectigo had also cross-signed all eight intermediates, creating alternative certificate chains involving the same compromised keys. It revoked those certificates on October 19, but clients without updated trust or revocation information could still accept an affected chain.

Google removed the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the Chrome Root Store, with distribution scheduled for October 27. This also affects legitimate certificates under that root. On October 22, eMudhra announced that it was leaving the global TLS certificate business, so organizations using its publicly trusted TLS certificates need a replacement plan.

Apple's response shows why updating trust isn't always straightforward. Apple began blocking the compromised TLS intermediates on October 19 and the affected root on October 23. Safari, Mail, and applications using Apple's security frameworks receive these protections automatically. But some macOS command-line tools, including curl and git, can still accept the affected certificates because they use a separate certificate bundle. Apple says a future software update will address this gap.

One release, both fixes

That brings us back to Node.js. Version 24.22.1 included the Brotli fix, TLS hostname-verification fixes, updated NSS root certificates removing trust in the emSign ECC Root CA - G3, and checks for blocked public keys.

Shipping a fix is only half the job. Trigger.dev updated its Node.js runtimes and removed trust in the compromised eMudhra CAs in v4.7.7, but existing deployments still need to be redeployed. The same applies to containers: patching the host doesn’t update an old Node.js binary or CA bundle inside an image.

What this means for machine identities

The two problems threaten credentials in different ways. Successful Node2Shell exploitation grants an attacker code execution inside the application process, putting credentials accessible to that process at risk.

With eMudhra, an attacker who can redirect a connection and present a forged certificate accepted by the client could impersonate a trusted service. This could expose authentication tokens sent to that service. But the same trusted connection could also be used to deliver malicious content to the application.

For example, the attacker could return a Brotli-compressed response to a vulnerable Node.js application. If the application processes it through the affected decoder, the certificate compromise could provide a delivery path for Node2Shell.

There's no public evidence that the eMudhra keys were exploited or that this combined attack has occurred.

What's next?

In the next blog of this series, we will look at whether the two vulnerabilities can be combined into a working attack chain. Can a forged certificate be used to deliver a malicious Brotli response to a vulnerable Node.js application? What conditions would make that possible, and where would the attack fail?

We'll also investigate the broader impact of the Brotli vulnerability. Node.js is one affected implementation, but the underlying library is used elsewhere. The question is which other applications expose the vulnerable decoder to untrusted data, and whether the impact goes beyond what Imperva demonstrated.

Our next blog will focus on what happens after a successful compromise, particularly the risks to application credentials, service accounts, and other machine identities.

00b81bbbd096.text:
A threat actor has been exploiting a critical-severity authentication bypass and a zero-day in Xen Orchestra, software maker Vates warns.

A web-based backup, management, and disaster recovery solution for XCP-ng and XenServer virtualization environments, Xen Orchestra operates as an agentless control center across hosts, VMs, storage, and pools.

The critical flaw exists in the REST authentication mechanism, where an authentication token is turned into {} and then treated as an unfiltered lookup, leading to the first token being returned by token collection. If the token is not expired, the provider authenticates as its owner.

This opens a route that exposes reusable login token IDs, allowing unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and gain administrator privileges.

“Xen Orchestra compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root,” Vates says.

The security defect impacts Xen Orchestra releases before 6.9.2 (stable) and 6.10.1 (latest), and Xen Orchestra Appliance, which contains Xen Orchestra.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Vates warned that the same threat actor has been exploiting this bug and a zero-day vulnerability that requires administrator privileges. The zero-day allows malicious VM imports that could compromise XCP-ng hosts, and a fix is still being developed.

According to the company, the attacker initially operated from 91.211.251.112:8001 and via the Tor network. No CVE identifier has been assigned to the security defects.

The company warns that unauthorized access is not logged, but has shared indicators of compromise (IoCs) associated with the observed attacks, and warns that they are limited to this specific campaign.

“Exploitation of the vulnerability by other threat actors using different TTPs and infrastructure cannot be ruled out. The absence of these IoCs alone is not sufficient to conclude that no compromise has occurred,” Vates notes.

The company recommends placing Xen Orchestra instances behind a dedicated network, blocking IP addresses and domain names associated with known malicious activity, blocking the empty token in a WAF rule, and rotating all potentially compromised credentials.

“In case of a confirmed compromise, a full reinstallation is recommended as cleanup alone cannot guarantee the removal of all backdoors left by the attacker,” Vates says.

Related: Asus, Zoom Release Security Patches

Related: Citrix, Ivanti Patch Critical and High-Severity Vulnerabilities

Related: Threat Actors Exploit Openwave, Cisco BroadWorks Vulnerabilities

Related: Exploited Outlook Zero-Day Among 1,094 Flaws Patched by Microsoft

Executive Summary

Unit 42 has identified Falcon (aka XG or Xiàng Gē), which is a command and control (C2) framework that compromises victims' browsers by running malicious JavaScript. An actor leveraged Falcon to compromise visitors of webmail portals and government web applications by placing malicious JavaScript directly within these sites.

Operating entirely inside the browser context, attackers have used the framework to sideload malicious Chrome extensions and steal the following information:

Passwords

Emails

Session cookies

Communications

Falcon also served as a delivery mechanism for an implant we call Antino, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel.

Our analysis identified the compromise of government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. The campaigns we observed targeted ministries of foreign affairs, defense and interior, and law enforcement agencies, consistent with strategic intelligence collection objectives.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed in this article through the following products and services:

Advanced WildFire

Advanced URL Filtering and Advanced DNS Security

Cortex XDR and XSIAM

Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security

Prisma Browser

Idira Endpoint Privilege Manager (EPM)

Idira Identity and Access Management (IAM)

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

Related Unit 42 Topics

Command and Control (C2), Chrome. JavaScript

Hiding in Plain Sight

Falcon C2 management panels are designed to remain semi-hidden. When accessed, the panel displays a blank page with no visible branding or login interface.

To deter casual inspection, the page disables the right-click context menu via a global contextmenu listener that calls preventDefault(). The login form also stays hidden until the F9 key is pressed three consecutive times; any other keystroke resets the counter.

Figure 1 below shows the JavaScript code for this key tracking.

Once triggered, the page displays a branded Falcon panel featuring a stylized bird logo and credential input fields. This operational security (OPSEC) mechanism ensures that it does not directly expose the login page to bots, unintended visitors and automated systems that grab webpage screenshots.

Figure 2 below shows a screenshot of the login panel.

Falcon is written in NodeJS and has two listeners. One listener is for the management panel interface on TCP port 8080 and the victim-facing listener is on TCP port 443.

On the victim-facing listener, we observed a JavaScript-based version of the classic game Tetris serving as the default page, designed to blend in further. Another instance hosted a game of Snake. Figure 3 below shows both versions.

Overlap with PeckBirdy

In January 2026, Trend Micro reported on a scripting framework dubbed PeckBirdy. They described it as a versatile tool for exploiting living-off-the-land (LotL) binaries (LOLBins).

Our comparison with PeckBirdy revealed that it shares near-identical URL structures, payload delivery mechanisms and communication protocols with Falcon. Table 1 compares the URL structures of the two frameworks.

Falcon

PeckBirdy

Description

hxxps[:]//{domain}/config/{ATTACK_ID}

hxxps[:]//{domain}/{ATTACK_ID}

Standard payload

hxxps[:]//{domain}/config/{ATTACK_ID}/hta

hxxps[:]//{domain}/{ATTACK_ID}/hta

HTA application loader

hxxps[:]//{domain}/config/{ATTACK_ID}/html

hxxps[:]//{domain}/{ATTACK_ID}/html

HTML loader

hxxps[:]//{domain}/config/{ATTACK_ID}/wscript

hxxps[:]//{domain}/{ATTACK_ID}/wscript

JScript loader for HTA

Table 1. URL structure comparison between Falcon and PeckBirdy.

Both frameworks use the same payload delivery sequence to execute HTA, HTML or JScript payloads, with the primary distinction being Falcon's inclusion of the /config/ path prefix.Both frameworks use AES for data encryption. PeckBirdy relies solely on AES with a predetermined encryption key, whereas Falcon negotiates an AES session key with the server, encrypted with RSA.Most significantly, both frameworks store their persistent session ID using the same Baidu-mimicking naming convention:

PeckBirdy writes its session ID to a browser cookie prefixed with Hm_lvt_

Falcon employs the same prefix for the same purpose, saving it as Hm_lvt_$ in the browser’s local storage and Hm_lvt__<session ID> within a browser cookie

Based on these extensive technical overlaps, we assess with high confidence that Falcon and PeckBirdy represent variants of the same core framework.

The Falcon Implant

When someone visits a website affected by Falcon, the website sends a request to the Falcon C2 server. The server generates an implant uniquely obfuscated for that browser session. The implant is generated by two files: victim_common.js and victim.js.

The first file holds the configuration block described below and the second file contains common functions for communication and command execution. The two files are combined, and then passed through an obfuscation routine that XOR encodes each character in the implant with a one-byte key and converts the result into an integer.

The result is a script with a large list of integers and a small section of code to decode and execute itself. Figure 4 shows an example of the obfuscated script.

Figure 5 shows the template configuration block. The $CLIENT_IP is the victim IP address, set by the server as it generates the implant.

Victim Persistence and Tracking

The implant generates a persistent 32-character lower case alphanumeric session identifier per victim using a three-tier storage strategy designed to survive session restarts:

Browser local storage: Reading and writing a key Hm_lvt_$, likely mimicking Baidu Analytics tracking identifiers to blend with legitimate Chinese web analytics telemetry

Cookie: Setting Hm_lvt__<session ID>=1 with a path of / and an expiry date of the year 2099

Falcon extension storage cache: Checking whether a storageApi object is defined; if so, the session ID is stored there as well

The storageApi is a dictionary within the Falcon browser extension, meaning it is present only if the victim has the Falcon browser extension installed. We detail the browser extension in the Falcon Browser Extension section.

C2 Communication

The implant establishes a TLS encrypted WebSocket connection to maintain a persistent connection as long as the browser tab of the affected webpage is open. It sends a heartbeat message {"heartbeat":"1"} every minute to keep the connection alive. The implant resets the timer on every inbound message, so an actively engaged session never emits standalone heartbeats.

The code supports a fallback protocol using the Comet communication protocol. If Comet is used, payload data exchanged with the C2 server is not encrypted. The WebSocket functionality supports AES encryption in combination with the TLS transport encryption as described below.

Cryptographic Key Exchange

The implant leverages the browser's native Web Crypto API to encrypt all exchanged data using AES. If the Web Crypto API is unavailable, the implant falls back to URL-encoding and Base64. The key exchange proceeds in five steps:

Step 1: The server offers its RSA public key

Upon WebSocket connection, the server pushes a message with an action pubkey containing a 2048-bit RSA public key in PEM format, as illustrated in Figure 6.

Step 2: The client generates 256-bit AES session key material

The implant generates a 32-byte AES key and a 16-byte initialization vector (IV) using the browser's crypto.getRandomValues. If unavailable, a fallback function generates the key material from an alphanumeric string.

Step 3: The client encrypts the session key material using the server’s RSA public key

Both the AES key and IV are individually encrypted using the server's RSA public key and then Base64-encoded.

Step 4: The client sends the encrypted AES key material to the server

The client sends the encrypted key material to the server in a key_exchange message, as shown in Figure 7.

Step 5: All subsequent exchanges have their payload data encrypted with the session key material using AES-256-CBC.

Command Dispatch

Following the key exchange, the implant registers with the server by sending information about its current execution environment. Figure 8 below shows the data before encryption.

The data includes the current URL and domain of the tab within which the Falcon implant is running. The data also includes the browser's User-Agent string and client IP address (set by the backend server during implant generation).

The implant first attempts to read the remark from the browser’s local storage, specifically from the _domain_google_mark field. If unsuccessful, it then searches for the string _domain_google_mark= within the current webpage’s cookies to retrieve the remark.

If the implant uses Comet for communication, it only supports the run and nothing commands, with the latter serving no operational purpose.

The run command enables an operator to execute arbitrary JavaScript code through evaluation by calling eval. The set_remark command applies a remark (or label/comment) to the session, helping the operator organize the sessions in the management panel. It updates the remark for the fields _domain_google_mark across the browser's local storage, document cookie and Falcon extension storage.

The implant implements four main command APIs that attackers can use in custom modules to exfiltrate data, notify an operator or annotate the session in the Falcon database. Table 2 below details the APIs.

Function

Purpose

xg_note

Set session label (remark)

xg_send

Send arbitrary JSON to the C2

xg_data

Exfiltrate arbitrary data

xg_notify

Send notification via Telegram

Table 2. Main command APIs.

Falcon Browser Extension

While the browser implant runs purely in the context of the browser tab, Falcon has two browser extensions to facilitate full control of a victim’s browser:

One for Firefox

One for Chrome

The extensions work with the implant.

We are currently unaware of how an operator is deploying these browser extensions. It is likely that they are using an initial implant to trick a target into installing the browser extension and granting the operator unfettered browser access.

The two extensions are functionally identical, this section focuses on the Chrome extension.

The extension masquerades as a PDF reader, as shown in Figure 9, using the name PDF Viewer.

The extension consists of 14 files, as detailed below in Table 3.

File

Description

sandbox.html

C2 command executor, message dispatcher

sandbox.js

page.js

Unused code, likely remnants from development

page.html

offscreen.html

Extension bootstrapping and setting up an internal MessageChannel messaging bus and downloading the Falcon implant.

offscreen.js

background.js

Background service worker that stores collected data in a first in, first out (FIFO) cache such as credentials, network requests and clipboard data.

Monitors the browser’s credentials store for credentials, cookies, history and downloads.

twitter-dm.js

Scrapes username and direct messages from Twitter/X when a user authenticates on x[.]com.

content-script.js

Clipboard manipulation, credential theft, network hooking, web storage theft. Sends data through background.js for exfiltration.

analytics-core.js

Hook fetch and XMLHttpRequest intercept HTTP requests

manifest.json

Extension manifest

icon16.png

Extension icons

icon128.png

icon48.png

Table 3. Falcon Extension Files.

An operator generates the extension bundle in the management panel, which provides the operator a ZIP archive that is ready to install in a victim’s browser. As manually installing an extension in Chrome involves many steps, it is possible that an operator instead socially engineered a victim into downloading and executing a small deployment utility that installed the extension via the command line.

We have observed evidence in the management panel that the operator possesses a utility for silent plugin installation for Chrome and Firefox as Figure 10 below shows. However, we have not been able to recover a sample for further analysis.

The operator can upload tools to the management panel and password protect them, preventing other people from accessing them. The panel shows that there are two tools uploaded. Table 4 below shows the translated columns.

Name of Document

Size

Description

Upload Time

firefox.zip

0.38 MB

Plugins for silently installing Firefox

2026-04-25T14:09:06.000Z

0.62 MB

Plugins for silently installing Chrome

2026-04-23T03:08:40.000Z

Table 4. Falcon management panel (tools) translation.

The extension requests a total of 40 permissions that grant the operator full control over the victim’s browser. These permissions include access to credentials, cookies and browser network traffic. Figure 11 below shows the extension manifest.

The manifest parameters are described below in Table 5.

Parameters

Description

manifest_version

Defines the manifest version (3)

name

Extension name (PDF Viewer)

version

Extension version (2026.5.13.1)

description

Extension description (Portable Document Format)

permissions

Individual permissions required by the extension (40 total)

host_permissions

A list of websites the extension is permitted to interact with and read data from. <all urls> specifies that the extension has access to all visited websites.

background

Defines the filename for the background service worker (background.js)

content_scripts

A list of scripts that should run on every URL that matches a certain criteria. The first script injects a content-script.js in all websites visited by a victim after the page has fully loaded. The second script injects twitter-dm.js on URLs matching x[.]com and twitter[.]com, more details in the Twitter Direct Message Exfiltration section.

sandbox

Defines the context from which untrusted code executes (sandbox.html)

content_security_policy

Defines the sandbox security policy and accessible objects

web_accessible_resources

Declares resources that are world accessible (by other webpages). Extension resources not listed here would result in a cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) error.

Table 5. Falcon extension manifest parameters.

Extension Initialization

When the extension is installed, enabled, or the browser starts, Chrome parses the extension manifest. The background service worker, background.js, runs and creates a hidden or offscreen document from the offscreen.html file.

The offscreen.html file loads offscreen.js (hereafter referred to as offscreen) and creates an iframe to load sandbox.html (which loads sandbox.js, hereafter referred to as sandbox) in parallel.

This structure is common for Chrome extensions that need offscreen documents. The sandbox acts as a code execution environment, allowing eval execution.

Offscreen starts by creating a MessageChannel message bus for communication

between extension components. It delays execution for 2 seconds to allow the message bus to be established before sending a request to the C2 server to download the Falcon implant. The code is passed to the sandbox through the message bus as shown in Figure 12.

The code is executed by appending a script tag to the sandbox.html document body. The implant code, now running inside the sandbox, establishes a WebSocket connection to the C2 server.

In parallel with the background/offscreen initialization, Chrome automatically injects content-script.js (hereafter referred to as content script) into every page visited by the victim due to its manifest definition in content_scripts.

The twitter-dm.js script is injected only if a victim visits twitter[.]com or x[.]com as defined in the manifest. The content script runs in an isolated context and only has access to the webpage's Document Object Model (DOM), but not to its JavaScript context.

To achieve full page context access, the content script injects a script tag into the page pointing to chrome-extension://<extension ID>/analytics-core.js (hereafter called analytics core). Because the analytics core file is defined in web_accessible_resources in the manifest, it is accessible to web pages and not blocked by CORS.

At this point, the extension has:

Full access to the browser's data store (via chrome.* APIs in background.js)

Full access to the context of every webpage the victim visits (via the content script and analytics core)

Web Proxy

Falcon allows an operator to use a victim’s browser as a proxy server and to use the victim’s browser data store, including session cookies and credentials for requests. An operator creates a proxy and attaches it to the victim’s Falcon session.

The operator then configures the victim’s browser with the Falcon server address and the designated proxy port. The operator is then able to send requests to the Falcon implant within the victim’s browser, with these requests encapsulated in a JavaScript snippet. They will then be sent to the victim’s browser as illustrated below in Figure 13.

The sandbox receives and executes the JavaScript. This script calls handleProxyRequest with the request data as an argument, which subsequently sends a message on the Chrome runtime message bus as shown in Figure 14.

The background service worker picks up the messages, constructs the request and sets the fetchOptions to use the victim's credential store in the request. Figure 15 below shows this, highlighted in bold.

The response from the request is Base64-encoded and returned in JSON via the C2 WebSocket. This enables an operator to browse resources using the identity of the victim, allowing for session hijacking and access to internal network resources.

Download Intercept

The extension can intercept and replace file downloads according to operator-defined rules. The operator can define broad rules targeting a list of domain and file extensions.

Figure 16 below shows an example rule that intercepts and replaces all executable downloads from google[.]com and dl.google[.]com with an operator-controlled URL.

The background service worker installs an event listener that listens for chrome.downloads.onCreated events. When detected, the background worker sends a message to offscreen over the Chrome runtime message bus, which it relays to the sandbox.

The sandbox applies the intercept rule set to the download URL to determine whether it should modify the URL. While the background service worker has the necessary privileges to intercept and replace downloads, the extension's architectural design keeps the intercept rules and C2 command processing (which requires eval execution) within the sandbox. This design necessitates passing messages across the message buses.

If the URL matches a rule, the extension cancels the original file transfer and removes the download from the Chrome download history. The new URL consists of the target and redirect URL, where the target URL is encoded and appended to the end of the redirect URL as shown below in Figure 17.

The download retains the original filename and will appear to the victim as ChromeSetup.exe while the origins will show as evil[.]com.

This technique enables an operator to achieve code execution on the victim’s system by intercepting a legitimate download and replacing it with the operator’s payload. It does so leaving little evidence that the file originated from a malicious source. The operator can use this to deploy additional malware and gain a stronger foothold in the target network.

Network Hooking

The functionality of analytics core is to install a hook for window.fetch, XMLHttpRequest.open and XMLHttpRequest.send. This hook enables the extension to intercept requests made from the current webpage and any third-party scripts loaded on the page. The operator can also define intercept rules that can replace a URL with an operator’s own URL (e.g., to hijack software updates).

For window.fetch, the hook intercepts HTTP requests that result in an HTTP 200 response and sets the content type to application/json or contains text/. The intercepted request and response data is posted to the MessageChannel as shown below in Figure 18.

For calls to XMLHttpRequest.send, the hook checks whether the HTTP response code is between 200 and 299, and whether the content type is application/json or contains text/. The hook also checks the responseType attribute to see whether it is text or an empty string.

The intercepted request and response data is posted to the MessageChannel as shown below in Figure 19.

The posted message signals the content script to relay the message from the MessageChannel onto Chrome’s runtime message bus using chrome.runtime.sendMessage as shown below in Figure 20.

The background worker picks up the message and stores it in a cache awaiting operator instructions to upload the data to the C2 server. The cache operates in a FIFO fashion and stores a maximum of 500 requests.

Discord Messages and Friends List Exfiltration

An operator can also target Discord chat messages and friend lists. They achieve this using passive network hooking described above, as Discord uses JSON in its HTTP communication. If configured, the operator can intercept requests matching a Discord URL pattern with victim data stored in a separate table.

Zalo Chat Database Exfiltration

Zalo is a chat application similar to WhatsApp that is popular in Vietnam. Falcon supports intercepting Zalo chat message databases using passive network hooking. Targeting Zalo provides additional insights into the targeted audience of the operator.

Gmail Exfiltration

While the ability to exfiltrate Gmail data is not a core functionality of the extension, it does provide an operator with the access needed to compromise a victim’s Gmail account and download email data. An operator issues a command that uploads a JavaScript to the extension, which sends a request to Gmail using the user’s Gmail session cookie to retrieve a list of authenticated users.

An operator can then select the accounts to collect data from, to be uploaded to the C2 server. This action is facilitated by the extension.

The exfiltrated email data includes:

Date

Receiver

Sender

Subject

Email body

Attachments

Clipboard Hijacking

As soon as the extension is installed, loaded or the browser starts, the clipboard hijacker is actively monitoring the victim’s clipboard events. It intercepts every cut, copy and paste event by adding document listeners as shown below in Figure 21.

By default, the hijacker runs without any rules. An operator has the option to define pattern matching rules and replacements (e.g., replacing account numbers or cryptocurrency wallet addresses).

The rules are stored in Chrome’s local storage chrome.storage.local in a key clipboard_replacer_rules. Figure 22 below shows an example rule.

Intercepted clipboard events are passed as messages on Chrome’s message bus. These messages are picked up by the background worker and stored in a cache similar to the intercepted HTTP requests. They then await an operator command to upload the data.

X/Twitter Direct Messages Exfiltration

The extension comes with a separate module for scraping direct messages from the X/Twitter social media platform. The module is defined in the extension manifest under content_scripts and is injected into any webpage whose URL matches the patterns *://*.twitter.com/* or *://*.x.com/*.

The module can only scrape direct messages when a victim browses a conversation. It cannot enumerate conversations or open other conversations.

The module is notable for using X and Y coordinate systems to identify messages received (left) and sent by the account owner (right), leveraging X/Twitter’s CSS layout. Along with the messages, the module extracts attachment references (URLs) and the associated timestamp. It attempts to translate the timestamp into a uniform format.

Because X/Twitter uses “today” or “yesterday” instead of timestamps for the most recent messages, the module attempts to convert them into timestamps. We found that the module supports six different languages, as shown below in Table 6.

Table 6. Module language support.

This language support provides insight into the target demographic to extract Twitter/X direct messages.

Continuously Monitoring - Credentials Store, History and Downloads

The extension supports monitoring for sensitive information. It collects some information automatically when the extension is loaded, other information requires an operator to issue a command to enable monitoring. Table 7 shows the various collectors and how they are enabled.

Collector

Collects

Description

Continuously collects data and stores it in the background service worker’s cache. Only the 500 latest entries are kept in the cache.

Cookies

Table 7. Falcon extension collection capabilities.

Possible AI-Assisted Development

The Falcon framework shows a high level of complexity in both design and capability. However, the overall code exhibits characteristics suggesting the malware authors likely used AI to assist with design and development. This conclusion is based on the coding style, including variable naming and code comments.

There are also inconsistent design choices that make little sense to a human developer. For example, the network hook for XMLHttpRequest checks for an HTTP response code greater than or equal to 200 but less than 300, while the hook for fetch checks against response.ok. Both result in the same outcome while the first is rarely, if ever, used when the response.ok shortcut exists.

Campaign Tracking

Falcon uses unique attack identifiers to organize campaigns. We identified campaigns targeting government entities across at least five countries, as shown in Table 8.

Region

Targets

Middle Eastern Country

Ministry of Defense

Ministry of Interior

Ministry of Foreign Affairs

National Agency for Network Services

Table 8. Campaign victims identified.

While all five campaigns leveraged Falcon as their primary C2 framework, each exhibited distinct tradecraft in implant delivery and target selection, demonstrating how the operators tailored their approach to specific environments.

The operator compromised the Middle Eastern country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs Roundcube webmail portal by inserting a script tag that loads the Falcon implant. This enabled the operator to intercept credentials and monitor user sessions.

In Southeast Asian country A, the operator used Falcon to load a custom username-harvesting module. This was followed later by a fake Adobe Flash update prompt that attempted to deliver the Antino implant to pre-selected users.

In Southeast Asian country B, the operator used the Falcon Chrome extension mimicking a PDF viewer to establish persistent access from a browser context.

In Southeast Asian country C, a separate Falcon campaign targeted a military entity.

The following sections detail our analysis of the campaign associated with the Middle Eastern country and Southeast Asian countries A and B.

Middle Eastern Country (Roundcube Webmail)

In April 2026, we observed a Falcon implant residing on the Roundcube webmail portal of a Middle Eastern Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The actor had injected a <script> tag into the portal header as shown in Figure 23.

The resource config_r5lfmqe3 returns the obfuscated JavaScript Falcon implant. This enables the actor to intercept credentials as users sign in. Based on the analyzed data, we assess with high confidence that the script executes on each Roundcube visited by a victim, granting the operator access to a victim’s inbox and account settings.

We observed a total of 39 Roundcube instances being affected within the target country. We have no evidence of any instances affected outside of the target country, suggesting this was a highly targeted campaign.

Southeast Asian Country A - Police Entity (Username Harvesting and Antino Implant Deployment)

In May 2026, we observed the Falcon implant deployed in a web application belonging to a Southeast Asian police entity. The operator deployed a custom Falcon module to harvest usernames and later target specific victims by displaying a fake Adobe Flash Player update prompt with a specific username.

The first module targets the text content of the HTML element with the ID leftusername. It reports the contents to the Falcon C2 using the built-in function xg_note.

This function annotates the session in the Falcon database and sets the implant’s remark attribute. This enables the operator to know which session corresponds to which username. Figure 24 below shows code from this first module.

The module first extracts the text contents of the leftusername element, as the harvesting module does. It compares the username against a hard-coded list of targeted usernames.

If the username matches and the fake Adobe Flash Player pop-up (shown below in Figure 26) has been shown fewer than 10 times, the module displays the pop-up shown below. The pop-up count is stored in the browser’s local storage in a key called popup_count.

Clicking the upgrade button serves the user with an implant, Antino, documented in the section: Antino Implant. The payload was served from hxxps[:]//microsoft-flash[.]com/download/Adobe_installer.exe.

Southeast Asian Country B - Justice Entity (Falcon Browser Extension)

In early 2026, we identified the compromise of an entity affiliated with a national justice department in a Southeast Asian country. Unlike other campaigns attributed to this actor, this intrusion likely relied on a different initial access vector: a malicious Chrome browser extension.

The extension (ID: mbidcmlcbgbphpoacojjbmfpohcimjji) mimicked a legitimate PDF viewer. It was sideloaded in Chrome's developer mode and ran persistently in the victim's browser with a broad permission set, as documented in the section: Falcon Browser Extension.

Communication with the operator's infrastructure was maintained over a long-lived WebSocket originating from the extension's own sandbox context. The compromised browser checked in every 3-4 minutes for more than 3 weeks.

Beyond ambient data collection, the extension provided the operator with persistent visibility into the victim's day-to-day work inside the national justice department's internal document system. This document system is used to route, print and track official correspondence between high-ranking officials and subordinate staff.

On one occasion, while the victim was actively viewing a routing slip in that system, we observed the operator capture a full-page screenshot of the rendered document. The captured document was a request for the approval of the release of persons deprived of liberty. This demonstrates the actor's willingness to conduct hands-on collection when material of intelligence value appeared during the victim's session, rather than relying solely on the extension's automated telemetry.

Alongside the screenshot, the extension exfiltrated plaintext credentials for the same system and recorded more than 20 additional routing-slip page views spanning late April–mid-May 2026. This demonstrates both the operator's interest in classified internal documents and their ability to independently replay access to the system.

Antino Implant

Antino is written in Rust and dates back to at least Oct. 6, 2025, based on the compilation timestamp of the earliest known sample. The name originates from the filename of the oldest known sample antino-client.exe, along with PDB strings in the binary, such as antino_client.pdb.

The Antino configuration is stored in the .cfg PE section and is XOR-encoded as Figure 27 below shows.

The .cfg section is 65,535 bytes while the configuration takes up 262 (0x106) bytes. The first 4 bytes are the length of the XOR-encoded configuration data, 258 (0x102) bytes. Antino decodes the configuration using a 2-byte key 0xABCD. The decoded configuration is in JSON format and contains Microsoft OneDrive credentials and a remark (campaign ID).
