Persistence

Antino uses passive execution to establish persistence in the Windows Registry. It first copies itself to the hard-coded directory %LOCALAPPDATA%\Windows GatherOSStateKit\tmp<8 char>.exe and attempts to copy two DLLs, DllSafeCheck64.dll and slc.dll, from its current directory.

Antino does not import either of these files, but we have observed it using DllSafeCheck64.dll for sideloading in older versions of Antino. This functionality is likely a remnant from those versions.

The implant then checks for the presence of a file named id. If it exists, Antino reads the contents as the bot ID. If the file does not exist, it generates a UUID string and writes it to the id file.

To achieve passive execution, the implant writes a diagnostic answer file to %TEMP%\SDIAG_<GUID>\result\result.ps1 as shown below in Figure 28. A diagnostic answer file is a configuration file that defines parameters for the diagnosed application.

Antino executes the Microsoft Scripted Diagnostic Native Host utility (sdiagnhost.exe), which parses the diagnostic answer file. The first XML section highlighted in red defines the header, and the text that follows is the path required to load the Program Compatibility Wizard (PCW). The contents highlighted in purple are the answer file folder name. The contents highlighted in blue are the answer file filename. The PowerShell snippet highlighted in light magenta is ultimately executed in the context of sdiagnhost.exe and adds Antino to the Windows Registry Run key.

Command and Control

Antino uses Microsoft OneDrive for C2 and uploads a heartbeat to the antino/heartbeat/<Bot ID>.json file in the OneDrive folder as a beacon. The heartbeat contains the hostname, username and remark from the Antino configuration.

Antino searches the OneDrive root folder for files following the command_req_<Bot ID>_<timestamp>.json format. Files matching the format indicate that a command has been issued to the bot. Figure 29 below shows an example command, system_info.

Antino supports 10 commands shown below in Table 10.

Download and execute a Rhai script

execute_program

Program execution

upload_file

File exfiltration via OneDrive, uploaded to antino/antino_upload/

download_file

File download from OneDrive, downloaded from antino/antino_upload/

Table 10. Antino commands.

Notably, Antino supports execution of Rhai scripts (embedded scripting for Rust) that easily extend the implants’ capabilities without compiling additional binary shellcode. We have not observed any usage of Rhai scripts in the wild.

Conclusion

Falcon's browser-native approach presents significant challenges for traditional endpoint and network security controls. It operates entirely within the browser sandbox, avoiding persistent file artifacts and encrypting all C2 traffic over WebSocket.

The discovery of Antino, a Rust-based implant that routes its C2 through Microsoft OneDrive, demonstrates further attempts to blend into network traffic. Organizations should monitor for the following anomalous activity:

Browser extensions installed in developer mode, particularly those mimicking common utilities (e.g., PDF viewers) and requesting broad permissions (e.g., <all_urls>, debugger, tabCapture, nativeMessaging, or webRequest)

Hm_lvt_ cookies or local-storage keys on internal or government web applications where Baidu Analytics has no legitimate reason to appear

<script> tags added to the templates or headers of internal webmail, ticketing or case-management portals loading resources from unfamiliar external domains, especially where the response is a heavily numeric JavaScript array with a small decoder loop

OAuth activity to Microsoft OneDrive tenants outside the organization's own tenancy, especially with repeated small JSON writes to paths such as antino/heartbeat/ or antino/antino_upload/

Kai has announced External Attack Surface Management (EASM), now available on the Kai Autonomous Defense Platform. The company also launched Kai Labs, an expanded research team focused on the hardest open problems where AI meets security.

Most exposure management programs only see inside, so they miss the exposures attackers find first. With EASM, Kai unifies internal and external exposures into a single remediation plan, accelerating the path to zero. The external view sharpens what counts as real risk and lets teams address exposures comprehensively from one platform.

“Attackers start outside, and for most organizations the outside is the part they understand least,” said Dr. Damiano Bolzoni, CTO of Kai. “Extending our platform to the external attack surface means teams see their exposure the way an attacker does and fix it in the same place they manage everything else.”

Kai unifies internal and external exposures into a single remediation plan

Many teams manage external and internal exposure with different tools, and the data from each is not integrated. Analysts reconcile external findings with internal data by hand to determine ownership, risk, and priority, which slows security down.

With EASM, Kai brings both surfaces into one platform and a single dataset, so external and internal exposure can be analyzed together at machine speed. The result is a clearer view of which exposures are real risk and single plan to close them. That matters because the external attack surface changes every day: new cloud services, forgotten subsidiaries, test sites left online, and APIs and AI services stood up without a security review.

Key capabilities include:

Discovery and attribution: Discovers the internet-facing assets tied to an organization’s domains, including assets that CMDBs and internal asset inventories commonly miss.

Exposed AI infrastructure: Finds LLM endpoints, MCP servers, and vector databases.

API visibility: Breaks published API definitions down into the individual endpoints they expose.

Attacker-style investigation: Investigates and uncovers exposures the same way an attacker would.

One asset record, one queue: Every external exposure joins the same asset record, aligns to the same owners, and is fixed through the same workflow as internal vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.

Introducing Kai Labs

Alongside EASM, Kai is launching Kai Labs, an expanded research team that tackles the hardest open problems where AI meets security. Kai Labs tests its ideas in real security programs, not just the lab.

Kai Labs is led by Kylie McClanahan, PhD, Research Director, whose career spans vulnerability management, prioritization, and remediation. The team pairs AI scientists with security researchers in detection, application security, offensive research, and AI red teaming.

Its first research areas are offensive learning, autonomous action, decision models, trusted autonomy, and security context, spanning how AI attackers learn, how fixes are generated and verified, and how defenders can trust autonomous action. Kai Labs publishes its findings through blogs, conference talks, and peer-reviewed papers.

The Git project has released security updates addressing six vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to execute code, write to unintended files or cause memory corruption when Git processes malicious repositories or other specially prepared input.

Code execution during cloning

A vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-111760 stems from an integer truncation in Git’s handling of its index. An extremely long file path can pass Git’s safety checks under one name and then be written under a shorter one.

By exploiting this discrepancy, an attacker can replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks. This can cause attacker-controlled code to run during a recursive clone. The fix rejects overly long index paths before their lengths can be truncated.

Five more vulnerabilities

When cloning an empty repository over v2 protocol, Git did not validate the target of the HEAD symbolic reference that a server advertised, so a malicious server could therefore use path-traversal components to make a subsequent branch update, with the files reference backend, write outside the intended reference directory. Git now validates that target, along with other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received over protocol v2, closing the hole identified as CVE-2026-113408.

Git’s code for stripping GPG signatures assumed a message held at most two signatures. A crafted message with more can overflow a fixed-size stack array, causing memory corruption or a crash, for example when someone merges a specially crafted tag. Hosting services that perform merges on behalf of users may be exposed, according to the advisory for CVE-2026-114467.

CVE-2026-114469 concerns binary patches. Git’s roughly 1 GiB limit on patch size checked only the size of the patch as supplied, so a small patch could expand past the limit when decoded and trigger an out-of-bounds read and a crash. Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing.

CVE-2026-105437 affects Git’s merge machinery, where a memory-size calculation can overflow on very large results, such as many conflicts combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute. This can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small and corrupts heap memory. Both local merges and services that merge untrusted content are affected.

The sixth flaw, CVE-2026-114466, affects git fast-import. Three features lacked safeguards when supplied through untrusted input streams. Two submodule-rewriting options could read arbitrary files, potentially leaking contents through error messages, while a third could create or append to files. Unless the caller explicitly allows unsafe features, they are rejected when supplied through the input stream. GitHub advises enabling that option only when the program generating the stream is trusted.

GitHub’s response

The patches ship in Git 2.56.1, with backports for the 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3 and 2.50.2 series. Maintainers recommend that users update to 2.56.1 or the patched release for their series, and that they also update any software that bundles its own copy of Git.

GitHub said it has deployed fixes across github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.

GitHub Enterprise Server administrators are advised to upgrade promptly to version 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 or 3.22.4. Patched Git builds are being coordinated for GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app, and GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also receive them.

What should users do

Users should install a patched Git from their operating system or Git distributor, and administrators should also update Git on automation and services that process repositories on behalf of others.

“If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes,” Elijah Newren, Staff Software Engineer at GitHub, said.

Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023).

QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well.

Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat.

Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works.

What we’re building and why it’s unique

Meerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm.

Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge.

Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a get or a put. Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper.

Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale. A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements.

The challenges of consensus at a global scale

While all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable.

Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers.

Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues.

Destructive interference and leaders

Consider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits.

Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the Prepare phase, and the Accept phase. In the Prepare phase, any proposer can send a ballot number out to a majority of acceptors. This ballot number serves as a promise – acceptors will only accept proposals with that ballot number or higher. Then, in the Accept phase, the proposer sends its proposal along with the ballot number to a majority of acceptors again. If a majority of acceptors still hold the ballot number of the proposal, the majority accepts it, and the proposer can safely decide the proposal.

Challenges arise when two or more proposers submit proposals at the same time. Specifically, another proposer can interleave its own higher ballot number in between the two phases, blocking any lower ballots. Two proposers can repeatedly block each other from progressing – effectively competing for acceptance.

When proposers compete and block each other in this way, we say that they destructively interfere. Destructive interference gets worse as more proposers propose their own ballots. The more concurrent proposers there are, the more likely it is that the system gets stuck repeatedly proposing. Even if none of the replicas have crashed or are unavailable, multiple proposers and misbehaving networks can block Paxos. Formally, we say that Paxos does not guarantee liveness (i.e., that proposals are eventually decided) without assuming that, at some point, all messages arrive within a bounded amount of time — an assumption known as partial synchrony.

To avoid multiple proposers constantly competing, most deployed consensus algorithms, like Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Viewstamped Replication, add a special leader proposer. The leader is the only replica that can make proposals. Centralizing the proposing power in one replica forces an order on concurrent requests, avoids competing proposals, and has the added benefit of getting decisions done in an optimal single network round-trip, instead of two. While the leader is healthy and the network is well-behaved, leader-based protocols are fast.

The trade-off is that the leader must remain operational and reachable. When it fails, becomes too slow, or is disconnected from the cluster, the system stalls. The only solution is for the remaining replicas to detect that the leader has failed, and elect a new one in its place.

When leader recovery is unstable

When a leader fails, the system must recover by electing a new one. Interestingly, leader recovery is often how destructive interference sneaks right back into a leader-based system.

Consider Raft. For safety reasons, Raft elects a new leader using a majority vote. A replica that suspects that the leader has failed announces itself as a candidate for leadership and requests a vote from other replicas. If more than half of the replicas agree to vote for the candidate, it becomes the new leader. If they don’t, then a new election is called, and the candidates try again.

Multiple replicas can become candidates — all they need to do is detect that the leader is down. The candidates may then all try to acquire a majority vote simultaneously. The problem is that the candidates will compete for the majority vote, which means Raft’s elections suffer from the destructive interference we just saw in Paxos: two replicas can mutually prevent each other from getting support from a majority and becoming the leader. The more elections fail, the more replicas will try to get themselves elected leader.

Even if the leader stops being faulty, elections continue to disrupt what could have been normal system functioning. This is known as a metastable failure: a failure pattern that perpetuates itself even when the initial cause of failure is removed. A two-second network outage — or a momentarily faulty network switch — can make the leader appear to be faulty and force a leader election, which can fail, and force further elections. The outage will be over in two seconds, but the election can continue for much longer as candidates continue to block each other.

Ideally, consensus algorithms wouldn’t need any recovery process, as they are complicated, prone to interference, and introduce another source of downtime.

When fault detection goes awry

The problem of destructive interference in leader elections is compounded by trigger-happy fault-detection, especially in wide-area networks. In order for leader-based consensus algorithms to choose a new leader, replicas must first detect that the leader has failed. However, if replicas detect leader-failures inaccurately, the system may spend an inordinate amount of time in recovery, not handling requests.

In a distributed system, where machines are separated over a network, fault detection will ultimately depend on expectations. A process cannot directly observe that a remote process has failed; it can only observe that an expected message has or hasn’t arrived. We need a predictable pattern of communication, such as heartbeats or acknowledgements, to tell us that a machine is healthy. If an expected message does not arrive within the expected time, we suspect a fault. The difficulty lies in managing those expectations.

In real networks, especially wide-area networks, messages don’t always arrive when predicted. There is no guaranteed upper bound on the time that it takes for messages to arrive. That’s not to say that the network is slow, or that it is unreliable — most messages arrive within the time we expect them to. Instead, sudden bursts of latency and losses in connectivity can, momentarily, and without warning, increase the time it takes for any message to traverse the network. We call such networks asynchronous.

The big issue with asynchronous networks is that if some server doesn’t reply in a given amount of time, we don’t really know if the server has failed or if the network is just slow — the two are indistinguishable over the network. Any practical fault detector has to make a guess based on how long it has been waiting compared to its expectation, and sometimes that guess will be wrong.

In leader-based algorithms, that guess is exactly what triggers leader elections. Sometimes the leader is down; sometimes its messages are late, or the connection is silently broken. The protocol cannot know which one happened before it reacts. If the guess is wrong, and a replica thinks the leader is faulty when it actually isn’t, then an election begins and the entire system must stop. Until the leader is replaced, no progress is made — and as we just saw, that can take a while.

Fault detection is fundamentally error-prone in asynchronous networks, and when the detector makes a mistake, we get downtime.

When fault detection is slow

Even when a fault detector guesses correctly, there are issues. Fault detectors react to failures by observing messages on the network, and so their response time has to scale with network latency — the detector’s timeout can’t be below the network latency. This is why Raft is commonly deployed with an election timeout of five to ten times the network round-trip time. It has to be high enough to give a chance for the leader to signal that it is alive, and avoid falsely triggering elections. The election timeout can be much lower than that, but since leader elections completely stop the system, timeouts are usually set conservatively high.

Roughly speaking, a round trip halfway across the world is measured in hundreds of milliseconds. If an election timeout is several round trips, detecting a failed coordinator can take around a second. Even when fault detection is completely accurate, it is slow, and it is slowest in high-latency global networks. Until the detector reacts, the system is down.

Why QuePaxa is the right fit

We realized that any algorithm relying on a strict leader or accurate timeouts was inevitably going to stall in a consensus system that runs over the Internet. We searched for consensus algorithms designed for asynchronous environments — protocols that didn't rely on a well-behaved network or precise timing to function. This led us to QuePaxa, published in 2023 by Tennage & Băsescu et al.

The most notable thing about QuePaxa is how it can efficiently reach consensus in a single round trip under favorable network conditions, but also gracefully degrades performance during latency spikes, connectivity issues, and server failures. QuePaxa achieves this by solving the exact problems we just discussed through three key design choices: having an optional leader, completely removing the reliance on fault detection, and designing for constructive interference between proposers.

In QuePaxa, much like in Paxos, there are two roles: proposers and recorders. Proposers submit proposals to be decided on, and recorders serve as intermediaries between proposers, recording every proposal they see.

Instead of having proposers compete to get their own proposals decided, in QuePaxa, proposers will cooperatively work towards a proposal that everyone supports. QuePaxa does this by assigning a priority to proposals, in the form of a random number. The optional leader gets an exclusive maximum priority. During execution, proposers submit their proposals to the recorders, who propagate the proposal to other active proposers. When proposers receive a proposal from a recorder with a higher priority than theirs, they adopt the new proposal as their own, i.e., begin broadcasting the higher priority proposal instead. In general, proposers in QuePaxa work together to decide on the highest priority proposal that they collectively know. This means proposers can’t lock each other out of deciding on a proposal, indefinitely.

The caveat is that it might not be possible to spread proposals around well enough to agree on a proposal, and so proposers have to try again, with each attempt constituting a round. However, as more proposers submit proposals, the more likely they are to converge on the highest priority proposal. This is what makes QuePaxa a randomized algorithm: the randomly generated priorities of non-leader proposers are likely — but not guaranteed — to lead to consensus on the highest known priority, in a round. Yet, given enough rounds, it is guaranteed that proposers agree on a proposal.

One proposer is designated the leader. The leader is the only proposer capable of deciding in a single round trip. The leader always proposes with the highest priority; if the leader knows it spread its proposal before any other proposer, then it can decide immediately. Clients aren’t forced to make requests to the leader — any proposer can propose. If the leader goes down, then clients can keep making requests to other proposers. The leader is completely optional. The leader is simply more likely to decide, than any other proposer, and do so faster, in a single round trip.

However, because the leader is the only one that can decide in a single round trip, we want to use it whenever possible. To exploit this fast path without creating a single point of failure, clients sending proposals to the system hedge their bets: they send their requests for proposals to every replica, and the non-leader replicas will wait for a small timeout, so the leader can propose and decide on its own. In our own implementation of QuePaxa, we actually deviate from the paper and have clients wait the hedge timeout instead of the replicas, to reduce the amount of messages we send over the network, but the overall result is the same.

This hedging timeout is very different from the timeouts used in Raft or Multi-Paxos. It is not fault detection, and so isn’t constrained by network latency; it is locally determined by replicas and can be as small as they want it to be. In Raft, having a five-millisecond timeout in a network with 100-millisecond latency would completely freeze the system. But in QuePaxa, a five-millisecond hedge timeout only increases the number of active proposers.

However, hedging isn’t free: the more proposers there are, the more proposals get broadcast, and the more likely it is that replicas fail to decide in a round. Instead, hedging provides a tradeoff: we can react faster to leader changes by lowering the hedge timeout, but we incur extra bandwidth costs and may take more time to decide. That’s a tradeoff we're more than willing to make.

If the QuePaxa leader goes down, we can recover as fast as we want — we’re not bound by network latency. This is how QuePaxa gets around fault detection: since anyone can propose, not just the leader, QuePaxa can proactively deal with leader failures by hedging, rather than reacting to failures.

How QuePaxa works under the hood

To understand how QuePaxa gives us all of these nice properties, let’s look at how QuePaxa actually works.

QuePaxa works in rounds made up of four phases. If a proposal hasn’t been decided on in the last phase, a new round is started, and QuePaxa starts over. At the start of each phase, proposers broadcast their currently adopted proposal to all recorders. Once a proposer receives a reply from a majority of recorders, they advance to the next phase. Here’s the general outline of the phases:

Phase 0 (Propose and Adopt): Proposers randomly select a priority, send their proposals to recorders, and adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority of recorders. If it’s the first round and the leader knows its proposal reached a majority of recorders first, the leader decides immediately.

Phase 1 (Spread): Proposers spread their adopted proposal to a majority of recorders.

Phase 2 (Check and Decide): Proposers ask a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal seen in the previous phase. If it matches their own adopted proposal, they decide on it.

Phase 3 (Carry Forward): Any proposer that failed to decide prepares for the next round by adopting the best proposal they see from a majority of recorders.

Let’s walk through a couple of example executions and unpack how each phase contributes to the overall behavior we want out of QuePaxa. Each execution will have two proposers (one of which is the leader) and three recorders.

The Leader Fast Path (Phase 0): The first phase does three important things: it randomizes priorities (which it must do to circumvent the FLP impossibility theorem), checks if the leader reached a majority of support first, and helps proposers converge if the leader didn't. The leader’s proposal is not randomized, and will always have the highest possible priority.

In the example above, the leader's proposal reaches a majority of recorders before anyone else, and receives replies confirming it. The leader can safely decide right away. This might seem dangerous, but it is entirely safe thanks to a property called majority intersection: any two majorities of recorders always share at least one recorder. Because the leader reached a majority, any other proposer querying a majority will inevitably encounter the leader's proposal and adopt it. Since the leader’s proposal has the highest priority, any other proposer will adopt the leader’s proposal. It is impossible to decide on any other proposal.

Concurrent Slow Path (Phases 0-3): When there are concurrent proposers, however, it is not guaranteed that the leader will immediately decide. The leader might fail to reach a majority of recorders first, or it might receive a single reply supporting another proposer. Let's look at what happens when another proposer contests the leader.

Phase 0: Pictured below, a second proposer (shown in red) reaches the second and third recorders first. The fast path is blocked. Instead of competing, proposers adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority and move to the second phase. The two proposers could both converge to the leader’s proposal in this phase. For illustrative purposes, our example will prevent convergence by delaying the leader’s messages.

Phase 1: Proposers spread the proposal they just adopted in Phase 0 to a majority of recorders. The recorders keep track of the highest-priority proposal they observe. It is a simple but critical step: it prevents the protocol from later deciding on a lower-priority proposal. This is once again thanks to majority intersection: any majority queried in the following phase must include at least one recorder that saw the adopted proposal, in this phase. For illustrative purposes, we prevent convergence in this phase by delaying the leader’s message to the third recorder, so the recorder does not adopt the leader’s proposal.

Phase 2: Now, a decision can happen. Each proposer determines if a higher-priority proposal gained enough support to overtake its own by asking a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal observed during Phase 1. If the highest proposal returned is still their adopted proposal, they decide. In our diagram, the leader sees its own proposal returned by a majority and safely decides. The other proposer receives conflicting summaries, so it cannot decide yet. Like in Phase 1, recorders keep track of the highest priority proposal they received.

Phase 3: If a proposer doesn’t decide in Phase 2, it moves to the final cleanup phase to prepare for the next round. Proposers spread their proposals again and adopt the best they find among a majority of recorders. Here, the remaining proposer discovers the decided proposal and adopts it, heading into the next round.

This is deliberate — if there was some decision in the previous phase, then a majority of the recorders will have that proposal, and any remaining proposers are guaranteed to adopt it. We see here another instance of cooperation between proposers — even when a round fails, proposers try to converge on the same proposal heading into the next round.

Moving to the next round: After the fourth phase, proposers move on to the next round. At this point, there is no more leader fast path, and the only way to decide is by converging in the third phase. Importantly, due to proposal adoption, it becomes exponentially easier to decide as rounds progress. The QuePaxa paper predicts that each round has a 50% chance of deciding, but in practice, that probability is much higher, thanks to convergence.

Putting all four phases together, we can see where QuePaxa gets its resilience. The first phase gives the leader its one-round-trip fast path. If that fast path fails, random priorities and proposal adoption help proposers converge instead of compete. The second and third phases make it safe to decide, thanks to majority intersection, while the fourth carries what proposers learned into the next round, in case proposers don’t decide.

No proposer has to detect that the leader has failed before making progress, and a failed round doesn’t throw away the work already done. When the network behaves, QuePaxa is fast. When it doesn’t, QuePaxa keeps moving.

How QuePaxa makes Meerkat possible

In our own evaluations of Meerkat, where we had servers spanning nearly all continents, we’ve directly experienced the impact that QuePaxa has on the overall performance and availability of the system. Meerkat continuously processes requests, even when the leader crashes, disconnects, or just becomes slow. At no point have we ever seen it completely stall. This is exactly what we wanted.

The rate at which Meerkat handles requests has also been generally predictable. Most decisions — upwards of 95% — are made by the leader in the first phase, which keeps our throughput fairly stable. In the instances where a decision isn't reached in the first phase, the throughput drops momentarily, down to at most a third of the usual rate, signaling that three round trips — so three phases — were needed to decide instead of just one. The system slows down, but does not grind to a halt.

QuePaxa also allows us to confidently switch out which replica acts as leader while the cluster is running. Since the leader isn’t the exclusive driver behind decisions and proposers are cooperative, a temporarily non-optimal leader isn’t as limiting as in other algorithms, where a leader misconfiguration could stall the system completely. We can dynamically tune which proposer is the leader without worrying too much about impacting the stability of a Meerkat cluster.

What we’ll be showing next

Designing Meerkat for a global network forced us to re-evaluate how we approach distributed consensus. Instead of sticking to familiar defaults that didn't quite fit our constraints, we looked to the decades of research produced by academia and industry. That search led us to QuePaxa.

Choosing QuePaxa meant choosing a less-traveled path. It has not been battle-tested as extensively as Raft or Paxos, and we’re also extending the original crash-stop design to support crash recovery. This demands careful engineering and stronger evidence of correctness than usual systems.

That is why we are formally verifying our QuePaxa implementation and Meerkat as a whole, alongside extensive simulation and fault-injection testing. Future posts in this series will explain how we verify Meerkat and QuePaxa’s Rust implementation, how we test failures that are difficult to reproduce in production, benchmarks, and what we have learned while turning an academic protocol into a production system.

Stay on the lookout for further Meerkat updates on the Cloudflare Blog, and if you want to learn more about research at Cloudflare, have a look at our work at Cloudflare Research.

Asus and Zoom are among the tech companies that have released fresh security updates for their products this week.

Computer maker Asus published an advisory describing four high- and medium-severity vulnerabilities in certain router firmware releases.

Successful exploitation of the flaws could allow attackers to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges or overwrite memory and cause a crash.

Zoom has patched two vulnerabilities in Workplace for Windows, including a critical-severity unauthenticated privilege escalation bug tracked as CVE-2026-108186 (CVSS score of 9.6).

The second issue (CVE-2026-108187, CVSS score of 8.1) could also allow remote, unauthenticated attackers to elevate their privileges.

Zoom Workplace for Windows versions 7.1.8 and later contain patches for both bugs. Zoom makes no mention of any of these flaws being exploited in the wild.

Key takeaways

Organizations experienced 2,550 weekly cyber attacks on average in October, down 9% month over month but up 32% year over year.

Education remained the most targeted sector, averaging 5,934 weekly attacks per organization, a 33% year-over-year increase, as all 23 tracked sectors saw double digit growth compared to last year.

Europe recorded the sharpest regional rise at 39% year over year, while Africa faced the highest volume at 3,834 weekly attacks per organization.

One in every 35 enterprise GenAI prompts posed a high risk of sensitive data leakage, affecting 90% of organizations that regularly use GenAI tools.

One in every 128 emails was classified as phishing, down from 1 in 91 in September; 79% of phishing emails contained links.

A total of 1,063 ransomware attacks were reported, the highest in recent years, and 35% more than in October 2025.

New n0n extortion group enters top 3 within a month after initial operation, relying heavily on AI-assisted tooling

October’s data shows a more mixed picture. Weekly attack volumes eased from September and phishing became less frequent, but attacks remain one third higher than a year ago, high-risk GenAI prompts continued to rise, and ransomware reached a record 1,063 reported attacks, with a new actor entering the top three. Together, these findings reinforce Check Point’s prevention-first view: organizations need AI-powered security, consistent visibility and shared intelligence across the full attack surface to reduce risk before it becomes business impact.

Global Cyber Attacks Ease from September but Stay Well Above Last Year

Organizations experienced an average of 2,550 cyber attacks per week in October 2026. That represents a 9% decrease from September, but still a 32% increase compared to October 2025. The monthly dip should not be read as a change in direction: attack levels remain roughly a third higher than a year ago, making resilience, exposure reduction and prevention increasingly important across networks, cloud, endpoints, email and AI services.

Education Still Faces the Highest Attack Volume While Agriculture Surges

Education remained the most targeted industry in October, averaging 5,934 weekly attacks per organization, up 33% year over year. The sector continues to face far more attacks than any other, likely reflecting the broad user base and open digital environments of schools, universities and research institutions.

Agriculture ranked second with 3,218 weekly attacks per organization, a 93% increase year over year, closely followed by Telecommunications with 3,068, up 19%. Notably, all tracked sectors recorded a double digit growth from last year, with several highly critical sectors such as Government, Energy & Utilities and Healthcare & Medical also placing in the top half of the ranking. These figures show sustained pressure on sectors with broad user bases, essential services and complex digital environments.

Africa Leads in Volume as Europe Records the Sharpest Increase

Africa recorded the highest regional attack volume in October and climbed back to top place for the first time since September 2025, averaging 3,834 weekly attacks per organization, up 38% year over year. Latin America ranked second at 3,483 weekly attacks, followed by APAC at 3,436. Europe experienced the highest rate of growth, with attacks increasing 39% compared to October 2025. North America also rose sharply, up 33% year over year. Although Europe’s overall volume remains lower than that of the leading regions, it recorded the fastest growth of any region, signaling an intensifying threat environment for organizations there.

In October, 1 in every 35 enterprise GenAI prompts posed a high risk of sensitive data leakage, affecting 90% of organizations that regularly use GenAI tools. A further 12% of prompts contained potentially sensitive information, keeping data exposure a mainstream governance concern. The global high-risk rate has risen steadily, from 2.3% (1 in 43) in August to 2.5% (1 in 39) in September and 2.9% (1 in 35) in October. The average user generated 91 prompts during the month, and each organization used an average of seven tools. With the risk of data leakage via prompts on the rise, it is increasingly important to understand what employees share, where it is processed and which controls apply.

Latin America recorded the highest regional rate of high-risk prompts at 1 in 26 (3.8%), above the global average. North America followed at 1 in 30 (3.3%) and APAC at 1 in 40 (2.5%). Given the average usage per user, this means that across the globe each user is likely submitting between 2 and 4 prompts which might expose sensitive data per month.

By industry, Business Services had the highest high-risk exposure rate at 5.4%, or 1 in every 19 prompts – almost double the global average. Government followed at 4.6% and Financial Services at 4.5%, with Healthcare & Medical and Information Technology also above the global average. These sectors routinely handle client, financial, citizen and patient information, which helps explain their greater exposure.

Sensitive Data Exposure Spans Core Business Information

Financial Data was the most common sensitive-data category, observed in GenAI prompts at 71% of organizations. Legal and Regulatory data and Network and IT Infrastructure followed at 70% each, Employee and HR data at 67%, and personally identifiable information at 62%. These percentages reflect the share of organizations where each category was observed, not the share of prompts. Network and IT Infrastructure information, such as hardware and network configurations and IP addresses, could give attackers valuable insight into an organization’s internal environment if exposed.

Email Phishing Risk Declines from September

One in every 128 emails, or 0.78%, was classified as phishing in October, down from 1 in 91 (1.10%) in September. Among phishing emails, 79% contained links and 14% contained attachments, confirming malicious links as the primary delivery method. Some phishing emails contained neither and relied on social engineering alone. Although phishing was slightly less frequent than in September, the heavy reliance on links underlines the importance of checking URLs before users click.

North America recorded the highest regional phishing rate, with 1 in 123 emails, or 0.81%, classified as malicious.

By industry, Construction & Engineering had the highest rate at 1.72% (1 in 58 emails), reflecting more than double the global average risk for phishing emails to employees in this sector. Real Estate, Rentals & Leasing followed at 1.05% (1 in 96), and Associations & Nonprofits at 0.97%(1 in 103..

Ransomware Climbs 35% Year over Year

* Ransomware data is drawn from double-extortion groups’ public “shame sites.” Although these sources have inherent biases, they provide useful insight into the ransomware landscape.

A total of 1,063 ransomware attacks were reported in October, representing a 35% increase compared with October 2025, and is the highest number reported to date. Business Services was the most targeted industry, accounting for 31.5% of reported victims. Consumer Goods & Services followed at 14.9%, with Industrial Manufacturing at 11.6%. Because business services providers often hold data or system access on behalf of multiple clients, a single incident can have consequences that extend beyond the organization itself.

These figures show where publicly claimed victims are concentrated, rather than the level of risk faced by an individual organization in each country.

The Gentlemen Leads the Ransomware Rankings as n0n Enters the Top Three

The Gentlemen was the most prevalent ransomware group in October, responsible for 13% of published attacks. Qilin followed with 12%, while n0n accounted for 8%, entering the top three only one month after appearing for the first time, and quadrupling its monthly share of published victims. The number of active groups has remained stable over the past three months, as new groups became active while others did not show continuous operations.

The Gentlemen: A fast-growing Ransomware-as-a-Service operation founded in mid-2025. It operates as both a RaaS provider and an Initial Access Broker, offering affiliates access to approximately 14,000 pre-exploited FortiGate devices, and supports Windows, Linux and ESXi environments.

Qilin: An established Ransomware-as-a-Service group with victim disclosures dating back to 2022. It provides affiliates with encryption, negotiation and support infrastructure, and has significantly increased its victim listings since March 2025.

n0n: A data-theft and extortion operation that emerged in September 2026 and had claimed more than 170 victims by early November. Its operators made extensive use of AI-assisted tooling, and initial access in observed cases relied on weak or stolen credentials rather than exploited vulnerabilities.

What October Tells Us

October’s figures show the average cyber risk easing month over month but remaining high year over year. Weekly attacks per organization fell 9% from September, and phishing became less frequent, yet attack rates are up in every region and industry compared with last year, high-risk GenAI prompts exposing organizations to data leakage continued to rise, and ransomware remained well above last year’s level and reached a new all time high. The quick rise of n0n, whose operators relied heavily on commercial generative-AI platforms, illustrates how adoption of AI tools accelerates and amplifies the operations and threats posed by attackers.

Organizations should focus on reducing exposure early, before attackers can act on it. Check Point’s prevention-first approach brings together AI-powered protection, shared intelligence and consistent governance across hybrid networks, cloud environments, digital workspaces and AI systems. As established and emerging risks converge, a unified security architecture can help teams prevent threats earlier, reduce complexity and secure AI adoption with greater confidence.

Shipping giant Maersk has confirmed that a threat actor breached systems belonging to a company it previously acquired and stole data.

Ransomware group WhiteArmor claimed the attack over the weekend, threatening that it would release about 100GB of information allegedly exfiltrated from the company's logistics and supply-chain platform.

Legacy system compromise

The investigation into the incident is ongoing, but the shipping firm says that current evidence indicates that "no sensitive data has been disclosed."

Maersk added that it does not expect disruptions to operations, and assures customers that they can continue booking and managing shipments through its systems as usual.

“The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI,” Maersk states.

A.P. Moller–Maersk is a Danish shipping and logistics group and one of the world’s largest container carriers by fleet capacity. The company operates ocean freighters, port terminals, warehouses, and air and land transport services across 130 countries.

It has 700 container ships, roughly 13.5% of the global fleet capacity, 60 terminals in 35 countries, and employs 100,000 people. Last year, Maersk reported $54 billion in revenue and $2.9 billion in net profit.

Maersk said the incident has been isolated, but did not share details about the affected system, the compromised data types, or when the intrusion occurred.

BleepingComputer reached out to Maersk with additional questions, but we have not heard back as of publishing.

Ransomware gang claims 100GB data theft

Over the weekend, the WhiteArmor ransomware gang listed Maersk on its data leak site and publicly asked for a ransom payment of $5million.

"Your contract-logistics arm, the former LF Logistics, runs fulfilment for many of the world's largest consumer brands. Five million dollars is roughly four hours of that EBITDA," the threat actor said.

"You have 30 days to contact us and pay USD 5,000,000 in bitcoin," reads WhiteArmor's public message.

WhiteArmor claims to hold approximately 100 GB of data allegedly stolen from Maersk's OCF/LF Logistics platform, which the group is using to support its extortion demands.

In 2022, Maersk acquired LF Logistics, the original developer of the OCF/LF Logistics platform, from the Li & Fung Group.

According to the threat actor, the data they hold includes nearly 30,000 drivers records, plaintext passwords, 33 SUPER_ADMIN accounts (the most privileged on a system), signed delivery receipts, and 14.44 inventory rows with purchase orders and Advance Shipping Notice (ASNs).

The hacker also claims to hold 27,842 mobile device logs that include phone numbers, emails, and IMEI (International Mobile Equipment Identity) numbers.

Maersk noted in the disclosure today that "the incident is isolated to a local system" and that it would notify customers "as more relevant information becomes available, and if we identify any need to inform impacted parties of any further findings."

"As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact," the company advises.

In 2017, Maersk was hit by NotPetya ransomware, forcing it to rebuild an infrastructure of over 4,000 servers and 45,000 workstations from scratch.

At the time, the company was forced to operate without IT for ten days, incurring damages of up to $300 million.

Attackers are using Alibaba Cloud to host self-managed instances of AntiFox, an open-source agentic penetration testing platform, to target web services and AWS environments.

The infrastructure hosting AntiFox was used for various malicious activities, including vulnerability exploitation, webshell deployment, credential validation, configuration discovery, and AWS secret harvesting.

Initially created as a fork of ARTEX 0.1.1, AntiFox has a Chinese-language interface and lets users deploy AI agents and automate common penetration-testing tasks, such as mapping exposed services and probing target endpoints for vulnerabilities.

Security researchers at Arctic Wolf observed malicious AntiFox-linked infrastructure hosted on Alibaba Cloud using valid AWS identities, including IAM users and, in some cases, assumed EC2 roles, to make authenticated requests to Amazon Web Services APIs.

“In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments,” Arctic Wolf says.

One case highlighted in the report involved deploying an ASPX webshell on an internet-exposed IIS server, executing OS commands, accessing application settings and database connection strings, and copying configuration and log files to a web-accessible directory.

The attacker also used valid IAM credentials and EC2 roles to probe Amazon Web Services (AWS) endpoints. In one intrusion, they cycled through multiple identities and made hundreds of API requests in about 30 minutes, the researchers note.

Although most of these attempts were blocked, the attacker was successful in some cases and obtained production secrets.

In a separate incident, the attackers used a valid AWS identity to read, copy, and delete S3 objects.

Arctic Wolf's report includes hunting guidance and recommendations for defenders that include correlating IIS webshell activity with unusual AWS access and reviewing successful API calls within bursts of denials.

The researchers also recommend revoking affected AWS sessions and keys and rotating credentials exposed through application files.

The AntiFox findings follow recent attacks involving ARTEX AI, another agentic penetration-testing framework developed in China that went closed-source after it was used in attacks on South Korean banks.

CrowdStrike also linked ARTEX to a cyberespionage campaign in which the Chinese hacking group Vapor Panda targeted more than 200 organizations across 14 countries.

For now, AntiFox remains available on GitHub, where it has been updated to version 2.0, which improves how the tool documents and reports findings.

Its publishers prohibit using the tool against live systems, in real-world penetration tests or security exercises, or for destructive or illegal activity, but they do not describe any technical controls that enforce those restrictions.

For years, eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) has been one of the most celebrated technologies in the Linux kernel. It lets developers run sandboxed programs inside the kernel without writing kernel modules, while powering everything from network monitoring to security tooling.

Linux is extremely popular in production servers and giants like Google, Cloudflare, and Meta rely on it daily.

The same eBPF capabilities that are attractive for defenders, however, can be a powerful weapon in the hands of attackers. Flare’s research found underground forum posts sharing eBPF rootkit code and step-by-step tutorials.

One Russian-language post described how to build an implant with process hiding and packet-triggered activation, and included screenshots the author presented as demonstrations.

What Makes eBPF Dangerous?

Traditional Linux rootkits typically rely on loadable kernel modules (LKMs) to hook system calls and hide malicious activity. These are well-understood by defenders, and most EDR solutions watch for suspicious module loads. eBPF, however, behaves in a different way.

An eBPF malware can hook into kernel functions, observe system calls, or inspect and modify network traffic using the same kernel-supported bpf() interface as legitimate tools like Cilium.

Its programs run without loading a kernel module, so a routine lsmod check can miss them. The challenge for defenders is determining who loaded the program and what it does.

The Next Linux Rootkit Is Already Being Discussed Underground

eBPF rootkits are moving from conference talks to underground forum tutorials, and by the time one loads on a host, it’s built to evade your usual checks.

Flare monitors forums, marketplaces, and paste sites in real time, so your team sees new tooling, exploits, and chatter early enough to track eBPF threats.

Free 2-Week Trial

From Classic BPF Backdoors to eBPF Rootkits

The first major wake-up call came in 2022 when PwC and Elastic Security Labs documented BPFDoor, a passive Linux backdoor attributed to a Chinese threat actor tracked as Red Menshen. The BPFDoor sample Elastic analyzed used a classic BPF socket filter to recognize specially crafted TCP, UDP, or ICMP packets.

Once triggered, it could open a reverse shell or redirect traffic to the implant. PwC discovered the malware in 2021, and public reporting in 2022 described activity targeting organizations in the Middle East and Asia.

Around the same time, Intezer and BlackBerry jointly disclosed Symbiote, a different flavor of Linux malware that weaponizes BPF for stealth. Rather than running as a standalone process, Symbiote uses the dynamic linker to preload a malicious shared library into affected processes.

The library intercepts calls to setsockopt() that attach classic BPF filters via SO_ATTACH_FILTER and prepends its own filter instructions to conceal selected traffic from packet capture.

Public research had already demonstrated offensive uses of eBPF. In 2021, researchers presented ebpfkit at Black Hat USA and DEF CON. TripleCross combines syscall hooks with XDP and traffic control programs to support library injection, execution hijacking, concealment, and command and control.

Boopkit uses getdents64 hooks to hide directory entries. An already installed implant can be triggered remotely in two documented ways, one involving a malformed TCP SYN and the other using ordinary TCP connections.

Lastly, in October 2025, Synacktiv reported LinkPro after investigating a compromise that began with an exposed Jenkins server. LinkPro used eBPF programs to hide activity on the host and activate the backdoor when it received a specially crafted packet.

Underground Adoption: From Research to Weaponization

Security researchers and state-sponsored threat actors have explored how eBPF can be used to build rootkits. Flare’s recent research found underground forum posts sharing code and step-by-step tutorials, showing that these techniques now circulate beyond academic papers and security conferences.

On the Russian-language Duty Free forum, a user published a tutorial on building an eBPF rootkit and cited BPFDoor and Symbiote as influences.

The guide includes source code and screenshots that the author presents as demonstrations. It describes how to activate the implant with a TCP SYN packet with a specific window size, hide processes by hooking getdents64, and encrypt command-and-control traffic with AES-256-GCM.

The guide also describes using XDP to inspect incoming plaintext HTTP traffic and drop packets that match a list of 43 IP addresses the author associates with antivirus vendors.

Flare also identified 10 related Pastebin posts containing XDP packet-processing code and timing thresholds expressed in microseconds.

eBPF Beyond Rootkits

Flare also found exploit code circulating across multiple platforms. The most frequently reposted exploit (at least six platforms) in the dataset targeted CVE-2017-16995, a 2017 Linux BPF verifier flaw involving incorrect sign extension.

Alongside the older eBPF exploits, researchers discovered some fresh exploits.

One example is an unverified Linux local privilege escalation PoC targeting kTLS and eBPF sockmaps. The proof-of-concept attempts to corrupt the page cache for /etc/passwd and inject an account with UID 0. Its claim of compatibility with all kernels from 4.18 onward is incorrect.

Upstream Linux 4.18 lacks a BPF helper the code calls. Successful privilege escalation on Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 has not been verified.

In one exploit sample we reviewed, the author credited Claude in a source code comment with generating the BPF instructions.

Why Detection Is So Hard

The fundamental challenge is that eBPF-based threats operate through a legitimate kernel interface.

Unlike a rogue kernel module, an eBPF program passes through the kernel’s built-in verifier and a malicious program that passes verification looks, to the kernel, like any other approved program.

Detection today focuses on monitoring bpf() syscalls, tracking loaded programs via bpftool, and watching for suspicious attachment points on sensitive syscalls like getdents64 and execve.

But these are reactive measures, and attackers have the advantage of operating through the kernel’s own sanctioned mechanisms.

What Defenders Should Do

Organizations running Linux infrastructure should take eBPF threats seriously:

Audit loaded eBPF programs regularly with bpftool prog list. Know what’s supposed to be there.

Restrict eBPF access via kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled=1 and limit CAP_BPF / CAP_NET_ADMIN.

Monitor for magic packets — several eBPF backdoors activate via specific TCP flags or window sizes.

Patch aggressively — BPF verifier bugs are a recurring vulnerability class, and weaponized exploits appear fast.

Watch for unexpected XDP programs on network interfaces.

Gather fresh threat intelligence – stay up to date on new attack vectors, tools and techniques which may help you tailor new detections and enforcement to block eBPF- based malware.

The Bottom Line

eBPF rootkits represent a genuine evolution in Linux threats as their implants can evade checks focused on loaded kernel modules. LinkPro went further by trying to hide its eBPF programs from bpftool prog list.

Investigators could still see associated BPF maps and links, illustrating why defenders should compare multiple sources of host telemetry.

Flare found underground posts sharing source code and instructions for hiding processes and activating an implant with a crafted packet. Synacktiv documented both techniques in its investigation of LinkPro, giving defenders a concrete example of how they can appear in an intrusion.

Learn more by signing up for our free trial.

Sponsored and written by Flare.

Summary

Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled attacks are accelerating, with AI as both a target and a force multiplier. Of the 103 AI-enabled incidents analyzed for this report, most involve AI accelerating familiar attack types (supply-chain compromise, phishing, extortion) and making them more convincing. The use of AI is evident throughout the attack lifecycle, though full automation remains rare. Note: The period of analysis for this report is between July 31, 2025 and July 31, 2026.

Developer tools are a prime target. Because AI coding assistants and proxy packages often have privileged access to credentials and code, threat actors use them as footholds for mass credential theft and lateral movement across downstream environments.

State-sponsored actors are beginning to experiment with agentic capabilities. Most of the state-sponsored activity in this report falls within Recorded Future’s AI Malware Maturity Model Level 2–3 (AI-assisted malware development), with one notable exception: a campaign against Taiwanese government entities that employed up to eight AI agents with limited human intervention.

Fully autonomous attacks remain rare, likely for both maturity and operational-risk reasons. Human oversight still appears necessary for reliable outcomes, which may limit the full automation of cyberattacks, especially in sensitive operations where an agent's error can have outsized consequences.

This restraint is unlikely to hold. As agentic techniques mature and diffuse across the threat landscape, autonomous and orchestrated campaigns are likely to become more frequent, alongside a growing underground market for illicit access to commercial models and rising "noise" from low-level automated intrusions that complicate the detection of serious threats.

As AI model training and distillation increase, AI tokens are becoming a piping hot currency for threat actors.

Cloud hosting provider Railway found out the hard way; it has confirmed a near 26-hour battle against attackers targeting AI provider credentials to sell to AI ‘transfer stations’ for use in model distillation. The crooks generated about $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges using the stolen credentials and potentially had access to up to 100,000 workspace credentials.

Railway said the attacker’s database searches looked for AI provider keys by name before anything else; some queries also targeted cloud, database, and payment service credentials.

The company disclosed the incident on October 22, and posted a follow-up report this week. Because of the ongoing investigation, it is not able to share the specific details and scale of the exploits, but advised users to revoke and reapply sensitive environmental variables stored on Railway prior to October 21.

“AI credentials are becoming the new credit card numbers,” said David Shipley of Beauceron Security. “So-called LLMjacking is expected to displace Cryptojacking as a cheap, scalable way to make money.”

A 26-hour battle

The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway’s build infrastructure. They were able to evade filesystem isolation protections and obtain an internal credential that they used to access stored build histories. From there, they retrieved a copy of Railway’s internal source code and analyzed it to identify additional avenues of compromise.

They then exploited another vulnerability involving an improperly configured trust relationship that allowed them to gain even more access to Railway’s infrastructure and obtain credentials used to decrypt customer environment variables.

In a nearly 26-hour battle, Railway’s engineering team worked 24-7 in shifts and the escalating situation became a “contest of agent speed,” the company explained. The threat actor chained various exploits, moved laterally across multiple systems, and “probed many potential routes, in parallel.” Defenders in turn hardened routes in parallel.

“This was not a single breach followed by a single fix,” Railway wrote.

The threat actors were “fully evicted” on October 21, but over the course of their time in the system, they obtained and decrypted a “subset” of customer variables, roughly 100,000, or “at most” 1.85% of workspaces. They also racked up $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges, with customers reporting their keys answered coding questions and performed training-data tasks they never ran. The company is working to reimburse customers, including for charges providers decline to refund.

The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to more than 1,850 users, which included GitHub and OAuth tokens that Railway says it reset. The company worked quickly with GitHub, GitLab, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, SpaceXSI, Stripe, and others to revoke potentially compromised keys.

In the wake of the attack, customers have been advised to remove public network access to databases; rotate any sensitive variables and keys; check GitHub account audit logs and review all app access; and check audit logs within registries such as Dockerhub.

On its own systems, Railway said it shut down any potentially compromised internal tooling; rolled all keys and “then rerolled them” after validating that intruders had been shut out; moved to a new generation of infrastructure; rebuilt tooling used to run its infrastructure; and added functionality to mass revoke Railway app permissions in the event of suspicious activity in the future.

Why attackers want AI keys

AI credentials are cheap to harvest at scale, Shipley noted; attackers can hit a provider like Railway rather than trying to target one company at a time. That access can then be resold to generate revenue through so-called AI routers, which provide access to models that users otherwise could not afford, or even reach.

This makes that access a hot commodity for tasks like distillation, which transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller one to cut costs and improve efficiency.

Training one model on another model’s answers at scale takes millions of questions, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, and a single account asking millions of questions stands out. Stolen keys spread those questions across thousands of real customers.

“Think of copying a textbook one page at a time, using library cards that belong to other people,” Dickson explained. Frontier AI is expensive to buy, and the owner of the keys gets the bill while the thief gets cost-free compute.

“It is the 2026 version of cryptomining; [the] same playbook with a different output,” he said.

Managing identities when so many are machine-held

Even though the facts are ugly, Railway deserves credit for a “remarkably candid report,” Dickson emphasized: It owns its own configuration mistake, it admits it cannot be sure it found every account the attacker created, and it commits to telling customers of issues more quickly in the future.

Railway is now moving to short-lived credentials and logging every decryption. That is the right fix, Dickson said, and every platform holding customer secrets should copy it.

“Railway customers should treat every secret stored on the platform as stolen until they have rotated it,” he noted. But that rotation has to beat the thief’s clock; an investigation by Wiz found that stolen keys were tested within 30 minutes of theft, then flooded with traffic four to seven days later.

Start with AI provider keys, then rotate cloud, database, and payment credentials, he advised. Check AI provider bills and usage logs for traffic internal teams did not generate, then report any unauthorized charges to Railway. Alert on any call from an unrecognized address.

Further, he said, limit the damage any one key can do. Set hard spending caps and usage alerts on every AI key, and scope each key as narrowly as the provider allows. This really works: In one case Wiz examined, a key restricted to a narrow set of model profiles left most of the thief’s traffic throttled.

Non-Railway users, meanwhile, should ask their platform providers two questions: How are my secrets stored, and who can decrypt them? A good standard practice: Issue fewer keys. “No one ever said during a key rotation that they wished they had issued more keys,” Dickson pointed out.

Ultimately, he said, a stolen AI key spends real money, and machines now hold most of the keys. “Protect machine identities like cash, because to a thief, that is exactly what they are,” Dickson urged.

d0660fa93fae.text: Hello and welcome to the Thursday, November 12, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich. We're recording today from Jacksonville, Florida. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cybersecurity Engineering. And as so often after a Patch Tuesday, we have a bit of a cleanup episode here today covering issues that we may have missed. Apache, for example, today released an update fixing a critical vulnerability in mod_http2. The vulnerability allows for remote code execution. The problem here is that during stream processing, the assign_headers function is used to assign request headers to specific streams. That's where a heap overflow happens. And well, that of course, then could potentially be used to trigger remote code execution. No working exploit has been made public yet. Disabling HTTP/2 can be used to mitigate the issue. Of course, you may run into other issues. If you, for example, have proxies translating to HTTP/2, you have always to be careful with HTTP request smuggling in this case. And Fortinet published 89 different advisories addressing more than 100 different vulnerabilities across its product portfolio. 17 of these vulnerabilities are considered critical, FortiMail being sort of the product with the most critical vulnerabilities being addressed in this update. Now, several of the critical issues may lead to arbitrary code execution without authentication. Too many vulnerabilities really to talk in detail on about each particular vulnerability. But well, if you have Fortinet products in your environment, there's probably a patch that you must apply. And now for these product. And as listeners probably expect when they hear about that many vulnerabilities all of a sudden popping up. Yes, AI took a part in discovering these vulnerabilities. And Ivanti also released its November 2026 security update. Now in this update, there is one patch for another SQL injection vulnerability, in Endpoint Manager. This SQL injection vulnerability may be leveraged to accomplish remote code execution. And then we also have a vulnerability in Ivanti CSA that allowed altering trusted EPM Core certificates without authentication. And then we got another, well, Saturday, Wednesday after patch Tuesday, thanks to Nightmare Eclipse. Nightmare Eclipse released what they're calling SignDrop. SignDrop is a privilege escalation vulnerability in the Windows Common Log File System. What makes this kind of interesting is that about a year ago, Microsoft added HMAC based authentication to CLFS log files to make it harder to abuse them in response to some of the vulnerabilities in this overall system. While SignDrop abuses exactly that new feature with some symlink and timing tricks, a regular user can escalate to system on Windows 11, 26H2 and Windows Server 2025. A proof of concept exploit has been posted to GitHub. So far, Microsoft has not confirmed the issue. There is no CVE number. I have not seen any reports of it being exploited. And as tempting as it may be, disabling CLFS log authentication is probably not a good workaround. Again, that was specifically established to prevent other security issues. It would bring back some of these older CLFS attacks that before that feature was introduced. And a quick follow up to the N-able N-central story from earlier this week. N-able has now released the 2026.4 hotfix 2 for N-central. And with that release notes explaining what they're fixing here. They're identifying three different CVE numbers that are addressed in this update.
