A rapidly expanding ecosystem of AI-enabled tools such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI — marketed for red teaming and penetration testing — are being used by attackers to execute offensive operations autonomously.

Their footprint is already substantial. Unit 42 has observed ARTEX used in intrusion attempts against multiple targets.

Our Incident Response team investigated multiple intrusions in which the attacker’s server hosted an ARTEX console or used infrastructure and user agents associated with ARTEX.

Separately, Unit 42 Managed Threat Hunting tracked a coordinated ARTEX campaign against customer cloud environments in sectors worldwide, including retail and consulting.

External scrutiny has already disrupted project lifecycles: the author of ARTEX recently made the repository closed-source and ceased public development to prevent misuse. Emerging alternatives are rapidly filling the void, introducing new capabilities that threat actors will inevitably co-opt.

Here, we share our observations of how attackers are using AI-powered red team tools, along with our recommendations for how defenders can mitigate.

Why Is ARTEX Such an Effective Tool for Attackers?

ARTEX and other red-teaming platforms are free, quick to deploy and need little more than access to a large language model (LLM).

ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent AI penetration testing framework first published in mid-2026. It has been widely forked since.

Attackers can use ARTEX to evaluate responses, adapt when something fails and keep pursuing their objective. They can target the identity workflows and APIs that organizations expose to the internet, and then use the associated credentials and trust relationships to reach the cloud.

AI-Powered Red Teaming and Pentesting Ecosystem Infrastructure

As of October 2026, Unit 42 identified 1,323 internet-facing hosts running CyberStrikeAI and 609 running ARTEX. Notably, 21 hosts were running both at the same time.

Unit 42 analyzed 14 tools across the pentesting and red-teaming tool ecosystem, highlighting 12 emerging tools alongside CyberStrikeAI and ARTEX.

These tools can be broken down into four categories of AI assisted red team activities.

Category

Tools

Goal

Reconnaissance and attack-surface management

ARL, ARL-Next, Scope Sentry, Nemo, XingRin, OpenEASD

Identify what assets exist, what is exposed and what changes

Agent-led testing and vulnerability hunting

CyberStrikeAI, ARTEX, Cairn, PentAGI, AutoHunter

Manage what should be investigated and how the system can act on it

Source-code auditing and verification

DeepAudit, AIxVuln

Identify where source code might be vulnerable and what supports that finding

AI-system security assessment

AI-Infra-Guard

Identify if AI infrastructure, agents, tools and model interfaces are vulnerable or unreliable

Table 1. Tool categories.

Implications For Defenders

Defenders should be aware of the following implications of AI-powered red teaming platforms:

Lowered Skill Floor for Attackers

Adversaries no longer require specialized tradecraft to execute multi-stage, adaptive penetration testing.

Off-the-shelf tooling combined with LLMs like DeepSeek allows financially motivated actors to launch and manage dozens of complex, concurrent network intrusions for minimal compute cost.

Risk of Internet-Exposed Assets

Any internet-exposed asset, regardless of organizational size or sector, is equally likely to be impacted by automated, persistent intrusion attempts.

Attackers using the autonomous AI penetration testing framework ARTEX are turning public password reset pages and exposed APIs into a path to cloud access, sometimes in less than a day. Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observed this activity across multiple organizations and sectors, without exploiting a single software vulnerability.

Because these autonomous platforms cannot target what they cannot find, continuous discovery and mitigation of exposed edge assets remains an effective barrier against automated campaigns.

Proactive AI Adoption Helps Defenders

Autonomous testing frameworks rely on foundational LLM reasoning patterns. Therefore, there is some predictability to AI-powered adversary tooling.

Security teams do not need to guess an agent's methodology; they can deploy identical open-weight offensive frameworks internally to surface, validate and remediate vulnerable exposure before external agents identify them.

Defenders Benefit From Tracking Ecosystem Shifts

The rapid adoption curve of tools in this ecosystem highlights how quickly operational trends can shift. Keeping an eye on these developments provides practical defensive advantages:

Observing emerging agent-led frameworks allows teams to test new capabilities early in controlled environments.

Monitoring the infrastructure hosting these tools makes it possible to update perimeter blocks before active targeting begins.

Current AI-Powered Frameworks Are Noisy

Current autonomous frameworks prioritize rapid trial-and-error over stealth. In our study of a tool called Cairn, it generated hundreds of thousands of noisy, high-frequency requests across multiple edge protocols from a single origin IP address.

Organizations with unified perimeter telemetry and centralized logging can readily distinguish this brute-force agentic traffic from legitimate users and block campaigns at the network edge before exploitation occurs.

Defensive Deception Could Help

LLM-driven testing tools use target responses as context for follow up actions.

Defenders may be able to take advantage of this to trick attackers using AI-powered red teaming tools into wasting resources.

When a target serves identical, generic error codes or enforces silent connection throttling, an AI agent lacks the contextual cues needed to adapt. Deprived of environmental feedback, autonomous loops burn context windows and compute budgets on dead ends.

Recognizing an AI-Driven Operator

ARTEX is forked and modified constantly. Furthermore, attackers rotate infrastructure quickly, so indicators lose value fast. How the operator behaves is more durable, and the behavior across our observations consistently pointed to an automated planner reacting to what it sees. Table 2 shows the hallmarks of this behavior.

Hallmark

What We Observed

Think-then-act cadence

Bursts of one to 14 requests about a second apart, then a pause of 25–31 seconds, consistent with an agent waiting on a model inference call

Machine speed

Pivots within about one minute of a credential download. More than 200 client secrets validated in about three minutes

Spec-driven targeting

Routes from downloaded OpenAPI specifications and source maps targeted almost immediately

Self-correction

Failed requests (HTTP 422) adjusted and retried successfully moments later

Checking its own work

A GET to the same path after almost every successful write. Write-then-delete tests on storage buckets.

Canary inputs

Bogus usernames before real ones, and placeholder values such as evil[.]com, test@example[.]com and deadbeefdeadbeefdeadbeef12

Parallel targeting

An application delivery controller, more than a dozen VPN appliances, a NAS device, workforce identity and cloud ports attacked within the same hour

Recheck loops

Polling every 48 seconds for three days, and attack sequences replayed identically about 30 seconds apart

Table 2. Behavioral hallmarks of ARTEX-driven activity observed by Unit 42.

Any one of these traits could come from an unusually configured tool or a person testing an API by hand. Seen together, they point to autonomous tooling.

Despite the autonomous tooling, humans were not entirely absent from the attacks we observed. In one engagement, the attacker switched from scripted clients to a desktop browser for the password reset and first token request. This suggests a human in the loop, or browser automation, for the most sensitive steps.

Conclusion and Mitigations for ARTEX Attacks

AI-driven tooling is not inventing new attacks. Self-service abuse, exposed APIs and stored credentials are long-standing weak points.

What has changed is the pace and the persistence. An ARTEX operator can test every exposed workflow in parallel and switch routes within minutes of being blocked. It can act on a stolen credential within a minute of finding it.

Because the framework is open source and widely forked, indicator-based detection will not keep up.

Defenders who remove machine-readable attack maps, require authentication everywhere and build detections around operator behavior will be best placed to stop an AI-assisted attacker.

Autonomous tooling probes faster than people can review alerts. Defenses need to block by default and remove the credentials these tools are looking for. Organizations should:

Remove public attack maps. Take OpenAPI specifications, source maps and configuration files containing tokens or client IDs off internet-facing applications.

Reduce and understand your organization’s public footprint. Certificate transparency can create target lists for threat actors. In cloud environments, it is vital to understand if host fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) are public knowledge. Consider private certificate authorities to limit information disclosure and locking origin traffic to content delivery network (CDN)-only ingress where possible.

Require authentication on every write endpoint, including development and staging APIs.

Harden self-service flows. Rate-limit and bot-protect registration, password reset and verification code endpoints. Remove unauthenticated account-existence checks.

Protect federated identities. Block local passwords for workforce accounts in customer and partner identity providers, and make sure a password reset can never unlink a federated identity.

Get credentials out of reach. Replace long-lived cloud keys with role-based access, keep administrator credentials out of provisioning records and move function secrets to a secrets manager.

Enforce least privilege for workload roles and any function that can create roles, keys or tokens.

Hunt for behavior, not just indicators. Look for:

Canary usernames in identity provider logs

First use of a cloud key from a new IP address

Write-then-delete storage tests

Early-phase probing that precedes a later intrusion

Arctic Wolf saw attackers use the AntiFox pentest platform to hit IIS servers and AWS accounts.

Arctic Wolf Labs has published research on attackers using AntiFox, an open-source, Chinese-language agentic penetration testing platform. These frameworks chain attack steps together with little human effort. In several intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were tied to confirmed attacks on internet-facing web services and the AWS environments behind them.

Two entry points showed up. In some cases, the attackers got into a public IIS application, though Arctic Wolf couldn’t identify the vulnerability. In others, they started with a valid AWS credential obtained by means nobody knows.

“Arctic Wolf is tracking the emerging use of self-hosted agentic penetration testing frameworks, including AntiFox, from public cloud infrastructure.” states the report published by Arctic Wolf, “In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments.”

The IIS attacks followed a similar pattern. The IIS worker process, w3wp.exe, created an ASPX web shell and then ran commands to gather information about the system. The attackers checked the user account, listed files in the application folder, reviewed file permissions using icacls and tested whether they could write files to the website’s main folder.

They then used PowerShell to read the web.config file, looking for database connection details and application settings. They also checked folders containing debug and error logs. Using credentials found in the configuration file, they tried to connect to an internal production database. Finally, they copied configuration files and logs into an upload folder that could be accessed through the website.

The AWS attacks moved quickly. AntiFox used valid IAM accounts and, in some cases, an assumed EC2 role. The attackers first checked their identity and permissions within AWS. They used commands such as GetCallerIdentity, GetUser, ListUsers, ListRoles, ListPolicies and ListKeys to discover available accounts, roles, policies and access keys. They also tried to obtain an authorization token for Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR).

In one intrusion, the source cycled through several AWS identities and sent hundreds of requests in about half an hour.

“The activity then rapidly enumerated services across the affected AWS environments, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock, using List, Get, and Describe operations.” continues the report. “After authorization failures, the activity continued across other services and concentrated on resources that remained accessible.”

Most requests came back as AccessDenied, but a few worked, and the attackers kept going where the doors were open.

Some sequences ended with a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Others focused on S3, listing buckets, objects and versions, reading objects, then copying and deleting them. Nobody has to stay awake for that kind of persistence, which is the whole point of the tool.

Arctic Wolf’s concern is simple. These frameworks make penetration testing techniques easier to reach for attackers, and they make those techniques faster and more consistent in live attacks.

For hunting, start with AWS activity coming from hosting providers the identity has never used. Look for one IP address using many access keys, users or roles in a short time, and for fast runs of List, Get and Describe calls across unrelated services, especially from Boto3 or Botocore. Check GuardDuty for odd IAM user behavior, credential access, discovery and unusual calls from hosting networks.

On the Windows side, watch for w3wp.exe starting cmd.exe, powershell.exe, whoami.exe, icacls.exe or archive tools. Look for new .aspx files in upload, temporary and image-conversion folders, and for config or log files saved there under .txt or image extensions. PowerShell commands that read WebConfigurationManager, ConnectionStrings or AppSettings deserve a close look, and so does any AWS activity that starts soon after.

Organizations should enable AWS CloudTrail logging and monitor access to sensitive S3 storage. They should also use S3 versioning and Object Lock to protect important data from deletion. Alerts should flag suspicious access to stored secrets, especially when it follows unusual account activity.

Companies should identify all internet-facing applications and prioritize patching and protecting file upload, conversion and document-processing services. If an IIS process launches an unexpected command shell, administrators should isolate the server, preserve logs and forensic evidence, remove malicious files and change all exposed credentials.

They should also revoke compromised AWS sessions and access keys, enforce IMDSv2 and apply least-privilege permissions to limit what applications can access. As Arctic Wolf warns, a series of mostly denied requests does not mean the attack was unsuccessful.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, AI Pentest Tool AntiFox)

The Baker Tilly Advisory Group is notifying clients that a data breach has compromised certain personal information about them and their dependents.

The company said the exposed data was stored on a platform operated by a third-party service provider Baker Tilly uses to serve clients.

Baker Tilly learned of the incident on September 6 and completed its review of the affected data on October 28, when it identified whose information was involved.

“On September 6, 2026, Baker Tilly became aware of a potential cybersecurity incident involving certain information stored on a platform operated by a third-party service provider used by Baker Tilly in connection with services we provide to clients,” reads the notification to customers.

“The unauthorized actor was able to obtain data relating to certain Baker Tilly clients,” the company added.

The breach notification does not provide a count of impacted clients, does not name the service provider, and leaves the specific data types exposed as a placeholder.

Data from the Office of the Texas Attorney General reports that Baker Tilly impacted 10,456 individuals in the state of Texas alone. The portal lists Social Security numbers (SSNs), full names, addresses, and other information as exposed data types.

Baker Tilly is a major accounting firm in the U.S., providing auditing, tax planning, compliance, advisory, and business operations services. Globally, the company operates in 147 countries and reports an annual revenue of $6.8 billion.

After discovering the incident, the company says it took immediate steps to contain it, contracted external experts to investigate, and notified law enforcement authorities.

Furthermore, it says it currently has no evidence of unauthorized activity on its own network, and added that it has no reports of identity theft or fraud linked to the exposure of customer information.

To mitigate the risks arising from the incident, the firm offers affected individuals 24 months of credit and identity monitoring through Experian.

BleepingComputer has contacted Baker Tilly for more information about the data breach, its source, the number of affected customers, and the type of data compromised, but we have not received a reply by the time of publishing.

BleepingComputer did not find any announcements from ransomware groups claiming the attack.

Update 11/11/26: Added additional information from ConnectWise and Huntress.

ConnectWise is investigating an active malware campaign targeting managed service providers (MSPs) that uses compromised ScreenConnect environments to deploy rogue remote-access clients to customer devices.

As part of its investigation, ConnectWise has disabled five third-party ScreenConnect extensions across approximately 400 partner environments as a precaution, warning that they may be associated with the attacks.

The campaign was first discovered Wednesday by cybersecurity firm Huntress, which says it has identified six compromised MSPs and 286 affected endpoints across 47 organizations, and that the number of victims continues to rise.

"Our SOC is working an active campaign that started around 17:47 UTC today targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances," Huntress posted to Reddit.

"We are currently tracking 6 compromised MSPs and 286+ endpoints, and those numbers are climbing. ConnectWise is engaged and working this with us."

ScreenConnect is a remote access and support platform used by MSPs and IT teams to remotely manage and troubleshoot customer devices.

According to Huntress, attackers are using ScreenConnect's Run Command functionality to deploy rogue ScreenConnect clients on managed endpoints, providing remote access outside of the legitimate MSP's ScreenConnect environment.

The researchers also warned of a potentially more dangerous technique in which attackers can compromise an MSP technician's workstation when they initiate a ScreenConnect session with an infected customer device.

Spike Brandt, Principal Threat Intelligence Incident Commander at Huntress, told BleepingComputer that the activity appears to involve abusing legitimate functionality rather than exploiting a software vulnerability.

"This appears to be abuse of legitimate functionality, aided using custom-built tooling that is, in some cases, compiled on the fly on the victim’s computer," Brandt told BleepingComputer.

"We have no information about how a “patient zero” computer or machine would have initiated this attack."

Huntress said it began receiving alerts when rogue ScreenConnect clients appeared on monitored endpoints and subsequently retrieved attacker scripts that were still accessible to analyze how the attacks worked.

However, the precise mechanism allowing malware to spread from an infected endpoint to a technician's workstation has not been publicly explained.

ConnectWise disables third-party extensions

In a security advisory published Wednesday night, ConnectWise confirmed unauthorized access to ScreenConnect partner accounts and the installation of unauthorized remote-access software in customer environments.

As part of its investigation, the company discovered five independent third-party extensions that may be associated with the attacks and disabled them across approximately 400 partner environments as a precaution.

ScreenConnect extensions are installed through its built-in Extensions marketplace via the ScreenConnect administration interface.

The extensions are:

Labtech Plus

RMM Plus

RMM+

RMM Plus Password Link

RMM+ Password Link

"Our initial assessment leads us to suspect the threat actor deployed additional remote-access software through independent 3rd party extensions that partners may have added to their environments," ConnectWise said.

The company stressed that having these extensions installed does not necessarily mean that a network was compromised and that the attacks remain under investigation.

"Disabling these 3rd party extensions is a precautionary containment measure. It does not establish that unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already present on affected devices has been removed," explained ConnectWise

While ConnectWise has disabled the extensions in affected cloud-hosted environments, it warned that on-premises ScreenConnect customers must disable them manually, as the company cannot do so from their end.

Partners were also instructed not to re-enable or reinstall the extensions until further guidance is available.

ConnectWise warned that disabling the extensions does not remove malicious software, persistence mechanisms, or unauthorized access that attackers may have already established on compromised endpoints.

The company advised partners to review authentication logs, extension installation records, administrative activity, Run Command history, and Toolbox records for suspicious activity.

It also urged technicians to avoid initiating interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially compromised devices and instead use separate security tools to investigate.

ConnectWise also said it has received reports of technician workstations being compromised during interactive ScreenConnect sessions, but these reports are still being confirmed.

The company added that it has no reason to believe partners that have not deployed the five identified extensions are impacted by this incident, but encouraged all partners to remain on heightened alert.

Huntress has not determined how the attackers are gaining access to affected MSP environments, but says its current telemetry points to compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions.

Huntress also warned that sequential identifiers used by the attackers suggest additional MSPs may have been previously compromised.

"Sequential attacker-assigned tags suggest other MSPs may have been compromised earlier, so ScreenConnect users should check their Run Command history even if they haven’t received alerts," Huntress told BleepingComputer.

Huntress also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations identify malicious activity, including rogue ScreenConnect client IDs and infrastructure used by the attackers.

The indicators include:

Attacker relay: 185.99.255[.]28 (hostname: screen)

C2 domains: newnewnew.gotdns[.]org, soxnewwork.homedns[.]org

Possible additional C2: cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com

Secondary C2: sc.payproofkit[.]com (155.94.150[.]39, hostname: WIN-FB5CKHMU4E1)

Stager: hxxps://ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4

Rogue ScreenConnect client IDs: 2588ef5c15954b10, ed630cc2c873b091

Installer pattern: /Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi?...&c=Exploited<N>

Attacker name: Addmin

Files: Panel-Lateral.ps1, runnew.cmd, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, Run-Lateral-Full.bat

The researchers are urging MSPs to review their environments for signs of compromise and avoid initiating interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially infected endpoints.

Huntress also told BleepingComputer that its researchers have contacted ConnectWise, the VPS provider hosting the attacker's infrastructure, cloud providers whose dynamic DNS services were used in the attacks, and the broader MSP community.

Earlier malware activity linked to rogue ScreenConnect identifier

BleepingComputer found an earlier malicious batch script that references one of the rogue ScreenConnect client IDs listed by Huntress, suggesting that the ID was used in malicious activity months before the current attacks were disclosed.

The script, named SSA-2026-STATEMENT-15518787.bat (VirusTotal), appears to impersonate a Social Security Administration statement and was first uploaded to VirusTotal on July 25, 2026.

The batch file attempts to add Microsoft Defender exclusions and creates persistence through the Windows Startup folder and the Run registry key.

It then contacts amexsafekeyupdate.com to retrieve installation commands for two separate installers.

VirusTotal sandbox activity associated with the sample includes downloads of ScreenConnect MSI installers from cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com and cyberrexdesign.screenconnect[.]com, with cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com also listed by Huntress as a possible C2 domain.

After launching the second installer, the script uses PowerShell to search running processes and Windows services for ed630cc2c873b091, one of the rogue ScreenConnect client IDs identified by Huntress.

If the identifier is found, the script considers the installation successful and sends a notification to the attackers through Telegram.

The earlier script also appears designed for a different distribution campaign, with its Social Security-themed filename suggesting it may have been used in phishing attacks.

Asked about the earlier activity, Huntress declined to comment on the specific July incident but said it has observed a significant increase in attacks using legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software as an initial payload in 2026.

The relationship between the July malware activity and the current ScreenConnect attacks remains unclear.

Certificate authority eMudhra has revoked eight additional intermediate CA certificates after an investigation into its recent certificate security incident found improper handling of private keys during the certificate-generation process.

The new revocations bring the total number of affected intermediate CA certificates to 16, including eight previously compromised certificates whose private keys were so weak that anyone could recover them almost instantly.

In a new incident report published Tuesday, eMudhra said that both sets of certificates were affected by a custom Python script used to transfer private keys between hardware security modules (HSMs) in April 2025.

HSMs are devices designed to securely generate and store cryptographic keys, preventing sensitive private keys from being exposed outside the hardware.

eMudhra says it developed the script to move certificate authority keys between different HSM vendors at its facilities after delays in obtaining new hardware.

However, the script contained a bug that reduced eight ECDSA private keys to a single byte, making them extremely easy to recover.

The same script also processed eight RSA private keys, which handled sensitive key information in the memory of the computer running the script rather than keeping it protected within the HSM.

While the RSA keys were not weakened like the original eight certificates, eMudhra says it could not demonstrate that it handled them under its certificate security policies.

"A re‑import performed from host process memory is not consistent with the CPS §6.2.6 and the RSA objects are therefore treated as not meeting that requirement," reads the incident report.

Due to this, the company revoked the additional eight RSA intermediate CA certificates on November 7, including certificates used to issue TLS and code-signing certificates.

Some of the affected RSA intermediates had been actively issuing certificates since May 2026, with the last certificate issued on November 3.

eMudhra says the affected customer certificates have also been replaced or migrated.

The investigation also found that an earlier problem in June 2025 could have revealed the flaw more than a year before it was discovered by a security researcher known as "Wayne."

At that time, eMudhra detected certificate revocation lists (CRLs) signed with private keys that did not match the corresponding CA certificates.

The company fixed the issue by signing the revocation lists with the matching keys but did not investigate why the problem occurred.

The new report confirms this was an early warning sign of the faulty key-generation process that went undetected until October 2026.

The investigation also found that eMudhra did not verify the strength of generated private keys or check that the keys used for certification matched those originally created in the HSM.

Major browsers blocked compromised certificates

As BleepingComputer previously reported, the incident was first disclosed on October 17, when a security researcher named Wayne discovered that eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys could be recovered by testing just 256 possible values.

Major browsers and operating systems trusted the compromised certificates, potentially allowing attackers to forge certificates for legitimate websites and intercept encrypted communications.

Mozilla, Google, Apple, and other software vendors subsequently released protections to block the compromised certificates.

Microsoft also released out-of-band Windows updates on October 26 to remove trust in affected eMudhra certificate trust chains on systems that could not receive automatic certificate trust updates.

Following the incident, eMudhra announced that it would exit the publicly trusted TLS certificate business and transition its remaining customers to another provider.

The company says it plans to stop issuing certificates under its remaining G1 hierarchy by November 16.

eMudhra has also commissioned an independent review by KPMG, with findings expected by December 4, to identify improvements to its certificate management and key-generation procedures.

The company says it has not detected any evidence that the compromised keys were used maliciously.

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of checkpoint files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

Key points and observations

CVE-2026-118383 is a critical use-after-free in MongoDB Server's primary catch-up process, with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.5. It affects replica set members, including those used by shards and config servers. Standalone mongod instances are unaffected.

Remote unauthenticated exploitation is possible, but only during a specific window that the attacker does not have visibility into.

We reproduced a crash (segmentation fault) on MongoDB Server 8.0.34.

An unauthenticated client can set up the crash with two ping requests, because vulnerable servers accept ping before login. Turning on authentication does not prevent this.

Upgrade every affected replica set member to a fixed release. Restricting network access can reduce exposure while you upgrade.

What happened

MongoDB announced a security update on November 10. The company said it found the vulnerability internally and was not aware of exploitation attempts at the time of its announcement. The advisory describes a use-after-free when a newly elected replica set primary completes catch-up. During catch-up, the member applies operations it missed before accepting writes as primary.

The vulnerability affects ordinary replica set members. It also affects the replica set members used by shards and config servers in sharded clusters. A standalone mongod does not perform replica set primary catch-up and is not affected by this vulnerability. The advisory rates the issue Critical and says the server may terminate unexpectedly or, under certain conditions, execute arbitrary code in the server process.

How to know if you are affected

The issue affects replica set members, including shard and config server replica set members in sharded clusters. Standalone mongod instances are not affected.

The MongoDB fix releases are:

MongoDB Server branch

First fixed release

9.0

9.0.7

8.3

8.3.16

8.0

8.0.37

7.0

7.0.48

6.0

6.0.30

5.0

5.0.35

4.4

4.4.32

Upgrade to the fixed release for your branch, or use a distributor package that includes the fix. Verify the version running on every member after the upgrade, including members in containers and any members that were offline during maintenance. MongoDB says Atlas clusters are upgraded automatically during maintenance. It urges customers who defer maintenance to apply the upgrade promptly.

Until you can upgrade, restrict network access to MongoDB to the specific systems that need access to it. This limits who can send the unauthenticated requests, but it does not fix the use-after-free.

Exploitation window and likelihood

When a replica set member wins an election, it first catches up on writes it missed, then starts accepting new ones. The bug is in the cleanup at the end of that catch-up step. Before any election happens, an attacker can leave two stale “waiters” on a member. A waiter is a pending notification MongoDB creates when a request asks to wait until replication reaches a certain point. Planting them does not crash the server by itself. The diagram below traces an election timeline and marks where the crash fires.

Plant during steady state: The attacker sends two unauthenticated ping requests that include a readConcern.afterOpTime value to a reachable, vulnerable replica set member. The waiters don't expire. They stay in place until the member restarts, rolls back, or steps down from primary.

Reach catch-up: Later, the same member has to win an election while it is behind another member. The attacker can't cause the lag or the election. Both have to happen on their own, for example during maintenance or an outage.

Crash when catch-up ends: When catch-up finishes, the new primary runs its cleanup twice, uses memory it has already freed, and crashes before it accepts any writes. Once the first two steps are in place, the crash does not depend on winning a timing race.

We created the lag and the failover ourselves, so the roughly 40 seconds our lab run took is not an estimate of how quickly a real attack would work. After the crash, our test cluster had no primary. Another deployment might elect a new primary and keep running.

What we reproduced

We built a four-member replica set from MongoDB's official Linux x86_64 binaries and created the two conditions an attacker can't control: one member falling behind on replication, and a failover that makes that member the new primary. Setting this up took admin access to the lab, to pause and stop mongod processes and to write data with an authenticated client. The attacker's part, the two ping requests, used no credentials, and we confirmed that the same unauthenticated client could not write to the database.

We ran the same failover three times, changing only the MongoDB version and whether we sent the two requests:

Run

Server

Unauthenticated waiter requests

Observed result

A

8.0.34

Both timed out after about 1.5 seconds with MaxTimeMSExpired

The target member exited catch-up twice, logged SIGSEGV, and the mongod process crashed

B

8.0.34

None sent

The target member exited catch-up once, became writable, and remained running through the observation window

C

8.0.37

Both rejected immediately with Unauthorized

The target member exited catch-up once, became writable, and remained running through the observation window

The video below shows run A from start to finish: the two unauthenticated requests, the failover we triggered, and the new primary crashing.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

In run A, MongoDB's log shows the new primary leaving catch-up mode twice within the same millisecond, followed by “Invalid access at address: 0” and “Got signal: 11 (Segmentation fault).” The backtrace points to CatchupState::abort_inlock(). Runs B and C went through the same failover, logged a single catch-up exit, and kept running.

Run C shows that the patched server refuses the requests. It does not test the other half of MongoDB's fix, which stops the double cleanup even when waiters are already in place; MongoDB's own regression tests cover that case. Our results show that the crash can be set up without credentials in this lab setup. They don't tell us how often it would succeed in other topologies, and we did not achieve code execution.

How to detect exploitation attempts

Start with MongoDB's structured server logs. In our vulnerable run, each planted request appeared as a COMMAND “Slow query” event (ID 51803). The useful fields were:

attr.command.ping

attr.command.readConcern.afterOpTime

attr.command.maxTimeMS

attr.errName (MaxTimeMSExpired)

attr.durationMillis

attr.remote

Look for an unauthenticated command with unusual operation-time values and an expired wait.

Also check the logs for the sequence that preceded a crash: a member enters primary catch-up (ID 21359), exits catch-up twice (ID 21363) in one transition, and then logs a fatal signal or backtrace involving CatchupState::abort_inlock(). A normal election or a single catch-up exit does not identify this CVE. The requests may arrive before the failover. Review earlier logs from the same member, not just events around the crash.

Whether these request fields appear in the logs depends on your logging settings. MongoDB documents that client operations enter the diagnostic log when they exceed the slow-operation threshold or when command verbosity is at least one. Check whether your logs retain the command object. Slow-operation sampling or a log pipeline may drop it. The attr.remote field may contain a loopback address rather than the original client IP.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Cloud Security Management reports findings for CVE-2026-118383. Check the vulnerability findings for affected hosts and container images.

Datadog Cloud Security Management also flags security groups that allow inbound MongoDB access from the internet, through the rule Inbound MongoDB access should be restricted. Use it to find exposed replica set members to patch first. Datadog Cloud SIEM detections for CVE-2026-118383 are currently being evaluated, and we will update this post when they are available.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-118383 affects MongoDB replica set members when a newly elected primary finishes catch-up. We reproduced a crash after two unauthenticated requests left abandoned waiters. The patched release rejected those requests. The vendor also identifies arbitrary code execution as a possible impact under certain conditions; our tests did not demonstrate it. Upgrade every affected member to a fixed release, verify the running versions, and investigate unusual readConcern.afterOpTime requests alongside catch-up and crash events.

890ee50f8873.text:
Sophos researchers are investigating an active campaign of malicious activity involving unauthorized ScreenConnect client deployments. ConnectWise released an advisory confirming the incident and is investigating multiple third-party extensions possibly linked to the activity. The advisory recommends disabling the identified extensions as a precautionary measure.

In one case observed by Sophos researchers, curl.exe downloaded ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi from 185[.]99[.]255[.]28 to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi. A ScreenConnect-generated command file then launched msiexec.exe to install the client silently. The researchers also observed ScreenConnect scripts staging batch files and using PowerShell with execution-policy bypass to retrieve a second-stage script from ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4.

The observed malicious activity has originated from three ScreenConnect instance IDs: d905b2b1b165d0a9, 4b8f4089ddaac6a9, and df1f7ef0cfacd0d8. These are likely compromised instances that are being used to execute commands and deploy the malicious instances. The IDs of those malicious instances are 2588ef5c15954b10 and ed630cc2c873b091.

Recommended actions

Organizations using ScreenConnect should follow the advice in the ConnectWise advisory. To identify malicious activity, review ScreenConnect command history for unexpected client deployments or remote commands. Usage of curl and PowerShell activity that downloads ScreenConnect installers or scripts from Windows Temp, followed by msiexec.exe installation, should also be investigated.

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs is investigating the applicability of existing countermeasures and the feasibility of developing additional countermeasures to detect activity associated with this threat. Activity is being reviewed across customer environments and will be escalated where identified.

0f0519b4a9d3.text: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register: “Maybe we should just go home.” “Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us. Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one. “It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review. “An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.” Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon. Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants are undoubtedly already scanning for vulnerable versions and reverse engineering the patch for their own attack purposes. So prioritize this fix, and keep an eye on your inbox for any suspicious files. Back-to-back months of 1K+ CVEs Despite the second month of more than 1,000 CVEs (October had 1,474), CVE-2026-124194 is the only one under active exploitation, and none of the 1,094 are listed as publicly known. Childs says this shouldn’t give organizations “false comfort.” “Logging back-to-back months above 1,000 CVEs proves automated bug-hunting has permanently reset patch volume,” he told The Register. “With AI making patch-diffing and exploit generation near-instant, the threat window opens the minute these updates drop.” For defenders, this means two things, Childs added. “What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action: patch Exchange and Domain Controllers (LDAP/Kerberos) first to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on your cloud services,” he said. Zero-click threats There are two zero-click threats in this month’s batch of fixes: CVE-2026-116928 and CVE-2026-119958. Both are critical, carrying 9.8 CVSS ratings, in part because they don’t require any user interaction to exploit. CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component that could lead to remote code execution. An unauthenticated attacker could abuse this search feature in Exchange “by sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment,” Redmond warned. “Exchange automatically processes the attachment for indexing, so the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute code with the permissions of the affected processing service.” CVE-2026-119958 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Windows' implementation of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely without user interaction. This one can be exploited by sending specially crafted LDAP requests to vulnerable systems, potentially compromising domain controllers. Childs also counts 30 CVEs that pose a “wormable risk,” requiring zero authentication and zero user interaction over a network. All of those are listed in his blog, so prioritize fixing those as well. And…Xbox remote code execution And finally, for funsies, a critical flaw in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service, CVE-2026-112967, that could allow remote code execution also made this month's roundup. It's a heap-overflow vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS rating that doesn't require authentication or user interaction to exploit. So don't take a gaming break between testing November's updates. Or, if you do, at least make sure vulnerable Windows systems running the Xbox Live Networking Service are on your patching list, too. ®

03c98e1134e4.text: Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four. Whatever the nature of the bug, Kumar asserts it was “a custom script run only on an isolated ceremony host and was not a function of the emCA software.” eMudhra needed that script because “global supply chain constraints” meant it couldn’t acquire the hardware security modules (HSMs), devices that generate and store cryptographic keys, that it wanted to use when creating a set of certificates for use in the USA. It therefore used HSMs made by a company called Utimaco to generate keys and planned to transfer the keys it produced to a different set of HSMs from a company called Crypto4A. Kumar explained that eMudhra decided on that move, which is unusual, because changes to policy about provenance of certificates meant it had to generate new certs by the end of May. The plan went sour when the company didn’t notice the errors in its script and didn’t test the keys it created. The rest is history: a Mozilla team member noticed that the company’s keys were woefully weak and pointed out that attackers could therefore issue fraudulent certificates that allowed them to impersonate servers, observe traffic, or even modify data in transit. Browser-makers quickly tweaked their software so it would not recognize certs from eMudhra. The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment. Kumar’s new post lists three steps eMudhra will take to wind up its certification business, one of which will see the company “Put in place improvements motivated by findings of [an] independent review to strengthen our general PKI operations.” Sounds like a plan. ®

CMMC: Understanding the Difference Between a POA&M and an OPA

November 10, 2026

Jason Spencer

BLOG

5 min.

Understanding the difference between a Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M) and an Operational Plan of Action (OPA) starts with recognizing that these two documents serve different purposes under 32 CFR Part 170 (the CMMC Program).

TL;DR – LA Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M) and an Operational Plan of Action (OPA) serve fundamentally different purposes under CMMC and confusing the two is one of the fastest ways to stall your certification.

A POA&M is tied to a C3PAO assessment finding, carries a 180-day closure deadline and directly impacts certification

An OPA tracks temporary vulnerabilities found during normal operations with no fixed timeline or certification consequence

Most compliance failures come from documentation mistakes, not security gaps

The Key Attributes of a POA&M and OPA

A POA&M is a formal remediation plan created in response to a C3PAO assessment finding where a security requirement is marked “Not Met”. It carries a strict 180-day closure deadline and directly impacts CMMC certification. An OPA, by contrast, tracks temporary vulnerabilities discovered during normal operations and carries no fixed deadline or certification consequence.

The following table provides a side-by-side comparison of the key attributes that distinguish these two documents.

Attribute

POA&M (Plan of Action & Milestones)

OPA (Operational Plan of Action)

Purpose

Documents NOT MET security requirements found during a CMMC assessment; tracks remediation to full compliance

Documents ongoing operational security activities, continuous improvement and risk management

Time-Bound

Yes — strict 180-day remediation deadline

No — ongoing with no fixed deadline

Trigger

Created when a practice is scored NOT MET during a C3PAO assessment

Created proactively as part of ongoing security operations

Certification Impact

Allows conditional CMMC Level 2 certification

Cannot cover or paper over a NOT MET requirement

Eligible Practices

Only 1-point practices (up to 22 maximum)

Applies broadly to operational improvements and enhancements

Score Threshold

Must score 80% or higher (88/110 practices MET)

No scoring threshold — exists independently of assessment

Close-Out

Formal close-out assessment by C3PAO within 180 days

Reviewed and updated as part of continuous monitoring; no formal close-out

Failure Consequence

Loses conditional certification if not remediated within 180 days

No direct certification consequence; may become findings in future assessments

Nature

Reactive — addresses deficiencies found during assessment

Proactive — addresses planned improvements and ongoing risk management

What Must a POA&M and an OPA Include to Pass a CMMC Assessment?

Knowing the difference between a POA&M and an OPA is only the first step. Organizations must also understand what each document needs to contain to satisfy assessor expectations and regulatory requirements. A strong POA&M goes beyond acknowledging a gap. It must include defined remediation steps, responsible parties, resource and budget requirements, milestones with specific dates and a firm 180-day closure commitment. A strong OPA must clearly identify the temporary vulnerability, describe the mitigation or correction plan, outline the current risk posture and explain the monitoring approach.

The table below breaks down the required content elements for each document type.

Strong POA&M Must Include

Strong OPA Must Include

Clear explanation of what is missing and why

Defined remediation steps with responsible parties

Resource requirements and budget implications

Milestones with specific completion dates

Evidence of active progress toward closure

180-day closure deadline commitment

Identification of the temporary vulnerability or deficiency

Explanation of how it will be mitigated, corrected or eliminated

Current risk posture description

Monitoring and tracking approach

No fixed deadline required - duration depends on circumstances

8 of the Most Common POA&M and OPA Mistakes Under CMMC

Even organizations with mature security programs frequently stumble when preparing POA&Ms and OPAs for CMMC compliance. These mistakes range from treating routine vulnerabilities as OPA items (when standard vulnerability management processes under RA.L2-3.11.3 and SI.L1-3.14.1 should apply) to submitting vague timelines that assessors will immediately flag. Other common errors include omitting required mitigation details from OPAs, resubmitting pre-CMMC implementation plans as POA&Ms, assuming compliance without completing a gap assessment or collecting actual evidence, making CUI scoping errors, practices not eligible for the POA&M and preparing for the wrong assessment criteria entirely.

The table below outlines eight of the most frequent mistakes and explains why each one matters.

#

Mistake

Why It Matters

1

Treating routine vulnerabilities as OPA items

Not every vulnerability warrants an OPA. Use standard vulnerability management (RA.L2-3.11.3 / SI.L1-3.14.1) instead.

2

Using vague timelines in POA&Ms

Assessors expect specific dates, resources and checkpoints - not general language.

3

Leaving mitigation details out of the OPA

CA.L2-3.12.2 requires documenting how deficiencies will be mitigated, corrected or eliminated.

4

Resubmitting the NIST SP 800-171 implementation POA&M

A pre-CMMC project plan is not a POA&M for assessment findings; these are distinct documents.

5

Assumed compliance without evidence

Organizations often assume compliance without completing a gap assessment or actual evidence collection.

6

CUI scoping errors

Organizations fail to understand FCI and/or CUI contracts and flows in their environment.

7

Preparing for the wrong assessment criteria

Failing to identify FCI for Level 1 or CUI for Level 2 compliance.

8

Practices not eligible for POA&M inclusion

Not POA&M eligible practices and objectives will lead to failure self-assessment and C3PAO assessment.

How Can Organizations Avoid POA&M and OPA Failures During CMMC Certification?

Knowing what belongs in a POA&M versus an OPA is the first step. Building them with the specificity, evidence and structure that will hold up under a C3PAO assessment is the harder one. GuidePoint Security CMMC Readiness Assessment and Advisory Services can help your organizations at every stage of the CMMC journey, from scoping and gap assessments through documentation, remediation and assessment readiness. Organizations that go through the process walk into their assessment with clean documentation, defensible evidence and a clear understanding of where they stand.

FAQs

What happens if a POA&M is not closed within 180 days?

The organization loses its conditional CMMC certification status. The C3PAO must verify closure before final certification is granted. There is no extension process.

When should an organization use an OPA instead of standard vulnerability management?

An OPA applies when a temporary deficiency falls outside routine patching or scanning cycles. Standard vulnerability management under RA.L2-3.11.3 handles known, recurring issues. Use an OPA for gaps that need a documented mitigation plan.

Why do organizations fail POA&M reviews during CMMC assessments?

Most failures stem from documentation gaps, not security gaps. Organizations submit vague timelines, omit mitigation details or reuse pre-CMMC implementation plans. Assessors expect specific dates, responsible parties and evidence of progress.

Do subcontractors need their own POA&M for CMMC?

Yes. Each organization seeking CMMC certification must maintain its own POA&M. Subcontractors cannot rely on a prime contractor’s documentation.

What happens if a vulnerability is found after a CMMC assessment?

Post-assessment vulnerabilities are tracked through an OPA, not a POA&M. The OPA documents the issue and mitigation plan without triggering a new assessment cycle.

Managed Security Services can give security teams greater visibility and access to specialized expertise, but finding a threat is only one part of incident response. Once an alert becomes an incident, the operating model between an internal security team and its managed security service provider (MSSP) becomes critical.

During an active incident, several actions may need to happen quickly: validate the threat, determine its scope, isolate an endpoint, disable an account, block malicious traffic, preserve evidence, engage IT teams, and escalate to business leadership. Each action can cross organizational boundaries and require a different level of authority.

That creates an operational seam. The MSSP may have the evidence and expertise to recommend an action, while the internal team has the business context, system access, and authority to approve or execute it. Organizations that define how that seam works before an incident can move from investigation to response with fewer delays and less ambiguity. Many MSSP relationships define what the provider monitors but not who is allowed to act. That gap rarely surfaces in a service review; it surfaces during an incident, often after hours, when a containment decision is waiting on an approver nobody can reach.

As Forrester notes in their recent report, Best Practices For MDR To-IR Handoffs, "During an incident, what organizations often miss are the processes they assume are a given and will happen as a matter of course, like handoffs between providers." The challenge is the transition from threat detection to coordinated action across multiple teams and stakeholders.

Where the MSSP handoff gets complicated and an incident is declared

Consider a compromised employee account. An MSSP might identify suspicious authentication activity, correlate it with other telemetry, investigate the behavior, and determine that the account is likely compromised. The logical containment step may be to disable the account or revoke active sessions.

Taking that action introduces considerations beyond threat detection. The account could belong to an executive, administrator, service owner, or employee supporting a time-sensitive business process. The response may require coordination with identity teams, the user’s manager, IT operations, or other stakeholders.

The same challenge applies to isolating endpoints, blocking network traffic, taking servers offline, or restricting access to critical applications. Technical urgency and business impact have to be considered together.

Here is how that can play out in practice. It is 2:00 a.m. on a Saturday. The MSSP confirms the compromise and recommends revoking the user’s sessions, but the agreed process requires customer approval before acting on executive accounts. The primary contact does not answer. The backup contact changed roles months ago. By the time someone with authority approves the action, the attacker has had hours to register a new MFA device and create mail-forwarding rules. Each team did its job; the gap was in the operating model between them.

This is where the relationship between internal teams and MSSPs needs to be operationally specific. Service scope should translate into a shared understanding of what the provider investigates, what it can act on independently, which actions require customer authorization, and how responsibility changes as an incident becomes more severe.

Those expectations should also extend beyond normal business hours. A response model that depends on reaching one specific internal contact can create a bottleneck during nights, weekends, or holidays. Organizations need primary and backup contacts, defined escalation thresholds, and predetermined rules for situations where an authorized decision-maker cannot immediately be reached.

The handoff also changes character at a specific point: when someone declares an incident. Before that point, the MSSP is triaging and escalating alerts. After it, the organization’s incident response plan takes over, an incident commander assumes coordination, often under external counsel, and obligations such as evidence preservation, regulatory notification timelines, and cyber insurance reporting may begin. The escalation framework should name who can make that declaration, what criteria trigger it, and how the MSSP’s role shifts once it is made.

Forrester warns that "Misaligned handoff protocols between MDR and IR providers lead to conflicting direction, inconsistent situational context, and slowed decision-making during the most time-critical phases of an incident."

For high-severity scenarios such as ransomware or confirmed data exfiltration, the response often extends well beyond the internal team and the MSSP. Breach counsel may be engaged early, the cyber insurer may require an approved incident response firm , and dedicated forensics teams may take over scoping. In many cases, these stakeholders are brought together only after a major incident occurs, making it critical to define expectations in advance around roles, decision authority, evidence sharing, communications, and reporting requirements.

Define four types of ownership

A practical escalation framework can start by assigning four types of ownership: investigation, containment, communication, and decision-making.

Investigation ownership establishes how far the MSSP should take an investigation before escalating it. Internal teams should know what information will arrive with that escalation, including affected assets and identities, indicators of compromise, investigation steps, severity, supporting evidence, and recommended actions. A consistent evidence package allows the internal team to build on the provider’s work rather than retracing it. Investigation should also account for a common transition during major incidents: the handoff from the MSSP’s security operations center (SOC) team to a digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) team. With many providers, that escalation involves a third party, which can introduce delays while contracts are activated, accounts are provisioned, access to data is established, and new investigators are brought up to speed. Organizations should define in advance how that transition occurs, what information is transferred, and who maintains continuity throughout the investigation. Providers with integrated MSSP and DFIR capabilities can help reduce additional friction during this phase of the response.

Containment ownership defines who has authority to disrupt potentially malicious activity. Organizations should document who can isolate an endpoint, disable an account, block infrastructure, quarantine messages, restrict network access, or take a system offline. Some organizations may authorize their managed security service provider to perform predetermined actions under defined conditions, while others may require internal approval. The important consideration is that both parties understand the boundaries and the process for exceptions. Containment ownership should also account for evidence: reimaging a system or deleting malicious artifacts too quickly can destroy the forensic data needed to understand scope. Ownership should extend beyond initial containment into recovery activities, including heightened monitoring, validation that the threat actor has been removed, and decisions about when systems can safely return to production. Unclear communication between internal teams, the MSSP, and third-party responders during this phase can create new risks, such as restoring access too soon or unnecessarily extending operational disruptions.

Communication ownership connects the security response with the rest of the organization. IT operations may need to rebuild devices. Identity teams may need to revoke credentials. Application owners can provide context about affected systems. Legal, privacy, communications, and executive teams may need to participate as severity increases. The escalation framework should identify who engages these stakeholders, through which channels, and at what point in the response.

Decision ownership becomes increasingly important as potential business impact grows. The team performing technical analysis may recommend containment, while an incident commander or business leader holds authority to approve an action with significant operational consequences. Severity levels should therefore map to specific decision-makers, including alternates when the primary owner is unavailable.

Clearly separating these responsibilities helps an organization use managed cybersecurity services as part of a broader incident response model rather than treating the provider relationship as an isolated security function.

Build escalation paths around scenarios

A useful escalation plan needs more than a contact list. It should map realistic incident scenarios to specific responsibilities, authority, communication channels, and expected response times.

For common scenarios such as compromised credentials, ransomware, cloud account abuse, suspected data exfiltration, or malware on a critical server, teams can document:

Trigger: What evidence or severity initiates escalation?

Investigator: Who validates the activity and determines scope?

Decision-maker: Who has authority to approve containment?

Executor: Who performs the technical action?

Communicator: Who coordinates with IT and other stakeholders?

Fallback: Who assumes responsibility if the primary contact is unavailable?

Time threshold: How long should the process wait for a decision before moving to the next escalation point?

The framework should be documented in incident response plans and playbooks, then be tested through tabletop exercises and operational reviews. Exercises can reveal outdated contact information, unclear approval authority, after-hours communication gaps, or technical actions that cannot be executed as expected. Real incidents can provide another feedback loop. If responders repeatedly lose time identifying an application owner or securing approval for containment, that friction points to a process that needs refinement.

This approach also acknowledges that the handoff is rarely a single moment. Investigation, containment, recovery, and communication may pass between an MSSP, the internal security team, IT, and business stakeholders several times over the course of one incident.

The larger challenge is not simply transferring responsibility from an MSSP to a customer. It is transitioning from a technical finding to the business decisions that follow. An MSSP may identify a compromised account, active ransomware, or suspected data exfiltration, but decisions about containment, recovery, communications, legal obligations, and operational risk ultimately belong to the organization.

Effective managed cybersecurity services depend on those transitions being deliberate. By defining who investigates, who contains, who communicates, and who decides, organizations can connect external security expertise with internal authority and business context.

An incident should put an escalation plan into action, rather than expose where one was missing.

LevelBlue helps organizations define these responsibilities before an incident tests them, through incident response planning and tabletop exercises that pressure-test escalation paths with both internal teams and their security providers.

Source: Jess Burn, Jeff Pollard, Joseph Blankenship, Liam Holloway, and Michael Belden, "Best Practices for MDR-to-IR Handoffs," Forrester Research, March 13, 2026.

Contributions by Kenneth Ng, Director of Operational Intelligence at LevelBlue.

IBM Consulting and Microsoft have combined their technologies and expertise with forward-deployed engineering support for qualifying engagements to help enterprises accelerate AI deployment.

Imagine Enterprise aims to help organizations—especially in regulated industries—combine human expertise with AI agents and connect them to unique enterprise data and daily processes. The platform is built to help organizations govern AI agents with controls, observability, and AI-compliance support designed to help secure industry-specific AI deployment.

IBM Consulting brings AI transformation expertise and a fleet of more than 6,000 AI agents and assets built on IBM Consulting Advantage, the company’s AI-powered delivery platform. Microsoft provides the AI, data, cloud, and security foundation that is designed to help the agents operate securely across the enterprise, while forward-deployed engineers from both companies can help customers move from experimentation to production.

Instead of organizations having to start from scratch, replace the platforms they already depend on, or spend months assembling the pieces themselves, Imagine Enterprise is designed around three simple advantages:

Instant Expertise: More than 6,000 AI agents and assets Starting with pre-built AI agents, assets, and deep industry expertise from day one. Organizations can begin with capabilities already built for their industry and adapt them to the unique needs of their business.

Fits the Enterprise: A platform that adapts Imagine Enterprise is designed to connect with an organization’s existing data, processes, systems, and technology environment. Enterprises can start where they are, build on what they already have, and scale over time, with enterprise security, identity, AI governance, and control built into the experience.

Intelligence Multiplier: Puts the knowledge of the business behind people and AI agents Imagine Enterprise brings IBM Consulting’s hands-on experience building and running more than 6,000 AI agents together with the Microsoft technologies to connect enterprise knowledge, data, and context across the organization. People and agents can operate with richer enterprise knowledge and context behind them, helping put what they already know to work across people and agents.

Supporting these advantages, Microsoft and GitHub technologies including Microsoft Foundry, GitHub Copilot, and Microsoft Copilot Studio help coordinate AI agents and enterprise systems, while Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft 365 infrastructure, Microsoft Entra, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Defender, and Microsoft Azure provide the data, identity, AI governance, security, and cloud foundation. IBM Consulting Advantage’s Process Studio, Context Studio, and Advantage Core help organizations design, deploy, and govern tailored AI agents.

From Emerging Technology to Business Opportunity

SEI, a leading global provider of financial technology, operations, and asset management services within the financial services industry, is looking to advance its enterprise transformation by exploring emerging and agentic technologies with IBM Consulting, with the support of Microsoft, and is leveraging other technologies from IBM Consulting and Microsoft to help improve how the company operates and enhance the experiences it delivers to employees and clients, supporting SEI’s commitment to sustainable growth.

“AI is evolving quickly, and our focus at SEI is on applying it with intention in ways that strengthen trust, enhance human decision-making, and create meaningful value across our business,” said Sneha Shah, Chief AI Strategist and Head of SEI Next. “Our work with IBM Consulting and Microsoft is helping us explore how emerging capabilities could support critical processes and be responsibly scaled over time, with the goal to create better experiences for our employees and clients. By combining emerging technology with SEI’s deep industry and operational expertise, we can move faster, scale more effectively, and create new opportunities for growth.”

“Clients are no longer looking for AI that simply helps people do the same work a little faster. They want to build an agentic business,” said Mohamad Ali, Senior Vice President and Head of IBM Consulting. “Microsoft and IBM are helping organizations bring human expertise and digital labor together in a way that can scale across the enterprise, to turn AI from a productivity aid into a real competitive advantage.” “Enterprise AI will be won by organizations that can turn their data, industry expertise, and AI into action,” said Rodrigo Kede Lima, President, Microsoft Frontier Company. “Together, Microsoft and IBM Consulting are bringing the best of our technology and expertise, to help customers move from AI ambition to business impact faster and with confidence.”

Imagine Enterprise’s industry-specific frameworks initially include financial services, insurance, and retail, and are designed to establish a repeatable blueprint for potential additional industries such as manufacturing, energy, public sector, mobility and more in the future.

Imagine Enterprise is available to clients by engaging IBM Consulting to deploy and operate the platform on the client’s behalf or co-innovating with IBM Consulting on enterprise-scale implementations. Self-management options are also available.

To learn more, visit: https://www.ibm.com/consulting/imagine-enterprise, or read the blog here.
