Who Checked the AI Agent’s ID at the Front Door?

November 9, 2026

Kevin Converse

BLOG

5 min.

I’ve worked with several security teams who were confident they knew how many agents were running in their environment. That confidence didn’t survive the assessment. What we uncovered were hundreds of agents operating on inherited authority, cached credentials, shared service accounts and user sessions that were never designed to be reused by autonomous systems. No one had authorized them. No one owned them. And no one knew the full scope of what they could do.

TL;DR – The cybersecurity industry is treating AI agent security as a permissions problem. It’s a delegation problem. The organizations scaling AI with confidence are the ones building trust chains now, not waiting for the standards to arrive.

Delegation, not permissions, is the gap. Agents don’t just access resources. They inherit authority no one explicitly granted.

Adoption is outpacing governance: most organizations can deploy agents fast, but few have lifecycle controls to match.

The first move is a registry, not a product: identify every agent, assign a human sponsor and define its purpose before buying anything.

Why AI Agent Security Is a Delegation Problem

The cybersecurity industry has spent the last year asking the wrong question about AI agents. Most have been focused on what agents can access, what permissions they hold and how to revoke them. Those are valid concerns, but they only scratch the surface. The deeper question is about delegation: who authorized this agent to act, on whose behalf, under what conditions and what happens when the chain of trust breaks.

Every Agent Represents a Trust Chain

When an employee delegates a task to an AI agent, a chain of trust forms.

The employee trusts the agent to act within certain boundaries

The organization trusts the employee to delegate responsibility

The systems the agent touches trust the credentials the agent presents

Each link in that chain carries an assumption about what the agent is authorized to do and in most organizations today, none of those assumptions have been formally defined.

This is what separates agentic AI from every previous identity challenge. Cloud identities, service accounts and workload identities all involve access. Agents involve authority. An agent doesn’t need permission to read a database; it needs authority to decide what to do with what it reads and then execute that decision across multiple systems before a human reviews the output.

This should raise major red flags for security experts. Privileged access management, role-based access control and service account governance all involve some form of delegated authority. For AI agents, that delegation is happening dynamically, at machine speed and without human knowledge that authority has been extended at all.

Six Problems Security Leaders Are Reporting

In the study Managing Agentic AI Through the Identity Control Plane: What Organizations Should Look For, conducted by IDC and sponsored by GuidePoint Security, panelists across industries described six interconnected problems in their own words:

Problem 1: “I cannot see or count my agents”

Problem 2: “Agents are breaking my identity tooling”

Problem 3: “Privilege is sprawling at machine speed”

Problem 4: “I can no longer trust the human signal”

Problem 5: “Governance and ownership are lagging adoption”

Problem 6: “There is a risk I do not control”

These remarks reveal something important about the nature of the risk. Identity tooling built for human lifecycles, where HR provides the join and leave signals, doesn’t apply to entities that never walk out the door. And when AI-generated impersonation can fake the human approval that the entire sponsor model depends on, the trust architecture has a gap before it even starts.

Why Maturity Assessments Miss the Real Gap

44% of organizations rank non-human identity and AI agent security as their top IAM priority over the next 12 to 24 months. But priority and readiness are not the same thing.

Across these six problems, the panel converged on one consensus: every agent needs a named human sponsor and managed lifecycle. That lifecycle includes gated intake, an approved purpose, scoped access, expiration and recertification and a clean revocation path.

However, adoption is outpacing governance and internally many organizations are struggling to communicate the issue. Managers closer to the problem report bigger gaps than directors, VPs and C-suite. The implication in this is that maturity decisions about where to invest and what to prioritize need to be informed by practitioners who have their hands on keyboards, not shaped exclusively by leadership’s more optimistic view.

What Organizations Can Do to Address the Gap

No single vendor is covering every part of the governance gap. The market is maturing quickly, but the best choice today is the one that closes the highest-priority gaps and can be operationally sustained by the team. Three steps to start:

1. Build an Authoritative Inventory

Not a one-time discovery sweep, but a registry. Every agent in the environment needs to be identified, bound to a named owner and assessed against a defined purpose.

2. Separate the Registry Decision From the Runtime Decision

Knowing who the agent is, its sponsor, its purpose and what it is allowed to touch can start now. How each agent proves its identity cryptographically at runtime, where emerging standards for workload identity such as SPIFFE and SPIRE are still maturing, is a decision that can wait for the market to settle.

3. Align Controls With Emerging Frameworks

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), the EU AI Act and the OWASP Non-Human Identity Top 10 all provide structure for building governance around this new identity class. Prioritize the agents with the most critical access first.

Start With Discovery, Not Standards

The industry will build the standards, protocols and tooling to manage delegation at machine speed. What it will not do is go back and redesign the trust chains that were never built in the first place. The organizations that start now, with discovery, ownership and lifecycle governance, will be the ones that scale AI with confidence.

GuidePoint Security Agentic AI Security Services are designed to help you with visibility, ownership mapping and a prioritized roadmap. We meet your organization wherever you are on the maturity curve with a vendor-objective approach, supporting your team in matching programs to your environment and risk profile.

For more details and insights on Agentic AI as the Identity Control Plane

Read our whitepaper: Managing Agentic AI Through the Identity Control Plane: What Organizations Should Look For

Watch our on-demand webinar: Securing Agentic AI at Scale

FAQs

What happens when an AI agent's trust chain breaks?

The agent continues operating with authority no one is monitoring. Without a revocation path tied to a human sponsor, compromised agents can move laterally across systems undetected.

How is AI agent delegation different from service account access?

Service accounts authenticate to a single system with static credentials. AI agents inherit authority from a human sponsor and make autonomous decisions across multiple systems at machine speed.

What risks do organizations face without an AI agent registry?

Unregistered agents accumulate privileges no one audits. When a breach occurs, security teams cannot scope the blast radius because they have no inventory of what agents exist or what they can reach.

Who should own AI agent governance inside an organization?

Identity and security teams share responsibility, but every agent needs a named human sponsor accountable for its purpose, scope and lifecycle. Without clear ownership, governance gaps compound as agent counts grow.

How do SPIFFE and SPIRE apply to AI agent identity?

SPIFFE provides a standard for issuing cryptographic identities to workloads and SPIRE is its runtime implementation. These standards are still maturing but will eventually let agents prove identity at runtime without shared credentials.

Introducing the GuidePoint Security Partner Portal

November 6, 2026

Mark Thornberry

BLOG

5 min.

Partnerships are a core part of how GuidePoint serves customers. Our partners give us a direct view of what customers need, where the market is moving and which technologies can create meaningful value. As GuidePoint enters its next stage of growth, we want to make it easier for partners to work with us at the pace our customers expect.

"The best partnerships are built on access: to the right people, the right information and a shared view of where customers are headed. The Partner Portal gives our partners that access in one place, so together we can move faster and bring the right capabilities to the customers we serve."

— Mark Thornberry, Chief Business Officer, GuidePoint Security

The GuidePoint Partner Portal is part of that investment. It gives partners better ways to engage with teams across the company, understand our capabilities and build on opportunities to support shared customers.

We designed the portal around your feedback. Here’s what it means for your team.

Navigate at Scale

Our regional model puts local expertise and customer relationships at the center of how we do business. Each of our eight regions brings knowledge of its market and the customers we serve together.

Vendor partners have asked for an easier way to navigate that model as their business with GuidePoint grows. The portal helps you find the right resources, the first time, across the entire organization, giving your team the information it needs to connect beyond the relationships you already have.

See How Our Services and Your Technology Align

You may know GuidePoint through a particular customer engagement, technology partnership or regional relationship. The portal helps you see the broader range of our cybersecurity services and how we position technology within those areas.

That context can help your team better understand where your solutions fit, align with how GuidePoint supports customers and identify ways to bring more value to the customers we serve together. When we understand each other’s strengths, we can develop an opportunity, prove it works and scale it together.

Stay Connected

Knowing what’s happening across GuidePoint makes it easier to plan your involvement.

The portal brings many programs and activities into one actively updated calendar. Your team can look ahead at events in the markets you support and more easily identify opportunities to spend time with our teams.

Vendor all-hands recordings will live here too, so colleagues who couldn’t attend can catch up and stay informed.

Find Marketing and Event Resources

Looking for GuidePoint’s brand or marketing guidelines, logos or media kit? The portal brings these resources together in one place, along with lead follow-up best practices for GuidePoint events. You’ll also find thought leadership resources that showcase our work and the cybersecurity challenges we’re helping customers solve.

Built for You, Managed by Us

Our team manages the portal and keeps its resources current, so there’s nothing for you to upload, update or maintain. That’s intentional. We want the portal to save your team time and we’ll keep adding resources as our work together grows.

Get Started

The portal is now available for all vendor partners who hold an active reseller agreement with GuidePoint Security. Eligible vendor partners have received an email invitation with instructions for setting up an account.

If you’re interested in becoming a GuidePoint Security vendor partner, connect with our Vendor Relationship Management team to learn more.

Thank you to the partners whose feedback helped shape this resource. We look forward to building on it as our partnerships grow!

Post-Quantum Cryptography Part 2: 2030 Is Not the Deadline

November 5, 2026

Timothy Amerson

BLOG

5 min.

TL;DR – GAO’s latest report shows why waiting for the compliance deadline could mean arriving years too late.

In Part 1, Post-Quantum Cryptography: Migrate by Risk, Not by Checkbox, I argued that post-quantum cryptography (PQC) cannot be treated as a compliance exercise. The Government Accountability Office’s (GAO) October 2026 report, GAO-27-108740, shows why: none of the 24 Chief Financial Officers (CFO) Act agencies fully addressed cryptographic inventory, funding assessment or testing and not one had tested PQC.

The audit ran February 2024 through September 2025, before Executive Order (EO) 14412 and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Memorandum M-26-15 accelerated the migration – so this is the baseline the Federal Government carried into the accelerated period. In GAO’s words, the gaps “increase the risk that their transitions to quantum-resistant cryptography will occur too late.” That makes the real deadline much closer than 2030.

GAO Put Numbers Behind the Problem

In Part 1, I wrote that when an organization cannot see its cryptography, the inventory gap is not a footnote – it is the program. GAO’s report, Quantum Computing: Federal Actions Needed to Prepare for Emerging Cyber Threat, puts numbers behind that point: only one of 24 agencies fully addressed the prioritized-inventory activities, 18 reported lacking cryptography expertise with no plan to close the gap, 23 had no documented inventory maintenance process, none fully addressed funding and none had tested PQC in their environment.

Figure 1. How the 24 CFO Act agencies scored against GAO's three preparatory practices. Source: GAO-27-108740.

These are not simply compliance findings. They are indicators of execution risk. If I cannot see quantum-vulnerable cryptography, I cannot prioritize it; if I cannot prioritize it, I cannot budget it; if I have not tested the replacement, I do not know what will break.

What Did Waiting Look Like?

The part of the report I keep rereading is not the scorecard. It is the explanations agencies gave, in good faith, for why each practice could wait a little longer: too early for automated tools or waiting on the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to name them (CISA says it never asked anyone to wait); too early to test (open-source PQC tooling has existed for years); too early to document funding without vendor pricing – which is how the Government arrived at an approximate $7.1 billion estimate OMB itself calls a rough order of magnitude.

Figure 2. The reasons agencies gave GAO for deferring action and GAO's response to each. Source: GAO-27-108740, pp. 26-33.

None of these reasons is unreasonable on its own. Together they form a dependency chain: no automation, so no inventory; no inventory, so no funding estimate; no testing, so no idea what breaks. Every year spent waiting for a better tool or a vendor quote is a year subtracted from the migration clock – the one clock agencies actually control.

Waiting for certainty is a decision. It just is not a documented one.

2030 Is a Compliance Line, Not a Risk Line

One concern I continue to have is that the December 31, 2030 deadline creates a false sense of time.

Executive Order 14412, Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks, requires Federal High Value Assets (HVAs) and high-impact systems to use PQC for key establishment by December 31, 2030 and for digital signatures by December 31, 2031. OMB Memorandum M-26-15, Execution of the Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography, implements that direction for civilian agencies in five phases, from discovery in 2026-2027 through full migration by 2035 – and frames 2030 as mitigating as much quantum risk as feasible by that date, not starting then. EO 14306 adds Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 by January 2, 2030.

The nearest milestones have already arrived: a named PQC migration lead within 30 days of EO 14412 and a PQC Migration Plan to OMB and the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD) within 120 days of the June 24, 2026 memorandum.

That date is October 22, 2026. The planning clock is not approaching. It is already running.

Figure 3. The three PQC clocks: the compliance clock set by policy, the migration clock each agency controls and the data confidentiality clock that neither policy nor the agency can reset.

But Even October 22 Is Not the Real Security Deadline

Compliance gives us dates. Risk gives us a different clock. The question is not when will a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) arrive, but how long does our information need to remain protected?

An adversary does not need a CRQC today to create a future compromise. They only need to collect the encrypted data today. That is the harvest-now, decrypt-later problem; EO 14412 names it in its first paragraph and GAO makes it concrete, citing collection techniques already in use, from Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) rerouting to supply-chain compromise. Two further GAO points belong in every briefing:

Detection will not save you. Using a CRQC to derive a private key from a public key “is not an event that can be detected by the victim organization’s cybersecurity tools.”

The exposure is in transit and in key establishment. Data at rest is generally protected by symmetric cryptography, which is not currently projected to be vulnerable. The harvestable risk sits in public-key exchanges – exactly why key establishment carries the 2030 gate.

Migrating a system in 2030 does not recall data an adversary collected in 2026. That changes the deadline.

The Deadline Is Driven by the Data

The concept is captured well by what is often called Mosca’s inequality, from Michele Mosca’s 2015 paper:

Data confidentiality lifetime + migration time > time until a CRQC = the organization is already at risk.

The migration itself takes years and the estimate keeps moving: the Global Risk Institute’s Quantum Threat Timeline Report 2025 puts the probability of a CRQC at 28-49 percent within 10 years and 51-70 percent within 15, up from its prior survey.

We do not need the exact arrival date to manage the risk. We do not wait to learn the date of the next ransomware campaign before building resilience or which credential an adversary will steal before strengthening identity controls. PQC should be treated the same way.

Uncertainty is part of the risk calculation. It is not a reason to postpone it.

Long-Lived Data Changes the Priority

Two systems can use the same vulnerable algorithm and carry completely different quantum risk. Data that loses its sensitivity next year is a different priority than personnel, health, investigative, intellectual-property or national-security information that must stay confidential for 10, 20 or 30 years. M-26-15 already points this way, directing agencies to “prioritize identifying and re-encrypting long-lived sensitive data.” GAO adds a nuance: a CRQC recovers keys slowly – hours to more than 200 hours each – so the adversary’s prize is a long-lived, heavily reused key. Key lifetimes belong in the risk score alongside the algorithm.

A checkbox tells me the control exists. Risk tells me whether it will still work against the threat it is meant to stop.

Discovery Cannot Stay a Spreadsheet Exercise

One department told GAO its unclassified environment supports more than four million endpoints – and it had no plan yet for inventorying the cryptography inside them. M-26-15 calls manual approaches “often insufficient” and directs automated discovery into a central Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM); EO 14412 gives CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 270 days to publish minimum CBOM elements. Build toward that format now; do not wait for it.

The goal is not simply to complete an inventory. The goal is to create continuous cryptographic visibility.

Testing May Be the Bigger Warning

One GAO finding concerns me even more than inventory: none of the 24 agencies had tested PQC in their environments. ONCD called testing encouraged, not required; GAO’s view is that OMB never called it voluntary and that open-source tooling was enough to begin.

Whatever the policy reading, the engineering reality is the same. PQC migration is not swapping one algorithm for another: larger keys, new handshakes and new libraries ripple through every dependent system, including the legacy ones. Policy now bakes testing into the schedule – M-26-15’s Phase 2 pilots in 2027-2028 and NIST’s own pilot due December 31, 2027 – and NIST has published the standards and the transition path in NIST IR 8547.

"Waiting until the deadline to discover that a critical mission system cannot support the new cryptography is not migration planning. It is crisis management."

— Timothy Amerson, Federal Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), GuidePoint Security

The Point I Keep Coming Back To

Cybersecurity is the Art and Science of Maintaining Operations.

PQC may be the best test of that idea in years. There are two ways to fail. Move too slowly and information protected today may eventually become readable by an adversary. Move without discovery, engineering and testing and we disrupt the mission ourselves. That is why the answer cannot be “move everything immediately.” And it cannot be “we have until 2030.”

Discover. Prioritize. Test. Migrate. Sustain. In that order.

Five Steps to Start PQC Migration Now

If I were sitting with an agency leadership team today, these are the five actions I would put on the board:

Identify the data that must remain sensitive into the 2030s and beyond. That is your highest harvest-now, decrypt-later exposure.

Establish continuous cryptographic discovery. Build toward a living CBOM rather than periodic spreadsheets. Do not wait for a government-furnished tool.

Prioritize by mission risk, data longevity and migration complexity. An HVA designation matters, but it is not the only thing that matters.

Begin representative PQC testing now. Phase 2 pilots start in 2027; the test plan has to exist first.

Connect the migration plan to funding, acquisition and modernization. PQC is not solely a CISO program; M-26-15 names the Chief Financial Officer, program offices and system owners as accountable.

The Federal Government now has policy direction, standards and hard milestones. What agencies cannot afford is to read those milestones as permission to wait.

December 31, 2030 is a compliance deadline. It is not necessarily your risk deadline.

For long-lived sensitive data in transit today, the exposure window may already be open. By 2030, agencies should be measuring what they migrated – not discovering where their vulnerable cryptography lives.

The quantum clock is running. Do not let the calendar make the risk decision for you.

Ready to Start Your PQC Migration?

GuidePoint Security works with Federal agencies and mission partners to assess cryptographic exposure, prioritize systems by mission risk and data longevity and identify discovery, inventory and testing capabilities that fit the environment – without anchoring the strategy to a single vendor. If you cannot yet answer what cryptography you have, what data it protects, how long it must stay protected and what will break when you migrate it, that is where the work begins.

Read Part 1 for the five-phase roadmap, then reach out for a cryptographic exposure assessment.

FAQs

What is harvest now, decrypt later?

Adversaries collect encrypted data today and store it. When a quantum computer arrives, they decrypt it. Data with long confidentiality needs is most at risk.

What is Mosca's inequality?

Mosca’s inequality says data is at risk when its confidentiality lifetime plus migration time exceeds the time until a quantum computer arrives.

How do I start a PQC migration plan?

Begin with a cryptographic inventory using automated discovery tools. Prioritize systems by data longevity and mission risk, then run pilot tests before full migration.

What happens if agencies miss the 2030 PQC deadline?

Data encrypted with vulnerable algorithms stays exposed to harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks. The longer migration takes, the wider the window an adversary has to collect and eventually decrypt sensitive records.

What is a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM)?

A CBOM is a living inventory of all cryptographic assets across an organization. OMB M-26-15 directs agencies to build one using automated discovery rather than manual spreadsheets.

The Third-Party Integrator Risk: OT’s Most Overlooked Attack Surface

November 4, 2026

Austin Turecek

BLOG

5 min.

Industrial Control System (ICS) and operational technology (OT) networks have continued to grow and expand in substantial ways. The demand on the networks have increased as markets have grown, the convergence of IT and OT have changed how these networks look and heightened interest from threat actors have significantly altered the approach to security in these environments.

TL;DR – A third-party integrator can help scale OT environments, but without following best practices, they can also introduce new security risks.

Rapid OT expansion has created the need for third-party support to help manage OT device integration and evolution.

CISA and the FBI highlight the growing exposure risk presented by third-party integrators, which cannot be addressed by least privilege access alone.

By following recommended best practices, including clear documentation, external-facing device reviews, remote access logging, visibility into new and updated devices and manual operations practice, you can reduce the risks associated with third-party integrator support.

Shifts in OT environments have not been small and in many cases, have required third-party support to help manage their evolution effectively. While integrators may help alleviate operational expansion and implement based on new requirements, they also introduce additional risks. Especially if these integrators and their clients don’t enforce proper cyber hygiene.

CISA Highlights the Growing Exposure Risk Created by Third-party Integrators

The OT third-party integrator risk concern was recently called out in a joint publication from CISA and the FBI. This publication “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators” highlights the growing exposure of ICS networks and includes a list of recommendations to help assess risk and reduce exposure. While these recommendations follow standard cybersecurity best practices, the historical need for system uptime and reliability has meant these practices sometimes fall on the back burner.

Notably, the core of these security recommendations builds on the “principle of least privilege.” This concept is a core tenet within many organizations, with system administrators restricting users to privileges based on their immediate roles and responsibilities. The goal of these controls is to limit the impact of an attack. If an account or system is breached, the principle of least privilege should minimize the overall reach and impact of an attack.

The Problem with Least Privilege in OT Environments

In reality, the application of “least privilege” poses a significant challenge within OT environments. Many of the foundational protocols, things such as Modbus, DNP3 and older versions of EtherNet/IP lack authentication and role- based access. While this may be difficult within the OT environment due to technical limitations with the basic protocols and the systems in use, additional steps can be taken to limit exposure of critical systems such as the following:

A dedicated integrator access zone or jump host in a DMZ, with no direct path into Purdue Level 1/2 and per-vendor accounts rather than shared integrator credentials

Just-in-time access to reduce the overall exposure of remote access solutions

Enabling MFA on remote access to reduce risks associated with account compromise

Continuous review of accessible user accounts, including integrator and vendor accounts and their activity to ensure permissions are appropriate

Regularly purge stale, unused or deprecated accounts and access as projects close-out

Best Practices When Engaging with Third-party ICS Integrators

In its own publication, CISA also provided a handful of best practices organizations should consider when bringing in third party ICS integrators.

Include Cybersecurity and Supply Chain Cybersecurity in Contracts and Service Agreements

As with all things security, proper implementation needs to start at the beginning. Prior to allowing any third party into your ICS networks, ensure documentation exists, highlight security expectations and accountability. Things such as change management, patching expectations and remote access method documentation can all help organizations understand security practices, even before they begin.

The security of your ICS network doesn’t just rely on your environment, but those that touch it. Proper data hygiene, secure remote access capabilities and documented change management and patch policies all contribute to the security of your environment, even before an integrator steps foot on a factory floor. Additional documentation around steps that will be taken to secure the environment, prior to entering the environment, can help demonstrate and support long term security initiatives.

Evaluate Devices with External Internet Exposure

Internet exposed assets represent a long-lived and frequently exploited path into ICS environments. VPN appliances, cellular modems and internet facing PLCs and HMI all introduce a new avenue of attack.

When working with an integrator, ensure that systems have only the necessary network access. While publicly exposing these systems on the internet may allow for quick and easy management, it also provides threat actors with a low-effort means into the environment. While more effort to configure, secure remote access tools with MFA and no inbound port forwarding can significantly reduce the exposure of a system, while still allowing for robust support.

In addition to configuring secure remote access, regular reviews of your external-facing Ips can help to ensure access in this form isn’t left unchecked.

Monitor and Log Remote Access

Given the criticality of most ICS environments, remote access should be carefully monitored and regularly reviewed. ICS integrators perform important work with ICS environments and as such, these accounts provide a high value entry point into the environment. Unrestricted and unmonitored access can quickly lead to operational blind spots, significantly reducing the environment’s overall integrity.

When possible, organizations should work with integrators to provision “Just-in-Time” access. “Just-in-Time” approval allows for targeted provision access, on approval. As opposed to an always on solution, integrators must request access to a specific system at a specific time. This access can be extended or revoked, at any time.

Access of this nature allows integrators to perform their tasks but also provide the system owners with more granular control. Initial access requires the approval of a trusted legitimate user, reducing the risk of unauthorized access and in the event of a breach or suspicious behavior, the access can quickly be revoked, isolating the overall impact.

In addition to controls such as “Just-in-Time” access, robust logging and monitoring of remote access and sensitive networks can help to identify and flag anomalous behavior. Forwarding logs to an OT aware SIEM can help ensure that alerts are triaged and handled appropriately.

This can easily identify off-hour activity or out-of-scope behavior from integrators. Additionally, consistent passive network monitoring can help identify new integrators systems and devices, even if they aren’t immediately communicated.

Request an Inventory of All Software and Hardware Supplied by the Integrator

Protection begins with visibility. It is impossible to protect the things which you do not know exist. When working with an ICS integrator it is important your team understands the software and hardware they are introducing into the environment.

Each new piece of software and hardware introduces a new potential means of compromise. An asset inventory supports vulnerability management and helps teams choose between patching and compensating controls. Undocumented software or hardware can quickly fall out of date and introduce new vulnerabilities in the environment.

Additionally, logic output should also be requested. PLC project and logic files, system backs ups and any integrator tool should also be collected and understood. These files and components create an actionable audit trail that can be leveraged to ensure system and environment integrity.

Practice Procedures and Maintain Capabilities for Manual Operations

ICS integrators can become a core part of an organization’s operations. In these situations, it’s important to ensure that they understand their roles and responsibilities within the organization.

Regular reviews with integrators can ensure they are ready and able to perform any necessary manual operations and fail-safe procedures. When performing tabletop exercises, reviewing policy and maintaining daily operations, these integrators should be present to ensure they are available and ready in the event of an incident.

The following list several best practices that should be regularly reviewed and verified with integrators.

Appropriate change management controls when interacting with and modifying PLCs logic. System owners should work with integrators and manage policy, to ensure that a reliable fallback logic is available and new logic is properly documented.

Policy exists to ensure that integrator-owned systems are regularly scanned to mitigate risks of malware.

Effective off boarding procedures should be in place to ensure inactive integrator accounts and systems cannot be used for an attack. Disable accounts and ensure unused systems/software are removed.

Ensure appropriate controls and segmentation exist between remote access solutions and high priority safety systems.

Start with a Risk Assessment

Outside of following these recommendations, regular risk assessments are highly encouraged. While some integrators have always put security first and built the systems and environments they support with this in mind, others may have focused their efforts on operational reliance and performance. The use of default credentials, insecure network configurations, outdated and vulnerable software and insufficient documentation is common in some ICS environments.

In these situations it is important to have a trusted partner capable of not only validating past work but also helping to support and foster an environment of operational and security excellence. GuidePoint’s consultants and engineers are well positioned to help organizations establish an OT security baseline so they can grow securely.

FAQs

What happens when a third-party integrator is compromised in an OT environment?

A compromised integrator account can give attackers direct access to controllers and sensors that run physical processes. Lateral movement from an integrator’s entry point can bypass IT security controls entirely. The impact ranges from production downtime to safety incidents depending on the attacker’s objectives.

How should organizations vet third-party ICS integrators before granting access?

Start with documented security requirements in the contract before any access is provisioned. Request evidence of the integrator’s own security practices including patch management and remote access policies. Verify that the integrator can support your logging and monitoring requirements.

What is the CISA advisory on third-party ICS integrators?

CISA and the FBI published “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators” in 2026. The advisory highlights the growing exposure of ICS networks through third-party access. It recommends applying least privilege controls and monitoring all integrator activity.

Why is unmonitored remote access dangerous in ICS environments?

Unmonitored remote sessions create blind spots where unauthorized changes can go undetected. Persistent VPN tunnels and always-on connections give attackers a low-effort entry point into critical systems. Without session logging, organizations cannot trace the source or scope of a breach.

Vulnerability scanning to identify technical weaknesses across their environment

Cyber maturity assessments to benchmark their security posture and prioritize what to improve first

Ransomware readiness assessments to understand how prepared they are for one of today's most damaging threats

Vendor risk assessments to evaluate the security of the third parties they rely on

Unlock exclusive rrelentless access to Security Colony.

Learn More

Breach monitoring to spot potential exposure of their data early

Ask the Expert forum access, connecting them directly with LevelBlue security specialists

Gary Gallen, Chief Executive of rrelentless and its parent, the rradar group of companies, sees the partnership the same way: "Cyber risk does not stand still, so neither can cyber insurance. Part of a 360-degree view of cyber risk

Security awareness training provider Pistachio, which joins as a partner at the same time, offers personalized training, simulated phishing campaigns and behavioral insights to strengthen the human side of security.

The result is legal, technical and people-focused support before, during and after a cyber incident, with LevelBlue providing the technical insight that helps policyholders see and close their gaps.

Bringing LevelBlue expertise to more organizations

As the world's largest and most analyst-recognized pure-play managed security service provider, LevelBlue supports thousands of organizations across 96 countries with managed security services, threat intelligence and risk consulting. Partnerships like this one with rrelentless let us extend that expertise to businesses that might otherwise never have access to it, through a channel they already trust.

Overnight on November 2, freezers in supermarkets across Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg and Ireland climbed to around 50°C, and stores awoke to spoiled stock. This is the second wave within a month, after a similar attack on hundreds of French stores in October. No one has publicly claimed either attack, and the attack vector hasn't been confirmed.

Regardless of who is responsible, the targets are what should worry us. These were refrigeration controllers: small, purpose-built devices that most of their asset owners likely didn’t think of as computers at all.

Invisible by design

The first problem is that nobody is looking for, or often even aware these devices are network connected. These devices often become effectively invisible once the integrator puts them in place. They perform their function reliably, and quietly. Unless something breaks, nobody thinks about them as computers that need ongoing security maintenance.

A refrigeration controller is installed by a contractor, commissioned, and then left to run. It rarely appears in an IT asset inventory, it often sits outside the security team's remit, and even worse, it may be reachable remotely so the maintenance provider can service it. That combination: connected, unmonitored, and effectively unowned, is an attacker’s dream target.

A patching problem with no easy fix

That invisibility creates a serious patching problem. Many embedded and industrial devices remain exposed not only to recently disclosed vulnerabilities, but also to flaws that were remediated decades ago, along with product-specific firmware weaknesses that may never be publicly documented.

The gaps come in several forms:

No fix exists. The manufacturer is unaware of the issue, has ended support for the product, or has no incentive to address it.

A fix exists but never reaches the field. The operator may not realize the device is vulnerable, may not know an upstream update is available, or may no longer have a clear owner responsible for maintaining it.

The fix is difficult to apply. There usually is no equivalent of Windows Update or Linux's `yum`/`apt` that can centrally track and deliver these updates. Updates may require a technician, a vendor-specific utility, physical access, or downtime that operators are reluctant to schedule.

Advance your IoT security with LevelBlue.

Learn More

The French attack shows how this plays out. Intermarché's owner said its systems were managed by Danfoss (an external engineering/product firm), and Reuters reported some of the November targets used the same technology. In August, Claroty's Team82 disclosed flaws in Danfoss refrigeration controllers, including a hidden credential that could grant admin access, and found thousands of the controllers reachable from the internet. The saddest part here: A firmware fix was available at the time of attack. Whether those flaws were used hasn't been established, but a fix that has been released is not the same as a fleet that has been patched.

Built for a different era, kept for decades

A lot of this equipment was also designed in an era, or for an environment, where security was not only not a primary focus, but often wasn't even considered. As a result, you still encounter weaknesses that the broader software industry has treated as solved problems for years: weak authentication, exposed services, hard-coded credentials, insecure update mechanisms, and other basic issues.

Those weaknesses persist because the hardware does. These devices can remain operational long after the vendor has ended support or stopped producing security updates. From an operational perspective, replacing a device that still does its job can be difficult to justify, even though it may be extremely vulnerable.

And even when manufacturers consider software security, hardware security often remains unaccounted for. Maintenance and debugging interfaces intended for technicians can sometimes provide surprisingly direct access to a device if someone can reach it physically. Features that are useful during manufacturing or servicing can become security liabilities when equipment remains deployed unattended, and a rooftop condenser or back-room controller cabinet is about as unattended as equipment gets.

This isn't a supermarket problem

It would be easy to file these attacks under retail and move on, but that misses the point. The broader issue is not at all specific to supermarkets or refrigeration. These kinds of niche embedded and IoT systems are deployed across retail, manufacturing, building automation, healthcare, critical infrastructure, solar, agriculture, and many other industries.

They are everywhere, but because they are purpose-built and usually quietly doing their jobs, they are often overlooked until an incident makes them visible. This month, that incident was spoiled food. In another sector, the same class of weakness could mean a stalled production line, a building with no climate control, disrupted energy assets causing blackouts, or tainted water at a utility.

What to do now

Organizations running embedded, IoT, and OT equipment, in stores or anywhere else can reduce exposure with a few practical steps:

Understand what you have. Inventory every connected device, including those installed and managed by third-party integrators, record the firmware version of each, and note the update mechanism/method.

Assign an owner and write processes. Every device needs a named person or team responsible for its security, not just its uptime, and they need to be aware of how to properly patch the device.

Take it off the internet. Devices should not be directly reachable from the public internet. Put remote vendor access behind a VPN or secure gateway with MFA and logging.

Patch, and plan for what you can't patch. Check vendor advisories, schedule firmware updates, and segment or monitor devices that are out of support until they can be replaced.

Change the defaults. Remove shared and default credentials and ask vendors directly about hidden or maintenance accounts.

Protect physical access. Secure cabinets and service ports on unattended equipment.

Alert on the physical outcome. Independent temperature or process alarms can catch tampering that the compromised controller itself would hide. Establish a baseline and expected value ranges, find a way to track them, and alert on them if they deviate.

Test it. Product (hardware/firmware) and OT- focused penetration testing finds the forgotten device before an attacker does.

The freezers in Sweden, Belgium, and France were doing exactly what they were built to do, until someone else told them otherwise. The lesson is simple: if it runs code, it can be compromised. And if your business depends on it, you can't afford to pretend it's just an appliance.

■記事概要

国内で相次ぐWEBシステムからの情報漏洩の状況をまとめ、第2報として公開します。

まず、前回の記事 の内容のサマリです。今年7月以降、WEBシステムからの情報漏洩が相次ぎ、被害がECサイトだけでなく、会員向けサービスや業務用システムなど、多種多様なサイトへ無差別的に広がり始めた状況をお伝えしました。その際は、WEBシステム構築に利用されるソフトウェアに共通する既知の脆弱性（CVE）だけでなく、個々のサイトやAPIの認証・アクセス制御などの不備を丁寧に探り、情報を窃取する攻撃手法が用いられること、及び対策の観点を紹介しています。また、探索範囲や攻撃量等の状況証拠から一連の攻撃でAIが悪用されている可能性に言及しています。なお、AI悪用についてはその後、それを裏付ける具体的な調査結果が国内のセキュリティ関連組織から相次いで公表され、弊社の調査でもその痕跡を確認しています。

本記事の前半では、10月末までの公表情報をもとに、その後の被害の広がりや攻撃・悪用の傾向を改めて整理します。結論としては、新たな傾向が現れたというよりも、前回お伝えした傾向がさらに色濃く表れている状況です。

後半では、本事案について関心が高いと思われる点を考察します。なお、本記事での集計条件は以下の通りです。

2026年10月31日までの公表情報を集計し、11月以降に公表された事案や続報に含まれる情報は含めていません。

国内で公表されたWEBシステムへの外部からの不正アクセスによる情報漏洩の関連と思われる事案を筆者の判断で抽出しています。ランサムウェア・記録媒体紛失・フィッシングを起点とする事案・他サービスから流出した認証情報を使うリスト型攻撃等は今回除外しています。

委託先・共通サービスの侵害は1事案にまとめて集計しています。利用企業側各社の公表は重複計上していません。実際に攻撃を受け被害が生じた件数を調査するためです。

■被害件数と漏洩規模

2026年の被害公表件数は10月までに288件となり、2025年の84件の3倍以上となっています。7月以降の増加傾向に加え、10月単月の公表が168件と突出しています。グラフで見るとその異様さが直感的にわかります。

図1：国内WEB侵害の公表件数推移

漏洩した情報の件数も大きくなっています。公表された漏洩規模を積み上げた参考値は、2026年の累計が約3.8億件相当となり、その約6割が10月の公表分です。2024年以降に公表された類似事案を漏洩規模で比べると、TOP10件は全件が、TOP20件のうち18件は2026年に公表された事案でした。なお、図表とは別に11月3日までに確認した新規事案と続報を反映すると、事案は10件、漏洩規模は約9,000万件増加しています。

図2：個人情報の漏えい規模

■侵害の実行時期

各社の公表情報で不正アクセスの発生時期を見ると、10月後半にも侵害が行われていることが分かります。事案が話題となり、以前の攻撃に気づいた事例だけが件数を押し上げているわけではありません。攻撃と被害はなおも継続中です。

以下のグラフは、10月に公表された168事案のうち、攻撃・不正操作の実行日が9〜10月と明記された38事案を元に作成しています。縦軸は公表日、横軸は実行日です。10月中旬以降も攻撃による被害が発生していることがわかります。

図3：公表日と攻撃・不正アクセス等の実行日

なお、これはあくまで推測ですが、WEBシステムへの不正アクセスがこれほど話題となり、10月7日以降、セキュリティ関連組織や政府からの注意喚起も広がるなかで、事業者の多くがこの問題を知らずにいたとは考えにくいところです。一連の攻撃では、既知の共通脆弱性（CVE）に加えて、各WEBシステム固有のセキュリティ上の不備や欠陥が幅広く悪用され、攻撃手法も必要な対策もシステムごとに異なります。こうした背景もあり、ある程度の警戒や点検をしていても、想定していなかったシステムや経路に穴が残り、そこを突かれているのではないでしょうか。

■被害対象の広がり

前回、被害がECサイトからさまざまな用途へ広がっているとお伝えしました。10月の公表では、この傾向がよりはっきり表れています。会員向けと業務・手続きを扱うシステムを合わせて、約3分の2を占めています。

図4：侵害されたサイト・サービスの用途

長年標的とされてきたECサイトの割合が減り、多種多様なサイトが標的になっています。7月以降の公表例から、印象的なものを挙げます。括弧内は公表された対象規模（漏洩の可能性を含む）です。

・葬儀会社の供花・供物の注文システム（約1万件）・ファッション誌のブロガー向け連絡・撮影やイベント参加などの案件管理システム（ブロガー約2,800人分）・5年前の音楽フェスのステージ前方指定エリア申込情報を保管する管理システム（約3,600件）・後払い決済利用者向けの請求書再発行申請システム（約2.9万件）・公演中止・延期に伴う電子チケットの返金申請・振込先管理システム（約1,500件）・地域の卓球協会の大会参加申込・責任者情報登録システム（申込責任者185人分）・地方の観光列車の乗客向け座席予約・情報管理システム（約1,400人分）・大学間連携の授業履修・インターンシップ出願管理システム（学生延べ約1,600人分）・ケーブル・配管の延焼防止材などを扱う部門の出荷管理システム（対象数量不明）・日本研究の英文資料を中心とする専門図書室の蔵書検索システム（対象数量不明）

■その他の被害傾向

ここからは7月～10月の公表事例248件について、いくつかの観点に分けて傾向をお伝えします。

まずは、漏洩している情報の種別です。公表された漏洩対象が氏名や住所などの基本情報にとどまる事案も23.0%を占めます。この点からも、情報の価値によって標的を選ぶのではなく、無差別に攻撃を仕掛け、取れる情報を盗むという傾向がうかがえます。

図5：漏えい等の対象となった情報の種類

続いて、不正アクセスの原因です。何らかの説明がある事案は47.2%で、そのうち問題の種類まで分類できるものは60事案、全体の24.2%でした。さまざまな不備が広く悪用されていることが分かります。なお、これはあくまで公表情報の統計である点にはご留意ください。筆者の体感では、WEBアプリの実装・処理の不備による被害が多いと感じています。

図6：原因の説明

次に、侵害されたシステム上での不正操作です。ここでは、内部情報の閲覧・取得（その可能性を含む）以外の不正操作を確認できた事例を集計しています。全体の約3割、73件でその記載を確認できました。なお、これらが全て攻撃者の意図した操作とは限らず、不正アクセス試行の中で異常動作を引き起こしてしまった事例も含まれているはずです。

図7：侵害されたシステム上での不正操作

次に、システム上の操作から利用者への影響に視点を移します。図7と重複する事案も含め、不正アクセス後に利用者に影響する何らかの不正利用・悪用が確認されたとの記載がある事案は24件で、全体の約1割でした。

図8：情報・機能の悪用と利用者への波及

なお、以下は今回の不正アクセス被害を受けた宿泊予約サイトの利用履歴がある弊社社員に届いたメールです。本文中には実際に宿泊したホテル名や宿泊日、本人氏名が記載されており、窃取した情報が、フィッシングメールをより巧妙にするための材料として使われています。

参考画像：宿泊予約に関する情報を記載し、カード情報の確認・更新に誘導するメール例

続いて、具体的な発覚のきっかけを確認できたのは全体の4割弱です。監視による検知に加え、高い負荷、不審な挙動、画面やデータの変化、外部からの通知、利用者の問い合わせなどがあります。「このメールは本物か」「身に覚えのない操作がある」という連絡も、侵害を調べる入口になります。ただし、何もないから攻撃を受けていないとは考えずに、常に警戒を行って下さい。

図9：異常発覚のきっかけ

公開情報をもとにした統計データの紹介は以上です。今回の集計では、原因や不正操作、発覚のきっかけなど、被害の詳細を公表いただいている事案も多く確認できました。こうした情報は、他の組織が同様の不備を探し、対策を進めるための重要な手掛かりになります。様々な葛藤の中で一部でも情報を公表いただいていることは非常にありがたく、前回の記事でも言及しましたが、今後さらにこうした情報の開示が広がることを期待しています。

■その他考察等

ここからは、これらの事例を踏まえ、今後の対策を考えるうえでの考察と私見を述べます。

■攻撃者の狙い、目的は

一連の情報の分析から、攻撃者の狙いは大きく三つあると考えています。

（1）情報の窃取と悪用取得した情報をフィッシングや詐欺、他サイトへのリスト型攻撃に悪用するため、情報を集める目的です。現在の攻撃の中心はこれですが、稀なケースでは窃取した情報の第三者への売却目的もあると考えています。

（2）ポイントやギフトなどの金銭的価値の獲得サイト内の機能を悪用し、ポイントやギフトなどを通じて金銭を得る目的です。今回の248事案のうち、ポイント・電子ギフトの不正交換発生を公表した事例は2件のみですが、それを標的にするような犯罪者テレグラムでの発言を弊社で確認しています。

（3）メール送信などに使える基盤の確保侵害したシステムを、フィッシングメールをばらまくための基盤として使う目的です。今回集計したWEB不正アクセスでは、メール・SMS送信機能を悪用した不正送信が7事案で報告されています。それ以外にも、企業のメール送信基盤などが悪用された事案があり、両方を合わせると、7〜10月公表分で少なくとも14事案（7月4件、9月3件、10月7件）を確認しています。

■実行犯はどのようなグループか

筆者が思い描くのは、国家を背景とするAPT（標的型攻撃）グループやランサムウェアなどで長年活動してきたプロのサイバー攻撃者ではなく、ここ数年で新規参入した「野良のサイバー犯罪者」です。単独犯や不特定多数のグループではなく、手法や狙う対象が微妙に異なる、限定的な数の複数クラスタが存在するように感じています。

長らく活動していたプロの攻撃者ほど高い技術力や経験、リソースを持たないはずの彼らが、低コストで高性能なAIと融合し、長期に渡り放置されてきたシステムのさまざまな不備やセキュリティホールを高速で探り、突くことによってこれほどの被害を生んでしまった点は非常にショッキングです。

余談ですが、AI利用の広がりとともに、攻撃者の脇の甘さも目立ち始めています。これは新参のサイバー犯罪者だけでなく、比較的高度なスキルを持つAPTグループの一部にも見られる傾向だと感じています。以前は攻撃に使うインフラの隠蔽にも力を入れていた攻撃者が、最近は活動や身元を隠すための運用上の秘匿（OPSEC）を十分に徹底できていないように見えるのです。

その背景に、作業量の増加や組織の拡大に伴うオペレーションの不備があるのか、AIを使っているため特定されないであろうという慢心があるのかは、まだ分かりません。実際、AIの利用によって攻撃の手法や手順（TTPs）が似通い、侵害の痕跡（IOC）にもグループ固有の特徴が表れにくくなっている面があります。そのため、活動の手掛かりが見えても、それを特定のグループに結び付けることは難しくなっていると考えています。

■10月以降に被害が急増した理由

被害急増の理由は、現時点では明確ではありません。一つの要因で単純に説明できるものではないと思いますが、低コストで高性能なAIの普及は主要因の一つと考えています。個人的には、特に2026年初頭前後からのAIの性能向上によって、「コーディング能力≒サイバー攻撃能力」だけでなく、自律的な判断能力や作業品質も高まったことが、大きく寄与している感覚があります。端的に言えば、指示したコンピュータ上の作業をミスなくこなせる範囲・速度・品質が、人間以上になったという感覚です。

そして、サイバー犯罪者は、まず試験的な攻撃を限定的な範囲で行い、そこで成果が見込めると判断すると、一気に対象を広げて情報の窃取や収益化に動きます。その成功を見た別のグループが模倣し、被害が急拡大することは、過去何度も事例があります。今回も、こうした試行（4～7月）から本格的な悪用への移行と模倣（8月以降）が重なっているのではないかと考えています。

■日本のみを標的とした活動か

一般論として、AIを悪用したサイバー攻撃は国内外を問わず多く行われています。今回のWEBシステムへの不正アクセスについても、海外に対しても攻撃を行っているグループは存在しますが、その一部が日本に特化した集中的な攻撃を行い、とりわけ多くの被害を出していると考えています。

AIを使った攻撃で高い成果を得るには、対象に応じて情報の収集・分析から攻撃に至るまでの手順や、AIが使うツールを整備・調整する、いわゆるハーネスエンジニアリングが必要であり、日本のサイトの構造やビジネス習慣に合わせて、こうした仕組みを作り込んでいることは十分考えられます。また、情報の取得から換金・収益化までの流れも組み立てる必要があることから、特定の国に集中して攻撃することには合理性があると見ています。

なお、筆者が調査した範囲では、AIを悪用したサイバー攻撃による大小さまざまな被害がこれほど広範囲に相次ぎ、連日のように報道され、政府や企業が対応に追われるなど社会問題化している状況は、日本以外では確認できていません。日本は、こうした状況を世界でも初めて経験している国なのかもしれません。

■被害がここまで続く理由

現在、国内の多くのWEBサイトでは、脆弱性診断やWAFの導入などの対策が行われています。被害を受けた企業の中には、セキュリティ対策に特に力を入れていた企業もあり、「何もしていなかった」とは一概に言えません。

それでも、なぜこれほど多くの被害が続いているのでしょうか。原因はまだ分かりませんが、セキュリティ診断の対象範囲や深さ、種別、パターンが十分でなかった、問題に気づいていてもリスク評価の結果として対応を見送っていた、管理対象から漏れたシステムがあったなど、さまざまな要因が絡み合っている可能性があります。

こうした構造的な要因を明らかにするため、被害を受けた企業と、攻撃を受けても事故を防ぐことができた企業の双方に広くヒアリング・調査を行い、次の攻撃の波に備えるべきだと考えています。

■まとめ

今回の一連のWEBシステムへの不正アクセスは、三つの想定外を明らかにしました。

一つ目は、AIの性能向上とその悪用が実害につながるまでの速さ、二つ目は、AIによる攻撃の脅威として、高度で巧妙な手法ではなく、認証やアクセス制御、実装・設定などの基礎的な不備が侵害につながっていることです。そして三つ目は、長年にわたりさまざまなセキュリティ対策を進めてきたはずの社会に、それでもこれほど多くの不備が残っていたことです。現在はその照準がWEBシステムに向いていますが、対象となり得るITシステムは他にも多く存在し、同様の流れが拡大し、より深刻な社会影響につながることを懸念しています。

そして、これらの状況は、攻撃者によるAIの活用が先行し、長年なんとか保たれてきた攻守のバランスが崩れつつあることを示しているように感じています。これまで、人間同士の攻防を前提としたセキュリティ対策のガイドラインや慣習が、約20年にわたって続いてきました。今まさに、それらを抜本的に見直すべき時期に来ていると考えます。ただし、システムやルールの変更、新しい方針の検討から整備、普及までには、非常に長い時間を要するでしょう。

それまでの間、各社が行える暫定的な対策として、まずはリスクの高いインターネット公開資産を削減し、スリム化・断捨離することが重要です。そのうえで、残ったシステムに対しては、AIを活用し、外部からのブラックボックステストと、設定・コードレビューの両面からセキュリティリスクを確認する必要があります。中長期的には、セキュリティを考慮したシステムの再構築やアーキテクチャの刷新も必要になるかもしれません。

AIはここ数年、さまざまな利便性や恩恵をもたらしてきました。しかし、ここに来てAIの負の側面が急速に顕在化し、私たちは過去にない極めて大きな難題を突きつけられているようにも感じています。

Google Cloud VMs on AMD Turin chips need a guest OS patch and a stop-and-start to protect against three CPU side-channel flaws, Google said this week.

The company has already applied mitigations against attacks between VMs, and between VMs and the host. Inside a VM, the flaws may let an attacker with code on the same processor core infer data from other processes or the kernel.

The affected machine series are C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D,, and G4, including bare-metal instances of C4D and Z4D. Turin is the code name for fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors.

All three flaws are Transient Scheduler Attacks (TSA). Two of them, TSA-SQ (CVE-2024-36350) and TSA-L1 (CVE-2024-36357), were first disclosed on July 8, 2025, for earlier EPYC processors.

AMD now says its Zen 5 processors, which include Turin, are "impacted differently from previously characterized AMD processors." The third flaw, CVE-2026-0004, is new. It may let an attacker who can run code on a system infer data in the processor's L1 data cache.

The Xen Project, which maintains the Xen hypervisor, calls the new flaw TSA-Fill. It also says an earlier statement has been corrected: "AMD had previously said that Zen5 CPUs were not vulnerable to TSA-SQ and TSA-L1."

Google rates the issue Medium. AMD classifies all three as local attacks with high attack complexity that require only low privileges, according to its Zen 5 bulletin and CVE-2026-0004 advisory.

As of today, none of the three is in the KEV catalog of exploited flaws kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Neither company reports any exploitation in its bulletins.

What Google Cloud Customers Need to Do

Google's security bulletin gives these steps for each service:

VMs: Install your OS vendor's fix when it ships. Starting this week, the company will update the CPU information that VMs report, so a patched guest kernel can turn on its mitigations. After that update reaches a VM, stop and start it. As the company puts it: "Rebooting the guest OS isn't enough."

Bare metal instances: If you run your own OS or hypervisor on a C4D or Z4D bare metal instance, apply your vendor's fixes when they are available.

Hypervisors inside a VM: The same CPU information update applies, so patched guest kernels can turn on their mitigations. Stop and start the VM once the update arrives.

GKE: Updated node images for Turin-based bare metal instances will be made available, and upgrading nodes picks up the CPU information update. As of today, the bulletin does not yet list them as available.

Cloud Run: No action is needed.

Customers on older Rome, Milan, and Genoa processors got the same stop-and-start instruction in an earlier bulletin at the time of the original disclosure on July 8, 2025.

The company lists nothing to do in the meantime for VMs whose OS vendor has not yet shipped a fix. It also does not say how to tell when the CPU information update has reached a VM.

A kernel commit that mitigates TSA on Zen 5, including the new variant, is in the Linux kernel source tree. As of today, Debian has fixed CVE-2026-0004 in its Linux kernel only in its unstable branch. Its security tracker still lists the kernels in bookworm, trixie, and forky as vulnerable.

For Turin servers on your own hardware, AMD says both platform firmware and OS updates are needed to mitigate the flaws fully. The mitigation may affect performance, and administrators should weigh the risk to their own workloads, according to its technical guidance.

The Xen Project has published hypervisor patches in its Xen advisory. It says microcode for all TSA flaws on Zen 5 has been in linux-firmware since September 23.

Security teams have more alerts, logs, and monitoring tools than ever. Yet when an attack happens, one simple question can still take too long to answer: Who or what is behind this activity, and what can they access?

A suspicious login might belong to an employee. An unusual API call could come from a machine account. Or an AI agent might be accessing sensitive systems using permissions nobody has reviewed recently.

Your SIEM or EDR may catch the activity. But without knowing who owns that identity, what permissions it has, and which systems it can reach, your SOC is missing a critical part of the story.

And that missing context can turn a manageable incident into a much bigger problem.

Join this expert-led webinar to learn how real-time identity context can help your SOC investigate threats faster, understand what's at risk, and respond with confidence.

The Blind Spot Between Identity and Security Operations

Here's the problem.

Identity and access management (IAM) teams know who has access to what. Security operations teams monitor suspicious activity and respond to threats.

But these teams often work with different tools, different data, and different priorities.

When an alert comes in, SOC analysts may know what happened but still struggle to understand what it means.

Consider a compromised service account. An analyst might detect suspicious activity, but several questions remain:

What applications and systems can this account access?

Could an attacker use it to move deeper into the network?

How much damage could it cause?

Can the account be disabled without breaking a critical business process?

These answers matter. Blocking the wrong identity can disrupt production. Waiting too long can give an attacker more room to move.

And with machine identities and autonomous AI agents becoming part of everyday operations, the problem is getting more complicated.

More Identities, More Access, More Risk

Traditional security monitoring was largely built around users, devices, and network activity.

Today, organizations also rely on service accounts, API keys, automated workloads, and AI agents that can act without direct human involvement.

These identities often have access to important systems and data.

If one is compromised, detecting the suspicious action is only the beginning. Security teams also need to understand its permissions, connections, and potential impact.

That's where identity context changes the investigation.

Instead of treating every alert as an isolated event, analysts can connect suspicious activity to the identity behind it, understand how far an attacker could move, and choose a response that limits damage without unnecessarily interrupting operations.

📅 Save Your Spot: See how identity context can improve your SOC response in this free webinar.

What Does a Better SOC Response Actually Look Like?

The goal isn't to add another dashboard or generate more alerts.

It's to give analysts the information they need when an incident is unfolding.

That means connecting identity intelligence with existing SIEM and EDR alerts, so teams can:

Investigate faster: Understand which human, machine, or AI identity is involved.

See the real risk: Identify permissions, connected systems, and potential lateral movement.

Contain threats safely: Respond to compromised credentials without unnecessarily disrupting critical automation.

Work better together: Give IAM and SOC teams shared workflows, clear escalation paths, and common response goals.

The difference is simple: knowing that something suspicious happened is useful. Knowing what it can affect and how to stop it is far more valuable.

Learn How to Close the Gap

In the upcoming webinar, Fuel the SOC with Identity Context: Securing Humans, Machines, and AI Agents, security experts will explore how organizations can bring IAM and security operations together.

Drawing on real-world enterprise deployments, the session will cover practical approaches to enriching security alerts with identity context, investigating lateral movement, understanding the potential blast radius of an attack, and improving incident response without disrupting production systems.

It will also explain how teams can align around shared metrics, escalation processes, and response playbooks.

Your SOC already has the alerts. Now give it the context to act.

Register for the free webinar and learn how to turn identity intelligence into faster, smarter security response.

N-able on Thursday said it's investigating a new public disclosure containing claims of additional vulnerabilities in on-premise versions of N-central running version 2026.4.1 HF2.

"Based on our initial review, the server issue described depends on a non-default configuration in which the Legacy API is turned on and exposed to the public internet," N-able said in a new advisory. "Legacy API is turned off by default in the product and is not recommended."

The company is urging customers to disable Legacy API immediately, if not already. It also noted that hosted environments are not affected by this issue.

The incident impacts the following services -

N-central On-premise (Americas)

N-central On-premise (APAC)

N-central On-premise (Europe)

The development comes days after N-able released 2026.4.1.26 to address a number of security flaws disclosed by independent security researcher Sean Bales earlier this week. The vulnerabilities are collectively tracked under the name Able2Shell.

The new shortcoming, also revealed by Bales, have been codenamed 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, adding the proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits successfully work against N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26), the update N-able released on November 10, 2026, to resolve Able2Shell.

According to the researcher, 4EverAble2Shell enables unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on N-central servers. Agent2Shell, on the other hand, leverages more than 10 zero-day vulnerabilities to run commands on managed Windows agents as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, assuming the attacker knows the target appliance ID.

Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, told The Hacker News that targeted N-central probing has been observed against 4EverAble2Shell within hours following the release of the PoC. The activity has originated from the IP address 157.20.241[.]16. There is no evidence of successful exploitation as of writing.

In the attack chain observed by the threat intelligence company, threat actors have been observed attempting to achieve initial code execution through a recently disclosed Apache Axis flaw (CVE-2026-90436, CVSS score: 9.8), followed by attempts to escalate privileges to root using 4EverAble2Shell, and then download and execute a shell script from 157.20.241[.]16 using curl.

Dewhurst said the development marks the first documented instance of exploitation attempts aimed at CVE-2026-90436, patches for which were released on November 6, 2026.

In a post shared on X, watchTowr also said it's seeing probes for 4EverAble2Shell targeting N-Centrals builds with the Legacy API enabled.

(This is a developing story. Please check back for more information.)

Since mid-August 2026, a phishing operation has been stealing live Google sessions from corporate users. Every check defenders normally lean on to judge a link came back clean, and the operator designed it that way on purpose.

The Threat Research team at Material Security spotted the campaign and has since taken down hundreds of attacker domains in an effort the team calls Operation CloudFire. Here’s what the researchers found.

The lure: Google Calendar invites

The messages show up as Google Calendar invites. Some arrive by BCC, and many come from an organization the recipient has already traded email with. The pretexts are deliberately boring: voicemail notifications, RFP and RFI requests, court summonses, and missed payment notices. Nothing about them stands out in a busy inbox.

Most of the links point to Google itself. The usual pattern runs through Google’s own /url redirector, with the real destination tucked into a query parameter. Other waves used share.google and Drive file links the same way, and one variant leaned on Intuit transaction notification links. Whenever a message gets scored, the domain, certificate, and reputation on display are all legitimate.

The capture: a reverse proxy in front of Google sign-in

Once a victim clicks through, the attacker runs a live reverse proxy in front of the real Google sign-in page. The victim types a password, gets a genuine prompt, and approves it while the operator watches in real time. The server passes each second factor along to Google as it comes in, whether that’s an SMS code, an authenticator code, Google’s Tap-Yes number matching, or phone-based account recovery. None of those controls stop the session from being captured.

The framework behind it, known as Nyasher, has been publicly documented since February, after researchers found a hardcoded key in its JavaScript.

Why the usual controls stay quiet

Reputation systems answer questions about ownership. They ask who registered a domain, what else it has hosted, and whether anyone has complained about it. This campaign was built so every one of those answers came back harmless.

It works in three layers. The first is Google’s redirector, which gives the initial hop a trusted Google URL. The second is a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge, and in some builds it’s the real widget served from Cloudflare’s own infrastructure. The third is the password capture page, and that’s where things get tricky for defenders. There’s no static site to scan. JavaScript builds the page in the browser after the visitor clears the challenge, so a crawler has nothing to fetch and a proxy log has nothing to record. As far as the researchers know, nobody had scanned those pages before the campaign was documented.

The infrastructure is also meant to be thrown away. Early waves used many lure domains spread across several registrars, and most were registered just days before use. Receiving endpoints went live one to twenty days ahead of the wave they served. One wildcard certificate was issued 46 minutes before the domain it covers was even registered. Blocking any single piece costs the operator a few dollars and an afternoon.

What stopping it took

Researchers tracked the campaign from the start, following each variant as lures, gates, and endpoints rotated. Once detections were in place, they caught more than 99% of the malicious messages, with a reclassification rate of 0.01%. It’s been steady work, since the attacker kept changing tactics, themes, and lure text to slip past static, machine learning, and agentic detections.

What worked was refusing to let any one signal make the call. Reputation alone wouldn’t have caught this. Neither would link analysis, since the first hop is a Google URL and the final page doesn’t exist until a browser builds it. Instead, the detection approach weighs technical indicators alongside the apparent intent of the message, where its links actually end up, and the sending relationship behind it. Any one of those can be enough to act on. A detection built around a single signal inherits that signal’s blind spots, and this operator has put real effort into mapping them.

Where the analysis happens matters too. Gateways built to inspect mail in transit aren’t a great fit for calendar invites, and much of this campaign arrives as invites. Calendar invites need to be treated as a threat surface of their own, with the account’s full history used as context next to the technical signals.

Where the damage lands

A hijacked session leaves its trail in Google Workspace audit logs. A live session reaches mail, Drive, and the ability to grant OAuth access in the victim’s name, so the blast radius goes well past the inbox.

That raises a couple of hard questions for security teams. Who’s actually reviewing those audit logs, and how fast can they act on what they find? Could the team revoke sessions, contain OAuth grants, and reset the affected account within an hour? Plenty of programs can’t, and an attacker holding a live session can do a lot in an hour.

Operation CloudFire: going after the infrastructure

By late September, the researchers decided that tuning rules, retraining models, and updating agents wouldn’t solve this alone. Detection protects customers, but it does nothing about an operator who’s already prepping the next wave. So the team went after the infrastructure.

Analysts pulled the gateway and backend URLs as messages were being sent and reported them through Cloudflare’s abuse reporting system. Cloudflare’s abuse team confirmed the fake interstitial and the proxied Google sign-in page behind it, then put its own phishing warning in front of those destinations.

That had two effects. First, the attacker’s infrastructure got burned. Every reported gateway and endpoint had to be re-registered, re-pointed, and re-certified before the operator could send again. Second, it protected people well beyond any one company’s customers. Anyone who clicked a reported link saw a warning page instead of a credential form.

One month by the numbers

These figures only cover organizations that agreed to share data, so the real totals are higher. Over one month of Operation CloudFire, researchers recorded:

68,676 campaign messages blocked

2,112 unique malicious URLs analyzed

897 unique domains taken down

8,570 unique compromised sender addresses across 6,354 root domains

The messages also followed a clear rhythm, with sends tracking US business hours.

Message delivery by time of day

The sender count explains how the campaign earned trust. The attacker controlled each compromised account before the first invite went out, and each one sent invites to the account owner’s saved contacts, among others. Recipients saw a name or domain they knew, on a domain with a clean history, at a sensible time of day. Reputation feeds had no reason to flag any of it.

Where things stand now

The phishing themes have moved from calendar invites to Google Drive file and document share invites. Researchers haven’t seen a matching jump in other lures or tactics, and activity from this group seems to have scattered. For now, the campaign looks finished.

Messages detected by week

Domains registered by interval

That’s a snapshot, and it could change fast. Rebuilding the infrastructure is cheap, and the framework has been public since February. The operator also shipped an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch alongside the live Google code. It includes a stylesheet path, a second harness, and a title string that decodes to a Microsoft sign-in prompt. None of those paths resolve today, and adding the new brand would only mean dropping in a file, with no code changes. The follow-on is built and waiting.

The researchers see the theme rotation as ongoing iteration and expect the next pivot to look a lot like this one, just with a different brand on it.

The full technical breakdown, including indicators of compromise and a timeline, is in the companion whitepaper. Teams hunting for this activity in their own environments should start there.

f735c8575244.text:
PTC has released patches for a new critical vulnerability impacting Windchill and FlexPLM software that, if successfully exploited, could result in remote code execution.

The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-126325, carries a CVSS v4 score of 9.2 out of a maximum of 10.0.

It has been described as a case of improper input validation and deserialization of untrusted data that could result in remote code execution via crafted requests.

"A critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability has been reported in PTC Windchill and PTC FlexPLM," according to a description of the flaw on CVE.org. "The vulnerability may be exploited through the deserialization of untrusted data."

The CVE record lists the following versions as affected -

PTC Windchill: 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0, 13.1.0.0, 13.1.1.0, 13.1.2.0, 13.1.3.0, 13.1.4.0

PTC FlexPLM: 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0, 13.1.0.0, 13.1.1.0, 13.1.2.0, 13.1.3.0

"If your Windchill or FlexPLM environment is hosted by PTC, the patches have been applied on their behalf. No action is required on your part," PTC said in a statement posted on its website.

"If your Windchill or FlexPLM environment is not hosted by PTC, we urge you to apply the patch as soon as possible to help protect your systems."

The disclosure comes nearly five months after another critical remote code execution (RCE) issue in Windchill and FlexPLM (CVE-2026-12569, CVSS score: 9.3) came under active exploitation.

Then, in July 2026, it emerged that threat actors linked to the Cl0p ransomware operation were weaponizing the flaw as part of a data extortion campaign designed to drop JSP web shells and exfiltrate sensitive product data from manufacturing companies and industrial enterprises.

"PTC software is a textbook target for initial access brokers and ransomware operators and a significant enabler of triple extortion campaigns," Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

"It allows malicious actors to reach far and wide within victim networks, encrypt and exfiltrate proprietary data, and disrupt industrial processes. In many cases, the impact across these environments has downstream implications for time-sensitive manufacturing, logistics, and fulfillment processes, resulting in material costs per hour of downtime."

Organizations running PTC Windchill and FlexPLM products are recommended to patch exposed systems as soon as possible and monitor for signs of code execution, backdoor access, or web shells on the host. If patching is not an immediate option, it's essential to apply network restrictions to limit the risk of compromise.
