565153bac6af.text: Microsoft has warned customers still clinging to Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 to consider the software "permanently vulnerable" as November's security fixes arrive for Subscription Edition (SE) alone. The warning appears in the release documentation for November's Exchange Server SE security update. Looking for Exchange 2016 and 2019 information? Tough. Microsoft stated: "Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 are no longer tested for vulnerabilities and there are no updates released. If you are using those versions of Exchange, you should consider them permanently vulnerable [Microsoft's emphasis] and should upgrade your organization immediately." You have been warned. Support for Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 ended on October 14, 2025, but the company announced an Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in July 2025. The plan was that this program would end on April 14, 2026, by which time customers would surely have made the jump to a later or online version, right? The company said: "This period will not be extended past April 2026 (you do not need to ask)." And... of course it was. As April 2026 rolled around, and it became clear that some customers were still stubbornly sticking with the old versions, Microsoft did the equivalent of heaving an exasperated sigh and offered another six months of paid security updates. Those final weeks also brought a separate treat: a Windows Server update breaking Exchange Server. This time it was serious. Microsoft released the final Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 security updates on October 13. No more patches, no more vulnerability testing, and apparently no more reprieves. According to Microsoft's Security Update Guide, the November update fixed nine vulnerabilities in Exchange Server SE, including a critical remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-118207. Microsoft isn't testing earlier versions of Exchange for the vulnerabilities. ®

ee890e2a9a1b.text:
A critical flaw in MongoDB Server allows an unauthenticated attacker to send two requests that trigger a crash on the database server. The crash occurs only if that server is later chosen to take over as the main server while it still lacks some recent changes.

MongoDB, the company that makes the database, released fixed versions earlier this week.

The affected servers are members of a replica set, a group of MongoDB servers that keep copies of the same data. One member, the primary, serves as the main server and handles all new writes, while the others replicate them. If the primary becomes unavailable, the other members hold an election to pick a new primary.

Researchers at Datadog Security Labs reproduced the crash in a lab and published their findings yesterday. On vulnerable versions, turning on authentication does not stop the two requests. An attacker cannot make the targeted member fall behind or win an election, or see when either happens, the researchers said.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-118383, is a use-after-free: the server ends up using memory it has already freed. MongoDB rated it 9.5 out of 10 on the CVSS 4.0 severity scale. The company said it found the flaw itself and was "not aware of any attempts to take advantage of this vulnerability."

Affected members include the shard and config server members of sharded clusters. A standalone mongod, a single server outside any replica set, is not affected.

Each affected branch has a fixed release, listed below and in the CVE record. Every earlier version in a branch is affected, back to the branch's first release.

MongoDB Atlas clusters automatically receive fixed versions during maintenance, the company said in its security announcement. Customers who defer maintenance should apply the upgrade as soon as possible.

Self-managed deployments need the fixed release on every replica set member. After upgrading, check the version each member is running, including members in containers and any that were offline during maintenance.

The 8.2 branch is not among the affected versions listed, and its newest release is 8.2.12. But a proof of concept published on GitHub reports that 8.2.12 still exhibited the bug in a lab test using a test-only setting.

The 8.2 branch reached end of life on July 31, according to the company's lifecycle schedule. Past that date, a version no longer receives fixes, including security fixes.

Until a member can be upgraded, the researchers advise restricting network access to the database to only the systems that need it. That limits who can send the two requests but does not fix the flaw.

A member who wins an election first catches up by applying the writes it missed before it accepts new ones. The flaw is in the cleanup that runs when this catch-up step ends, according to the Datadog researchers' technical analysis.

The two requests are ping commands that carry a readConcern.afterOpTime value. Each asks the server to wait until replication reaches a certain point, and the server records a pending notification for it, called a waiter.

Planting the waiters does not crash the server. They do not expire, and stay in place until the member restarts, rolls back or steps down from primary.

The crash needs the member who received the requests to win a later election, even though it is behind another member. When catch-up ends, the cleanup runs twice, reusing memory that was already freed, and the new primary crashes before it accepts any writes. Once those conditions are met, the crash does not depend on winning a timing race, the researchers said.

In the lab, the researchers caused the member to fall behind and forced a failover themselves by using admin access to pause and stop mongod processes. Only the two requests came from a client without credentials, and that client could not write to the database.

On version 8.0.34, the member crashed with a segmentation fault, leaving the lab cluster without a primary. Another deployment might elect a new primary and keep running.

In the fixed version 8.0.37, the server rejected both requests as unauthorized at once, and the member kept running. One part of the fix lets only system users use readConcern.afterOpTime.

MongoDB says the flaw may also result in arbitrary code execution in the server process under certain conditions. In the lab, though, "we did not achieve code execution," the researchers said. Their results also do not show how often the attack would work in other setups.

The proof-of-concept code reproduces the bug in a lab replica set, according to its author. Its reliable mode requires a test-only setting that a remote attacker cannot enable. Its stated impact is a crash or memory corruption, with no claim of code execution.

The second part of the fix stops the cleanup from running twice even when waiters are already in place, the researchers said. They did not test that part themselves.

In the proof-of-concept lab test, which ran with authentication turned off, the fixed 8.0.37 accepted the planted waiters but ran the cleanup only once.

To look for planting or a crash, check the server's structured logs for these signs from the researchers' vulnerable run:

Log event: a COMMAND "Slow query" entry (ID 51803) for an unauthenticated ping carrying readConcern.afterOpTime that ended with MaxTimeMSExpired.

Log event: a member entering primary catch-up (ID 21359), then exiting it twice (ID 21363) in one transition.

Log event: a fatal signal or backtrace involving CatchupState::abort_inlock() after those exits.

A normal election or a single catch-up exit does not point to this flaw. The requests may also arrive before the failover, so check earlier logs from the same member too.

Whether the request fields are logged depends on logging settings, and the attr.remote field may show a loopback address instead of the client's real IP.

A newly identified state-level actor has used compromised mobile operators in Asia to intercept calls and texts, mainly targeting subscribers in Taiwan. Enea has watched it since early 2025.

Enea, a firm providing software for telecommunications and cybersecurity, named the actor SilentAir in its November 11 research, which also covers Liminal Panda, a group that has attacked mobile operators.

The company said it saw a possible but unproven connection between the two groups.

SilentAir Targets Taiwanese Subscribers

Enea is highly confident that SilentAir operated at state level. The actor launched Signaling System No. 7 (SS7) and Diameter attacks from hijacked equipment in operators across at least six Asian countries, hitting targets in a dozen more countries and territories.

The attacks came in waves, from a handful of subscribers to several thousand in a month, with quiet spells of months in between. Interception accounted for 18.30% of SilentAir's activity, against 2.07% for the surveillance companies behind most signaling attacks.

For some targets, two-factor authentication (2FA) codes arrived moments after interception began, which Enea said showed an aim of breaking into their other accounts. Most of its other activity was silent SMS, texts that never show on the phone, sent largely to Taiwanese users around midnight.

Enea linked SilentAir to China-nexus operations with low confidence, citing the Taiwan focus, the lack of Chinese targets, working hours matching China's time zone and lulls over Chinese holidays. Some targets were political and government VIPs.

Read more on telecom espionage: Singapore Takes Down Chinese Hackers Targeting Telco Networks

Liminal Panda Expands GTPDoor

Enea said its firewalls spotted and blocked GTPDoor and other Liminal Panda activity at several customer operators from early 2026, detecting several hundred attempted command-and-control (C2) exchanges.

GTPDoor, a Unix backdoor, hides its C2 traffic in the GPRS Tunneling Protocol (GTP), which carries roaming data.

Enea said it had seen at least five to 10 operators infected by Liminal Panda, directly or through strong indications, and believed the true figure might be several dozen, concentrated in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

It also found a new GTPDoor version that rode on GTP-U, the part of the protocol carrying user data. That traffic is far heavier and, according to Enea, less closely watched, and unlike the control side it carries over into 5G. Enea believed the new version mostly served as a fallback.

CrowdStrike linked Liminal Panda to China-nexus operations in November 2024, also with low confidence.

Enea said it helped customers clear out Liminal Panda and alerted operators hosting SilentAir sources. It said both groups had been set back for now, but warned the conditions remained for them, or others, to return.

In this article

LEGO has taken BrickLink offline after detecting unusual activity

The company has not confirmed a hack or whether customer data was affected

Users should watch for suspicious payment requests and avoid reusing passwords

LEGO collectors looking for a missing piece have a bigger problem to contend with: accessing the specialized marketplace BrickLink.

LEGO has taken BrickLink offline after detecting what it calls “unusual activity.” The company says it is investigating before bringing the marketplace back, but has not disclosed whether attackers accessed its systems or whether customer information was affected.

BrickLink allows users to buy and sell LEGO parts, sets, and minifigures, making it a useful resource for collectors and a business platform for independent sellers. LEGO acquired the fan-founded marketplace in 2019. Its disruption leaves more than unfinished builds on hold: sellers also depend on access to orders and their storefronts.

The BrickLink website previously said it would remain unavailable until at least Wednesday, November 11. That date has now been removed, with no replacement given.

We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform. Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink.

Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues.

This work is still on-going and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible.

Updated: 11th November 2026

According to the BBC, LEGO had not provided details confirming a hack or explaining whether customer data was affected.

Specialist LEGO publications reported that BrickLink went offline around November 5. An article published the following morning described a notice saying the site was unavailable while teams carried out “necessary work.” That report also noted that users could not access storefronts, profiles, order histories, or the Designer Program page.

In November 2023, BrickLink also closed down after it noticed what turned out to be credential stuffing attacks.

The BBC also reported the experience of a BrickLink customer who received repeated payment links for a limited-edition preorder she said she had already paid for. The dispute was subsequently resolved, and LEGO told the BBC it was not aware of wider payment issues. But there is no established connection between that payment problem and the activity that prompted the shutdown.

How to stay safe

Until we know what the issue is, it is hard to provide targeted advice, but users can take a few proportionate precautions:

Watch for unexpected account or payment messages. A request to “restore access,” confirm payment information, or resolve an urgent account problem deserves scrutiny, because these are common phishing themes.

Verify requests through an independent route. Use the official website or an established support channel rather than following links in an unexpected email or text.

Use unique passwords. If your BrickLink password is also used elsewhere, change it on those other services now. Use a password manager to generate and store strong, unique passwords. Change your BrickLink password once the site is available again.

BrickLink’s shutdown is disruptive, but the available evidence does not yet justify calling it a confirmed data breach. For now, the priority for users is to follow official updates, check unexpected payment requests carefully, and watch for scams exploiting the outage.

2a284e1cbb49.text: Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments. Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing. ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015. Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes. Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected. The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control. Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console. Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA. Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity. The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe. ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access. In a security advisory, the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family. It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit. ConnectWise stressed that the 400 environments were identified because they had the extensions installed, not because they were necessarily compromised. The company said: "At this time, we have found no evidence of a compromise of ConnectWise infrastructure or a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself." There's another nasty trick buried in SCKit. According to Huntress, the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it. If the technician connects through ScreenConnect, the toolkit attempts to transfer malware back to their workstation, steal authentication cookies, and use their access to infect other machines. That could give attackers a route from one compromised customer into others managed by the same IT provider. However, Huntress says it has yet to see that part of the attack succeed. "We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far," the researchers wrote. Huntress also suspects that some of the malware's C# code was generated using an LLM, pointing to unusually detailed comments explaining what the code is supposed to do. Apparently, even malware authors appreciate a little help with their homework. Both Huntress and ConnectWise are urging administrators not to investigate suspected infections by remotely connecting through ScreenConnect, since doing so could put the technician's own machine at risk. Administrators are being advised to use other security tools to investigate affected machines, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients, and check what commands have been run. Any malware left behind will also need to be removed before the machines are brought back online. Huntress warned on Reddit that some machines were becoming reinfected within minutes of being taken out of isolation because the malware had not been properly removed. Simply disabling the vulnerable extensions won't necessarily undo the damage, either. As ConnectWise warns, "Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints." And with the attackers already able to install their own remote access software, kicking them out could prove considerably harder than closing the door they came through. ®

fb298703ac38.text:
In his LABScon 26 keynote, Dino Dai Zovi, SVP and Head of Security at Adyen, argues that defenders can’t keep pace with AI-enabled attackers through software alone. He makes the case that the hardware-based security already protecting everyday payments can close that gap.

Using tap-to-pay as an example, Dai Zovi notes how a secure element in a smartphone completes a transaction that malware on the device cannot touch. At the same time, data from the UK’s AI Security Institute on autonomous cyber capability shows end-to-end intrusions that once took days or months are now approaching minutes, with open-weight models only months behind frontier models.

Arguing that the main risk from AI is not AI agents turning on humanity but humans using AI to achieve malicious goals, Dai Zovi proposes engineering for resilience using hardware-based controls. He draws on analogies with bank vaults and nuclear weapon safety principles to show how hardware controls have long contained risks that would otherwise depend on people or software behaving correctly. He then works through an AI cyber range on the assumption that none of its vulnerabilities can be patched, and shows how a handful of hardware boundaries leave an agent with nothing useful to take.

He closes with a question. If the technology to contain AI already runs at scale in systems used many times a day, should we choose to apply it?

This presentation is essential viewing for security engineers, architects and leaders thinking about how to defend against AI-accelerated attacks.

About the Author

Dino Dai Zovi is SVP and Head of Security at Adyen. He previously served as Head of Applied Security Engineering at Block, where he led security for Cash App and for Square’s expansion into EMV card payments, including the work that inspired the PCI SPoC mobile PIN entry standard. He is best known for winning the first Pwn2Own contest in 2007, co-authoring “The iOS Hacker’s Handbook” and “The Mac Hacker’s Handbook,” and co-founding Trail of Bits, Capsule8 and the Pwnie Awards.

About LABScon

This presentation was featured live at LABScon 2026, an immersive 3-day conference bringing together the world’s top cybersecurity minds, hosted by SentinelOne’s research arm, SentinelLABS.

3d7b45a0cca7.text:
Apple's HomeView, which debuts on Friday, is a smart home device—think of it as a an iPhone-Apple Watch hybrid sitting on your counter—that can be personalized for up to six people and connected to each of their iCloud accounts. Using ambient face and voice data, it is designed to seamlessly switch between users while maintaining each of their privacy. You can ask HomeView about your schedule for the day and what movie your friend recommended in a text, but you'll be stopped from asking about your roommate's travel plans or her texts from last night. The feature doesn't rely on one of Apple's battle-tested biometric locks, like FaceID or TouchID, though. Instead, it uses new “person recognition” technology built off of an Apple architecture for securing sensor data.

This is a key departure for Apple. On the one hand, the company has still been very careful to think about security and privacy comprehensively. Not only does HomeView check for your face and voice before accessing your data from iCloud, it is also designed like an Apple Watch to check that your iPhone or iPad is on the same Wi-Fi network as the HomeView and has been recently unlocked (with FaceID or a PIN). On the other hand, expanding the architecture used to process biometric data and authenticate users creates more opportunities for mistakes and potential vulnerabilities. And when it comes to attempting to access users' Apple data, both law enforcement and exploit brokers consistently go to great lengths to attempt to break the company's on-device defenses.

FaceID is built for the use case where a person is staring at their device head-on from less than an arm's length away. It provides reliable security that’s difficult to defeat because it stores your biometric data on a special, physically isolated chip known as the Secure Enclave—first introduced in 2013 for the iPhone 5s. The architecture is so robust that Apple also relies on the Secure Enclave as the foundation of a device's entire encryption scheme. But Apple concluded that FaceID wasn't the best fit for the HomeView, because it needs to bounce quickly between users and relies on AI processing, which can't all be squeezed into the Secure Enclave.

As a result, HomeView uses Apple's recently announced Secure Exclave (note the “x”) to handle the video and audio data the device uses to evaluate who is in a room at a given time. Apple says it has actually been laying the groundwork for the Secure Exclave for a long time—early versions of the architecture were already in place for the iPhone 16 and 17 and MacBook Neo. Instead of being an entirely separately chip, the Secure Exclave is a dedicated, memory-protected space in recent Apple processors. It is in Apple's latest S11 chip for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, as well as the A20 Pro chip for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

Even though the Secure Exclave isn't based on the tried and true Secure Enclave technology, Apple argues that it is robust and expands the company's ability to secure a range of features, including improving the security of existing mechanisms. In a blog post on Thursday, the company even goes into some detail about how it used the mathematical technique known as formal verification to vet the “microkernel” designed for the Secure Exclave.

“This work both benefits our newest features and strengthens the security of features we already ship, such as ‘Hey Siri’ detection,” the company writes in a blog post. “Our goal is to keep ambient sensor data secure even against highly sophisticated attacks.”

HomeView and the MacBook Neo also use the Secure Exclave to govern the indicator light that tells users when their camera or microphone is active. The goal is to isolate this process and the chain of command governing it to make it even more difficult for attackers to try to disable an indicator light when it should be on or stop it from coming on in the first place.

The HomeView's “person recognition” technology is simply not as comprehensive as FaceID, though, and it is possible that the technology is more susceptible to reconstructed 3D depth map attacks—and potentially voiceprint attacks—than FaceID.

Of course, you don't have to have a HomeView in your house. Or if you do, you can use it on guest mode or a less involved “personalized” mode that only incorporates things like your playlists for other users to access as well and doesn't access calendar or Messages data. But as Apple forges deeper into AI integration, HomeView's departure from FaceID provides insight into the scale of the changes Apple is planning.

7e4fdba1b4c5.text:
Lego Group has taken its BrickLink Marketplace offline after identifying “unusual activity” on the platform.

An update was posted on November 11 by the Danish toy firm which said, “Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink.”

The company is currently investigating the activity and said it needs to “fully understand” what has happened before bringing the site back online.

“That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues.”

It is not yet known how long the downtime is expected to last and when the service will be reinstated.

BrickLink is an online marketplace owned by Lego Group where independent third-party sellers can buy and sell individual Lego parts – like eBay for Lego. Lego Group acquired the online marketplace in 2019.

The Lego marketplace has previously found itself at the center of security issues. In 2022, Salt Labs investigated BrickLink and found API vulnerabilities that could have allowed an attacker to take over user accounts, leak personal data and gain access to internal production data. Lego resolved the issues after Salt Labs disclosed the issues to the toy firm.

In November 2023 BrickLink was taken offline for a number of days due to a suspected cybersecurity incident.

Professional Lego reviewer Jay Ong, who runs Jay’s Bricks Blog, covered the downtime and noted that users were prompted to update their passwords. However, in an email he received at the time of the incident, he was reassured that his BrickLink account had not been compromised.

An active threat campaign is combining port scanning, password guessing, and Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands to compromise exposed Microsoft SQL servers and deliver malware.

The attackers are using predefined username and password lists to brute-force into these servers and exploit their administrative capabilities to execute commands on the underlying Windows systems.

The activity highlights the persistent challenge of securing privileged access across complex and often legacy infrastructure, said Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security. “While internet-facing databases are sometimes the unintended result of technical debt or misconfigurations, relying on static, standing credentials is what turns that exposure into a critical vulnerability,” he said. “When administrative logins can be brute-forced, attackers gain immediate, unchecked control to deploy malware without needing a single complex exploit.”

The campaign delivers two distinct payloads: an XMRig-based Monero cryptocurrency miner that hijacks the compromised servers’ computing resources, and a Gh0st remote access trojan (RAT) variant that gives attackers remote access and capabilities such as keylogging and data theft.

Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Brute-forcing SQL logins to get Windows commands

The campaign begins with a Go-based payload named “dllhost.exe,” which runs the open-source Naabu port scanner, FortiGuard researcher Xiaopeng Zhang said in a disclosure shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Thursday.

The payload retrieves target IP ranges from an attacker-controlled server, converts them into CIDR ranges, and scans randomly generated addresses for systems with TCP port 1433 open. This is the default port used by Microsoft SQL Server.

Once reachable servers are identified, the malware records their IP addresses and launches a brute-force attack using a separate executable named “dwn.exe.” The tool attempts to authenticate with usernames such as “sa” and “admin,” alongside a predefined password list containing more than 2700 entries.

Successful logins give attackers more than database access, Zhang said. The malware executes a series of malicious T-SQL commands contained in a file named 2018.sql, using SQL Server’s administrative functionality to run commands on the compromised Windows machine.

Among other things, the commands enable xp_cmdshell, a SQL Server feature that allows database administrators to execute Windows command shell operations. The attackers then use it to download or extract executables into the server’s “C:\Users\Public” directory and run them.

Jason Soroko, senior fellow at Sectigo, said the campaign effectively turns a database login into a way to execute malware on the server. “Organizations should remove direct internet access to SQL Server, restrict connections to approved systems, and enforce strong, unique credentials,” he said. “Administrative access should be limited to accounts that need it.”

Soroko also recommended keeping xp_cmdshell disabled unless required and monitoring attempts to enable it.

A cryptominer and a Gh0st RAT come along for the ride

The malicious T-SQL commands deploy a loader that retrieves additional executables from the attackers’ FTP infrastructure, including a Monero cryptocurrency miner and a variant of the Gh0st RAT.

FortiGuard observed a payload, MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe, posing as a legitimate browser update but actually turning out to be an XMRig-based cryptocurrency miner. It uses the compromised server’s CPU resources to mine Monero and communicates with mining pools using a wallet address embedded in its configuration.

The Gh0st RAT variant was delivered through “Winlogon.exe.” The researchers identified functionality for keylogging, file management, data theft, remote shell execution, and process management, alongside more than 30 control commands. Its capabilities also include screen capture and remote desktop access through plugins.

The attack was found using multiple persistence mechanisms to maintain access. The initial payload creates a scheduled task running every 30 minutes, while the downloader establishes another task to repeatedly execute daily at 1 AM. The Gh0st RAT, meanwhile, adds itself to the Windows registry’s Run key, installs a Windows service and creates a scheduled task that launches it every 30 minutes.

Barney said cryptominers may serve as a distraction from the more serious implications of an intrusion. Attackers, he noted, can use mining activity as “a smokescreen for establishing long-term persistence through remote access tools.” FortiGuard said it provides detection coverage for the campaign through its FortiGuard IPS, Web Filtering, and Antivirus services. For those who aren’t its customers, the company shared a list of indicators of compromise (IoCs) to help catch potential infections.

Conclusion

This analysis examined a campaign that abuses exposed Microsoft SQL Server instances to deliver additional malware. The payload, a UPX-packed Go binary that uses the Naabu scanner, retrieves a target IP range from its C2 server, probes TCP port 1433 to identify reachable servers, and records each successful response in Result.txt.

The downloaded go.vbs starts go.bat, which launches dwm.exe to brute-force MSSQL logins using a predefined list of users and passwords. It then executes the T-SQL commands in 2018.sql on each compromised server. Those commands enable xp_cmdshell and download or extract a loader into C:\Users\Public. The loader, in turn, pulls additional malicious executables from an FTP server.

During my analysis, malware samples were downloaded: “MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe” is an XMRig miner that uses the compromised server's CPU to mine Monero; “winlogon.exe” is a Gh0st RAT that provides keylogging, screen capture, file management, a remote shell, and more than 30 control commands for remotely controlling the compromised MS SQL servers.

Check Point Research has identified active, in-the-wild exploitation of PHP2Shell, a vulnerability in PHP that also affects Check Point Security Gateways. In the observed incidents, the attacker exploited PHP2Shell to gain initial access, then used a local privilege escalation vulnerability to obtain root privileges and establish persistence.

Security fixes for Check Point Security Gateway and Management were available one week before the attack, on October 23rd. Only a couple of dozen unpatched systems, in a single region, were compromised in the observed incidents. Affected customers were notified in real time. Check Point Research, through its Incident Response teams, worked to remediate affected systems.

We recommend that customers install the November Jumbo Hotfix on all Management Servers and Security Gateways as soon as operationally possible.

Overview

As part of BLAST and our Frontier AI Readiness Program, Check Point continues to release monthly security fixes that include fixes for vulnerabilities and security hardening.

Recent security incidents, such as PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) and HTTP2Shell, also known as Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497), a Brotli decompression vulnerability affecting Node.js and other software, led us to release hotfixes that are now part of the November Jumbo Hotfix.

Check Point is reporting active exploitation of PHP2Shell together with a local privilege escalation vulnerability (CVE-2026-123039). Indicators of compromise are shared below to help customers investigate.

Observed Attacks

Check Point Research investigated the exploitation of a chain of PHP2Shell and the Dynamic CLI privilege escalation vulnerability against internet-facing gateways. Exploitation activity dates back to October 30 and was observed as active until November 4.

Initial access was gained through exploitation of PHP2Shell in the Mobile Access Portal. While a hotfix for PHP2Shell has been available since October 23rd, we included it in this November Jumbo Hotfix. The privilege escalation vulnerability was then required to elevate permissions.

This activity provided initial access to the customer network and, in many cases, led to a foothold in the network. In a limited number of cases, the attack also involved destructive activity and was ideologically motivated.

Check Point Research, through our Incident Response teams, contacted affected customers on the day the investigation started and worked to remediate affected systems.

Prioritize upgrades of internet-facing Mobile Access deployments.

12c69006eb43.text:
Key findings

Beginning on 30 October 2026, an attacker executed scanning and exploitation activity against organizations with unpatched Check Point Security Gateways, using Mobile Access portals with PHP2Shell as initial access followed by CVE-2026-123039.

The first wave, on October 30, targeted Israeli organizations and included destructive activity against some of them. A broader second wave on November 2 targeted organizations across multiple countries and sectors, with no evidence of destructive activity

In the investigated intrusion, PHP2Shell provided initial access, followed by privilege escalation through the DynamicCLI interface, tracked as CVE-2026-123039. The attackers then deployed PHP webshells, the persistent TSGA backdoor and its embedded TSProxy networking component.

The attackers pivoted from the gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt notes during the destructive stage.

TSGA and TSProxy are modified variants of PhiliKit, a malware framework previously documented in attacks exploiting Ivanti vulnerabilities. Both tools share distinctive code, configuration, and cryptographic material with the framework

Although ESET associated PhiliKit with China nexus UNC5221, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.

The note left during the destructive activity uses the Dream Security brand. Dream had recently published research on PHP2Shell exploitation of Palo Alto Networks devices by China nexus actors. While this timing raises the possibility of retaliation, the available evidence does not establish a clear motive.

Introduction

We have now confirmed that, in late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways. Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Following initial access, the attacker escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI IPC interface. The attacker then used privileged command execution to deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence.

A second scanning wave on November 2nd targeted some Israeli organizations previously targeted during the first wave, alongside additional organizations worldwide, with no apparent focus on Israel. Neither wave showed a clear sector preference, suggesting opportunistic initial-access attempts rather than sector-specific targeting.

Infection Flow

On October 30, 2026, the first signs of exploitation appeared on the targeted Check Point Mobile Access gateways. PHP session artifacts were created under /opt/CPcvpn-R81.20/tmp/, including session files containing the upload_progress_pwn marker associated with the exploitation activity. During the same window, the portal’s Apache/PHP workers experienced hundreds of segmentation faults, providing additional evidence of repeated exploitation attempts against the service.

Figure 1 – Infection chain

After gaining access to the Mobile Access portal, the attackers escalated privileges to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI interface. With privileged command execution, the attackers placed PHP webshells in <templates>, a directory used by the Mobile Access portal to construct its login pages. These webshells provide a way to send commands through the web portal, establishing a stronger foothold within the compromised environment.

printf <base64 Webshell> | base64 -d > <templates>/zz<random>.tpl

The attacker used multiple .tpl files with names matching the pattern zz*.tpl Each initially received a small command-execution shell, which was then replaced with a more capable version. The expanded shell requires the hardcoded key zz2026 and supports operating-system commands, PHP code execution, and file uploads. Uploaded files are saved to the fixed path /tmp/.up.tpl. The attackers subsequently issued commands to copy that file into the portal’s directory as challenge_render.tpl.

The attackers then moved from web-based access to a standalone passive backdoor, launching the TSGA malware (/tmp/CPconfigdaemon) in the background and redirecting its output to a hidden temporary log:

nohup /tmp/CPconfigdaemon >/tmp/.bd.log 2>&1 & printf started

When executed as root, the malware relocates itself and relaunches under the name slot_CPconfigdaemon in the boot persistence directory. The executable also carries a second component, TSProxy: an embedded shared library that it writes to /lib/libcpfwcommon.so. Its injection code loads this library into selected appliance processes, where it intercepts networking functions to handle specially marked attacker connections while allowing ordinary traffic to continue. This combines a persistent standalone backdoor with concealed access through existing appliance services.

The attackers then deployed the gogo scanner on the gateway to discover internal assets and services across the network and continued to move laterally to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, authenticating with the vpxuser service account. On the ESXi host, they staged the destroy_v6 wiper to /tmp/des wiper and executed it. Finally, the attackers left a note that accompanied the destructive activity named DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt.

Figure 2 – Destructive activity note

Technical Analysis

Webshells

The expanded PHP webshell requires a hardcoded key to access its command-execution, PHP-evaluation, and file-upload functions. It supports both plain-text and Base64-encoded, XOR-obfuscated commands, and saves uploaded files to /tmp/.up.tpl.

Figure 3 – Webshell code

Wiper

The Linux ELF wiper destroy_v6 accepts a target directory as a command-line argument. The optional -f flag enables fast deletion, while -w specifies a pipe-separated list of directories to exclude. The wiper recursively traverses the target directory, deleting files regardless of extension and skipping excluded subtrees. By default, it attempts to overwrite files with zeros before deleting them, fast mode skips the overwrite step. It also writes DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt to each processed directory. This politically themed note includes a timestamp and explicitly rejects ransom negotiations.

TSGA – slot_CPconfigdaemon

The TSGA implant, deployed as slot_CPconfigdaemon, is a Linux gateway implant with substantial Check Point-specific functionality. It provides encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection, and binary firewall-log tampering.

TSProxy

TSProxy is a Linux shared-library backdoor embedded in TSGA and dropped as /lib/libcpfwcommon.so and supports encrypted SOCKS-style proxying.

Tools relationship

Both TSGA and TSProxy are Check Point-specific components linked to the previously reported PhiliKit-associated toolset. PhiliKit is a passive backdoor and installer targeting Ivanti VPN appliances and was previously reported following the February 25, 2026 upload of a sample named philistine to VirusTotal.

TSGA and the PhiliKit implant have roots in Tiny SHell, and share a core set of remote-control capabilities. Both implement authenticated, encrypted communications through TCP port 11072 and the Unix socket /tmp/.p_sock. The analyzed PhiliKit build restricts its TCP listener to loopback, whereas TSGA listens on all IPv4 interfaces. Both provide interactive shells with pseudo-terminal allocation, configurable terminal dimensions and bidirectional input/output. Operators can execute arbitrary shell commands and Python or Perl scripts, retrieve their output, transfer files using operator-selected paths, and collect selected or full appliance configurations over the encrypted channel.

TSProxy shares distinctive configuration with libdssafe.so, the networking component embedded in PhiliKit package: identical operator credentials, transport secrets, three matching activation-selector digests, and the same TLS certificate and private key. These overlaps strongly support a shared tooling lineage.

Attribution

The implants delivered to the gateway, TSGA and TSProxy are part of the PhiliKit malware family, which has been associated with the China-nexus group UNC5221 and previous exploitation of Ivanti appliances. In addition, gogo scanner has also been reported in connection with Chinese-nexus threat actors exploiting Ivanti vulnerabilities.

The infrastructure IP addresses used by the attacker were hosted on LightNode VPS infrastructure, a service previously associated with activity by Chinese- nexus threat actors.

The scanning activity was concentrated between 00:00 and 09:00 UTC, corresponding to 08:00–17:00 in China and broadly aligning with typical Chinese working hours.

With all the above, the following attributes that appeared in the described campaign do not appear to fully align with known Chinese-nexus groups (and specifically UNC5221) motives and interests:

Destructive operation

Focus on Israel and wiper note in Hebrew referring to the Israeli-Palestine conflict

Philikit name derived from the malware internal name philistine

Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.

A flaw fixed in Node.js this week lets unauthenticated clients crash servers that use the runtime's built-in HTTP/2 support on the 24.x and 26.x release lines. A second HTTP/2 flaw can cause a server to send a client pieces of its memory, including responses intended for other connections.

Fixed versions were released for all three supported lines: 22.23.5, 24.22.3, and 26.13.1.

The crash flaw, CVE-2026-123863, needs only a default HTTP/2 server that replies before the request body has fully arrived. The Node.js project calls that behavior typical. The crash works over both TLS and cleartext connections.

The memory flaw, CVE-2026-123866, affects all three lines. From 24.22.0 and 26.9.0 onward, a client alone can trigger it. On 22.x and older 24.x and 26.x builds, it can still be triggered when the server itself closes a stream partway through a response, for example after an idle timeout.

A separate flaw in Node.js HTTPS servers, CVE-2026-123864, can allow an unauthenticated client to read memory from other connections, "including TLS private keys and other users' requests," the project says. It affects all three supported lines.

The flaw needs a handler that calls res.flushHeaders() before the request body has fully arrived and later calls res.end() with data. Reading the leaked memory also needs a route that sends back or stores a request body. Plain HTTP servers built with node:http are not affected.

The release fixes 16 vulnerabilities in Node.js itself, seven of them rated high. The other four high-rated flaws, and the servers they affect, are:

CVE-2026-123865: a client can make any default HTTP/2 server hold memory and file descriptors permanently, on all three lines.

CVE-2026-123874: a client can corrupt server memory on 24.x and 26.x when the server serves files with stream.respondWithFile() or stream.respondWithFD(). On all three lines, canceling such downloads can also crash the server (CVE-2026-123875, rated medium).

CVE-2026-126051: a client can crash a TLS server on 24.x and 26.x if the server uses the SNICallback, OCSPRequest, newSession or resumeSession hooks, or server.addContext().

CVE-2026-123872: on a TLS server with stricter client-certificate rules for some hostnames, a client approved for another hostname can switch to a stricter one during TLS 1.2 renegotiation without meeting its rules. All three lines are affected.

The eight flaws above are all in Node.js's own HTTP/2, HTTPS and TLS server code, so they matter where a Node.js process accepts those connections itself.

Updating to the fixed version for each line is the only fix in the project's security advisory. It lists no workaround for servers that cannot update yet.

End-of-life lines, including 20.x and 25.x, get no fix in this release, and the project says such versions are always affected.

The advisory does not report any attacks using the flaws. It also does not say whether servers that met the conditions for the HTTPS flaw should replace their TLS keys or other secrets after updating.

Five of the flaws, including CVE-2026-123863 and CVE-2026-123864, were reported by Chris Rohlf in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research, according to the advisory.

Google and Mozilla have released fresh Chrome and Firefox security updates that resolve more than 180 vulnerabilities.

The Chrome refresh fixes 83 security defects, including five critical-severity use-after-free issues in ServiceWorker, CSS, Layout, Skia, and Accessibility.

All the remaining 78 bugs are high-severity weaknesses, mostly use-after-free (24), out-of-bounds read/write (10), type confusion (9), uninitialized resource (9), and incorrect/missing authorization (8).

Google discovered 52 of the vulnerabilities internally, and Anthropic and OpenAI researchers reported 18 more. No monetary reward will be handed out for any of these flaws.

The internet giant has paid a $4,000 bug bounty reward for a high-severity use-after-free in V8, but has not determined the amounts to be handed out for the remaining 12 externally reported flaws.

The latest Chrome iteration is now rolling out as versions 157.0.8103.78/.79 for Windows and macOS, and as version 157.0.8103.78 for Linux.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Firefox 160 arrived this week with patches for 99 vulnerabilities, including 57 high-severity security weaknesses.

Most of the flaws are use-after-free, incorrect boundary, and sandbox escape issues. The browser refresh also resolved invalid pointer, privilege escalation, information disclosure, and same-origin policy bypass bugs.

Mozilla included patches for most of these security defects in Thunderbird 160, which landed this week with 103 fixes. Thunderbird 153.7, Firefox ESR 153.7, and Firefox ESR 115.45 also rolled out with dozens of vulnerability patches.

Google and Mozilla make no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.

An attacker has tested stolen access to more than 60,000 GitHub repositories and inserted credential-stealing code in thousands of them, several security firms report.

Aikido Security said the operation, which it calls wfx-loot, began on November 10. It identified roughly 4,800 compromised accounts behind probe pull requests submitted to 61,764 repositories.

The requests were used to establish whether the stolen access permitted changes to a repository. “The pull request does nothing by itself,” StepSecurity explained, noting that malware was subsequently deployed in repositories where the permissions and configuration allowed it.

Aikido found signs that the stealer ran in more than 1,800 repositories. SafeDep separately counted 8,093 public repositories that received malicious commits, a figure that does not necessarily indicate successful execution.

“The attacker does not exploit a bug in GitHub Actions,” StepSecurity noted. The intruder instead relies on valid tokens belonging to developer and bot accounts.

The attacker placed the malware in existing or new GitHub Actions workflows, shell scripts run by CI systems, and npm installation hooks. The npm method also poses a risk to developers who install dependencies while the malicious changes are present.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The script looks for GitHub tokens, repository secrets, cloud credentials and AI service keys. It also reads GitHub Actions runner process memory and has functionality designed to expand access and establish persistence in AWS and Azure.

The attacker usually reversed the code changes and deleted workflow runs to conceal the activity.

StepSecurity traced 173 probe pull requests to tokens issued to the Fly.io GitHub app. The firm said it could not determine how the tokens were obtained and had no evidence that Fly.io’s infrastructure had been breached.

Affected software releases include a Packagist package and versions of two Go modules.

Aikido identified similarities with October’s GhostAction campaign but assessed that the two operations probably involved different actors.

The security firm warned that organizations should assume all accessible secrets were compromised if the malware executed. Organizations have been advised to revoke compromised tokens, rotate exposed secrets, and check for unauthorized cloud changes.

Related: Notion Customer Data Compromised in Fireworks AI Hack

Related: 500,000 Active Credentials Left Exposed on GitHub

Related: Meta Says Hackers Took Code, Personal Data of 1,500 in GitHub Breach

Police in nine countries, working with Europol, took down servers behind the Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC malware operations this week and recovered more than 6 million credentials stolen from infected computers. Europol announced the action as the latest round of Operation Endgame, the international campaign against the services that give ransomware gangs their way into a network.

Those logins are what reach ordinary users and companies. The suspects sold credentials they had harvested from victims’ machines, and buyers used them for further attacks, ransomware among them. Victim data tied to CastleRAT will go to notification services including Have I Been Pwned, so people and organizations whose passwords were taken may soon get an alert.

Europol and private-sector partners took 235 servers and 257 domains out of the criminals’ hands. Gootloader lost 14 servers and 218 domains. CastleRAT lost 120 servers and 39 domains. StealC lost 102 servers.

Gootloader is a loader, malware whose job is to get onto a machine and pull down other malware. Its operators planted fake legal documents on compromised websites, often hacked WordPress sites, and visitors who downloaded them were infected. Those infections led on to ransomware and extortion. Besides the servers and domains, 681 infected websites were cleaned up.

CastleRAT is a remote access trojan, a program that lets an attacker control an infected computer from a distance. It has been known since 2025, and Europol says it was built to be hard to detect. Europol links it to encrypted data, crippled IT systems, and companies and other organizations forced to pay ransoms.

StealC is an infostealer that can also drop other malware onto a machine. It pulled passwords, saved logins and digital identities off infected computers so they could be sold and used for fraud. This week’s action against its 102 servers continues work against StealC that began in June 2026.

Europol is urging WordPress users to change their credentials, turn on multi-factor authentication and patch vulnerabilities.

Israeli-American cybersecurity startup Daylight has raised $80 million in a Series B funding round that brings the total raised by the company to $120 million.

The investment round was led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives’ Growth Equity, with additional support from Okta Ventures, Bain Capital, Craft Ventures, Vintage Partners, and Maple Capital.

Founded in 2024, with headquarters in New York and Tel Aviv, Daylight has built Aura, an AI-native platform that hunts for, analyzes, and contains cyber threats in real time.

Combining AI automation with human expertise, the platform continuously builds, runs, and customizes agents that handle day-to-day operations based on customers’ workflows, risks, and priorities.

Daylight provides these capabilities as part of a flexible service model. Customers can select the service to be fully managed, co-managed, or supported by forward-deployed engineers.

As AI agents handle routine operations, customers can use Aura to investigate their security environments, access security data, and manage security operations.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Daylight also covers AI platforms that organizations use, offering protection against prompt injection, risky MCPs, and rogue AI-driven activity.

“As these agents become more capable, they’ll fundamentally change how threats are detected, investigated, and contained, with expert security engineers implementing, governing, and continuously improving their operations,” Daylight co-founder and CEO Hagai Shapira said.

“At Daylight, we’re already bringing this vision to life through an agent-native model that combines the speed and scale of AI with the judgment and oversight of human experts. We’re building the foundation for a new era of security operations,” Shapira added.

The company plans to use the fresh funding to accelerate its platform’s development, expand its security and technology teams, grow its presence in the US, and enter new markets in the EMEA and APAC regions.

The federal, state, local government, and education sectors are under growing cyber pressure, and the attack surface is shifting to where they now serve citizens most. According to Check Point’s 2026 Cyber Security Report, government organizations faced an average of 2,680 cyber-attacks per organization each week in 2025, a 17% increase from 2024, making government the second most targeted sector worldwide. As government organizations move services online, deploy citizen self-service portals, connect APIs, and integrate AI into mission-critical workflows, every new capability creates a new entry point. A successful attack doesn’t just disrupt IT-it can interrupt essential services, expose sensitive citizen records, compromise internal secrets, and undermine public trust.

The data reflects that reality. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report recorded 3,634 public-sector incidents and 2,410 confirmed data disclosure breaches, with exploitation of vulnerabilities accounting for 40% of initial access, and personal data, internal data, and secrets among the most compromised. That makes runtime web application and API protection especially critical for government organizations running legacy systems, third-party applications, and public-facing services that cannot always be patched immediately.

Check Point has been addressing this risk inside government trust and compliance requirements since achieving FedRAMP Certification for its Check Point Platform for Government in 2025. Now Check Point is expanding its FedRAMP-Certified packages to include Check Point WAF, bringing prevention-first web application security, API protection, Bot mitigation, DDoS defence, CDN-integrated delivery, and GenAI application security into the same government-certified platform.

Security Built for Modern Government Applications

Government organizations no longer operate static websites. Today’s public sector runs digital citizen portals, API-driven benefit and payment systems, cloud-native applications, and AI-enabled interfaces that connect identity, records, contractors, and partner organizations across the public sector. This growing interconnection makes the application layer more dynamic, complex, and exposed.

AI is also transforming both the speed of attacks and the security model required to stop them. Frontier AI technologies demonstrate how vulnerabilities can be discovered and validated autonomously at unprecedented speed and scale. Attackers are already using AI-powered tools to generate payload variations and exploit weaknesses faster, making signature-based protection increasingly ineffective. As a result, pre-emptive, AI-driven prevention that can stop unknown attacks without signatures or emergency updates is becoming essential.

Modern Web Application and API Protection (WAAP) must secure far more than a single website or API endpoint. Government organizations need prevention-first protection across the entire application environment, including:

Pre-emptively prevent known, unknown, and zero-day web and API attacks before they reach the application

End-to-end API security with automated discovery, schema validation and authentication enforcement

Availability of critical services with strong bot mitigation and DDoS protection against automated abuse and disruption

Block GenAI application attacks including prompt injection, data leakage and harmful content

Simplify operations with centralized management that reduces tool sprawl and complexity across the full application stack

Check Point WAF brings all these capabilities into a single consolidated platform, purpose-built for the modern application reality that government organizations face today. By adding it to the FedRAMP certified packages, federal organizations can now secure public-facing applications and APIs through the same government-certified platform they already trust with the prevention, visibility, and control needed to protect modern application environments without adding complexity or managing separate tools for every risk.

Why This Matters Now

The public-sector application attack surface is expanding quickly as government organizations modernize services, expose more APIs, and begin adopting AI-enabled workflows. At the same time, AI is accelerating the speed at which attackers find and exploit those weaknesses.

According to Check Point 2026 Cloud Security Report, 70% of organizations run GenAI workloads in production, yet visibility has not kept up. Only 5% of organizations have full visibility into how AI is used, and just 14% actively enforce and audit an AI security policy.

PHP2Shell shows how fast the window closes. Two critical PHP flaws, each rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale, let an attacker run code on a server with one crafted request, with no password, account, or user interaction. Attacks started before the patch landed on October 21, 2026, and government organizations took sites offline to cope. Check Point WAF preemptively blocked PHP2Shell with no signature, rule, or configuration change.

This is why expanding Check Point’s FedRAMP certification packages to include Check Point WAF matters. It is not just another security product. It is a way to help public-sector organizations protect the applications, APIs, and digital services that citizens, employees, contractors, and partners depend on every day.

Available Through the FedRAMP Marketplace

Check Point is listed on the FedRAMP Marketplace, with Check Point WAF included in the certification, making it easier for federal mission owners to discover, evaluate, and procure the solution.

Branch Traffic Has Changed. Security Has to Follow.

A traditional branch was simple in nature: a location that connects back to headquarters where applications, data, and security controls were housed. Today the landscape is wildly different. A branch may connect directly to SaaS apps, clouds, data centers, the open internet, and other locations within the enterprise. And while all those connections are being made, often many at one time, employees expect video calls and cloud applications to perform just as well in the office as they do at home.

The branch itself has become more complex, too. Connected devices can range from printers and ‘smart building’ systems to specialized IoT equipment. Employees may also access AI applications and services directly from the network. And many branch locations are expected to manage all of this without dedicated security personnel on site.

Routing all that activity back through headquarters can introduce unnecessary latency and cost. However, without the right controls you’re opening yourself up to new exposure. The modern branch needs connectivity, protection, and resilience to work together.

Now is the Time for Connectivity to Adapt to the Application

Not every application needs the same network path.

Video calls? Highly sensitive to latency and packet loss. Large backup transfers? Often prioritize cost over speed. Internal business applications? Might need an encrypted route back to a data center.

Software-defined wide area networking (SD-WAN) gives organizations more control over those decisions because, rather than relying on one fixed route, SD-WAN can evaluate available connections and steer traffic based on the application, business policy, and real-time network conditions.

Multiple links can add another layer of resilience. If one connection degrades or fails, traffic can move to a healthier path automatically. But branch continuity depends on more than WAN alone. Firewall clustering and hardware redundancy can help keep both connectivity and protection available when individual components fail.

For businesses that depend on real-time transactions, voice and video, cloud apps, or always-on access to corporate resources, that resilience helps keep a local issue from becoming a larger business interruption.

See how Hybrid Mesh connects security across the distributed enterprise. Download Our CISO Guide

The Branch Has Become A Bigger Security Surface

Direct internet access improves performance, but it also changes where traffic needs to be inspected and protected. Branch firewalls increasingly need to secure traffic locally while supporting the same high-bandwidth applications they are helping accelerate.

And the risk now extends well beyond internet traffic: printers, cameras, building systems, medical devices, and industrial equipment can all expand the internal attack surface. Many of those devices were never designed with modern cybersecurity in mind, making visibility, segmentation, and threat prevention increasingly important inside the branch as well as at its perimeter.

And of course AI adds another consideration entirely. Employees may use third-party AI applications, agents, or connected tools directly from the branch. Security teams need visibility into that activity and the ability to apply policy, including controls that help prevent sensitive data from being shared through prompts. Meanwhile, attackers are using AI to accelerate and develop new exploits, malware, and phishing tools. Branch security therefore needs strong prevention at the point where traffic is already being inspected, rather than relying on another, additional layer.

Every Branch Should Be Easier to Operate

A distributed enterprise may have dozens, hundreds, or thousands of locations. Managing each branch as its own network creates complexity that grows exponentially with every new site that needs to fit within the existing architecture.

Centralized policy, zero-touch provisioning, network-health monitoring, and unified visibility can make branches easier to deploy and manage while keeping protection more consistent across locations.

That matters especially when there is no security specialist sitting at every branch. Centralized management allows teams to deploy and maintain protection across large numbers of sites without turning every new location, policy change, or connectivity issue into an on-site project.

Go deeper into secure SD-WAN, resilient connectivity, and modern branch security. Download Our Branch Security E-book

Bring Connectivity and Security Together at the Branch

Hybrid Mesh Network Security connects the branch with the security architecture protecting data centers, clouds, applications, and users across the enterprise.

Check Point Firewall combines advanced threat prevention with Check Point SD-WAN to help organizations protect branch traffic while optimizing how applications connect. AI security at the firewall adds visibility and policy controls for employee AI usage, while centralized management and zero-touch deployment help maintain consistent protection across distributed locations.

Integration with Check Point SASE extends that approach beyond the branch, helping connect users and locations to the applications and resources they need while keeping branch security part of the broader enterprise architecture.

Organizations who prefer a hybrid security approach can benefit from a hybrid SASE deployment. This way, they can cater to remote users with cloud-based security (SSE) connected to on-prem SD WAN, and also protect office users through network firewalls embedded with SD WAN for optimized branch connectivity.

0f52fff49b5d.text:
What you will learn

How coding agents borrow the permissions of your CI/CD pipeline, why enforcement is thinnest in those environments and how to scope agents to the task, treat pipelines as privileged identities and check each action at runtime.

A coding agent working in PocketOS’s staging environment hit a credential error, found an unrelated API token and used it to delete the production database and the backups stored alongside it.

Nobody attacked anything, and according to the founder, all it took was nine seconds.

Most of the conversation about coding agents is about the code they write, but engineering and security leaders need to be able to say what an agent can set in motion, and whose authority it uses when it does.

Enforcement is thinnest where AI agents do their work

In Delinea’s 2026 Identity Security Report, Fall Edition, 2,254 IT and security leaders told us where AI access is checked at the moment of action, before the action runs. CI/CD pipelines came in at 35% and Kubernetes at 28%, the lowest of the six environments we asked about. And 47% of organizations lack enforcement at the moment of action across at least two of the six.

Those are the environments developers hand off to agents first, and they're where deploy roles, cluster permissions, and production credentials live.

The agent doesn’t need the prod credential

Say you ask an agent to bump a service in staging. It updates the deploy workflow and opens a pull request. On GitHub, a pull request from a branch in the same repo runs the workflow as modified in that PR. If the workflow can pick up the pipeline’s cloud role, and that role reaches prod as well as staging, the agent’s edit now has production authority behind it.

The agent never touched a prod credential. It borrowed the pipeline’s.

Over-scoped CI roles were a problem long before agents showed up. Workflows branch too, but someone wrote and reviewed every branch. An agent can write a new one and trigger it in the same session.

Permissions that were safe for a predictable job become much broader once the identity using them can improvise

Identity has to follow the action

Security teams already know how to limit privileged access. Agents need those same controls applied to each action because they decide what to do next on their own.

Scope the agent to the task, not the person who launched it. You might be allowed to query the production database, but your agent shouldn’t inherit that because you started it. A policy that can tell the two apart lets your query through and stops the same query when the agent sends it.

Treat the pipeline as a privileged identity. The deploy role is what actually touches prod, so it deserves the scrutiny you’d give an admin account: one role per environment, and a human review before anything reaches production.

Keep enforcing policy after access is granted. Authentication only checks who's connecting, so a command an agent runs 40 minutes into the session goes through unchecked. Access should exist only while the task needs it, and each consequential action should be checked against policy before it runs.

Where Delinea fits

Delinea extends Privileged Access Management from the point of access to the moment of action. For the connections it brokers, including databases, servers, Kubernetes and MCP tools, access is granted just-in-time for the task, and in a brokered session the credential is injected at the proxy so it never reaches the agent. Each query, command and tool call is checked at runtime, and one that’s out of scope doesn’t run.

Start with one agent-assisted workflow

Pick one agent-assisted workflow and trace it to production. List each identity it touches, from the agent to the runner to the deploy role to the cluster, and what each one is allowed to do. Then find the point where a production action from a staging task would be stopped. If the answer is “we’d catch it in the logs,” you’ve found your gap.

Explore the findings in Delinea’s 2026 Identity Security Report, Fall Edition: The AI Enforcement Gap.

Zoom fixes two Windows Workplace flaws, including a critical bug that could let unauthenticated attackers remotely escalate privileges.

Zoom has released security updates to fix two vulnerabilities in Zoom Workplace for Windows. One is critical and could let attackers gain higher privileges on affected systems.

The vulnerabilities are:

CVE-2026-108186 (CVSS 9.6): An input validation flaw that could allow an attacker to gain higher privileges through a network connection, without logging in.

CVE-2026-108187 (CVSS 8.1): An origin validation flaw that could also allow an unauthenticated attacker to gain higher privileges remotely.

If successfully exploited, either vulnerability could allow attackers to increase their privileges without having an account or any special permissions on the affected system. Users should install the latest Zoom Workplace updates to protect their systems.

The first flaw was reported by the internal security team, while the second one was reported by the research shmoul.

CVE-2026-108187 affects Zoom Workplace for Windows releases earlier than 7.1.5, while CVE-2026-108186 impacts versions from 7.1.0 up to, but not including, 7.1.8.

The flaw can corrupt memory through a specially crafted message. Attackers could exploit it to target meeting participants, execute code without user interaction, steal data, activate cameras or microphones, and install malware.

In August, Zoom patched four vulnerabilities, including a critical zero-click flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-53413. CVE-2026-53413 is a memory corruption issue found by A Security that could allow a meeting participant to execute code on another participant’s computer.

Due to its impact, the researchers dubbed the flaw “Zoomsday,” it affects Zoom clients on all supported platforms and is linked to the proprietary protocol used by the annotation function. Zoom has now begun rolling out security updates to address the issue.

“Ⓐ Security, the Autonomous Offensive Security and Remediation Platform, discovered a critical flaw in Zoom that let an attacker take complete control of another user’s device during a live call. No click, no download, and nothing required of the victim but being in the meeting.” reads the report published by A Security. “The vulnerability is present in every version of Zoom on every device and operating system: Windows, Mac, iPhone, Android and Linux. The vulnerability exists in all versions up to and including 7.0.5.”

The flaw can corrupt memory through a specially crafted message. Attackers could exploit it to target meeting participants, execute code without user interaction, steal data, activate cameras or microphones, and install malware.

In July, Zoom fixed another critical Windows vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-53412 (CVSS score of 9.8), that could allow unauthenticated attackers to hijack user accounts. The flaw affects older versions of Workplace, the Windows VDI Client, and the Meeting SDK for Windows.

At this time, Zoom is not aware of attacks exploiting one of the above vulnerabilities. Users are recommended to apply the latest updates.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini
