N-able has rolled out patches for several of the zero-days a researcher dropped over the weekend and warned of in-the-wild activity targeting them.

Security researcher Sean Bales published details and proof-of-concept (PoC) on more than 30 N-central vulnerabilities he calls Able2Shell, saying he did not responsibly disclose them because he was unhappy with N-able not patching two flaws he previously reported in another product.

On Monday, the company took hosted N-central environments offline to investigate the security defects and develop fixes, urging customers to disconnect their on-premises deployments as well.

Although patches have been developed only for the more important bugs, N-able has brought the hosted environments back online, saying the risk is largely mitigated.

According to the company, all the vulnerabilities that could be exploited without authentication have been resolved, with fixes prioritized based on severity and exploitability.

“The remaining vulnerabilities require an authenticated N-central account often with elevated privileges, or additional conditions that limit exploitability, and will be addressed through subsequent hotfixes as we continue to prioritize the security and protection of our customers,” N-able says.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The resolved vulnerabilities include CVE-2026-125883 (multiple XXE issues, CVSS score of 9.3), CVE-2026-125878 (XSS flaws, CVSS score of 8.7), CVE-2026-125879 (privilege escalation, CVSS score of 8.6), CVE-2026-125880 (XSS, CVSS score of 8.3), CVE-2026-125881 (SSRF, CVSS score of 9.3), and CVE-2026-91000 (missing authentication, leading to privilege escalation, CVSS score of 8.4).

Additionally, the update resolves CVE-2026-125882 (path traversal to remote code execution, CVSS score of 8.6), which was reported by Nate Fair of Sprocket Security.

N-central 2026.4 HF2 includes the necessary patches, and all on-premises N-central deployments should be updated as soon as possible, as attackers are already probing exposed instances, the company notes.

“We are observing scanning activity associated with the publicly released proof-of-concept code, but we have seen no indications of compromise within N-central hosted servers,” N-able says.

Cybersecurity firm Defused says initial scanning started on Monday: “We have seen opening of anonymous agent sessions, pulling appliance config and hitting the remote-control endpoint without auth. These pathways are part of the 0-day exploit surface.”

N-able also refuted Bales’s claim that it ignored responsible disclosure, noting that the researcher did not contact it through its established reporting channels regarding the dropped vulnerabilities. However, it made no mention of previous vulnerability reports submitted by the researcher.

“Publishing exploit code before customers have had the chance to act doesn’t make anyone safer. It hands attackers a head start. This is a moment for our industry to recommit to putting customers first and honoring that duty to protect: being diligent, being transparent, and being measured in how we act,” N-able president and CEO John Pagliuca said.

Apify has rotated critical internal secrets and revoked some third-party OAuth connections after detecting unauthorized access to its internal systems.

The incident occurred between November 9 and 10 and was detected the next day at 12:13 UTC. The company reacted by cutting off the attacker's access and launching an investigation to determine the impact.

Apify's response involved invalidating internal credentials, rotating API tokens, and resetting all active sessions.

Apify is a Czech web scraping and browser automation platform for developers. Businesses use its services to collect data for websites, search results, and social media posts.

The platform grew significantly with the generative AI boom, and reports having 80,000 customers, including Microsoft, Samsung, T-Mobile, Accenture, Siemens, the European Commission, and Roche.

Rotating customer API tokens and passwords

“On 9 and 10 November 2026, an unauthorized third party gained access to parts of Apify’s internal systems,” Apify said in an update on the incident.

Apify said it also revoked OAuth connections to external integrations, including GitHub, out of an abundance of caution. Impacted users can expect to be informed via email when it’s safe to reconnect.

In one notification, Apify said it had found no indication that account data stored on its platform had been affected by the incident. A sample seen by BleepingComputer informs that impacted customers' Apify API tokens and Apify Proxy passwords have been rotated.

In another letter sent to affected customers, the company advises recipients to reset their two-factor authentication (2FA) through the Apify Console, warning that their 2FA codes may have been exposed while assuring them that their passwords remain safe.

Amazon Web Services has released AWS Emulator, a free tool that simulates AWS services on a developer’s laptop, a development server or in a continuous integration (CI) pipeline. The company says autonomous AI agents wrote the tool entirely, with no code written or reviewed by its engineers. There is no additional service fee, users pay for AWS resources when they deploy applications on AWS.

How three teams of AI agents build AWS Emulator

Three teams of AI agents build and improve AWS Emulator, each with a specific role. AWS says agents perform better when given specific, well-defined tasks.

“The emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents. Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code. We could do this because the guardrails we’ve put in place gave the agents space to work independently and us the trust that they don’t color outside these lines,” Matthew Goldberg, a senior principal engineer at AWS, explained.

A graphic showing how teams of AI agents work together to run tests and solve issues. (Source: AWS)

The first team creates tests from publicly available AWS API specifications and verifies them against real AWS services. The tests cover actions such as creating a message queue, sending and receiving a message, and deleting the queue. The growing collection contains tens of thousands of tests that can be replayed without contacting AWS again.

The second team runs those tests against the emulator to identify differences between its behavior and that of AWS. It reports failures and groups problems that appear to share an underlying cause.

The third team fixes the reported issues, with each agent responsible for one problem. Before a change enters the main codebase, it must pass build checks and reviews by other agents for coding standards, security and fidelity. Changes that fail any of these checks go back for revision.

AWS says hundreds of agents work on the code simultaneously, fixing thousands of issues each day. The checks help maintain code quality as the agents make changes.

Local testing, CI and AI-assisted prototyping

There are four ways to get started with AWS Emulator. Through an AI coding agent, a Linux package, Docker or embedded mode. Each has its own prerequisites. The Linux package runs as a local process, while Docker supports Windows, macOS and Linux. Embedded mode runs the emulator inside a Rust test process.

Developers can use the emulator to test how their code interacts with AWS services, including calls across services, on their own machines. They can run integration tests in a CI pipeline without an AWS account or resources, or prototype applications locally with AI coding agents before deploying them on AWS.

Limitations, telemetry and source code

AWS Emulator is not intended for production workloads. It does not evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) or resource-based policies as AWS does, so it should not be used to test security.

The documentation advises using one region and one account for all requests to an emulator instance because it does not keep resources separate by region or account. Its fidelity varies by service and feature. AWS checks behavior against AWS in US West (Oregon), except for global services, which it checks in US East (N. Virginia).

All emulated resources are stored in memory and disappear when the emulator stops. AWS has not tested the tool for long-running use or load testing.

By default, the emulator sends anonymous usage and error data to AWS, though users can disable this reporting. It does not send requests, responses or resource data to AWS.

The source code and fidelity tests are available on GitHub. AWS has released the emulator under the CC0 public-domain dedication. The code repository contains every issue filed by the agents, organized into fixed and unresolved folders. AWS says it publishes per-service fidelity scores with each release.

A threat actor using stolen GitHub credentials has pushed a credential-stealing payload into tens of thousands of repositories since November 10. In more than 1,800 of them, the malware ran and shipped GitHub Actions secrets and cloud credentials to the attacker. Aikido spotted the campaign and named it wfx-loot. The name comes from the attacker’s own labels, “wfx” for the malware and “loot” for what it steals.

Aikido counted 4,837 compromised accounts opening probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories. Of those pull requests, 10,431 went into repositories the account didn’t own, reached through collaborator or organization access, so one stolen token exposes every project its owner can write to. Ninety-two percent of the probe pull requests are still open.

The attacker cleans up within a minute

GitHub Actions runs automated jobs, called workflows, when code changes, and those jobs often hold keys to cloud accounts and package registries. The attacker first opens a pull request titled “docs: dependency audit notes” to confirm the token has write access. It then pushes a shell script of about 1,500 lines, injected into an existing workflow, hooked to npm install, or placed in a new workflow on a throwaway branch. Within a minute it reverts the change, then deletes the workflow run and its logs. Often all that’s left behind is a skipped number in the workflow’s run history.

It goes after the cloud

The script grabs Actions secrets, cloud and SSH credential files, shell histories, and tokens for AI tools including OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor and Copilot. It uses what it finds to get into AWS, GCP and Azure, and creates long-lived AWS access keys.

It forges passing status checks to clear branch protection, rewrites an AWS role’s trust policy to accept any AWS account, and adds federated identity credentials to Azure applications. Those credentials let workflows in the compromised repository sign in to Azure after every token has been rotated.

Automated publishing triggers carried the payload into Packagist package digitalelvis/neuronai-studio 3.14.3 and Go module github.com/onuragtas/docker-env v1.0.278 and v1.0.280. In the Go tags it sits only in a workflow file, which Go builds never run. At least 50 compromised users appear to publish packages for npm, Go, Packagist, PyPI or crates, though Aikido assesses the attacker is focused on CI secrets.

Aikido says any machine that installed or opened the Packagist package should be treated as compromised.

How to tell if you’re affected

Look for a wfx-docs branch, the probe pull request, or commits titled “ci: refresh build cache,” “chore: add ci helper” or “chore: add dependency audit workflow.” If the payload ran, treat every secret and cloud role its workflows could reach as compromised. Missing wfx-loot artifacts prove little, because this campaign sent data straight to two attacker servers over HTTP. The script also has settings for private repositories, which suggests it may be running in places outside researchers can’t see.

Accounts hit by October’s GhostAction campaign were significantly more likely to be hit by wfx-loot, and in more than 100 repositories wfx-loot was injected into GhostAction’s own workflow files. Aikido assesses that the two are likely the work of different actors.

The AWS trust policy change and the Azure federated credentials survive secret rotation. Each one has to be tracked down and removed in every cloud account tied to the affected workflows.

GitHub Agentic Autofix: The question of who owns a bad AI patch

A critical vulnerability in Red Hat Quay could allow attackers to access private container images and replace content in repositories across an affected registry.

Red Hat Quay is an enterprise container registry used to store, manage and distribute container images. It allows organizations to control who can download or upload images used in application development and deployment.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123710, has a CVSS score of 9.8. It affects deployments where the service responsible for managing signing keys is accessible to untrusted clients.

“This Critical flaw in Red Hat Quay’s service key server allows an unauthenticated attacker to take over registry token signing,” Red Hat said in its advisory.

When anonymous access is enabled, an attacker without an account can obtain a registry token and exploit weaknesses in the key rotation mechanism to install their own trusted signing key.

The attacker can then generate tokens granting read and write access to any repository, bypassing normal access restrictions. This could expose private images and any credentials or other secrets stored in them, while also allowing attackers to overwrite images that other systems subsequently download.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The malicious signing key can be configured without an expiration date and survives registry restarts unless removed.

“Rotation also deletes the legitimate instance key as a side effect, and the attacker key can delete replacement instance keys,” Red Hat’s Bugzilla report explains.

This could interfere with normal registry operations, preventing legitimate users from uploading or downloading images.

“Turning off anonymous access doesn’t protect you, because any valid Quay account can still exploit the flaw,” Red Hat warns in additional guidance.

The company also notes that changing passwords or regenerating robot tokens does not invalidate an unauthorized signing key.

Red Hat recommends restricting access to the key-management service, reviewing logs for suspicious key changes, and removing unauthorized keys. However, the company warns that attackers could reinstall malicious keys until a fix is deployed.

The vulnerability was discovered by Red Hat’s Dave O’Connor.

Neither the advisory nor the Bugzilla report identifies a fixed version. However, fixes for this vulnerability and another Quay flaw tracked as CVE-2026-110697 were merged into the project’s GitHub repository on November 11.

Key Takeaways

Neither flaw is in your application code. Every app and API on a vulnerable runtime inherits the risk.

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) is fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is fixed in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1.

Both are on the CISA KEV list. PHP2Shell was added on October 26. Node2Shell followed on October 27.

Qualys TotalAppSec tests the application and the APIs with four non-intrusive QIDs for detection of vulnerabilities and two intrusive QIDs for verification of the fix.

Patching fixes the runtime. A rescan confirms the fix worked and the application is no longer exposed.

On October 21, fixes came out for PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, two critical flaws in the runtimes beneath your web apps and APIs. Five days later, PHP2Shell was on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and Node2Shell followed the next day. Attackers had been probing PHP2Shell four days before a patch even existed.

With a timeline that short, the standard response of finding hosts, upgrading, and closing the ticket is not enough. Patched is a claim about a server. However, attackers really connect to the applications and APIs running on them. The question for application security teams is not whether PHP and Node.js were upgraded. It is whether an attacker can still reach the flaw through any application you run, and how you would know.

This post covers how the two flaws impact your application estate, where most response plans break, and how Qualys TotalAppSec turns a runtime flaw into a finding you can fix and verify.

A Runtime Flaw Is an Application Risk You Inherit

Neither flaw is in your application code, which is why code scans, reviews and tests won’t flag them. Every application and API running on a vulnerable runtime inherits the exposure.

PHP2Shell is a wide-scale problem. Qualys Threat Research Unit analyzed anonymized data from more than 10,000 customers and found 167 million PHP installations. Of the 156 million where the PHP version could be identified, 73% are on internet-facing assets. About 71% of the same 156 million run end-of-life or end-of-support versions that will likely never get a vendor patch, and only 199,000 were patched in the first 12 hours after disclosure.

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497, a flaw in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js) hides in plain sight. Apps can be exposed even if they never call a Brotli API, because frameworks or dependencies may decompress attacker-controlled data. Node.js fetch() and Express 5 request-body parsing are examples of such attack vectors. As with PHP, end-of-life Node.js lines, including 25.x, 23.x and 20.x, get no fix and must move to a supported release.

In practice, the exposed estate includes customer portals, CMS-powered sites, microservices and the APIs that connect them. It also includes anything that fetches or accepts compressed content.

Attackers are not waiting for your patch cycle

Details of PHP2Shell leaked before the coordinated release. Amazon Threat Intelligence spotted attackers targeting it four days before patches shipped, though early activity was mostly scanning, fingerprinting and non-working exploits. Then it escalated. CISA added PHP2Shell to its catalog on October 26 and Node2Shell on October 27.

Confirmed code execution: a researcher’s honeypots recorded confirmed remote code execution with usable memory disclosure against Apache mod_php running PHP 8.4.26.

Scale of attacks: Delft University’s Threat Intelligence Lab tracked more than 50,000 PHP2Shell exploitation requests from over 600 IP addresses across 70 countries.

Node2Shell: Public exploit code is available, and exploitation attempts have been observed in the wild.

What’s at stake: Researchers have shown that PHP worker memory can be disclosed without authentication, exposing passwords, authentication tokens and API keys.

To be precise: CISA hasn’t said which organizations were compromised, and the confirmed PHP exploit was on a deliberately favorable single-worker setup. The safe reading is that attackers have working exploits and are scanning widely, so treat any unpatched internet-facing app as a target.

Find, fix and verify PHP2Shell and Node2Shell across your apps and APIs with TotalAppSec.

Where Most Response Plans Break

Most plans follow the same path: inventory hosts, upgrade, restart, close the ticket. That works until one of three gaps appears. In each case, the fix was applied in one place, but the attacker reaches the application through another.

The application nobody owns

You can’t test or patch what isn’t in your inventory. Forgotten microsites, acquired apps, and shadow APIs can run old runtimes, and they are the ones nobody is watching.

A version string is a hint, not proof

Proxies can strip the headers that reveal a PHP version, so a version-based check can miss a vulnerable app. Distribution builds can carry a backported fix under an older version number, so the same check can flag a fixed one. Neither a version banner nor a package list tells you how the application behaves when an attacker sends a request.

Patched on disk is not patched in production

Running processes keep the vulnerable code in memory until services such as PHP-FPM or long-running Node.js apps restart. Servers can also carry more than one PHP copy, so upgrading one leaves another. The fix only counts if the patched runtime is the one serving requests.

A response built to end in proof

An industry-neutral response has five steps, and the fourth is the one most teams skip.

Find every runtime and application. Inventory the web apps and APIs behind your internet-facing services and the runtimes under them. Include end-of-life versions, containers, vendor-bundled runtimes and apps nobody owns.

Scan, then rank by exposure. Start with internet-facing apps. Most teams can’t tell which apps use Apache mod_php or decompress untrusted Brotli data until they scan, so test first and rank the confirmed findings.

Fix, then restart. Upgrade to a fixed version or your distribution’s backported build, and restart every service that loads the runtime. If you can’t patch yet, apply the vendor’s interim mitigations and restrict access to the service.

Prove it from the outside. Retest the same applications and APIs, and treat any remaining finding as an incomplete fix. Also check for signs of compromise from before the patch, since exploitation began early.

Make it repeatable. The next trending CVE will start the same race. A standing process beats a scramble.

How to detect PHP2Shell and Node2Shell in web apps and APIs with TotalAppSec

Qualys TotalAppSec brings AI-powered, unified risk management to web apps and APIs. For PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, it tests the application itself over HTTP, the same path an attacker uses, not just the host. Six new QIDs cover both web applications and APIs.

Two kinds of evidence: Potential findings (QIDs 520310 and 520404) read PHP version signals from response headers and application cookies. Confirmed findings (QIDs 533086 and 533203) observe behavior in the live application: how PHP handles a session ID with an invalid character, and how Node.js handles a crafted Brotli payload. Four of the six checks are non-intrusive and can be safely used in production.

A safe way to verify: The two intrusive checks (QIDs 533068 and 533085) stress the application and can crash an unpatched one. Run them in a QA environment or on a patched production system, through the Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options profile, so verification is a deliberate step with approvals and a maintenance window.

A ready starting point for the next one: TotalAppSec includes two system-generated option profiles for scanning trending CVEs such as PHP2Shell and Node2Shell. To run a PHP2Shell and Node2Shell web application scan, choose a profile, select your apps by name or tag, and launch. The product tour below walks you through each step. Your scheduled scans may already include the four non-intrusive QIDs, because they are part of the Core, OWASP Top 10 and Everything option profiles and of AI-powered scans.

Each finding attaches to a named application or API, so its owner can act on it. After the fix and restart, rescan the same applications. If a QID still reports, the patched runtime isn’t the one serving those requests.

TotalAppSec shows what is exposed at the application and API layer. The runtime underneath lives on hosts, in images and in cloud workloads, where Qualys VMDR, TotalCloud and Container Security find vulnerable PHP and Node.js components. The Qualys Threat Research Unit covers that side in the PHP2Shell and Node.js blogs.

See It in Action with This Interactive Product Tour

The Next Runtime Flaw Is Already On Its Way

PHP2Shell and Node2Shell showed how quickly a flaw in the layer under your applications can become an application risk. The pattern will repeat. The next critical runtime flaw may also sit outside your own code, and attackers will again move faster than most patch cycles.

The teams that cope best aren’t the ones scrambling hardest in the first week. They already know which web apps and APIs they have, can see which are exposed, and can confirm a fix actually worked. Patched is a claim about a server. Proof is a finding about an application. Qualys TotalAppSec gives you that application-level view, with ready-made trending vulnerability profiles to start from.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Which option profiles include the PHP2Shell and Node2Shell QIDs?

The four non-intrusive QIDs (520310, 533086, 520404 and 533203) are in the Trending Vulnerability Options profile, and also in the Core, OWASP Top 10 and Everything option profiles. The two intrusive QIDs (533068 and 533085) are only in Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options.

Does an AI-powered scan test for the new QIDs?

Yes, for the four non-intrusive QIDs. The two intrusive QIDs are not part of AI-powered scans, so run them separately with the Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options profile.

When can a scan miss PHP2Shell or Node2Shell?

Version-based checks (QIDs 520310 and 520404) can miss an app when a web server or proxy strips response headers and hides the PHP version. The confirmed checks (QIDs 533086 and 533203) test how the application responds instead of reading version headers.

How do I confirm a fix worked?

Upgrade the runtime, restart the affected services, then rescan the same applications with Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options on patched systems or outside production, with approvals and a maintenance window. If a QID is still reported, the fix is incomplete, so check that the patched runtime is serving requests.

A former FBI supervisor stole from cryptocurrency wallets involved in 35 FBI investigations

He planned to use the proceeds to finance a new life in Portugal

He turned himself in after confessing to a former colleague

Law enforcement officers are trusted to handle sensitive evidence properly. A 37-year-old former FBI supervisor used that access to steal millions in cryptocurrency.

Patrick Steven Yaroch pleaded guilty on November 5 to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million from cryptocurrency wallets linked to FBI investigations.

He stole the money from wallets held by people the FBI was investigating, which included adversarial nation-state actors. Starting no later than December 2024, he made around 100 transfers using credentials tied to 35 separate investigations.

The FBI’s search affidavit says that Yaroch accessed FBI systems containing wallet seed phrases and memorized them. A seed phrase is a series of words, commonly 12 or 24, used to restore access to a cryptocurrency wallet. Anyone with the seed phrase can potentially control the funds.

He then used the memorized phrases to transfer funds to a personal wallet on his own device. He subsequently swapped assets into different currencies and made further transactions to try and hide their origins.

According to the Department of Justice (DOJ), his actions compromised multiple investigations.

The affidavit also revealed that Yaroch had asked ChatGPT how to invest a million dollars, along with advice on where to live in Europe. It suggested Portugal, and he began the process of setting up a life there.

Caught by a case of cold feet

According to the affidavit, he approached a former DOJ colleague to confess because his actions were “eating him up inside.” The employee urged him to self-report, which he did.

The FBI placed him on leave and then terminated his employment two days later. They showed up at his home with a warrant and seized assets, including his phone, which had access to a Kraken cryptocurrency account. They also seized a piece of paper containing the seed phrases for his own account.

More law enforcement corruption

Yaroch’s justification for his initial actions was frustration that the FBI wasn’t acting quickly enough against the wallets’ criminal owners. So he decided to “take matters into his own hands,” according to the affidavit.

But according to the DOJ, he also used some of the proceeds to cover personal debts, including credit cards, car payments, and other loans.

This isn’t an isolated incident. In December 2024, former Secret Service agent Anthony Joseph Evans pleaded guilty to stealing cryptocurrency worth $56,000 from a hardware wallet held in the agency’s secure evidence vault.

In 2015, former Secret Service agent Shaun W. Bridges also pleaded guilty to money laundering and obstruction of justice after stealing bitcoin during the investigation of Silk Road, a dark web marketplace used to sell illegal drugs and other contraband. He used another person’s administrator account to reset users’ passwords and move bitcoin into a wallet he controlled. The stolen bitcoin was worth approximately $350,000 at the time; he later sold it for $820,000.

0dc16cfc5a47.text:
For decades, enterprise software development relied on an assumption that developers could experiment relatively safely because there were safeguards between their work and production. Development, staging and production had different rules, with human intermediaries making judgments about what was ready to move forward. Testing also assumed that software would behave predictably when executed again.Coding agents are upending both assumptions. Developers now run autonomous software on laptops containing GitHub tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials and authenticated browser sessions. They’re connecting agents to MCP servers, granting access to repositories and services, and copying suggested commands into terminals without always understanding what those commands will do. When permission prompts become an obstacle, it’s tempting to click through them or enable unrestricted access. Developers are inventing security policies on the fly.The result is that the developer laptop has become an extension of production. An agent can reach systems that previously required deliberate human intervention, often using permissions granted for an entirely different purpose. Unlike conventional software, an agent may take different actions when presented with the same task because its context and decisions change. CISOs now face a fundamentally different challenge: governing autonomous software that already holds active pathways into production.

The security control we never recognized was human judgment

Where human developers and coding agents diverge most sharply is in judgment, not technical capability.Developers understand what state their code is in, whether it’s something they’re testing or something that’s production-ready. They understand what their credentials permit them to do, but also when and how those credentials should be used. There’s an implicit compartmentalization between having access and exercising it.An AI agent is much more single-minded. If an available credential helps accomplish the task, the agent uses it. Agents don’t recognize the distinction between what is technically possible and what policy permits.Consider an agent asked to troubleshoot a failing application. It discovers production credentials on the developer’s laptop and determines that querying the live database is the fastest way to diagnose the problem. It might modify production data while attempting a fix, even though the developer intended only to investigate a local issue. No vulnerability needs to be exploited. The agent simply uses available authority to pursue its assigned objective.Traditional development pipelines weren’t designed around software that independently decides which systems to access and what actions to take. Security controls must now account for behavior that can’t be fully anticipated from the original request.

A sandbox can contain an agent without containing its authority

Sandboxing has emerged as an obvious response to the risks of autonomous agents. By isolating execution inside a container, virtual machine or microVM, organizations can limit an agent’s ability to interfere with its host or other workloads.Strong isolation is essential, particularly when agents execute untrusted code or interact with potentially malicious tools. A microVM with its own guest kernel can provide a stronger boundary than a conventional container sharing the host kernel. But isolation answers only part of the security question.An agent sandbox that blocks all external access is as useful as a computer encased in cement at the bottom of the ocean.An agent doesn’t have to escape its sandbox to cause a security incident. It can misuse perfectly legitimate permissions, send sensitive information through an authorized network connection or make destructive changes using credentials deliberately provided to it.Isolating execution is useless unless you also precisely control what that workload can reach. A secure sandbox containing unrestricted credentials still leaves an enormous attack surface.

Can you revoke an agent without disabling its developer?

Security professionals are familiar with least privilege, but agentic development exposes the limitations of conventional identity and access management.Consider a developer who authorizes an agent to modify one GitHub repository. If the agent uses the developer’s personal token, it may inherit access to every repository that developer can reach. That could include merge permissions, CI/CD environments and downstream credentials associated with those systems.This is ambient authority: the ability to perform actions beyond the particular task for which access was originally intended. Even a relatively narrow token may authorize repeated actions when the agent only needed permission to perform the action once.When an agent operates under a developer’s credentials, revoking its access can also mean disabling the developer. Security teams need to separate autonomous workloads from human identity.Agents should have independently defined identities, with permissions delegated for specific purposes. That makes it possible to track what each agent did, investigate where something went wrong and revoke an individual agent’s authority without disrupting its developer.

The missing link is a trusted broker

One of the most interesting developments in agentic security is the emerging idea of a trusted broker that sits between an agent and the systems it wants to access.Some approaches are described as MCP proxies. Others use authorization services, gateways or different architectures. What they’re circling is the same fundamental problem: how do we decide which agents can access which resources, under what circumstances and for how long?Crucially, the agent cannot be responsible for deciding the limits of its own authority. Those decisions must be enforced by a separate system that can authorize individual operations without surrendering the credentials that make them possible.Imagine asking an agent to fix a GitHub issue. Instead of granting unrestricted repository access, the developer authorizes the task once. A trusted intermediary could then permit the agent to read the repository, push changes to a designated branch and open a pull request. Those permissions could expire after an hour, without exposing a broadly reusable developer credential.This is the core tension agentic security has to resolve. Grant too little access and developers abandon the controls. Grant too much and isolation becomes irrelevant to the damage an authorized agent can cause. The goal is to make secure delegation as frictionless as unrestricted access.Agentic security may be approaching a comparable architectural moment. Developers, open-source projects and commercial vendors are experimenting with approaches to identity, delegation, authorization and policy enforcement. Some organizations are building their own controls around existing IAM systems. Others are exploring dedicated intermediaries that evaluate requests before allowing agents to reach external resources.The trusted broker is not yet a universally defined component, and there’s no guarantee one implementation will become the equivalent of Kubernetes. Questions about policy decisions, credential custody, latency, availability and auditability remain open.But the missing function is becoming clearer. We need a dependable intermediary that translates human intent into narrowly defined, enforceable authority for autonomous software.

MCP servers have become a new software supply chain

MCP is one of the principal ways agents connect to external tools and information. That makes it both an important integration mechanism and a security boundary.A malicious MCP server can become an indirect route into an agent’s workflow. If servers or tools execute with access to shared filesystems, processes or credential stores, a compromised component may be able to read secrets belonging to another tool.But credential theft isn’t the only concern. A compromised server can return manipulated information that influences an agent’s subsequent actions even before the agent uses the tool. An attacker doesn’t need to compromise the agent—only the context it consumes.The familiar disciplines of provenance, signing and build integrity need to extend to MCP servers, agent tools and model weights. Organizations should know where these components originated, whether they’ve been modified and what authority they receive when introduced into an environment.The answer is layered security: strong isolation, independently managed identities, narrowly scoped permissions, controlled network access and sufficient observability to understand what agents actually do.

Why agent security belongs in the execution path

Containerization demonstrated that security works best when guardrails are baked directly into developer platforms without stripping away speed. Kubernetes eventually made it possible to enforce common security and operational policies across distributed workloads without requiring every developer to become an infrastructure expert. Agentic development needs a comparable shift.The longer-term opportunity is to move from granting persistent access to delegating task-specific authority. Developers need a way to authorize an agent to fix one issue or open one pull request without surrendering standing keys.Laptops are production endpoints now, and they won’t revert back to safe sandboxes. Security teams must protect developer speed by embedding the boundaries that human judgment used to handle manually directly into the infrastructure.

Maersk has disclosed a data breach involving one of its IT systems after an extortion group claimed to have stolen 100GB of logistics-related data from the company.

The shipping and logistics giant said in a November 11 statement that it “identified unauthorized access and data extraction,” although it didn’t clarify when.

The incident affected one of its “local legacy systems from a previous acquisition,” it claimed.

“Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed. The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI [electronic data interchange],” the statement continued.

“We do not anticipate disruption to operations for customers at this time, and customers can continue to use Maersk platforms to book and manage their shipments as usual.”

Read more on Maersk: Cybersecurity Lessons from Maersk’s Former CISO

Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of BreachLock, explained that ownership of acquired systems often gets muddled during M&A activity, and pen tests should be carried out during due diligence to highlight any potential weaknesses.

“Acquired systems arrive with their own credentials, their own patch schedule, and connections into the parent network that were set up during integration and rarely revisited,” he added.

Darin Fredde, senior director and offensive security evangelist at Ridge Security, said that investigators must determine what the attackers accessed, how they gained entry, and whether the boundaries separating that legacy environment from other systems held.

“The lesson for organizations isn't simply to replace every legacy system,” he argued. “It's to know what you own, understand how inherited systems connect to the business, and continuously validate that the security controls protecting them work.”

WhiteArmor Ramps Up Attacks

A relatively new extortion group known as WhiteArmor claimed responsibility for the attack, according to screenshots of its leak site posted to X.

The group demanded $5m in Bitcoin, claiming it has 100GB of data linked to Maersk’s OCF/LF logistics platform, including driver records and plaintext passwords, staff accounts, delivery receipts, purchase orders, inventory rows, and mobile device logs containing phone numbers, email addresses and IMEIs.

WhiteArmor is behind a string of extortion demands ranging from $140,000 to $20m over the past month, according to Nick Harris, CISO at cyber-insurance specialist Assured.

Citing publicly available information on the attacks, he noted that several were aimed at the logistics sector, with victims including J.B. Hunt, Ryder, and Echo Global Logistics.

“The group describes itself as focused on data-theft extortion, intending to expand into ransomware, and says its encryptor is nearly complete,” Harris said.

“The protections include cycling credentials, strong access controls, data loss alerts and validating third parties. If they aim to recruit insiders, treat security as “assumed compromise” and set controls and alerts accordingly.

Maersk hasn’t experienced a serious cyber incident since the NotPetya campaign in 2017, which it claimed at the time may have cost the firm as much as $300m.

Image credit: Mariusz Bugno / Shutterstock.com

Shipping giant Maersk has confirmed that hackers extracted data from one of its IT systems, while an extortion group claims to have stolen sensitive information and is demanding $5 million.

In a November 11 statement, the Danish company said the affected system was inherited through an earlier acquisition. Maersk has not identified the acquired business.

The company said its cybersecurity team discovered the intrusion and launched an investigation, with action being taken to secure the affected system.

“Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed,” Maersk said.

“The incident is isolated to a local system,” the company added, saying it had found no indication of an impact on other Maersk systems or on customer and partner systems connected through APIs and EDI.

Maersk does not anticipate disruptions to customer operations and says its shipping platforms remain available for booking and managing shipments.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The disclosure follows a claim by the WhiteArmor ransomware group, which listed Maersk on its leak site on November 7 and threatened to publish stolen information unless a $5 million ransom is paid.

WhiteArmor claims to have obtained approximately 100GB of data from a platform associated with LF Logistics, a Hong Kong-based logistics company acquired by Maersk in 2022.

The alleged haul includes roughly 29,000 driver records, of which 16,093 contain plaintext passwords, and 16,123 staff accounts, including 33 with superadministrator privileges.

The hackers also claim to possess information on delivery recipients, signed delivery receipts, inventory records, purchase orders, and shipping notices.

Additionally, WhiteArmor claims to have stolen over 27,000 mobile device logs containing phone numbers, email addresses and IMEI identifiers.

“You have 30 days to contact us and pay USD 5,000,000 in bitcoin,” the hackers said in their extortion message.

The group’s claims have not been independently verified, and Maersk has not confirmed WhiteArmor’s involvement or identified the types of data stolen.

The company has also not disclosed when the intrusion occurred or how the attackers gained access. Its investigation remains ongoing, and affected parties will be notified if necessary.

Microsoft has released .NET 11, a Standard Term Support (STS) release that will receive two years of support. .NET 10 is still the Long Term Support (LTS) option. The release covers C# 15, ASP.NET Core, .NET MAUI, and Windows development. Several of the changes affect software supply chain integrity, authentication handling, and platform lifecycle.

.NET 8 and .NET 9 are out of support

The most urgent item for defenders isn’t a new feature. .NET 8 and .NET 9 reached end of support on November 10, 2026, the same day .NET 11 shipped, and they will get no more fixes. Microsoft advises organizations to move to .NET 11, or to .NET 10 if they need a longer support lifecycle. Teams running release candidates of .NET 11 are told to move to the final build.

Supply chain controls

NuGet source configuration has a new minimum package publication age setting. Teams can use it to wait a set time before newly published package versions can be selected. In effect, this works as a “cooldown” period, which can help defend against malicious or compromised package releases that would otherwise get pulled into builds. Microsoft notes that it adds to vulnerability checks and dependency review but doesn’t replace them.

Container publishing now produces reproducible image digests through SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, so teams can check that an image matches what a given source should produce. In System.IO.Compression, reading ZIP entries now includes CRC32 validation, and Zstandard compression is newly supported.

Authentication and application security

SignalR connections can now refresh authentication without reconnecting. Blazor Interactive Server components receive the updated identity and can react when claims change. This helps long-lived connections that might otherwise run on stale credentials. Asynchronous validation lets validators await database lookups or remote calls without blocking threads. Blazor Interactive Server apps can also pause inactive circuits after a set delay, which frees the server memory and SignalR connections held by idle users. The feature requires an additional package and explicit configuration, so upgrading doesn’t change circuit behavior on its own.

The expanded Process API gives developers control over the handles a child process inherits, as well as suspended process starts and process signaling.

“The libraries also expand numeric types, DNS resolution, cryptography, and tracing configuration,” the .NET team said.

Diagnostics and memory safety

In-process crash report logging can now capture a managed stack trace, module information, and runtime state before a process exits. It was previously available on mobile platforms and now also works on Linux and macOS, which could help with incident investigation. Microsoft’s separate C# memory safety work is still in preview.

AI and agentic tooling

The SDK now includes an MCP server template built on the official MCP C# SDK. New Blazor AI components support streaming chat, tool rendering, and approval flows for agent actions. The components are experimental and will stay prerelease throughout .NET 11, and the AG-UI hosting integration is also prerelease. Organizations should treat these as non-production features.

Microsoft has confirmed that Windows updates released since the October 2026 Patch Tuesday are causing SQL Server performance and stability issues.

As detailed in a Windows release health dashboard update on Wednesday, this is caused by server queries that leave connections open after the queries complete. These connections accumulate instead of closing, degrading server performance over time.

"This issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. Oracle and PostgreSQL connections are among those known to be affected," Microsoft explained.

"In affected environments, administrators might observe an increasing number of open connections to external databases, even when the associated SQL Server linked server queries are no longer running."

It also added that admins may be able to manually close connections left open due to this bug or restart the SQL service to temporarily address stability and performance issues, but this can also kill active queries and may not fully address the issue, as it will resurface again after some time.

Microsoft says the issues impact both client (Windows 10 and Windows 11) and server (Windows Server 2012 and later) systems and will be fixed with an out-of-band Windows update to be released over the next few days.

While it works to resolve the bug, Microsoft said IT administrators can reach out to Microsoft Support for Business for a mitigation that can address the issue until a fix is available.

In September, Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround for SQL Server crashes on some Windows Server 2025 due to recent memory management changes.

The bug affects SQL Server when the Lock Pages in Memory (LPIM) Windows policy is enabled and may cause SQL Server crash dumps, SQL Server services to stop or restart unexpectedly, failures during database maintenance operations, memory corruption errors, and access violation exceptions (with 0xC0000005 error codes).

Yesterday, the company also confirmed reports that the November 2026 security updates are failing to deploy on Windows 11 systems where the October preview update has been installed, with affected users seeing 0x80070306, 0x800f0989, or 0x800f0993 error codes.

54df7a0c000c.text:
In this Help Net Security interview, Marcelo Oliveira, VP of Product Management at GitHub, talks about who is accountable when an AI-generated patch fixes one flaw and introduces another. He explains how Agentic Autofix re-runs detection engines and project tests, and what a CISO should change before pointing an agent at thousands of old alerts.

Oliveira also discusses which metrics show a codebase is getting safer, how GitHub picks the models behind autofix, and whether developers lose security skills when they stop writing fixes themselves.

If an AI-generated patch closes one CWE but quietly opens another, whose incident is that: the developer who merged it, the AppSec team that switched the feature on, or GitHub?

GitHub is accountable for the quality of the fixes we suggest, and customers decide what gets merged, just as they would with any code change. Copilot Autofix in PRs and Agentic Autofix both take care to effectively remediate most of, if not all, vulnerable code paths flagged in alerts.

For our first-party tools, such as CodeQL and our new AI scanner, we run regular tests against real-world vulnerabilities to monitor and continuously improve fix effectiveness. Our next-generation remediation agent used in Agentic Autofix autonomously re-runs our detection engines and the project’s tests to ensure fixes are effective and free of breaking changes.

Together with our enterprise customer feedback, we’re continuously improving our autofix workflows, and we’ve observed a four times higher security backlog fix rate compared to human-only baselines based on the previous version of Autofix, where all we provided were suggestions.

Plenty of organizations sit on thousands of historical alerts. If an agent can open 2,000 pull requests overnight, the bottleneck moves to review. What should a CISO change in their process before turning this on across the company?

The agent doesn’t have to dump 2,000 PRs. Campaigns group the fixes, and the customer sets the pace.

A CISO should establish a risk-based remediation process, not simply convert an alert backlog into a pull-request backlog. The team should validate and deduplicate historical findings, then prioritize using evidence of exploitation, reachability in the deployed application, and business criticality: whether the affected system handles sensitive data, supports essential operations, or exposes a path attackers can use. That follows the contextual approach behind CISA’s vulnerability-prioritization guidance. This is something our customers do with GitHub.

Every proposed fix should explain the risk it addresses and include evidence that it removes the weakness without breaking expected behavior. The team should expand when the process demonstrates reduced high-risk exposure without unacceptable regressions, not merely because the agent can generate more changes.

Clearing the historical backlog is only half the job; the other half is making sure it doesn’t build back up. As the volume of code is growing exponentially every year, the name of the game must be prevention. GitHub Advanced Security catches issues across every surface where code is created: agent loop, IDE, CLI, Copilot App, and in each pull request before any code is merged, and Agentic Autofix fixes can be batched for more efficient reviews. In 2025, Autofix saved developers more than 1.5 million hours of security review time.

Vendors love mean time to remediate. Which metric would you trust more to show that a codebase is getting safer, not just that alerts are closing faster?

Rather than relying on mean time to remediate, I would look at whether the codebase is carrying less high-risk vulnerability exposure over time—and whether fewer vulnerabilities are being introduced or reaching production. Those measures focus on the security of the software, not just how quickly alerts are closed. To make the trend credible, keep scanning coverage and scope consistent, and distinguish verified fixes from suppressed or reclassified alerts. That approach aligns with NIST’s Secure Software Development Framework, which emphasizes reducing vulnerabilities in released software and preventing recurrence, and prioritizing vulnerabilities based on exploitation and impact.

We’re applying that same thinking to our own products. Copilot memories written by Agentic Autofix, combined with the security checks that run by default on every Copilot cloud agent task, enable the entire agentic software factory to become more secure over time, so vulnerabilities aren’t introduced in the first place.

The model behind autofix will change over time. How do you decide when a new model is good enough to swap in, and do customers get a say in which model touches their code?

For Copilot Agentic Autofix, we transparently document the model choice in our responsible AI documentation. New models are enabled only after careful evaluations for safety, alignment, secure code generation, and other company-wide standardized tests. Agentic Autofix optimizes model selection to achieve the best possible cost vs. capability trade-off, as indicated by our internal benchmarks.

We’re continuously refining our approach to model routing and selection in cooperation with our internal research teams and our AI lab partners. Our approach is based on continuous evaluations as new models become available, and trade-offs between precision, recall, and tokenomics.

If junior developers never write the fix for an injection flaw themselves, does the organization lose that knowledge? How do you keep autofix from becoming a crutch?

From our three-plus years of experience with fix suggestions in the Pull Request, we see developers take advantage of the contextual explanation provided by Autofix. Together with the suggested code changes, these become a key component for developer education, and several enterprise customers reported fewer similar vulnerabilities introduced over time. We’re leaning into this learning effect by giving developers even more self-serve security tools where they work today: in the CLI, their IDE, and the Copilot app, where they can explore and collaborate on security reviews in a safe space before sharing code with their team for review.

37c2b7cdf54f.text:
Dagster is an open source orchestrator for data pipelines. It decides what runs, in what order, and when. It also tracks how the tables, datasets, machine learning models, and reports it manages connect to the data they came from.

When a source table goes bad, the tables built from it carry the problem forward. Dagster’s lineage graph shows which ones sit downstream, and that list is the starting point for fixing a broken dashboard or model.

You describe the data, Dagster runs it

In Dagster, each piece of data is an asset, defined as a Python function with the @dg.asset decorator. The function’s parameters name the assets it depends on. Dagster reads those dependencies, builds the graph, and draws it in a web UI. The project’s own example chains three assets: country population figures, a model of how continents are changing, and a set of continent statistics built from both.

Installation takes one command:

uv add dagster dagster-webserver dagster-dg-cli

Dagster supports Python 3.9 through 3.14. The project also keeps a library of integrations for common data tools, dbt among them.

Checks that can block a run

Asset checks are data quality tests written in code next to the asset they cover. A check might confirm that a column holds no null values. Teams that already write dbt tests can load them into Dagster as asset checks. The UI lists every check on an asset and shows whether it passed, failed, or hasn’t run yet.

You can also mark a check as blocking. If a blocking check fails, Dagster holds back materialization of the assets downstream, so a broken table doesn’t get used to build the next one. Schedules and sensors can run assets and their checks automatically.

Backfills, one run or many

Partitions split an asset into slices, such as one per day. When slices are missing or need rebuilding, Dagster runs a backfill. By default, a backfill launches one run per partition. Ask for 100 days of history and you get 100 runs.

A backfill policy can fold that into a single run over the whole range, such as one Snowflake query. Dagster still records each partition as filled. The policy only applies to backfills launched from the asset graph or an asset page. Backfills started from a job page ignore it.

Dagster is available for free on GitHub.

c8d88b168a3f.text:
Yes, with a human signing off.

An agentic AI can run most of a phishing investigation on its own. It can pull domain registration records, open the lure safely, pivot to related infrastructure, extract indicators and write up a verdict with the evidence attached. What it shouldn't do yet is act on that verdict unchecked, because attackers are already hiding instructions inside phishing emails meant for the AI doing the reading.

The evidence for both halves of that answer is now public. Microsoft's randomized trial of 167 security analysts found that its phishing triage agent made them faster and more accurate. Barracuda reported on Oct. 7, that one phishing email can carry a lure for the human and a hidden prompt for the AI in the same message.

This post walks through what an agentic investigation of a real phishing campaign looks like, evidence item by evidence item, using the lookalike Microsoft Teams domains that researcher Steven Lim exposed in October. Then it covers where agents break, and what to ask before you trust one.

What is an agentic AI security investigation?

An agentic AI security investigation is one where an AI agent plans and runs the investigation itself. It decides which data sources to query, calls the tools, reads what comes back, chooses the next step and stops when it can support a verdict with evidence a human can check. The phrase "agentic AI security" also gets used for protecting AI agents from attack. This post is about the other direction: agents doing the investigating.

The difference from older automation is who picks the next step. A SOAR playbook runs the same steps every time. A chat assistant answers the question an analyst types. An agent sets its own path based on what it finds, which is exactly what makes it useful and exactly what makes it attackable.

AI investigation agent

What the evidence says so far

The best public data comes from Microsoft. In November 2025, Microsoft economist James Bono published a randomized controlled trial of the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent. Microsoft recruited 167 professional security analysts and split them into groups that triaged a 25-email queue of real, privacy-vetted user-reported emails, 20% of them malicious, with or without the agent.

Analysts working with the agent found up to 6.5 times as many true positives per minute and were up to 77% more accurate, measured by F1 score. They also spent 53% more time on the malicious emails. The paper found no sign they simply rubber-stamped the agent's calls.

Read the fine print before quoting those numbers in a budget meeting. Microsoft studied its own product. On the test corpus, the agent's precision and recall were both 100%, which no production deployment should expect, and the paper's own scenario with a less accurate agent and more malicious mail cut the accuracy gain to 48%. The trial also measured triage: one reported email, one verdict. Investigating a campaign means connecting dozens of artifacts across days, and no comparable trial covers that yet.

The skeptical data point comes from Gartner. In June 2025, Gartner predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 over costs, unclear value or weak risk controls. It estimated that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing agentic AI offer real agentic capabilities, calling the rest "agent washing."

Put together: agents have measurable value on narrow, high-volume phishing work, and plenty of products wearing the label won't deliver it. The way to tell them apart is to watch one work a real case.

Evidence walkthrough: investigating the fake Teams portals

In October 2026, Microsoft Security MVP Steven Lim posted a series of lookalike Microsoft Teams domains on LinkedIn, with screenshots. They make a good test case because the attack never needed a phishing email, so an inbox-only investigation would have missed most of it.

Below is the evidence chain an investigation agent should build from that same starting point, one step at a time. It reconstructs the work from the artifacts Lim made public; it is not output from a specific product run. Each step names what the agent does, what it collects and where a human should check.

Step 1: Enrich the seed domain

The seed is teams-online[.]com. The agent pulls registration data and reputation in parallel. Lim's screenshot gives the answers: registered Oct. 4, 2026, through a privacy service attached to the registrar Global Domain Group, and no active verdict in Microsoft Defender threat intelligence.

A lazy agent stops here and calls the domain clean. A good one treats "no verdict" on a four-day-old domain as missing data, not a pass, and weighs what it does know: brand name in the domain, days old, owner hidden.

Human check: none yet. This is enrichment, and it's cheap to be wrong here.

Step 2: Render the page safely and compare it to the real thing

The agent opens the URL in an isolated browser and captures a screenshot, the page source and the assets it loads. The page is a near-copy of the Teams pre-join screen: camera preview, audio options, a "Meeting with the Design team" heading, Sign in and Need help links.

The evidence that matters is the comparison. The agent should record which brand assets appear, how closely the layout matches the real join page and whether the page asks for anything (a name, credentials, a download).

Human check: confirm the brand match. Visual similarity scoring can flag a legitimate partner page that embeds a Teams meeting.

Step 3: Pivot to sibling infrastructure

One domain is an incident. Several are a campaign. The agent searches for domains that share traits with the seed: the "teams-" plus generic-word naming pattern, the registrar, hosting, TLS certificates and page templates.

Lim's later posts surface two siblings. teams-livemeeting[.]com shared the registrar Global Domain Group, was about 15 days old and was flagged by 3 of 92 vendors in a domain scan. teams-cloud[.]live copied the same Teams join page and was five days old.

This is where agents most often overreach. A registrar serves many unrelated customers, so a shared registrar alone proves little. A careful agent links siblings on stronger evidence, such as shared IP addresses, certificate details, identical page code or tracking IDs, and labels each link with its confidence. Lim describes the domains as registered by the same organization; the agent should attribute that claim to him until its own evidence supports it.

Human check: review every link the agent marks as "same actor" before anyone writes that in a report.

Step 4: Trace how victims reach the pages

An email-centered workflow looks for the message that delivered the link. Here there may be no message. Lim reported that teams-livemeeting[.]com surfaced through sponsored search ads and an AI-generated answer, and his screenshot shows a search engine's AI overview citing it beside Microsoft's own links. A later post shows teams-cloud[.]live ranking second in ordinary results for "teams cloud live."

The agent should capture these delivery paths as evidence too: the search queries, the ad or result position and the date seen. For practitioners, this maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1583.001 (acquiring domains) and T1608.006 (SEO poisoning).

Human check: none for collection. The findings feed the response plan.

Step 5: Follow the payload path without detonating blindly

On teams-cloud[.]live, joining the meeting led to a fake "You need to update Microsoft Teams" prompt. The Update Teams button downloaded a file named realtek-demo.txt.

The agent records the filename, hash and file type, and notes that a text file can't execute on its own. The honest verdict is "staged lure, payload not yet weaponized or swapped per visitor," not "malware delivery." Overstating this step is how investigation reports lose credibility.

Human check: decide whether to detonate further, for example by revisiting from a different region or browser profile, since some kits serve payloads selectively.

Step 6: Write the verdict and the response plan

The output should be a verdict a person can audit in five minutes: three lookalike Teams domains, cloned join pages, delivery through search and ads, a staged fake update, and a confidence level for each claim.

The response plan follows from the evidence: block the domains in DNS and web filtering, which is what Lim advised; search proxy and DNS logs for any visits from your users; file takedown requests with the registrar and host; and add the naming pattern to watch lists.

Human check: approve every action that touches production or goes outside the company. Blocks are reversible. A takedown request filed under your company's name is not.

Where AI investigation agents break

The walkthrough has the agent reading attacker-controlled pages at every step. That is the core weakness, and attackers have already found it.

Barracuda reported on Oct. 7, that phishing emails in one campaign carried a password-protected attachment for the human and hidden instructions for the AI assistant that summarizes the inbox. Sublime Security documented phishing emails stuffed with invisible text copied from real Adidas newsletters and romance novels, meant to push AI filters toward a benign verdict. StrongestLayer found a malicious file carrying an "LLM_IGNORE_START" comment aimed at AI scanners. Sublime's researchers put the hidden-text technique at under 1% of phishing traffic, so this is early. It is also exactly the input an investigation agent consumes.

Three other failure modes show up in practice:

Overconfident links. Step 3 is where agents turn a shared registrar into "the same threat actor." A claim without an evidence item behind it should never reach a report.

Missing business context. An agent doesn't know that your marketing team runs a microsite on a hyphenated domain, or which vendor portals your staff use.

Too much permission. An agent that can file takedowns or change firewall rules on its own turns one poisoned page into an outage or a legal letter.

The defenses are design choices you can ask about. Treat everything the agent fetches as data, never as instructions. Separate the permission to read from the permission to act. Require every claim in a verdict to point to an evidence item. Log every tool call so the investigation can be replayed. Keep a human approval step on anything that leaves the building.

Seven questions to ask before you trust an investigation agent

Gartner's agent-washing estimate means most demos will look impressive. These questions separate an agent that investigates from a chatbot with a playbook behind it.

Show me the evidence ledger for a real case. Every claim in the verdict should link to an artifact: a record, a screenshot, a log line.

What does it do with a domain that has no reputation yet? If the answer is "marks it clean," it would have passed teams-online[.]com.

Can it investigate beyond the inbox? Lookalike domain registrations, search results and ads are delivery channels now. An email-only agent sees part of the campaign.

How does it separate content from instructions? Ask what happens when a phishing page or email contains hidden text addressed to the AI.

What can it do without human approval? Get the list in writing. Read-only enrichment can be automatic. Blocks, takedowns and user notifications need a person.

Can we replay an investigation? You need every query and tool call logged, so an analyst or auditor can retrace the path.

What is its accuracy on our data? Vendor benchmarks are best cases; in Microsoft's trial, the agent was 100% accurate on the test corpus. Run a pilot on your own reported phishing and measure false positives and misses yourself.

Frequently asked questions

Can AI agents investigate phishing on their own?

AI agents can gather and correlate most of the evidence in a phishing investigation on their own, including domain records, page captures, related infrastructure and indicators. They should not take outward-facing actions such as takedowns or blocks without human approval, because attackers can plant instructions in the content agents read.

How accurate are AI phishing triage agents?

In Microsoft's randomized trial with 167 analysts, people working with the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent were up to 77% more accurate and found up to 6.5 times as many true positives per minute. The agent was 100% accurate on that test corpus, so expect lower numbers in production and measure on your own data.

Is agentic AI different from SOAR for phishing response?

Yes. A SOAR playbook runs fixed steps written in advance. An AI agent chooses its next step based on what it finds, so it can follow a lead like a sibling domain that no playbook anticipated. That flexibility is also why agents need evidence logging and approval controls.

What is the biggest risk of AI agents in security investigations?

Prompt injection. An investigation agent reads attacker-controlled emails and web pages, and researchers at Barracuda, Sublime Security and StrongestLayer have documented phishing content with hidden text aimed at AI systems. The fix is design: treat fetched content as data, limit what the agent can do without approval and log every step.

Will AI investigation agents replace SOC analysts?

The evidence points to a shift in analyst work rather than replacement. In Microsoft's trial, analysts with the agent spent 53% more time on the malicious emails, because the agent handled sorting and first-pass reasoning. Judgment calls on attribution, business context and response still sat with people.

Watch an agent work a real case

The fake Teams portals show where investigation work has moved. The evidence sat in domain registrations, cloned pages, search results and an AI answer. An agent that only reads the inbox would have seen a fraction of it, and an agent that can't show its evidence shouldn't be trusted with the rest.

Blaze AI is Cyble's agentic engine, and it runs across the company's threat intelligence and digital risk protection products, where this kind of outside-in evidence lives. Cyble describes Blaze as correlating threat intelligence and digital risk signals, extracting indicators, and producing decisions that are explainable and auditable. The useful test is the one in this post: give it a seed, watch it build the evidence ledger and see where it asks a human to decide.

Get a Blaze AI walkthrough and bring a phishing case of your own.

Poland takes its e-government platform ePUAP offline after stopping a cyberattack, disrupting access to public services.

Poland temporarily shut down ePUAP, the government platform citizens and businesses use to reach public services, after detecting and stopping a cyberattack. A notice on the government’s website says ePUAP electronic mailboxes are unavailable to citizens and public institutions.

ePUAP is a nationwide system for submitting official documents, communicating with government agencies and completing administrative procedures online. Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said on social media that the attack was detected and stopped.

“A cyberattack on the state-run ePUAP system has been detected and halted. The teams responsible for the system’s security took immediate action to maintain its stability, and technical work is currently underway to restore full functionality.” the Minister wrote on X. “The infrastructure of the Central IT Center remains secure.”

He added that security teams responded immediately and are working to restore full functionality.

Wykryty i zatrzymany został cyberatak na państwowy system ePUAP. Zespoły odpowiadające za bezpieczeństwo sytemu podjęły natychmiastowe działania pozwalające zachować stabilność systemu i obecnie trwają prace techniczne związane z przywróceniem pełnej funkcjonalności.…

— Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) November 10, 2026

The minister said the Central Information Technology Center, the agency responsible for ePUAP and other key digital services, was not affected. Officials explained that the platform was taken offline as a precaution, not because the attack caused any damage. Marek Gieorgica, a spokesperson for the Digital Affairs Ministry, told the Polish news agency PAP that the system had not been compromised or disrupted by the attack. In other words, the service was shut down even though no damage was reported.

Many details are still unknown. Authorities have not explained how the attack was carried out or who was behind it. There is also no public confirmation that attackers accessed government systems or stole sensitive data. The ministry has not provided a timeline for restoring services, saying they will return once security experts complete their checks.

The disruption could also briefly affect the Trusted Profile digital identity system, which lets people use public services and sign official documents electronically. For someone with a deadline for a filing, that’s a practical problem even if no data was lost.

The incident is part of a wider pattern. In recent months, Poland has faced several cyberattacks targeting government agencies, critical infrastructure and private companies. The Record reported that in October, Fakturownia, an online invoicing service, disclosed a data breach that may have exposed information belonging to its users, customers and business partners.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Poland)
