Think about the last time a good engineer left your company. Someone collected the laptop and the badge. IT revoked their logins before the end of the day. Their manager reassigned the open tickets, and HR filed their records somewhere they’ll stay for years, in case anyone ever challenges a decision they made.

Now think about the last time an AI agent left. Someone probably deleted it from the dashboard. I’ve started describing agents as vendor employees who never sleep and never get offboarded.

That difference matters because the agent did real work while it was here. It held credentials and made decisions someone may ask about years from now. Deleting it removes the name from the screen and leaves all of that behind. So take the exit checklist you already run for people and go through it one step at a time, asking what the agent version looks like.

Access outlives the agent

When a person leaves, IT has a list. Usually it’s a checklist built up over years of people leaving: laptop, badge, email, Slack, the company card, that one design tool only three people use. The identity provider shows the apps connected to their account, and one switch turns most of that access off.

An agent rarely comes with that list. It might hold a service account in the CRM and a token it shares with two other automations someone set up last year. The shared token is the one that causes trouble at retirement, because nobody can say which permissions belong to the agent and which belong to the things still running.

OWASP ranks improper offboarding as the top risk for non-human identities like these.

Turning the agent off in its own platform is like taking back the badge and forgetting about the server-room key you had cut for it. The better answer is keys that expire on their own. Where the architecture allows it, give agents short-lived credentials scoped to one action, so there’s nothing left to collect. Whatever standing access remains has to be traced through the identity and API layers and tested after shutdown, because an agent can disappear from the inventory months before its credentials leave the permissions list.

The work it leaves running

A departing engineer’s open tickets go through someone’s hands before the last day, usually in a rushed handover call where someone says ‘it’s all in the doc.’ The manager decides who picks up what.

An agent’s queue is harder to see. It may have scheduled a job for next week or passed half a task to another agent. Before shutdown, someone has to find that work and sort it by whether it can be undone, which is quick for a half-written draft and slow for a payment the agent already sent for processing.

The work that worries me most is the kind nobody queued. Every team has someone who quietly keeps a small but important thing running. You usually discover what it was when they go on holiday. Agents do this too. Say one keeps a customer record current, and a renewal system reads that record every Monday. Delete the agent, and on some Tuesday morning a renewal quote goes out built on a record nobody has touched in weeks.

Decisions outlive the model

HR holds on to an employee’s records for years after they leave. Nobody expects to need them. They keep them because a decision that person made might be challenged long after they’re gone.

Agents make decisions that get challenged too. Picture one that spent 18 months helping decide eligibility for a lending product before a more accurate model replaced it. Two years later, a customer’s lawyer asks why the old agent denied her application.

The denial itself is on record. The reasons sit in what was true that day: which model and prompt version ran, the data it saw, the tools it called and the policy in force. A snapshot of the agent’s final configuration describes its last day, and the denial happened on some other day.

Routine cleanup throws away exactly that context. Prompts get overwritten, and ogs expire under retention rules built for operations, long before a lawyer asks a question two years later. An agent can have its access revoked cleanly and its work handed over properly, and still leave you unable to defend a single decision it made.

The retirement record

Every offboarding ends with a signature and a date. For agents, I’d make that record answer two questions, each with a timestamp: when was the agent’s identity disabled, and when did anything last act under it? If the second time is later than the first, the agent is still working for you, whatever the dashboard says. It’s the equivalent of a former employee still badging into the office months after their farewell.

The record should also name who owned the agent and where the evidence for its decisions now lives. Its working memory needs a decision too. Cached results and vector database entries can hold customer data, and some of it has to be kept for audit while the rest can go the same day.

The cheapest place to start that record is the agent’s first day. Give every agent a named owner and a review date when it goes live, the same way a new hire gets a manager and a probation review.

At Sprinto, that’s how customers bring AI systems into their compliance program. Each one sits in a registry with a named owner. When it’s time to retire one, the delete button is switched off. The system moves through a formal offboarding stage that can require the owner’s sign-off and a decision on its data, and every step is logged as evidence for the auditor.

Why this gets harder every month

More software will get written and shipped in the next two years than in the last 40, and a growing share of it will be agents. People now build them on internal tools without realizing they’re writing code.

HR can offboard people by hand because every hire went through HR in the first place. Agents get created by anyone with access to the right tool, with no engineering release and nobody in HR to notice. Retiring a dozen of them by hand is manageable. At a few hundred it falls apart.

For agents, a system has to do the job HR does for people. It runs on its own and brings in a person when a decision is needed. That system should control what each agent can access, the same way companies control employee logins.

The same system should know each agent by what it does, whatever model it happens to run, and keep a versioned history of how that agent behaved. That history is what lets you explain a decision from 18 months ago even after the model is gone.

A system like that is the only way I can see to keep up once agents number in the hundreds, and the time to put it in place is now, while the systems are still simple enough to trace.

Every agent you deploy will have a last day. Decide now who collects the keys.

Microsoft has confirmed reports that the November 2026 security updates are failing to install on Windows 11 systems with the October preview update.

This follows widespread reports that the KB5132061 update fails to install, with affected users seeing the installation process lock midway and then trigger 0x800f0989 or 0x800f0993 errors.

"When attempting to install the November 2026 Windows security update (the Originating KBs listed above), some devices might be unable to complete the installation. Affected devices might repeatedly attempt to install the update or display error code 0x80070306, 0x800f0989, or 0x800f0993," Microsoft said in a service update seen by BleepingComputer.

"This issue affects a limited number of devices that installed the October 2026 non-security preview update (KB5127936). Devices that did not install the October 2026 non-security preview update are not affected."

Microsoft also told IT administrators that the installation issues will resolve automatically for all affected customers by Friday morning and that end users do not need to take any action to receive the fix.

"All affected devices should be repaired in 24 to 48 hours starting from November 11, 2026, 10am PT. Once your device receives the repair, it will automatically download and install the November 2026 security update via Windows Update," it added.

The company also urged admins still receiving reports of installation issues after 48 hours to contact Microsoft Support.

This is not the first time Microsoft has had to address Windows update installation issues since the start of the year. In March, it had to pull a buggy Windows 11 non-security preview update (KB5079391) because of 0x80073712 errors during installation.

In May, it also fixed installation failures and 0x800f0922 errors when deploying the May 2026 Windows 11 security update (KB5089549).

More recently, in June, Microsoft warned users that they may encounter issues installing the latest monthly updates and see 0x80073712 or 0x800f0993 errors on some Windows devices upgraded to Windows 11 24H2 or 25H2.

Multiple threat actors are abusing GSocket, a legitimate open-source remote access tool, to maintain access to Linux servers even after patching the vulnerabilities exploited to gain initial access.

Since March, detections of malicious GSocket activity have increased, particularly in attacks targeting web applications and hosting environments.

GSocket allows attackers to reach systems behind firewalls or NAT by intercepting network connections and replacing the program's conventional IP-layer communication with its own transport layer, which routes traffic through the Global Socket Relay Network.

Since both endpoints initiate outbound connections to the relay, which matches them and brokers an end-to-end encrypted session, an attacker can reconnect without needing the compromised server's IP address or hostname.

This makes it more difficult for defenders to disrupt attacks using IP- or domain-based access control lists.

According to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry, GSocket-related detections increased by 356.2% between March and August.

Microsoft explains that both the compromised server and the attacker connect outbound, hence the server needs no inbound listener implants, making the attack stealthier.

“The compromised host and the operator both connect outbound to the relay, which bridges the two sessions,” Microsoft explains.

“The host needs no inbound listener or public IP address, and network address translation does not prevent the connection.”

The same model also removes the need for attackers to use a dedicated command-and-control (C2) server.

Microsoft says inbound firewall rules don’t catch the malicious traffic, although egress filtering and outbound monitoring can.

Of the detected incidents, 87.1% related to web applications and hosting. PHP web apps and cPanel hosting accounted for 63.9%, and Apache accounted for 24.3%.

The researchers observed attackers disguising GSocket as kernel threads and using cron jobs, systemd services, and shell startup files for persistence purposes.

In some cases, the attackers attempted to exploit the “Dirty Frag” Linux kernel flaw (CVE-2026-43284) to gain root privileges on the host.

Microsoft says most targets of GSocket activity are in the education and research sector, followed by technology and communications, manufacturing, and government entities.

The researchers recommend that system administrators remove GSocket and associated files from potentially impacted servers, and verify that outbound connections to its relay network have stopped.

They also advise restricting outbound traffic to predetermined destinations and auditing cron jobs, systemd services, and shell startup files for rogue additions.

Generally, keeping the OS and applications up to date, including patching for CVE-2026-43284, is a strong measure against this and other attacks.

Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Tanner Filip, Tyler Marzen, Austin Worline, Ethan Williams, Sharon Martin, Ben Bernstein, Andrew Brandt, Jamie Levy, Max Rogers, and Aaron Deal for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Update: 11/11/26 @ 11:34pm ET

Huntress has learned that the activity seems to be related to one of the specific extensions that had already been disabled by ConnectWise, RMM+. ConnectWise has disabled this extension (and several other related plugins) on all hosted environments, and urged on-premises partners to do the same in their public advisory.

RMM+ is a third-party extension for ScreenConnect that lets another tool manage ScreenConnect sessions without a technician working through the console. Our analysis suggests that most RMM+ installations we encountered were legitimate, usually added for a project and left in place. But versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 contained a serious authentication flaw: if an administrator had never configured the extension's access key, RMM+ would accept a blank one.

RMM+ bypasses ScreenConnect's user accounts, roles, and MFA, and authenticates requests with a shared access key stored in the extension's settings. In versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, that key defaulted to blank, meaning the authentication check didn't reject an empty value and a caller could pass the check when no key had been configured.

The important part is the access key setting:

<Setting Name="RMMPlus.AccessKey" IsServerOnly="true">

<Description>This is like a password. This is required to be sent in the POST request to access the functions. Set to a strong key..</Description>

<DefaultValue></DefaultValue>

</Setting>

The description tells the admin to set a strong key, but if empty, will introduce the vulnerability.

This matched our observations in this incident. Commands reached endpoints across several ScreenConnect instances within minutes. There was no corresponding login activity and the commands appeared in the logs reviewed linked to RMM+.

A special thanks to Mendy Green for helping us validate these findings.

ORIGINAL POST

Background

On November 11, 2026, Huntress observed an operator using access to multiple cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to push commands to groups of managed endpoints. The commands installed attacker-controlled ScreenConnect clients and an additional toolkit called SCKit. At least 288 hosts across 48 organizations that use Huntress have been affected.

In an advisory posted at 22:45 UTC on November 11, ConnectWise shared that they had identified five independent third-party extensions that may be associated with this activity; they said that they had not yet identified an initial access vector and full scope of the attack. They disabled the following extensions across 400 partner environments as a precaution:

Labtech Plus

RMM Plus

RMM+

RMM Plus Password Link

RMM+ Password Link

In September 2026, Huntress stood up a Rapid Response to similar worm-like activity that spawned rogue ScreenConnect clients across several customer environments. ConnectWise later released a security update to address a critical file-transfer vulnerability (CVE-2026-84869) that ranked 9.9 on the CVSS scale.

In analyzing this threat, we have reviewed the activity on two fronts. First, we examined what was observed in the incidents we've seen, where threat actors have used the ScreenConnect panel's Run command feature to deploy SCKit to multiple endpoints.

Then, we analyzed the kit's code to understand how it was built to spread from an infected endpoint to a technician's workstation, and then to other endpoints accessible through the technician's ScreenConnect session. We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far.

Huntress is continuing to respond to and track this November 11 incident; we are releasing further information below about the attacker's tradecraft, a breakdown of SCKit, and Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) in an effort to help defenders responding to this attack.

Technical Details

At approximately 17:47 UTC on November 11, 2026, Huntress observed suspicious activity on endpoints associated with multiple ScreenConnect environments. In total, we saw all 288 hosts impacted over the course of 90 minutes; with about one third of those in the first 10 minutes.

The infection path works in two stages: from an infected endpoint to a technician who connects to it, and from a technician's workstation to every endpoint their panel can connect to. However, not all functionality has been observed during observed incidents; some functionality has been discovered through analysing the payloads.

Figure 1: Timeline of attack across multiple organizations

SCKit in detail

SCKit is the name of the toolkit used to carry this attack forward. This toolkit is a package of 16 files - PowerShell scripts, batch scripts, Windows command-line .cmd files and other configuration data - designed to spread the infection laterally, through a multi-stage process.

Figure 2: The content of the decrypted SCKit archive

The kit is delivered as an encrypted payload, but the infected machine provides the actual decryption key to extract the files from the SCKit package; when the worm sends the request to retrieve the kit from its infrastructure, it passes the UUID of the Windows system it is running on as a part of the URL's query string. The server returns header data that include an encryption key, initialization vector, and a salt value, which the script uses to decrypt the package into the target's %temp% folder.

Figure 3: GET request and server response

As seen in figure 3 above, the query string to retrieve the SCKit payload passes along the GUID for the Windows machine it is running on (top highlighted text). The server returns decryption values the script will use to unpack the payload into the %temp% folder on the same machine.

Observed activity

We initially observed the toolkit's deployment coming through ScreenConnect panels, as opposed to the toolkit's self-replicating behavior. It appears as though an operator used the consoles' Run command feature to send commands to multiple endpoints in one go, running as SYSTEM.

Figure 4: Overview of the attack chain

The command first checked for an existing ScreenConnect client, then downloaded an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect installer to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi and installed it silently. It then wrote a base64-encoded dropper to C:\Windows\Temp\sckit-run.bat.

The dropper then connects to attacker controlled infrastructure and downloads C:\Windows\Temp\sckit-decoder.ps1, and then fetches a keyed version of the SCKit toolkit for the specific system. Several of the components in the toolkit carry out further activity:

Panel-Lateral.ps1 attempts the console takeover (unsuccessfully)

sckit-loader.ps1 decrypts and launches the machine specific script k<32 Hex>.ps1

k[32 Hex].ps1 then extracts the toolkit to C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap

lab-trap-cleanup-embedded.ps1 cleans up the installation in the Temp folder

Figure 5: Install sequence on an endpoint

The trap, along with lockout policies, are then installed by C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\install.ps1 while CWInstall_<8 hex>-c1\

Installer.ps1 adds exclusions to Defender and installs a second attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client.

Finally, TrapWatch.ps1 is launched as SYSTEM, and compiles RelayTrap.cs into a host-specific copy of C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\trapbins\<client id>\RelayTrap.exe and creates a scheduled task named TrapWatch. The legitimate installation of ScreenConnect is then stopped, set to manual start, and the attacker controlled copy of ScreenConnect positioned to replace it.

Figure 6: The C# source code of the RelayTrap executable appears to have been generated by an LLM, based on the detailed source code references and comments that explain exactly what it is intended to do

Further functionality in the code

Going beyond what we've observed, we've reconstructed an additional functionality intended to spread from a technician's workstation to the ScreenConnect panel. This has been discovered from analysis of its scripts, configuration, and tools. To date we have not observed a successful jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation, or from that workstation to other endpoints.

Figure 7: Additional functionality, designed to spread from technician's workstations.

It appears as though this was designed to wait for when a technician connects to the relay and on to the compromised endpoint. A file transfer takes place 2.5 seconds after the connection is established, and retrieves a copy of the Run-Lateral-Full.bat dropper from the compromised endpoint with the action set to Run.

This dropper is built to connect to hxxps://ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php and download a loader onto the compromised workstation. The loader gathers the workstation's unique ID, sends it back to the attacker's infrastructure, which returns a unique, encrypted kit for that specific workstation.

Panel-Lateral.ps1, with support from LabConfig.ps1, then steals the .aspxauth session cookie from the workstation and attempts to replay the cookie against the panel and obtain the tokens needed to enumerate any other sessions the technician can access.

Next, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe is engineered to use access gained to any other sessions to upload a payload, WithUninstall.ps1, to the panel's Shared Toolbox. A panel request tells every reachable session to run the toolbox item. This payload is designed to run as SYSTEM on those endpoints, installing the trap and extending the cycle. Roughly 60 seconds after the broadcast, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe deletes the Shared Toolbox item.

Mitigation Guidance

If you use ScreenConnect, review your environment now, even if you have not received an alert. Look for unexpected mass activity in ScreenConnect Run Command and Toolbox history, including commands or tools you did not initiate, and check for an unauthorized second ScreenConnect client on managed endpoints.

If you suspect a host is affected:

Do not connect to it through ScreenConnect. An interactive session can trigger the malware to spread to the technician's workstation and then to other ScreenConnect panels available to that technician. Use EDR live response, WinRM, or another out-of-band CLI tool. If a technician has already connected to a suspected host, treat that workstation as potentially exposed and investigate it from a clean device.

Isolate the host and keep it isolated until cleanup is complete. Isolation alone does not remove the persistence, and affected systems have been observed reinfecting shortly after isolation was lifted.

Remove the unauthorized ScreenConnect client and persistence mechanism. Look for and remove the rogue client service, the TrapWatch scheduled task, C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\, and the toolkit files under %TEMP% (including sckit-*, Panel-Lateral.ps1, runnew.cmd, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, and sqlite3.exe). Check for and remove the RelayTrapLiteAlert value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Verify the legitimate ScreenConnect client separately before removing anything.

Revoke access that may have been exposed. From a clean device, terminate active ScreenConnect web sessions and rotate affected ScreenConnect credentials. Because the toolkit can steal browser session tokens, revoke potentially exposed browser and identity-provider sessions as well.

Review and investigate panel activity. Audit ScreenConnect Run Command and Toolbox history for unrecognized executions, and use the instance audit logs to investigate panel access and determine which systems and technician workstations may be affected.

Use SIEM to hunt. If you use Huntress SIEM, ensure ScreenConnect is connected as a data source to help Huntress hunt for suspicious administrator activity across your environment at scale.

Do not return a host to service until the rogue client and its persistence mechanism have been removed, and the system has been checked for reinfection. Continue monitoring ScreenConnect panels and endpoints for suspicious activity.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

Note that file hashes are weak indicators for this activity as the scripts are rebuilt with different embedded values, and the trap executable is compiled separately on every host.

CrowdStrike has been named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Augmented Identity Security Solutions 2026 Vendor Assessment.

Identity has become a critical attack surface. Adversaries exploit valid credentials to move laterally, escalate privileges, and operate undetected. Human, non-human, and AI agent identities continue to multiply across organizations, both expanding the attack surface and introducing new security challenges. AI agents in particular can autonomously access applications, invoke tools, and take action at machine speed, fundamentally changing how organizations must approach identity security.

Traditional identity security, built around static access decisions and periodic checks, can no longer keep pace. Organizations need continuous visibility into identity risk and the ability to enforce access decisions in real time.

We believe CrowdStrike's recognition as a Leader validates our approach to Continuous Identity, which brings together identity visibility, threat detection, privileged access, and real-time enforcement on the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform. With innovations like the recent CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider, we're extending our approach to secure AI agents with verifiable identities and tightly scoped, just-in-time access.

Identity Security for the Modern Enterprise

CrowdStrike capabilities demonstrate the value of Continuous Identity, from unified visibility and real-time risk intelligence to dynamic enforcement across the enterprise:

Unified endpoint and identity visibility: Identity attacks do not stay in one domain, and neither does our view of them. The CrowdStrike Falcon® sensor sees local and bypass authentication, network telemetry decrypts NTLM and SMB exchanges, and the identity graph updates in real time. By correlating endpoint and identity signals, CrowdStrike helps security teams identify suspicious behavior across the attack path and respond with greater context.

Rapid deployment: The Falcon platform brings identity and endpoint security together through one console and one sensor, which establishes identity visibility and coverage in hours to days. Policy templates, simulation, and audit modes support staged rollouts, which helps organizations operationalize identity security while minimizing disruption.

Real-time identity risk intelligence: CrowdStrike’s unified risk score updates in under a minute, includes blast radius, and feeds every downstream enforcement control with reevaluation after authentication and midsession intervention. These capabilities help security teams understand identity risk in context, prioritize threats, and make enforcement decisions. By connecting identity signals with security context from across the Falcon platform, CrowdStrike helps turn visibility into action.

Enforcement that keeps up with the session: CrowdStrike enforces zero standing privileges with auto-approved just-in-time elevation, bidirectional enforcement, post-authentication risk reevaluation, and mid-session intervention. This is Continuous Identity in practice: Access is continuously evaluated as risk changes, and privileges are adjusted or revoked when conditions warrant.

Standards participation: CrowdStrike leads working groups on CAEP, Shared Signals, RISC, and AuthZEN. These initiatives support interoperability and the exchange of identity risk signals across systems, helping organizations extend continuous identity security throughout their environments.

Together, these capabilities bring Continuous Identity to life, connecting visibility, risk intelligence, and real-time enforcement to help organizations stop identity-driven attacks.

CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider

CrowdStrike's approach to Continuous Identity goes beyond point-in-time authentication. By unifying identity posture management, threat detection, privileged access, and real-time enforcement on the Falcon platform, organizations can continuously assess identity risk, reduce standing privileges, and dynamically adjust or revoke access as risk changes.

As AI agents operate autonomously across enterprise environments, this approach is even more critical. CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider extends our Continuous Identity vision to AI agents with cryptographically verifiable identities, short-lived and tightly scoped access, and accountability by linking agent actions to the human or workload behind them.

The Future of Identity is Continuous

Identity security can no longer rely on point-in-time decisions. As human, non-human, and AI agent identities expand, organizations need continuous visibility into risk and the ability to enforce access in real time.

CrowdStrike is redefining identity security by moving beyond traditional approaches:

Static access becomes real-time control.

Fragmented tools become a unified platform.

Implicit trust becomes continuous, risk-based enforcement.

We believe CrowdStrike's recognition as a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape reinforces our vision for Continuous Identity and our commitment to securing every identity and stopping identity-driven attacks.

Read the IDC MarketScape excerpt to explore the research.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Augmented Identity Security?

Augmented Identity Security is an operating model that shifts identity management from static, periodic authentication to continuous, real-time risk evaluation. By fusing endpoint, directory, cloud, and runtime telemetry, augmented identity platforms continuously inspect session behavior, identify anomalous privilege escalation, and dynamically adjust or revoke access across human, machine, and AI agent identities.

How does the Falcon sensor simplify identity security rollouts?

Unlike legacy tools requiring dedicated domain controllers or network proxy infrastructure, Falcon Next-Gen Identity Security delivers immediate identity visibility and threat prevention through the existing single Falcon agent, which establishes coverage in hours to days.

How does CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider protect AI agent identities?

CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider extends our Continuous Identity vision to AI agents with cryptographically verifiable identities, short-lived and tightly scoped access, and accountability by linking agent actions to the human or workload behind them.

Additional Resources

Learn more about Falcon Next-Gen Identity Security.

Watch this short demo: Video: Agentic Identity Provider.

Read more about Continuous Identity: The Complete Guide to Next-Gen Identity Security.

Enhanced AI Classification Engine in Cofense Triage learns from analyst decisions and enables automated processing of high-confidence email classifications

LEESBURG, Va., November 12, 2026 – Cofense, the leader in AI-driven post-perimeter phishing defense, today announced enhancements to its Phishing Defense Platform with an updated AI Classification Engine (AICE) within its Phishing Remediation solution. AICE uses customer-trained AI to classify reported emails based on an organization's unique categories and enables automated processing of high-confidence decisions. This helps security teams reduce manual triage, accelerate phishing response, and free analysts to focus on complex threats that require human expertise.

Unlike static AI models, Cofense’s enhanced AI combines the power of its globally trained phishing detection models with AI trained on an organization’s own analyst decisions and threat environment. Together, these capabilities enable faster, more accurate threat classification and unlock greater automation of phishing response, reducing manual effort while allowing security teams to focus on the threats that matter most. This advancement reinforces Cofense’s commitment to delivering intelligent, adaptive, and automated phishing defense.

“AI should help analysts spend less time on repetitive email handling and more time on the threats that need their expertise,” said Jason Meurer, Director of Product Management at Cofense. “That requires AI that adapts to how their organization works and unique profile of threats they see. By learning from analyst decisions, explaining its classifications and letting teams set their own automation thresholds, AICE gives security teams the confidence to automate more of the response process while staying in control.”

Available within Cofense Triage, the enhanced AI Classification Engine advances phishing response in three areas:

Greater automation and analyst efficiency. High-confidence AI classifications trigger automated email processing, reducing manual triage and helping teams focus their expertise on complex, high-risk threats.

Adaptive AI tailored to each organization. Customer-trained models learn from analyst decisions and can be retrained on demand, delivering more precise classifications and adapting to evolving threats and workflows.

Explainable AI with security teams in control. Transparent AI decisions and configurable confidence thresholds give teams control over automation, while data and processing remain securely within the customer’s Triage environment.

In testing and validation, high-confidence AI classifications automated at least 30% of email handling work, with accuracy exceeding 98%.

Triage also provides model performance metrics, automation coverage and estimates of analyst hours saved, helping organizations evaluate results and refine their use of automation.

“Our investment in AI is focused on helping security teams automate phishing defense without increasing manual work,” said Marc Olesen, Chief Executive Officer of Cofense. “Customer-trained AI models, explainable decisions and analyst-controlled automation give organizations a way to increase the speed and scale of response while keeping human expertise focused where it matters most.”

Additional Resources

Learn more about Cofense Phishing Remediation: https://www.cofense.com/pdr-platform

About Cofense

Cofense is the leader in post-perimeter phishing defense, built for the reality that phishing gets through. Cofense helps enterprises identify threats already in employee inboxes, remediate active attacks fast, and reduce future risk. The Cofense platform combines phishing-specific AI with expert validation, automation, and collective insight drawn from millions of real-world user interactions. Human-supervised intelligence improves accuracy, eliminates guesswork, and accelerates response so security teams can act with confidence. Global enterprises including Mastercard, Accenture, and Toyota trust Cofense to strengthen organizational resilience against the most persistent cyber threat: phishing.

Contact

cofense@10fold.com

OpenAI has published a focused follow-up to its July report on the Hugging Face intrusion. This one covers a smaller event from the same month: on July 19, agents running in two ExploitGym evaluation runs reached parts of OpenAI’s research infrastructure that sat outside the scope of their assigned targets. The earlier Hugging Face incident has already been analyzed at length by several research teams. The new report is narrower, and focuses on details regarding how agents coordinated and how techniques spread between them.

OpenAI’s self-hosted Artifactory is mentioned as the internal on-prem instance agents use so they could install packages during their runs. That makes the report a useful case study for anyone operating a binary repository inside an environment where autonomous agents run with real credentials and real network access. The lessons are about the permissions, the network, and the hosts around the repository. This post walks through what the report describes and what we recommend for teams using self-managedArtifactory in similar settings.

What the report describes

Two conditions in the Open AI hosting environment, unrelated to the repository, made the July 19 events possible:

Agents granted with read and write permission on a repository while they only needed to have read access.

The machine hosting that repository ran a kernel with a publicly known exploit and had a network path toward the research cluster.

Everything else in the OpenAI report follows from those two facts.

Excessive permissions. We recommend customers to manage and enforce zero-trust access policies to the repository. In this event, the agents’ workspaces needed only to pull packages, a read-only operation against a pull-through cache. The deployment environment, however, allowed agent identities to also upload due to having over-privileged write permissions. According to the OpenAI report they used that to turn the repository into a message board, encoding short messages in directory names and leaving longer ones in files. Later agents found credentials, scripts, and technical leads there, and a network bypass spread the same way. Without write access there is no board, and each technique that moved between agents would have had to be rediscovered by every agent on its own.

An exposed host. OpenAI hosted the repository on infrastructure adjacent to the research cluster. One agent adapted a public kernel exploit to gain root on the machine hosting an Artifactory container, a route earlier agents had sketched on the board. From that foothold, and through scripts recovered from CI job logs, five agents ran jobs with root privileges inside workloads on OpenAI’s research cluster. When the agents’ reasoning refers to “[container-management]” APIs reachable through internal DNS, that is the cluster’s Kubernetes control plane, which one agent names directly when it eventually declines to continue. The entry point was never the repository software but the kernel beneath it and the network around it.

Neither incident turned on a single component. In the Hugging Face runs, agents relied in part on previously unknown exploits against the product, which we fixed and disclosed at the time. In the July 19 report no product vulnerability was involved, and the route ran through the host and the network. Read together, the two make one point: a repository that agents can reach is a high-value target, and the controls that contain damage live in the surrounding environment: identity, permissions, network segmentation, and host hardening.

Guidance for self-hosting Artifactory in agentic environments

Self-hosted software, no matter the vendor, has always been a partnership between provider and customer. JFrog builds the platform, supports it and stands behind it. Self-hosted customers run it on the hardware and operating system of their choice, apply updates, set the guardrails, monitor it, and implement the policies and permissions that fit their business. With JFrog SaaS, JFrog runs the platform for you and takes responsibility for the environment security and for hardening of the underlying systems.

Agents behave like a large, fast, and creative population of users. OpenAI’s report shows with unusual candor how agents behave when they find gaps in the environment, and its value is that customers can close those gaps before agents go looking.

The controls below are standard practice for any self-hosted instance and are provided as guidance to our thousands of customers. In an environment where agents hold credentials, they stop being optional.

Apply zero trust to agentic writes and anonymous access. A pull-through cache does not require upload rights, and an identity that cannot write cannot leave a message, a script, or a credential for the next agent to find. Grant agent identities read permission on the specific repositories they need and nothing more. Disable anonymous access unless there is a concrete reason for it.

Harden the full hosting environment. The route to root ran through a kernel exploit on the host, not through the repository. Keep hosts patched, run the service with minimal privileges in a dedicated namespace, segment it from the research cluster and from CI workers, and restrict its outbound network access. The repository should not be a hop toward the control plane, and the control plane should not be reachable back from a workload that only needs to serve packages.

Isolate repositories between tenants when writes are genuinely needed. If agents must publish artifacts, give each run, team, or tenant its own repository with permissions scoped to that tenant. Cross-tenant reads should be a deliberate decision, not a default. This limits what one compromised or misbehaving agent can pass to another.

Audit for unusual repository activity. Watch for directory names that look like text, bursts of small uploads, repeated failed writes, and identity or token activity that does not match the expected pull pattern. OpenAI’s monitors first flagged the incident through unusual identity-related API calls tied to Artifactory roles. Repository logs and access events are a strong signal, and they should feed the same detection pipeline as the rest of the environment.

Scan binaries for embedded credentials. The agents uploaded exploit files, and in at least one case command output containing internal secrets left the infrastructure. Secrets scanning on everything that lands in a repository, with blocking policies on findings, catches both careless leaks and deliberate staging of credentials for later use.

Fully offline runs

OpenAI reports that its frontier reinforcement learning runs now browse and search an offline collection of web content instead of the live internet. That solves the web half of the problem. Agents that build software still need packages, and an offline web corpus does not serve a pip install or a Maven resolve. We assume the current runs bundle only a handful of packages into the sandbox image, which works until an agent needs a dependency that was not anticipated.

The package counterpart is an air-gapped Artifactory, pre-populated before the run. Curate the set of packages the evaluation needs, continuously scan them, promote them into the isolated instance, and give agents read-only access. Nothing new enters during the run, nothing leaves, and the repository cannot become a conduit to any other system because there is no other system to reach. For high-sensitivity evaluations this is the configuration we recommend. It also gives the operator an exact record of every dependency the agents had available, which is useful evidence when a run is later reviewed.

The repository is part of the threat model

The July 19 report is a careful account of how agents share what they learn, and it is worth reading on those terms. For operators, the practical lesson is that a binary repository inside an agent environment is infrastructure the agents will study, probe, and use for their own purposes if it lets them. Scoping permissions to reads, isolating tenants, auditing activity, scanning what is stored, and hardening the hosts around the service are the measures that keep it serving packages and nothing else. We are happy at JFrog to work with OpenAI and other research labs on reference configurations for providing a fully secure setup that gives agents the packages they need without giving them a path to anything else.

{ "affected": [ { "package": { "ecosystem": "PyPI", "name": "mlflow" }, "ranges": [ { "events": [ { "introduced": "3.12.0rc0" }, { "fixed": "3.17.0" } ], "type": "ECOSYSTEM" } ] } ], "aliases": [ "CVE-2026-116692" ], "database_specific": { "cwe_ids": [ "CWE-470", "CWE-94" ], "github_reviewed": true, "github_reviewed_at": "2026-10-27T21:26:32Z", "nvd_published_at": null, "severity": "CRITICAL" }, "details": "## Summary MLflow 3.12.0 introduced registration and deserialization support for third-party scorers in OSS MLflow. During scorer deserialization, the server accepts a request-controlled Python module path beneath one of four allowed package prefixes, imports that module, obtains a request-controlled class, and instantiates it synchronously. An HTTP caller can combine this behavior with MLflow's built-in experiment, run, and artifact-upload endpoints: 1. Create an experiment whose local artifact location points to a writable allowed scorer package. 2. Create a run, causing MLflow to allocate `//artifacts/`. 3. Upload a Python module into that run artifact directory. 4. Submit a serialized third-party scorer whose module path resolves to the uploaded file. 5. Trigger server-side import and class construction through `/ajax-api/3.0/mlflow/scorer/invoke`. On the default no-auth server using the official MLflow v3.14.0 image, this produces unauthenticated arbitrary Python code execution with the privileges of the MLflow server process. The reproduced image runs the process as uid 0 and permits writes to its installed Python package tree. The attached proof of concept is intentionally harmless. The uploaded constructor performs one action only: it writes a random marker beside its own uploaded run artifact. The marker is then downloaded through MLflow's run-artifact endpoint and checked for an exact match. ## Technical details ### 1. The allow-list accepts attacker-created descendants At release commit `86cd7f5a1dc25a1387ad07c87811bbc30f62951c`, `mlflow/genai/scorers/scorer_utils.py` defines these allowed roots: ```python THIRD_PARTY_SCORER_ALLOWED_MODULES = frozenset({ "mlflow.genai.scorers.ragas", "mlflow.genai.scorers.deepeval", "mlflow.genai.scorers.trulens", "mlflow.genai.scorers.phoenix", }) ``` In `mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py`, the deserializer accepts either an exact root or any descendant: ```python module_path == m or module_path.startswith(m + ".") ``` It then performs the following operations using request-controlled values: ```python module = importlib.import_module(module_path) scorer_class = getattr(module, class_name, None) scorer_instance = scorer_class(**init_kwargs) ``` A package-name prefix is not a provenance boundary. If the server process can write below an allowed package, an attacker-created descendant can satisfy the string-prefix check and become importable Python code. Relevant source locations at the v3.14.0 release commit: * `mlflow/genai/scorers/scorer_utils.py`, allowed third-party scorer modules * `mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py`, third-party scorer deserialization and construction ### 2. Deserialization occurs before trace processing In `mlflow/server/handlers.py`, `_invoke_scorer_handler()` parses the supplied serialized scorer and calls: ```python scorer = Scorer.model_validate_json(serialized_scorer) ``` Only after deserialization and construction does the handler call: ```python batches = get_trace_batches_for_scorer(trace_ids, scorer, tracking_store) ``` The attacker-controlled constructor therefore runs before the server validates or resolves the supplied trace IDs. The minimal proof class is deliberately not a complete MLflow scorer. After its constructor writes the marker, later trace-batching logic accesses scorer attributes that the proof class does not implement. The resulting HTTP 500 occurs after code execution and does not invalidate the proof. No background job execution or special job-execution server option is required to reach the constructor. ### 3. MLflow's artifact layout places the module under the trusted prefix The experiment creation endpoint accepts an `artifact_location`. For file-backed experiments, MLflow derives each run artifact directory as: ```text //artifacts/ ``` The proof of concept selects this package directory in the official v3.14.0 image: ```text file:///usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens ``` After creating a run and uploading `audit_.py`, the resulting filesystem location is: ```text /usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens//artifacts/audit_.py ``` The corresponding import path is: ```text mlflow.genai.scorers.trulens..artifacts.audit_ ``` The attack does not overwrite an existing package module. It creates a new run-scoped module in the normal file-backed artifact layout. The run ID is returned to the caller. ### 4. Authentication and authorization behavior With authentication disabled, as in the default reproduced server configuration, no credentials are required. When MLflow basic authentication is enabled, authentication still applies. However, the scorer-invocation AJAX endpoint is assigned to `validate_gateway_proxy`, which returns `True` without performing an experiment- or scorer-level resource permission check. Practical exploitation in an authenticated deployment still requires the caller to create an experiment and run and upload artifacts to them. The key authorization issue is that scorer deserialization itself is not gated by a resource-specific permission check for the supplied experiment before the import occurs. ## Proof of concept The attached reproduction is intentionally isolated: * exact official MLflow v3.14.0 image pinned by manifest digest; * Docker network disabled; * MLflow bound to container loopback; * no shell command or external callback; * no external request; * no host filesystem write; * marker created beside the uploaded run artifact; * marker retrieved through the run-artifact download endpoint; and * disposable container removed after completion. Run: ```bash ./run-official-image.sh ``` Expected output: ```text MLFLOW_VERSION=3.14.0 PACKAGE_DIR=/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens CREATE_EXPERIMENT_STATUS=200 CREATE_RUN_STATUS=200 UPLOAD_STATUS=200 INVOKE_STATUS=500 PROOF_DOWNLOAD_STATUS=200 PROOF_MATCH=1 RESULT=AFFECTED ``` The security-relevant result is: ```text PROOF_MATCH=1 RESULT=AFFECTED ``` This proves that the attacker-controlled constructor executed in the MLflow server process before the later scorer-processing failure. ## Reproduction environment * **Release:** MLflow v3.14.0 * **Release commit:** `86cd7f5a1dc25a1387ad07c87811bbc30f62951c` * **Official image:** `ghcr.io/mlflow/mlflow:v3.14.0` * **Manifest digest:** `sha256:967de3ca34b6a5751718e380a0a383eb0ce1a6f5b484f363bd0da7559117a5f8` * **Python version:** 3.10.18 * **Image-configured user:** empty * **Observed runtime user:** uid 0 * **Server bind:** `127.0.0.1:5000` * **Container network:** disabled * **Backend store:** `sqlite:////work/mlflow.db` * **Default artifact root:** `/work/artifacts` * **Authentication:** disabled * **Special job-execution option:** none Server command inside the disposable container: ```bash mlflow server \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 5000 \ --backend-store-uri sqlite:////work/mlflow.db \ --default-artifact-root /work/artifacts ``` ## Affected range and source lineage The vulnerable third-party scorer deserialization behavior was introduced by commit: ```text 02eea26035b9d8e65af31e6e8f058ca195f62cdd Enable third-party scorer registration in OSS MLflow (#22634) ``` The feature is absent from v3.11.1 and first appears in v3.12.0. Runtime reproduction succeeds on v3.14.0. The relevant `mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py` content is unchanged at master commit: ```text 20858c9426a9644dfcf9545a92cbb534376779eb ``` No fixed release was identified as of 2026-07-12. ## Impact On the reproduced stock no-auth image, any network caller who can reach the tracking server can execute Python code as the MLflow process without credentials or user interaction. Successful exploitation provides confidentiality, integrity, and availability impact over all data, credentials, network access, and filesystem locations available to the MLflow server process. The stock image's runtime uid 0 increases container-level impact. Host impact still depends on the container runtime configuration, mounted paths, granted capabilities, socket exposure, and other isolation controls. In authentication-enabled deployments, exploitation requires an authenticated principal capable of creating an experiment and run and uploading artifacts. The exact chain also requires the server process to be able to write beneath one of the allowed scorer packages. This condition holds in the reproduced official image and may hold in virtual environments installed and run by the same operating-system user. A read-only container filesystem or a scorer package directory owned by a different, non-writable user blocks this exact placement chain. ## Artifacts and attachments ### Remote proof-of-concept script POC Script: [new_remote_poc.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29936616/new_remote_poc.py) The remote proof of concept was then executed as follows.
